A sample of "low-fat dairy whitener" manufactured by Nestle India, drawn from the premises of Hotel Lalit in Connaught Place in the national capital, has been found "unsafe and substandard," the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said on Saturday (October 3, 2026).
In a post on social media, the food regulator said the sample was collected from the premises of Bharat Hotels Ltd (The Lalit), Connaught Place, New Delhi.
According to the FSSAI, the report of the food analyst’s laboratory declared the product “substandard” and “unsafe,” indicating non-compliance under the Food Safety and Standards (FSS) Act, 2006.
A copy of the laboratory analysis report was provided to the food business operator (FBO) for reference and necessary action, the regulator said. A notice has also been issued to Bharat Hotels Ltd over the non-compliant product.
The FBO was given an opportunity to appeal against the food analyst's report under the relevant section of the FSS Act, 2006, within the prescribed period. The FBO has also been directed to immediately stop the sale of the identified unsafe food product, the FSSAI added.

Industrialist Anand Mahindra shared a viral video of a three-wheeler driving through central London streets, with a touch of Gujarati caption — “UK ma riksha aavi gai chhe… Mahindra ni chhe, aapda”. The viral clip featured a vehicle, likely a Mahindra Treo model, manoeuvring among cars and cabs, accompanied by playful on-screen Gujarati text inviting people to experience it in London. Loosely, it translated to: “Look, a Mahindra rickshaw is now in the UK — and it’s one of ours!” The sight of the quintessential Indian three-wheeler navigating British roads has sparked a wave of amused and prideful reactions across social media, with many users celebrating the ‘reverse colonisation’. Viewing the export as a humorous symbolic milestone, one user wrote, "UK waalo ko 200 saal baad reverse colonisation ka taste mil raha hai! Sir, ab London ki baarish mein bhi auto driver bolega: 'Arey saheb, wo side nahi jana, traffic bohot hai!' Proud moment!" Another similarly quipped that "a rickshaw on British roads is the most confident import since tea." Many found entertainment in the merging of the two worlds, imagining an "autowala with British accent," while another suggested to fellow travellers, "Next time you go to London, take a proper spin around, in your own rickshaw!!!" From a business and branding perspective, netizens lauded the automaker's global footprint. “It's the cheapest advertising for which you got paid, sir. Kudos to Mahindra group for taking Bharat's brand outside Bharat,” read one comment. Pointing to the booming domestic EV market, a Gujarati user added, “Have London ma pan aapdi riksha India ma FY26 ma pehli vaar 8 lakh thi vadhu electric 3-wheeler vechaya — next stop electric Mahindra riksha nu export?” However, some users felt the international spotlight called for a modern makeover, with one noting, “Our humble rickshaw definitely needs to change the way it looks. A design challenge.” Mahindra & Mahindra has been exporting its electric three-wheelers to the UK since at least late 2021 and early 2022. These vehicles are primarily distributed through specialised local dealerships like the Cheshire-based Tuk Tuk (UK) Ltd, commonly known as The Tuk Shop. Rather than serving as traditional passenger taxis, these exported EVs are being adapted for a diverse range of niche functions. The cargo-focused variant, the Mahindra Treo Zor, is increasingly being utilised by small businesses for eco-friendly, last-mile urban deliveries. Meanwhile, the passenger-oriented Mahindra Treo is proving popular for promotional activities, hospitality transport, and recreational trips. The vehicle's unique adaptability was further highlighted in October 2022 when the Gwent Police in Wales officially added a Mahindra Treo to their fleet, according to a report byThe Times of India. In December 2021, Anand Mahindra took to social media to congratulate the first UK buyers taking delivery from The Tuk Shop, stating that they had “seen the future and it's electric and three-wheeled”. Boy recounts 1994 park attack on tape played at trial of alleged sex predator
Richard Neil has pleaded not guilty to 17 historical charges, including kidnapping, sexual assault
WARNING: This article contains graphic content and may affect those who have experienced sexual violence or know someone affected by it.
As police drove him to Toronto's Hospital for Sick Children, the 10-year-old boy kept asking if they were nearly there.
"My stomach's turning," he told the two officers, as he lay in the back of the vehicle.
Thirty-two years after the child was tied to a tree and sexually assaulted, an audio recording of his September 1994 interview with police was played for the jury Monday at the trial of his alleged attacker.
Richard Neil has pleaded not guilty to 17 charges related to the incident, as well as two other similar past attacks on an eight-year-old boy and a 15-year-old girl. The list of allegations includes kidnapping, sexual assault causing bodily harm and administering a stupefying drug.
The three attacks in southern Ontario parks between 1992 and 1995 confounded investigators for three decades. Advances in DNA technology — including investigative genetic genealogy — finally helped police link the three crime scenes to Neil, a prosecutor told the jury Monday in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Brampton, Ont.
Neil, now 67, was arrested in 2024.
The court heard the former postal worker doesn't dispute what happened to the three children, but insists he wasn't involved.
"He did a lot of rude things to me," the 10-year-old boy told Peel Regional Police about the unidentified attacker in 1994.
The victim, whose identity is covered by a publication ban, recounted saying hello to a stranger in Brampton's Norton Place Park after school that day. They struck up a conversation. The man claimed he had lost his wallet with $900 inside.
The boy said the pair walked around the park and chatted on a bench, until the man's mood suddenly soured, ostensibly accusing the boy of stealing his wallet.
"He tied my foot to the tree ... so I couldn't get away," the boy is heard telling police on the audio tape.
He described a series of lurid acts carried out by the man in a wooded area of the park, including urination, oral sex and anal penetration.
"It hurt," the boy told police.
After the attacker got away, the boy ran out of the woods, exiting near a branch of the Royal Canadian Legion adjacent to the park.
Witness recalls seeing boy run from park
David Kilpatrick, now a 71-year-old retiree, testified Monday about stopping at the Legion that evening to have a beer and play a round of pool.
Everything changed when he spotted the child wearing only his pants.
"I see this young boy coming out of the woods … shirt in hand, screaming, so I knew something was wrong," Kilpatrick told the court.
"You have to call my mom," he said the boy urged him. "I've been attacked."
Kilpatrick said the boy provided a basic description of the attacker: a white man with black hair, wearing a grey track suit.
He ran the boy into the Legion, told the bartender to call 911 and rushed into the woods himself to find the assailant, to no avail.
Kilpatrick fought back tears Monday as he spoke from the witness box. He said he promised the 10-year-old that day he would find his attacker.
"I was wound up like a clock," he told the court. "Still am, just talking about it now."
DNA tied 3 assaults to 1 man: Crown
That evening, the boy led investigators to the spot where he'd been attacked. DNA recovered from the Brampton park — as well as semen and men's underwear worn as a mask, each found separately at the scenes of two other assaults — proved crucial in linking the three incidents to one man, Crown attorney Shazin Karim told the jury.
In the first attack at Kitchener's Idlewood Park on Aug. 21, 1992, a boy said he'd been lured away from his sister and a friend by a man who promised to show him dozens of bicycles in a wooded area, Karim said.
She told the jury the assailant held a pocket knife and threatened to kill the eight-year-old "if he said a word."
On Aug. 31, 1995, at Oakville's Wildwood Park, a girl out walking her dog was approached by a man who threatened her with what appeared to be a loaded gun, Karim told the court in her opening statement. She said the 15-year-old cried as the man set up a video camera to record the assault.

Trump offers to help Russia after Siberia plague institute death: ‘It’s a rough disease’
Trump called the suspected outbreak a ‘big problem for Russia’ as authorities monitor contacts of the victim

The United States is prepared to offer assistance to Russia after a laboratory worker died at a plague research institute in Siberia, US President Donald Trump confirmed on Monday at the White House.
Addressing reporters as he departed the White House for a trip to Nebraska, Trump described the outbreak as a "big problem for Russia." The laboratory worker had fallen ill and died under undisclosed circumstances, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of people.
While news of the death generated public health fears across social media, Russian authorities insisted on Monday that the situation was under control. "Well, I hate to see them having it," Trump said. "It's a rough disease."
He stated that the US would do what it could to help Russia. Trump has said he considers Russian President Vladimir Putin someone whom he can work with, despite ongoing tensions over Russia's war against Ukraine. "We'll help," Trump said. "Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we're always will to help."
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday he doesn’t think there is cause for alarm, but the U.S. is watching the case closely, aware that “it could spread quickly” despite the quarantine and other public health protocols.
Russian authorities have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring contacts of the woman who died at the plague research institute.
Authorities said they found no evidence that her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with. But the case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
The woman worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, southeastern Siberia. A state TV station in Irkutsk reported Monday that she died last week in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk.
The hospital has been placed under quarantine, Mayor Maxim Modin said Friday, no longer admitting or discharging patients, and its laboratory halted carrying out routine tests. The hospital's outpatient clinic kept operating as usual, he said.
Anna Popova, head of Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk and met with Gov. Igor Kobzev and other officials on Friday.
Kobzev said everyone who came into contact with the woman is under medical supervision. He didn’t identify the infection and called it a suspected case of “a particularly dangerous infection.”
Rospotrebnadzor was implementing “a full range of anti-epidemic measures,” he added.Rospotrebnadzor said Sunday the woman was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” or origin, and said “extensive” testing found “no microorganisms associated with the patient’s professional activities.”
The agency also said it didn't uncover any incidents at the institute “involving pathogenic microorganisms."
Independent local news outlet Lyudi Baikala quoted sources it did not identify as saying the 28-year-old lab technician died from pneumonic plague and that several Irkutsk hospitals were placed under quarantine.
Asked Monday to comment on the case, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the public and media should follow official statements from Rospotrebnadzor, rather than "rumors or speculation.”Rospotrebnadzor did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Additional reporting by AP.

Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China and Europe, as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU.
The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely, and the EU imposes duties of up to 45%.
EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist “made in Europe” barriers on British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market.
Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales in China.
Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who have flocked to cheaper Chinese models, and could deter brands such as Chery, which is in talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant, from investing further in the UK.
“There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.
“Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.”
Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”.
Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures.
Figures released on Friday showed that British new car registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s Sealion 7 among the top sellers.
The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China.
Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.”
.
Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.”
Victor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.”
He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.”
Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors.
Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid cars rocketed after the EU tariffs were imposed on EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers.
Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms.
Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.”
He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.

CM Sukhu announces Rs 1 cr each for Himachal’s three Asiad gold-winning kabaddi players
Himachal Pradesh Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu on Monday announced a cash award of Rs 1 crore each for three kabaddi players from the state who were part of the gold-winning women’s team at the just-concluded Asian Games in Japan – Pushpa Rana, Jyoti Thakur and Bhawna Thakur.
The chief minister also announced Rs 1 crore for Renuka Singh Thakur, a member of the women’s cricket team that won the gold at the Asian Games, beating Sri Lanka by 147 runs in the final.
The kabaddi trio called on Sukhu on Monday, who congratulated them on their outstanding achievement and honoured them with Himachali caps and shawls.
Led by Pushpa, the women’s kabaddi team defended their gold medal with an unbeaten run at Aichi-Nagoya, defeating Iran 37-34 in a thrilling final to lift the crown for a fourth time.
According to an official statement, Sukhu said the state government would soon organise a felicitation ceremony in the players’ honour, where they would be presented with Rs 1 crore each.
The three players would also be employed in government service, Sukhu said, adding that those who do not wish to join the police force would be offered appointments in the sports department, enabling them to continue pursuing their sporting careers while contributing to the promotion and development of sports in the state.
The state government has increased the prize money for gold-winning international athletes by revising its sports policy, with special emphasis on strengthening sports infrastructure across Himachal, Sukhu said.

Bengaluru youngsters to get a shot at Australian Open Ball kids squad selection at KSLTA
Young tennis enthusiasts in Bengaluru will have a chance to get closer to Grand Slam tennis when the Australian Open Ball Kids selection trials are held at the Karnataka State Lawn Tennis Association (KSLTA) on October 10 and 11.
The Kia India Ball Kids programme is open to children aged 12 to 15 years, with the Bengaluru trials forming part of a national selection process that will culminate in four youngsters being selected to represent India as official Ball Kids at the Australian Open 2027 in Melbourne.
Speaking about the initiative, Sunil Yajaman, Hon. Jt. Secy, AITA and Hon. Jt. Secy, KSLTA, said, “Junior tennis is all about creating opportunities. An experience like this can give youngsters exposure to a Grand Slam environment, build their confidence and inspire them to dream bigger. For many children, simply being around the world’s best players could be an experience they remember for the rest of their lives.”
He added, “We are thankful to Australian Open & Tennis Australia who have chosen Bengaluru to host this selection and give an opportunity to the desiring kids in Karnataka to try their hand in working at the prestigious Australian Open 2027, which is the first grand slam event of the year.”
The programme has an added resonance given that Roger Federer himself served as a ball boy at the Swiss Indoors in Basel in 1993-94, long before going on to become one of tennis’s greatest champions.

Digvijay Pratap Singh overcomes emotional week to clinch ITF M15 title in Baku
Digvijay Pratap Singh clinched the men’s singles title at the ITF Men’s World Tennis Tour M15 in Baku, Azerbaijan.
The second-seeded Indian (ATP 552) delivered a commanding performance against the tournament’s top seed, Great Britain’s Millen Hurrion (ATP 537), securing a 6-4, 6-4 straight-sets victory in the championship match on Sunday.
The triumph carried emotional significance for the RGTA athlete. Digivijay dedicated the win to his grandfather, who sadly passed away on October 1, right in the middle of the tournament week. Despite the profound personal loss, Singh showcased elite mental fortitude to navigate a highly competitive draw and finish the week as champion.
He opened his campaign on the hard courts by overcoming Russia’s Dmitry Bessonov 6-1, 6-4 in the first round, followed by a hard-fought 6-3, 7-6 victory over Great Britain’s Oscar Brown in the Round of 16. In the quarterfinals, he maintained his momentum to edge past Turkey’s Arda Azkara 7-5, 7-6.
His toughest test of the tournament came in the semi-finals against seventh seed Marcus Walters of Great Britain. In a grueling, back-and-forth three-set battle, Digvijay held his nerve during two crucial tie-breaks to eventually emerge victorious with a 7-6, 4-6, 7-6 win, booking his place in the grand finale.

Fenesta Open announces Rs 11 lakh Player Development Scholarship
The Fenesta Open National Tennis Championship has introduced a Rs 11 lakh Player Development Scholarship to support the continued development of players across five singles categories, the organisers said on Monday.
The scholarship, announced by DCM Shriram Foundation, the CSR arm of DCM Shriram Ltd, will be awarded to winners and runners-up in the men’s, women’s, U-18, U-16 and U-14 singles categories at the 31st edition of the championship.
The Fenesta Open already offers a prize pool of over Rs 21.55 lakh.
The new scholarship represents an additional commitment towards supporting players beyond their performance at the Championship.
Under the new structure, winners in the men’s, women’s, boys U-18 and girls U-18 singles categories will receive a scholarship of Rs 1.05 lakh each, while runners-up will receive Rs 60,000 each. Winners in the boys and girls U-16 and U-14 singles categories will receive a scholarship of Rs 70,000 each, while runners-up will receive Rs 40,000 each.
-PTI

The mechanical keyboard isn’t always so mechanical anymore.
Over the past six years, keyboards with optical, Hall-effect, and other “contactless” switches have become increasingly common, often going for higher prices than traditional mechanical keyboards, which already command a premium over basic membrane boards. In return, they promise some theoretical advantages, particularly for gamers. In daily use, though, the differences can be pretty subtle.
So what exactly are you paying for? In this guide, we break down how the newest switches work, why contactless designs are becoming more popular, and where their advantages—and disadvantages—really matter.
First, let’s recap what happens when you push a key with a traditional mechanical switch inside.
As you can see in the diagram of a Cherry MX Brown switch below, standard mechanical switches have two metal leaves—in this case, the “crosspoint”—that are shaped differently, with the top of the larger leaf bent away from the smaller leaf.
An exploded view of an MX Brown switch.
Credit:
Das Keyboard
When you press a mechanical switch, its plastic stem moves downward toward the keyboard’s PCB, and a spring wrapped around the stem compresses. As you release the button, the spring expands, forcing the stem back up to its original position.
When a switch is at rest, a protruding piece of the plastic stem keeps the switch’s two leaves from making contact. As the stem goes downward, that piece moves with it, allowing the leaves to touch and close a circuit on the keyboard’s PCB, which sends a signal to the keyboard’s microcontroller, telling the computer which input was made.
A transparent profile view of an MX Red switch at rest.
Cherry
A transparent profile view of an MX Red switch at rest.
Cherry
A transparent profile view of a depressed MX Red switch.
Cherry
A transparent profile view of a depressed MX Red switch.
Cherry
A transparent profile view of an MX Red switch at rest.
Cherry
A transparent profile view of a depressed MX Red switch.
Cherry
But because mechanical switches rely on the physical contact of internal components, they can degrade over time.
Why new switches?
The switches in this guide differ from traditional mechanical switches because they don’t register input through contact between two metal leaves—hence the term “contactless.” Manufacturers often claim contactless switches last longer than regular switches, and they’re not susceptible to oxidation or corrosion, which can affect mechanical switches after prolonged use.
An example of mechanical switch leaves showing oxidation, courtesy of Reddit user Hapimp.
An example of mechanical switch leaves showing oxidation, courtesy of Reddit user Hapimp.
Credit:
Hapimp/Reddit
But there are other things to keep in mind for longevity. Contactless switches require specific PCBs, which are less common than those used for standard mechanical switches. And while hot-swappability can extend a keyboard’s life by making it easier to replace a broken key or change switches, hot-swappable PCBs for contactless switches—and prebuilt keyboards that support contactless switches and hot-swapping—are harder to find.
Newer standard mechanical switches, including some Cherry MX2A-series switches rated for 100 million keystrokes, can have lifespans similar to those of contactless options. If longevity is a priority, contactless switches may still be worth considering, but be sure to compare their ratings with those of standard switches.
Some users and companies claim that contactless switches feel smoother when pressed and reset because no metallic leaves touch. But other parts of the switch, like the spring and stem, can also create friction. I’ve occasionally noticed smoother presses with certain contactless switches (more on that later), but some premium standard switches, especially properly lubricated ones, can also feel extremely smooth.
If you want the best-feeling switches, look beyond whether they operate mechanically or through light beams or magnets. Factors like the switch’s specs, force curve, and materials can have a greater impact on how a switch feels.
Customizable actuation
Many contactless switches have customizable actuation points, a feature that isn’t possible with traditional mechanical switches. That can be helpful if you want some keys to feel stiffer or lighter than others (I prefer a stiffer spacebar, for instance), more flexibility over how keys respond, or analog input.
But software may not accurately reflect a switch’s actual actuation point. Review website RTINGs tested 14 keyboards with adjustable actuation from 11 brands and found that, on each keyboard, the keys actuated at a different distance than the one set in the companion app. We’re talking about differences of fractions of a millimeter, but it’s worth keeping in mind if you’re considering contactless switches for customizable actuation.
Some keyboards with contactless switches go further by letting users program keys so that one full press results in two inputs. For example, you can set a key to input “A” if you press it down 0.5 mm and then “B” if you press it down another 0.5 mm.
Some keyboards with contactless switches also support analog input, which lets the keyboard detect how far a switch has been pressed and adjust the input accordingly, giving gamers a joystick-like experience. Traditional mechanical keyboards don’t support analog input.
Gaming advantages
Contactless switches are becoming more common largely because of their potential appeal to gamers. Vendors often claim keyboards with contactless switches register input faster than traditional mechanical keyboards, mostly because the switches don’t require debouncing.
Debounce delay is the time between when a key on a mechanical keyboard is pressed and when the keyboard accepts the keypress as an input. The delay is necessary for standard switches because their metal leaves can rapidly bounce off each other when they make contact during a keypress. Debouncing ensures that the keyboard’s microcontroller doesn’t interpret these bounces as additional inputs (which would cause pressing “a” to register as something like “aaaa”). Keyboard firmware often handles debouncing, but hardware, such as an FPGA, can also do it.
Most of us never notice debounce delays, and manufacturers rarely disclose how much debounce delay keyboards use, though keyboard enthusiasts often point to 5 ms to 20 ms as common. Cherry says some of its MX2A switches require “less than 1 ms” for debouncing. And keyboard manufacturers occasionally implement longer-than-necessary debounce times to compensate for switch degradation over time.
But keyboard latency, or the amount of time it takes from when you start pressing a key to when you see that key registered on-screen, depends on more than just sensing technology. Other factors include the keys’ travel and actuation times and the keyboard’s polling rate. A Bluetooth keyboard with full-height optical switches and a 133 Hz wireless polling rate, for instance, will still display more latency than a traditional mechanical keyboard with low-profile switches and an 8,000 Hz polling rate through a wired connection.
Again, for many of us, none of this matters. It’s primarily professional gamers who need a keyboard with ultra-low latency, and that’s assuming they’ve already reduced latency in more essential areas, like their GPU, CPU, and monitor.
And because contactless switches frequently target gamers, there are way more linear options than tactile or clicky ones.
Optical switches
Optical switches, which rely on an infrared (IR) light beam to actuate, first hit consumer keyboards in 2016.
Optical switches work differently depending on the manufacturer, but generally, each switch contains a light beam that is redirected when the switch is depressed. This causes the beam to either hit or stop hitting a dedicated photoelectric sensor, registering an input. When the spring resets the switch, the light beam returns to its original position.
A diagram of a Razer optical switch in its resting position.
Razer
A diagram of a Razer optical switch in its resting position.
Razer
A diagram of a depressed Razer optical switch.
Razer
A diagram of a depressed Razer optical switch.
Razer
A diagram of a Razer optical switch in its resting position.
Razer
A diagram of a depressed Razer optical switch.
Razer
Most optical switches rely on an IR light and a sensor that are integrated into the keyboard’s PCB.
“In both Razer Optical Switches and Analog Optical Switches, the IR emitter and sensor are mounted on the keyboard’s PCB, with the switch stem acting as the ‘shutter’ for the light path,” a Razer spokesperson told me. “This PCB‑based design has remained consistent across generations. What has evolved over time are the exact positioning, components, and firmware processing—advancements that enable features like adjustable actuation points, Rapid Trigger, and full travel‑distance tracking in our analog switches, rather than simple on/off detection.”
Are optical switches faster than traditional mechanical switches?
Companies selling optical switches often claim they are faster than traditional switches. Because they don’t require debouncing, that’s technically true. And PC gaming peripheral companies often pair optical switches with high polling rates for even wider claims of ultra-low latency.
A marketing image from Razer claims that optical switches have lower response times than magnetic and traditional mechanical switches. Take it with a grain of salt.
Credit:
Razer
A marketing image from Razer claims that optical switches have lower response times than magnetic and traditional mechanical switches. Take it with a grain of salt.
Credit:
Razer
But would an average person notice quicker input when typing an email with an optical keyboard? Almost certainly not.
I asked Razer’s spokesperson if the design of optical switches precludes Razer’s optical keyboards from hot-swappability. Since optical switches aren’t subject to the same amount of degradation as traditional mechanical switches, the representative argued, users won’t need to swap them over time. But that argument is about longevity, not customizability.
“While the switches themselves are not soldered on, the keyboards are engineered as a fixed assembly to maintain the precise alignment required for consistent and accurate performance,” Razer’s rep told me.
An ad for an optical keyboard PCB for keyboard builders.
An ad for an optical keyboard PCB for keyboard builders.
Credit:
ePathBuy
Electrostatic capacitive switches
Electrostatic capacitive (EC) mechanical keyboards differ from traditional mechanical keyboards, but they remain closely tied to the technology’s origins.
IBM’s Model F—one of the first and most influential mechanical keyboards—used a capacitive PCB with its famous buckling spring switches. When a buckling spring switch is depressed, a capacitive flipper attached to the bottom of the switch’s spring is forced forward. This changes the capacitance of the two capacitive pads beneath it, registering an input.
In today’s EC keyboards, each switch has a conductive element. When the switch is depressed, the capacitance between the conductive element and the capacitive sensor pad on the PCB beneath it increases as the conductive element moves closer to the sensor pad.
A depiction of a standard mechanical switch actuating (left) versus a Varmilo EC switch actuating (right).
Varmilo
A depiction of a standard mechanical switch actuating (left) versus a Varmilo EC switch actuating (right).
Varmilo
A diagram of a Model F keyboard’s buckling spring switch.
Today’s EC keyboards, including new, non-IBM “Model F” keyboards and Topre keyboards, all use a capacitance-sensing PCB but with varying switch designs.
Topre switches
Topre switches are among the best-known—and most expensive—EC switches. Topre keyboards are lauded for their “thocky” sound: a clean, soft, distinct thud that’s not rattly or clacky (assuming you’re using ping-free, quality stabilizers).
The Type-S Topre silent electrostatic capacitive switches I’ve used have had remarkably smooth travel as they depress and reset, making every part of the keypress feel predictable and intentional.
HHKB’s Professional Classic Type-S keyboard has Type-S Topre silent EC switches. Even without arrows or a numpad, it is $269 as of this writing.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
HHKB’s Professional Classic Type-S keyboard has Type-S Topre silent EC switches. Even without arrows or a numpad, it is $269 as of this writing.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
Topre keyboards are unique among so-called “mechanical keyboards” in that they work similarly to rubber-dome membrane keyboards. With the other switches mentioned in this guide, the resistance you feel when pressing a key comes from the switch’s spring. In a Topre switch, that resistance comes from the rubber dome.
The Professional Classic Type-S keyboard’s Topre switches.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
The Professional Classic Type-S keyboard’s Topre switches.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
More details on how Topre switches work come from Topre Corporation’s 1986 patent (PDF):
A keyboard switch is provided with an insulating substrate, a first electrode laid on the insulating substrate, a second electrode formed of a conical coil spring and facing the first electrode, a dielectric disposed on the first electrode, a button positioned on the top portion of the second electrode, and a rubber cap disposed between the button and second electrode, for giving snap feeling to an operator when the button is depressed and the capacitance of the switch exceeds a given value. The capacitance varies with the change in the facing area, which changes substantially in proportion to the depth of depression of the button. The switch is capacitive-coupled for a switching operation and the snap feeling is given to the operator when the capacitance exceeds the given value.
EC switches don’t always look different from regular mechanical switches. Varmilo and NiZ’s EC switches, for example, have Cherry MX-style, cross-shaped stems and plastic housing. NiZ EC switches use a conical spring and rubber dome and forego metal leaves, just like Topres do. But Varmilo’s EC switches look like standard mechanical switches and even have metal leaves (these leaves never touch each other; they’re for creating variable capacitance, which occurs as the distance between them changes).
A profile view of an EC switch from Chinese manufacturer NiZ.
NiZ
A profile view of an EC switch from Chinese manufacturer NiZ.
NiZ
The Naevies EC switch is compatible with MX-style keycaps, stabilizers, and mounting plates.
Hall-effect switches are based on the Hall-effect principle, which American physicist Edwin Hall developed in 1879. In simple terms, if a magnet is placed near an electrical current flowing through a conductor, the current’s electrons are pushed toward one side of the conductor. This creates a small voltage, which is perpendicular to the direction of the electrical current’s flow, across the conductor.
In 1968, Honeywell made the first keyboard with Hall-effect sensors. Of course, other keyboard types were cheaper to produce, relegating Hall-effect keyboards to an afterthought for decades. Hall-effect sensors started making a comeback in the ’90s—Sega used them in its Saturn and Dreamcast controllers, giving them a reputation for durability and resistance to stick drift, something Switch 2 owners wish Nintendo would emulate.
And with that reputation, Hall-effect sensors became increasingly common among keyboard builders in the 2010s and showed up in prebuilt gaming keyboards in 2021, starting with Wooting’s Two HE.
An exploded view of Corsair’s MGX Hall-effect keyboard switch. The magnet is south of the “double-rail structure” stem.
Credit:
Corsair
An exploded view of Corsair’s MGX Hall-effect keyboard switch. The magnet is south of the “double-rail structure” stem.
Credit:
Corsair
Each Hall-effect switch has a magnet inside its stem. Pressing the switch moves the magnet closer to the keyboard’s PCB, which houses a Hall-effect sensor for each key. Each sensor contains a semiconductor element that conducts the electrical current. As the switch’s magnet moves closer to its dedicated sensor, its changing magnetic field alters the voltage produced across the sensor’s semiconductor element. When the keyboard’s microcontroller detects a change in a sensor’s voltage, it registers input.
Gateron’s Nebula magnetic switch.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
Gateron’s Nebula magnetic switch.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
Hall-effect keyboard building
Some nuances make building a keyboard with Hall-effect switches more complex than building a keyboard with standard or other types of contactless switches.
It’s even possible to find a hot-swappable Hall-effect keyboard, keyboard kit, or keyboard PCB that isn’t compatible with your Hall-effect switches. Hall-effect switches come in 3-pin or 5-pin varieties, and the polarity of the switch’s magnet must be compatible with the PCB’s sensors, or depressing the switch may not trigger the sensor beneath it.
Additionally, Hall-effect switches have various magnetic flux ranges, usually measured in Gauss, that indicate the minimum and maximum magnetic field strength the switch supports. This matters for some users, particularly those who want their keyboard to detect very light presses. And a switch with a broader magnetic flux can support a larger analog range.
So one company’s Hall-effect keyboard may have north-facing magnets with a magnetic flux range of 120 Gs to 750 Gs, while another has south-facing magnets with a magnetic flux range of 102-905 Gs. Swapping the two keyboards’ switches could cause compatibility issues, as one keyboard’s sensors or firmware may not support the new switches’ magnetic flux range.
Magnetic flux and polarity specs are hard to find because there’s no standard for measuring magnetic flux, and many users don’t seek or need this information. Monsgeek, one of the companies that provides magnetic flux specs for switches, told me that “most casual users don’t need to worry about magnetic flux numbers, but for enthusiasts who like to fine-tune actuation distance, rapid trigger, or overall switch feel, these specifications can be helpful and make the keyboard easier to customize.”
Keychron doesn’t provide magnetic flux specs for its magnetic switches because magnetic flux “is an internal engineering parameter of magnetic switches, not a user-facing performance metric,” Paul Tan, Keychron’s COO, told me.
Keychron’s keyboard firmware and launcher calibrate the magnetic sensor to each switch so “users experience consistent performance regardless of minor variations in magnetic field strength,” Tan said.
TMR switches
TMR keyboards became available in 2024 and are marketed as using more advanced sensing technology than mechanical, optical, and Hall-effect keyboards. Like Hall-effect switches, tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) switches use magnets, but TMR keyboard PCBs use a different type of sensor.
An exploded view of a TMR switch with a TMR sensor, courtesy of keyboard manufacturer Uniqmag.
An exploded view of a TMR switch with a TMR sensor, courtesy of keyboard manufacturer Uniqmag.
Credit:
Uniqmag
TMR sensors have two ferromagnetic layers made of thin-film magnetic materials. One has a fixed magnetization direction, while the other can change if a magnet is placed near it. An even thinner insulating barrier separates the two layers.
When you depress a TMR switch, the magnet inside its stem moves toward a dedicated TMR sensor on the keyboard’s PCB. This changes the alignment of the two ferromagnetic layers, which alters how easily electrons can tunnel through the insulating barrier (a quantum phenomenon known as tunnel magnetoresistance) and changes the sensor’s electrical resistance. When this change in resistance occurs, the sensor produces an electric signal, which the keyboard’s microcontroller registers as an input.
Hall-effect versus TMR keyboards
In general, TMR sensors consume less power than Hall-effect sensors. This can result in a TMR keyboard having a longer battery life than an equally specced Hall-effect keyboard. But additional factors, such as battery capacity and lighting, affect how long a wireless keyboard will last before you need to charge it, too.
A higher peak sensitivity means a keyboard’s sensors produce a larger electrical response to changes in the magnetic field caused by the position of the switch’s magnet. TMR keyboards can have higher peak sensitivity than Hall-effect keyboards because a TMR sensor can produce a larger electrical signal in response to changes in the magnetic field caused by depressing a switch.
Higher peak sensitivity lets a sensor detect small changes in movement, which could allow you to set a switch’s actuation points in 0.01 mm increments instead of the more common 0.1 mm, for example. This level of customization is more common among TMR keyboards but is also available in good Hall-effect boards. Keep in mind, though, that software often inaccurately depicts the actuation points of keyboards, albeit by amounts that are hard to notice, according to RTINGs’ testing).
In fact, some Hall-effect keyboards have a higher peak sensitivity than some TMR keyboards. Other factors, including the sensor and its placement and the keyboard’s polling rate and firmware, can affect a keyboard’s peak sensitivity. On rare occasions, electromagnetic noise or external magnetic fields can make magnetic-switch keyboards act erratically around other electronics, as seen in the video below.
Hall-effect sensors generally have a lower signal-to-noise ratio than TMR sensors, so they often rely on signal amplification. Because TMR sensors can provide a stronger signal and better signal-to-noise ratio, they can be less susceptible to electrical noise than Hall-effect keyboards.
Price and availability
TMR keyboards have been around for less time and generally have higher wafer and packaging costs, so they tend to be more expensive than similarly specced Hall-effect keyboards, although there’s also less variety. Additionally, TMR switches, PCBs, and barebones kits can be difficult to find, making TMR keyboard building even trickier than building a Hall-effect, EC, or optical keyboard.
Due to the operating principles of Hall-effect and TMR switches, the Hall sensor must be directly aligned with the magnet inside the switch to ensure proper performance. This requires the sensor to remain in a fixed position on the PCB, which makes implementing mechanical, hot-swap sockets challenging without causing interference.
Some companies have marketed TMR keyboards as Hall-effect boards. This seems counterintuitive, given the benefits TMR can offer over Hall-effect. In a September blog post, Keychron said it added the “HE” tag to the name of its TMR keyboards because “early on, TMR wasn’t widely known. Using the widely known ‘HE’ magnetic in the keyboard industry helped the market quickly understand our keyboard using magnetic switches—though our fundamental tech has always been Keychron.”
Keychron calls its keyboard “HE,” but it’s actually TMR.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
Keychron calls its keyboard “HE,” but it’s actually TMR.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
Inductive switches
The first inductive-switch consumer keyboards released last year. Ducky and Epomaker marketed their respective keyboards to gamers looking for analog input and lower power consumption than Hall-effect keyboards can provide. Inductive keyboards can consume less power than Hall-effect and TMR keyboards because they don’t require a dedicated sensor for each key, although other factors can affect battery life. They’re also generally less susceptible to interference from other devices’ magnetic fields because the switches don’t contain magnets.
Each switch has a conductive metal actuator, often cone-shaped, that descends toward the keyboard’s PCB when the switch is depressed. As the cone moves toward the PCB, it eventually enters and distributes an electromagnetic field created by coils on the PCB. This creates eddy currents, which increase the coils’ effective inductance, following Lenz’s law. Sensors on the PCB pick up the coils’ change in inductance, causing the keyboard to register an input.
An exploded view of an Unionwell inductive switch.
The MX Multipoint Cyan in its regular, non-exploded form. Cherry
Cherry’s MX Multipoint Cyan inductive switch uses a metal actuator element (south of the cyan-colored stem) instead of a cone.Cherry
The MX Multipoint Cyan in its regular, non-exploded form. Cherry
Some manufacturers, like Cherry, also claim that inductive-switch keyboards offer higher precision, including with analog input. But because inductive switch keyboards are newer, it’s difficult to gauge that claim. For example, after testing the One X, RTINGs reported that “accuracy is impressive but not better than some of the highest-performing Hall-effect keyboards to date.”
Availability
The only companies currently making inductive switches appear to be Cherry, Kailh, and Unionwell. Aesco also says it makes inductive switches through a collaboration with Unionwell and Kailh. Only Kailh seems to be selling switches individually, meaning most inductive switches are available only through prebuilt keyboards.
A handful of companies, including Ducky, Aesco, Aula, Epomaker, Black Shark, DAREU, and Redragon, currently sell inductive keyboards. DIY options are even rarer.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

As an Indian woman, I often feel myself oscillating between states of anxiety or anger. The anxiety is about doing the mental maths of how to stay safe – thinking about what I’m wearing, where I am going and how I’ll get there, and so on. The anger is at the sheer absurdity of this, and the stories of of sexual violence and harassment I read about every day. I am not the only one.
Last week, two particularly enraging incidents captured national attention. First, a video showing a group of men accused of harassing and molesting two teenagers at night in Bihar’s Jamui went viral. Then, a 17-year-old, out with a friend in Delhi, was allegedly gang-raped in a park by men posing as police. After, women in Bihar told Outlook how the incident in Jamui triggers greater controls and pressure on them. In Delhi, authorities curbed access to public parks and a premier women’s college, Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), briefly moved classes online.
I have noticed this pattern repeatedly: after incidents of sexual violence go viral on social media, the fallout further ensnares women. We are the ones who get told to avoid certain places, regulate our behaviour, dress modestly or be home earlier, thereby placing the burden of escaping this menace on us. Feminist activist Kavita Krishnan has described this phenomenon as “perhaps the most widespread form of gender-based violence in India”.
Instead of figuring out why sexual violence remains entrenched in our society, how patriarchal agency perpetuates such violence or what kind of social conditioning is needed for men, women are instead expected to take up less public space. (It is another matter that women might not be safe even inside their own homes.)
Regulating women is easy because “it does not require any institutional cost and, most of all, it sends the signal to concerned parents that the problem is being handled”, says Meena Kandasamy, a feminist author, whose latest novel, Fieldwork As a Sex Object, is about a woman’s life being upturned when a deepfake video using her face goes viral. “Their target audience is not the young women who feel unsafe but the rest of society.”
In my experience, this repression happens at three levels: first in the realm of family, then in broader society, and ultimately by the state. It begins at home, under the guise of protection, with arbitrary curfews or dress codes. It gets reinforced at a community level with institutions and social groups through moral policing, victim-blaming and the expectation that women should not put themselves in “unsafe” situations.
Then there is the response of the state. Restricting access to parks after sunset can surely reduce the number of people in those places, but it doesn’t address why women are unsafe there. Harassment and sexual violence are, unfortunately, not tied to timings or daylight. And further restricting women’s lives is not the solution to injustices foisted on them. All three, Kandasamy says, consider women as a “problem to be handled”.
“She’s not a citizen (for the state), a member (for the community), or an adult (for the family). She is treated like an inanimate but precious object – like a diamond that has to be locked up to prevent theft,” she said.
‘Moral policing’ of the wrong target
Women, however, are pushing back against this approach. In recent days, students from Delhi University have come out on the streets demanding safer public spaces including more street lighting, usable public toilets, more housing and scholarships for female students. Vedayana, 20, a student at Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), says locking up parks is not the solution: “If you are not putting up safety measures to make it accessible to women, then it is as good as saying that the park is only for men.”
The scale of the issue is devastatingly clear. A recently published survey of more than 4,000 women in New Delhi and Bengaluru, found that 65% of women in New Delhi and 29% in Bengaluru experienced harassment in public spaces in the past year.
Another 2024 study from India and Pakistan found that women’s overall mobility remains abysmally low, and what freedom they do have is almost entirely tied to education, employment or unpaid care work. Substantive mobility for leisure or pleasure is practically nonexistent.
Despite how widespread and urgent the problem is, the political response can further shake public confidence. A female minister from Bihar, commenting on the molestation video said: “Moral policing can be done in a more decent and elegant fashion.” Another minister from the state drew fire for describing it as an “isolated” incident”.
Minimising crimes against women reflects a political culture in which accountability becomes optional. Students such as Vedayana want this to change. Political parties, she tells me, should pledge to not give tickets or positions to anyone accused of sexual harassment. “We don’t want the leaders sitting at the top to perpetrate and preach rape culture,” she adds.
Parliament is not immune to accusations, either: the BJP politician Brij Bhushan Singh, who formerly headed the Wrestling Federation of India, was recently accused of sexual harassment by six female wrestlers – he denies the allegations, and was acquitted by a magistrate, in a case that is undergoing appeal. According to an analysis of 2024 parliamentarians by the Association for Democratic Reforms, 15 winning candidates declared cases related to crimes against women.
For Vedayana, changing the mentality has to begin early with families and the way boys are raised. “If you are in a position of authority, use it to influence people by speaking out against patriarchy and groom your sons first.”
What else we’re reading about
Golden girls | Indian women’s cricket team beat Sri Lanka by 147 runs to win gold at the Asian Games last week. Smriti Mandhana’s smashing 79 off 45 deliveries helped India reach a formidable 216 in 20 overs. Deepti Sharma’s three-wicket haul helped India end Sri Lanka’s hopes with just 69 runs on board. Sri Lanka settled for silver, while Pakistan claimed the bronze after beating Bangladesh.
Moma | A solo exhibition by one of south Asia’s most distinguished artists, Nilima Sheikh, opened at New York’s Museum of Modern Art at the weekend. Fractured Skies, presented in collaboration with the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art in Delhi, will run until next June.
EC under fire | An explosive Indian Express investigation has revealed how two of the top three election officials objected at least 14 times over a period of 10 months to changes made by the Election Commission over its controversial exercise that has struck 130 million people from the voter rolls.
Count it
A number worth knowing
105
An inquiry committee probing the theft of donations from Ayodhya’s Ram Temple has uncovered 105 instances of cash being removed or concealed. The thefts were caught on CCTV cameras.
According to a preliminary report, some of the accused allegedly hid the money on themselves during the process of counting donations and then walked out.
Vibe check
Tony Klor’s city vlogs from Indian towns are “hella dope,” to use his own words. The 32-year-old American has visited about 200 cities around the country, taking his Instagram followers to places that rarely feature on a travel itinerary.
It’s a treat to watch him having the time of his life. He marched with Anganwadi workers in Nashik chanting “pay my didis”, ribbed with middle-aged uncles sweating it out in a park, whom he christened “Nizamaddies”. Wandering through the mining town of Ballari, which he describes as “highkey vibey”, he films its temple, church and mosque.
“A lot of people who watch my videos are Indians and they have no idea about these magnificent places in India,” the tech professional-turned-content creator says. “India is like the easiest place to make a friend in the world. People invite me to their weddings on the street that I met five minutes before that. Hospitality is so, so next-level.”

China funding UK research and sending it to Beijing's spies, MI5 warns

More than 100 academics linked to British institutions have unwittingly assisted China's espionage operations against the UK via a front company working for its intelligence and security services, MI5 has warned.
In the highly unusual public alert, the UK's internal security service warned universities and academics that continuing ties with China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) could ultimately lead to criminal charges for aiding a foreign state.
Security minister Dan Jarvis said MI5's warning exposed attempts by Chinese intelligence agencies to use British academic research to undermine UK national security.
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London said the accusation was "imaginary and purely fabricated".
Universities UK, which represents more than 140 institutions, meanwhile said it was reviewing the alert and focusing on "supporting our universities as they assess any implications for existing or future partnerships".
In June, MI5 and its closest partners in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, issued a joint warning that China's military intelligence services were targeting professional networking sites and online job platforms.
This new UK-specific alert goes further, revealing what the service says is a threat that has been growing within British academic institutions.
MI5 says that the CGTRI, sometimes translated as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), has "very strong ties" to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS).
"MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage," it says.
"More than 100 UK-linked academics have contributed to projects funded by MSS via CGTRI," adding that in some cases the researches would not be aware of the front company's role in their project.

UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including AI, cyber-security, covert communications systems and steganography, which means hiding a secret message or file inside an ordinary message or object.
"This activity supports Ministry of State Security espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security," MI5 said.
The security alert said that many academic institutions and individuals will have engaged with the CGTRI "in good faith" because the link back to Chinese state security had been "obfuscated".
It continued: "UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions."
The public alert raises the prospect that British academics who do not act on it immediately could ultimately fall foul of the law.
It stressed that the National Security Act, a key piece of legislation passed in 2023 to counter state espionage, created a new offence of assisting a foreign intelligence service where the individual ought to reasonably have known what they were doing so.
Jarvis said: "This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security, and that of our allies."
He said he had now written to all university vice-chancellors to end relationships with the organisation.

Conservative MP Sir Iain Duncan-Smith, co-chair of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, told the BBC that several reports had suggested "British universities' dependence on Chinese students has opened them up to all sorts of problems" and that security checks should be stepped up.
Responding to the alert, Universities UK said universities "take their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously".
"The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes," said chief executive Vivienne Stern, "while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation".
"Close engagement between Government and the higher education sector is vital to ensuring that universities and the country continue to benefit from international collaboration while effectively managing national security risks."
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London hit back - saying it had already made "solemn representations" to the UK.
"The accusations made by the UK intelligence agency against the relevant Chinese entity are imaginary and purely fabricated," they said.
"Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations. Such exchanges and collaboration are mutually beneficial.
"We urge the UK intelligence authorities to stop spreading falsehoods and stop undermining educational exchanges and research cooperation between China and the UK."
