A new tool is allowing Mac users the ability again to easily turn off Apple Intelligence with one click and free up to 12GB of storage.
Unlike with previous versions of macOS, macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn’t have a toggle for turning off Apple Intelligence. That makes disabling AI features that you may not want more difficult. It also means that the AI models necessary for running Apple Intelligence will take up space on your disk, even if you don’t use them or if you go through your settings to individually find and disable AI capabilities.
In response, a developer known as Om Lahore on GitHub last week created RemoveMacAI, a command-line tool that allows macOS 27 users to “turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27″ in a way that is “fully reversible,” per the GitHub page. They said that Apple’s Intelligence models take up “about 12GB,” but the models can actually take up over 30GB, The Verge noted.
RemoveMacAI “turns off Siri, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, the ChatGPT extension, and all the summaries, then it deletes the models and stops macOS from downloading them again. Dictation still works because it’s a separate setting,” the developer said in a Reddit post first spotted by MacRumors.

2 killed, including student, in ‘horrific’ school bus crash in Florida
The bus was transporting 39 people to Winter Haven High School when an oncoming car crossed the centre line and caused the crash
A school bus flipped over onto its roof during a multivehicle crash in central Florida on Monday morning, killing two people – including a 10th grade girl – and injuring several others, authorities said.
Some 39 people were on the school bus that was headed to Winter Haven High School in Winter Haven when an oncoming car crossed the centre line and caused the crash, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said at a news conference.
“It was a horrible crash,” Judd said. “It was a terrible, tragic morning. We had a beautiful 10th grade girl lose her life.”
The bus had been travelling along a Winter Haven road shortly after 6am local time when an oncoming car crossed the centre line and crashed into the side of the bus near the rear wheels, Judd said.

The weekend’s elections in Brazil not only put Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the lead in the presidential race, but also underscored how far the former president has come in building a political dynasty.
As his far-right senator son heads into a runoff against the leftist incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a sweeping far-right victory in congressional races also secured seats for Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, two of his sons and one of his brothers.
Few in the family have spent much time working outside politics since the patriarch led the way four decades ago, but the offices they now hold have had a significant upgrade.
Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro, 44, who divided her campaign with caring for her husband as he serves a sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup, ran for public office for the first time and was elected senator.
Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, regarded as the most radical of the siblings – he ran his father’s social media accounts and was indicted by federal police for leading a so-called hate cabinet that spread fake news and attacks on opponents – was also elected senator for the first time.
His previous political career amounted to 25 years as a city councillor in Rio de Janeiro – starting at the age of 17, when his father put him up for a seat against his own mother, Rogéria Bolsonaro, who had divorced Jair. Carlos won. (Rogéria also ran last Sunday for a seat in the state legislature, still using the Bolsonaro surname, but lost.)
The patriarch’s fourth son, Jair Renan Valle Bolsonaro, 28, who dropped his two middle names on the ballot to run simply as Jair Bolsonaro, jumped from city councillor to federal congressman.
Of Bolsonaro’s five children, only his 15-year-old daughter has never held political office.
Even the former president’s younger brother, Renato Bolsonaro, 62, nicknamed the “brother who can’t win” after losing seven consecutive elections for lower-level offices, was elected. He went from fewer than 10,000 votes in a mayoral race two years ago to 380,000 votes for congress.
During the campaign, Renato caused some friction within the family by saying that “Flávio is not Jair. He doesn’t draw crowds”. At the polls, however, Flávio ended up winning more votes than his father did in 2018 and 2022, although the result is seen by some as more of an anti-Lula vote than a strong preference for the senator.
The number of Bolsonaros in office could have been even higher had “son 03”, Eduardo Bolsonaro, 42, not abandoned his seat in congress and gone into self-imposed exile in the US, where for more than a year he has lobbied for what Lula and many others see as Donald Trump’s attempts to interfere in Brazil’s elections.
Although Michelle is the most recent member of the family to enter politics, it is she who is often considered to be the leading figure among the Bolsonaros. In a July poll, she was named the most powerful woman in Brazilian politics, well ahead of the current first lady, Janja Lula da Silva, in addition to a supreme court justice and many members of congress.
“She is a phenomenon,” said Camila Rocha, a researcher at the Brazilian Center for Analysis and Planning, who has interviewed voters and studied the Brazilian right for a decade. “Even Bolsonaro voters don’t like his sons very much, but many of them like Michelle, who is very charismatic.”
The daughter of a housewife and a retired bus driver from the metropolitan region around Brasília, Michelle was working as a parliamentary secretary for another politician when, at 25, she met Bolsonaro, then a 52-year-old congressman. She is his third wife.
When he took office as president in 2019, Michelle made history by becoming the first and only Brazilian first lady to deliver a speech at an inauguration. She did so in Brazilian Sign Language, which she had mastered while working as an interpreter at evangelical church services – her religiosity is seen as one of the main assets behind Bolsonaro’s close relationship with evangelical voters.
Despite playing by Bolsonaro’s party’s rules, Michelle was at the centre of one of the most contentious moments of Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign, when she said that she had been “humiliated”, “disrespected” and “mistreated” by the senator. Reports of friction between her and her stepsons are frequent. Given her popularity, Flávio had to apologise publicly – although Michelle accepted it, the two did not campaign together.
Polls suggested Bolsonaro supporters would have preferred the former first lady as the presidential candidate, but the patriarch opted for his eldest son, and gave her the senate mission instead. “That was the mission my husband entrusted to me, and I will represent him, God willing,” she said in August.
Michelle and Bolsonaro’s sons were also widely seen as helping secure victories for other far-right candidates from Bolsonaro’s party, which will have by far the largest bloc in the next congress.
“Although the family has been in politics for a long time, many voters still see the Bolsonaros as representing ‘renewal’ and an anti-system vote,” said Rocha.
“So, to change everything, these voters want to throw a ‘bomb’ that blows up congress and Lula. And that bomb is the Bolsonaro family,” she added.

Well, it’s safe to say no Bahrain Grand Prix has been affected by torrential rain quite like the 2026 race.
For one thing, it was held several thousand miles from Bahrain itself. The ongoing war with Iran ruled such things out, so the Sepang International Circuit in Malaysia stepped in to fill its spot. One of the best examples of a late-’90s “Tilke track”—named for its designer, Herman Tilke—it’s characterized by a couple of long straights and the always-brutal tropical weather that provides one of the toughest physical challenges on the calendar. And this weekend was no exception.
Heavy rain arrived about half an hour before the start time, delaying things significantly. Although the sport has two different kinds of treaded tires for use in the rain, the full wet tire generates so much spray, and such slow lap times, that it’s essentially only useful for circulating behind the safety car. If it’s wet enough to need it, it will be too wet to see where you’re going. The intermediate tire, by contrast, has much shallower grooves and is good for racing on damp but not soaked tracks, although it quickly overheats and degrades as the track dries.
Chaos ensues
The organizers decided on two formation laps behind the safety car; circulating at lower speed would allow the drivers to get an idea of the track conditions and let their intermediate tires pump some water off the track surface, the idea went. But that didn’t take into account a bug lurking in the cars’ software.
Driving slowly behind the safety car with reduced hybrid power in some parts of the track due to the extremely wet conditions convinced several of the cars that they were being tricked into breaking a hard-coded rule meant to prevent cheating, triggering an automatic 60-second shutdown of their electric motors that caused chaos as car after car slowed for the one in front, then took varying lengths of time to reboot their systems.
The cars assembled on the grid before the first attempt at a race start.
Credit:
JADE GAO / AFP
The cars assembled on the grid before the first attempt at a race start.
Credit:
JADE GAO / AFP
“It was like the Lego race,” said Max Verstappen of Red Bull, referring back to the human-size Lego cars that F1 used for a driver parade at the 2025 Miami Grand Prix. “At some point, we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn’t understand what was going on. Then we did a lap and then I see eight other cars crawling still… I mean that’s not what you want, right, for the sport.”
The race organizers aborted the entire start. The bug had never come up in testing, and the FIA had to hastily write and distribute a software update to fix it. An hour after the first aborted start, the cars lined up on the grid again, ready to finally race.
“In wet conditions, there are some different software settings for the cars for safety reasons to reduce the power in certain sectors from the maximum to a lower level,” explained Nikolas Tombazis, head of single-seater racing at the FIA. “And this year, we’ve had very little wet weather running or none at all, almost. So it wasn’t maybe adequately checked.”
The software was developed by the FIA with the teams and engine makers. “So it’s common software for all cars,” Tombazis said. “And basically there was a combination of events between those software settings and the fact that some cars went incredibly slow during the formation lap and those entered a sort of a bug into the software which was stopping those cars to reaccelerate and to go to normal speeds.”
“And as a result of that, we had quite a few cars affected by that problem and which caused them to stop,” Tombazis said. “Perhaps I should also add that as soon as the formation lap problems happened, we understood the problem very soon afterward and we issued some an updated software to the teams. It took about sort of 20 minutes for the software to be issued. Some explanations teams had to update the software in the car. They had to ask a couple of questions and we had to make sure they all had done that work. So all of that took maybe about 20 minutes or so and so that was what caused that delay for the second start.”
(Indeed, the delay led Verstappen to joke that his team got their update applied faster thanks to their Oracle-supplied data connection.)
More chaos
The delay to the start was long enough that the rain had abated and the puddles of standing water had all drained, leading just over half the grid to gamble that it was dry enough to risk starting on either the soft or medium slick. Only nine drivers opted for the intermediate tire, including Verstappen (on pole), championship leader Kimi Antonelli, and his Mercedes teammate George Russell. Lewis Hamilton, starting second, was among those choosing to start on either the soft or medium slick tire; this was a mistake, as the formation lap proved the track was still much wetter than expected—too wet for slicks, certainly.
So it wasn’t a surprise to see the slick-shod cars quickly left behind as they struggled to put down power on the wet tarmac. Despite being on the intermediates, Verstappen got a terrible start and was left in third, behind both Mercedes.
“I was not surprised because my start was horrendous,” Verstappen said. “Again, dropping the clutch and not having power. The engine just completely died on me. But then you just have to settle in, try not to overreact as well, and just slot in, try to keep your position there. The race is long, a lot of things can happen, and step by step, I could close the gap.”
And he did, passing Russell on lap six and then closing up behind Antonelli quickly thereafter.
Lewis Hamilton and the other slick-shod cars got left behind at the start as track conditions proved far too wet for their tires.
Credit:
Jayce Illman/Getty Images
Lewis Hamilton and the other slick-shod cars got left behind at the start as track conditions proved far too wet for their tires.
Credit:
Jayce Illman/Getty Images
Meanwhile, at the back of the pack, some of the drivers who started on slicks made stops to change to the intermediates. McLaren’s Oscar Piastri was among the first who quickly began scything through the field; within a lap, he’d caught up and passed everyone who went by as he stopped. Others followed suit, though Hamilton was not among them, telling his race engineer on lap 5 that he’d gamble on the conditions coming back to suit him. It was a decision that would show the depth of experience that the seven-time world champion brings to the sport.
The race restarted on lap 13, and Verstappen pounced on Antonelli, taking the lead, with Russell following into second. Hamilton, meanwhile, was in 15th, although not for long. Within a lap, he was up to 11th. Within 10 laps of the restart, he was in 5th.
Slightly further back, another legend of the sport was also having a good day.
Fernando Alonso’s Aston Martin might have been a laughingstock at the start of the season, as it was multiple seconds slower than the cars of the frontrunners, but the Adrian Newey-designed aerodynamic update that arrived in Hungary closed some of the gap to the rest of the field. And Honda has now introduced a second power unit upgrade that has helped drivability even while at a power deficit to the others. It’s not quite as effective a package as Hamilton’s Ferrari, but Alonso began moving forward, and by lap 40, he was in 10th place, the final points-paying position.
Fernando Alonso will race in F1 for at least one more year; he entered the sport in 2001.
Credit:
Jayce Illman/Getty Images
Fernando Alonso will race in F1 for at least one more year; he entered the sport in 2001.
Credit:
Jayce Illman/Getty Images
Up front, Verstappen was building a commanding lead, and Antonelli had overtaken Russell for second, having first asked the team unsuccessfully if they’d simply tell Russell to let him by.
Extra chaos
Then Alex Albon’s Williams suffered a gearbox failure on lap 43, triggering a virtual safety car. Verstappen and Hamilton stopped for tires, followed a lap later by Antonelli, Russell, and the other Red Bull of Isack Hadjar. The broken transmission of the Williams prevented it from being easily moved, so a full safety car was declared, bunching the pack up.
The race would restart on lap 52 (of 55), but not before Russell came to a stop by the side of the track just past the pit exit on lap 50. “Another [power unit] failure, when we were on course for a pretty certain podium. It’s a tough one to take. It’s unfortunately happened too many times this season, and, yeah, this is just where we are,” Russell said after the race as he acknowledged his title chances for 2026 were over.
The final three laps were frenetic. Hamilton passed Hadjar for third, a wonderful recovery drive back to the podium after being more than a minute off the lead at one point during the race. His Ferrari teammate Charles Leclerc trailed behind, also passing the second Red Bull and fully salvaging Ferrari’s day. Ahead of the red cars, Antonelli was closing down on Verstappen but without being close enough to attempt an overtake. And Alonso was making moves, too, ending his day in eighth place, Aston’s best finish of the year.
Everyone knows this looks bad
Kimi Antonelli (R) looks set to join Max Verstappen (M) and Lewis Hamilton (R) as one of F1’s greats.
Credit:
Clive Mason/Getty Images
Kimi Antonelli (R) looks set to join Max Verstappen (M) and Lewis Hamilton (R) as one of F1’s greats.
Credit:
Clive Mason/Getty Images
On a chaotic day, F1’s biggest talents shone their brightest. Between them, Hamilton, Verstappen, and Alonso have 13 world championships, and this year, Antonelli has given every indication his name belongs alongside theirs, even if he does need to do something about his weakness for exceeding track limits. And the racing we got was actually rather thrilling. But some of that was still overshadowed by all the chaos that had to happen first. And everyone knows where to point the finger.
“The power units are exceptionally complicated. The more complicated you make things, the more there is to go wrong. So that is obviously something we need to bear in mind for the future,” said Russell. “It just proves that we shouldn’t have any of that stuff on the electronic side,” said McLaren’s Lando Norris.
“It is clear the regs are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the PUs, for the manufacturers. It is too complicated,” said Williams’ Carlos Sainz. “Again, my only question mark is who, five years ago, decided that this was the direction to go? We are doing the best with what we are given as a sport and as regulations. The FIA and F1 are doing the best they can with what was decided four or five years ago, but clearly what was decided four or five years ago is wrong.”
Next year, the power units will be rebalanced with more power from the V6 and less from the electric motor, with another change coming in 2028. Then it’s all change in 2031 (or perhaps 2030), when F1 will likely go back to V8s and much smaller hybrid systems.
Jonathan is the Automotive Editor at Ars Technica. He has a BSc and PhD in Pharmacology. In 2014 he decided to indulge his lifelong passion for the car by leaving the National Human Genome Research Institute and launching Ars Technica's automotive coverage. He lives in Washington, DC.

A new California law bans child marriage. What's the global outlook on the practice?
It's been a landmark year for activists seeking bans against child marriage in the U.S. On Sept. 30, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Bill AB 1267, setting 18 as the minimum age for marriage in the state, with no exceptions.
The bill, sponsored by Unchained at Last and the California Commission on the Status of Women and Girls, was authored by Assemblymember Gail Pellerin. It repealed provisions that had allowed minors to marry with parental consent and judicial approval, a system that meant California had no statutory minimum marriage age. The law also removes the parallel exception that allowed minors to enter domestic partnerships.
Its passage marks the culmination of a nearly decade-long campaign by survivors and advocacy groups to outlaw marriage before 18 in the state. California is now the 18th state to prohibit child marriage without exception; such marriages remain legal under varying restrictions in 32 other states.
The signing also brought survivor voices to the forefront. Newsom signed the measure alongside advocate Courtney Stodden, who was 16 when her parents permitted her to marry 50-year-old actor Doug Hutchison and has since become an outspoken campaigner against child marriage.
"The heart of this effort has always been the survivors," Pellerin said after the bill was signed. "They told us what it means to be a child in a marriage you did not freely choose."
She pointed to the difficulties minors can face in seeking legal help, leaving home or escaping adults who may be enabling the marriage. "Because of them, California children are safer."
A global perspective
The issue of child marriage — when one partner is under age 18 — is a global concern. The United Nations calls it a "human rights violation," citing a litany of concerns for child brides: "early pregnancy and social isolation, interrupting her schooling, limiting her opportunities for career and vocational advancement and placing her at risk of domestic violence." Yet every year, the U.N. estimates that 12 million girls become child brides.
Child grooms, the U.N. further notes, may be forced into "an adult role for which they are unprepared," with pressure to drop out of school and support a family.
The U.N. has set the goal of ending child marriage by the year 2030.
Since 2021, countries as diverse as Sierra Leone, England, the Philippines and the Dominican Republic have been passing legislation to set the marriage age at 18, with no exceptions.
In the United States, the current push for a national law is controversial — some have criticized provisions in the proposed legislation, and others oppose it altogether.
And legislation is not necessarily the solution. In India, marriage under age 18 is illegal, yet the latest National Family Health Survey conducted in country found that one in five women ages 20 to 24 married before turning 18. UNICEF estimates that at least 1.5 million girls under the age of 18 are married in India each year.
The U.S. effort
Even as states like California create new laws regarding child marriage, the United States as a whole is debating the issue — and raising the possibility of a nationwide ban.
On July 16, U.S. Rep. Gwen Moore of Wisconsin and Sens. Dick Durbin, Brian Schatz and Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Child Marriage Prevention Act, a federal bill aimed at combating child marriage.
This legislation would push states toward a nationwide minimum marriage age of 18. "In 34 states, including Wisconsin, child marriage is legal. Many of these marriages are between young girls and adult men. It's time we end this predatory practice," Moore said in a statement emailed to NPR. "I know that advocates have pushed for reform at the state level, which has led some states to change their laws. This federal legislation would help bolster and support those efforts, including helping states get the data to understand its prevalence in their jurisdictions and then take action to address it."
In announcing the bill, its four congressional cosponsors cited data showing that more than 314,000 minors were legally married in the United States between 2000 and 2021, including girls as young as 10. The figures, compiled by child-marriage advocacy groups from state marriage records, indicate that most of the underage girls were married to adult men.
Unchained At Last, a nonprofit worked to end forced and child marriage in the U.S., estimates that at least 66,415 of these marriages — about one in five — occurred when the bride was at an age when sexual relations would be considered a crime (the age varies from 14 to 18 depending on the state). In roughly 90% of that subset, according to the organization's founder, Fraidy Reiss, marital exemptions in state statutory-rape laws shielded the adult spouse from prosecution. Married minors may also face legal barriers to hiring an attorney, filing for divorce or obtaining protection from abuse.
The Tahirih Justice Center, an organization with a long history of advocating for survivors of forced and child marriage, has been a key partner in developing and supporting this legislation.
"The one thing we hear all the time from places — Cameroon, Guatemala, you name it — is: 'It makes my work harder when a politician can say to my face, the United States allows child marriage, so why should I do anything?' The best thing that we can do to help the global movement is to get our house in order," says Casey Carter Swegman, director of public policy at Tahirih.
Swegman says that a child's apparent consent does not necessarily mean that the decision to marry was made freely. "A 15-, 16- or 17-year-old who has been pressured and coached by family members may tell a judge that she consents because refusing could expose her to punishment or violence at home," she says. This is especially troubling, Swegman says, when pregnancy, potential evidence of sexual abuse, is treated as justification for allowing the marriage to proceed.
"A child is coming before your court pregnant by an adult person — that should be a red flag for statutory rape, not a green light for marriage," she says.
Although the proposed bill has won support from many child-marriage advocates, others have questioned whether its provisions go far enough and warn of possible unintended consequences that it has overlooked.
"If I could heart a provision of this bill, it would be [the proposal] to provide financial incentive to states that have banned child marriage — that I can get behind," says Reiss. "While I applaud Congress for introducing and considering legislation to combat child marriage at the federal level, I am appalled that two sections of the Child Marriage Prevention Act would make a mockery of the bill's title."
Section 6, she says, would provide federal grants to states to "study" child marriage instead of banning it. "If states are given money to examine something that's a human rights violation instead of banning it outright, it would be devastating," says Reiss, who says she was forced to marry at age 19.
Section 10 would allow some minors as young as 16, whether in the United States or abroad, to qualify for a U.S. spousal visa under certain circumstances. This would actually encourage a particularly heinous form of child marriage, says Reiss: the trafficking of minors to the U.S. under the guise of marriage, and it would discourage U.S. states from setting their marriage age at 18, no exceptions. "If the bill were amended to set the spousal visa age at 18, it would be a 'game-changer' by sending a clear message to states and halting legal trafficking," she says.
There has been opposition to the idea in some states. For instance, some Republican lawmakers in Missouri have opposed state bans on child marriage, arguing that such restrictions constitute government overreach and interfere with parental authority.
In 2024, in an interview with the Missouri Independent, Republican state Rep. Dean Van Schoiack called a proposed ban "government intrusion in people's lives." Asked what would be lost if 16- and 17-year-olds could no longer marry, he replied, "Liberties that people currently have."
Missouri banned the practice in 2025.
How the U.S. bill compares to other global efforts
As Congress prepares to debate the U.S. bill, other countries have already adopted more sweeping national restrictions. The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2024 in Sierra Leone sets 18 as the minimum age of marriage without any exceptions for parental consent, religious marriage or pregnancy. Section 15 declares that any child marriage contracted after the Act took effect to be void. The legislation even penalizes people who facilitate or attend a child marriage.
In November 2024, Colombia, where 23% of girls are married before they're 18, passed a law banning such marriages outright. In a similar move, on Sept. 25, 2025, Bolivia banned child marriage without exceptions, removing provisions allowing 16- and 17-year-olds to marry with parental consent or judicial approval.
But laws are not always a solution. In many countries in sub-Saharan Africa and in India, there are national laws banning child marriage but weak enforcement often limits their effectiveness.
"In countries like India, child marriage persists despite strong laws due to deeply ingrained cultural factors, making solutions very complex," says Renu Singh, executive director of Young Lives India, a research program that studies how poverty and inequality shape children's lives as they grow into adulthood.
The Young Lives study began in 2002, in India, Ethiopia, Peru and Vietnam.
In India, Young Lives has followed 3,000 children in the southern Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana — from childhood into their late 20s. Researchers have repeatedly interviewed them and their families about education, health, employment, marriage, fertility, household circumstances and personal aspirations. They found that many of the children they'd followed married early.
Working with India's National Commission for Protection of Child Rights, they analyzed 2011 Census data to map child marriage at the state and district levels. That research reported 12.1 million marriages involving people below India's respective legal marriage ages (21 for boys and 18 for girls) and identified hotspots that could help the government target interventions.
"We found that there were so many varied and complex reasons driving these marriages," says Singh. "It wasn't just low-income groups who got their children married off." Some parents, she says, who were deeply concerned about the safety of an unmarried daughter, saw marriage as a security net. Young Lives found that girls with older brothers were more at risk of being married early because of the social custom of giving dowries — when the bride's family gifts the bridegroom's family money at the time of marriage. In a household with a boy and a girl, the girl was married especially early, so that her older brother could get married too.
"Boys were often married off early as well, especially if the family wanted to get dowries for their sons to offset the financial losses they faced when they gave their own daughters away in marriage. And this was the case across all income groups," says Singh.
India's national law has helped establish that child marriage is unacceptable and punishable, Singh says — but lasting change also requires communities to stop accepting and supporting the widespread practice.
NPR has reported on how this practice unfolds in India: "Our parents just hold the weddings in secret," a 16-year-old told our correspondent. "At night — very rushed." Our story continues: "She was married when she was 9 years old. A bunch of other girls nod. They were all married around that age, too. A shy girl in a pink T-shirt says she didn't even understand what was happening at the time."
For legislation to be effective, Singh says, parents, relatives, religious leaders and others must no longer regard an early marriage as normal, protective or beneficial for a girl.
"The U.S. also has major issues with deeply entrenched gender roles, with patriarchy, with extreme — I would say almost obsession over the control of female sexuality. These are the [reasons] the social pressure for this practice continue," says Swegman. In addition to a national law, it's clear that attitudes must change too. "This requires belief and behavior change, services, support, thoughtful conversations on the community level," says Swegman.
The campaign for stronger laws in the United States is a part of a growing international effort to move child marriage higher up the global political agenda.
One of the key figures behind the U.N. resolution declaring a day "to end child, early and forced marriage" is Bhuwan Ribhu, a lawyer and the founder of Just Rights for Children, a child rights network. Just Rights for Children has filed a series of Public Interest Litigations in India that would reframe child marriage as child rape, securing legal protections for the young women.
"Establishing an official International Day to End Child, Early and Forced Marriage gives us an annual platform to hold governments accountable and enforce laws that protect children. Now is the time to build on this commitment and end child marriage by 2030. Today, the world has spoken in one voice: the crime of child marriage must end," Ribhu says.

The Allahabad High Court has initiated suo motu proceedings on noise pollution following reports of the death of a 7-year-old Class 2 student at a school in Balrampur while a procession carrying loudspeakers and a music system was passing nearby.
The incident occurred on September 22 at Divine Public School on City Palace Road in Bhagautiganj, Balrampur. The deceased was identified as Vaishnavi Tiwari. According to reports, the procession was part of the 10-day Ganpati Utsav, which started on September 14.
Observing that the incident raises larger questions over the unchecked menace of noise pollution, a Division Bench of Justice Rajan Roy and Justice Manjive Shukla on Wednesday (September 28) ordered the registration of a separate suo motu PIL while hearing an existing case concerning the use of pressure horns, modified silencers and hooters.
The court, however, clarified that it had not established any connection between the alleged loud noise and the child’s death.
The Bench maintained that the broader problem of noise pollution and the enforcement of statutory safeguards required separate consideration. It observed that violations of the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, were frequently witnessed in public spaces despite the existing legal framework.
The PIL will examine the authorities responsible for controlling noise pollution, the enforcement measures currently in place, and whether regular monitoring is required, The Bench said.
The court also stressed the need for greater public awareness, observing that a lack of awareness may contribute to violations. At the same time, the Bench said continued violations despite enforcement measures should attract accountability under the applicable law.
The court made the Uttar Pradesh Director General of Police, the Uttar Pradesh Pollution Control Board (UPPCB), the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), Lucknow civic authorities and officials from key government departments parties in the matter. The Balrampur District Magistrate, Superintendent of Police and Chief Medical Officer were also directed to be impleaded. The State was asked to obtain reports on the incident and submit details of measures taken or proposed to enforce noise-control laws.
The court also expressed hope that the child’s parents and school authorities would not face unnecessary pressure or interference. The matter will now be heard on October 12.

Sixteen founders across 10 new-age tech companies earned a combined ₹43.4 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 8.2% from ₹40.2 Cr in FY25, according to data compiled by Inc42. Average fixed remuneration per founder increased to ₹2.7 Cr from ₹2.5 Cr. Of these, 12 founders received increases in fixed pay, three saw reductions, and one reported unchanged remuneration. Honasa Consumer cofounder Ghazal Alagh recorded the highest percentage increase, with her fixed remuneration rising 60% to ₹2.4 Cr from ₹1.5 Cr. Delhivery cofounder Sahil Barua followed with a 21.4% increase to ₹3.4 Cr from ₹2.8 Cr. Nykaa founder Falguni Nayar saw the steepest percentage decline at 14%, with her fixed pay falling to ₹74 Lakh from ₹86 Lakh. Swiggy cofounder Sriharsha Majety’s remuneration declined 12.5% to ₹1.4 Cr from ₹1.6 Cr. Lenskart cofounder Peyush Bansal drew the highest fixed remuneration among the founders tracked, despite a 1.7% decline to ₹5.7 Cr from ₹5.8 Cr. Meesho cofounders Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Kumar followed with ₹4.8 Cr each, while Paytm founder Vijay Shekhar Sharma received ₹4 Cr, unchanged from FY25. However, fixed pay tells only part of the story. Peyush Bansal received ₹12 Cr in bonuses and performance incentives – more than twice his fixed remuneration – along with perquisites and retirement benefits. Fellow Lenskart cofounder Neha Bansal received ₹6 Cr in bonuses and performance incentives, in addition to her ₹2.7 Cr fixed pay. Share-based compensation also featured prominently. Majety’s ESOP gains stood at ₹549.3 Cr, while Delhivery cofounder Kapil Bharati recorded ₹6.9 Cr in ESOP gains. Separately, the cost of stock options granted to FirstCry founder Supam Maheshwari stood at ₹31.7 Cr. He also received ₹2.1 Cr in perquisites and ₹84 Lakh in performance incentives. These components require separate treatment. Stock-option costs and ESOP-related benefits do not necessarily represent cash received by a founder during the year and should be distinguished from fixed salaries and cash incentives. Inc42 has been tracking founders’ remuneration since FY23, covering the startup ecosystem’s shift from the era of funding boom to the funding winter and now, more recently, towards profitability and IPOs. Lightweight. Lots of style options. Better battery life. Better mics for call quality.
TIRED
Many of the same last-gen features. Meta's AI isn't all that smart. Audio playback could be louder. People might think you're a creep.
I’ve been on a call with my insurance provider for over an hour when the fire alarm in my apartment starts blaring. The sound is extraordinarily loud, piercing through the entire building. It overwhelms the voice on the other line, which comes through the speakers of my new Meta Nova smart glasses.
I manage to dart outside, keep the call going, and eventually learn this is a false alarm. I breathe a sigh of relief, but the helpful human on the other end sounds very worried and asks if I’m OK. Turns out, they hadn’t heard the sirens at all, just me screeching, “OH JESUS WHAT IS HAPPENING?” The six-mic system on Meta’s new smart glasses does quite a good job of culling background noise over calls. I hadn’t expected to try that feature out in that way, but I can confirm it works.
This may not be a use case that would inspire someone to buy a new pair of Meta’s smart glasses. Especially not its camera-equipped ones, which have become prime targets of controversy about them being used by creeps and abusers. (Meta launched camera-free audio-only glasses, but we haven't tested them yet.)
In fact, none of the upgrades in Meta’s new Gen 3 glasses are revolutionary. The glasses get nine hours of battery life, one more than the previous generation. They have a superior mic array—though identical to the Meta Glasses that debuted in June—a dedicated button for Meta’s AI assistant, and a slimmer, lighter fit that comes in dozens of color and frame combinations. They have the same 12-MP cameras that can capture 3K video as the Gen 2 models.
Photograph: Courtesy of Meta
Photograph: Courtesy of Meta
The pair of glasses I’ve been using are the Meta-designed, non-Ray-Ban-branded Meta Nova glasses. You can also shop styles like the Adventurer Lisa or Capri editions. (The Ray-Ban-branded Gen 3 models are more expensive, starting at $499.) The Nova comes with much of the same software for $299. They have translucent brown frames and rounded lenses and are the first pair of Meta glasses I’ve worn that I feel actually look decent on my face.
The camera housing on my Meta Nova glasses is smaller than on the Gen 2 glasses. From a distance, they might even read as rivets at a glance. (I asked my colleague Reece Rogers how they looked on my face, and from a few feet away in the WIRED office, he didn’t even notice they were camera-enabled glasses at first.)
They feel and function the same as before. You can interact with an AI assistant or snap photos and video with the press of a button. Conversation Focus, a mode that helps hard-of-hearing people better pick up spoken words, is a feature that only works in early access on Meta’s Ray-Ban and Oakley smart glasses. It seems very helpful, but my Meta-designed frames don’t have it yet.
They also don’t have integration with Meta’s Muse AI, which the company says is coming later this year. I’m intrigued by that, even if having access to a camera on your face will certainly help a service that seems better at surveilling than helping its users. That said, I’ve found Muse more useful than Meta’s current AI assistant, and I look forward to asking my entirely too cute AI buddy to assist me via my glasses.
Unfortunately, Meta’s current AI assistant on the glasses is still terrible. I tried to ask what features the glasses I was wearing had, and it failed miserably. The AI couldn’t get any of the details right, even when I told it specifically which frames I was wearing and let it snap a picture of the Meta product page for reference. I wouldn’t want to depend on the AI to help me sort out anything with some real complexity.
If you pretty much ignore the AI entirely, the Gen 3 glasses do just about everything Meta promises. They capture nice photos and video, all while maintaining an indicator light that has recently been made more tamper-proof. (That’s not necessarily enough to deter the creeps.) The frames are wearable, and the software is competent enough. They’re also pricey, so maybe you can save some cash sticking with the Gen 2. They’ll all do what you probably expect them to do. Just maybe don’t be weird about it, all right?

Luke Littler missed out on the chance to hold the senior and youth world titles simultaneously after suffering a surprise semi-final defeat at the World Youth Championship.
The 19-year-old world number one was beaten 6-5 by world number 68 Cam Crabtree, who will face German Jan Schmidt in the final on 29 November.
That match will take place on finals day at the Players Championship Finals in Minehead – an event Littler has also yet to qualify for having skipped the majority of Pro Tour events this season.
He is currently ranked 126th in the Players Championship order of merit and only the top 64 qualify.
Four Players Championship events remain, but two of those are in Den Bosch in the Netherlands - where Littler withdrew from events recently after being subjected to boos by the crowds.
Littler has won successive full World Championships and won the youth title as a 16-year-old in 2023, but the semi-final loss to 23-year-old Crabtree was his second successive exit at that stage having lost to Beau Greaves in 2025. He could though enter four more times, with the tournament open to players aged 23 or under at the start of the season.
The loss is the latest in a series of surprise exits for Littler, who was knocked out of the World Grand Prix in the first round by Luke Woodhouse and lost to Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals of the World Series of Darts finals.

Nigeria mourns as 32 killed in military plane crash
- Published
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has declared three days of national mourning after a military aircraft crashed in southern Ondo State, killing 32 people.
Authorities say the plane was on a routine mission from Benin City to Lagos when it came down near a naval base on Monday morning.
A resident told the BBC that the plane had crashed near a swamp and that clothes and shoes had been found at the site. Smoke could be seen rising from the area.
Tinubu offered his deepest condolences for the 25 passengers and seven crew members on board and has ordered a full investigation.
The president also ordered national flags to be flown at half-mast across the country as a mark of respect for those who died.
"This is a painful moment for our Armed Forces and for the entire nation," Tinubu said.
"Our Air Force personnel put their lives on the line every day to secure Nigeria. Their sacrifice will never be forgotten," he added.
Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo earlier said he had been informed "of the disappearance of a military aircraft with tail number NGR 931, enroute Lagos from Benin at 0913 hours earlier today".
He said "efforts to raise the aircraft on radio proved abortive" before subsequent confirmation that it had crashed near a naval base in Igbokoda, Ondo state.
He said search and rescue efforts were ongoing.
The crashed plane, described as an ATR-42 aircraft, carries between 30 and 50 passengers, according to its manufacturers.
Tinubu has ordered the Air Force to immediately begin a thorough investigation into the cause of the crash to help prevent similar incidents in the future.
The identities of those who died have not yet been released. Authorities say the names of the officers will be published after their families have been informed.
The Nigerian Air Force plays a key role in the country's military operations, including efforts to tackle armed groups and insecurity in several parts of the country.
The accident is one of the deadliest air disasters in Nigeria in recent years.
In May 2021, Nigeria's army chief, Lt-Gen Ibrahim Attahiru, was killed in a plane crash alongside 10 other officers in the north-western state of Kaduna amid bad weather.
In February of the same year, seven people died after a military plane crashed short of a runway in the capital Abuja.

Michael Douglas is wading into the “nepo baby” debate.
The “Wall Street” actor, who is the son of the late Hollywood legend Kirk Douglas, opened up on a recent episode of the “SmartLess” podcast and said the title “really pisses” him off.

Beyond the discussion of nepotism, Douglas also noted that the best advice he could give to aspiring actors is to recognize “good material.” “The problem we all have is we don’t play an instrument, or we don’t paint, or we don’t write,” he said. “We’re standing there. Popular on Variety

‘Did Rahul and Sonia Gandhi win elections through vote chori’: BJP as poll process row intensifies
BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra asked if the governments in Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Himachal Pradesh were formed through the alleged vote theft.
The stand-off between the Congress and the BJP over alleged irregularities in the election process intensified on Tuesday with the ruling party demanding that the opposition leaders clarify whether they won their own elections through “vote chori”.
Addressing the media, BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra asked if the governments in Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Himachal Pradesh were formed through the alleged vote theft.
“Have Rahul Gandhi and Sonia Gandhi become MPs through vote theft? They themselves are also MPs. If we became MPs through vote theft, did they also become MPs through vote theft? Were the governments in Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Himachal Pradesh formed through vote theft?..." Patra said.
BJP accuses Congress of 'false allegations'
Deep Dive
The BJP accused the Congress party, and the leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, of levelling false allegations against the Election Commission of India and the process followed for Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
Patra said Gandhi’s accusations that the poll panel and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar were involved in “vote chori" and making "illegal and unilateral" changes to voter registration Form 6 are unfounded and an attempt to create “anarchy”.
“Rahul Gandhi alleged that the Supreme Court had declared Form 6 illegal and ruled that it was altered unilaterally to help the BJP. The Supreme Court never declared Form 6 illegal,” he said. The apex Court accepted a petition to review records to clarify who made the modifications," Patra said.
He also denied Gandhi's claims that the EC’s decision regarding the SIR of electoral rolls in Bihar was not unanimous.
“The ECI in its statement said clearly that the SIR order was a completely unanimous decision passed by all three Election Commissioners on June 24, 2025. The decision has been legally validated and upheld by a Supreme Court judgement on May 27, 2026,” he said.
On Monday, Rahul Gandhi alleged that CEC Gyanesh Kumar and everyone else involved in "criminal assault on democracy" will be held accountable, after the Supreme Court said it did not approve any modifications to Form 6 being used during the SIR.
In a post on X, Gandhi said it is now established beyond doubt that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar changed Form 6 "illegally and unilaterally", and asserted that the CEC, as well as everyone else involved in this "criminal assault on democracy", will be held accountable.
10 questions for Rahul Gandhi
The BJP, which has been accusing the Congress of trying to create distrust in public institutions and constitutional bodies, on Tuesday accused the grand old party of trying to create anarchy.
Patra said, “ I have 10 questions for Rahul Gandhi. He should tell us why. Is the Congress attempting to dismantle and insult democratic institutions like the ECI and the Supreme Court simply because they fail to win elections?”
Patra said both Gandhi and his mother, Sonia Gandhi, also contested and won the Lok Sabha elections, and if they accuse the poll panel of “vote chori”, they should explain their own victories.
He said the Congress should explain why it celebrates victories using the exact same electoral machinery, but cries “vote chori” when it loses. He said an attempt was made to create the impression that the names of 13 crore people were sought to be deleted through the SIR.
“I have just been shown that BJP-backed candidates have won in 11 Himachal district councils. This has just happened. The elections to these district councils, as I told you about the elections in Tripura, are conducted through ballot papers. Now, look at this: BJP-backed candidates have won in 11 Himachal district councils. How did this happen? These elections were held through ballot papers, right?..."
On the Opposition's rally against the poll panel irregularities, Patra said, “We believe that even today, the Congress party is going to attempt to create an atmosphere of anarchy in the country by using the Election Commission. We have been hearing about the so-called rally and march. Before their rally takes place, it is our responsibility as a political party to accurately place the issue before the people of the country and explain what is happening in the Election Commission and what is happening in the entire matter before the Supreme Court. For the past few days, misconceptions and fake news have been spread regarding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR)..."

Convicted murderer Christa Pike is unconscious, intubated and receiving breathing assistance from a ventilator after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her, her attorneys said on Friday (October 2, 2026), providing the first detailed account of the extent of injuries she suffered during the lethal injection.
Hospital staff are working to save Pike’s life and clear the lethal drug pentobarbital from her system, her attorneys said in an emergency court filing seeking an order requiring Tennessee’s Department of Correction to preserve evidence from Wednesday night’s botched execution.
Pike remains in critical condition, her lawyers said, two days after the state administered two doses of pentobarbital but failed to kill her. She has suffered significant injuries to both arms, they added.
“At no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” Pike’s lawyers said in a filing in the Chancery Court for the State of Tennessee Twentieth Judicial District.
The filing provides the fullest picture yet of the medical consequences of an attempted execution that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee said followed the state’s established protocol. It was the state’s second botched execution this year and Lee has halted any further state killings for the rest of 2026 and ordered an independent review of what happened.
Pike’s attorneys have said the execution team’s difficulties administering the drug were related to intravenous access, an issue they had warned the state and courts about before the execution.
Pike, 50, was convicted of killing her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, when Pike was 18. She had been scheduled to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than two centuries.

Opinions on Keurig’s K-Cup System fall into two camps: fans who value the convenience of a quick java hit and coffee purists who sideline it as flavored water. I land somewhere in the middle: I grind my own beans and brew them through a reusable filter, but I let the machine do the rest. So, perhaps, I’m the customer that Keurig has in mind with its new Alta system.
The Alta is Keurig's first single-serve coffee maker that uses plastic- and aluminum-free coffee pods—finally launching after years of development. If Alta takes off, we are likely seeing the beginning of the end for the disposable K-Cup, which launched in 1998.
Whatever your thoughts are on how the perfect cup should be made, for nearly 50 million homes in the US (and not counting the many more in offices), Keurig is coffee. For almost 30 years, we’ve been trained to ditch the old drip-coffee maker for disposable single-serve pods. But now, Keurig wants us to leave (eventually) the K-Cup and embrace the AltaRounds pod, a compostable, compressed coffee round that works the same: Drop it into the machine, press a button or two, and out comes joe.
During a presentation in New York City, Phil Drapeau, Keurig’s senior vice president of Future Coffee Systems, said customers wanted more than brewed coffee. They wanted to make fancy espresso drinks, from simple cappuccinos to salted caramel concoctions I sampled at the event (PSL fans, rejoice). But to do so, Keurig needed to invent an entirely new system.
“We wouldn’t be able to do any of that with K-Cup,” Drapeau says. “It will fail. You have to brew it at the right temperature and extract. You can’t be constrained by the K-Cup system.”
Robot Barista
If the K-Cup was about bringing Dunkin’ home, then the Alta is about mimicking brewing third-wave coffee in the kitchen. Keurig looked at how coffeehouse baristas brew espresso, and how it can simplify the process by applying the K-Cup experience.
With the AltaRound, you don’t need to measure and grind beans, tamp, or adjust pressure and temperature. The round is covered with a plant-based seaweed wrap that ensures the coffee stays compressed and fresh. After you insert it, pick a drink via the touchscreen, and the machine punctures the AltaRound and applies 10 bars of pressure to extract the liquid. Spent AltaRounds are dumped into a container.
The first-gen Alta coffee machine is sleek but enormous. It would take the space of my existing Keurig, coffee grinder, and Breville Bambino, and then some more. On the plus side, it has a built-in milk frother for drinks like lattes—it’s a separate process (a Keurig rep told me someone successfully made latte art with it)—and a built-in K-Cup brewer too. Keurig says this lets users keep brewing coffee styles not yet available in the Alta or if they want something quick. (At launch, AltaRounds come in single espresso, double espresso, and regular coffee.)
The machine is wonderfully easy to use, but the process from inserting the AltaRound to drinking takes some time. It's still faster than using a traditional espresso maker, and you do get flavorful coffee with that must-have crema on the surface. A fellow journalist/coffee enthusiast didn’t find it special, but for a K-Cup drinker like me, it’s a game changer.
Keurig is offering a bundle in the US that includes the Alta brewer (in four color choices), four boxes of AltaRounds, and Flur glasses for $500. The preorder has already sold out, which suggests strong interest. There’s no announcement on when the Alta will be on sale en masse and exactly how much (likely also $500, but without the bundled extras), but a pack of eight AltaRounds will cost $10 to $11. (Stay tuned for our full review.) With that high price, it will be some time before the K-Cup dies (well, plastic never dies) and the Alta takes its place.
It’s no secret that Keurig has been exploring a revolution in coffee pods to replace the K-Cup, and has already been beta-testing a prototype in homes. Customers have also been asking for something environmentally friendly that’s compostable and free of plastics and aluminum. (Foil wrappers and cardboard are still used in AltaRounds packaging.)
The K-Cup has been exhausted in terms of innovation. Specialty coffee for the Keurig doesn’t taste great (Nespresso does it better), and Keurig hasn’t been able to innovate beyond the K-Cup’s original intention: basic brewed coffee.
Beyond sustainability, the Alta’s technology echoes issues that plagued the K-Cup. To tell the machine which pod you inserted and to adjust the right settings, each AltaRound has a QR code that the brewer scans. In the past, Keurig ran afoul with consumers and advocates when it tried to implement a printer-toner-style DRM that would have shut out third-party pod makers. For now, Alta users can choose AltaRounds flavors from Keurig and Peet’s, both owned by the same parent company. Will Keurig allow other makers into the Alta system down the road, as it eventually did with the K-Cup? Time will tell if this is the pod revolution we’ve been waiting for.

Luke Hartley realized how important Elon Musk's Starlink was to him when it fell overboard.
Two weeks into his voyage across the Pacific in October 2023, Hartley's sailboat, Songbird, was hit by an intense squall that knocked the Starlink dish balanced on the front of the boat over the side.
It was a major blow for the music teacher turned sailing influencer, who tells me he made far more money posting about his three-year voyage around the world on TikTok via Starlink than he ever had in the US education system. Without satellite internet, he had no way to upload the videos that were funding his voyage, check weather forecasts, or call his family.
From the remote Pacific to the front lines of Ukraine, Starlink's network of orbital internet satellites has become indispensable to 13 million people in more than 167 countries. Starlink accounted for more than 60% of the $18.6 billion in revenue SpaceX generated last year, and was the only part of the business to turn a profit.
Musk has grander ambitions for the flying crown jewels in his empire. The company plans to launch tens of thousands more satellites in the coming years as it targets new markets, in a push to transform Starlink from a boutique service for rugged survivalists into the world's premier wireless carrier and broadband provider.
Beyond the profits, Starlink has also provided Musk a vital source of influence and soft power that stretches the globe.
The world's richest man's attempt to gut government bureaucracy with DOGE, his massive political donations, and his erratic and incendiary posting habits on X have cost him Tesla customers and inspired boycotts and protests against his other companies. But Starlink is so useful in far-flung and war-torn places — and has so few alternatives — that it has granted Musk a rare level of immunity to political gravity. It's also left governments, adventurers, and digital nomads struggling to reconcile their reliance on the technology with the controversies that swirl around Musk.
"We can criticize Musk till the cows come home, but it's an incredible product," says Hartley, who has mixed feelings about depending so heavily on Starlink. "It has a very controversial name behind it, but it is also a way for me to talk to my mom and inspire folks. Both things can be true."
Nowhere is this dance between reluctance and reliance more delicately choreographed than in Ukraine, where Starlink has been essential in the war against Russia. Starlink satellites have been widely adopted across the Ukrainian military as a comms system that cannot be hacked or jammed by Russian radio warfare. The service has allowed ground teams to adapt their targets mid-mission and remotely control drones with flawless video almost to the moment of impact, with no need for giant antennas that could reveal their position.
The technological advantage has come at the price of giving a mercurial CEO the power to tilt the balance of the war.
In 2023, Musk sparked global headlines when he revealed he refused a request to activate Starlink to assist a Ukrainian assault on Crimea because he was concerned that "SpaceX would be explicitly complicit in a major act of war."
The billionaire also threatened to stop supplying Ukraine with Starlink terminals the year prior over a funding dispute, and Reuters reported last July that he jeopardized a 2022 Ukrainian counteroffensive by cutting Starlink access to frontline troops.
Musk did not respond to the report, but he previously said in a March 2025 X post that he would never turn off Ukrainian terminals or use the threat of doing so as a bargaining chip, no matter how much he disagreed with the country's government.
More recently, Musk has given Ukraine an edge. In February of this year, SpaceX clamped down on Russian forces' illicit use of Starlink terminals after Ukraine's then-defense minister made a personal appeal to Musk. The cutoff severely disrupted Russia's military and allowed Ukraine to retake valuable territory.
Some servicemembers and researchers say Ukraine's dependent yet unstable relationship with Starlink leaves them uneasy. "If you are military and you're operating a drone, you cannot rely on something unpredictable. All the systems should be under control," says one drone pilot and sergeant in Ukraine's unmanned brigades. "But we have no alternative right now," he adds.
Alessio Terzi, an assistant professor at the University of Cambridge's Bennett School of Public Policy, tells me that governments risk entering a "Faustian pact" with Musk that would see the billionaire decide how, when, and where its citizens and militaries access the internet.
He said that the closest analogy for this level of geopolitical power is not pre-war titans of industry like Henry Ford and Thomas Edison but the East India Company, the British trading conglomerate that ruled over much of the Indian subcontinent. The company was granted exclusive rights to operate the trade routes between Asia and Britain in 1600. It leveraged that monopoly to grow into a quasi-empire with its own system of taxation and standing army that ruled over millions for nearly three centuries.
We can criticize Musk till the cows come home, but it's an incredible product.Luke Hartley
Terzi says that SpaceX's market share of everything sent into space — close to 80% in 2025 — outstrips the East India Company's share of global shipping at its peak. He adds that Musk and SpaceX are leveraging their own monopoly over satellite communication to act more like a sovereign state than a private company.
"This is a mega-company that is chipping away at some roles that would normally fall on the government," says Terzi.
A star is born
When Musk first announced plans for Starlink in 2015, launching internet satellites was an ambitious side quest. At the time, SpaceX's main mission was to lower the cost of launching cargo into space by perfecting its Falcon rocket, which could be partially reused over multiple flights rather than self-destructing on impact.
One former SpaceX employee said that SpaceX initially based its Starlink division in Redmond, Washington, in part to avoid distracting employees working on Falcon at the company's main facilities in Texas and California. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
By 2020, however, Starlink was at the center of SpaceX's plans. That year, Musk suggested the satellite internet service could become a $30 billion-a-year cash cow.
The company spun up a production line for Starlink user terminals in a corner of its Hawthorne, California, facility that was so far away from the main campus that early employees bought bikes to travel from one side to the other. The bikes were regularly stolen, another former employee said. In typical SpaceX fashion, the production line quickly expanded, the former employee said, so much so that it spilled out into unfinished buildings with compacted dirt floors.
Musk took a hands-on approach to the project, the person added, including telling employees to contact him if they encountered any roadblocks and providing technical feedback on new versions of the terminal.
"If his internet was down, then we were in trouble," the former employee said.
In Starlink's early days, Musk framed it as an effort to "rebuild the internet" into a space-based network that would eliminate lag while reaching the estimated 42 million Americans with no access to broadband internet. It had the added bonus, Musk said, of providing a steady stream of revenue to pay for SpaceX's Mars colonization efforts.
Musk's rivals are also chasing this vision. Jeff Bezos' Amazon and Paris-based Eutelsat OneWeb have attempted to build their own satellite constellations, but the dominance of SpaceX's rocket business — the company launched its Falcon 9 rocket 165 times last year, more rockets than the rest of the world combined — gives it a steep advantage. When Amazon put 24 of its Project Kuiper (now Leo) satellites into orbit last October, they traveled on a SpaceX rocket.
Recently, Musk has gone from describing Starlink as cheap internet for rural communities to something more fundamental: an oxygen source for an AI-saturated world. In SpaceX's August 2026 earnings call, Musk speculated that demand for Starlink would skyrocket as it became the connectivity network for fleets of robotaxis and armies of humanoid robots. (Tesla has already begun outfitting its Cybercab robotaxis with Starlink dishes.)
Beyond the financial success Starlink has afforded Musk, it has also become a useful tool for him and SpaceX to generate positive headlines. The company regularly offers Starlink for free in countries hit by natural disasters and it waived fees for Starlink access in Iran during a government crackdown on protests.
SpaceX has also used Starlink discounts to defuse the data center backlash that has spread across the US. The rocket giant's Colossus data centers in Memphis and nearby Southaven, Mississippi, have attracted opposition and lawsuits from local residents complaining about noise and pollution from the gas generators powering the sites. SpaceX responded in June by offering residents in Memphis 50% off Starlink for their "partnership and support." SpaceX extended the same offer to residents of rural Vermilion Parish in Louisiana, where it is building a $100 billion spaceport that will eventually support thousands of Starship flights a year.
Musk's ambitions for the service are growing more galactic. In SpaceX's August earnings call, he predicted that Starlink could provide the majority of the world's internet within the next 10 years.
One area where Starlink has already become a must-have is in the air. Executives said on the call that in-flight WiFi powered by Starlink, which has been adopted by more than 40 airlines, has become so popular that some passengers — including YouTube influencer Mr Beast — are booking short-haul flights instead of going direct because they have Starlink.
The satellite internet service has become a major selling point for airlines that offer it and a headache for those who don't. United Airlines has used its Starlink in-flight WiFi to try and woo Delta loyalty flyers, after Delta picked Amazon's Leo for its fleet.
SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell signaled on the call that the company plans to turn its mobile service into a full-fledged mobile carrier that will aggressively target AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile. "I anticipate us to be able to acquire quite a few of their customers because I think our service will be better," she said.
Limited by liftoffs
To take on the telecoms, SpaceX is planning to fill the heavens with a lot more Starlink satellites.
The company has submitted proposals to regulators to launch 100,000 of its V3 Starlink satellites, which are larger units that can only be launched on SpaceX's massive Starship rocket.
Analysts say that this proliferation won't be enough to take on the likes of AT&T. Tim Farrar, president at technology consultancy TMF Associates, tells me that while low-earth orbit satellites are great at providing coverage to remote and rural areas, they struggle to provide service in densely populated cities. As they whiz around the planet at 17,000 miles an hour, Starlink's satellites spend a small fraction of their time in orbit over these areas, and far more time crossing large uninhabited expanses of ocean and wilderness.
Starlink would provide Taiwan a backup network for military and civilian comms that would be exceptionally hard for China to jam.
Pierre Lionnet, a space economist, says that as the company launches more satellites to try to meet rising demand in urban areas, the amount of capacity being wasted will increase, shrinking SpaceX's margins. "The problem of growing this capacity is that it means that the same satellite will spend a larger amount of time circling the earth in areas where there is no additional demand," he says. Lionnet estimates that the company would be unlikely to turn a profit on a 100,000-strong network of Starlink satellites at the current cost of launching cargo into orbit.
SpaceX is working hard to bring that cost down with Starship, its most advanced rocket, which executives estimate will reduce launch costs by 10 times compared to the Falcon 9. In September, SpaceX hit a major milestone for Starship when it deployed working Starlink V3 satellites into orbit for the first time.
Until Starship can ramp up to full commercial operation, SpaceX will face pressure to maximize revenue from the satellite capacity they do have, Lionnet says. That means adding new enterprise customers, such as governments and airlines, and launching Starlink in new countries.
When connectivity becomes power
Global expansion gives Musk new soft power opportunities, but also risks entangling other parts of his business empire in geopolitics.
Following the example of Ukraine and the US government — for which SpaceX has built Starshield, a secure military version of Starlink — other nations are looking closely at Starlink for military purposes. In July, Taiwan changed foreign ownership rules that previously collapsed negotiations with SpaceX to bring Starlink to the island nation.
Phoebe Pham, a researcher at Taiwan's state-backed Institute for National Defense and Security Research, says that low-earth orbit satellite internet networks like Starlink would be critical for the country in the event of a conflict with China, which views Taiwan as a breakaway province.
Some military analysts have predicted that in an assault on Taiwan, China would likely cut the undersea cables that provide internet to the island and launch a barrage of cyberattacks against the island's communications infrastructure. For the Taiwanese government, Starlink would provide a backup network for military and civilian comms that would be exceptionally hard for China to jam.
"It would be wrong to say they're not looking at lessons learned from Ukraine," Pham says.
In Taiwan, government approval or adoption of Starlink could be complicated by Musk's business interests in China and his previous comments about Taiwanese independence. He suggested in 2022 that the island become a "special administrative zone" similar to Hong Kong and described Taiwan as an "integral part" of China in 2023. Tesla has operated a giant EV factory in Shanghai since 2019, and around a fifth of the automaker's revenue last year came from the Chinese market.
Pham says that if Starlink applied to operate in Taiwan, the government would have to weigh the risk that Musk's business interests in China could be used as "potential leverage." It could seek to avoid giving Musk the kind of unilateral decision-making power he has enjoyed in Ukraine, she added.
"The question is, who makes these decisions about the activation and coverage?" she says.
Starlink has also run into geopolitical roadblocks in India. In June, Bloomberg reported that officials hit the brakes on the service's long-awaited launch after raising concerns over reports from local Iranian media that Starlink kits were being used in Iran, despite a state-mandated block on internet access during the conflict with the US and Israel. SpaceX executive Lauren Dreyer said in response to Bloomberg's report that the company remained in "active and productive discussions" about bringing Starlink to India, adding that SpaceX had set up a bespoke deployment model for operating Starlink in the country.
Ukraine is now exploring alternative methods for frontline communications. A senior figure at a company manufacturing drones for the country's military says Ukraine is planning for the day Starlink goes offline, whether because Musk has pulled the plug or as a result of direct Russian attacks on Starlink's satellites.
"Hopefully, it will not happen tomorrow. But if it happens in a year, Ukraine will be ready," the person says. "Every army should prepare for this scenario because it's not just a question if Elon Musk will shut it down. In the military, you always need to have backup options for connectivity. Otherwise, you may lose everything."
