IPO-bound Razorpay announced today that it has deepened its partnership with AI major OpenAI to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT. Under the partnership, the company's growth marketing platform, Razorpay Engage, will enable brands to prepare product catalogues, launch and manage campaigns on ChatGPT Ads. Brands onboarded by Razorpay include Tanishq, Fastrack, Traya, Tata Neu, Rivaah by Tanishq, Shaadi.com, Axis Max Life, Palmonas and Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies (NMIMS). Razorpay Engage To Become ChatGPT Ads Layer Razorpay Engage will provide the technology and operational infrastructure for businesses looking to get started with ChatGPT Ads. Its offering will include assessing catalogue readiness, improving and structuring product feeds, creating and managing campaigns, and measuring and optimising campaign performance. The platform will also use an AI agent built around ChatGPT Ads best practices to help create and manage campaigns across different contexts where consumers may encounter a brand's products. The agent will monitor campaign performance and make ongoing adjustments, while Razorpay's team will provide human oversight where required. “The way people discover products is changing. The next customer may not search for a product or scroll through an ad; they may simply ask an AI assistant for help deciding what to buy. For businesses, we believe that opens up an entirely new moment to be discovered,” Razorpay COO Rahul Kothari said. The Broader Context Behind OpenAI-Razorpay Partnership The partnership comes as consumer discovery of brands is shifting from traditional keyword-based searches on engines to conversational interactions with AI chatbots. An early trend of users describing what they are looking for to an AI bot, comparing options and refine their choices via subsequent conversations is emerging at the moment. As this trend gains more footing, ChatGPT started rolling out ads on ChatGPT in India, with the initial rollout covering logged-in adults on the Free and Go plans at the end of August. Ad agencies WPP and Omnicom are OpenAI’s first agency partners in India. For brands, this creates a new channel where products need to be structured and represented with sufficient information and context to surface across different consumer queries. Razorpay said managing this process manually at scale can be challenging. The advertising push builds on Razorpay's earlier efforts to turn ChatGPT into a commerce channel. The fintech company has been working with OpenAI and NPCI on infrastructure that allows merchants to create ChatGPT-native storefronts, sync product catalogues and eventually complete purchases within the chat interface. In August, Razorpay said it was working with around 50 brands and several ecommerce marketplaces on agentic-commerce pilots. The company has also earlier said that its technology can reduce the time required for a Shopify merchant to set up a ChatGPT storefront from around eight to 10 weeks to roughly 30 minutes by automating catalogue syncing and the submission process. The broader proposition is that merchants need more than visibility on AI platforms: they also need structured catalogues, storefronts and payment infrastructure that can work inside conversational interfaces. Razorpay has been building these layers as it seeks to establish itself as an infrastructure provider for AI-led commerce. This also marks a continuation of Razorpay's partnership with OpenAI and NPCI around agentic payments. The company has been experimenting with UPI Circle and UPI Reserve Pay to enable purchases within ChatGPT, while keeping payment credentials away from the AI model and requiring user consent for transactions. Razorpay's push comes as other payment companies, including Cashfree and Pine Labs, are also building infrastructure for agentic commerce, suggesting that payment providers see the AI interface as a potential new layer between consumers and merchants rather than simply another checkout channel. The partnership also marks another step in Razorpay's expansion beyond its core payments business. Razorpay was founded in 2014 by IIT Roorkee alumni Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur and has expanded from payments into a broader suite of business and banking solutions. Razorpay launched Engage in 2023 as a full-stack growth marketing platform, offering businesses customer acquisition, retention and engagement tools. The platform provides personalised incentives, gift cards and targeted rewards across an inventory of more than 5,000 options. Its AI push, meanwhile, extends beyond commerce and advertising. In August, Razorpay launched Vulcan, a proprietary AI foundation model designed to improve payment success, fraud detection and transaction routing, underlining the company's broader attempt to build AI into its payments infrastructure. Razorpay has also been developing Agent Studio, its platform for deploying task-specific AI agents for businesses. Around 200 businesses were using the platform in beta as of August, with use cases including reconciliation, abandoned-cart recovery, subscription recovery and finance operations. The company has previously described this as a broader “distribution layer” across different agentic touchpoints, including merchant websites, independent agent platforms and large language model platforms, rather than a bet solely on ChatGPT. The startup, which has raised over $800 M from investors like Tiger Global, Y Combinator, Lightspeed, is gearing up for a public markets debut soon.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

The zardozi embroidery on a Dior dress, the T-strap leather sandals at a Prada show, the mirror-work technique used on a Fendi bag – for decades, the skill of Indian artisans has been an invisible force behind some of the world’s most coveted fashion.
Now, that work is beginning to claim its own place in the spotlight, and the Mumbai-based textile and embroidery atelier Chanakya International is at the forefront.
Chanakya marked its 40th anniversary this month, celebrating with three exhibitions that trace its journey from an embroidery powerhouse to a present-day craft and cultural institution. The person steering it is 49-year-old Karishma Swali, whose father set up the group’s operations in the 1980s.
“What we have as a country is unique,” she tells me of India’s rich textile and craft heritage. “It’s unparalleled in many ways, and it’s the only place where we continue to practise it.” During the Renaissance, she says, France and Italy had established and varied traditions. “But what we have in India today is [what] other parts of the world have lost.”
Chanakya has a network of 1,400 artisans, and says that some are 13th-generation craftspeople, skilled in hundreds of embroidery traditions and supplying almost every luxury label you can imagine. Among the techniques they have revived is the Mughal-era silver filigree lace, or chaand jaal, reintroduced in a lighter form that has since become a regular feature in couture collections.
In 2023, Dior held a show at Mumbai’s Gateway of India, showcasing its partnership with Chanakya, in a high-profile acknowledgment of Indian craftsmanship. The runway saw sari-inspired skirts, vibrant madras-checks sets and Nehru-collar jackets.
These collaborations are supported by expert craft knowledge passed down and refined over generations, and they need institutional support to survive. The Kalhath Institute, a craft-preservation centre in Lucknow, runs residencies that pair artists from across the world with local artisans.
Kalhath’s co-founder Mohammed Amine Dadda tells me that Indian craftsmanship’s defining quality is “intelligence of the hand” – a sensitive, slow and cumulative process underpinned by patience and dexterity. “Without this technical mastery, and the considerable time required to create the most demanding pieces, haute couture and contemporary luxury simply could not bring their most ambitious creative visions to life.”
This mastery is not limited to textiles. When it comes to jewellery, global luxury brands have long sought Jaipur-based the Gem Palace, established in 1852 by the Kasliwal family, who still run it today. Samarth Kasliwal, 33, says part of the appeal lies in the visual language of Indian artistry itself. “There is something about Indian artistry that is inspired by nature,” he tells me, pointing to the recurring use of floral patterns and animals across Indian art and design. These motifs are universal, and travel across the lines of culture and language.
One recent collaboration Kasliwal is particularly proud of is a collection for Dior featuring green onyx and rock crystals, with engravings of birds, animals and flowers. The combination, he says, is reminiscent of traditional Indian jewellery, while drawing on techniques that remain central to the atelier’s work today.
With increased visibility, the question of credit and appropriation has become harder to ignore. Last week, a Ralph Lauren gown from the designer’s spring 2027 collection attracted criticism after many Indians pointed out that the embroidery the brand described as “embellishments” looked a lot like Indian zardozi, but without any accompanying credit. (Ralph Lauren did not respond to my request for comment.)
Then, Fendi came under fire when people noticed that a baguette bag from its autumn/winter collection featured mirrorwork often seen in Gujarati crafts. In April, Fendi credited Chanakya artisans in a social media video showcasing the same embroidery. But the product description on its site failed to mention any Indian inspiration, and its final label read “Made in Italy”.
After I asked Fendi about the discrepancy, the brand cited its “creative partnership” with Chanakya of more than three decades, saying it “remains committed to supporting and recognizing India’s rich craft heritage”. The website descriptor now reads: “Made in Italy and India with Chanakya”.
A recent Financial Times report noted that under EU rules, garments embroidered in India can still end up with a European label – so long as the final construction and finishing take place in Europe.
Last year, Prada was accused of appropriating Indian culture with Kolhapuri-inspired sandals, a controversy that showed us these debates around recognition can sometimes produce a more structural response. “We acknowledge the sandals … are inspired by traditional Indian handcrafted footwear, with a centuries-old heritage,” Lorenzo Bertelli, the corporate social responsibility chief at the Italian fashion house, had written in a letter to the Maharashtra chamber of commerce at the time.
Prada subsequently partnered with state-backed organisations in Maharashtra and Karnataka to produce a limited-edition collection, Made in India, and committed to a three-year training programme for artisans specialising in the craft.
Might these collaborations, controversies and corrections represent a shift in India’s place in the fashion industry? Anthropologist Phyllida Jay, author of Inspired by India: How India Transformed Global Design, appears to think so, placing the debate in a longer arc. “The stories of the ateliers producing highly skilled Indian craft in the elevated realm of European luxury and high fashion is part of a broader paradigm shift,” she writes, “where over 70 years after the end of colonial rule, India is being looked at in a different way on the world stage.” It is, in a way, a reversal, moving from a colonial history of extraction toward one in which Indians themselves get a voice in how their craft is represented.
Swali is ensuring this visibility also lives on through the Chanakya School of Craft, which she set up in 2016. Its 18-month programme provides free embroidery training and a travel honorarium to dozens of women, some of whom have gone on to work at the main atelier. Others have set up their own independent studios.
I had a chance to visit the space – inside a high-rise in Lower Parel, where those as young as 18 learn intricate needlework alongside grandmothers in their 60s. “Craft in India has never been institutionalised,” Swali says of the ethos behind the initiative. “It’s intergenerational,” she says, adding that women have often been excluded.
India’s culture of craft has always been precious. Growing up, I loved having the choice to affordably create any type of clothing. At one point, I had a small army of tailors, each with a different specialisation, whom I’d go to for different needs. I’d buy ajrakh and mashru silks from Dastkar or Nalli, and hand it to the right Masterji to stitch, embroider and tweak to my size. So, to me, Indian craftsmanship is not just a part of luxury, but a luxury itself.

13,138
Foreign investors have pulled out Rs 13,138 crore (£1.02bn) from Indian equities in the first half of September, wiping out about half of the net inflows recorded in August.

The true measure of my love for my friends is in the number of memes I send them. One of the accounts I rely on is Bahaish Kapoor’s. The screenwriter-turned-meme evangelist pairs black-and-white Bollywood stills with contemporary gen Z sass, and lets incongruity do the rest. What makes an image meme-worthy? “I always look for people who are in a deep philosophical, romantic, dramatic action moment which I can repurpose to bring in a whole new meaning,” he tells me. “I try to mix and match and see what’s working.” His 340,000-plus followers include Sharon Stone and Hrithik Roshan.

£800m in, £800m out - Why Man City scandal shines light on Man Utd finances
- Published
The Premier League panel's report laid it out in black and white.
"The club's income was hugely overstated by over £830 million."
In other words, Manchester City's owners circumvented the league's financial regulations over a number of years by pumping money into the club that should not have been recorded as sponsorship income.
The damning judgement landed less than five days after Manchester United's extended filing to the New York Stock Exchange which detailed their end of year accounts to 30 June 2026.
Contained within it was an interest payment of £37m, an increase from £34m the previous year.
And respected football finance blogger Swiss Ramble now estimates that United's net interest payments since the leveraged Glazer takeover of the club in 2005 have risen to a total of £852m.
Without excusing City's owners in any way, it has not escaped the attentions of many fans from both Manchester clubs that while the arrival of one ownership group in the city resulted in money being ploughed in, it meant a similar significant sum being paid out in interest for the other.
Maintaining financial discipline
United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."
This came after a third-place finish in the Premier League, which confirmed a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence.
Record revenues of £677.6m, projected to go as high as £760m in 2026-27, is something to celebrate.
Yet Berrada's cautious stance underlined a few home truths.
In confirming they had spent £191.7m on new players; notably Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, and costs associated with them, plus academy players such as England youth international Tynan Thompson, since 30 June, with payments due 'in the next five years'. United also revealed they had borrowed an additional £90m. It took their overall debt to £1.15bn.
To put that into context, in accounts to June 2021, the comparable sum was £667m.
Prior to 30 June, United's transfer debt was £375m. Of that, £218m must be paid before 30 June 2027. United have also said in addition to Baleba, Santos and Tielemans, they are liable for another £122.8m in potential contract payments if players they have already signed hit pre-agreed targets – although presumably the club would be happy if they ended up paying this.
When they restructured their debt in June, United added $125m (£94.36m) to their main debt. On 23 September, they said £63.5m had been spent on land for their proposed new stadium, the precise funding model for which is still to be determined.
Many fans, particularly those who do not want a new stadium, feel that money would have been better invested in Michael Carrick's squad.
Yet, as Berrada said, United are taking a 'disciplined approach' on that.
In 2025, United had the fifth highest wage bill in the Premier League, at £313m. The absence of European football means that sum dropped to £302m in 2025-26. No other clubs have released their figures yet, but it would be a major surprise if United climbed any higher, meaning Carrick over-achieved by finishing third. United's wages to turnover ratio is 45%. No club had a better figure than that last season.
While there are variables and also notable exceptions, including the Old Trafford outfit themselves who over the past decade, have topped the annual salary cost table but not the actual Premier League, and in 2024-25 finished 15th despite those fifth highest wage costs, there is a general correlation between salaries and performance.
Yet, while United were relatively restrained on the transfer front in terms of spending this summer – their £148m outlay was below that of newly-promoted Ipswich and Hull among others – their recent net spend has been high. The reason for this is clear.
When the most recent transfer window closed on 1 September, they had generated £47m from sales. It put them 11th in the Premier League. Only Liverpool of their 'big six' rivals brought in less.
Since they sold striker Romelu Lukaku to Inter Milan for £74m in 2019, United have only generated more than £25m for a player on four occasions – for Mason Greenwood, Scott McTominay, Rasmus Hojlund and Alejandro Garnacho.
It was instructive this summer a series of young players were sold, either for a lower fee than anticipated in the cases of Radek Vitek and Toby Collyer, who joined Middlesbrough and West Brom respectively, or none, like defenders Tyler Fredricson and James Overy. In all cases though, the transfers included significant sell-on and buy-back clauses, which is part of a strategy by United to generate more revenue from player sales.
In June 2023, Premier League clubs voted to cap future leveraged buyouts at around 65% of a club's value. The move seemed to be in response to ALK Capital's takeover of Burnley in December 2020.
Many United fans feel the move was 18 years too late.
The negativity around Manchester City's scandal has indirectly, shone a light on the situation at Old Trafford.
Given there is little realistic chance of the substantive debt being paid off, Berrada and his colleagues must navigate the tricky balance of keeping costs under control, trimming the outstanding transfer fees, not extending the revolving credit limit and funding a new stadium – all while spending enough to deliver on the pitch.
In 2017-18, United made £80m in prize money from their run to the Champions League quarter-finals. In 2024-25, they got £31m for reaching the Europa League final. In their recently negotiated shirt deal with Adidas, a £10m annual reduction is applied if the club miss out on reaching the Champions League.
When Carrick sends his team out against bottom-club Tottenham at Old Trafford on 10 October, they will be attempting to drag themselves up from 12th place in the table.
The overall target is undefined, but it is pretty clear Champions League qualification will be a significant part of it.

Shares of Mamaearth parent Honasa Consumer jumped as much as 8.2% to ₹478.20 on the BSE in early trade, after the beauty and personal care (BPC) company issued a strong business update for Q2 FY27. At 10:03 IST, the stock was trading 6.9% higher at ₹472.35. The company’s market capitalisation stood at ₹15,368 Cr (about $1.6 Bn) In an exchange filing, Honasa said it expects net sales value (NSV) growth in the low thirties on a YoY basis for the quarter ended September 2026, supported by growth across its focus categories and brands. The company also expects a low double-digit operating margin, with strong YoY improvement, as it works towards expanding its EBITDA margin. Its flagship brand Mamaearth is expected to register NSV growth in the high teens during the quarter, supported by higher brand penetration and offline expansion. Meanwhile, newer brands are expected to post NSV growth in the mid-forties. This younger brand portfolio comprises The Derma Co, Aqualogica, BBlunt, Dr Sheth’s, Staze, Lumineve, and Reginald Men. Offline channels continued to lead Honasa’s growth, with both general trade and modern trade expected to post strong growth. The company attributed this to deeper direct distribution in general trade and better execution at retail outlets. Online channels are also expected to sustain their growth momentum. The growth estimates are on a like-for-like basis, with the Q2 FY26 base adjusted for a change in the Flipkart group’s settlement mechanism that affects revenue recognition for marketplace sellers. In the preceding quarter, Honasa’s consolidated net profit more than doubled to ₹90.5 Cr from ₹41.3 Cr in the year-ago period. Operating revenue rose 27% YoY to ₹755.9 Cr, while EBITDA more than doubled to ₹110 Cr from ₹46 Cr. In Q1 FY27, Honasa’s focus categories grew more than 35% YoY, while its younger brands grew over 40%. Both general trade and modern trade grew more than 40%, and its distribution network crossed 3 Lakh FMCG retail outlets. The latest update follows Honasa’s overhaul of its offline distribution under Project Neev, which began in late 2024 and stabilised during 2025. The exercise removed the super-stockist layer and strengthened direct servicing of retailers through distributors. Alongside the distribution reset, Honasa narrowed Mamaearth’s focus to five core categories — face wash, shampoo, sunscreen, moisturiser, and baby care — after its expansion into too many categories diluted focus and execution. The company has been pursuing diversification through younger brands, spanning skincare, haircare, colour cosmetics, and men’s grooming. Honasa also proposed acquiring a 58% stake in nutraceuticals startup Fluence Pharma for ₹135 Cr, but called off the transaction in August after certain closing conditions were not fulfilled. Despite this, it said it remained committed to entering nutraceuticals through organic and inorganic opportunities.

Romania reports 2 dead and 11 rescued after fire onboard a vessel in Black Sea
Romanian authorities report that two people have died and 11 crew members were rescued after a commercial vessel caught fire in the Black Sea
BUCHAREST, Romania -- Romanian authorities said on Monday that two people have died after a fire on a commercial vessel which later sank in the Black Sea. Eleven crew members were rescued.
Romania’s Coast Guard was alerted at around 11 a.m. local time, the Interior Ministry said. The vessel was in Romania ’s exclusive economic zone, about 30 nautical miles (55 kilometers) south of Sfantul Gheorghe in Tulcea County.

Are extended warranties on TVs and laptops ever really worth it?
Or are they just another useless upsell?
Have mercy on retail clerks. To keep their jobs, they're often asked to push promotions they know most customers don't want, such as memberships and credit cards. Upselling looks good on a manager's ledger, even if it irritates a good portion of their customers.
If you've been shopping for smart TVs, laptops or just about any major piece of electronics in the past decade, you've no doubt been pitched on the idea of an extended warranty, AppleCare+ and Best Buy Protection being a couple of familiar examples. At a glance, they're more reasonable than most in-store promotions. Everything breaks eventually, and the cost of some repairs can be eye-watering. Just ask anyone who's smashed the display on their MacBook.
Despite this, you can safely skip an extended warranty in most circumstances. They mostly exist for the sake of an upsell, which you can tell by the strings attached and the fundamental nature of consumer electronics. When an extended plan is justified, you'll likely know before you walk in the door.
Why extended warranties are usually a waste of money
For starters, extended warranties are typically focused around defects, and any TV, laptop or similarly expensive device is likely to be covered by the manufacturer for 90 days to a year or more. This matters because if a product is defective, it's going to fail under relatively normal strain, by definition. You're liable to find out quickly if it's faulty, though there are obviously outliers.
Another point is that while planned obsolescence is real, a product that survives the first year is likely to survive past the two- or three-year window that's common for many extended warranties. In an accelerated longevity test by RTINGS, 102 TVs were run nonstop between November 2022 and September 2025. Only two actually failed before they reached 3,000 hours, and most made it to at least 8,000. This longevity test employed TVs that had already been used for hundreds of hours, so the results didn't show an initial spike for models that failed right away — a spike that would be present if the TVs were all brand-new. But again, those failures often are covered by the manufacturer and wouldn't require an extended warranty. If you watched TV for four hours a day, every day, it would take you over two years to reach that 3,000-hour mark, by which point just 2 percent of the TVs had failed.
Unbiased reliability figures are harder to come by for laptops, but it almost doesn't matter for a couple of reasons. The first is that planned obsolescence factor. Within two or three years, just about any device you buy — especially a laptop — is going to be supplanted by something with improved performance for a similar price. Meanwhile, equivalent products are going to become cheaper and cheaper, especially if you're willing to buy a used or refurbished model.
That factors into the second point, which is the cost of an extended warranty vs. just saving up for a replacement or repair. To cover a $1,300 TV, for example, Best Buy charges approximately $160 for two years of Geek Squad TV Protection, and $280 for five years. While the cost of replacing the display panel could vastly exceed either sum, the retailer estimates that other repairs will typically fall between $255 and $395. You could spend most or all of the cost of a repair on a warranty you may never use, and you'll still be stuck with old hardware if you successfully pursue a claim.
Some warranties include loopholes, on that note. We can't make blanket statements, but it's important to watch out for clauses that prevent you from seeking repairs if there are signs of liquid exposure or anything else that could be branded user error, regardless of whether it's the source of your problems. In other situations, you may be forced to use a manufacturer's warranty first if it's still in effect, Geek Squad Protection being a prime example.
When does an extended warranty actually make sense?
Though TVs are rarely mission-critical, there are professionals who simply can't afford any downtime with a laptop or other productivity tools, and put the equipment they own through the wringer. The cost of an extended warranty is nothing by comparison, though if you're in this camp, it's essential that you pick a plan that allows for loaner units or rapid repairs or replacements. In fact, you may be looking at special business-oriented warranties that aren't pitched over the checkout counter.
If you hate the idea of downtime but you're not necessarily a professional, it can make sense to invest in a plan like AppleCare+. That incorporates theft and loss replacements for some devices and vastly reduced prices for fixing accidental damage, including liquids. Considering that many cities have an Apple Store or at least an authorized service site, same-day repairs and replacements are a real possibility.
Unfortunately, most vendors don't have such an extensive support network. If you need a repair, there's a strong chance your device is going to be shipped to a depot in another city, then back a few days later. And they may ship it back unrepaired if they can't replicate the issue you reported — something we've experienced directly. Every warranty is a gamble, in that respect.

Donald Trump said that his super PAC MAGA Inc. would now pay for advertisements that the White House has run at taxpayer expense and stirred an outcry among Democrats and some Republicans.
Trump posted on Truth Social on Monday: “The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money. This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”
The White House has deemed the spots to be public service announcements, comparing them to government-funded ads that promoted vaccines under President Joe Biden and the Affordable Care Act under President Barack Obama.
Watch on Deadline
But the Trump spots feature himself and promote his presidency. One of the ads is almost identical to a spot that Trump posted on social media to promote his 2024 presidential campaign. More than $10 million has been spent on the series of ads, per CNN, citing estimates from analysis firm AdImpact.
Airing during football games and news programming, among other dayparts, the ads prominently featured the line, “Paid for by the U.S. government.” The group Public Citizen filed an FCC complaint, arguing that broadcasters could be held liable for an illegal use of government funds. But FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said last week that he didn’t see anything “out of the ordinary” in the airing of the spots, calling them a “normal PSA.”
“U.S.A money” he calls it.

Think about what you’re wearing right now. Did you pick it out? Or was it chosen for you by an algorithm you haven’t even considered?
Can thrift shops save us from Shein?
Ultra-fast fashion is everywhere. Thrift shops offer a way out.
You may think it’s the former, but with the state of the fashion industry, it’s likely the latter. There was a time when taste was decided by designers at luxury fashion houses, à la Karl Lagerfeld at Chanel, or Anna Wintour-type magazine editors (think of the famous cerulean sweater monologue from The Devil Wears Prada). Now, in the era of fast fashion, our clothing options are often dictated by computers.
Amy Odell writes the Back Row newsletter and hosts a podcast with the same name. She told Vox that what’s known as fast fashion has been kicked into hyperdrive by companies like Shein.
“I’ve also heard it called instant fashion,” she says. “The way it works is that they use algorithms to track trends and what people are interested in, and then they make a few hundred of a very large number of different items and they test demand.” She says this model has allowed companies like Shein to introduce around 4,700 new apparel styles per day. (For comparison, fast fashion brand Zara produces around 20,000 a year.)
Some are trying to claw back their personal style by hitting the thrift store instead. Traditionally, it’s where people go to find less expensive clothes. But fashion journalist Hannah Marriott says it can be so much more than that.
“For the last probably a hundred years, [the thrift store] has had lots of moments where it’s been cool within countercultures,” Marriott told Vox. “Whether it’s grunge, or the surrealists in the 1920s, or the Rolling Stones in the 1960s, secondhand clothing was cool because of the stigma.”
So how did thrifting go from stigmatized to chic? And are thrift stores still thrifty now that they’re more mainstream, especially in an era of ultra-cheap Shein clothing? We find out that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Marriott, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
There’s sometimes this stigma that’s attached to buying secondhand clothes. How has its perception changed over time?
Secondhand clothing used to be something that there was a real sense that if you couldn’t buy new, you would buy secondhand. At the same time, it has had lots of moments where it’s been cool within countercultures.
People within countercultures — whether it’s grunge, or the surrealists in the 1920s, or the Rolling Stones in the 1960s — secondhand clothing was cool because of the stigma. It’s also been a really important resource for people on lower incomes for a long time.
I think it was a gradual shift by various things that happened in the pandemic, including this absolute influx of apps [like The RealReal and Depop] that got very, very popular during that time, particularly among younger Gen Z consumers.
Thrifting became a social currency on social media platforms, especially on TikTok. It’s a vast ecosystem at the moment, and all of them have slightly different business models, slightly different fees that they charge, and slightly different audiences that they’re reaching. The stigma has really gone away, and it’s almost reversed.
What does that ecosystem look like?
There are different layers to it. There are consignment places like The RealReal where they take quite a big cut, but they will promote your items for you. I think those sites tend to work best if you’ve actually got designer clothes that have quite a big margin, particularly handbags.
Then there are other sites that are a bit more laid-back: eBay maybe skews a bit older, Depop skews a bit younger and trendier. There’s Vinted, which I know from the UK, but is making inroads into the US now. There’s ThreadUp as well. Poshmark.
It’s an absolutely vast ecosystem at the moment, and all of them have slightly different business models, slightly different fees that they charge, and slightly different audiences that they’re reaching.
One of the biggest secondhand shops here in the US is still Goodwill. Can you walk me through how Goodwill has adapted and changed to the secondhand boom?
Neighborhood thrift stores of that kind are the sort of stores that people on lower incomes do rely on more. It’s less trend-led than something like Depop. And it is somewhere that people have often been going for decades to get clothes that they can afford.
Goodwill undeniably has put its prices up. Inflation is such an issue for everyone, so I’m sure that there would be an element of prices going up anyway, but a lot of shoppers feel strongly that they’ve gone up a lot — that you can’t find bargains anymore, that the bargains get sent online to either their website or are bought by resellers who sell them for an inflated price online.
It’s hard to get to the bottom of exactly how true all of that is, especially because Goodwill is run as 150 autonomous [nonprofits], and each of them set their own prices. But what I would say is you are seeing things like the Goodwill branch in Connecticut charging $75 bucks to go on a thrift tour coach to get early access to a Goodwill store, and then you get to go to another store. You used to be able to buy 10 things in Goodwill for $75.
It’s so interesting that thrifting used to be this edgy original thing, but it’s really gone mainstream. Has it sold out?
I remember when I was much younger, people would say, “Ooh, you got that secondhand.” I just don’t think anyone would ever say that now because that’s kind of how we shop.
But I still think it is great if you find something original that you love that no one else has, and I still think you’re more likely to find it secondhand or in certain other under-the-radar brands that aren’t fast fashion.
I think maybe this is a reaction to 30 years of fast fashion just getting faster and faster and faster. I think we’re all feeling a bit tired of that business model, so we’re trying to find other ways to shop and express ourselves.

A 1-kg mass of hair was removed from the stomach and small intestine of a nine-year-old girl in a rare surgery at a private hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam, authorities said on Saturday.
The girl, who was diagnosed with Rapunzel syndrome, underwent the surgery at NIMS Medicity in nearby Neyyattinkara, they said.
She was admitted to the hospital with persistent abdominal pain and vomiting, according to a statement issued by the hospital. Ultrasound and CT scans revealed severe intestinal obstruction, and a subsequent endoscopy confirmed a large mass of hair accumulated in the stomach and small intestine.
The hairball was completely removed through a complex surgical procedure led by Dr Biju I G Nair, senior consultant in the Department of Paediatric Surgery at the hospital. The girl recovered well, resumed eating normally and was discharged, the doctor said.
Dr Nair said a trichobezoar, or hairball, forms when a person repeatedly pulls out and swallows hair. The swallowed hair cannot be digested and can gradually accumulate in the stomach, forming a hard mass that may cause intestinal obstruction over time, he said.
Rare condition
Rapunzel syndrome is an extremely rare condition in which a trichobezoar extends from the stomach into the small intestine. It is usually seen in adolescent girls, according to medical literature. Hospital authorities said fewer than 100 cases have been reported worldwide.

This story originally appeared on Vox and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
On a bright, sunny day last May, I stood on a boat surrounded by the turquoise waters of the island nation of Palau. I was there in the western Pacific watching scuba divers as they prepared to bring up evidence of a mysterious aquatic world.
Palau is famous for its spectacular and rich coral reefs. But these divers were planning to descend past those sun-lit marine communities and down into a lesser-known twilight zone known as the “mesophotic coral ecosystem.”
Mesophotic essentially means “middle” and “light,” which is where these ecosystems are—not quite in the bright daylight, not quite in the profound darkness, but somewhere in between. For simplicity’s sake, we’ll call these communities, which range from some 30 meters to 150 meters below the surface, the “deep reefs.”
One of the divers on the boat with me was a zoologist and curator at the California Academy of Sciences named Luiz Rocha, who has spent decades studying these deep reefs and their secrets.
“Anything between 30 meters and 150 meters is really, really unknown,” he told me.
Because these deep reefs are so unknown, researchers like Rocha are left with big questions. They want to get a baseline picture of what is going on in these ecosystems—even just who lives there!—so that they can better understand how they function. They’ve also tried to work out whether (or not) these deep reefs might provide a refuge for species living in shallower coral reefs.
I was in Palau for Vox’s Unexplainable podcast because, in an effort to gather more information about these mysterious places, Rocha left some scientific structures down in these twilight depths back in 2016. Those structures then spent almost a decade becoming encrusted with all kinds of marine life. And now, Rocha was back to retrieve them, hoping that he—along with many other scientists — would be able to open them up, like a box of scientific puzzle pieces, full of clues about this under-understood marine world.
One thing that’s often acknowledged in papers about mesophotic coral ecosystems is that scientists don’t know as much as they’d like to. A National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration article about them from 2019 is full of “mays,” as in: They may “serve as essential fish habitat for economically and ecologically important species.
Researchers do know some things, of course. They know that these deep reefs can be found in many of the same regions as shallower coral reefs—so mainly the tropical and subtropical parts of the world, like Micronesia, the Caribbean, and even the Gulf of Mexico. They’ve found that there are many species that seem to be unique to these places, and recent research points to their potential susceptibility to climate change.
Researchers have also gotten a sense of some of the key differences between these deep reefs and their shallower coral neighbors. In shallow reefs, hard corals team up with photosynthesizing algae. The algae provide the corals with nutrients, and the corals secrete a calcium-carbonate matrix that helps create the architecture of the reef.
As you go deeper, though, the light begins to fade, and the opportunities for photosynthesis start to fade with it. The temperature also drops. So the animals living down in the deep reefs are ones that can survive in a dimmer, cooler world.
Scientists can dive into the deep reefs to try to learn more about these understudied places—as Rocha has—but exploring down at 100 meters requires more difficult, riskier technical diving than exploring at shallower depths. The deeper you dive, for example, the faster gases get pushed into your tissues, which imposes limits on these really deep dives.
“We have a very, very short time,” Rocha says, “And by short time, I mean five minutes. Six, seven minutes.”
Scientists can take some pictures in that time, make some measurements, or collect a few samples, but then they have to move back upwards—a process that can take hours, since they must rise slowly to avoid decompression sickness.
It is, obviously, not particularly efficient to study an ecosystem in five- to seven-minute intervals. People have also used remote-operated vehicles and submersibles to explore the deep reefs, but those have their own issues, and cameras can’t always capture all the detail you might want, or photograph more secretive, cryptic animals. So huge gaps remain in scientific knowledge about these ecosystems.
“Whenever we go somewhere,” Rocha says, “the first thing we find is new species. It’s the most basic thing in science you can do.” But this effort goes beyond just cataloging new species of fish, sponges, or sea slugs.
Rocha wants to answer fundamental questions like: What is the main energy source for everything down here in the dim light? What does the food chain look like? How have things evolved to live at these depths? How similar are they to the shallow ecosystems, and how different? How are they affected by climate change—and what’s the most efficient way to protect them?
But Rocha says that “in some ways, we don’t even know what questions to ask. We really only know what the crucial questions are when we have a baseline understanding of the ecosystem. And for deep reefs, we don’t have that yet.”
Rocha is not deterred by the enormous number of question marks that surround these deep reefs. For years now, he has been gathering bits of basic information about them, often via those very short dives.
About a decade ago, though, Rocha got interested in another method for sampling the biodiversity of this sort of marine ecosystem—a technique involving “autonomous reef monitoring structures” or ARMS.
Basically, each ARMS is a stack of several PVC plates, separated at uniform intervals and attached to a base plate. They look like little gray, featureless hotels. You take them to a place that you want to study, bring them down, secure them, and then leave them alone for a while to let them collect … life.
“As soon as you drop any kind of clean structure on a reef,” Rocha says, “it starts getting colonized by larvae of everything around it—of sponges, gorgonians, corals. And then, because there’s a lot of hiding spots between the plates—so between the floors of the hotel—they start getting colonized by shrimp, by mollusks, by ascidians, by anything you can imagine in the ocean. And it becomes this stable, diverse mini reef, if you will, packed with a lot of biodiversity that would be very hard to collect all at once in any given reef.”
A few years after that initial drop, you come back, collect the ARMS, and then study the mini reef that has grown on them. You can sample and touch and analyze things to your heart’s content.
It’s not only a very effective way to collect lots of creatures, all at once, but also a great way to do so in a standardized way. If you went down—or sent a robot down—to collect an encrusted rock from a reef, you could learn a lot about the life on it, but it would be hard to compare the life on that rock to life on other rocks from other reefs, or even the same reef, because each rock would have its own unique characteristics. Not so for ARMS.
“ Every one’s the same,” Chris Meyer, director of the Smithsonian Global ARMS program, told me. “It’s prefab housing, and then you just look to see who moves in.”
To Rocha, this seemed like a great way to get a really good, long look at the deep reefs instead of the brief glimpses he was getting from diving. It was also, he told me, fairly cheap to deploy them. So from 2016 to 2018, with some private funding, he and his colleagues left ARMS in some of the deep reefs around Palau—as well as in Guam, the Marshall Islands, and French Polynesia. They installed some around 50 meters, and some around 100, and then some around 10 meters, so he could compare the deep reefs to their shallower neighbors.
After that, he waited.
In fact, he waited a little longer than he would have liked, because the retrieval of ARMS is more expensive than deploying them, so he had to work out more funding.
Eventually, private funders agreed to underwrite the retrieval of the ARMS that Rocha had left. Which is how he and his fellow divers finally found themselves on a boat in Palau again, ready to pull up these structures from the deep.
Over the course of a few days, I watched a whole team of people pull several ARMS out of the deep reefs of Palau. Some of the ARMS were relatively sparse, but others were almost fuzzy with organisms—vibrant with red and orange and green and pink and white. One had a massive sponge attached to it; another had several delicate fronds dangling from it like coralline ferns. The ARMS collected each day traveled to the Palau International Coral Reef Center in bins full of seawater, where the scientists quickly got to work—seeing and touching (and smelling) this mysterious ecosystem right up close.
The process was, as it turned out, equal parts magical excitement and well-oiled, Cheez-It–fueled disassembly line. After the plates were taken apart, Meyer took photographs of the plates—what he called a “time capsule of the place.” Others in the lab picked carefully through trays of debris, hunting for tiny crabs and worms and mollusks, or scraped samples off the plates and deposited them in tubes.
They collected sea squirts, said to be our closest invertebrate relatives. They collected sponges—flat ones that felt dry underwater, thick ones with bristles like tiny, unmoving caterpillars, one as thin as a flake of skin and shot through with silver filaments. They collected strange, soft corals known as octocorals, and they collected colonies of animals called bryozoans, which created what looked like swirling, two-dimensional honeycombs.
“We’re looking for every unique thing, which we call a morphospecies,” a Smithsonian research biologist named Sarah Tweedt explained. “And we’re trying to get some representative tissue samples from all of these things so that we can sequence the DNA—and match the DNA to the organism.”
That is, of course, assuming there is already a known genetic match in our existing DNA libraries.
On the first day that I spent with the team, a Cal Academy curator named Terry Goslinger identified several potential new species. He is an expert on colorful, delightful sea slugs known as nudibranchs, and so, because of his deep knowledge (and because nudibranchs’ bright hues and patterns make them somewhat easier to tell apart than some other underwater creatures), he was able to make some on-the-spot calls about whether or not certain species were likely to be new to science, pending genetic testing to confirm.
Many of the animals were trickier to pin down, though. The researchers did their best to identify the creatures they were finding, but even now, several months out, there’s still a lot of work to be done. Of the close to 3,000 specimens, only a small fraction were identified at a species level. The numbers are a little bit inexact because researchers are still processing the data, but when I checked in with a Cal Academy postdoc working on the project, Susanne Bähr, in July, she told me that only 3 percent of samples had been ID’d by species, and a little less than 20 had a genus designation. Many, many more were only identified at higher, broader taxonomic levels. Genetic testing of the samples, paired with photographs and descriptions of the samples, will help people work out more specific species, and also help them identify whether certain species are new to science.
The most important parts of this work will involve more than just identifying species. In fact, the more time I spent with these researchers in the lab (including one evening spent with them as they worked past midnight), the more I got the sense that, while they seemed excited about seeing new species, they seemed equally excited to witness relationships between animals.
When I walked into the lab one day, for example, several people urged me to go over and look through a microscope at a creature known as a pompom crab—a tiny yellow crustacean holding purple anemones in its modified front claws. Tweedt was extremely jazzed when she found something referred to as a “skeleton shrimp,” which looked to me like the marine equivalent of a stick insect, blending in on something called a hydroid. She pulled me aside another time, around 1 in the morning, to show me “the frosting on the cake” of the day, which turned out to be some bright red sea snails and the bright red octocorals they seemed to live on
As she put it in a later conversation, these relationships are, in many ways, the key takeaway from this ARMS project, and what distinguishes it from efforts to bring up a few individual samples at a time. Studying them, or even just looking at the fuller picture ARMS provide, is what will let researchers tackle some of the outstanding questions about these ecosystems. Bähr, for example, is already working with the data from ARMS retrieved in Guam, trying to analyze how much overlap (or lack thereof) there is between species at different depths in the deep reefs.
Really, though, this is all just the beginning. In one of our conversations, Rocha compared the work they are doing now to ecology work done in the mid-20th century to understand how species’ vertical distribution changes as you go up a mountain. This drove home for me how far behind researchers working on the mesophotic deep reefs are compared to their colleagues working on, say, shallower coral reefs. I asked him what kept him working on such a difficult puzzle.
“It’s the reward at the end of it,” he said. “If it’s a hard puzzle, at the end of it, the reward is always bigger.”
“But in our lifetimes, will we assemble the deep reef puzzle?” I asked.
“No, we will not assemble the puzzle, no,” Rocha said, “but we’ll generate some good pieces for the next generation to assemble.”

Anthropic vs. the pope
Claude’s creators are worried the LLM could be conscious. The Catholic Church disagrees.
Hi readers, happy Friday! It’s been a big week for the AI debate — not the one about whether it will cause the robot apocalypse, though there’s still plenty to worry about there, but instead about whether the technology is conscious.
The folks at Anthropic, the AI company behind the large language model Claude, certainly seem to think it is — or at least, they’re extremely open to the possibility.
As the New York Times reported earlier in the week, the company has spent the last year grappling with the question by speaking with religious thinkers from many faith traditions in an effort to chart a moral course for the LLM (that is, to keep it from killing us all, so maybe it is all one big debate).
In the process, the Times reports, some of those thinkers observed that members of the Anthropic team were “relating to [Claude] like a conscious being” and even, according to it, a degree of “moral status.”
On the flip side of this debate is Pope Leo XIV, who decidedly does not seem to buy into AI consciousness arguments. His “Magnifica Humanitas” encyclical earlier this year argued that AI will never be able to replace humanity — and reportedly “alarmed” Anthropic’s co-founder, Christopher Olah.
Since then, Pope Leo has continued to emphasize the differences between humans and machines this week. “There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others,” he posted on Friday. “Algorithms lack the spark of humanity.”
Loneliness machines
Conscious or no (and that’s a no from me), it’s hard to argue that tech companies don’t want you to interact with their models like people. That includes OpenAI and Meta, both of whom introduced “cute” new AI agents — called Dots and Muse, respectively — last month.
As my colleague Adam Clark Estes reported this week, though, the promise of a companionable, always-there AI might not be the best idea in the world — especially for children. A new study, still under review, suggests that AI use may be causing loneliness in middle schoolers.
Adam spoke with the lead researcher on the study, UNC Chapel Hill professor Anne Maheux, who explained that “middle school students using AI for emotional intimacy and companionship developed greater loneliness over time.”
According to Maheux, one big point where AI chatbots fail compared to human beings is “friction,” or the complicated push-and-pull dynamic of any connection with a real human being. By contrast, chatbots are “sycophantic, highly agreeable, anthropomorphized,” she says, which can lead to kids “developing expectations or understandings of interactive relationships that are actually fundamentally at odds with a normal human relationship.”
People, in other words, still matter, no matter how much the AI companies want us to build our lives around machines instead.

England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender
- Published
Harry Kane will write another chapter in his illustrious England history by equalling Peter Shilton's record tally of 125 caps if he plays a part in the Uefa Nations League meeting with the Czech Republic at Wembley.
England's captain is already his country's record scorer with 89 goals in 124 appearances in a full international career he started by opening his account 79 seconds into his debut.
Since that 4-0 win against Lithuania at Wembley in March 2015, he has been England's mainstay. He is still irreplaceable at 33 and their top scorer in major tournaments with 21 goals in 36 appearances across six of those showpieces, ahead of Gary Lineker's 10 goals in 18 appearances.
He is in the process of building a monument to his goalscoring brilliance at elite level as he currently stands 36 goals ahead of England's second-highest scorer Wayne Rooney, who boasts a record of 53 goals in 120 games.
Kane is unquestionably England men's most important and influential player of the modern era. The only blemish on his magnificent career is the failure – not his alone it must be stressed – to add to the one men's World Cup won in 1966.
Irrespective of that space for silverware on his CV, how highly does Kane rank in the pantheon of greats who have represented the England men's team? Could he even be the greatest? He has made himself a serious contender.
- The great number nine decline - where have England's strikers gone? 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Can Kane buck history and win Ballon d'Or? 
  - Published7 September
Moore? Charlton? Rooney? - where does Kane rank?
This argument will instantly cut away from Kane to Bobby Moore, the elegant, unflappable defender who remains the only England captain to lift the World Cup, leading his team to triumph at Wembley in July 1966 as West Germany were beaten 4-2.
Moore was only 25 at the time, and had enjoyed success at club level with West Ham United, winning the FA Cup and European Cup Winners' Cup before the World Cup. He won 108 caps between May 1962 and November 1973.
And then, of course, the conversation must turn to Sir Bobby Charlton, who survived the Munich Air Disaster with Manchester United in 1958 to become arguably England's most famous footballer of his era.
Charlton was a global beacon of dignity and world-class ability, winning the World Cup then, two years later, captaining Manchester United when they became the first English team to win the European Cup, scoring twice as Benfica were beaten 4-1 at Wembley.
He remains third on England's list of scorers, with 49 goals in 106 games.
Sir Geoff Hurst will always claim a special place with his hat-trick in the World Cup final win, while many others will have their supporters from recent times, including the likes of Wayne Rooney and David Beckham.
Former England midfielder Danny Murphy, said: "Bobby Moore will always be in people's conversation. Sir Bobby Charlton also, because of what they did and the memories they created.
"As you move forward, for me as a kid Gazza [Paul Gascoigne] burst on the scene and became a hero, especially as a creative midfield player myself.
"I think Rooney was arguably the most all-round footballer we have ever had, the most talented I've seen – but no-one can argue with Harry Kane's quality, numbers and longevity. It is the record of an England great."
He added: "There is one thing there is no debate about. Harry Kane is England's greatest goalscorer.
"No-one can take that away from him. The numbers over such a period of longevity are incredible. This, in itself, deserves all the accolades in the world. To stay at that level and not have anybody displace him is testimony to his ability and professionalism.
"He's a born goalscorer. He's a super professional. He's technically brilliant. He's been an absolute credit to himself and his family in the way he's conducted himself and the longevity he's had in his career.
"Is he England's greatest player? This is all about opinions and eras, but his record and longevity alone informs you that he is an England great. He is in that elite group."
'We are guilty of underestimating what is in front of us'
Kane's status as an England great is beyond question. Where he stands in that list of greats will be shaped by eras and opinions, according to former internationals Paul Robinson and Murphy.
Robinson told BBC Sport that the scale of Kane's greatness may only be fully appreciated in years to come.
He said: "Harry Kane is an England great. There is no argument. He will always be part of that conversation now.
"I think we are guilty in the modern era of underestimating what we've got in front of us. We are quite happy to look through rose-tinted spectacles at what we had in the past.
"We will talk about Bobby Moore and Sir Bobby Charlton, but football now is a completely different game. The life of a footballer is completely different and it's almost like they are playing a different game.
"What Bobby Moore and Sir Bobby Charlton achieved, nobody in an England shirt has done since. You respect what they did in the era, and the status and legacy that comes with winning the World Cup and everything else they did, but we must also say it is a different game now."
Kane's double in Saturday's 7-0 win in Croatia took his tally to 11 goals in 12 games for England in this calendar year. He has also scored in six consecutive England away games, with only Sir Tom Finney having a longer run, seven between September 1946 and May 1948.
Last season alone, Ballon d'Or contender Kane scored a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for England and his club Bayern Munich.
He has scored five hat-tricks in an England career which includes 110 starts, with a 66% win rate.
"The biggest compliment you can pay Harry Kane is to ask yourself how long we've been pondering the question 'what will England do if Harry Kane gets injured?'," Robinson added.
"There is no-one close to his class in that position. It is taken as read the captain is playing and without the captain, we would be in trouble.
"I think we'll appreciate him even more in another 10,15, 20 years when you look back and see what he has achieved. People will point to the lack of silverware with England, but he can't play everywhere can he?
"We look back with nostalgia and fondness, saying we've had this great and that great – and England have – but make no mistake Kane is right in that debate and will be for years to come."
'The big moments haven't yet happened for him'
Kane's lack of a major international trophy will undoubtedly be the argument used to counter suggestions he is England's greatest.
He has come close, only to lose two World Cup semi-finals and two European Championship finals.
The next Euros in the United Kingdom and Ireland in 2028 could be his last chance to change that unwanted record.
Murphy, said: "The only thing really missing from him is the icing on the cake, namely getting over the line in a major tournament, which is looking less likely for him as the years go by.
"I suppose that will always be one criticism of him, as well as many England players and generations. Nobody has managed to get them over the line since 1966, and the responsibility usually does fall on the strikers or the captain.
"He didn't score in the World Cup semi-final against Croatia 2018 or in the Euros final against Italy at Wembley. He missed a penalty against France in the World Cup quarter-final in 2022, then obviously he didn't score in the Euro 2024 final against Spain or the World Cup semi-final against Argentina.
"People will look at that and say in the big moments, it didn't happen for him.
"I don't adhere to that observation at all because it's not just him and he did so much to get England in those positions. Anyone can miss a penalty. The reality is the team itself, the tactics, all those things factor into why England haven't got over the line."
As Kane stands on the brink of equalling the England caps record, he still has time – and the enduring quality - to state his case as an all-time great even more forcefully in the future.

The Supreme Court on Monday (September 28, 2026) questioned the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) over its proposed deadline – of nearly two years — for implementing front-of-pack warning labels (FoPL) on packaged foods, asking why it wanted to “waste so much time” on fresh public and industry consultations when the issue concerned citizens’ health.
The court’s remarks came as it pressed the food safety regulator to expedite the introduction of warning labels on packaged foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fat.
Responding to the court’s September 10 order, which raised several questions over the size, colour, and placement of the proposed labels as well as the timeline for their implementation, the FSSAI said in an affidavit filed last week that the draft regulations would require a four-month process of consultation and finalisation. It proposed notifying the labelling norms by July 1 next year, following which food business operators would be given another 365 days to transition to the new regime to ensure minimal hardship.
“Why voluntary compliance for a year? Why do you need so much time? Why do you want to start afresh with the exercise of hearing and calling for objections? You started in 2022. What did you do in the last four years?” a Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran asked while reserving its order in the matter.
PIL petition
The top court was hearing a public interest litigation (PIL) petition filed by non-profit organisation 3S and Our Health Society, seeking the introduction of FoPL guidelines on the lines of those in force in foreign jurisdictions. The petitioner, represented by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dwivedi, has argued that such labels are necessary to warn children and other consumers about packaged foods containing high levels of salt, sugar and saturated fat, and their potential adverse health effects.
Additional Solicitor-General Brijender Chahar, appearing for the Centre and the FSSAI, explained that the exercise initiated in 2022 concerned the Indian Nutrition Rating (star-rating) system and was based on a different yardstick from the warning-label regime now under consideration.
“Today, the yardstick is completely different. We have set four months for drafting the regulations. The rest we leave it to my Lords — how much time should be given for compliance,” Mr. Chahar submitted.
Public health goal
Justice Pardiwala appreciated the steps taken by the regulator so far, but said much more remained to be done to give meaningful effect to the court’s objective of protecting public health. The Bench also indicated that it would seek to strike a “balance” while fixing a reasonable timeline to roll out the warning labels.
“We appreciate whatever you have done so far, and we appreciate your initiative, but there is a lot which is required to be done to give meaningful effect to what we want to achieve… We are undertaking this entire exercise for the good of the nation, for the good of the citizens, so we expect the authority to accept our order in its true spirit,” the Bench said.
The Bench further made it clear that its forthcoming directions would be binding on the regulator and said it expected the FSSAI to implement them “scrupulously” and in their “true spirit”. The court also indicated that it would keep the matter pending to monitor compliance with its directions.
“We will now pronounce the final order. We will again keep it for some time to ensure due compliance with each and every direction. Do not disappoint us on the day when the matter comes up for reporting compliance,” the Bench told the regulator.
Single-phase proposal
In its affidavit filed earlier, the FSSAI had told the top court that it was prepared to roll out FoPL for packaged foods in a single phase, departing from its earlier proposal for a two-stage implementation based on the number of “nutrients of concern” present in a product.
“The FSSAI proposes to adopt a single-phase approach for the implementation of Front-of-Pack Nutrition Labelling. To finalise the draft regulations, it requires a four-month period, and there shall be a ‘voluntary implementation period of 365 days’ by Food Business Operators (FBOs),” the affidavit had stated.
On the design of the warning label, the regulator modified its earlier proposal for a red hexagon and suggested placing the hexagon against a white, square-shaped background, drawing from the labelling format followed in Canada.
The FSSAI also clarified that the warning requirement would not be confined to products containing high levels of two or more nutrients of concern. Packaged foods exceeding the prescribed threshold for even one such nutrient would carry the warning.
Under the proposed framework, the warning label would be prominently placed on the top-left corner of the front of the package for greater visibility. The warning would also appear in a font larger than that used for the nutritional information displayed on the back of the pack.
Note of caution
Earlier, the top court had also flagged a possible unintended consequence of the proposed regime. It had noted that requiring manufacturers to reduce salt, sugar and fat — ingredients that add to taste, texture, and shelf life — could prompt greater reliance on artificial preservatives, emulsifiers and other additives.
The Bench had therefore asked the FSSAI to examine this possibility and consider corresponding regulatory safeguards to ensure that reducing one set of potentially harmful ingredients does not result in their substitution with other additives that could pose health concerns.
For determining the products that would require such warnings, the FSSAI has proposed adopting threshold values for added sugar, added fat used in cooking, and salt per 100 g/ml, as prescribed in the Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, issued by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN).
