'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria
- Published
Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak.
The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners.
Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital.
The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests, including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers.
Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation.
"I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts.
When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin.
The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window.
"One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door. That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says.
Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites.
The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity.
Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday.
The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding.
As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive.
He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe.
"People were calling for help, some were already very weak."
But no-one came to help, he and others allege.
"While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency.
"We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door.
"We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died."
Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies.
The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye.
"The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC.
As the organisation involved is a federal body rather than a force under his jurisdiction, such as the police, the governor is unable to exert direct influence but he welcomes the investigation that has been ordered by the government in capital, Abuja.
A 10-member committee has now been set-up to determine exactly what happened.
It has two weeks to establish the causes of the deaths and identify who was responsible and can recommend legal action against anyone found culpable.
No officer, regardless of rank, would be protected and any attempt to obstruct the investigation would be taken seriously, Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said.
As he leaves the cell after talking to the BBC, Muhammad says he hopes that by speaking out he can help find justice and bring some closure to this traumatic event.

Pakistan-made cosmetics that continued to find their way to Hyderabad more than a year after India shut the door on imports from the neighbouring country have now led investigators to Mumbai’s Crawford Market, pointing to a wider supply chain behind the banned products.
The development comes amid a separate public-health concern over some of the skin-whitening products. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) last month specifically warned consumers against two Pakistan-made creams after tests found excessive levels of heavy metals.
Both ‘Goree Beauty Cream’ and ‘Chandni Whitening Cream’, named in the September 8 CDSCO alert, were among the products found during raids on three shops in Hyderabad this week.
An officer involved in the investigation said the cosmetics seized in Hyderabad were allegedly being sourced from Crawford Market in Mumbai. “Investigators are now looking further up the chain to establish how the products entered India and reached wholesale and retail markets despite restrictions on their import.
Imports from Pakistan prohibited since May 2025
India prohibited the direct or indirect import or transit of all goods originating in or exported from Pakistan on May 2, 2025. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade imposed the restriction through a notification, citing national security and public policy.
The prohibition extends to goods entering India indirectly, meaning routing Pakistan-origin products through another country does not by itself make their import permissible.
Cosmetics imported into India are additionally governed by the Cosmetics Rules, 2020. Products must be registered with the Central Licensing Authority before import and are required to comply with prescribed quality and safety standards.
The CDSCO had stepped up scrutiny even before the latest Hyderabad seizure. In July, it directed its zonal offices, State licensing authorities and officers at ports to maintain enhanced surveillance following instances of imported cosmetics being sold in domestic markets without valid import registration certificates.
Heavy metals found in two creams
The health regulator followed this with a more pointed warning on September 8. After testing Goree Beauty Cream and Chandni Whitening Cream, it said neither had been issued a registration certificate for import and that the products contained heavy metals beyond specified limits, which could pose health risks, including toxic effects. Consumers were advised not to purchase or use them.
The Hyderabad investigation has meanwhile opened another line of inquiry. According to the officer, investigators found that an ointment originating from the United Kingdom was allegedly being mixed with cosmetic products and the resulting preparation sold for skin-lightening purposes.
Samples of the products have been sent for forensic examination, and investigators are awaiting the laboratory findings to establish their composition and determine the substances present in them.
Officials have raised concerns about potentially carcinogenic substances, but the forensic results are awaited. The precise health implications of the seized preparations are therefore yet to be established.
The latest investigation follows raids by the Hyderabad police and CDSCO at Beauty Ladies Emporium, Beauty Queen Shop and S.J. Medical Shop in the Habeeb Nagar and Nampally areas, where cosmetics valued at about ₹7 lakh were seized.
The stock included several Pakistan-made whitening creams, soaps and other cosmetic products. Five persons were identified in connection with their alleged sale and distribution.
The Crawford Market link also comes against the backdrop of enforcement action in Mumbai itself, where Pakistan-made cosmetics valued at about ₹12 lakh were seized during a raid in July.

For a long time, fungal infections have meant itchy skin, discoloured nails and sometimes hair loss.
These symptoms are collectively called dermatophytosis and are caused by a group of fungi called dermatophytes.
‘’Unfortunately, immunocompromised patients can get lesions all over their body. The itchiness and the lesions can get so severe that people even get suicidal thoughts,” said Shivaprakash Rudramurthy, professor of medical mycology at the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER), Chandigarh.
Global warming
Dermatophytes are molds: fungi that grow in long strands. The other common category of fungi is yeast, which are single, oval-shaped cells. Among the yeasts, Candida auris is rapidly emerging as a multidrug resistant pathogen in ICU facilities. It enters the blood stream and causes severe infections, most of which are untreatable by the available antifungals. According to Prof. Rudramurthy, those infected suffer a 30-40% mortality rate.
C. auris has become a menace only in the last two decades. The first report was in 2009 in Japan. Several other fungal species have become more pathogenic only in recent times. The cause of this rise remains unresolved but scientists and medical doctors have some ideas.
Fungi grow best in damp places below 30° C, so they can grow on our skin, especially in moist areas of the body, like armpits and the genital area. However, bloodstream infections in humans were rare because they could not survive in the body’s 37° C temperature.
“Fungal infections are common in cold-blooded animals with lower body temperatures,” Sriram Varahan, a mycologist at CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad, said.
“But global warming puts a selective pressure on fungi such that only the more heat-tolerant ones survive. These ones can survive inside our bodies too, if they gain access to it. This is called the fungal infection — mammalian selection hypothesis.”
Clinical samples
Today, roughly 20% of infections reported in hospitals are fungal in nature — yet most hospitals in India lack the capabilities and infrastructure to identify fungal pathogens, Prof Rudramurthy said.
This prompted PGIMER to begin storing fungal pathogens some 25 years ago. Today, the institute holds a stock of 15,000 clinical fungal isolates across India and helps other medical centres and clinicians identify and culture them for study, free of cost.
The C. auris isolates from PGIMER’s repository have come handy for Kaustuv Sanyal and his research associate Aswathy Narayanan, both at the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research, Bengaluru. They study how fungal pathogens divide and their genomes evolve.
In a recent study published in Nature Communications, they characterised the clinical isolates of C. auris found across India. Their focus was the pathogen’s ability to resist antifungals. They were able to establish their findings in patient samples and go beyond earlier studies in model systems.
“More than 90% clinical isolates of C. auris are resistant to common azole-based antifungals, such as fluconazole,” Prof. Sanyal said. Some “30% of them are resistant to another class of antifungals called the polyenes. They mostly respond to a different class of antifungals called the echinocandins.”
A drug may not work on a pathogen for many reasons, including the drug’s target becoming mutated or the drug’s effect being negated by the pathogen’s own biomolecules. Dr. Narayanan and her collaborators at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Thiruvananthapuram, found significant changes in drug-resistant C. auris genomes that could explain why Indian clinical isolates were able to resist azoles and echinocandins.
Susceptibility tests
A fungal cell has two protective layers surrounding it. The outermost is the cell wall and the inner one is the cell membrane. Azole and polyene antifungals target a fat called ergosterol that is enriched in the cell membrane. Echinocandins target the cell wall.
“When we grow C. auris isolates in the presence of fluconazole, the pathogen fights back by making extra copies of the Erg 11 gene. This in turn helps in higher production of ergosterol, thereby eliminating the effect of the azole drug,” Dr Narayanan said.
The study found parts in the C. auris genome where additional copies of the Erg11 gene were present.
With echinocandin drugs such as caspofungin, the team found mutations in the Fks1 gene that allowed the pathogen to resist the drug’s action. The team also found genetic changes promoting higher tolerance of echinocandins.
“Fks1 mutations can enable C. auris to survive even caspofungin doses up to 16 ug/ml. That means a patient with such a pathogen will need the drug at a concentration higher than 16 ug/ml,” Prof. Sanyal said. “Today, clinicians would not know that because they test the pathogen’s ability to survive only until 2 µg/mL of caspofungin — as defined by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and followed globally.”
The logical thing for clinicians would be to look for mutations like in the Fks1 gene and decide the limits for tests to decide the antifungal dose for patients. But due to associated costs, a more practical way is to increase the limits of susceptibility tests for caspofungin to higher than 16 ug/ml, Prof. Sanyal added.
C. auris, without any specific gene mutation or gene duplication, still responds to high concentrations of caspofungin in unexpected ways. While the pathogen dies at lower concentrations of the drug, at exceptionally high ones, it survives. This is paradoxical.
“This is because caspofungin at high doses activates compensatory pathways in the fungus,” Prof. Sanyal explained. “The fungus starts producing chitin, the raw material of the fungal cell wall, in large quantities. Any damage that caspofungin brings about on the cell wall is compensated by the extra chitin production. And thus the cell wall remains intact despite the antifungal.”
Such examples of paradoxical growth are called the Eagle effect, named for the U.S. pathologist Harry Eagle.
Beyond the arms race
The studies underline the importance of clinicians conducting more nuanced susceptibility tests to decide the antifungal doses. They show that fungi are protected from antifungals by genetic mutations as well as by making more copies of protective genes.
Prof. Sanyal also stressed on the need for a combination of therapies to target cellular compensatory pathways, keeping the major antifungals effective against drug-tolerant species.
However, Dr. Varahan said he believed scientists and doctors need to think of gentler alternatives: “When we target [a molecule] without which an organism cannot live at all, evolution ensures that its population survives with a changed molecule. So instead of participating in an arms race, it is perhaps better to target the less critical molecular pathways, inhibition of which will allow the pathogen to still survive but not cause a disease.”
It seems the idea of dousing fungal pathogens with antifungals is nearing its end. The next-generation of antifungals will need more planning.
Somdatta Karak heads science communication at CSIR-CCMB.

The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination”.
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates, where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”

There’s no place like Kansas, a state whose howling winds are so fierce that in the 1800s, the roaring soundscape drove local farmers into madness. It is so windy in Kansas that every so often, trains get swept off their tracks or trampolines get hurled into the air and flung into neighbors’ trees.
The Senate’s new permitting plan could change how America gets energy for a generation
This messy bipartisan bargain that could bring down your power bill.
But today, the same gusts that whisked away Dorothy’s home have made Kansas the third-most wind-powered place in the country, its great plains dotted with thousands of twirling turbines responsible for generating over half of the state’s energy.
And for years, Kansas has been trying to share.
But that’s easier said than done in the US, where building power lines across state borders can be an onerous, litigious, and bureaucratic slog. The Grain Belt Express, a proposed 800-mile high-voltage line carrying Kansas’ windy riches across Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana, has been trying to get built for the past 16 years. When completed, it will allow Kansas to pump five times as much wind power into Missouri as it does now. But though the project received its first approval in 2013, it will likely not open until 2029 at the earliest, beset by regulatory hurdles across multiple jurisdictions and an endless stream of legal challenges that immediately halt progress every time a new injunction is filed. Alas, the express — which only broke ground this year — was forced to run oh so local.
But other projects like it might soon enjoy far more reasonable timelines. On Wednesday, a bipartisan group of Senators announced a deal called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA — an acronym that’s led to a slew of cringeworthy euphoric Baja Blast references from abundance Democrats, clean energy advocates, and oil industry lobbyists alike. If passed, it would significantly curtail Americans’ ability to endlessly litigate against energy projects they don’t like, and empower the federal government to push critical multistate projects forward even if one state or municipality drags its feet. That could remake the way the nation’s energy infrastructure gets built, including its interstate transmission lines, for decades to come.
But the bill also suggests that easing the way for clean energy in the US may require simultaneously creating the conditions for more oil and gas infrastructure in a country that already has a lot of it. It would also mean defanging some of the landmark regulatory norms that for decades have, for example, given Americans a say over developments that could contaminate their drinking water and helped tribes protect sacred heritage sites. These laws were necessary in the first place because prior to the 1970s, American communities frequently found themselves both literally and figuratively steamrolled by developers singularly focused on building things quickly with little regard for the oil spills, river fires, and bifurcated neighborhoods they left in their wake.
And yet today, half a century later, that same dilemma has, in some ways, turned on its head. America builds things too slowly, and in particular, it builds the kind of infrastructure desperately needed to usher in a transition to clean energy with little of the urgency you’d expect from a world in the throes of climate change-related disaster. Exasperatingly, some of the same protections that have played a critical role in making this nation safer may also be standing in the way of building a nation that is more affordable and sustainable in the long run.
There are still plenty of reasons to feel hopeful about the world’s transition away from fossil fuels, even in the US, which has lagged behind our peers while still building an extraordinary number of solar and wind farms, particularly in Republican-led states like Kansas and Texas. And yet, many of these projects have languished in never-ending Ticketmaster-esque queues to connect to the nation’s decrepit power grid, a direct result of the permitting hellscape that prevents much-needed high-voltage cables like the Grain Belt Express from coming online.
This new bill aims to ease many of the bottlenecks that stymie clean energy, but it also throws a bone to fossil fuels, which, like renewables, would benefit from less onerous environmental reviews and quicker permissions. This is, after all, a bipartisan bill in a Congress that, at least for now, remains Republican-led, under the tutelage of an aggrieved president who has sabotaged some of the nation’s most promising clean energy projects with an often petty and relentless fervor. Some Democrats in Congress, along with other environmentalists, have raised serious concerns about the bill. Those initial objections may prophesize an uphill battle for it when it comes to a vote, likely after the November midterms.
Even so, with American electricity bills spiking to frightening new heights, and a data center buildout that could all but snap the power grid in half, this ambitious deal is, at the very least, an indication that some of the nation’s representatives are finally listening. And if it passes into law in the months to come, it could very well remake how Americans get their energy for a generation.
So why are environmentalists mad?
By most accounts, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act almost didn’t happen.
For months, the proposed permitting deal has been stalled by the Trump administration’s failure to assure Democrats that the president would lay off his attacks on “windmills” and other clean energy projects. But in recent days, lawmakers appear to have come close to a fragile détente on the back of a “very reasonable opening proposal” from the White House, according to Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island and ranking member of the Environment and Public Works Committee.
If the BAAJA is passed, it will codify new protections that legally prevent presidents like Trump from meddling with already-permitted energy projects or singling out specific forms of energy, a prohibition that will also apply if a Democratic president attempts to halt an approved gas line or a petroleum refinery. The Biden administration’s freeze on approvals for new natural gas export plants, for example, would not be allowed.
It’s this element of the proposed bill that worries many environmentalists most. According to a transcript obtained by Punchbowl News, during a coalition call on Thursday, dozens of advocates from prominent environmental groups — including the Sierra Club, the National Wildlife Federation, and the Environmental Law & Policy Center — expressed their misgivings about the bill and strategized about how to lobby Democrats against it.
Most environmentalists acknowledge, however, that we need to spruce up the power grid and fix how permitting works for clean energy projects and transmission lines. As clean energy advocates know all too well, the projects they support are, paradoxically, more likely to be hampered by environmental reviews than fossil fuel projects are, because renewables usually require more space and represent the bulk of new energy developments. But many advocates understandably take issue with the idea that reforming this overcomplicated process may require weakening the right to challenge other projects, a right affirmed by the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act.
The bill’s fate may ultimately depend on whether this trade-off is worth it. The BAAJA still does leave some room for court challenges if they’re filed within 150 days of an approval. But it will still place a much larger burden for determining these damage thresholds on federal agencies, which are, of course, currently controlled by Trump.
“The question’s not whether that would be a good idea — it’s one of the basic building blocks for converting more of our energy system to renewables,” the environmentalist Bill McKibben wrote of grid expansion and permitting reform on his Substack this week. “It’s how many pounds of flesh the fossil fuel industry would demand in return, and how close to vital organs that flesh would be located.”
The problem is, no matter how many Congressional seats Democrats seem poised to scoop up in November, they will still need to get Republicans on board if they want Americans to be able to really see the benefits of solar, the cheapest energy source of all time, reflected on their power bill. And for most of the nation, if not Earth itself, that transition can’t come soon enough.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

A wild African black panther prowls for prey. An orphaned baby pangolin must learn how to climb on its own. And a green turtle struggles to make it back to the water after laying her eggs on a remote island, rescued by local humans who carry the exhuasted turtle to the water’s edge. These animals and many other species are featured in Africa: Earth’s Wild Home, a new documentary series from National Geographic. It’s meant to launch a new franchise, with separate series documenting the wildlife and environmental ecosystems of all seven continents in turn.
The seven-episode documentary series took four years to complete, with filming taking place across nearly 30 different African countries. Each episode focuses on a specific ecosystem, from the jungle and the desert, to the plains, mountains, and islands of Africa, and closes by spotlighting the various scientists, photographers, and NatGeo explorers whose work made the series possible. The final episode focuses on the local conservation leaders and researchers working to preserve Africa’s rich biodiversity for future generations.
The producers found the perfect narrator in Wunmi Mosaku, who has delivered powerful performances in such works as Sinners, Loki, and Lovecraft Country. “I was incredibly honored that they even know my name at Nat Geo,” Mosaku told Ars. “It was wonderful to be asked to narrate the series, it means so much to me. As someone who was born in Nigeria and raised in England, I’ll take any opportunity I can to reconnect and celebrate this incredible continent where life is so diverse and so extreme and beautiful and relentless and peaceful. I wanted to be a part of that because it’s a part of me.”
“There was so much I didn’t know,” said Mosaku. “I have been to Nigeria, obviously, and Ghana. I’ve worked in Kenya and South Africa. But there’s so much to see. I don’t think you could even explore it in a lifetime. So many things were shocking to me. Seeing snow and monkeys living in the snow in Africa, I had never seen that before.”

By the time Mr. Saravanan turned 87, he had a severely narrowed aortic valve that was impacting his daily activities to an extent where he required oxygen support for about a month. Post the successful completion of a Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation (TAVI) procedure, however, he recovered at an impressive pace. In just four days, he regained the strength to venture outdoors and cast his vote for the municipal elections. He lived an independent lifestyle till he crossed the milestone of 93 years old and finally breathed his last due to a fall while playing with his grandchildren.
Mr. Saravanan’s journey tells us the story of how far medical advancement in treating aortic valve disease has progressed. For those who qualify, TAVI offers a unique technique to replace the faulty aortic valve without undergoing the traditional open-heart surgery.
Understanding the aortic valve
The aortic valve forms one of the four valves within the human heart structure. It lies between the largest artery called the aorta and the main ventricle of the heart that pumps oxygen-rich blood across the entire body system. Each beat allows the leaflets of the valve, also known as cusps, to open for the outflow of blood and shut to stop any back flow.
With increasing years, calcium deposits on these valves make them thickened and rigid. The term for this is ‘aortic stenosis’. This condition is most prevalent as age advances over 70 years, when the calcification of the valve becomes prominent due to wear and tear. In many cases, patients present with aortic stenosis at an earlier stage of life due to a birth defect in the aortic valve. Being born with only two cusps of the valve instead of three, makes such valves prone to wear out sooner.
Why the narrowed valve is a problem
With a narrowing of the aortic valve, the heart needs to exert additional pressure to ensure flow of the blood through the restricted space. Early signs could be subtle: a task which had been manageable might now need an extra halt in between; routine tasks could suddenly drain energy like never before.
As symptoms intensify with time, the patient might encounter shortness of breath, discomfort in the chest area, dizziness or even fainting spells. These indicate worsening of the condition and must be addressed without further delay. A test known as an echocardiography is a painless diagnostic procedure using ultrasonic waves to assess the extent of narrowing of the valve, besides assessing cardiac function.
Commencement of symptomatic severe aortic stenosis marks an ominous milestone. It heralds rapid progression towards end-stage illness. Untreated, aortic stenosis inevitably results in heart failure and can lead to sudden cardiac death.
When the valve needs replacing
For several decades, severe aortic valve diseases were treated only with open heart surgery. TAVI has revolutionised the entire process for eligible patients. . In TAVI, a biological valve, usually bovine or porcine tissue stitched within a metallic frame, is placed at the tip of a catheter. The catheter is then typically inserted through the leg artery and moved all the way into the heart. At the site of the damaged valve, the new valve is deployed and it starts operating instantly.
Unlike traditional surgical procedures for valve replacement, TAVI doesn’t involve cutting through the chest bone. It is often performed under local anaesthesia with mild sedation depending on individual patient circumstances.
Its main benefit lies in quick mobilisation and most patients can be discharged within a few days after the procedure.
There can be no denying the fact that TAVI is evolving rapidly as an interventional cardiovascular technique. Its origins lay in its development for patients who were deemed too risky for any kind of surgical intervention. Over time, it has become the procedure of choice in most patients with aortic stenosis over 65 years.
Matching patients to treatments
It is important to understand that TAVI is not an option for everyone with aortic stenosis. It should be considered carefully in younger patients and in people with certain types of bicuspid aortic valve, an enlarged aorta or a need for additional bypass surgery.
Many factors come into play when determining what would work best for a given patient. Among the factors to consider are: age, general health status, longevity prospects, valve robustness, anatomical considerations, and potential need for further procedures down the line.
Advanced imaging technologies enable the medical team to analyse the anatomy of the patient, select the most appropriate path of intervention and decide on the correct valve and its size. There cannot be any one-size-fits-all strategy here. The treatment must focus on the unique circumstances of each person.
It is important to keep future treatment options open as each tissue valve can only last upto 10-12 years. This is why the heart team plays a significant role. Cardiologists, cardiac surgeons, and imaging experts work together to plan the most suitable treatment option for that individual.
What patients should know
For patients diagnosed with aortic stenosis and found suitable for TAVI, the procedure can improve quality of life and help them live longer. By easing symptoms such as breathlessness, tiredness and chest discomfort, it may make everyday activities easier again. The decision should also be part of a lifelong heart valve plan that considers how long the replacement valve may last and what treatment options might be needed in the future.
(Dr. G. Sengottuvelu is senior consultant – interventional cardiology, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. drgseng@gmail.com)

Utah regulators on Monday announced a plan to allow an artificial intelligence product to evaluate patients for acne treatment and write new drug prescriptions without prior human review.
A startup called Nolla Health will launch an AI-powered service in the state that will assess a patient for mild-to-moderate acne treatment using a structured intake and by analyzing photos of their skin. The product may determine whether one of a list of low-risk drugs is appropriate. In the first stages of the pilot, the decisions of the AI will be reviewed by a licensed clinician who will sign off on prescriptions, but Nolla may eventually be allowed to prescribe drugs without this review. The company last year announced it raised $4.5 million from investors including General Catalyst, and Nolla aspires to direct treatment for a host of conditions using AI.
The new pilot is part of a significant expansion of a closely watched “AI sandbox” program that allows Utah’s Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy, or OAIP, to waive regulations for companies that want to test AI products under state supervision.

A study published in September in Nature by neuroscientist Sergiu Pașca’s group at Stanford University reports an experiment that sounds almost like science fiction. Human brain tissue grown from stem cells was transplanted into mice in which much of the cerebral cortex had been genetically prevented from forming. The transplanted tissue grew into this vacant space, produced several types of human brain cells, became electrically active, connected with the mouse nervous system and was associated with measurable differences in behaviour.
Yet, an important limitation must be stated at the outset. The researchers have not created a human brain inside a mouse. The transplanted tissue remained immature, lacked the ordered structure of a normal human cortex, and the study cannot establish that human neurons directly caused any particular behaviour. What the experiment offers is a narrow glimpse of human brain development as it unfolds inside a non-human living nervous system.
Our blind spot
Understanding how the human brain develops matters both for evolutionary biology and for medicine. The cerebral cortex expanded greatly during human evolution, developing specialised cells and connections involved in language, planning and complex social behaviour. Studying how these features emerge may help explain what makes the human brain distinctive.
It is also medically important because many neurological and psychiatric disorders may begin during development, long before symptoms appear. The main challenge is access. Scientists cannot experimentally manipulate a developing human brain as they can in laboratory animals. Imaging can track structural changes, while foetal and post-mortem tissues provide useful snapshots. Still, neither allows researchers to alter a gene or developmental process and observe the consequences over time. Human developmental neuroscience has therefore long faced a major experimental blind spot.
Growing brain tissue
Stem cell technology opened up another avenue to study the developing human brain. Scientists can take ordinary human cells, re-programme them into an earlier, flexible state called induced pluripotent stem cells, and guide them to become nerve cells. When these cells are grown together in three dimensions, they can organise into structures called organoids. A brain organoid is a small piece of laboratory-grown neural tissue that reproduces some features of early brain development. Organoids allow researchers to observe how human neurons develop, introduce disease-related genetic changes and test responses to drugs.
However, tissue grown in a lab dish lacks key features of a living brain, including normal blood circulation, sensory inputs and long-distance connections with other parts of the nervous system. Researchers, including the Stanford group, have therefore transplanted human brain organoids into rodents, where the living environment supports better survival and maturation. Yet this creates another constraint: the rodent already has its own cortex, so the transplanted human tissue must compete for limited space and neural connections, and has never amounted to more than a fragment of the host’s brain.
A third window
The Stanford researchers opened up a third possibility. Instead of engineering a better graft, they re-engineered the host. Using genetic techniques, they produced mice in which much of the neocortex and hippocampus never formed. Because the mice were also bred to lack a functioning immune system, the human tissue would not be rejected. Human cortical organoids were then transplanted into the vacant space soon after birth. The researchers call the approach xenocortication. ‘Xeno’ refers to something originating from another species, while the cortex is the outer region of the brain involved in many higher functions.
In the Stanford experiment, freed from much of the competition from mouse cortical tissue, the human grafts expanded substantially, and by three months, they made up about 92% of the animal’s cortical tissue. They produced several types of developing cortical neurons, along with progenitor cells and astrocytes, at a stage of maturity roughly equivalent to that of the human cortex late in the second trimester of pregnancy. The grafts generated deep-layer neurons carrying the molecular signature of von Economo neurons, large, distinctively shaped cells found in humans and a few other large-brained mammals, but absent in rodents, and long associated with social cognition and psychiatric illness. Such neurons are almost impossible to grow in a dish.
The grafts also became electrically active, producing slow waves that swept across the tissue every few minutes, a pattern characteristic of developing, rather than mature, cortical networks. They formed connections with surviving parts of the mouse nervous system, and human nerve fibres reached as far as the cervical spinal cord, something not seen in mice with an intact cortex. This is the conceptual leap of the study: human neural tissue was no longer a fragment lodged inside a rodent’s brain, but tissue occupying almost all of the space where that animal’s cortex would have been.
Reading behaviour
The next question was whether this integration had any functional effect. The starting point was itself surprising. Mice lacking most of their neocortex and hippocampus (roughly half the brain by volume) remained active and mobile, ran at normal speeds and responded normally to heat and touch. To detect subtler differences, the researchers combined conventional behavioural tests with a machine-learning system called Motion Sequencing (MoSeq). A depth camera recorded freely moving mice, while the software divided their movements into 60 recurring sub-second patterns, such as rearing, pausing, and turning, creating a detailed behavioural fingerprint rather than relying solely on speed or distance travelled. By this measure, mice lacking much of their cortex behaved differently from normal animals. Xenocortical mice showed an intermediate pattern, suggesting that transplantation altered behaviour without fully restoring it. In a Y-shaped maze used to test working memory, normal and xenocortical mice performed above chance, whereas mice lacking much of their cortex did not. This suggests possible partial functional compensation, but does not prove that human neurons restored memory.
Why this matters
To show what the platform can do, the researchers exposed the mice to five hours of severe oxygen deprivation. The response was confined to the human tissue: a molecular marker of oxygen stress appeared in the graft but not in the adjacent mouse brain, and not at all in animals without a graft. Two days later, the xenocortical mice walked differently, shifting to a more stable stance without any change in their speed. Imaging 10 days on showed changes in the graft’s blood vessels. Under the microscope, the graft’s supporting cells had multiplied and become more complex.
This creates a potentially powerful experimental pathway. Scientists could introduce a disease-related mutation into human cells, allow the resulting neural tissue to develop within a living nervous system, observe changes in cells and circuits, assess whether behaviour is affected, and then test possible treatments. Such models could help study developmental brain disorders, the oxygen deprivation around birth that can lead to cerebral palsy, human-specific neuronal diseases and evolutionary differences between human and animal brains. They may also provide a platform for drug testing and, eventually, for evaluating regenerative or cell-based treatments for severe early brain injury.
Limits and ethics
The model is still far from reproducing a developing human brain. The grafts did not reproduce the full balance of excitatory and inhibitory neurons. Human neurons also mature far more slowly than mouse neurons, creating a mismatch between the developmental timelines of graft and host. Although anatomical connections were observed, this does not prove that they directly controlled behaviour. Any behavioural changes, therefore, arise from a hybrid system in which human tissue interacts with the remaining mouse brain.
These scientific limits also shape the ethical questions. There is no evidence that the animals developed human consciousness or a human-like mind. However, future models may contain larger, more mature, and better-organised human neural tissue, with greater integration into the host brain. At what point might this alter an animal’s cognition, perception or capacity for experience in ethically significant ways? The researchers anticipated this question and consulted bioethicists at Stanford before beginning. The paper argues that going further towards grafts with mature cortical layering, or transplantation into embryos or into non-human primates, will require a greater degree of scrutiny before such experiments begin.
Ultimately, xenocortication is important not because it creates a human brain in another species, but because it may provide a third window to study human brain development.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com; Dr Veera Rajagopal is a physician-scientist & geneticist working in drug discovery. veera.scientist@gmail.com)

Rumors that Cornell University was forcibly removed from the Ivy League, the collegiate athletic conference that includes eight of the United States' oldest and most-prestigious universities, circulated in late September 2026.
The rumor circulated as the university was scrutinized over a lawsuit that accused seven male students of drugging and raping a female student in 2024. As Snopes previously reported, the lawsuit, filed in September 2026, led to the Tompkins County, N.Y., district attorney reopening his office's investigation into the case.
People across various social media platforms shared the rumor, expressing their apparent satisfaction with the purported decision, writing, "Cornell getting dropped from the Ivy League is music to my earssssssssssss."
Cornell getting dropped from the Ivy League is music to my earssssssssss!!
— Seema Genche (@seemagenche) September 30, 2026
However, the rumor that Cornell University was "dropped" from the Ivy League was false.
There was no evidence to suggest that the rumor had any merit. The official Ivy League website featured Cornell University as of this writing, complete with its upcoming game schedule and standings for multiple sports.
Further, the "About the Ivy League" page on the organization's website stated, "The League's world-renowned schools – Brown, Columbia, Cornell, Dartmouth, Harvard, Penn, Princeton and Yale – serve as the standard bearers for inspiring and transforming student- athletes to boldly take on the world's challenges and lead lives of great impact."
Searches of Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo revealed no credible media outlets reporting on the rumor, which would have been a major headline given the widespread media coverage of the "Cornell 7" case.
Looking closer at the most-popular versions of the claim circulating on social media, it's clear that the accounts spreading the rumor used the exact same language — "Cornell getting dropped from the Ivy League is music to my earssssssssssss" — indicating that it was either the work of bots posting the message across a variety of accounts or, less likely, a copy-and-paste campaign.
A 2009 piece in Cornell's student-run independent newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun, dug into the history of the school's affiliation with the prestigious organization.
It said the name Ivy League originated in 1937 but "did not become formal until November 1954, when the presidents of Brown, Columbia, Cornell, Dartmouth, Harvard, Penn, Princeton and Yale affixed their signatures to the 'Common Statement of Ivy Group Institutions.'"
Further, it said the Ivy League "distinguished itself from other schools with a few basic rules: no postseason competition, and no financial aid to players except for legitimate academic or need-based scholarships."
Snopes reached out to Cornell University and the Ivy League for comment and will update this article if we hear back.

Drones buzz overhead, troops hunker underground in Ukraine's hellish kill zone
KYIV, Ukraine — The front line in the Russia-Ukraine war stretches the entire length of this country, from north to south. It has barely budged in four years and is sometimes compared to the static, deadlocked, trench warfare of World War I.
Yet straddling this front line is the kill zone, dominated by constantly evolving drone technology that's defining this conflict — and the future of warfare.
"This kill zone is a belt of territory which is full of Russian drones, Russian mines and also artillery. It's nonstop reconnaissance and surveillance," said Ukraine's Sr. Lt. Taras Myshak, the spokesman for Ukraine's 59th Separate Assault Brigade. He spoke with NPR on Zoom, just a few miles from the front line in eastern Ukraine.
Ukraine has a similar arsenal threatening the Russian forces that are dug in on the other side of the line.
The most important thing to know about the kill zone is that any sign of movement — just sticking your head out of a foxhole for fresh air — can get you noticed, and attacked, by the drones constantly buzzing overhead.
Myshak says even routine movements, like rotating troops in and out of this zone, is a nightmare.
"Not far from where we are talking today, we have a group that moved through the kill zone, and they will walk four hours just to go 1 kilometer," he said. "Because all the time they hear the drone, and they have to hide and wait. Then the drone passes, and they can move."
Nightfall doesn't make it any safer to move because the drones have thermal cameras that detect body heat and make it even harder to hide.
"In the night, it's even more dangerous," he said.
A front line that barely budges
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it advanced rapidly in conventional fashion with large columns of troops in armored vehicles. Later that fall, Ukraine's counteroffensive drove the Russians back in some places.
Since then, the two armies have settled in, and the front line has moved only incrementally, mostly with limited gains by Russia. This line now stretches more than 700 miles. On either side of the line, the kill zone is a band roughly 10 to 20 miles wide and dominated by drones.
"The kill zone is basically a product of drone warfare," said Rob Lee, a U.S. Marine veteran who now lives in Ukraine and monitors the war for the Foreign Policy Research Institute of Philadelphia.
Because Ukraine has far fewer troops and relies heavily on drones, it has a remarkably small presence on the front line.
Lee said that in many places, Ukraine has fewer than 10 soldiers per mile, in small groups, spaced out hundreds of yards apart.
"Those infantrymen are maybe two positions where it's two to four people," said Lee. "They're underground for the most part. They're trying to remain hidden."
These troops are not really trying to hold back advancing Russian soldiers, he added. They act more as spotters, relaying Russian movements to Ukrainian drone operators behind the front lines, who then track down the Russian intruders from the air.
Lee says the front line is so saturated with drones that it's virtually impossible for either side to pull together a large ground force without being detected and drawing fire.
Military vehicles like tanks and armored personnel carriers are even easier to spot and attack.
"Because of such a high density of drones, it became very difficult to bring vehicles near the front line at all," he said.
Neither army planned to fight this way.
Ukraine had no real drone industry at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the country will make 10 million this year.
Russia has ramped up its own drone production. It's expected to make more than 7 million this year, including jet-powered aircraft that are often evading Ukraine's defenses.
Starting from scratch
When Dima Putiata joined Ukraine's military four years ago, he knew nothing about drones and didn't think this was a manly way to wage war.
"When I saw that we have drones, I was not smart enough. I said, 'No, we don't need to have it. Let's fight like men.' I was a little bit maybe romantic in this way," said Putiata.
In addition to skeptics like Putiata, few Ukrainian troops were trained to use these new weapons.
"No one had drone operators," he recalled. "It's just, 'Oh, you're a driver? You can use it.' Or, 'Oh, can I use a drone? You can try.'"
By the time he left the military in May, Putiata, a sergeant, was commanding 26 drone crews in and around the kill zone in northeastern Ukraine.
Both sides have rapidly embraced the technology even if they don't know where it's headed next, he said.
"They understand how to use it here and right now, maybe not really understanding how to use it in the future," he noted. "My point is, you just need to keep going and adapting."
Recognizing the role of drones
Two years ago, Ukraine became the first country to establish drones as an independent branch of its military.
This innovation now includes the widespread use of ground drones, which look like trollies and perform a wide range of tasks that have become too dangerous for troops.
The robots deliver food, medicine and ammunition to the front line. The robots can be loaded with machine guns that now carry out regular attacks.
The ground robots are also being used to evacuate wounded soldiers from the kill zone. But drone operators and combat medics have separate skills, and it turns out you need both.
"The drone operator doesn't know how to properly evacuate a wounded soldier, and the medic doesn't know how to operate a ground robot," said Lyuba Shipovich, a Ukrainian American who heads a private group, Dignitas, that trains troops on drones.
"So now we're trying to create combined program that will train both the medic and the robot operator," she said.
Media coverage tends to focus on long-range airstrikes that Russia and Ukraine are inflicting deep inside each other's territory.
But the vast majority of the fighting is in the kill zone, with drones now responsible for 80% of all casualties, according to Rob Lee and other military analysts.
Dima Putiata, the former Ukrainian soldier, says what started in this war has already spread to other conflicts.
"With drones, this is the cheapest flying munition that can be massively produced. You can destroy a lot of stuff," he said. "It's much cheaper than it used to be to have a war, unfortunately."
A kind of war, he predicts, that the world will see more often.
NPR's Hanna Palamarenko contributed to this story.

F1 in the wet and the future of engines - Q&A
- Published
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won his first race of the season in a dramatic rain-affected Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
Kimi Antonelli finished second in the Mercedes and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who fought his way back to the front after an incorrect tyre choice at the start, completed the podium.
Antonelli extended his lead in the championship to 84 points, after team-mate George Russell retired with an engine failure.
This weekend, it's the Singapore Grand Prix - Formula 1's original night race.
Before the race at Marina Bay, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
Do we miss out on exciting wet-weather racing because an overly cautious approach is applied when rain occurs prior to the start of the race? We are watching the best drivers in the world, who have wet tyres, but it seems when it rains prior to the start of a race, the action gets under way too late. - Sam
This question comes up a lot whenever there is a wet race, but in this specific situation the delay in starting the race was not caused by any conservatism when it comes to wet running.
The cars were sent out on formation laps when the track was still pretty wet on Sunday in Malaysia, but then a bug in the wet-weather engine settings affected a number of cars, including those of Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton on the front row.
That meant the formation laps had to be aborted, and a new code written and given to the teams to upload to ensure that did not happen again.
It just so happened that in the intervening 25 minutes, there had been no more rain, so the track was pretty dry by the time the race started. Although it has to be said that it took a safety car on lap nine before the drivers who had started on treaded intermediate tyres came in for slicks.
On a generic level, there is no fundamental objection in F1 to racing in the wet - most of the drivers enjoy it. But there is now a collective agreement that they will not race when they can't see where they are going.
So races are not started when that is the case - as it was at the original start time in Malaysia.
But if you cast your mind back to Brazil in 2024, and Verstappen's brilliant drive from 17th on the grid to victory, that was run in wet conditions.
- F1 needs to have hard look at itself - Sainz 
  - Published19 hours ago
After the Bahrain Grand Prix, Lewis Hamilton said that, had he started on the intermediate tyres, he could have won the race. Given the race data and his pace, do you think that's a realistic claim had Ferrari put him on the inters at the start? - Michael
The truth is that Hamilton - and anyone else - will never know, because there was no direct comparison between his pace and Max Verstappen's in similar conditions.
In the first few laps, Hamilton was on slicks and Verstappen on intermediates. When Verstappen switched to slicks, Hamilton's tyres were much older.
On the very few laps when Hamilton was in clear air before he caught Isack Hadjar, his pace when generally nowhere near Verstappen's but then his tyres were nine laps older, so you would not expect it to be.
And then once he finally passed Hadjar, there were only three laps to go.
On one of them, Hamilton was within 0.1secs of Verstappen, on the other two he was 0.5secs and 1.2secs off. But how much were either of them pushing?
What we can say is that Verstappen looked imperious all weekend, and it was probably going to be difficult for anyone to beat him - even Hamilton, who, it's worth saying, on Saturday was not sounding that confident of challenging him.
But it's just a whole load of ifs, buts and maybes, isn't it?
Malaysia, true to form, brought a great race, chaos and weather. It was sold out. Fans have loved it, missed it, drivers liked the track. We know why it dropped off the calendar but what would it take to come back permanently? - Nick
Simple answer - money.
Malaysia dropped off the calendar because the government there was no longer willing to pay the rights fee, feeling that the expense did not justify the return.
It returned only because the Crown Prince of Bahrain was keen to stage his race, F1 was happy to accommodate him, and he managed to strike a deal with the Malaysian government.
There's no doubt the race was a success. It had a record crowd of 261,000 this year, more than double the previous largest weekend attendance of 126,690, reflecting F1's growth around the world.
If Malaysia was keen on returning to the calendar on a more permanent basis, there is no reason why F1 would not listen to them.
But whether that led to a deal would depend on whether one could be struck that satisfied both parties.
With Red Bull running their own powertrains, what part does Ford play? - John
Max Verstappen's victory in Malaysia on Sunday was not only a landmark because it was Red Bull's first of the season - it was also their first as a power-unit manufacturer.
Red Bull Powertrains was set up specifically to make an engine for the new 2026 regulations, so the team could be in control of their own destiny following Honda's official withdrawal from F1 at the end of 2021.
Ford came on board as a partner early on, and this is much more than simply a badging deal in return for finance/sponsorship money.
Team principal Laurent Mekies said on Monday: "Ford has been with us on this project since pretty much the very beginning.
"They are a key strategic partner for us on these operations. They are helping us on a number of topics.
"Specifically, to give you a few examples, they are manufacturing some of the key elements of the engines.
"So, some of these key elements are manufactured in Milton Keynes (at the Red Bull campus), some of these key elements are manufactured at Ford. And they are a 200,000-people company. And therefore, also in terms of engineering, if and when we need specific support on some topics, we are able to get access to some very good specialists they have.
"Some of these specialists are actually with us in Milton Keynes, and they are able to help us on some specific topics. So it's a mix of manufacturing of key components and some very specific engineering support on some other topics."
Singapore Grand Prix
9-11 October
Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app
Max Verstappen spoke recently about how much he enjoyed the endurance racing at the Nurburgring. And how he liked "pure" motorsport with the V8 engines and would welcome that or even the V10s back in F1. Is that even possible now? Or has F1 fully embraced the electric/hybrid system, and there is no going back? - Peter
This is a really complex topic, with many conflicting elements to it.
Verstappen - and Fernando Alonso and Lando Norris - has expressed his view this year that to return to "pure" racing, F1 should go back to naturally aspirated engines with no hybrid element.
FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has also been pushing a return to naturally aspirated engines, first V10s early last year, and more recently V8s.
Ben Sulayem has cited the evocative sound of V8s as one his main reasons, as well as lighter cars.
But naturally aspirated engines would use more fuel, so the cars would for half the race or so actually be heavier than they are now. The FIA has even investigated the idea of refuelling returning - which is not popular with the teams.
In F1 these days, only Alonso and Lewis Hamilton survive from the days when the drivers could push flat out throughout a grand prix with no concerns about tyre management.
But occasionally circumstances align to allow that to happen again. And in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, on the low-abrasion Baku circuit in the final stint, it did.
Race winner George Russell said afterwards: "The final stint, I think, is the most amount of fun I've had in a race for as long as I can remember because the tyre felt great. We were pushing flat out every single lap. It was like qualifying one after another.
"You needed to be so alert around this circuit because the walls are so close, especially through the castle. You're threading the needle.
"Those final 10 laps felt really, really fun. And it almost felt like the stories I hear of the drivers in the early-mid 2000s, of when every lap was like a qualifying lap.
"The heart rate is higher, you're pushing the limit every single lap, there's no management. We've had a lot of conversations this year about power-unit energy management, but the tyre management is still there and it has been there for years and years (since Pirelli came in in 2011).
"But just with how the temperatures and the circuit fell out today, with the tyres there was no management, and that was exceptionally fun."
On a romantic level, there is an argument that this is what F1 should be about - drivers pushing themselves and their cars to the absolute limit all the time.
And, it's worth pointing out, tyres are as much of a problem on this front as engines - much more so, in fact, before this year.
But it's not as simple as that.
Statistics show that the years of refuelling from 1994-2009 had the least amount of on-track overtakes in history.
Then there are the optics of using more fuel at a time when F1 is trying to go net-zero carbon by 2030, even if the racing is a tiny percentage of the sport's overall footprint.
Naturally aspirated engines would also be extremely loud - which would put at risk races such as Miami and Las Vegas close to or in population centres.
And then there's road relevance. The manufacturers are not in F1 for fun. They're in it for marketing reasons. Most road-car engines these days are turbos, and have some degree of hybridisation.
The upshot of all that is that it looks like F1 is heading to a new engine formula - for either 2030 or 2031 - that features V8 turbos with in the region of 15-25% electrical power, mainly to be used as a push-to-pass system.
Bosses are aware of the mistakes with energy starvation that have been caused with the latest rules, and the idea will be to allow the drivers to operate with maximum power all the time, with the electrical elements used to facilitate overtaking.

What is the purpose of a battery symbol next to a USB Port?
Typically, it means faster charging speeds and bi-directional charging.
The more USB ports on a device, the better, but things can get confusing when they all have a different symbol on them. Among the markings seen next to USB ports, it's not uncommon to see a battery icon, which typically indicates that it's a USB Power Delivery port. Known as USB PD for short, this port means it can deliver higher power levels than a typical USB port, but can also charge connected devices.
The USB PD charging protocol has a long history and was first introduced in 2012, meaning it predates the debut of the USB-C port. However, USB PD was updated in 2021 and is now able to deliver up to 240W of power, meaning it can support more demanding devices like high-end laptops or some monitors. Beyond supplying more power, the USB PD port has some cool use cases that you might not know about.
What can you do with a USB port with a battery symbol?
When you see a battery symbol next to a USB port, it can mean a few things. Most commonly, the icon means that port is USB PD compatible and can offer a more sophisticated charging protocol. Using USB PD, you can charge your laptop faster since Power Delivery conducts an intelligent digital handshake between device and charger that provides the right amount of voltage and current without the risk of overheating.
The battery symbol could also translate to another useful feature in the form of bidirectional charging. When looking at your laptop's USB ports, you can use the one with a battery symbol to charge another device, like your smartphone or AirPods. Even further, some laptops' USB ports with this symbol can charge a device even when it's asleep or shut down thanks to "Always On" charging. Keep in mind that leaving your smartphone plugged into your laptop's compatible port can completely drain the battery. Luckily, most laptop makers have included a way to disable this charging feature.
Does a battery symbol always mean USB PD?
As much sense as a battery icon makes, USB PD has somewhat of an identity crisis when it comes to the symbol that represents it. According to the USB Implementers Forum, the nonprofit corporation that created and set the official USB standards, the official symbol is a battery shape made with negative space.
Members of the USB Implementers Forum include Apple, Microsoft and HP, but not all companies align with how they indicate that a USB port is equipped with the Power Delivery charging protocol. Across devices, there can be the official battery symbol from the USB Implementers Forum, a different battery logo, a lightning bolt (not to be confused with the Thunderbolt symbol) or even simply the letters "PD" to indicate that it's a USB PD port. On top of that, some companies will have USB ports that are compatible with the USB PD protocol but don't indicate it, like Apple's Thunderbolt ports for its MacBooks. If in doubt, it's best to check the manufacturer's specifications in a user manual.
