"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

It's been more than four years since the launch of LIV Golf rocked the game.
A brash breakaway league, bankrolled by Saudi Arabian billions, luring top players with promises of big money.
Still it divides opinion in golf, and has split the loyalty of its champions.
But it could all come to an end soon.
After the League's Saudi backers pulled its funding - having spent more than $5bn (£3.6bn) - this week's abortive season finale could be the end.
That's unless a new deal is struck, soon.
BBC Sport visited the final event of 2026 at an exclusive golf club in Indianapolis, and found a strange atmosphere of surface-level optimism, but deep uncertainty.
Get ready for LIV 2.0... or the end?
LIV staff have learnt to put on a brave face. And that was no more necessary than this week at Chatham Hills Golf Club.
Despite endless questions about the future, they still had a tournament to host, and LIV Golf's white knight was in town - "the investor", as he was most frequently described.
The phrase "LIV 2.0" was used on countless occasions by the league's leadership - and that is the dream they are clinging to.
It stands for a new chapter, a second life for LIV.
There did appear to be genuine optimism that a deal could be struck.
LIV Golf chief executive officer Scott O'Neil believes he can pull off the near-impossible, and so do many of those closest to him.
But there was widespread acknowledgement that, if they do achieve it, the process to get there won't be easy.
One insider remarked "it's darkest before dawn". Another said "it will get worse before it gets better".
Work is said to be happening at "breakneck speed" behind the scenes, because of the pressure of players needing clarity on their futures, events needing to be organised, and sponsorships agreed.
However, there were players, caddies, staff and volunteers who shared a more pessimistic view with BBC Sport, with one describing it as the "last hurrah".
One senior figure within golf's media remarked: "We're at the hospice, not the funeral."
What would new era of LIV look like?
Much of the format is expected to stay the same in any new LIV - a shotgun start, team competition, music blaring from speakers and party holes.
But change will be felt in the boardrooms and in players' pockets.
The "free-spending" days are over.
If LIV does get a second chapter, it will need to be run in a more financially-disciplined way, given overall losses of this era of LIV are expected to have run into several billions of dollars.
BBC Sport has had it confirmed by multiple sources that the prospective investor behind plans for LIV 2.0 is Ted Goldthorpe, head of the credit division of international investment firm BC Partners.
Indeed, one insider referred to him simply as "TG", a nickname that suggests he has become a familiar face.
Goldthorpe attended LIV's most recent event in Bedminster, New York, and O'Neil said he was spending time "looking under the hood" of the league.
But in Indianapolis, Goldthorpe kept himself out of public view, even ushered out of a side door of the clubhouse to avoid media huddled by the front entrance.
He did, however, meet players as a group and set out his vision for the future - the primary aim being to make LIV sustainable, and ultimately profitable.
Selling franchises will certainly be part of the plan, and BBC Sport heard from one of the team's general managers about "significant interest" from investors.
O'Neil said the ambition was to set LIV up so it was "built to last".
There would be a reduced schedule of 10 events a year, across five continents.
The final location of those may well depend on which players stick around, with Australia's former Open champion Cameron Smith particularly popular in Adelaide, for example.
O'Neil said the schedule would be aimed at maximising LIV players' ability to be match-fit come the majors.
Players have been promised equity under a deal with a new investor, but quite what that equates to remains unknown.
They will also get key commercial rights back - called 'Name Image Likeness' rights - which means they can maximise their own endorsements.
Prize money was roughly half this week compared to previous events, and that is a sign of things to come.
Over on the American-based PGA Tour - which LIV players are banned from - prize money has increased in recent years, in large part because of LIV.
If the PGA Tour follows through on its plans to have a two-track system - with a Championship Series and a Challenger Series - it is likely that LIV prize money would sit somewhere between those, and higher than the European-based DP World Tour prize money.
'57 players with 57 different mindsets'
If there are no players, there is no LIV 2.0.
So the next few weeks will be critical in providing the specific details players say they're currently lacking to make decisions over their future.
When asked if there was a critical mass of players needed to sign up for the future before a transaction could be done, O'Neil said: "The entirety of our focus is to get to this transaction and get through it.
"Without the players, that becomes very difficult. I have a good level of confidence in my conversation that we'll have a critical mass of the right players to move this league forward."
Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell, who joined LIV in 2022, told BBC Sport the mood among the players was "subdued".
"There are 57 players out here on LIV and there are 57 different mindsets," said the 2010 US Open champion.
"Some guys have some exemptions in other tours, some have nowhere to go [if LIV folds]."
He said he would be "taking a step back" to work out his future after the Indianapolis event.
"If LIV 2.0 goes ahead, we'll look at the schedule and how it all plays out, and see if that suits me and my lifestyle," McDowell added.
"I have an opportunity to go back to the European Tour and play there as well.
"Whether the two of those can happen simultaneously, whether I can only do one or the other, there are questions like that we don't know the answers to. Until I get that, it's very difficult to make any decisions."
When asked by BBC Sport about his future, Smith, who joined LIV just after winning The Open in 2022, said there would be a "little bit of time to think about that once the season is done".
Would he like to stick with LIV? "I really love LIV," he said. "It has done wonders for my family, for golf in Australia, my friends, the people that we've got to meet around the world. It would be a shame for it to be done, but we'll see what happens."
Other players did not feel comfortable speaking on the record.
One senior player said there is an "emotional" feeling among the group as they await clarity.
Another told BBC Sport "it's been great", before quickly adding "it is great".
It was made clear Jon Rahm - whose future is the source of considerable speculation - would not speak to media aside from his tournament obligations.
American Bryson DeChambeau declined an interview request from BBC Sport.
But after Thursday's first round, he said: "We definitely have a lot against us.
"If it works, it works, awesome. If it doesn't, we'll figure things out. Time will move on, and I would say that time heals things.
"I hope people can see that we actually bring value to the game of golf. My wish is that people give us one more shot and be open minded."
Signs of a strange week
Several people over the past few days privately told me this week had been "extraordinary". Here are some examples.
On Monday, Englishmen Lee Westwood and Tyrrell Hatton were sitting side-by-side in the front row of their flight from Dublin to Indianapolis when official confirmation finally came that their season would be ending early this week.
While the Saudi Public Investment Fund had said it would continue funding LIV until the end of the season, the decision to cancel the team event at the end of August in Michigan was necessary financially, and allowed LIV bosses to "focus on the next chapter".
In the press release about the schedule change came significant news regarding the Indianapolis event too - no live music sets on the weekend, which have been seen as a staple at LIV events over the past four years.
Later on Monday it was announced that routine player news conferences the following day wouldn't happen. It was felt, BBC Sport understands, that players would be left fielding questions they simply didn't know the answers to.
There were reports of vendors suing LIV over unpaid invoices, and of prize money being paid more slowly than normal - although BBC Sport understands that latter issue has been resolved.
Then, at 16:30 local time on Tuesday, the driving range emptied, as players headed for a meeting with "the investor". Fifty minutes later they emerged from the clubhouse, with most swerving awaiting media.
A few stopped to chat, but appeared careful about what they divulged. Martin Kaymer said it was "productive and positive".
Sergio Garcia agreed it had been "productive", but when pushed on his future walked away and said "we'll see".
American Brendan Steele was the only player BBC Sport spoke to in the week who has nailed his colours to the mast - he wants to remain a LIV player.
"It feels new life has been breathed into [LIV]. There was a lot of excitement and energy in the room.
"I'm committed to being here, this is where I want to be."
A critical month ahead
When asked by BBC Sport if he had doubts about LIV's existence beyond this week's event in Indianapolis, O'Neil said the "facts are good" and finished his answer by saying "I wouldn't bet against us".
So what's he basing his optimism on?
In terms of uptake of LIV worldwide, LIV said Adelaide attracted a record 115,000 fans - said to make it Australia's highest-attended golf event - and had a global broadcast audience of 5.5m.
Meanwhile, 100,000 fans attended the event in South Africa, and 50,000 went to the recent UK event, according to LIV.
LIV said 30% of its event-goers had never attended a professional golf event before.
O'Neil said that annual attendance in 2026 would surpass that of 2025, with two fewer events.
LIV Golf said revenue grew by more than100% from 2024 to 2025, and the first half of 2026 suggested this would increase again.
O'Neil also said sponsors were not "running for the hills" despite the uncertainty.
Growth is clearly promising. But there will be no doubt in the minds of Goldthorpe and the LIV hierarchy that turning this into a profitable organisation will take a serious shift in outlook, and of course in spending.
Once everyone packs up from Indianapolis on Sunday night, the focus will turn entirely to securing a transaction to give LIV 2.0 a chance of getting off the ground.
There are a few options available - filing for bankruptcy, pre-packaged insolvency, or someone comes in and pays the outstanding bills.
If all outstanding payments were settled, including on player contracts - such as Rahm, who is understood to be owed millions – then players wouldn't be able to break their contracts early.
O'Neil said there was a deadline for players to sign up to LIV 2.0, but wouldn't provide details of what that was.
The manoeuvrings of the PGA Tour and DP World Tour will be crucial.
There are undoubtedly difficult decisions ahead.
This is the end of an era for LIV.
What no one knows yet is whether it is the end full stop.

Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Later on Sunday, a Russian airstrike hit Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest city, killing one person and injured another six, mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram.
- In Kyiv, Merz said Germany’s financial help was not only about protecting Ukraine’s territorial integrity. “We do it deeply in our own interest, for it is a matter of Europe’s security,” he said, adding that Russia was carrying out cyber-attacks and disinformation campaigns targeting European democracy. Russia has said accusations of hybrid warfare are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
- Zelenskyy said on Sunday he believed Russia might have shared jet-drone technology with its ally North Korea. Earlier in the war, North Korea supplied Russia with millions of artillery shells, and it has since provided ballistic missiles that Moscow regularly uses to attack Ukrainian cities. Asked if Russia had shared with North Korea the technology behind its latest generation of jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy told journalists: “They [Russia] are sharing with North Korea all the technologies. I don’t know about the ballistic and etc but I think yes, because North Korea helped them with missiles.”
- Meanwhile, Ukraine’s military has again used drones to deliver food and medicine to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine,  foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sunday. Oleshky, a frontline town on the Dnipro River, which separates Russian and Ukrainian forces, has become “a hell on earth” under Russian occupation since 2022, according to residents. Sybiha, who has previously accused Russia of starving residents, said the latest delivery contained almost four metric tons of food and medicine. Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said last month that Russia had not agreed to Ukrainian proposals to allow civilians to evacuate.
- As Zelenskyy on Sunday said the US wanted to hold a new round of peace talks with Ukraine and Russia by the end of October, India said it was seeking a greater role in brokering an end to the war, the foreign minister said. Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said at a Munich Security Conference in New Delhi on Sunday that India had been advocating for a peace deal “for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy, so we have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard”. He said India was starting with Black Sea safety of shipping but also including discussions about grain and energy exports and “on non-attack possibilities”.

Ola Electric founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal has pledged a 4.32% stake in the electric two-wheeler maker to fund his participation in the company’s proposed rights issue of up to ₹1,000 Cr. In an exchange filing yesterday, the company said the pledge was solely meant to finance Aggarwal’s subscription to the issue and that there were no other pledges outstanding on his securities. “No shares are being sold. The promoter will invest alongside all other shareholders on the same terms,” Ola Electric said. Citing the promoter’s disclosures under SAST regulations, PTI reported that the arrangement involves pledging 20 Cr shares in favour of CTL Trusteeship Limited to secure non-convertible debentures issued by Krutrim Data Centre Pvt Ltd. The report described Krutrim Data Centre as a non-operative promoter group entity owned by Aggarwal, separate from Krutrim SI Designs, which operates the AI and cloud infrastructure businesses. The debenture proceeds will fund Aggarwal’s participation in Ola Electric’s rights issue, it added. Ola Electric’s statement did not disclose the amount raised against the shares or the financing terms. According to the draft letter of offer filed last week, Aggarwal held a 26.52% stake in Ola Electric as of June 30, 2026. The 20 Cr pledged shares represent about 16.3% of that holding. The draft document said Aggarwal has committed to subscribing to his full rights entitlement, subject to provisions allowing him to renounce entitlements in favour of promoter group members or specified investors. He may also subscribe to additional shares or any portion left unsubscribed, subject to minimum public shareholding requirements. The disclosure comes after Ola Electric’s board cleared the rights issue on September 28. The issue is part of a broader ₹1,500 Cr fundraising plan approved by the board on September 5. The company has not announced whether or how it will raise the remaining ₹500 Cr. Ola Electric said it chose the rights issue route to enable participation by eligible retail, institutional, and promoter group shareholders. Debt Repayment, Expansion Drive Fundraise Of the proceeds, the company plans to deploy ₹350 Cr towards repaying or prepaying borrowings of Ola Electric and its material subsidiaries, including accrued interest and applicable prepayment penalties. Another ₹400 Cr is earmarked for organic growth initiatives across its electric mobility and energy storage businesses, including manufacturing, R&D, stores, dealerships, service infrastructure, and sales and marketing. The remaining net proceeds will go towards general corporate purposes. The company expects to deploy the funds during FY27 and FY28. As the shares will be partly paid-up, shareholders will pay a portion on application and the balance through a subsequent call. The draft document envisages completing the first and final call by October 31, 2027, although the board can revise the schedule. The proposed issue follows Ola Electric’s ₹780.2 Cr QIP in June. Of the ₹744.9 Cr net proceeds, it earmarked ₹225 Cr for debt repayment, ₹335 Cr for organic growth initiatives, and ₹184.9 Cr for general corporate purposes. Fundraising Amid Falling Revenue, Market Share The fundraising push comes amid continued pressure on Ola Electric’s business. Its consolidated operating revenue fell 45% to ₹455 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹828 Cr in the year-ago quarter, while net loss narrowed 21.5% to ₹336 Cr from ₹428 Cr. For FY26, operating revenue halved to ₹2,253 Cr from ₹4,514 Cr in FY25, while E2W deliveries fell to 1.74 Lakh units from 3.59 Lakh units. More recently, Ola Electric recorded 13,449 registrations in September, down 3.5% MoM, giving it around 6.5% of the E2W market, according to Vahan data as of October 1. The company described FY26 as a “year of structural reset”, during which it rationalised its retail network, cut costs, strengthened service operations, and focused on improving unit economics. It has since opened its first dealer-operated stores across seven states. Last month, it outlined plans to build a network of more than 500 dealerships over the following two quarters, with dealer partners handling local sales and service and company-owned outlets transitioning into product experience centres. Beyond E2Ws, Ola Electric is expanding its battery cell manufacturing and battery energy storage businesses. It also launched the S1Z escooter range in August, powered by its internally developed Bharat Cell LFP technology. At 13:20 IST, Ola Electric's shares were trading at ₹36.76, down 0.89% from the previous day's close.

While thousands of Indian students head overseas annually for medical degrees, comprising a heavily monitored segment under the National Medical Commission (NMC) and the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS), parliamentary disclosures indicate that centralised tracking of specific discipline-wise student outflows remains complex.
But for many, the journey culminates in a grueling, high-stakes afternoon inside an Indian examination hall. When the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) released the results for the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE) June 2026, the pass rate had plummeted sharply to just 12.4%, triggering nationwide discussions, student protests, and scrutiny over what is locking foreign medical graduates out of medical practice.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
The panic after the paper
Dr. Chaynika Soni, a medical intern in a Government Hospital in Rajasthan who cleared the exam in her second attempt after graduating from Belarus in 2024, recalls, “Every single year after the exam, you’ll see the same thing. Students come out saying, ‘The paper was impossible.’ ‘It was too hard.’ ‘Nobody could solve it.’ Coaching centers will upload videos saying, ‘The paper was unexpected.’ Telegram groups will be filled with panic.”
This panic was visible during the June session, where candidates faced sudden structural shifts. Describing his experience with the exam pattern, Dr. Kshitij Anand said, “The questions were relatively long and time-consuming. I felt the questions were completely unrelated to what I studied. There were some questions I could get direct answers for, but it wasn’t much. They give you questions and options in a way that you take time to figure out answers but not enough time to think.”
He adds that the introduction of unfamiliar video modules caught aspirants off guard: “The Board gave us video questions which I agreed were manageable, but it was a new pattern. The FMGE conducted last January was way more image-based, and the options were comparatively easier to tap than this one. Also, the diagrams I have never seen before.”
Acknowledging these pressures, Professor Dr. Karan Juneja, National Convenor of IMA Junior Doctors’ Network, points out that “More video-based questions (this time), clinical-based questions will be tough for FMG’s [as they are] not exposed to Indian setting and less time make the exam tough.”
Inside the recall analysis
As the National Board of Examinations does not release official FMGE question papers, student-reconstructed “recall” papers serve as the baseline for preparation. A look at the high-weightage sections — Community Medicine (PSM), Internal Medicine, and Obstetrics and Gynaecology — reveals distinct hurdles.
Community Medicine heavily tests India-specific public health administration, including domestic health committees like the Bhore or Kartar Singh committees, local staffing norms at Primary Health Centres, and administrative schemes that foreign universities naturally omit. For a student trained overseas, this often translates to unfamiliar civic administration rather than core medicine.
Conversely, Internal Medicine acts as a control case focused on universal clinical reasoning, ranging from ABG analysis to emergency cardiac protocols. Meanwhile, Obstetrics and Gynaecology balances international diagnostic criteria with clinical application, though candidate performance frequently hinges on interpreting embedded clinical images, manoeuvres, or diagnostic scans.
Weighing these system dynamics, Dr. Samar Kumar, National FMG In-charge for the Federation of All India Medical Association (FAIMA), explains, “In departments such as Medicine, Surgery, and Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Indian hospitals generally see a very large number of patients. This gives doctors and students exposure to a wide variety of clinical presentations and allows them to learn how to manage patients even when resources are limited. I would particularly highlight Community Medicine... If an FMG studies Medicine, Surgery, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, and Community Medicine properly, focuses on clinical concepts, and practices clinical and image-based questions, they should find these areas much more manageable in the FMGE.”
Conceptual depth and the gap in coaching materials
Beyond traditional curriculum differences, candidates found that the depth of questioning defied standard coaching modules. Dr. Ruhi Kumari, who appeared in the June session, explains, “We weren’t trained that way. For example, there was a question on cholera; the answer was an increase in cAMP. I knew it was an increase in cAMP (cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate), but the options were given in biochemistry language. Like, you have to know what cAMP is in biochemistry; only then can you answer that. No coaching institute is teaching anyone like this. Only USMLE tutors do. Because USMLE has always asked in-depth questions. Many clinical questions expect you to have clinical experience. But that’s just unfair, because I will only get that experience after I visit the clinic.”
Dr. Kumari further notes the obsolescence of traditional prep material: “Marrow [an online platform) questions were considered the standard before this exam, but I can tell you they are not anymore. There were a lot of questions that weren’t even asked in many previous years' papers, that flustered everyone... Honestly, I am not sure which resource would give me the most apt training, because no institute is teaching you like that at present. Doing INICET papers is not going to help you, or even NEET-PG papers.”
Logistics, exam conditions, and the transparency debate
The academic difficulty was further compounded by severe logistical hurdles on test day. Dr. Samar Kumar outlines the physical toll: “The first issue was related to examination centres. Multiple centres had inadequate facilities. Some did not have coolers or fans, and in some cases, even drinking water was not adequately available. As you know, the FMG examination is five hours, and overall it takes eight hours. Maintaining concentration in such tough conditions, especially during extreme summer, is something beyond the capacity of many students and FMG doctors particularly when they are not provided with adequate facilities.”
He added regarding the sudden format changes, “The second and most important issue was the sudden introduction of video-based questions in the FMG June 2026 examination. FMGs opposed this later as well and conducted protests regarding this issue in Delhi, Gautam Nagar. The demand of the students was to provide compensation for the sudden introduction of video-based questions, but NBEMS denied the demand.”
Adding to student frustration is a perceived lack of institutional accountability. Dr. Kumar said, “Moreover, the FMG examination does not have any kind of transparency. The questions and answers have never been shown to FMGs. Thus, no one knows how they failed by just one mark, five marks, or ten marks... Then why does NBEMS say that they cannot show the questions and answers together? Why can’t the examination questions and their corresponding answers be disclosed?”
FMGE versus NEET-PG and the time crunch
Comparing the screening test to domestic evaluations, Professor Dr. Karan Juneja, National Convenor of IMA Junior Doctors’ Network, notes that “NEET PG exam standard is being given in FMGE exam as the board-making exam is the same NBE.”
While Indian MBBS graduates prepping for NEET-PG sit within a mature ecosystem of shared question banks and peer networks, foreign-trained graduates often experience thinner access to these informal pipelines.
Dr. Samar Kumar contrasts the two exams, “Recently, FMGE has also included video-based and lengthy clinically oriented questions, which adds another dimension to the examination... FMGE continues to have 300 questions, whereas NEET-PG has moved from the earlier 200-question format to 180 questions. Therefore, FMGE tests not only clinical knowledge and application but also a candidate’s ability to maintain concentration and consistency throughout a long examination. NEET-PG, on the other hand, has its own competitive dynamics, including negative marking and a highly competitive selection process. But if you remove these factors from NEET-PG, then it becomes easier than FMGE.”
This time crunch is intensified by structural scheduling. Dr. Anjali Ayappan from Kochi points out, “Two months is simply not enough preparation time for FMG students, especially considering the amount of syllabus and the situation most FMGs are already in. And bringing the next exam forward to October is especially bad for the June pass-outs. They barely get any time to prepare after the result, and then suddenly they’re expected to appear again in October.”
The long road to registration
Clearing the exam is only the first milestone; graduates face a complex administrative labyrinth before they can practice. Dr. Parvathy Sabu, who cleared the exam and works in a Government Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, said, “Internship posts for FMGs are fewer across almost every State, and protests to increase seats are seen often... By the time you get PR [permanent registration], best-case scenario, approximately 8 years have gone by (including course duration) and a lot of money. Abroad MBBS is a very long-term investment that many don’t realise initially. I think the integration into Indian healthcare and internship issues are the biggest challenges faced by FMGs.”
Reflecting on these cumulative pressures, Dr. Madhavi Gurung, an FMG aspirant who studied in the U.K., concludes, “Many of my friends skipped FMGE and are now doing residency in the U.S., some are working non-training jobs in the U.K., and some are on track to settle in Australia. The struggle doesn’t end after NEET-UG. And with rising competition and reservation quotas, the system is tough. Every year wasted in endless NEET attempts can drain your mental health and confidence. I’m now planning to take AMC Part 1 by the end of this year and hopefully move abroad permanently.”

The vanishing world of India's street magicians
- Published
Sitting in his cramped Delhi home, Ishamuddin Khan can still make a rope appear to rise into the air.
The 55-year-old magician spent decades performing a trick once dismissed as legend, and still keeps photographs and newspaper clippings from his years of international fame.
These days, he spends more time looking back at those memories than performing the trick.
"The times have changed," he says. "Street magic is dying a slow death. It is on a ventilator."
Khan's story reflects a wider change in India, where traditional street performers are finding it increasingly difficult to make a living from their craft.
Magicians, jugglers, puppeteers and acrobats once made a living from crowds in public spaces. Changing entertainment habits and tighter restrictions have made audiences harder to find, pushing many out of the profession.
Khan, one of India's best-known magicians, comes from the Madari community, which has a long tradition of performing in public spaces.
There are no official figures, but Khan says community records identify about 400 Madari families in Delhi, with hundreds more in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Telangana.
Despite their small numbers today, the Madaris trace their roots back centuries.
Historian Ashok Mathur says Madari traditions have roots in Indian folklore, mythology and the long history of travelling performers.
"For generations, these skills were passed through families," he explains.
Khan followed the same path, learning magic from his father and uncles and performing from the age of 12. By his early 20s, he had mastered the rope trick that would later make him famous.
The trick – in which a rope appears to rise into the air before a boy climbs it – was long associated with the mythology of Indian street magic and widely considered impossible, until Khan performed it.
He says it took six years to master the trick, which he first performed publicly in 1995 outside Delhi's iconic Qutub Minar. Two years later, he performed it before 30,000 people on a beach in Karnataka.
His trick brought international attention, and that led to tours to the UK, France, Germany and Japan.
Khan hoped the fame would shine a light on India's traditional performers. For a while, it did. But the attention faded.
As audiences turned to new forms of entertainment and public performance opportunities dwindled, many magicians found it harder to make a living from skills passed down through generations.
One of them is 40-year-old Imam Khan.
Once a magician, Imam now makes a living collecting bottles and recyclables from Delhi's streets. He spends much of his time rag-picking near a western Delhi dump, earning about 200 rupees ($2; £1.57) a day.
Experts say the decline in street performance has multiple causes, chief among them the changing nature of public spaces.
Anurupa Roy, founder of Katkatha Puppet Arts Trust, says performers increasingly struggle to find audiences as public spaces shrink.
"Closed parks and residential societies that bar outsiders are limiting spaces for performance."
Researcher and performer Komita Dhanda says changing attitudes to public spaces are also driving the decline.
"With tighter security, especially in busy town and city centres, there is little space left for street performers," she says.
It is not just individual artists who struggle to get permission. Dhanda says her well-known street theatre group, Jana Natya Manch, often faces hurdles performing in public spaces.
For many artists, the challenge is not just finding a venue but navigating unclear rules over what is allowed.
Most street performers rely on voluntary payments, but experts say the line between performing for money and begging can blur.
Unlike the UK, India has no federal busking framework. Performers instead navigate state-level rules on public order, obstruction, noise and public land.
"This is why street performers often have to face municipal and police regulations governing public spaces, as well as state-specific anti-begging laws," says lawyer Kaushik Mitra.
For many artists, Covid made a bad situation worse.
When India imposed its 2020 lockdown, public performances stopped. Many magicians returned to their villages; some never came back.
"We saw a decline in public performances after this period," Dhanda says. "The brunt was especially harsh for street magicians and performers, many of whom did not return to cities."
For the artists who did return and continue the trade, the challenges only increased.
Shahim Khan, 42, still performs magic on Delhi's streets, sometimes with his 12-year-old daughter, Alia.
Much of his work is now confined to industrial areas, far from the busy public spaces where he once performed, hitting his earnings hard.
Before the pandemic, he could stage four or five shows a day, earning 1,000-1,200 rupees.
"Now I barely manage two shows and earn 200-400 rupees," he says.
The rise of short-form digital entertainment has added to the pressures on traditional performers, experts say. So have changing attitudes towards street arts.
"There was a lot of Western interest in things like the rope trick decades ago. But forms and tastes have changed, and so has what India chooses to showcase," Dhanda says.
For Khan, the loss is about more than money. He fears an art passed down generations could disappear if no-one learns it.
"A trick can survive only if someone learns it," he says.
His son, Altamash, began performing with him as a teenager but now works decorating parties with balloons. In his 30s, he has largely left performing behind.
Years without regular practice have dulled his skills. When he demonstrated his juggling for the BBC, he struggled to find the rhythm.
"I am slowly forgetting all the tricks," he said.
Khan had hoped his son would carry on the family tradition. Altamash had hoped to make a name for himself too, but it did not work out.
"I knew I may not achieve the fame my father has, but I did not think there would come a time when performing would not remain an option," he says.

A while back, I was at physical therapy, and the topic of tennis came up. Someone said something about yellow tennis balls, and I was like… “What? They’re green.” And then someone else chimed in, “No, they’re yellow!” And then someone across the room hollered, “No, they’re obviously green.”
What color is a tennis ball?
A neuroscientist and artist argue there’s no such thing as a color.
There was basically a physical therapy uproar. And when I started asking other people how they saw them — yellow or green — they told me they couldn’t even believe there was a debate. So I called up Bevil Conway. He’s a neuroscientist who heads up a lab at the National Eye Institute. He’s working on a book called Color Coded, which is due out next year. And he’s also a working artist — which is actually how he got into studying color in the first place.
Conway told me there’s a pretty good reason for why so many people disagree about tennis balls. He said it’s simple: “There’s no such thing as a color.”
In the latest episode of Unexplainable, I talked with Conway about what color even is, the viral dress fight (black and blue or white and gold?), and why we get so upset when people don’t see color the same way we do. Below is an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. Listen to the episode anywhere you get your podcasts or you can watch on Netflix.
So you are an artist. You are also a neuroscientist. You study color. You’re also working on a book about color. Are there still color mysteries? Are there things science doesn’t know about color?
There are lots of mysteries about color. For a long time, people thought that color was a little bit like a filter, that everything that’s really important is in black and white, and then there’s a color filter you put on top of it.
But a bunch of years ago, my lab were blown away to discover that there’s as much brain involved in processing color as there is in face recognition.
The same amount of processing power?
Yeah, there’s tons and tons of tissue [and] pretty fancy bits of brain that are doing pretty high-level things — parts of brain we think of as being involved in social cognition and in high-level reasoning and visual memory. Color must be more than just this little add-on. It’s doing something much deeper. So we’re trying to understand what those bits of brain are doing.
So what is color? How does it work? How do our brains and eyes perceive it?
The classic definition would be: Color is the visual feature that you get from wavelength properties of the light entering your eye. People typically see the long wavelength end as red light, and then going through short wavelengths, you know, following ROYGBIV: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
If color were just wavelength, then an object under blue light would look blue, and the same object under yellow light would look yellow. And that wouldn’t be very helpful — because what you want is a signal that tells you about objects, immune to the lighting condition. You want them to always have that color.
A perfect example is a peach. If you look at a peach outside and you look at it inside, it’s always gonna look like a peach color. But if you looked at the pattern of wavelengths that are coming off of the peach, they’re very different under different lighting conditions. They should be different colors if color were just wavelength, but they’re not. Those two different compositions of wavelengths look the same color.
What I think is so cool about color is it’s so fundamental for how we need to experience the world — but the mechanics of how it does it teaches us a lot about the brain.
What we’re talking about is color constancy. That is, an object’s color is constant despite the viewing conditions.
So if the peach is fundamentally a different color inside and outside, and our brains are telling us that it is still, you know, peach colored, how are our brains deceiving us?
So it’s not fundamentally a different color. It’s the same color. That’s the cool thing. The problem is that you are carrying around, Noam, in your head an idea that color is wavelength, and that is the mistake.
Color is not wavelength! And we’ve known this for a long time. But the problem is that we want something that is an empirical, measurable number that’s outside of an observer, that’s a thing out there in the world, that would be the same number regardless of who looks at it. And color, at its core, is not that.
Color is dependent on your own visual system interacting with the world. And that doesn’t mean it’s any less real. It just means that its reality is dependent on psychological neural brain processes. And that’s what makes color fascinating.
Color is, you’re saying, something that is essentially created in the brain.
Absolutely, yes. Color is a generative product of the brain that gives us reliable, useful, true, meaningful, objective information, but it itself is not [those things]. It’s some generative product of your brain in order to come up with this information that’s useful and meaningful about the world.
[Your brain is] actually creating that thing that is a color. Colors don’t exist out there in the world independent of a viewer to see them.
Is this related to “the dress” — you know, like 10 years ago when that photo of a dress went viral, and a bunch of people on the internet thought it was blue and black, and a bunch of other people thought it was white and gold, and everyone got super upset? Is this the same type of thing, of seeing something in different lighting or different contexts and perceiving a different color?
It is. So the dress was fascinating because people with normal color vision looking at exactly the same thing were asserting very different perceptions.
And, you know, from a deep kind of philosophical point of view, it’s important because they weren’t saying, “Yeah, it kinda looks different to me, but I understand how you could see it as different.” They were like, “No, it is white and gold.” And other people were saying, “It is different colors.” That was, for me professionally and personally, a really big deal because it underscored this fact that color is this generative, constructive thing that your brain is doing, making all kinds of assumptions, filling in the gaps about lighting, about what you think you’re seeing.
In the case of the dress, it’s such a crappy little photograph, very blurry. It doesn’t give you a lot of context. And your visual system, your own brain, has to make a guess about what the lighting is. And if your brain guesses that the lighting is nice, warm, direct sunlight, then it implicitly subtracts out a little bit of the yellow from the image, and you see it as blue and black. Whereas other people looking at exactly the same pixels on the same monitor who assume that the lighting is cool, indirect, shaded light from blue sky, their brains color-correct the image, subtract out some of the blue, and they see it as white and gold. And so you have these two groups of people whose brains have just made different assumptions.
Why do you think that left people feeling so unnerved? When this happened, people could not possibly believe someone else could look at that dress and see a different color.
It was amazing! And, you know, it’s still, to date, I think, the most viral image in the history of the internet. Right when it came out, my initial reaction too was like, “Huh, that’s weird. I wonder what’s going on there.” And a lot of my colleagues thought, “Well, maybe it’s got to do with proportions of rods and cones, or people are looking at different displays, or maybe people are just silently color blind.”
But I think the idea that your own brain could play such a fundamental role in determining what the pattern of wavelengths means, even for vision scientists, wasn’t sitting front of mind.
I think the reason that it played so deeply, if I could wax poetic, it’s that our contemporary society depends on a shared experience, right? Our laws depend on a common idea of what’s right and wrong.
Yeah, like whether my red is your red; we still need to be able to point at something and agree that it’s red.
Yes, and here was an example where it was like: “That isn’t white and gold, that’s blue and black, clearly. Do we live in a shared reality?”
And if you can’t trust your eyes, what can you trust? I think people genuinely felt like, “Is this the beginning of the end?” Like, “Is our whole society collapsing?” I mean, look at Twitter, there were all sorts of expletives flying around.
Have you ever gotten into an argument about a color? I once got into an argument about tennis balls and what color they were.
Yeah, what color are they? I’m curious.
I couldn’t believe anyone thought they were yellow! I always thought they were green.
They’re totally yellow. I mean, we can get into one now. You’re wrong. It’s so funny — I really thought that they were definitionally yellow.
So what is going on with tennis balls?
Tennis balls are funny. I mean, if you ask people to pick their best example of green and blue and red and orange and yellow and so on, there’s a lot of variability. Green and blue is the most variable. Some people’s best example of green is another person’s best example of blue.
Meaning, you could ask me to pick a color that would be perfectly green, and then someone else would be like, “No, that’s blue.”
Yeah, exactly. And this isn’t language-based. This is true across all cultures.
We just perceive blues and greens kinda badly or vaguely?
Yeah, and one of the ideas that we have about that is that blues and greens aren’t really the colors that are tied to objects.
So if I ask you what colors are objects, it’s a weird question! It’s like, objects can be any colors. But it turns out, if you actually go and measure, you know, the colors of things that you choose to label in the world, most of them are, like, yellow, brown, red, pink, some purples, not many.
Yeah, I guess green and blue is the background. Like green’s the forest, and blue is the sky.
Yeah, exactly. And, and even in nature, there are very few natural blue objects, and that’s partly what made blue as a pigment so desirable. So what’s weird about yellow is that yellow, if you just ask people in the rainbow to pick where yellow is, people are incredibly consistent.
So people really know yellow.
They really know yellow. And I think what’s going on with the tennis ball is that it is a little bit fluorescent. It’s actually emitting a little bit more light than it’s taking in because it’s reprocessing it, short-wavelength light in the visible spectrum.
So they’ve picked this bright yellow, which is right at the peak of our visual system sensitivity. So the color of the tennis ball is the optimal wavelength that we can detect with our eyes, and it’s right in that range where it’s technically probably closer to green than it is to yellow. But because it’s so bright, and yellow is considered a bright color, the brightest color, people could be persuaded to see it in a yellow direction.
What I hear you saying is that I’m right — and it’s green.
Yeah, yeah. Although, I still like it as yellow.

California’s attorney general and three city attorneys announced a $272.5 million settlement with Lyft after allegations that the company “committed wage theft by misclassifying drivers as independent contractors rather than employees” between 2016 and 2020, according to a Thursday statement.
The case dates back to May 2020, when then-Attorney General Xavier Becerra, who is now the Democratic candidate for governor, sued both Uber and Lyft. That lawsuit said the ridehailing companies evaded state law when they declared that their drivers were not employees.
Thursday’s settlement affects only Lyft, while the case against Uber continues.
“We are proud to announce this landmark win for workers, the largest misclassification settlement in California’s history,” Attorney General Rob Bonta said in the statement. “Rideshare companies like Lyft have enjoyed massive growth and profits on the backs of drivers over the past decade, many who are from immigrant communities and communities of color.”
The city attorneys echoed this sentiment.
“Los Angeles and our statewide partners will not allow businesses to exploit their workers and evade their obligations under the law,” Los Angeles City Attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto said in the same statement. “When companies misclassify their workers, they deny them critical protections and shift the burden onto taxpayers. This historic settlement sends a clear message: Companies must follow the law, pay their fair share, and play by the rules.”
Ever since these rideshare companies began in the early 2010s, they have been scrutinized for underpaying and mistreating drivers. The specific state law that California used to challenge the companies is known as Assembly Bill 5 (AB5), which enshrined a three-part test to determine if someone is properly classified as an independent contractor or an employee.

OpenAI will add a digital watermark to text and code generated in the EU
This is to comply with the region's new AI transparency rules.
OpenAI just announced its plans to comply with part of the European Union's new AI transparency rules. The company will soon begin adding an invisible watermark to text and code generated in the EU. This follows a similar move by Anthropic earlier this year.
OpenAI is using a proprietary system called textGrain that "adds an invisible statistical signal to the model's word choices." Once added, a detector can spot these signals and ascertain if there's a watermark.
The company says the system "matched or exceeded" the performance of other approaches, like SynthID for text. However, it still cautions that "strong performance under ideal conditions does not guarantee reliable detection in everyday use."
That's corporate speak for "it may not always work." It admits that shorter text is harder to detect, with around an 80 percent success rate. The same goes for "content such as mathematics." Even editing text seems to bring down the success rate. OpenAI does plan on making the technology available in open source so others can tweak it.
The watermark will not be enabled by default, except for "eligible ChatGPT and Codex text output in the European Union." Customers will be able to opt-in "for select models," though it didn't specify which models would be available to the general global public.
OpenAI is being a bit more cautious when it comes to the detection software. Access will initially be limited to "approved researchers and expert organizations." Also, the detector doesn't identify the user or reveal prompts or conversations.
Article 50 of the EU's AI Act mandates that providers of generative AI systems make text outputs identifiable in a machine-readable way. This already pertains to new companies entering the market, but pre-existing entities have until December 2 to comply. This includes organizations like OpenAI and Anthropic, of course, but also Microsoft, Google and Meta, among others.

Samoa leader apologises for Nazi salute after video from 2007 emerges
- Published
Samoa's prime minister has apologised after a video emerged of him giving a Nazi salute while saying "Heil Hitler" at a family gathering.
In the seven-second clip filmed in July 2007, Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt is seen leading about a dozen people in the salute. "Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler!" he says, then thanks the group for responding.
Schmidt has acknowledged that his words and gesture "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt", adding that the clip was recorded at a private gathering and "not intended for the public".
"I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism," Schmidt said in a statement published on Facebook on Monday.
The footage was first reported by local outlet the Samoa Observer in a news story on Sunday.
It said the video was filmed at a Schmidt family reunion in July 2007, when Schmidt was deputy speaker of parliament and quoted a family member who said he was the master of ceremonies at the gathering.
Samoa, a tiny island nation of about 221,000 people, sits about halfway between New Zealand and Hawaii.
It was under Germany's control in the early 20th century, but the colonisation ended shortly after World War One broke out.
Schmidt, who has Samoan and German heritage, took office as the country's eighth prime minister in September 2025.
He wore a Jewish prayer shawl during his swearing-in ceremony and has made clear his support for Israel during the early days of his premiership, saying that Samoa "stood with Israel".
"If people around the world don't like it, that's up to them, but Samoa stands with the land of God... There is only one God our country believes in, the God of Israel," he had said.

Colombia launches joint task force to protect pipeline and fight ELN rebels
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has launched a joint task force that will fight rebel groups and drug gangs in the country's northeast
BOGOTA, Colombia -- Colombia's president launched a joint task force Monday that will fight rebel groups and drug gangs in the country's northeast, as the government changes its strategy in dealing with criminal groups, replacing peace talks with various military offensives.
President Abelardo de la Espriella said one of the main missions of the newly designated task force Urano will be to stop Colombia’s largest remaining rebel group, the National Liberation Army, from stealing gasoline and diesel from a pipeline that runs from the country's Caribbean coast to a refinery in Barrancabermeja.
De la Espriella accused the group, known also as the ELN, of stealing fuel from the pipeline to “feed” criminal economies.
“They use it to make cocaine, to power illegal mines and to generate income for terrorist activities,” he said Monday at a ceremony in Valledupar.
For almost two decades, Colombia’s military deployed joint task forces — with troops from the army, the navy and the air force — to fight rebel groups in rural areas. The task forces were overseen directly by commanders in Bogota and helped the military achieve key victories against the FARC rebels until a peace deal was signed with that group in 2016.
The strategy was dropped two years ago by former President Gustavo Petro's administration, as officials tried to give army commanders in rural areas greater control over operations. Some critics said the decision weakened Colombia’s military.
De la Espriella, a conservative who was sworn into office in August, has canceled peace talks with the nation’s remaining rebel groups.
He said that by bringing back the joint task forces, the government will be able to confront rebel groups and drug gangs with greater force. He added that the Urano task force will also include police officers.
“There will be no negotiations or empathy with terrorism,” he said.

A chronic autoimmune skin condition in which the body’s immune system mistakes melanocytes (cells which produce melanin, giving colour to your skin, hair and eyes) as enemies and attacks them. This leads to patches of depigmentation anywhere in your body. This condition is known as vitiligo.
Types of vitiligo
The main types of vitiligo are non-segmental and segmental vitiligo.
Non-segmental vitiligo is the most common form, where colour loss appears symmetrically on both sides of the body, such as both hands or both knees. Segmental vitiligo, on the other hand, often starts at a younger age and affects only one side or a single specific area of the body.
What causes vitiligo?
While the primary reason for vitiligo is not fully understood, it is seen to be caused by various factors, from genetics to immune dysfunction.
Research has shown that vitiligo is primarily a T-cell–mediated autoimmune disease where CD8+ cytotoxic T cells attack and destroy skin pigment cells called melanocytes, leading to white patches on the skin.
Having a family member with vitiligo or other autoimmune diseases is shown to have an increased risk, suggesting shared genetic susceptibility. Environmental factors like oxidative stress, skin trauma, and certain chemicals can sometimes trigger or worsen vitiligo in genetically susceptible people.
Vitiligo is also often associated with other autoimmune conditions, especially autoimmune thyroid disease, so clinicians may screen for these in some patients.
Symptoms of vitiligo
The main symptom of vitiligo is depigmentation and the appearance of patches on your body. This can be anywhere from your face and hands to your knees or feet. Hair in the affected area may also turn white.
There are various ways through which doctors can help you diagnose vitiligo and determine what type of vitiligo you may have. One major examination done is the Wood’s lamp examination, where ultraviolet light is used to distinguish vitiligo from other hypopigmented conditions.
Treatment options
Treatment for vitiligo is mostly connected to re-pigmentation, or slowing progression, depending on the type of vitiligo and patient preference rather than a guaranteed cure.
There are various types of topical treatments (like creams for external use) which can often help with inflammation, as well as medical light treatments like narrowband UVB phototherapy and excimer laser or lamp. Availability of certain treatments also changes from country to country and by the patient’s age group. There are situations where oral medication is also used for the short term. People with stable vitiligo can also consider surgical options if other treatments are not working, and depigmentation therapy if a major part of the person’s natural pigmentation is lost.

Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford
- Published
President Donald Trump has said the US moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
Speaking to reporters as he departed for Nebraska on Monday, Trump said the US had known of a "threat", which led them to move the bombers.
Earlier on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to Trump's comments last week, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.
- What prompted the US bombers to leave RAF Fairford? 
  - Published2 hours ago
- What makes RAF Fairford one of the UK's most important military sites? 
  - Published6 days ago
Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
While speaking to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.
Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident.
"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."
He added Washington "actually knows the people that made the threat", but he did not confirm who.
The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairford remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran.
One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb - a covert drone attack on five Russian bases in June last year - as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance.
"Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously," the source said.
Trump's comments, and those of Vance before him, stand in stark contrast to those of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
While both Trump and Vance pointed to an unspecified threat, Rubio was much more guarded in his language, noting that it was "not unusual" for military units and assets to rotate and be moved around the world.
RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Following the release of the first five men, Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident.
Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
Speaking earlier on Monday, Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.
He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."
Rubio said the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very co-operative since the incident.
Vance later said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington felt Iran was doing what it had "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".
Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but he did not provide further details, while Rubio said it had "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
The redeployment from RAF Fairford will reduce America's capacity to "quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat", Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute told the Reuters news agency.
However, the use of the base had already been limited given London's stipulation that it should only be used for defensive strikes, he added.
The planes could potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf to reduce the need for air-to-air refuelling but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, Bergs added.

The former India captain oversaw the men’s and women’s teams as DC’s director of cricket between 2023 and 2024, and was the head coach of the Pretoria Capitals in the SA20 for the 2025 season.

Parth Jindal, Delhi Capitals chairman and co-owner, said: “Dada is and has always been an integral part of the Delhi Capitals family. The Russian ‘lab leak’ and America’s great weakness
After Trump withdrew from the WHO and slashed funding for medical research, American scientists told me they feared China would take over as the world leader in science. Situations like this underscore how risky that move was, writes Holly Baxter

There’s a lot we don’t know about what has happened in Siberia. What we do know: A 28-year-old laboratory worker at an anti-plague research institute in Irkutsk died last week after developing severe pneumonia. Russian authorities have described her illness as pneumonia of unknown origin and said tests found no connection to the dangerous pathogens she worked with. But reports have circulated that she may have accidentally broken a test tube containing plague bacteria, and the hospital where she was treated has been quarantined. Around 200 people who may have had contact with her have reportedly been placed under observation.
So, no, it’s not Covid again. And it might not be a plague outbreak at all. But the possibility of a laboratory accident involving Yersinia pestis, the bacterium responsible for plague, is sufficiently alarming to have attracted international attention.
Pneumonic plague is particularly dangerous because it can spread between people through respiratory droplets. However, it is a bacterial disease rather than a viral one, meaning it’s generally treatable with antibiotics when caught quickly. It’s also not that transmissible: you’d have to be in very close contact with an infected person to catch it. None of this was the case with Covid.
Dr. Simon Clarke, an associate professor of cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, puts the lab-leak theory in useful perspective. “It is not unheard of for pathogens to escape from labs,” he says. High-containment laboratories are designed around precisely this possibility, with multiple layers of protection, safety cabinets, airflow systems and strict procedures. Lab-acquired infections are rare, and “a broken tube would not automatically lead to exposure or infection.” But it is unusual, he says, for test tubes to be used that much at all these days, which raises its own questions.
All of this means that “an awful lot must have gone wrong” for a worker to become infected in the way that’s been reported.
The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute is a large research facility that deals with the kind of plague bacteria still circulating among animals in Siberia (and other parts of the world.) Irkutsk itself is a long way away from major international cities like Moscow and St. Petersburg — the distance is similar to the distance between New York and Los Angeles, necessitating seven-hour flights or multi-day train rides across desolate landscapes — and the Siberian region, which borders Mongolia and China, has very different weather patterns to the European parts of Russia, which border places like Finland and Ukraine.
All of this context is important, when you consider how successful a quarantine might be and why a plague lab might be based in Irkutsk in the first place. Indeed, the whole institute is currently locked down with around 60 people inside, according to local media reports. But none of this is fully reassuring to a world that’s still reeling from the Covid pandemic.
The Trump administration says it is watching the situation. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that he was “monitoring it closely,” and that he doesn’t believe it’s a cause for alarm. American agencies including the CDC and the State Department are, like everybody else, seeking more information. Unfortunately, the Trump administration has somewhat kneecapped itself in this regard.
The U.S. formally withdrew from the World Health Organization in January, ending its membership, funding and personnel involvement amid claims of political motivation and a lack of transparency. The WHO isn’t perfect — and Russia is certainly not the most transparent country in the world — but it was the best we had when it came to information-sharing during Covid.
America can, of course, still gather intelligence on the current situation. It can certainly speak directly to Russia. But global disease surveillance works best when information moves quickly and scientists and public health officials have established channels through which they can share it. And although Putin and Trump have shared a few friendly visits, Trump himself complained during the early days of the Ukraine war that he’d have a phone call with Putin that he thought had gone well and then hear a couple of hours later that Russia had just bombed a hospital.
America is currently trying to work out what its place is in the next era of biomedical science. The Trump administration has restricted federal support for research, disrupted the NIH, made it harder for talented foreign students to get visas to study at elite universities in the US, and made it harder for US scientists to collaborate with scientists across the world. When I asked researchers in cutting-edge genetics and cancer research in New York what the effect had been on their work, they said that it had been slowed and fractured to the point that they believed China would now take over as the global leader in biomedical breakthroughs. In their view, the damage has already been done.
Being longtime allies, China and Russia already have closer comms than the U.S. has with either country. If China becomes the world leader in medical research, it will bring Russia along for the ride. They will share developments and experiments both publicly and privately, especially during times of emergency and quarantine. They will be more honest with each other than they will be with the rest of the world. Current research suggests America still has significant advantages in the quality and commercial reach of its biomedical science. But China is closing the gap, particularly in areas such as clinical trials, drug development and manufacturing.
The country that can sequence a pathogen fastest, develop a diagnostic fastest, test a treatment fastest and manufacture it at scale is building the infrastructure that determines how quickly it can protect its own population when something unexpected happens. This is also where Trump’s hand-wavey, vibes-based approach to medicine starts to become extremely concerning for Americans.
America spent decades building an extraordinary scientific and public health infrastructure partly because infectious diseases do not respect national borders. Now, at the moment when biological technology is becoming more powerful, more consequential and more strategically important, the country is pulling back from some of the international institutions and research structures that helped give it that advantage. A steadfast belief in rampant individualism has eroded America’s ability to wield bigger, more effective influence from within a group.
Meanwhile, over 1,000 miles away, Russian officials don’t seem to be able to agree on whether there was a lab leak or not — but enough local media (and social media) exists around Irkutsk that details have emerged of hospital lockdowns and mask mandates. Contacts at the UN told me that they started hearing rumors about a Russian lab leak last week, but nothing concrete had been confirmed by anyone within the country’s diplomatic corps. This is how information does tend to filter out of Russia: through hearsay, with an effort at state control that doesn’t entirely hold, and a lot of bluster about how the media can’t be trusted. It’s not a winning strategy.
Still, the Irkutsk incident may turn out to be nothing more than a frightening story about a laboratory worker who died from an illness that was never the pneumonic plague; or perhaps it will prove to have been the plague, and a serious breach, followed by successful quarantines and lessons learned. But it is hardly the only pathogen we should be worrying about.
From Ebola to the other coronaviruses already circulating in the world, there are viruses and bacteria with the potential to become epidemics given the right, or wrong, conditions. The only real defence is the unglamorous stuff: open communication, functioning institutions and countries willing to share information before a pathogen has crossed their borders.
One would hope the most powerful countries in the world might understand that. But none of it guarantees a shareable soundbite — so perhaps hope is all we have left.
