Delhi’s new draft electoral roll has 97,53,577 names. In February 2025, 94,94,607 people voted in the Delhi assembly elections. Eighteen months later, the roll of eligible voters has just 2,58,970, or 2.7%, more names than the number of people who turned out to vote last year.
Now, in 24 of Delhi’s 70 assembly constituencies, the gap has disappeared altogether: The draft roll contains fewer names than the number of people who actually voted in those seats in 2025.
The numbers raise a fundamental question about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR): Has the exercise removed large numbers of people who were genuine, eligible voters and actually cast their ballots in 2025? Or did the electoral rolls used for that election contain a large number of names that should never have been there — including people who had died, shifted or were duplicated? The Election Commission of India (ECI) needs to account for the discrepancy.
An Alt News analysis of constituency-wise data procured and compiled by Mandate Analytics from ECI’s own records shows that the draft roll published on August 31, 2026, under the SIR has fewer names than the number of people who voted in the 2025 election in 24 constituencies.
Delhi SIR in Numbers
The SIR, which began in Bihar in June 2025, has resulted in more than 13 crore names being excluded from draft electoral rolls across 30 states and union territories, according to The Indian Express. In Delhi, the draft roll has shrunk by 58,73,159 names, or 37.6%, compared with the 2025 electoral roll.
The SIR began with a base list of 1.45 crore names — 11.16 lakh fewer than the electoral roll used for the 2025 election. Every elector on the base list was to receive an enumeration form from a booth level officer (BLO) and return the completed form. Forms that were not returned were marked “uncollectable” and assigned one of the ASDDO categories: absent, shifted, dead, duplicate or other. These electors were then excluded from the draft roll. Across Delhi, 47,56,722 forms, which is nearly a third of the base list, were marked uncollectable.
The exclusions were unevenly distributed. In South East Delhi, an average of 43.5% of the base-list names in each constituency were marked uncollectable, compared with 24.3% in Outer North Delhi.
The 24 Constituencies Which Throw up a Puzzle
In February 2025, Sangam Vihar had 2,05,647 names on its electoral roll, and 1,25,723 people voted. BJP’s Chandan Kumar Choudhary won the seat by 344 votes — the narrowest margin in the city. The SIR draft roll now lists 1,14,412 electors in Sangam Vihar: 91,235 fewer than the 2025 roll and 11,311 fewer than the number of people who actually voted.
The disparity extends across 24 constituencies. A total of 28,89,268 people voted in these seats in 2025, while the SIR draft roll now has just 27,66,145 names. This means that, even under the impossible assumption that every person on the current draft roll voted in 2025, at least 1,23,123 people who actually voted last year are no longer on the draft rolls of these constituencies.
That is a floor, not an estimate of the actual number. The real number of 2025 voters missing from the draft rolls can only be higher.
These 24 constituencies had 49,14,127 electors in 2025, of whom 58.8% voted. The SIR draft roll now contains 27,66,145 names — just 56.3% of the 2025 electorate, below the 58.8% turnout. In Tughlakabad, 56.1% of electors voted in 2025, while the draft roll contains just 49% of the 2025 electorate. In New Delhi, 56.7% voted; the draft roll contains 48.1%.
Across these constituencies, the electoral roll has fallen by 21,47,982 names, or 43.7%, since 2025. Of these, 4,10,759 names were already absent from the SIR base list, while 17,37,223 forms were marked uncollectable during the revision. Tughlakabad has the highest uncollectable rate in Delhi, at 47.8% of its base list.
All seven constituencies in South East Delhi — Jangpura, Kasturba Nagar, Sangam Vihar, Kalkaji, Tughlakabad, Badarpur and Okhla — are among the 24 constituencies where the draft roll is smaller than the number of people who voted in 2025.
In four seats the gap between the draft roll and 2025 turnout is larger than the margin that decided the seat. These are: Sangam Vihar, New Delhi, Delhi Cantt and Rajinder Nagar. In New Delhi, Arvind Kejriwal lost by 4,089 votes. The seat had 1,08,788 electors in 2025; the draft roll has 52,368, which is 9,318 short of the number of people who voted.
The Cuts are not Over
It is also worth remembering that the draft roll is not the final roll; it is likely to shrink further.
After the uncollectable forms were set aside, a second round of exclusions began. Electors whose names appeared on the draft roll are now being served notices requiring them to produce documents. Those unable to establish their eligibility risk being excluded from the final roll. In these 24 constituencies, 9,78,541 electors — about 35% of those on the draft roll — have been served notices. Across Delhi, the figure is 33.13 lakh.
The impact could extend well beyond these 24 constituencies. If just one in 10 of the electors served notices is ultimately excluded, 39 of Delhi’s 70 constituencies would have fewer names on the final roll than the number of people who voted there in 2025.
The Question the EC has to Answer
In other words, in February 2025, the ECI’s roll for these 24 constituencies had 49.14 lakh names, and 28.89 lakh people voted. Its own revision now leaves just 27.66 lakh names on the draft roll — fewer than the number of people who actually voted in those constituencies 18 months ago. And the roll is still shrinking.
The numbers demand an explanation. Either the SIR has excluded large numbers of genuine, living residents who voted in the 2025 election, or the rolls on which the ECI conducted that election contained lakhs of names that should not have been there. Either way, the discrepancy is one the Commission needs to account for.
It is also, in substance, the same Election Commission. The Delhi election was conducted under chief election commissioner (CEC) Rajiv Kumar, with Gyanesh Kumar and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu as election commissioners. Gyanesh Kumar took over as CEC on February 19, 2025, just days after the results. He has since overseen the SIR exercise.
Questions from Inside the Commission
These numbers come at a time when the SIR is itself facing scrutiny within the Election Commission.
An investigation by The Indian Express, published on September 23, reported that two of the three members of the Commission, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, objected on record at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders issued during the nationwide rollout of the SIR. In several instances, they recorded that decisions had been taken without their knowledge. The report does not examine Delhi, but one of the concerns it raises is directly relevant to the revision here.
Who decided? The ECI has repeatedly responded to allegations of electoral-roll manipulation by pointing out that rolls in each constituency are prepared and maintained under the authority of the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO), a statutory official. But according to The Indian Express, both Commissioners raised concerns that this safeguard was being weakened. Joshi flagged the increasing centralisation of the electoral-roll database, while Sandhu recorded that state election officials had said they did not have full access to ERONet, the software used to maintain the rolls.
That raises a question for Delhi: when 17.37 lakh names were marked uncollectable across 24 constituencies, and all seven constituencies in South East Delhi were among those with the highest rates, who made those determinations? Were they made by the constituency-level EROs, as the statutory framework envisages, or were decisions being taken or directed elsewhere? The ECI has not publicly explained this.
Alt News has sent questions to the Election Commission of India seeking an explanation. This report will be updated if and when a response is received.
The constituency-level data used in this report was procured and compiled by Mandate Analytics from records published by the Election Commission of India and the chief electoral officer (CEO), Delhi. Alt News independently verified the figures against the original ECI and CEO Delhi documents. The constituency-wise figures for electors issued notices are as compiled by Mandate Analytics.
SIR-related data for Delhi and other states is available at macinsights.in.

Norway is planning a temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places, amid rising global concern at the spread of the AI-enabled recording devices.
The Oslo government is planning a bill to prevent the use of the camera-enabled spectacles in parks, beaches, museums, shopping centres, schools, daycare centres, healthcare facilities, gyms and public events, although private use would still be allowed.
There is already a growing patchwork of restrictions on the use of the glasses including in UK and US courtrooms and in pubs, cinemas and restaurants where owners have raised privacy fears.
Torgeir Micaelsen, Norway’s minister of digital affairs, said he was “worried that new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without knowing it”.
“We do not want a society where people worry about being recorded without their knowledge, photographed or filmed in places and situations where they are accustomed to not being monitored,” he said.
Norway’s Labour party, which heads a minority government, needs the support of other parties to pass the proposed ban. It said it planned to submit a bill “as soon as possible”, while tasking an expert group with drawing up permanent regulations on the issue.
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta sells “smart” versions of Ray-Ban and Oakley glasses that allow users to film, take photos, make phone calls, play music and execute AI prompts. It has sold at least 9m pairs of the Ray-Ban versions since the start of 2023.
In the UK restaurateurs such as Jeremy King, who created the Wolseley and Delaunay restaurants, and pub chain Wetherspoons have already said they do not want customers using the devices. Cinemas said in August they had begun introducing policies to ban or restrict the use of smart glasses citing both privacy and film piracy concerns.
Last week the governor of California, Gavin Newsom, vetoed legislation that would have penalised citizens for using smart glasses to record people without their permission in changing rooms, doctors’ offices and other spaces people generally consider private. The state already has laws governing unlawful recording.
In France, the child welfare group E-enfance said it had this year received about 20 reports of women being filmed without their knowledge using glasses fitted with a camera, the majority of which involved Meta smart glasses. It said the incidents often followed the same pattern: a young girl or woman approached in a public place, filmed without her knowledge, with the clip then posted on social media in the form of a prank or a street interview.
Meta has stressed that each pair of glasses is fitted with a tamper-proof LED light that blinks white when the user is recording or taking pictures. It advises users: “Not everyone loves being photographed. Stop recording if anyone expresses that they would rather you not.”
A Meta spokesperson said: “We’re excited that our glasses continue to be very popular for listening to music, making calls, or getting live translations, so we’re continuing to expand styles and features around the world. Every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video. It can’t be turned off and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it -- something smartphones and other camera’s don’t have.”

From floating saunas to clinical trials: How heat might help mental health
The belief that heat can benefit the mind and relieve psychic suffering has a long history across human societies. But when Eva Hilland scanned the scientific literature for the kind of evidence that would support recommending heat as a legitimate intervention for mental health, she came up with very little.
"There are many knowledge gaps," says Hilland, a cognitive neuroscientist at Oslo Metropolitan University. Although, what existing evidence she did find seemed promising. "So we just saw the potential."
Sauna-going – sometimes paired with cold plunges or winter swimming – is attracting a new generation of followers, from the U.S. to Hilland's sauna-steeped country of Norway.
The trend not only reflects the reach of the broader wellness and longevity movement, but also a thirst for communal experience and social connection, particularly in the wake of the pandemic.
The science is just beginning to catch up with many of the theorized benefits. Though considerably less studied than the cardiovascular impact, mental health has emerged as one of the more exciting and appealing applications.
Sauna survey
Hilland, whose research group focuses on neuroimaging and genetics, is one of the scientists now diving into this research domain of heat and mental health. And she's leveraging the sauna popularity surge in her own city, Oslo, to do it.
With funding from a local municipality, she's recruiting 50 people for a randomized controlled trial to see whether coupling sauna with a simple set of mental health habits improves stress, well-being, sleep and more.
Instead of visiting a windowless research lab, her study participants take two sessions a week at one of the floating sauna villages that have cropped up in Oslo's inner harbor – a waterfront that has transformed into a world-class destination for heat-seekers in just the past decade.
Large surveys of sauna users reflect what many readily share: It's the psychological benefits more than anything else that keeps them coming back, whether that's stress reduction, elevated mood, improved sleep or the ineffable post-sauna glow.
Some of these self-reported improvements may have less to do with sweating and more to do with the digital detox, time in nature, mindfulness and social connection that sauna-going facilitates.
But the weight of the evidence suggests heat itself is also "powerful physiological stimulus for promoting mental health," says Christopher Lowry, an integrative physiologist and neuroscientist at the University of Colorado, Boulder.
What we know heat does
While warm baths were commonplace in psychiatric asylums a century ago, the modern evidence base largely rests on translational work done with animals and cell models, and a small number of human studies, most of which lack strict control groups.
In his lab, Lowry has extensively explored the physiological mechanisms linking temperature and mental health.
When our skin senses heat, those signals travel to a primitive part of the brain that tells our body to cool down. That process overlaps with a pathway involved in mood and pleasure, which is implicated in depression.
Heat also triggers a specific anti-inflammatory response. A similar phenomenon occurs during exercise, a well-established treatment for depression and other mental health conditions. And separately, Lowry says, animal studies find heat activates a group of "serotonin neurons" in the brain that may "provide stress resilience and antidepressant effects."
In humans, the strongest data come from a landmark trial, published ten years ago, and led by a team at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and co-authored by Lowry.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
A total of 30 people with depression were randomly separated into two groups. About half spent around two hours in a whole-body infrared machine designed to raise their body temperature to 38.5 C, or about 101 F. The rest received a sham treatment.
Within a week, a majority of those in the treatment group had a 50% reduction in their symptoms and the effects persisted throughout the six-week follow-up period.
Training the body to cool down
Those findings are what originally inspired Ashley Mason to enter the field.
A clinical psychologist who studies mood disorders and sleep at the University of California, San Francisco, Mason now has funding from the National Institutes of Health and others to study various forms of heat therapy for depression, sleep and loneliness.
The renewed scientific interest in using heat for psychiatric conditions, in part, reflects an intriguing observation – people with depression tend to have difficulty with thermoregulation.
"What we know from a bunch of literature is that depressed people seem to run hot," says Mason, also a professor of psychiatry and behavioral science. "When their depression improves, their thermoregulatory system seems to also change."
In fact, Mason's lab recently tracked this association between self-reported symptoms of depression and body temperature using wearable device data collected from close to 20,000 people.
Even when controlling for factors like weather and medical conditions, symptom severity correlated with higher skin temperature and less daily fluctuation in body temperature, meaning their bodies weren't cooling down as much at night.
It may seem counterintuitive to heat folks up even more, but Mason says doing so seems to function like a "thermoregulatory workout" – training their system to become more efficient at cooling down in the long run.
"So when you are actually done being exposed to that heat, your body temperature drops for a much longer period of time than you were spending in that heat," she says. "Days, possibly weeks, we still don't know."
Several older studies have also shown that successfully treating people with antidepressant medication or other therapies improves their thermoregulation.
The implication, Masons says, is that acting on this "bi-directional" relationship – both via heat and traditional therapeutic approaches – could have a synergistic effect.
To test this hypothesis, she has run two small pilot trials combining eight weeks of cognitive behavioral therapy and four sessions in an infrared hyperthermia machine. In both studies, most of the participants were in remission from depression by the end of the study.
Her team is now carrying out the same protocol with a larger pool of patients at UCSF, Harvard and the Cleveland Clinic.
Mason stresses the results should be viewed as preliminary. The studies were not powered to show the treatments were effective, but they do lay the groundwork for the larger, well-controlled trials that could deliver that kind of evidence.
"Heat does seem to be a promising therapy, but we're very much at the beginning of this research," she notes.
If these future studies pan out, it may have a place alongside other non-pharmacological approaches for mental health, like exercise – at least in some cases.
"For people with depression who have tried a lot of different types of treatment, do I think that there's room for heat therapy to have a seat at the table?" she says. "Absolutely."
Exactly how you get hot may not matter so much as long as people are sweating.
However, the boom of interest in age-old forms of heat therapy like sauna may be a natural entry point for many.
"The science is new, but the practice is not," Mason says.

Washington, Oct 06: The US launched the largest denaturalisation effort in modern history by moving to strip 40 individuals, including one of Indian origin, of their American citizenship, the Department of Justice said.
The 40 individuals facing denaturalisation actions in multiple US courts have been accused of serious offences, including acting as an agent for a foreign government, committing voluntary manslaughter, and aggravated sodomy against a special-needs man.
Balwinder Singh of California is facing denaturalisation action in the state’s Eastern District court for using a fraudulent identity to gain admission to and acquire a US citizenship.
“Today’s announcement marks the largest denaturalisation effort in modern history,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche on Monday.
Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, a naturalised US citizen’s citizenship may be revoked and certificate of naturalisation cancelled, if it was procured illegally or by concealment of a material fact or by willful misrepresentation.
“Every single one of these individuals lied their way into US citizenship,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division.
“This administration will continue to pursue the largest denaturalisation effort in department history to restore trust and integrity in US citizenship. Our message is clear: the United States will not tolerate deception in the naturalisation process,” Shumate said.
According to the Department of Justice, Singh, in 1992, submitted an immigration application under the identity of Balwinder Singh.
In 2003, he sought and received permanent resident status under a second identity.
“Fingerprints establish that Singh submitted both applications. In 2009, Singh naturalised under his second identity. The complaint alleges seven counts for his numerous misrepresentations and unlawful acts that adversely reflect his moral character,” the Justice Department said.
The department said it is seeking to revoke the citizenship of Jinchao Wei, a China-born former US Navy sailor convicted of espionage-related offences.
According to the Justice Department, Wei enlisted in the Navy in 2021 and by February 2022 had begun conspiring to sell military secrets to China.
He became a US citizen in May 2022 under provisions designed to expedite naturalisation for people serving honourably in the US armed forces.
Wei was convicted in August 2025 of conspiracy to commit espionage, espionage and unlawful export of technical data related to defence articles. He was sentenced to 200 months in prison and discharged from the Navy.
Among those against whom denaturalisation actions have been initiated are those from Pakistan, Mexico, Cambodia, Nepal and Afghanistan.

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

Egyptologists have long debated whether the earliest pharoahs of the First Dynasty were buried with various servants and officials to serve them in the afterlife—a form of human sacrifice. But there is very little archaeological evidence available, given that many of the earliest Egyptian tombs were plundered and/or hastily excavated. A new paper published in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology reassesses a collection of skulls excavated from tombs in the 1920s and concludes that over one-third show evidence of blunt force trauma. This suggests that they may have been victims of so-called “retainer sacrifice.”
Author Roselyn Campbell is a bioarchaeologist at Purdue University who has long been fascinated with the history of human sacrifice. “I’m interested in how we as human beings decide which types of violence are okay and which are not, and how we even define violence,” Campbell told Ars. “It’s very context specific. We have to be careful not to extend our own ideas about what violence is and how it’s used into other cultures. With Egypt, we have such a long history of European and colonial archeology; they came in with very specific ideas about what this culture was. You really have to make an effort to contextualize the legacy data we have.”
Naturally she found the debate over whether ancient Egyptians practiced retainer sacrifice pertinent to her interests. “People tend to fall into one of two camps,” said Campbell. “Either retainer sacrifice definitely happened, end of discussion, or it definitely didn’t happen, end of discussion. But nobody’s actually looked at the bones in a very long time.” Forensic science has advanced considerably over the last century, so re-analysis could be useful. Complicating matters is the fact that older sets of remains are often incomplete and/or modified for preservation, destroying vital forensic information in the process.
Cold case files
As a case study, Campbell turned to a collection of human remains first excavated by famed British archaeologist Flinders Petrie in the 1920s, from the Abydos site in southern Egypt. Abydos is the site of a royal necropolis where many of the early pharoahs were buried, along with many ancient temples. (It’s also the home of what may be the world’s oldest brewery.) This particular set of remains—46 crania stored at Cambridge University— came from the Umm el-Qaab cemetary, which contains subsidiary burials presumed to be retainers of deceased First Dynasty rulers. Petrie noted several grave markers with names and official titles, mostly lower to mid-level officials and artisans.

Fuel is being shipped from South Korea to Russia via sanctioned tankers as Moscow scrambles for supplies amid the war in Ukraine, a move one expert said “undermines” Seoul’s public backing for Kyiv.
Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.
Three of the vessels were under sanctions by the UK and EU, and one took on its cargo through a ship-to-ship transfer in South Korean waters – a method that can obscure where a cargo came from and lets ships avoid calling at port terminals.
“It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia”, said Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank. “This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”
Seoul has sent Ukraine humanitarian aid and non-lethal military supplies such as helmets, body armour and demining vehicles, and in 2023 pledged $2.3bn in support, most of it in loans.
But South Korea has long sought to balance its support for Ukraine with its desire to improve ties with Russia. Throughout the war, Seoul has ruled out sending weapons directly to Ukraine, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Moscow has signalled an interest in restoring relations with South Korea, including trade ties.
While the fuel trade involves vessels sanctioned by some of Seoul’s western partners, it does not appear to breach South Korean law. South Korea’s own measures against Russia rely mainly on export controls on goods such as industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
The shipments, however, risk making Seoul look like a weak link in western efforts to pressure Russia, as relations with Kyiv come under strain over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul says was meant to remain secret.
It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show.
The largest carrier, the sanctioned Layla, made two voyages from the south-eastern port of Ulsan to Vladivostok leaving on 19 July and 10 August and carrying 57,000 tonnes of diesel in total. On the first trip, it told South Korean authorities its destination was Vladivostok, but on the second it said it was bound for Niigata in Japan.
Another sanctioned tanker, the Russian-flagged Astoria, which is also under Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 tonnes of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August, declaring Japan as its destination, before sailing to Vladivostok.
The third sanctioned tanker, the Chongchon, never berthed. It took on about 26,000 tonnes of fuel from an unsanctioned tanker, the Celeste I, at an anchorage off the southern South Korean port of Yeosu in early August, then headed to Vladivostok after declaring Singapore as its destination.
The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to requests for comment.
Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, says Moscow has been forced to import fuel products to feed the “Russian war machine”.
According to data from the maritime analytics firm Kpler, the buyers included Rosneft, Russia’s state-controlled oil company, which is under UK, US, EU and Australian sanctions, and NNK, a Russian oil group whose owner, Eduard Khudainatov, and one of its companies, NNK-Oil, are under UK sanctions.
In August, Russia imported 368,000 tonnes of oil products by sea, more than seven times the previous month and the highest monthly total since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Kpler data analysed by CREA. South Korea accounted for 112,000 tonnes, or 31%, of that amount, second only to India.
Loadings at South Korean ports began to surge in July, just as the country’s president, Lee Jae Myung, pledged $100m for Ukraine’s reconstruction at a Nato summit in Turkey.
A 2025 trade association survey found that nearly 80% of South Korean firms that had stopped exporting to Russia since the war began were open to resuming trade.
In March, as the war with Iran shut the strait of Hormuz, South Korea capped exports of certain fuels and imported Russian naphtha under a US sanctions waiver.
On 1 October, the UK temporarily exempted South Korea’s existing gas contracts from a ban on maritime services for Russian LNG that takes effect in January 2027.
When contacted, South Korea’s foreign ministry did not address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said that as “a responsible member of the international community, the government supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”
It said it had expanded its export controls on Russia under the Foreign Trade Act “beyond strategic items to 1,402 non-strategic items with a high potential for diversion to military use” and was “strictly enforcing” them.
The government “continues to monitor the implementation of its export controls on Russia and, where necessary, takes action in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations,” the ministry said.
The UK Foreign Office did not answer questions about the UK-sanctioned tankers using South Korean ports, or say whether the shipments had been raised with Seoul.
A spokesperson said: “The UK remains firmly committed to the effective monitoring of our sanctions and to working with international partners to increase economic pressure on Russia and reduce the revenues funding its illegal war against Ukraine.”

Quick Answer
The ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 is a practical, performance-driven business laptop featuring a powerful Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, an exceptional keyboard, excellent port selection, and easy RAM/storage upgradability. However, its main drawbacks are mediocre battery life, a dim display limited to 45% NTSC, and an underwhelming webcam.
ASUS offers the ExpertBook series in many configurations. If you want the best business laptop Asus offers, consider the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra. If you are a business owner who wants a premium design without compromising essential business features, the ASUS ExpertBook B Series is worth considering. Finally, the ASUS ExpertBook P Series is for those looking for an affordable business laptop without paying a premium.
In that regard, the ASUS ExpertBook P3 is a sweet spot for people looking for an affordable business laptop. It doesn’t try to compete with the flashy, ultra-thin consumer aesthetics of the Apple MacBook Air or Dell XPS line; instead, it positions itself as an aggressive challenger to the Lenovo ThinkPad and HP EliteBook ecosystems, as well as other business laptop ranges.
I have been using the ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 version (2026) for the past several days. Overall, it has been a solid business laptop. The model I am testing comes with a powerful Intel Core Ultra 7 255H and delivers excellent performance, a reliable port selection, the best keyboard in its class, and plenty of business-focused features.
ASUS has also expanded the ASUS ExpertBook P3 G2 series, now offering more choices than before with both Intel and AMD configurations across different sizes, while also addressing some of the shortcomings we noticed with the earlier ExpertBook P series.
In this full, detailed review, I will share my experience with the ASUS P3 G1, compare it to the original P3 launched in 2025, and see how it stacks up against the recently announced ASUS P3 G2 series. By the end, you should have a better idea of whether the Asus P3 G1 still makes sense or is worth going for the latest generations instead.
Table of Contents
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 Review
Design and Build: Practical Over Premium
Asus ExpertBook laptops are easy to spot from miles away. Most models across the lineup look the same and follow a very similar design language, with an understated gray finish and a clean, minimal look.
Asus ExpertBook P3 G1 also follows the same design. It may not impress you with flashy looks or an ultra-slim profile, which is something the ExpertBook P3 isn’t trying to do anyway. This is a practical, business-first laptop.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 comes in two chassis variants. The 1A variant has a plastic chassis, and the 2A variant has a metal chassis for those who want an even sturdier, more premium build.
My unit comes with a plastic body, but it doesn’t feel cheap by any means. In fact, it is a step up from some of the older ExpertBook laptops I have reviewed in the past.
Although the chassis is plastic, the matte, grainy finish hides it and gives it a much more premium feel. I love minimal laptop designs, and the ASUS ExpertBook takes that approach even further with nothing but the ASUS logo on the lid. The matte, grainy finish is also fingerprint-resistant; as a result, smudges don’t show up, and it stays clean.
The same treatment continues when you open the lid. The hinge is now slightly stronger. The display is stiffer than ideal to position, but it still wobbles a bit when you type and change its angle.
The lid opens up to 180 degrees, allowing the display to lie completely flat on the surface. It can come in handy if you want to share your screen with someone across the table. One limitation, though: since this variant doesn’t have a touchscreen, you cannot really use the display while it is lying flat.
Build quality is stronger than last generation, but it still has noticeable flex, especially in the center of the keyboard and between the touchpad and the keyboard. Thankfully, I didn’t notice it while typing. The deck doesn’t bend much under normal use unless you press harder.
The rounded corners also make the laptop more comfortable to hold during longer carrying periods.
One thing Asus continues to get right is port selection. In a world where fewer ports have become the norm for a premium experience, Asus ExpertBook P3 supports all major ports, including one Thunderbolt 4 USB-C, one USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C, two USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-A ports, a full-size RJ45 Gigabit Ethernet port, HDMI 2.1 TMDS, a 3.5mm audio jack, and a Kensington Nano lock. You get pretty much every port you expect from a business laptop. That also means you can connect most everyday accessories directly to the laptop without carrying a separate dongle.
The chassis is also MIL-STD 810H tested across 24 procedures. The laptop should handle everyday wear and tear. Note that the laptop is not water-resistant.
The keyboard supports backlighting. This makes it easy to see and type in low-light conditions. The backlight also doesn’t leak when you’re looking straight at the laptop. It also has durable keys, and ASUS claims the keyboard is tested for up to 10 million keystrokes to withstand wear and tear over time.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 is available in both 14-inch and 16-inch sizes. My review unit is the 14-inch variant with a WUXGA 16:10 display. The side bezels are fairly noticeable, and there is a rather large chin at the bottom that also houses the Asus ExpertBook logo. Above the display is a physical privacy shutter, which I truly appreciate for business-centric users who want better privacy.
Display: Good for Work, Not for Creative Use
The 14-inch display is a sweet spot if you want something compact without giving up too much screen space.
ASUS ExpertBook doesn’t get the kind of high-end OLED displays Asus offers on some of its high-end laptops or even more affordable VivoBook models. It is a 14-inch IPS-level display with WUXGA 1920 × 1200 resolution, a 16:10 aspect ratio, a 60Hz refresh rate, up to 300 nits of brightness, and 45% NTSC color coverage.
The display quality is decent and gets the job done, especially if you’re buying the ExpertBook primarily for office work. It is perfectly fine for browsing and using office apps like spreadsheets and documents, but if you work on photos or video editing, you will probably want something with better color coverage.
The display also has an anti-glare coating, which does a good job of cutting down reflections and makes it easier to use in bright environments. However, the trade-off is that a matte finish coating removes some of the visual punch you get from glossy panels. Colors aren’t as vibrant, although the text remains sharp.
Watching videos and content on this WUXGA IPS-level panel isn’t a pleasant experience, but as I said, for everyday tasks such as browsing, spreadsheets, and other office applications, it feels comfortable to use, and the text looks sharp enough to read clearly.
Performance: More Power Than Most Office Users Need
Performance is easily one of the ExpertBook P3’s strongest aspects. Asus offers it with either a Core Ultra 5 225H or Core Ultra 7 255H. My unit came with an Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, paired with 16GB DDR5 RAM and a 512GB M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD.
At the heart of the configuration is the Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, a high-performance processor with 16 cores, 16 threads, a maximum clock speed of 5.1GHz, and integrated Intel Graphics. In everyday use, this combination handles almost any task without breaking a sweat. Whether you’re using multiple graphics-heavy applications, running dozens of browser tabs, or switching between office apps all day.
Another advantage is upgradability. Asus ExpertBook P3 comes with two DDR5 SO-DIMM slots, and the existing RAM isn’t soldered to the motherboard, so you can upgrade later if you want to, and it won’t cost you a bomb upfront, which is the case with most modern laptops.
It also has two storage slots: one M.2 2280 PCIe 4.0 slot and one M.2 2230 PCIe 4.0 slot, giving you more room to expand the storage later.
One thing I did notice is that the laptop gets quite warm at the bottom even during something as basic as browsing the web. You can definitely feel the heat when using it in your lap. It is not entirely surprising, though, considering the Core Ultra 7 255H is an H-series processor designed for higher performance.
Keyboard and Trackpad: The Keyboard Is the Star
The keyboard is easily one of my favorite things about the Asus ExpertBook P3. It offers one of the best typing experiences I have had on a laptop after Mac. A lot of that comes down to the 1.5mm key travel, which delivers a great typing experience. The keys are also large and well spaced, giving your fingers plenty of room to move around. It didn’t take me long to get comfortable with this keyboard.
The trackpad is also large enough for daily use. The large surface area makes it easy to move the cursor and also use gestures.
I have no issues with the keyboard and trackpad, though some users may find the fingerprint sensor placement inconvenient because it is integrated into the power button. To prevent accidental presses, ASUS made the power button slightly firmer.
Battery Life: The Biggest Compromise
This kind of performance is always welcome, especially if you regularly handle high-demand tasks. The trade-off, though, is battery life. My configuration comes with a 50Wh, 3-cell battery, and the ExpertBook P3 takes a noticeable hit here.
Even for basic use, I was getting only about 8-9 hours. On medium to heavy gaming, the battery life dropped to 4 to 5 hours, which isn’t the performance you want if you plan to use it on battery power all day.
ASUS bundles a 65W USB-C charger in the box, and it can take your laptop from 0 to 100 in less than 2 hours. That’s fairly quick, but I really wish Windows laptop makers offered more travel-friendly options instead of big, bulky charging bricks and three-pin plugs.
Sound: Decent, but Nothing Special
The speakers are decently loud, but they don’t get particularly loud. ASUS uses two built-in speakers with Dirac audio support. Thankfully, Asus includes a built-in 3.5mm headphone jack, so you can plug in wired headphones or earphones directly without relying on the built-in speakers.
Windows 11 Home: Still Too Cluttered
I have never been a fan of Windows’ cluttered experience. If you’ve used Windows for years, you probably won’t mind much, but if you are coming from a Mac or Linux, you’ll have to deal with Windows’ cluttered experience first.
It took me more than three hours to set up the device, including the unwanted Windows updates I had to install during setup. Plus, the Windows update prompts never stop. Even Microsoft has promised to improve the Windows laptop experience by eliminating these unwanted distractions.
Since this is an ExpertBook, ASUS includes business-centric features, including AI ExpertMeet for meetings. However, this configuration lacks some useful Copilot+ AI features for those who care about privacy and want to run AI features locally on the device. The Core Ultra 7 255H delivers up to 13 TOPS of NPU performance, well short of the 40+ TOPS required for a Copilot+ PC. You may need to rely on cloud processing for more demanding AI features.
Camera: Still Needs Work
ASUS has been pretty good at improving the little things in everyday use, but the camera is still one area that needs work. My configuration comes with a 1080p FHD IR camera with Windows Hello support and a physical privacy shutter. Even on the maxed-out ExpertBook Ultra, the camera quality is rather underwhelming, especially on business laptops like this, where it matters a lot.
Even in good lighting, the camera adds plenty of noise, and in low light, it gets worse. However, you can always connect an external camera if camera quality matters to you. But this is something Asus needs to improve.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 Review Verdict: Powerful and Practical, but Battery Holds It Back
Overall, if performance is high on your priority list, then the ASUS ExpertBook P3 might be a better choice. Everyday tasks feel quick and responsive, plus it also has plenty of power for more demanding tasks. The excellent keyboard, with 1.5mm key travel, makes typing sessions comfortable, and the full selection of ports lets you connect any peripherals without constantly reaching for or using a dongle. The biggest advantage of the Asus ExpertBook P3 is plenty of room to upgrade later. It offers dual SO-DIMM slots for memory and dual M.2 slots for additional PCIe storage.
Among the pros are also some compromises. Battery life takes a noticeable hit when you push the processor harder, and while the laptop can handle some AI workloads locally, it cannot run the full set of Copilot+ PC features.

- Great keyboard with 1.5mm key travel
- Plenty of ports
- RAM and SSD are upgradeable
- Fingerprint-resistant matte finish
- 180-degree hinge
- Good business and security features

- Average battery life
- Poor color coverage

Indonesia court to rule on bid to annul vice president's election win
Plaintiffs led by a former Indonesian deputy law minister filed a petition last month, arguing that Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka's overseas education credentials did not satisfy Indonesian eligibility requirements.
JAKARTA: Indonesia's Constitutional Court will issue a ruling late on Tuesday (Oct 6) on a case that seeks to annul Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka's election win because of alleged gaps in his education record, a move that could see him lose office and further undermine President Prabowo Subianto's administration.
Prabowo became the eighth president of Southeast Asia's largest economy after a successful but often controversial election campaign alongside Gibran, the 39-year-old eldest son of Prabowo's predecessor, Joko Widodo.
Last month, plaintiffs led by a former Indonesian deputy law minister filed a petition to the court asking its nine-judge panel to annul Gibran's vice presidency, arguing that his overseas education credentials did not satisfy Indonesian eligibility requirements and were improperly accepted by election authorities.
Indonesian election law requires presidential and vice-presidential candidates to have completed senior high school or an equivalent level of education. Plaintiffs argued Gibran failed to adequately prove he had met the criteria.
Judges are scheduled to deliver their verdict on Tuesday after holding several hearings with experts, diplomatic attaches, and the education ministry, the court's website shows.
The challenge hinges on whether Gibran's overseas studies met the requirements and whether election officials were justified in relying on government-issued equivalency certificates to support his candidacy.
Gibran attended Orchid Park Secondary School in Singapore and later studied at UTS Insearch in Australia before obtaining a bachelor's degree through the Management Development Institute of Singapore (MDIS).
Indonesian education ministry official Taufiq Damarjati told the court on Oct 2 that the ministry's equivalency assessment was based on Gibran's overall educational history, while acknowledging that no diploma was submitted during the application process, court transcripts show.
Prabowo has replaced several senior officials, including the national police chief and the Coordinating Minister for Human Development and Culture, local media reported, moves widely seen as a reflection of strains in his relationship with Widodo.
Widodo threw his support behind Prabowo, his former defence minister, during the presidential campaign.
A controversial 2023 ruling by the Constitutional Court exempted Gibran from age restrictions, paving the way for his candidacy. The move sparked protests and criticism from students, activists and legal scholars, with analysts saying it allowed Widodo to retain influence even after leaving office.

(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Athira Elssa Johnson writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
A treatment can make a difference only when patients can access it. The cost of medicines, their safety and regulation, and whether people can get the care they need are all part of that question. This week, our coverage also looks at vaccination, infectious diseases, artificial intelligence, prevention and new medical research.
Questions around the cost of medicines came into focus after the Supreme Court described the overpricing of essential cancer drugs as “broad daylight dacoity”. The report examines concerns around medicine prices and what they mean for access to treatment.
A regulatory warning against the indiscriminate use of painkillers and antibiotics highlighted the risks of inappropriate medicine use, including kidney disease. India has also ordered a crackdown on nicotine pouches, citing health risks.
Food regulation also featured this week. Krishnadas Rajagopal reports on FSSAI telling the Supreme Court that front-of-pack nutrition labelling will be rolled out in a single phase.The regulator has also proposed that only milk-derived products be represented as ‘paneer’. Bindu Shajan Perappadan explains what analogue paneer is and why FSSAI is acting against it.
Vaccination and infectious diseases
Vaccination has been another focus, with attention on missed doses, vaccination records, catch-up vaccination, adult immunisation and changing needs across different stages of life.
In our Health Webinar, experts discussed childhood and adult vaccination, travel vaccination and common concerns around vaccines. The discussion also looked at the importance of maintaining vaccination records and understanding changing immunisation needs.
Ahead of winter, Sayesha Gupta, Megha Jacob and Karan Babbar looked at vaccination among older adults and why Delhi’s grandparents may need protection alongside their grandchildren.
The wider question of preparedness also remains important. India stressed the need for resilient health systems and pandemic preparedness at the United Nations.
On the infectious disease front, reports showed that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to two new health zones. An mpox case has also been confirmed in a northeastern Congolese city at the centre of the Ebola outbreak.
In India, C. Maya reports on scientists at IAV, Keralam developing a dengue early-warning system to forecast trends and help anticipate outbreaks.
AI and healthcare
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used in medical imaging, clinical decision-making and drug and vaccine development. Its expanding role also raises questions around patient safety, inaccurate information, data and the potential misuse of AI in biology.
The latest Health Wrap examines these issues in ‘AI in healthcare: promise, risks and patient safety’.
Other developments include a partnership between Anthropic and OpenEvidence to expand access to medical AI; Afshan Yasmeenreported on HEADS, an initiative using AI to help address gaps in mental healthcare. In Assam, inputs from ASHAs are being used to develop an AI-enabled training platform for cervical cancer screening.
Health data is also coming under scrutiny, with the CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic called to appear before an Australian AI probe following a breach involving a health database.
Nutrition and prevention
Nutrition and preventive health also featured prominently. A study found that consuming an additional 100 grams of ultra-processed food a day was associated with a 14% higher risk of a heart event. The findings add to research examining the relationship between ultra-processed food and cardiovascular health.
Suparna Mukherjee looks at what people should know about artificial sweeteners and health, particularly as their use becomes more common.
Managing conditions, new research
Several stories this week examine conditions that can be difficult to recognise, diagnose or manage.
I look at GERD and why persistent reflux symptoms need to be distinguished from what is commonly described as heartburn.
Another report looked at research linking pregnancy-related forgetfulness, popularly called ‘momnesia’, to disruption in a brain circuit, offering another possible explanation for cognitive changes during pregnancy.
Swagata Yadavar reported on village health centres in Haryana screening people for heart disease and identifying those who need further care.
Divya Gandhi reports on a study found that deaf adults have distinctly superior peripheral vision, adding to research into how sensory systems adapt to differences in sensory input.
Dr. V. Divya Sai looks at what happens when cancer treatment is no longer working and treatment options change. Dr. C. Aravinda examines why male contraception continues to lag behind other forms of contraception.
Researchers at RGCB in Keralam have developed nanopore sensors aimed at detecting biomarkers associated with neurodegenerative diseases, while IIT Palakkad researchers have developed sensors for faster heparin monitoring.
Another report looks at the U.S. FDA’s approval of an AbbVie drug for Parkinson’s disease. The Health Ministry’s latest advisory on stem cell therapy for autism has also drawn attention, read our explainer here.
