“I am not trying to make any excuses here, but I am just saying that that was the true reflection of where we were as a nation in Indian football terms,” he added.
“There were no games that were happening for players to stay in shape and have game time, and when you are facing teams who have a setup where they are playing regular football, they will have some (extra) sharpness even if they are a lower-ranked team. That’s something which we were missing in very crucial games.”
But he believes there are signs of better days ahead. The new ISL season begins on October 10 in its old format, while the national team trained for three weeks in Bengaluru before this window.
“I think (this) was the first camp when we had everyone,” Gurpreet said. “Now, we can plan better and see how we want to go (ahead as a team),” Gurpreet added.
A work in progress
Gurpreet has been in the national team for a decade now, and has played under four managers – all from different countries, Jamil being the only Indian tactician among them.
“Coach Khalid is very thorough in his preparation. He does a lot of hard work from morning till evening, in terms of how training has to be set up and how the opponent plays. I’m not going to sit here and compare coaches; I’m just going to talk about what is currently in front of us,” he said.
“I feel like it (team composition) is something which will take time because, since coach Khalid has come, we are trying to find a core group of players we can rely on every single game when we face tougher opposition. Every time, there has been something missing, be it injuries or non-release of players.”
A different test
Brazil gave India and Gurpreet a taste of elite opposition. Today, another former world champion awaits.
“When the news came out, as a player you’re just trying to make sure, checking facts that it is happening or not,” he said. “And then you feel that, okay, it is a great opportunity.”
The two matches so far have provided the Blue Tigers a stage to prove that they have worked on their weaknesses. A 1-1 draw with Panama, ranked 94 places above India, and a pressing game against Brazil earned them praise despite a 0-4 loss.
But for Gurpreet, there will be personal demons to confront — avoiding the mistakes he did against Brazil and staying composed in an era of trolls.
“Fifteen years ago, there was not much involvement of social media, with fans giving their opinions and listening to what is happening around the ecosystem. But now, we have overexposure to everything,” Gurpreet said.
“That is something we, as players, have to learn how to deal with, because now it has become a part of the job. If people are talking good, great. If people are talking bad, no problem. That’s part and parcel of life.”
Gurpreet has been here before. Despite making nine saves against Qatar in 2021, he let in the lone goal that handed India a 0-1 loss.
“When the opposition player comes and tells you that you deserve to be on a different level in terms of the way you play, that is the best compliment that you can receive,” he said.
India did not lose another game in 2021 since, with Gurpreet between the sticks. It won five matches, drew four, while he had four clean sheets and lifted the SAFF Championship title.
Two mistakes and two goals in a friendly can not define a career built over 15 years. And it won’t. Uruguay is next, and for Gurpreet, the only response that has ever mattered is the one he makes with his gloves.

On 02 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) held a protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park grounds demanding accountability from the Election Commission of India (ECI) and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Protesters raised concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleged voter deletions, and transparency in the electoral process. Despite Mumbai Police denying permission for the gathering, thousands attended the protest and raised slogans. Police later registered an FIR against the organisers and 400–500 unidentified participants for allegedly violating restrictions on the assembly.
In this context, a video (here & here) is circulating on social media claiming that CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was attacked at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park during this protest. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke was attacked during a protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park on 02 October 2026.
Fact: The video is from 15 June 2026 and shows Abhijeet Dipke being assaulted by unidentified individuals during a youth protest against paper leaks and unemployment in Jaipur, Rajasthan. There are no reports of him being attacked at the Mumbai protest. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video shows that the same video (here & here) has been available online since at least 15 June 2026. These posts describe it as Abhijeet Dipke being attacked in Jaipur, Rajasthan.
According to media reports (here, here & here), on 15 June 2026, Dipke was manhandled and slapped multiple times during a youth protest at Shaheed Smarak in Jaipur, Rajasthan. He had reportedly organised the protest to speak out against paper leaks and unemployment, and to demand the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. As supporters carried Dipke on their shoulders toward the stage, several people emerged from the crowd, pulled him down, and struck his face. This sparked a quick retaliatory scuffle from CJP supporters before the police stepped in and detained the suspects.
Afterwards, Dipke condemned the assault, calling it a sign of fear and cowardice from his opponents. Furthermore, there are no news reports of Dipke being assaulted at the Mumbai Shivaji Park protest
To sum it up, an old video of Abhijeet Dipke being assaulted in Jaipur is falsely shared to claim he was attacked in Mumbai.

In an Asian Games, where the overarching storyline from the shooting galleries was one of underwhelming returns, Haryana’s Neeru Dhanda single-handedly rewrote the narrative.
Her gold ended India’s 48-year wait for an individual trap title, with the previous one won by the late Randhir Singh.
Neeru’s triumph is part of a 15-medal haul — three gold, eight silver and four bronze — that left India second only to China, with 28, on the shooting medal table. Yet the numbers tell only part of the story. Three years after a record 22 medals in Hangzhou, the decline was stark.
The most glaring drop came in gold medals: India had won seven in the previous edition, five of them in ‘team’ events. According to the International Shooting Sport Federation’s (ISSF) general regulation 3.3.2.3, these events are meant for “three (3) members of the same gender” which award medals based on the sum total of the scores of each of the participating shooters in the individual qualification round.
This time, India couldn’t win a single ‘team’ gold. That these events are not on the Olympic programme is a fair argument, but the inability to convert opportunities does expose a worrying loss of depth. The silver and bronze medals helped keep the overall tally respectable.
The disappointment was particularly pronounced in rifle and pistol, the two disciplines that have traditionally supplied India with a steady stream of elite performers. India had only four individual medals from non-shotgun events: Elavenil Valarivan’s silver in 10m air rifle, Rudrankksh Patil’s bronze and Himanshu Singh’s silver in the same event, and Esha Singh’s silver in 25m sports pistol.
Moreover, a handful of household names never made the podium. Double Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker, who could have won a maximum of four medals, returned without one. Suruchi Singh, one of the revelations of Indian shooting in recent years, also failed to medal individually. She managed to salvage her campaign with a mixed-team gold medal, this edition’s first, alongside Kamaljeet Singh.
Perhaps it was the agony of falling short elsewhere that made Neeru’s campaign stand out even more. That she managed to pull it off even after being hospitalised in Bhopal for three days with suspected H1N1 before flying out to Japan made her campaign all the more memorable.
Her 28 out of 30 in the individual trap final became the new Games record before a mixed-team gold came along when she teamed up with Kynan Chenai. She returned from Aichi-Nagoya with two gold medals and a silver from the trap women’s team, becoming the first Indian woman to win an individual Asiad gold in a shotgun event.
Neeru may have done the heavy lifting at the Aichi Prefectural General Shooting Gallery, but there are questions unanswered. The contentious selection process may be the biggest of them all.
It is understood that the country’s quota had been capped at 30, six fewer than usual, forcing a few difficult selections. Shooters capable of competing in multiple events were preferred over specialists to maximise India’s entries, while recent form was assessed through the National Rifle Association of India’s (NRAI) Moving Average Method (MAM).
Under the MAM, a shooter’s four best qualification scores at recognised competitions held within a 180-day window are averaged to determine their ranking and eligibility for representation. Additional ancillary points are awarded for reaching a final.
The system, however, carries an inherent risk. The window will always favour shooters who peak at the right moment, while potentially undervaluing those with a proven record of delivering at major championships. At an Asian Games, where experience under pressure can be decisive, that distinction matters.
The omission of established names such as Paris Olympic medallists Swapnil Kusale and Sarabjot Singh, former world champion Samrat Rana, and Hangzhou gold medallist Sift Kaur Samra proved that experience and potential can’t be treated as mutually exclusive. There is a case for a provision that guarantees a place in the squad for shooters who have reached a defined level of international success for a set period of time.
There are, of course, positives. Despite everything, it is a sizeable haul, and the emergence of a few new names gives the sport a foundation to build on. But for a programme that has expanded its depth and ambition over the past decade, merely maintaining a respectable medal count cannot be the benchmark.
India needs its rifle and pistol shooters back among the principal protagonists, while also ensuring Neeru’s triumph isn’t a shotgun outlier. With less than two years to go for LA2028, the NRAI must prioritise addressing the gaps.
The clock is ticking.

A purported screenshot circulated online in fall 2026 of a purported Truth Social post, dated Sept. 22, in which U.S. President Donald Trump wrote that he had "spoken to God" and that "tonight is Armageddon.".
The image spread on multiple platforms, including Instagram, Threads and Facebook. Many commenters appeared to believe Trump actually posted the remarks. The full text of the alleged post read as follows:
I have spoken to God and he has given me a vision of an ocean filled with blood a city of dust a golden throne for me to sit on, eternally!!!, Tonight is Armageddon, the final judgement of good and evil!!!! Lock your doors and do not directly at the flash!!!! God bless us all!!!
President Donald J. Trump
(X user @ZiemowitSzcze11.)
Despite the username matching Trump's real Truth Social username, there's no evidence Trump actually published the post. The earliest version of the image we found appeared on a Polish X account that captioned it (translation via X): "Well, fake, but would you be surprised?" (archived).
We searched Trump's Truth — an online archive of Trump's Truth Social posts — for the word "Armageddon," and none of the three results related to the quote above.
(Trump's Truth)
We also looked all posts Trump actually published on Sept. 22 and found he published four that day. None of the four posts matched the timestamp or content of that in the screenshot.
The fake quote appeared to echo whistleblower reports received by the Military Religious Freedom Foundation that U.S. military commanders told troops their action in Iran was "all part of God's divine plan," allegedly "referring to Armageddon and the imminent return of Jesus Christ."
Trump has echoed similarly apocalyptic language, posting in May 2026, for example, that "a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again" — referring to U.S. attacks on Iran. He's also faced criticism for his posting an image depicting him in the likeness of Jesus Christ.

Seoul – South Korea is preparing a response to force North Korea to apologize for a mine blast in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that seriously wounded two South Korean soldiers, a defense ministry spokesperson said Tuesday.
South Korea is also calling on Pyongyang to come to the table to discuss the misalignment of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL), which bisects the DMZ, the spokesperson said.
The Sept. 21 blast wounded three South Korean troops, two of them seriously.
The spokesperson, Chung Bin-na, did not specify what measures would be taken in response to the blast, which South Korea has said was caused by North Korean mines, citing the results of a joint investigation with the United Nations Command.
Chung said North Korea must remove the mines it planted in the DMZ south of the MDL, but also said there were differences in the exact line that separates the Korean Peninsula as recognized by the two Koreas.
Differing views of the border line are one factor contributing to tension in the area, Chung said.
Some sections of the MDL, which stretches more than 200 kilometers between the east and west coasts with 1,900 markers, have become difficult to identify after decades of limited access inside the DMZ since it was drawn up in 1953 at the end of the Korean War.
North Korea on Friday rejected as “groundless” Seoul’s accusation that North Korean mines seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the DMZ and dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology, state news agency KCNA reported.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of the North’s leader Kim Jong Un, said Pyongyang had not deliberately planted mines in the border zone, KCNA reported.

In October 2024, students at Cornell University received a campus crime alert about a reported sexual assault. At the time, it was just a campus story. Nearly two years later, on September 16, the victim, known only as “Jane Doe,” filed a civil lawsuit that brought national attention to her story. People across the country are asking what happened and why criminal charges never followed.
How did the Cornell rape case go so wrong?
A former sex crimes prosecutor explains where the Cornell case should go next.
Doe alleges that seven men drugged and sexually assaulted her at the Chi Phi fraternity house two years ago. Her lawsuit also accuses the university, fraternity and sorority organizations, and a local bar of failing to protect her.
The lawyers for several of the men have denied the allegations and any wrongdoing. Cornell says its disciplinary actions led to suspensions and expulsions for some of the young men, and that the Chi Phi fraternity remains barred from campus.
Doe went to campus police in November 2024, and the district attorney’s office reviewed her account and declined to bring charges. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has said that what she described to Cornell police didn’t meet the state’s requirements for criminal charges.
Van Houten reopened the investigation late last month while continuing to defend his original decision to not pursue charges, but it’s now out of his hands: On Thursday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul named the state attorney general, Letitia James, as special prosecutor to investigate the allegations, saying she had “lost faith” in Van Houten.
To break down why Van Houten didn’t pursue the case at the time and what should have happened instead, Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Lauren Hersh, a former Brooklyn prosecutor who led the office’s sex trafficking unit and CEO of World Without Exploitation, about how authorities handled Jane Doe’s allegations, the limits of New York’s consent laws, and what needs to change.
Hersh also explains where she believes the case should go next and what a special prosecutor can do to investigate (the interview took place prior to James’s appointment).
Below is an excerpt of Hersh’s conversation with Noel edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
I want to start with what we know in 2024. A young woman who we know as “Jane Doe” goes to the Cornell campus police and says she had gone to a frat house while under the influence of alcohol.
At the frat house, she was given more alcohol and ketamine. Several men had sex with her while she was intoxicated. This is what she tells Cornell campus police. What, in your view, is supposed to happen next?
There are a number of things that could happen. What I would say about these cases is there is no perfect scenario of what is supposed to happen, because what is critically important is we listen to the desire of the survivor.
We want to take this at her pace. We want to be guided by her wishes. We want her to decide if she is ready to go forward, if she wants to speak to campus police, the Title IX office, if she wants to speak to the local law enforcement. There are a lot of variables here, but for me, what is critically important is that we’re listening to the survivor and what she ultimately wants to happen.
In the present day, the district attorney who was involved has said that his office reviewed Jane Doe’s statement at the time and found at the time that what she described didn’t meet the legal definition of a crime.
I think people want to understand, Lauren, how is that possible?
To be really candid with you, Noel, this is an area that seems super unclear to me because the role of the district attorney in that moment is to investigate.
When you first get a case file, you first get a victim statement, and especially with facts as horrific as these facts are, or our understanding of this six-page document that the DA read — I would never say that this is a clear-cut case where there’ll be a conviction at the end. We never know that.
What I can say with 100 percent certainty is if you get a document like that, as a prosecutor, that is a significant investigative lead. And so, as a prosecutor, what I believe to be good practice is starting to pull the layers back, trying to understand what transpired here. Interviewing the victim. That feels critical. That never happened. We now know that there are all these text messages that were shared between these boys, and the prosecutor’s now saying, “I didn’t know about the text messages.”
It’s my understanding that there were a lot of boys on that particular text thread. And so a good investigator would have gone to that fraternity house and tried to interview some of those boys, tried to understand what were the contemporaneous statements made at that time. Were there any text messages? Was there any social media activity? And I believe that had they done that in a timely fashion, they likely would have come up with these text messages at that time and not two years later.
What you’re saying is interesting because the DA has come out publicly and defended himself by saying, essentially, the details of this lawsuit, which was filed in September of this year, are different from the details in the young woman’s 2024 statement to the police.
He has used that in his defense, right? “Here’s what I knew at the time versus what this young woman is saying today.” I think I hear you saying that maybe that’s not an excuse?
You’re asking about the inconsistent statements, and I find it troubling that the DA is leading with this notion that the victim has inconsistent statements because that feels to me like here we are making excuses and blaming the victim.
To my knowledge, the DA has not yet interviewed this victim. Perhaps he’s talking about the civil complaint, which I would think is written in a way where she has worked with her lawyer to put this together. And the initial statement, the initial six-page document that the DA read, my understanding is that it is basically a summary of a conversation.
Inconsistencies come in all shapes and sizes, so it’s hard to know exactly what we’re talking about here, but it is very common for there to be some inconsistencies. That is not a dealbreaker, despite the fact that this prosecutor wants the public to believe that it is.
What do you make of the prosecutor speaking publicly in the way that he is at this moment?
I find it rather confusing. I’m not really understanding why he is doing a media tour rather than sitting in his office doing the work, interviewing this particular victim, interviewing witnesses, seeing what evidence actually exists.
It seems to me that the DA has gotten to a conclusion before he’s done the work in actually investigating the case, and it is deeply troubling. And I think the governor should consider appointing a special prosecutor because I am not certain, based on this media tour, that this DA is able to give this particular survivor a full and fair investigation of the facts.
Drugs and alcohol are central to this case, right? The young woman admits she had been drinking and she was using ketamine. Under New York law, how does that affect whether or not someone is believed to be capable of consenting to sex?
New York law is actually really problematic here. It’s a place where I believe we are desperate for a legislative fix. I think that there have been a lot of advocates who’ve been championing a correction to this voluntary intoxication loophole for a lot of years, and we’ve not been able to get it.
New York law makes it very, very hard to prosecute a person when the victim is voluntarily intoxicated, but not unconscious, and this new law would allow the prosecutors the ability to bring cases when the victim is so severely intoxicated but not physically helpless and where a reasonable person should have known the victim’s condition.
In this particular case, based on what we’re hearing, she was in a condition where a reasonable person should have known her condition. And so in this particular instance, the DA is right. This is a very, very hard case to prove in this moment, but I’m a big believer. We don’t not prosecute cases because they’re hard cases. But at the same time, we know that a change to the law is critically important.
You clearly want more investigation here. What questions do you want asked? Who do you want to be [interviewed]?
Before I say who and how and what that investigation looks like, I think it’s really important to say that when two years have passed and the DA did not investigate these cases immediately, we have a big problem on our hands.
The fact that the DA did not investigate this from the moment he found out about this, it’s really problematic because as we know, evidence disappears, memories fade. When you’re dealing on a college campus with a specific culture, there may be a narrative that takes hold. And so it’s important to talk about the time lapse and how that harms the case.
That said, I still believe that the investigation is critically important. I don’t believe that this DA is the right person to do the investigation. I think a special prosecutor should be appointed. And then I think that the prosecutor and law enforcement should be interviewing everybody who was in that fraternity on that night. Anybody who saw this victim before, saw this victim after. Were there any statements in the immediate aftermath of her leaving that fraternity? Was there an outcry witness? We know that some text messages have come to light. Are there other text messages? I suspect that there are.
I’d want to interview as many of those boys as possible to understand what was going on because some of those text messages that have come to light — one says, “Free pussy” — don’t sound like a mindset that is engaging in consensual sex.
I think it is critically important that we understand all of the correspondence of that night. I think we want to see what is out there that helps us get closer to understanding what transpired that night.
I’ve seen two lines of thinking about this. One is that this is a horrific incident that never should have happened, but it is in some ways singular. But I’ve seen another line of thinking that says, “No, this is a systemic failure. This kind of thing goes on on college campuses, and the steps that follow the outcomes are often the same.”
I wonder if you think this is a systemic failure, and if you think it is, what would need to be done to fix this problem?
That’s a big question. I do think it’s a systemic failure. I also think it’s a cultural failure. And the reason that I would say this is because I don’t think this is isolated to this specific college campus. I think that sexual assault is happening across the country on college campuses everywhere.
In terms of additional systemic failures, I’ve been working with the Epstein survivors for the last year and a half, so I’ve seen so many systemic failures, so many prosecutorial failures, so much failure with law enforcement. I think that this is yet another example of prosecutorial failure.
I think the law enforcement failed this young person — the fact that there’s no investigation that happened immediately in the aftermath of this incident, no investigation. We just continue to fail survivors all over the place, and we have to start doing better.

Author Chetan Bhagat has a new productivity proposal for India's workforce: avoid looking at the clock and the number of hours you are expected to put in at your desk, and instead focus on how much work you can actually get done. He argued that even four hours of dedicated work can be enough for a day, reigniting an old workplace debate over whether longer hours mean greater productivity. Bhagat made these remarks at the 18th edition of the Project Management South Asia Conference (PMSAC) in Bengaluru on 3 October and said, "I work 4 hours a day, and that is enough if you do it with full dedication." "If you genuinely do work for 4 hours in a day, that is enough, good enough. It doesn't mean you have to include meetings, breaks, Wi-Fi issues, and other hunky-dory stuff that the offices often witness. In those 4 hours, you have to prioritise everything you put on the table," he added, according to media reports. However, he also stressed the importance of prioritising everything that an employee puts on the table. According to Bhagat, people should not simply start focusing on putting only four hours a day into their work and consider the rest of their day to be free. Instead, his idea is to encourage people to figure out what deserves their attention the most and complete that task with utmost dedication and discipline. His remarks come at a time when workplaces in India and around the world are grappling with questions over how long employees should work and how their working hours can be used more effectively, even as the rapid rise of artificial intelligence (AI) fuels uncertainty over the future of jobs and how work itself could change. Bhagat's remarks stand in sharp contrast to views expressed by some industry leaders, including Infosys co-founder NR Narayana Murthy, who has advocated a 70-hour workweek for young Indians, linking longer working hours with the need to improve the country's productivity and competitiveness. Murthy later said that he had worked more than 70 hours a week for over four decades and, during the period when India followed a six-day workweek, his weekly working hours often reached 85-90. Commenting on how employees can prioritise work-life balance, Bhagat noted, "No one cares for you unless you are. Do what makes you feel happy; follow 11 rules of life," a reference to his 2024 book, 11 Rules for Life: Secrets to Level Up. His argument attempts to shift the productivity debate away from how many hours an employee spends at work to what they accomplish during those hours. But whether four hours of focused work can really be enough for a day may depend on the nature of the job, workload, and responsibilities. A video showing a group of people marching on a road while waving Bangladesh’s national flags is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it shows illegal migrants raising Bangladeshi flags in Virar, Maharashtra. Some social media users have also linked the video to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, suggesting that the visuals highlight the need for the exercise. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows illegal migrants raising Bangladeshi flags in Virar, Maharashtra.
Fact: The viral video does not show illegal migrants raising Bangladeshi flags in Virar, Maharashtra. It shows participants carrying Bangladeshi flags during a Hero bike advertisement shoot in Virar on 03 October 2026. Prakash Kawale, Senior Police Inspector at Bolinj Police Station, confirmed to Factly that the video was from the shoot. Dinesh Jaiswal, owner of DJ Location, the production house involved, also confirmed this, adding that the shoot was cancelled after a ruckus and that all the participants were Indian. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed several details that raised questions about its authenticity. A mounted camera is visible at the beginning of the video and again around the 12-second mark. A cloth diffuser, typically used to control lighting during a shoot, is also visible. These details indicate that the footage was recorded during a shoot.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) featuring similar visuals. According to these reports, a Bangladeshi flag was used during a commercial advertisement shoot in Virar, a suburb in Maharashtra’s Palghar district, which triggered protests from local groups. The reports noted that some locals complained to the police and later burned the Bangladeshi flags used by the production crew. One of the reports also captured the aftermath, showing several youths attempting to burn a Bangladeshi flag.
We contacted Mr Prakash Kawale, Senior Police Inspector at Bolinj Police Station in Virar, regarding the viral video. Speaking to Factly, he confirmed that the video was recorded during an advertisement shoot. According to him, “This was an ad shoot by a Hero Bike company on 03 October 2026.”
We also learnt from the inspector that the shoot was carried out by DJ Location. We also contacted Dinesh Jaiswal, the owner of the production house, who confirmed that the video was recorded during an advertisement shoot for a Hero bike. He said the shoot was cancelled after a ruckus broke out, following which the concept was dropped. He added that all the people involved in the shoot were Indian and clarified that the video was from an advertisement shoot, not a real incident involving illegal migrants.
To sum up, this viral video does not show illegal migrants raising Bangladeshi flags in Virar, Maharashtra; it is from an advertisement shoot.

Separatist party projected to win Quebec election, adding new test to Canada's unity
- Published
Canadian media projects the sovereigntist Parti Québécois (PQ) will secure a minority win in Monday's provincial election in Quebec, making Paul St-Pierre Plamondon the incoming premier.
It marks the first time the PQ has been in power since 2014. It could prove to be a test for Prime Minister Mark Carney, setting up confrontations with Quebec over issues like immigration and the monarchy.
The party has also pledged to hold a referendum on Quebec's independence, similar to an upcoming vote in province of Alberta later this month.
The majority French-speaking province has held other votes on this, in 1980 and 1995. Polls indicate only 30% of Quebecers back such a move.
Plamondon has said that vote would occur after US President Donald Trump is out of office.
Carney may find himself managing dual unity crises in different parts of the country, depending on the outcome of the separation vote in Alberta. Trump is due to leave office in roughly two years, meaning that if Plamondon keeps his pledge, a third plebiscite on independence would likely be scheduled for 2029 or 2030.
Separate from sovereignty, Plamondon has made it clear he is willing to fight Ottawa if it is seen as overstepping matters of provincial interest.
He suggested during the campaign that he was going to pressure Ottawa, external on issues like immigration, vowing to fight any increases mandated by the Carney government.
He also pledged to "abolish the monarchy in Quebec" and reroute money spent on its institutions to social services instead.
"We are going to do what we have to do to get the monarchy out of Quebec, repatriate those funds, and send them to social causes," he told reporters in late September.
For example, Plamondon suggested defunding Quebec's lieutenant-governor's office - responsible for representing King Charles III in the province - saying he would instead spend that money to tackle homelessness.
Plamondon was among the Quebec lawmakers who refused to pledge allegiance to the King in 2022, paving the way for a provincial law that now makes the oath of allegiance optional.
His plan to withdraw financial support for the lieutenant-governor's office is likely to face significant legal challenges, given the monarchy's central role in Canada's constitution.
Such a move would also put future Quebec laws in doubt, as one of the key roles of the lieutenant-governor is to give royal assent to new legislation.
Pressed about these hurdles, Plamondon has told reporters that he is ready for a legal battle with the federal government.
The success of the Parti Québécois on Monday is in part due to public fatigue with the previous Coalition Avenir Québec government.
Coalition Avenir Québec made safeguarding Quebec's identity and language central to its eight years in office, but its longtime leader, François Legault, eventually lost significant support among voters.
Efforts to revive the party by replacing Legault with a new leader, outgoing Premier Christine Fréchette, were unsuccessful.
Fréchette conceded her own re-election race in Trois-Rivières shortly before 22:00 local time. She said in a speech that she would work with St-Pierre Plamondon on the transition.
"Governing Quebec is the greatest honour I have ever had," she said. "I have Quebec tattooed on my heart."
The Quebec Liberal Party secured the second-most seats, while the Quebec Conservative Party gained seats.
Prime Minister Carney, who leads the federal Liberal party, remains popular in Quebec, though support for him had recently dipped, external as US President Donald Trump imposed new tariffs on Canada in August, following a breakdown in trade talks.
Quebec is among the hardest hit by the latest US tariffs, with experts at global forecasting firm Oxford Economics projecting a C$2bn blow for the province.
Carney congratulated Plamondon on his victory late on Monday and vowed to work together with the party.
"Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada," he said in a post on social media. "I look forward to working with you to support Québec's businesses and workers impacted by tariffs, create more good jobs, work to end homelessness, and get more homes built across Québec."

In a single generation, energy drinks have conquered the beverage world. Starting as an upscale version of the humble NoDoz pill, then sugared up for guzzling, they are now the caffeine jolt of choice for the sluggish and the sleep-deprived. In an odd commercial convergence, they have also hooked up with the burgeoning wellness movement by adding favorites like ginseng, vitamins, and amino acids to the mix, making the energy drink seem like a friendly sports drink. Presto! An $85-billion-a-year (and growing) global market is upon us.
Which is fine. Caffeine in whatever form, be it in coffee or tea or Coca-Cola, has long been a staple of the American kitchen table.
But there is a large problem with allowing market forces alone to square the deal: Energy drinks are not safe, especially for teens and pre-teens. Too much caffeine (and perhaps the sporty added favorites, too) can push the naïve teen heart or mind into overdrive, leading to acute illness and even death. A decade-plus ago, the evidence was strong enough to lead the American Medical Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics, and even Congress to advise extreme restraint.
In response, many producers agreed to not advertise to those under 12 years of age — but declined to protect 13 to 18-year-olds. They anticipated that, after a few years of further “debate,” politicians would move on from the issue. Which they did.
Meanwhile, the financial clout of the industry has grown considerably, resulting in a new, more dangerous problem.
Faced with promises of big cash pay-outs, American universities have entered the fray on the wrong side of the argument. The first mega-splash came over the summer, with the $20 million-a-year agreement between Monster Energy and college sports’ Big 12 Conference (which includes the caffeine-avoidant Brigham Young University). The deal makes Monster the Big 12’s “official entitlement partner” and specifically includes placement of a Monster patch onto every game jersey.
Not to be outdone, Celsius, another prominent energy drink, has partnered with ESPN to sponsor College GameDay, the hub of the let’s-have-fun-and-watch-TV-sports-all-day movement. Why support a TV show? As an ex-teen boy, I know why: College football is the promised land of uber-impressionable boys dreaming of becoming bros. Or as John Higgins, professor of cardiology at UTHealth in Houston, an expert on the risk the drinks pose to the young, put it to me, “An energy-drink logo on a Big 12 jersey tells [a] child: this is part of sports, performance and success.”
Celsius makes the same point in market terms. “College is where the next generation of fans and consumers are shaping culture,” the write, calling their collaboration with ESPN “a natural evolution of that commitment” in a press release. There it is: fans and consumers together as one, indivisible! Forever!
To make the misalliance even more concerning, some of the universities receiving the dough are also doing research that demonstrates the benefits of the drinks. One study, for example, found that “active individuals may improve acute metabolic outcomes via consumption of a caffeine- and protein-containing energy drink.” Indeed, this sort of play-to-be-paid approach with energy drinks is now global.
Some wealthy countries, including Norway and Kuwait, have imposed strict rules to formally ban sale to teens. Others are considering the same. Most notably, the European Food Safety Authority is updating its guidance on energy drinks, having given the drinks a soft pass a decade ago.
In most countries, however, well-funded measures developed by the energy drink oligarchy have been successful at keeping regulation at a distance.
So here we are with a mega-cash cow that poses a recognized health threat to young people. Despite the hard work of many physicians and citizens who are speaking out, the U.S. is still dithering about how best to move forward.
But take heart! In recent years, there have been two great public health triumphs in protecting teens from commercially lucrative harm: Both cigarettes and alcohol have real restrictions on access and on advertising as well.
Mothers Against Drunk Driving, or MADD, was founded in 1980 by a mother whose 13-year-old daughter was killed by an intoxicated driver. The story of moms (and dads) forcing profound change is grassroots campaigning at its most inspiring. Because of their work, we now have designated drivers, a national drinking age, and a definition of when blood alcohol levels are too high. And by an older MADD estimate, drunk driving death have fallen 55%.
A similar parent-powered movement appears to be forming against energy drinks. In Texas, parents have demanded that school districts ban all energy drinks in the public schools. Similar actions have come from Tennessee, Kentucky, and beyond.
The rise and fall of Joe Cool, the Camel cigarette advertising gimmick that launched a thousand teen smokers, was accomplished with a more top-down approach. Using cold hard facts, the Federal Trade Commission brought a lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds stating that the cigarette maker caused “substantial injury to the health and safety of children and adolescents under 18.”
Surely those seeking to restrict access to energy drinks can draw on these successes. But the anti-energy drink campaign lacks a key ingredient: There is a paucity of cold hard facts about the harm being done. Even now, we cannot say with any confidence how many people die annually from energy drink ingestion.
Unlike deaths from a drug such as fentanyl, no government agency tracks the number of deaths connected to energy drinks nationally. Some data are available: Emergency room visits by teens and young adults from energy drink ingestion doubled from 2017 to 2023. America’s Poisons Centers reported a 24% increase in calls for “pediatric exposure to energy drinks” between 2022 and 2023. The state of Connecticut formally into their General Assembly entered the heartbreaking details of more than three dozen local deaths strongly linked to energy drinks. Compelling information, but not strong enough to convince a politician.
In the absence of population-based evidence, the energy drink cabal is having an easy time of it, lazily deflecting criticism about risk by citing an alternative explanation to each death: Maybe the deaths were due to the person drinking too many energy drinks (which the makers themselves advise against). Or maybe the death was from another medication they were taking, or from a preexisting heart condition or the use of an illicit substance.
Thus far the U.S. has done very little. A disappointingly wimpy government attempt to start the ball rolling includes the Susan Katz Caffeine Safety Act (named for a 21-year-old woman who died of cardiac arrest after consuming an energy drink), which would impose mandatory disclosure of caffeine amounts in beverages and food. But this bill has failed in both 2025 and 2026 to pass in Congress.
The Food and Drug Administration has issued “Guidance for Industry” on how various commercial concerns should (not “must”) display caffeine amounts in their drinks.
My guess is that parents of school-aged kids, supported by physicians, will be the ones to bring enough focus to the danger to finally address this problem. But this will take time that some unlucky teens simply don’t have.
Kent Sepkowitz is a professor emeritus of medicine at Weill-Cornell Medical College.

Hyundai's all-electric hot hatch goes on sale in the UK, starting at around $25,000
The EV maker has no plans to bring the Ioniq 3 to the US, though.
Hyundai's Ioniq 3 and its extremely attractive price tag has landed in the UK. First introduced in April, the all-electric compact hatchback is now available to order, starting at £18,495, or around $25,000. That final price is thanks to a £3,750 Electric Car Grant in the UK that each Ioniq 3 model qualifies for.
Ashley Andrew, president of Hyundai Motor UK, said in a press release that the Ioniq 3 had more customers registering interest before launch than any other Hyundai introduced in the country. For that starting price, you get the Advance trim that's equipped with a 42 kWh battery and provides a 213-mile range. Alternatively, you can pay all the way up to £31,945, or around $42,000, for the top-end N-Line Evo version that comes with a 61 kWh battery and up to 308 miles of range. The Ioniq 3 was built on a 400V architecture, and it can charge from 10 to 80 percent in about 29 minutes (it might vary slightly depending on which size battery you choose).
Hyundai said the Ioniq 3 is its first vehicle in Europe to use its new Pleos Connect Infotainment system that's based on the Android Automotive OS and offers a more intuitive design. Depending on the trim, you can get either a 12.9-inch or 14.6-inch infotainment display, along with optional features like heated seats and steering wheel or Hyundai's smart driving features like Highway Driving Assist 2 and Blind View Monitor.
Hyundai describes the Ioniq 3 as an EV hatchback built for everyday European needs, so it's not surprising that it won't be coming to the US. On top of that, Hyundai's latest EV is being built in Turkey meaning that it would be subject to US tariffs that would take away from the main selling point of affordability. Instead, US customers have similar options with Hyundai's slightly larger Ioniq 5 or more recently, the Kia EV3 that starts at around $31,000.

What are emotions, really? And why do we have them?
Simply put, emotions are intangible responses to what we see happening around us. They arise spontaneously, without conscious thought.
Emotions allowed early humans to efficiently dodge dangers as they explored the world around them. While the world and our lives in it are very different today than the way they were for our ancestors, our emotions haven’t changed.
Despite being so fundamental to our survival as a species, however, scientists are still piecing together how emotions arise in our brains. In a study recently published in Science, in fact, scientists have just reported mapping the brain-wide activity patterns that trigger emotions.
The team found that once an emotion was set off, it outlasted the trigger that sparked it in the first place. If this sounds familiar, it’s because this is what you feel when you accidentally stub your toe, burn your hand, and even when you enjoy your favourite flavour of ice cream.
In all these examples, there is incoming sensory information that prompts an emotional response while the good or bad feeling lasts even after the body part has been reflexively pulled back or after the ice cream is finished.
Stories hidden in blinks
In the new study, scientists led by Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University examined how emotions emerged in response to unpleasant (but not painful) sensory stimuli.
The participants were subjected to an eye puff assay: a machine called a tonometer blew light puffs of air into their left eye in specific sequences. Each puff lasted about 60 ms, the gap between puffs was 3-8 s long, and the entire session lasted 5 minutes. The scientists varied the gap between puffs so that participants didn’t reflexively tense up for the next puff they knew was coming.
Also read: Making the brain transparent
During the entire duration, a high-speed camera recorded the way participants closed their eyes and their behavioral and subjective responses.
As expected, repeated puffs of air to the eye elicited reflexive blinking as participants instinctively pulled back from the tonometer. They also kept the eye closed for certain durations or squinted or blinked rapidly during the gaps. As part of their subjective reports, the participants said this experience was “unpleasant” and “annoying”.
The scientists recruited a separate group of participants who were, at the time of the study, inpatients at the Stanford university hospital and had electrodes planted in their brains to check for epileptic seizures. Members of this group who consented to participate underwent the same eyepuff assay. The scientists found that these participants’ behavioural responses were consistent with those of the previous group. They also blinked reflexively and kept their eyes closed for (relatively) long periods.
The real story emerged in the brain activity patterns.
Enter: ketamine
Each puff causes a signal to be broadcast throughout the brain, like a “breaking news” alert, followed by a slower, more persistent signal. In this second phase, based on data from the electrodes in the brains of participants, scientists found that specific circuits in the brain were activated, which were linked to the generation of an emotional response in the individual.
To confirm this possibility, the scientists administered ketamine to some of these participants and had them redo the eye puff assay. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved ketamine’s use as an anaesthetic and at lower doses as an antidepressant. Ketamine also induces short-term dissociation: i.e. for a brief period, it alters subjective perceptions. By injecting it, the team could separate a person’s reflexive response from the emotional one.
The scientists found that being subjected to air puffs in the eye when a person was on ketamine changed neither the initial reflexive behaviour nor the initial burst of neural activity in the brain. However, it caused the subsequent slower brain response to dissipate much faster, so much so that the volunteers no longer described the experience as annoying but as a “tickling of the eyeball”.
Consistent with this ‘weaker’ subjective experience from ketamine, the participants’ behaviour also changed. They didn’t blink or close their eyes between consecutive air puffs. Instead, they held their eyes open even though they knew more puffs were in the offing.
Ketamine is known to block a sensor in the brain whose job it is to integrate signals coming from different corners. This means in the participants injected with ketamine, the brain may not have integrated the various signals into a coherent emotional response.
Of mice and men
Even though vertebrates have brains of vastly different sizes and complexity, the overall ‘brain plan’ is highly conserved. (The brain plan is akin to the building plan of a house or apartment.) To zero in on those systems responsible for emotions and which have survived evolution, Deisseroth’s team repeated their experiments with lab mice. The mice went through the eyepuff assay, had their brain activity measured with surgically planted electrodes, and had ketamine injected.
The team noticed the same patterns in mice as they had in humans. Injecting ketamine substantially changed the spiking activity in some neurons but not others. Only those neurons (or brain regions) coordinating the second phase — the slower response after the burst — were affected by ketamine. The initial burst didn’t change in any way, just as with the human participants.
The scientists could also study the neural activity following a puff in greater detail in the mouse model. They found that the fast/reflexive responses corresponded with a sharp rise in activity in some of the midbrain regions. This included the thalamus, where incoming sensory signals converge before being relayed onward, and the periaqueductal grey, which is involved in emotional behaviours.
They also found that the second phase of neural activity corresponded with activity in the brain’s emotional centres (described by the umbrella term ‘limbic regions’) and the frontal cortex. Again, as expected.
Then they dissected the brain activity patterns by stages, focusing on how quickly activity in brain regions shot up after the eyepuff and how long it took to fade away. They noticed that activity patterns in most of the pertinent regions increased at an explosive pace right after the eyepuff — but the rate of decrease was more interesting.
A pattern appears
The patterns in different regions slowed at different rates, fading first in the midbrain regions and last in the frontal cortex. The thalamus was active both in the first and the second phase. Considering the thalamus is the brain’s coordinating centre for all sensory signals, it makes sense that it would be active in the first phase. Incoming sensory signals go on to higher brain regions from the cortex. So it also served the role of handing off the baton, so to speak, and thus essayed a sort of bridging role across timescales.
The new study is the first to report this sort of differential pattern across different parts of the brain vis-à-vis emotions. At this point, it is not possible to say with any certainty what the implications are for the brain’s cortical and mid-brain areas.
With computational models of neuron firing activity in the mouse and the mouse’s behaviour following the eye puff assay, the team found that the timescale of neural activity was an important factor that shaped the emotional response.
Indeed, if the sensory signals dissipate before the brain has a chance to integrate the information, the person won’t be able to learn the lesson: “protect yourself from that obnoxious thing”. On the other hand, if brain activity is more strongly coupled to the fast and slow phases that Deisseroth & co. observed, such activity also lasts longer than normal, causing its own problems. Over-stabilised brain states have been correlated with depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder, all of which cause people to experience uninterrupted or mistimed thoughts and emotions.
Beyond the binary of health and disease, the fast and slow phases of brain activity highlighted in the study could reveal the fundamentals of information processing in the brain. People differ in how their brains process information about their environment — in turn a product of their genetic makeup and their upbringing in their formative years.
First steps
Why do we have emotions? For now it may be more gainful to flip the question: what would happen if we didn’t have them?
In the absence of an instinctive reaction that our emotions afford us, the brain’s response would be based entirely on risk-benefit analyses, which can be very time consuming. Over time we’d struggle to make decisions both big and small. What should I wear today? What should I make for dinner tonight? What should I study? Whom should I marry? Purely rational thought would turn such questions into never-ending decision-making exercises with no final answer.
The new study has revealed what happens in the brain in the first seconds when an emotion takes root. One hopes future studies will reveal the specific information encoded by this primal circuitry, how they encode different emotions, and how they evolve with time.
Dr. Reeteka Sud is a neuroscientist by training and senior scientist at the Center for Brain and Mind, Department of Psychiatry, NIMHANS, Bengaluru.

IPO-bound study abroad platform Leverage Edu is targeting ₹600 Cr in revenue in FY27, up over 60% from the ₹372 Cr it reported in FY26, sources told Inc42. The startup’s management wants to reach this revenue milestone before taking it public. Alongside its listing preparations, Leverage Edu is exploring a ₹500 Cr pre-IPO funding round to bring a large private equity firm onto its cap table. The startup has held talks with a couple of global PE firms and is expected to close the round soon, the sources said. “Akshay has committed to the board that the company will list by the end of next year. He is currently out in the market to finalise investment bankers for the IPO,” one of the sources said, referring to founder and CEO Akshay Chaturvedi. Leverage Edu did not respond to Inc42’s questions till the time of publication. Preparing For A Public Listing Inc42 earlier exclusively reported that the startup is planning a ₹2,000–3,000 Cr IPO, comprising a fresh issue of shares and an OFS. The split between the two components is yet to be decided. The startup is targeting a valuation of over $900 Mn for the IPO. Pitch decks prepared by investment bankers and accessed by Inc42 position Leverage Edu alongside platform businesses such as Zomato, ixigo, and Shadowfax, with expectations of similar valuation multiples. It turned EBITDA profitable in FY26, posting an EBITDA of ₹9.5 Cr, according to the sources. Meanwhile, Leverage Edu has been expanding its international presence. The startup’s services spanning fintech, accommodation, travel, and career support account for 25–33% of its total revenue. It also claimed to have added over 55,000 students in FY26, taking its total customer base to over 1.75 Lakh. Leverage Edu has raised about $73 Mn in funding to date from investors including Blume Ventures, DSG Consumer Partners, and Kaizenvest.

You can get Microsoft 365 for free through an eligible Education plan, free web and mobile versions of Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and other apps, or a 30-day Microsoft 365 trial with full desktop apps and 1 TB of OneDrive storage.
Microsoft 365 (formerly Office 365) is a subscription service that gives you access to various Microsoft products. This includes productivity apps like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and OneNote; 1 TB of OneDrive cloud storage; and tools like Teams, Forms, and Loop.
As of writing, a paid subscription starts at $1.99 a month or $19.99 a year for Microsoft 365 Basic and goes up to $19.99 a month or $199.99 a year for Microsoft 365 Premium. Whether getting a subscription is justified depends on which of the included apps and services you use and how much.
If you’re not too sure about that and don’t want to buy a subscription right away, you can get Microsoft 365 for free using the following methods. Which method to pick depends on whether you’re a student/educator and your requirements.
Get the Microsoft 365 Education Plan
Microsoft 365 Education is a special plan for students and educators that provides free access to Microsoft 365 apps and services. You need a valid school, college, or university email address to be eligible. You’d have one if you’re a student or educator at an accredited institution with a Microsoft Education license.
To check if you qualify, visit the Microsoft 365 Education portal, type your institution-issued email address, and hit Next. If you’re eligible, you’ll be prompted to log in with the same email address. Or you may receive a verification link in your inbox. Subsequently, you’ll be able to use the Microsoft 365 apps within the browser or download them to your devices, based on the plan your institute offers.
Microsoft 365 Education is currently available in three plans: A1, A3, and A5. Your institute will most likely offer an A1 plan since it’s free, though some may offer an A3. The major difference between them is that A1 is web-only, whereas A3 supports downloads, so you can use the apps even when you’re offline.
If you don’t have an institute-provided email address or it isn’t eligible for the Education plan, you can get Microsoft 365 for free using the next method.

Use Microsoft 365 for the Web or Native Mobile Apps
Unless you have advanced needs — creating and running macros (VBA) in Excel, multi-device installation rights, or fully offline mode — you don’t really need a Microsoft 365 subscription. The online version of Microsoft 365, which offers access to basic versions of its apps, along with 5GB of free cloud storage, should serve your needs just as well.
All you need for this method is a Microsoft account and a web browser. In your preferred browser, visit the Microsoft 365 online portal and sign in with your Microsoft account. Create a new Microsoft account if you don’t have one.
Next, click the app launcher icon in your dashboard and select the app you want to use. This will open the app in a new browser tab, where you can create a new document or work on an existing one in your OneDrive storage. Any changes you make to the document are automatically saved to the cloud. Keep in mind, though, that the app’s functionality halts completely when you lose the internet connection.
Just like Microsoft 365 for the web, Microsoft also offers mobile apps for many of its productivity apps. So, if you just want to work on a Word, Excel, or PowerPoint document, you can download their mobile apps on your phone or tablet and use them. Just note that these apps offer limited functionality, similar to the web version. However, unlike their web versions, mobile apps support some offline functionality, allowing you to view a cached version of the document or edit local documents, even without an active internet connection.
Get the Microsoft 365 Free Trial
Microsoft offers a 30-day free trial to Microsoft 365. This trial gives you full, unrestricted access to the service, including complete offline capabilities and the ability to download desktop apps to your PC or Mac. You also get 1 TB of OneDrive cloud storage.
A free trial is great for someone who wants full-blown access to Microsoft’s productivity suite for a brief period. It also makes sense for those who want the Microsoft 365 service without committing to an upfront payment.
To subscribe to a 30-day Microsoft 365 free trial, you need a Microsoft account and a valid payment method. Open a browser and go to the official Microsoft 365 free trial page. Click the Start Free Trial button, and log in with your Microsoft account when prompted. If you haven’t taken a free trial with this account previously, you’ll be asked to add a valid payment method. Complete the checkout process. You now have complete access to Microsoft 365.
Set a reminder to cancel the subscription before the 30 days are up. If you forget, Microsoft will convert the trial to a monthly or annual subscription and charge you for the same on your added payment method.
Identify Your Use Case to Find the Right Method
You can use any of the above methods to get Microsoft 365 for free. However, not all of them offer the same level of access. As such, it’s important to identify your use case before choosing a method.
For example, if you want a full-blown Excel experience for a few weeks, the free 30-day trial makes more sense. Meanwhile, you might want to subscribe to the Microsoft 365 Education plan if you’re a student or educator and want desktop access to productivity apps for a longer period. Or use their mobile apps on your phone or tablet if you only need to view or maintain a few Excel sheets.

“Rendering Doom in a database is obviously a bad idea,” Lukas Vogel writes in a lengthy blog post explaining how exactly he managed to render Doom using an SQL database.
OK, that’s not entirely accurate. The SQLDoom project uses a small Python client to handle input and output, drive the game’s timing, and display each frame to the screen. Behind that, a series of CedarDB tables tracks the game geometry and state, while about 1,300 lines of SQL queries spread across 89 common table expressions implement the game logic and generate 35 bitmap framebuffers per second.
In this, SQLDoom is a major improvement over Vogel’s previous DoomQL project, which last year set out to build “a multiplayer Doom-like shooter entirely in SQL.” Unfortunately, that effort ended up with raycasting-based, grayscale ASCII graphics that were more akin to the simplistic 90-degree-angled maps of Wolfenstein 3D. The newer SQLDoom, on the other hand, generates full-color 640×480 frames that look like they could have come from the original Doom executable.
It’s all just data, man
Converting Doom‘s classic WAD files to a relational database was relatively simple and straightforward, Vogel writes, because of the way the original game broke levels down into vertices, lines, sectors, and so on. Even Doom‘s famous binary-space partition trees can be broken down into SQL using a sort_key for objects that’s pre-computed for each position at load time. With this set in your table, a simple “ORDER BY” statement can determine every frame which parts of walls to display and which to ignore, vastly improving performance.

The Karnataka government has increased the cash awards for the State’s Asian Games 2026 medallists, with gold medallists set to receive ₹1 crore, silver medallists ₹75 lakh and bronze medallists ₹50 lakh.
For the first time, the government has also sanctioned a ₹5 lakh incentive for each of the 20 Karnataka athletes who qualified for and participated in the Asian Games.
Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar and Deputy Chief Minister and Youth Empowerment and Sports Minister G. Parameshwara felicitated Karnataka athletes who won medals at the Asian Games 2026 at Vidhana Soudha on Tuesday (October 6, 2026).
Speaking at the event, the Deputy Chief Minister said the government was taking steps to recognise sporting achievements while providing athletes with financial and employment security.
The eight Karnataka athletes who won medals at the Asian Games will receive the enhanced cash prizes. In addition, each of the eight medallists will get a ₹5 lakh participation incentive. Earlier, the cash awards were ₹35 lakh for gold, ₹25 lakh for silver and ₹15 lakh for bronze.
Mr. Parameshwara said representing the country at an international event was itself a significant achievement and that the incentive was intended to recognise the efforts of athletes.
Group-B jobs for Asian, Commonwealth medallists
Asian Games and Commonwealth Games medallists will also be eligible for direct recruitment to Group-B posts in the State government.
Eligible and interested athletes can be recruited through a selection committee headed by the Chief Secretary, the Minister said.
The government has also introduced a 2% reservation in direct recruitment for achieving sportspersons. A notification issued on October 3 provides for the reservation in Group-A, B, C and D posts across the State Government.
Four athletes get ₹10 lakh under ‘Guri: Olympics’
Four athletes — M.R. Poovamma, Sneha S.S., Shreyanka Patil and Shilpa K.S. — have been selected under the ‘Guri: Olympics’ scheme for 2026-27. Each will receive ₹10 lakh towards training, preparation and other requirements for Olympic-level competition.
Mr. Parameshwara said the government would continue to support athletes through financial assistance, training and opportunities to compete in international events.
The measures, he said, were aimed at encouraging athletes to pursue sport without having to worry about their future employment and livelihood.

'I've lost my peace' - Cape Verde hero Vozinha on newfound fame
- Published
Cape Verde's heroic World Cup goalkeeper Vozinha says he craves the "peace and tranquillity" of the life he led before he shot to fame.
The 40-year-old shot to global prominence in June when he almost single-handedly kept Spain at bay as Cape Verde drew 0-0 with the European champions on their World Cup debut.
Vozinha's follower count on social media sky-rocketed over the course of the game, from about 50,000 to more than one million.
But his fame shot up even further when Argentina needed extra time to beat Cape Verde in the round of 32.
Vozinha says his life was easier before his World Cup heroics.
"I've lost my peace and tranquillity," he told the Observer., external
"I no longer have any privacy, or at least much less than I used to.
"Now I go out, I go to a restaurant, and there's always someone who wants to take a photo with me or asks me for an autograph. Or, worse, someone is filming me.
"That's what has changed most in my life, and I don't think there's anything I can do about it."
Vozinha's mother became part of the fairytale too. After he revealed that she had could not afford a visa to watch his World Cup debut, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries announced that the visa fee had been waived.
Now Vozinha has revealed that his mother is visited on a daily basis by fans wanting to talk or to take photographs with him.
"A lot of people want to be famous and have a public profile, but they only see the positive side of that reality," said Vozinha.
"To be honest, if I were offered the life I have today or the life I had before, I'd choose the one I had before."
His World Cup performances for Cape Verde, a West African island nation with a population of 525,000, earned Vozinha a nomination for men's goalkeeper of the year at the Ballon d'Or awards.
"It's nice to feel like a kind of ambassador, but I want to make it clear that what we achieved was a collective effort," Vozinha said.
"We made history and the best news would be if we could harness that momentum to develop our country and improve the living conditions of our people."

Snapchat’s distinct navigation uses custom icons across its main features: the bottom bar accesses Snap Map, Chat, Explore, Stories, and Spotlight. In chats, color-coded arrows and squares signal message types (pink for audio-less snaps, purple for video/audio snaps, and blue for text chats), while outlined versions show opened status or screenshots.
Snapchat successfully positioned itself as “the social media platform for Gen Z”. With its ephemeral nature and best retention features such as Snapstreaks, Snapchat is one of the most popular social media platforms currently.
However, I took my time to understand the platform better and finally became a user. But still, I am far from being a snapper, a word I use for those who are obsessed with Snapstreaks, including my close friends.
Despite being a user for months, I still find the Snapchat interface harder to navigate. Part of the reason is that it is completely detached from the common interfaces used in other social media platforms.
Moreover, Snapchat uses its own terms, such as Planets, Best Friends, and Chats, which can confuse new users. So, as part of our icon explanation series, in this guide you will learn everything about icons and their meanings on Snapchat. For quick reference, here is the Snapchat legend, followed by various icons on each screen and what they mean.

Snapchat also uses various colored arrows and squares to represent the type of snaps. If you see a pink arrow icon, it means you sent a snap without audio. If you see a purple arrow, it means you sent a video snap; in other words, you sent a snap with audio or video.
If you see blue, it means the chat was sent; in other words, you sent a chat message. If you see gray, it means your chat is waiting for the person to accept you.
If the arrow turns into an outline pink arrow, it means the recipient has opened your Snapchat without audio. If you see purple, it means the recipient opened your Snapchat with audio or video, and it’s the same for the blue outline arrow.
