Democrats' advantage is clear with less than a month to go in the midterm elections
President Trump was elected in 2024, in large measure, with a mandate to bring down prices. But that hasn't happened. Instead, Trump is facing record-low approval ratings, and voters are blaming him for costs that have continued to rise since he took office this second time around.
As a result, Republicans are likely to pay the price at the ballot box next month. One month out from Election Day, the electoral landscape has shifted even more so in Democrats' direction.
They are favored to win the House, albeit with a fairly narrow majority. The Cook Political Report forecasts a five-to-15-seat net gain for Democrats at this point. That would give them in the range of 220 to 230 seats come January. (218 is needed for a majority.)
The Senate has shifted more dramatically over the last several months. Six seats have moved more in Democrats' direction since June in comparing Cook's ratings from then to now. When the cycle first started, the Senate was a long shot for Democrats. Now, it's within reach.
And that's largely because of the national mood, which is usually the case in midterms. Trump has just a 37% approval rating, according to an average of the polls. That's tied for the lowest pre-midterm approval in the last half century.
The only other president to be that low in that time was George W. Bush in 2006. Back then, Iraq was spiraling into civil war, and Republicans lost both the House and Senate.
Trump is also facing a historic intensity of opposition; 53% in the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll said they strongly disapprove of the job the president is doing, the highest ever recorded in the survey. That's not a great sign for Republicans with Trump insisting that the midterm elections be about him.
As it is, history is unkind to the president's party in midterm elections. They usually lose about two dozen seats in the House and four in the Senate. It's even worse for the party in power when the president's approval rating is below 50%, as Trump's is now.
Loading...
There are multiple reasons Democratic gains might be limited, including mid-decade redistricting helping to insulate Republicans, fewer competitive-to-potentially competitive House seats, with most in districts Trump won in 2024, Republicans' campaign spending edge and the unpopularity of the Democratic Party.
That said, the headwinds the GOP is facing are very real.
Republicans have lost their edge on the economy
Economic issues continue to rate as the top problem and most important issue facing the country.
Most presidents get more blame and credit than they deserve for the economy, but the war with Iran and Trump's tariffs were choices that have directly led to increased costs on many goods and energy.
The economy is increasingly bifurcated with the wealthy doing well and regular people struggling. Wealthy Americans are seeing increases in their wealth and stock portfolios, which are dominated by AI companies.
It's a different story for many others. Inflation is outpacing wages, meaning people's paychecks aren't taking them as far. There isn't a lot of turnover in the labor market, so if someone doesn't have a job or is looking to change, it's not an easy thing to do.
Plus, many are turning against AI. In many places, it's driving up utility costs and, along with the rising national debt, is making borrowing more difficult.
All of that is coming at a time when gas prices have skyrocketed because of the Iran war, and interest rates are creeping higher. In trying to tame inflation, the Federal Reserve hiked rates this fall. That makes it more expensive to borrow money and harder to pay for things like houses and cars.
The blame for that sort of thing often gets pointed directly at the White House and the party in power, and right now, that's Trump and Republicans.
An AP/NORC poll released last week, for example, found that 65% said higher-than-usual prices are more because of Trump's policies than factors outside of his control.
Just 26% said they approved of the job he's doing on the economy.
An NBC News poll from September found that for only the second time in the Trump era, respondents said they trusted Democrats more than Republicans on the economy. (Though it was within the margin of error, the movement in the survey was clear.)
The only other time Democrats led on that question was in 2018 – the last midterm year when Trump was president. Democrats won 42 seats and control of the House then.
Add the widely negative views of the economy to the administration's immigration enforcement tactics, discretionary domestic cuts, the slashing of regulations and the government workforce, and it's all firing up Democrats.
An opposition party enthusiastic to vote is a major warning sign for the president's party, especially in a midterm year.
History is not on the side of the president's party in midterm elections
In 18 of the 20 midterms since World War II, the president's party has lost House seats. On average, it's 26 seats, and it's nine more than that when a president's approval rating is below 50%.
The last three midterm elections have seen fewer lost House seats, despite unpopular presidents, in large measure because the universe of competitive districts is smaller.
The president, himself, though, has acknowledged multiple times the political headwinds his party faces in midterms.
"Whether you have a great president or not, Republican or Democrat, they don't do well in midterms," Trump said Friday at a campaign rally in Alabama. "I don't know why. Nobody's explained it."
There are reasons, however.
First, turnout in midterms is historically about 30% lower than in presidential years. So, the voters most fired up to vote show up in outsized numbers.
Anger is a great motivator, and often the voters more aligned with the opposition party most want to register their frustration. And, as noted earlier, the intensity of opposition to Trump is at historic levels.
A CBS poll out Sunday found Democrats with the enthusiasm edge – 84% of Democrats and 82% of independents surveyed said they are "definitely" going to vote compared to 77% of Republicans.
What's more, a key indicator of which party does well in midterms is pointing in the Democrats' direction. Surveys, including the NPR/PBS News/Marist poll, ask a version of: "If November's election for Congress were held today, which party's candidate are you more likely to vote for in your district?"
In an average of the 2026 polls, Democrats have a nine-point advantage on this question, known as the congressional ballot test. Democrats tend to need a larger lead on the question historically than Republicans, given how districts have been drawn. But +9 is in the range of what Democrats need.
To put a finer point on it: in each of the past seven midterm elections, the party with the advantage on the congressional ballot has made gains.
Loading...
With independents and Latinos, two swing groups, souring on Trump during this second term, that's an added problem for Republicans in competitive districts.
Their jobs are made even tougher when Trump says things like "pretend" he's on the ballot and makes the election a "referendum" on him.
The White House's theory of the case is that Trump has had success turning conservatives out when he's on the ballot, and Republican candidates need them to show up in big numbers.
But whether that's enough is going to be tested. In swing districts and some key Senate races, candidates also usually need voters in the middle to win.
The bottom line is with less than a month to go until all the votes are in, the political compass is pointed in Democrats' direction. For multiple reasons, Democrats' gains might not be as big as similar numbers might indicate in past elections, but there is no doubt that, right now, they have the wind at their backs.

Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
- Published
Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.
Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF forces have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city.
Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and federal government forces alongside allied fighters in parts of Ethiopia's northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries.
The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours.

  - Published2 days ago
Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides.
However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.
Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied.
Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.
The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

High-flying lawyer goes on trial for writing bad cheque allegedly to cover for collapsing firm
Nicholas Cartel is self-representing against criminal charge stemming from probe into $7M embezzlement
A Toronto lawyer who co-founded a law firm with his wife that collapsed spectacularly three years ago, after millions of dollars in client money was discovered missing from the firm's trust account, went on trial Monday on a fraud charge stemming from the police investigation into the case.
Nicholas Cartel, 62, faces one count of fraud over $5,000 based on allegations that he deliberately wrote a bad cheque for $300,000 in an attempt to cover up a shortfall in the trust account at Cartel & Bui LLP, the firm he ran with his wife.
The alleged fraud occurred in February 2023, when Cartel & Bui LLP was handling a property sale for a client. The law firm needed to pay out $2.22 million in proceeds to the client but didn't have sufficient funds in its trust account because Bui had been embezzling money from it for years, according to her own evidence in a separate civil case.
Bui is facing 32 criminal charges in a separate case stemming from the embezzlement.
The February 2023 incident foreshadowed a series of events in which more than 25 property owners and buyers in southern Ontario ran into problems closing on real estate deals because money was missing from the Cartel & Bui trust account.
One couple lost $2.16 million they had entrusted to the firm to buy a house in Toronto, while other clients — or home-purchase insurers — were out as much as $729,000.
Cartel is not facing criminal charges in relation to those other cases, and has long maintained his innocence. He says he operated a separate legal practice at the firm focused on class actions and litigation, while the theft of client money occurred in the real estate side of the business run by his wife, Singa Bui.
With respect to the criminal charge alleging that he deliberately wrote a bad cheque, Cartel does not deny writing it but says his actions didn't amount to fraud.
He also maintains that prosecutors have improperly withheld evidence from him and misleadingly presented other evidence. At the outset of his trial Monday, he told the court he intends to bring an application under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to have his criminal charge stayed.
Bank employees testify
At the start of Monday's trial in provincial court in Toronto, prosecutor Dihim Emami called a witness from Royal Bank of Canada's investigations department to testify about records associated with the personal chequing account on which the $300,000 cheque was drawn.
The witness, Adkin Holder, a former Toronto police fraud-squad detective, testified that the account's opening documents showed it belonged to Cartel and that for months before the bad cheque was written, the account had a negative balance.
He said that because of that, a $300,000 cheque would have failed to cash, and the receiving bank could have been at risk of losing the money if it was unable to recover it from the person who wrote the cheque.
Cartel later asked Holder whether it was possible the account was in fact a joint account at the time the bad cheque was written, which Holder agreed was possible.
Prosecutors then entered records showing that the account statements bore only Cartel's name, while statements for other joint accounts bore both his name and Bui's.
A second witness, from TD Bank, where the law firm had its trust account, began testifying Monday afternoon about transactions in that account and is expected to resume Tuesday.
Already jailed for contempt of court
Cartel has already spent 30 days in jail over the collapse of his firm, after a judge in separate civil lawsuits against him and his wife ruled in August 2024 that he had committed contempt of court by failing to produce records or answer questions about where the missing trust-account money went.
He filed an appeal of that ruling, but it was dismissed this past August because he failed to move it forward.
He is also on the hook for millions of dollars in default judgments against him obtained by former clients of his firm, though has said he will contest them.
His attempt to overturn one of those judgments, for $500,000, was rejected by the Ontario Court of Appeal in February.
Defendant dismissed his criminal lawyer
Cartel hired veteran criminal lawyer Richard Posner to defend him late last year, but split with Posner 4½ months later amid a dispute over his fees and trial strategy, according to records obtained by CBC from a separate case in which Cartel challenged Posner's billings.
Those records show Cartel wanted his lawyer to try to get his charge dismissed as an abuse of process — a rare remedy available when a defendant can show that the prosecution's conduct seriously compromised the accused's right to a fair trial.
"In my respectful view, there is no basis for advancing an abuse of process claim in this case," Posner emailed Cartel, according to documents from their fee dispute.
"If you want to bring this motion, you will need to discharge me and find another lawyer or represent yourself."

At another point, Cartel and Posner differed over whether they should agree at trial to certain of the prosecution's alleged facts.
"Why dispute or make the Crown prove things that are plain and obvious from the business records? In my view, it makes no sense to do so, but the choice is yours," Posner wrote to Cartel.
Ultimately, Posner wrote to Cartel in April of this year: "Based on the tenor and content of your email, along with your previous communications with the members of my office, it is my respectful view there has been a breakdown in our solicitor-client relationship. Accordingly, I will be requesting to be removed from the record on the next court date."
Cartel replied: "I was going to terminate your services Monday, in any event…. I have long ago lost any faith that you or your firm could represent my best interests."

Cartel told CBC News on Monday, on the sidelines of his trial, that he and Posner had settled their dispute out of court.
He is representing himself in his criminal trial. The judge, Rachel Grinburg, referred to that fact in court several times Monday, emphasizing that she wanted to ensure the proceedings were fair to him.
His law licence has been provisionally suspended since April 2024 by the Law Society of Ontario, which has levelled 20 disciplinary accusations against him, including 12 counts of misappropriation of client funds.
Bui was disbarred by the Law Society in December.

There’s been a lot of doom and gloom from the auto industry lately when the subject of China comes up. Automaker CEOs, in particular, warn that allowing low-cost, high-tech Chinese electric vehicles to be sold in the US would effectively spell the end of their businesses.
Hyundai CEO says only a ‘level playing field’ can minimize damage from China
Hyundai CEO José Muñoz says the US could be overrun like Europe without protections in place.
Hyundai CEO José Muñoz is not as pessimistic as some of his counterparts. He says he’s confident the right mix of protectionist policies and improvements on the product side can keep China at bay. Even though his company is feeling the squeeze from China, Muñoz isn’t ready to throw in the towel. But he also acknowledges that China could flood the US with affordable imports without established protections in place.
“As long as there is a level playing field for everybody,” Muñoz said at the reveal of the new 2027 Hyundai Tucson in New York City last week. “That’s all we ask, right? We compete everywhere in the world, and then we have seen that in the markets where that position is respected, so it’s really good for us.”
Chinese automakers have expanded rapidly in Europe, gobbling up market share and damaging domestic brands like Volkswagen, Volvo, and Mercedes by offering vehicles at much lower prices. US automakers warn the same could be true for them if China were allowed to import its vehicles here.
“We compete everywhere in the world, and then we have seen that in the markets where that position is respected, so it’s really good for us.”
— José Muñoz
Steep tariffs and laws that prohibit the sale of cars with software from China have basically made it impossible to sell Chinese vehicles in the US. But in recent months, the dam appears to be weakening. President Donald Trump has said several times that he would be open to Chinese automakers building manufacturing plants in the US if they hire American workers. And experts across the board believe it’s only a matter of time before China finds a way to sell its cars in the US.
But if Chinese brands eventually set up manufacturing inside North America or enter via partner channels, it’s not clear whether Hyundai has a defensive strategy ready. I asked Muñoz whether his company had begun to plan for the eventuality of Chinese imports available in the US market. He said it had not.
“We don’t develop strategies specifically because of the Chinese or because of other types of consumers, or other types of competitors,” he said. “We are always trying to do better.”
If Hyundai has any strategy, Muñoz added, it’s vertical integration: bringing down costs by making its tech and components. “This allows us to be more competitive,” he said. “Better quality over cost.”
“We don’t develop strategies specifically because of the Chinese or because of other types of consumers, or other types of competitors.”
Muñoz cited Hyundai’s $5.8 billion investment in Louisiana to produce green steel as an example of the company’s efforts to vertically integrate in the US. Hyundai expects the investment to provide better, more competitive, and more environmentally friendly steel. He says the same philosophy applies to software and other technologies that Hyundai wants to develop internally.
“So there is always room to do better,” he continued. “So if the Chinese competitor were to enter in the market, we would see what would happen, but I don’t know, I don’t have a crystal ball. I just look around, for example, Europe, and see what has happened, and then you may expect similar type of behaviors.”
Chinese vehicles sold in Europe are on average about 30 percent cheaper than comparable European-made rival models, even when factoring in EU import tariffs. The US has already fallen behind the rest of the world when it comes to EV adoption, after Trump and Republicans in Congress eliminated federal subsidies. In Europe, EVs account for over 20 percent of sales; in China, it’s over 60 percent. In the US, it’s less than 6 percent.
Political polarization certainly plays a role in depressing sales, as does inadequate charging infrastructure. But the lack of affordable electric models is regularly cited as the biggest barrier to adoption in the US. On that front, Muñoz thinks the US can still catch up.
“I think the American market is the most competitive in the world,” he said, noting that Hyundai still records robust EV sales here. That may be true, but the company’s hybrids are what’s keeping its EV business afloat. Hyundai has added hybrids to a wide range of vehicles, including its top-selling Tucson.
Unlike other automakers, Hyundai hasn’t retreated from EVs. It continues to sell its Ioniq 5 and Ioniq 9 here in the US, as well as a growing number of hybrids. In fact, the Hyundai Group recently surpassed Honda to claim second place in US hybrid sales behind Toyota.
Muñoz acknowledged that the US was still catching up to China’s dominance in EV batteries. Hyundai operates a battery manufacturing joint venture with SK On in Georgia near its massive Metaplant, where it builds all of its EVs and hybrids.
“Obviously if you don’t have the critical mass, the volume, it’s very difficult to be competitive,” he said. “One of the biggest pieces of cost is the battery. That is the key element, right? But there is a lot of production of batteries in the United States with some of the best global manufacturers. So I’m not concerned.”

Unannounced protest on Gurugram’s Sohna Road triggers hours-long traffic jam
Some students staged a sit-in outside the State Council of Educational Research and Training office over some admission issues
An unannounced student protest on Gurugram’s Sohna Road triggered a traffic jam along a nearly three-kilometre stretch on Monday afternoon, with an ambulance remaining stuck for over 40 minutes. Paramedics and motorists watched helplessly as tightly packed cars, trucks, and motorcycles filled every inch, making it impossible for the ambulance to move.
Desperate two-wheeler riders tried squeezing through narrow footpath edges, only to block lanes. The jam choked key arterial roads, from the busy Rajiv Chowk underpass and junction past Tau Devi Lal Sports Complex up to Civil Lines and the District and Sessions Court.
An HT spot check found bumper-to-bumper traffic for over two to three hours. “We had not moved an inch in nearly 40 minutes,” said a commuter in his car en route to Old Gurugram. “Inside the underpass, the trapped exhaust fumes and blaring horns were suffocating. The worst part was seeing an ambulance siren wailing right behind us with nowhere to go.”
Gurugram traffic police officers said some students staged the unannounced sit-in outside the State Council of Educational Research and Training office over some admission issues. “The traffic police were prompt in diverting traffic to ease the congestion. Our teams were deployed on the ground continuously to monitor the situation,” said Gurugram traffic police spokesperson Vikas Verma.

Inside Chief Justice John Roberts are two wolves.
The Supreme Court is looking for a way to kill climate lawsuits
They just can’t come up with a legal argument that would allow them to do so.
The first wolf is a staunch conservative who spent much of his career litigating on behalf of corporate interests. This wolf looks at a series of climate change lawsuits that could potentially cost the oil industry billions of dollars or more, and recoils in horror.
The second wolf is a judge tasked with following the law wherever it leads. And that wolf seemed baffled by the oil industry’s arguments in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, a Supreme Court case where two oil companies are asking the justices to shut down dozens of climate change lawsuits.
The Court’s decision in Suncor is likely to shape the future of climate litigation in the United States. If the oil industry prevails, that will probably shut down climate change-related suits in state courts — and it may shut them down entirely because it is unclear whether federal law allows these suits to proceed in federal court. If the oil industry loses, by contrast, it could face dozens of suits in state courts across the country seeking billions of dollars or more.
And the outcome in Suncor is likely to turn on which wolf shows up to the justices’ conference on how to decide the case. Roberts, who asked the most ambiguous questions at Monday’s oral argument in Suncor, clearly wants these lawsuits to disappear. But he also appeared doubtful that the oil companies’ weak legal arguments will allow him to make that disappearing act happen.
Notably, Justice Samuel Alito, who owns stock in oil and gas companies, is recused from hearing the case. So, in the likely event that all three of the Court’s Democrats hold together against the oil companies, Roberts would split the Court 4-4 if he decides to join them. That would leave the Court unable to render a decision, and a lower court opinion, which rejected the oil companies’ bid for lawsuit immunity, would remain in effect.
That said, at least two other justices asked questions suggesting that their votes may potentially be in play. Justice Clarence Thomas, who otherwise appeared sympathetic to the oil companies, repeatedly asked whether his Court has jurisdiction to hear Suncor in the first place. Meanwhile, while most of Democratic Justice Elena Kagan’s questions seemed to favor allowing the climate change lawsuits to proceed, she did ask some questions at the end that indicated that she may be looking for a narrow reason to hand the oil companies a win.
The bottom line is that it is difficult to predict how this case will turn out, as more than one justice asked questions that suggest that their vote is, at least, in play. But the outcome is likely to hinge upon the tension within Roberts — who both signaled that he wants the oil companies to win, but who also expressed deep skepticism of their primary legal argument.
So what is Suncor actually about?
Suncor is one of many lawsuits brought by state or local governments (in this case, the plaintiff is Boulder, Colorado) who’ve sued oil companies claiming that those companies should be liable for the harms caused by climate change within those governments’ jurisdictions. In this particular case, the defendants are Exxon Mobil and Suncor, a company that operates two oil refineries in Colorado.
The lawyer for these two companies, Kannon Shanmugam, told the justices that there are about 60 similar cases brought by municipal governments throughout the country. And, in one of his more pro-oil moments during Monday’s oral argument, Roberts predicted that if Boulder wins in the Supreme Court, there will be numerous other copycat lawsuits filed by other municipalities.
The question in Suncor is whether state courts, including Colorado’s own courts, are forbidden from hearing these sorts of climate change lawsuits.
As Roberts pointed out in one of his less pro-oil moments during Monday’s argument, “there are a lot of familiar situations where conduct outside of a state has broad effects on other states…and yet we allow the state courts in a particular state to bring litigation.” He pointed to “mass tort” suits and “complaints about operations of the internet” as two examples where state courts hear lawsuits involving harms that arise across state borders.
The oil companies’ primary argument is that suits involving air and water pollution are special. But their evidence supporting this argument is confusing and difficult to parse.
Briefly, the oil companies point to several cases, many of which were decided more than a century ago. These cases held that, before Congress enacted the Clean Air Act in 1963, states could sometimes sue other states for cross-border pollution, even though no federal law forbade such pollution. The Supreme Court created “federal common law” permitting these suits, and the oil companies claim that this federal common law preempted any state lawsuits that covered a similar subject matter.
This federal common law, they now argue, has itself been displaced by the Clear Air Act and its partner statute, the Clean Water Act, but the principle that state suits involving air and water pollution are preempted is somehow still in effect. Although there is no provision in the text of the Constitution that supports this argument by the oil companies, those companies claim that their argument is implicit in the “structure of the Constitution.”
The oil companies’ primary legal argument is difficult to understand
If you are confused by all the arcane history and logical leaps contained in the oil companies’ argument, don’t worry. So were most of the justices. Only Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who repeatedly claimed that his Court’s precedents bar Boulder’s lawsuit, seemed to buy what the oil companies are saying without reservation. Most of the other justices expressed at least some reservations.
Justice Amy Coney Barrett, for example, argued that even under the older “federal common law” regime, states still retained some authority over environmental lawsuits, although she noted that the Court’s previous decisions do not really define the scope of that authority. Kagan pointed out that the many suits challenging climate change are similar to past litigation against tobacco and opioid manufacturers. But those suits were heard by state courts.
Many of the justices appear bothered that these lawsuits exist, but the most skeptical justices couldn’t agree on a legal theory they could use to shut them down.
It seems unlikely, in other words, that there are five votes for the oil companies’ convoluted claim that the “structure of the Constitution” somehow bars state courts from hearing climate change lawsuits. But several of the justices did appear troubled by what could happen if dozens of state courts reach conflicting judgments on who is responsible for climate change and who should receive compensation because of it. And some of these justices floated alternative theories for how to hand the oil companies a win.
At one point, for example, Barrett floated the possibility that, if the plaintiffs lose in Suncor, they might file a new suit under the now-defunct federal common law that existed prior to the Clean Air Act. Kagan, meanwhile, suggested that perhaps the Clean Air Act could be read to preempt these suits like Suncor. According to Kagan, that law “sets up an extremely complicated scheme about how regulations of emissions should operate,” and allowing states to hear lawsuits like Suncor would “get in the way of how Congress decided to regulate greenhouse gases.”
And Roberts didn’t so much offer a legal argument in favor of the oil companies’ position as express incredulity of what would happen if those companies lose. “Presumably if you prevail,” before the Supreme Court, Roberts told Kevin Russell, the lawyer for Boulder, “the next day a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit, copy your pleadings, and then there will be at least 50…how do you think that will work out on the ground?”
All of which is a long way of saying that the outcome in Suncor is uncertain. The oil companies led with a weak legal argument, and only Kavanaugh seemed to fully embrace that argument. Many of the justices appear bothered that these lawsuits exist, but the most skeptical justices couldn’t agree on a legal theory they could use to shut them down.
For what it is worth, the oil companies actually do make a strong policy argument that it is a bad idea to allow state courts to do so. As they argue, climate change is a global problem caused by many polluters (and companies like Exxon that supply the oil burned by polluters) throughout the world. It could be impossible to determine which specific companies caused the specific problems caused by climate change in Boulder, Colorado. And even if this obstacle can be overcome, there are many thorny questions about which state’s law should apply when pollution from one state crosses over into another, not to mention the difficult diplomatic issues that could arise if a state court orders a foreign company to pay a large sum of money.
But under our Constitution, the proper solution if the oil companies want federal law to preempt state court suits like Suncor is that they can lobby Congress, and Congress could then draft a statute that balances these companies’ interest in avoiding many conflicting legal decisions with the interests of plaintiffs like Boulder who say they are experiencing real harms from climate change. Congress has the power, for example, to combine all of these state lawsuits into one grand federal lawsuit, where a single proceeding could determine how to portion out the costs of climate change to various energy companies, and how to divide whatever these companies are ordered to pay among the various plaintiffs.
But that solution would undoubtedly require compromises that companies like Exxon will not like. So, instead, they’ve asked the Supreme Court to give them the legal regime that they want, despite the fact that they could not articulate a persuasive legal argument for that outcome. It remains to be seen whether this Court will give the oil companies a win anyway.

Italy’s Meloni follows pop stars in seeking to trademark her voice to combat AI deepfakes
Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni has applied to trademark her voice with the European Union intellectual property office in a bid to bolster protections against AI-generated deepfakes
ROME -- Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni has applied to trademark her voice with the European Union’s Intellectual Property Office, seeking to protect herself against AI-generated deepfakes.
The application filed with the EU agency includes a four-second audio recording of Meloni repeating the phrase, in Italian, “Io sono Giorgia Meloni” (“I am Giorgia Meloni”), according to the EU office's records on Monday.
The filing, first reported by Italian daily La Repubblica, was confirmed by an Italian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
Meloni’s move comes as governments, regulators and public figures grapple with the rapid spread of artificial intelligence tools capable of convincingly replicating voices and images.
The recorded phrase echoes Meloni’s famous declaration at a 2019 political rally: “I am Giorgia, I am a woman, I am a mother, I am Italian, I am Christian.” The slogan became widely known in Italy and inspired a viral dance remix. “Io sono Giorgia” was also the title of her 2021 autobiography.
Manipulated images of Meloni have repeatedly circulated online in recent years and have at times been passed off as authentic. Among them was a fake image showing her sitting on a bed in her underwear.
Meloni has warned that deepfakes can “deceive, manipulate and harm anyone,” urging users to verify online content before sharing it.
“I can defend myself, but many others cannot,” she said in May, after fake images of her surfaced online.
Pop star Taylor Swift was among the most prominent targets of deepfakes in 2024, after sexually explicit AI-generated images falsely depicting her spread widely online, fueling calls for stronger legal protections against unauthorized digital replicas.
Matthew McConaughey was one of the first major celebrities to use trademark registrations to secure rights to voice clips and motion elements.
Fellow actor Scarlett Johansson also raised concerns about AI-generated voices after objecting to an OpenAI chatbot voice that she said sounded “eerily similar” to her own. She had declined to participate in the project. OpenAI denied intentionally imitating Johansson’s voice and later withdrew the feature.
And in Japan last week, a court awarded legal protection to the human voice for the first time. The case involved a popular Japanese anime voice actor who demanded that TikTok close an account over its unauthorized use of an AI clone of his trademark baritone.
Italian media reported that even if Meloni's application is approved, the trademark will not automatically prevent AI-generated imitations of her voice. It could, however, provide an additional legal tool against unauthorized use.
The filing follows a separate legal battle launched by Meloni in 2024 against a man accused of creating and posting deepfake pornographic images using her likeness. The case remains pending before an Italian court.

What you should know about the Russian “plague lab”
You’re probably worrying about the wrong things.
The death of a 28-year-old lab tech halfway around the world is not typically the sort of thing the White House monitors.
But when that tech dies of severe pneumonia…while working at a Siberian plague research lab…foreign governments (and pretty much everyone in my timeline) tend to pay more attention.
The World Health Organization says that there’s little cause for concern, to be clear. Testing has turned up no connection between the woman’s work and her cause of death.
And even if she did contract pneumonic plague, that’s hardly a doomsday scenario. The plague comes in three flavors — bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic — and they all crop up from time to time, particularly in places like Central Asia and Africa. If caught early, pneumonic plague is typically curable with common antibiotics. A man in Arizona caught the disease from his cat in 2025, for instance, but didn’t spread it to anyone else.
Of course, the real fear (and the reason so many people are talking about this today, I suspect) is that Russia has, at various times in its history, worked to develop more deadly and contagious forms of plague for use as a biological weapon.
There’s no evidence linking that program to this lab or this death in Siberia. Still, the general threat of biological warfare is so ominous and urgent that now seems like a worthwhile time to understand it a bit better.
Go a little deeper
In her very recent and slightly spooky book, Biological War: A Scenario, journalist Annie Jacobsen lays out how world governments and health authorities are poised to respond to the hypothetical leak of a weaponized pneumonic plague from a Russian lab. At the risk of being euphemistic here, let me say that she concludes things would not go well.
But wait! There’s even more doom and gloom where that thought experiment came from. AI chatbots have made it hypothetically possible for more-or-less ordinary people to grasp the research and techniques they’d need to hack together their own biological weapons.
Just last month, the AI giant Anthropic disclosed five cases where scientists had tried to use its software on research that could have been used in weapons development. And while the company apparently shut those attempts down, their mere existence is fairly frightening.
Can anything be done about these risks, now that they’re here? My colleague Noel King asked Jacobsen that very question in early September. Jacobsen essentially said that the public needs to demand policies aimed at avoiding the “nightmare scenario,” whether that’s an inadvertent lab leak or terrorist attack. Such policies might include things like independent testing of AI models or stricter licensing requirements for high-risk labs.
But it’s unclear what authority could rein in bad state-level actors. And it’s hard to imagine a public upswell for such niche scientific regulations, particularly at a moment when we don’t lack for other doomsday threats. For now, I suppose, I’ll take (partial, provisional) solace in the fact that this Russian situation doesn’t look like one of them.
One link for later
➨ Curtail your catastrophizing. Catastrophizing is a common thought pattern where you assume the worst possible scenario. (For instance, perhaps you read about a quarantine in Russia and began to fear for the end of the world!) Catastrophic thinking can help prepare us for difficult or frightening situations, but it can also be a major source of stress. Try interrogating your doomsday thoughts and noting when the worst case doesn’t come to pass.

COVID-19 made the weaknesses in our pandemic preparedness at national and global levels painfully clear. But a new study highlights that even at the first, local steps of an outbreak with pandemic-potential, we are worryingly underprepared.
Health officials in New York set up a regional test of healthcare facilities to identify and respond to a patient with a mystery infection that could pose a pandemic-level threat. But things didn’t go well. Overall, responses were slow, appropriate use of personal protective equipment was spotty, and only 60 percent of facilities passed the basics of the test—an overall failing grade.
“These drills identified needs for health care workers and health care facility staff member training to achieve earlier identification, masking, and isolation of potentially infectious febrile patients,” the officials wrote in the study, which was published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.
The drill centered on “professional patient actors,” who staggered into healthcare facilities feigning expected symptoms of an H5 bird flu infection—a virus type thought to have pandemic potential. The actors wore makeup to look unwell, used eye drops and petroleum jelly to mimic having conjunctivitis (aka pink eye), and had a fake cough. They complained about feeling weak and feverish and reported taking a Motrin (fever reducer) before coming in. When questioned, they said they hadn’t traveled out of the country and, if asked about any sick contacts, would respond, “Does a sick bird count?” They would tell a sad tale of trying to save a sick duck they found in a park. In the story, the duck doesn’t make it, and the now-ill patient didn’t wear any gloves while handling it. The chatty actor would tell this story without prompting.
To pass the test, a healthcare facility needed to mask the patient and put them in an isolation room. Ideally, the masking would occur within a minute or less of the patient walking in, and isolation would occur in 10 minutes or less. For this drill, both masking and isolation were enough to pass, regardless of timing.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.

The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

A video showing a man with a disability being assaulted by a group of men is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it shows a Muslim being harassed in India. Let us verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals showing an old handicapped muslim being harassed by a few men in India.
Fact: The viral video is scripted content from a YouTube channel called Muklesur Bhaijaan 2.0, which regularly posts similar videos on social media. The channel’s bio states that it shares scripted content. We also found several other videos on the channel featuring the same elderly man. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of the key frames from the viral video led us to a YouTube channel named Muklesur Bhaijaan 2.0, where the same video was uploaded and published on 15 December 2025, with the description ‘ak muslim chacha ko mara chapri na | #shortsvideo bike rider | bike rider vs chapri.’

The Nobel Assembly said Deisseroth is based at Stanford University in California, while Hegemann is at Humboldt University in Berlin and Nagel at the University of Würzburg in Germany.
Thomas Perlmann, the secretary of the medicine committee, said he was able to reach all three winners by phone Monday.
The prize was announced at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, kicking off Nobels week.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).
Last year, the prize went to three scientists researching the immune system.
Monday's medicine prize is followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday and literature on Thursday.
After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Oct. 12.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

Our skin, hair and nails require adequate protein, energy, vitamins and minerals for growth, repair and normal functioning. When deficiencies are significant or prolonged, some may become visible. But many of these signs also overlap with hormonal disorders, chronic illnesses, dermatological conditions, stress, poor sleep and other factors. So when and how do you know if there is a nutritional deficit?
What the signs can indicate
Iron deficiency, particularly when it progresses to anaemia, can cause pallor of the skin and mucous membranes, and may be associated with diffuse hair shedding. Spoon-shaped nails can also occur with iron deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency may cause hyperpigmentation, particularly over the knuckles, as well as changes in the tongue and oral mucosa.
Zinc deficiency can affect skin integrity and hair growth, while inadequate protein intake can affect hair structure and growth and, in severe cases, cause marked changes in the skin and hair. Vitamin C deficiency can result in bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Dry or scaly skin may be associated with inadequate vitamin A, essential fatty acids or zinc.
Cracks at the corners of the mouth can occur with iron, vitamin B12, zinc or riboflavin deficiency. A smooth, red and sore tongue, or glossitis, can be associated with deficiencies of vitamin B12, iron, folate or niacin.
Ramya Subburaj, senior clinical dietitian and head of the department of dietetics, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, said these signs should be viewed as clues rather than proof of a deficiency. “There is considerable overlap between nutritional and non-nutritional causes,” she said, noting that a person with hair loss should not assume that poor nutrition is necessarily responsible.
What ‘ferritin face’ really means
Terms such as ‘iron-deficiency face’ and ‘ferritin face’ circulating on social media are not recognised medical diagnoses. Iron deficiency can cause anaemia and pallor, but there is no specific facial appearance through which low ferritin can be diagnosed.
Ferritin is a protein that stores iron and its level is used to assess the body’s iron stores. Low ferritin can occur before iron-deficiency anaemia develops. However, it does not produce a distinct facial appearance.
Pushpa Gnanaraj, senior consultant, dermatology, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, said pallor associated with anaemia may be visible in the skin, lips, gums or inner eyelids because of reduced haemoglobin. But dullness, dark circles or changes in facial appearance are not specific to low iron stores.
Vinitha Krishnan, chief clinical dietitian, nutrition and dietetics, SIMS Hospital, Chennai, said any changes associated with depleted iron stores are generally subtle and non-specific. Similar features can occur with inadequate sleep, stress, dehydration, allergies, ageing, thyroid disorders or other nutritional deficiencies.
A proper history and clinical examination are therefore important. Depending on the symptoms, investigations may include a complete blood count, ferritin and iron studies, vitamin B12 and vitamin D. Thyroid testing, zinc assessment or other investigations may be considered when clinically indicated. Dermatological conditions such as eczema, psoriasis, fungal infections, autoimmune disorders and pigmentary diseases may also need to be ruled out.
Correcting deficiencies
When a confirmed nutritional deficiency is responsible for a symptom, correcting it can lead to improvement. The timeline, however, depends on the nutrient involved and the severity and duration of the deficiency.
Pallor and some symptoms associated with iron deficiency may begin to improve within weeks of appropriate treatment, while mouth ulcers and glossitis can also improve after the underlying deficiency is corrected. Hair shedding and thinning generally take longer to recover because hair grows slowly; improvement may take several months. Nail changes can similarly take months to grow out.
Reshma Aleem, senior clinical dietician, Rela Hospital, Chennai, said the extent and speed of recovery depend on whether the deficiency is mild, moderate or severe and on how effectively it is corrected.
Fixing the basics
A varied diet remains the foundation. Adequate protein, pulses, whole grains, vegetables, fruits, nuts and seeds, along with eggs, dairy, fish, lean meat or fortified foods according to dietary preference, can provide a range of nutrients.
Experts caution against taking supplements based only on a social-media checklist. Excessive intake of some vitamins and minerals can itself cause adverse effects and may interfere with the absorption or metabolism of other nutrients. More importantly, treating an assumed deficiency can delay the diagnosis of the actual cause.
The appropriate approach is to investigate persistent changes, confirm a deficiency where indicated and then correct it with dietary measures or supplementation under clinical guidance.

Poland's antitrust regulator accuses Google of unfair market practices
The penalty could be up to 10 percent of Google’s annual revenue.
A Polish regulator said that Google isn't playing by the rules when the tech giant displays articles from local media publishers in Google Search, Google News and Google Discover. Poland's Office of Competition and Consumer Protection, abbreviated as UOKiK, said that Google leaned on its dominant market position and failed to provide necessary data when negotiating compensation with the country's news publishers.
Tomasz Chróstny, president of UOKiK, said in a press release that there were rules that clearly laid out what info Google was required to provide to publishers to figure out proper compensation and that the company still failed to do so. The agency could hit the company with a fine amounting to up to 10 percent of Google's annual revenue, according to Chróstny. We reached out to Google for comment and will update the story if we hear back.
Like the UOKiK, the European Commission previously opened an antitrust investigation against Google, looking at if the company offered appropriate compensation for articles used in its AI Overview or AI Mode features. Prior to Google, the Polish authority also accused Apple of using its App Tracking Transparency feature of creating unfair competition in the personalized ads market.

Hospitals across the State are up against a shortage of drugs for treating non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Several commonly prescribed drugs for blood sugar management (metformin), hypertension (telmasartan), and cholesterol (atorvastatin) are in short supply in hospitals, even as authorities have assured that these will be back in stock within a week.
“It is not as though we are running short on all drugs. But NCD drugs are medicines that people should be taking without fail as a matter of routine and disruptions in its supply can be worrying. We anticipated this shortage last month and moved fast to make local purchases so our patients do not miss the medication,” the medical officer at a family health centre in Thiruvananthapuram said.
“NCD drugs are in short supply but we have not had any issues because our hospital management committee has adequate funds, apart from the substantial resources that our block panchayat sets aside every year for purchasing drugs, for making local purchases. If a substantial amount of drugs has to be purchased, then we float a tender. However, there are also health institutions in smaller panchayats which might be struggling to make local purchase because of insufficient funds,” the superintendent at a taluk hospital in the suburbs said.
Ideally, when a patient registered at the NCD clinic of a particular healthcare institution comes for review, the hospital should have at least 30 days’ stock of the NCD drugs for the patient to take home. In the present situation, many hospitals are not able to ensure that.
Medical officers said this year, the Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) released only the drug supplies of the first quarter and that the second quarter release of June did not happen at all which led to the shortage of some drugs, including NCD drugs.
The KMSCL purchases around ₹700-800 crore worth of medicines every year for supplying to around 8,000 government healthcare institutions. In its last procurement exercise, 180 items reportedly received no bids, while suppliers quoted higher prices for another 171 items. This resulted in re-tendering and delays in placing fresh orders.
According to sources, the supply orders given in January-March, for some 18 non-bidder drugs, were cancelled by the new government because the prices quoted were considered far too high, which triggered the present shortage. However, fresh procurement orders have been placed and the supplies are expected to arrive within a week, it was pointed out.
The fact that the KMSCL owes over ₹2,200 crore to various pharma firms, for drugs purchased for hospitals as well as the drugs purchased by hospitals for patients under the Karunya Arogya Suraksha Padhati, has not helped the situation. The massive delays in payment is one of the reasons why many pharma forms do not respond to tenders floated by the KMSCL.
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan had directed that the procurement procedures for the next financial year begin in October itself and that the entire process be completed by the end of December.
He also directed that middlemen be removed from the tender processes and that agencies dealing directly in imported medicines also be allowed to take part in tenders. He said a comprehensive overhaul was under way at the KMSCL
According to sources, there are also efforts to form a consortium with medical service corporations of other States so that common purchase tenders can be floated, which might likely bring prices further down.

బ్యాంకులకు వారానికి ఐదు రోజుల పని విధానం అమలు చేయాలని బ్యాంకు ఉద్యోగ సంఘాలు చాలా కాలంగా డిమాండ్ చేస్తున్నాయి. ఈ డిమాండ్పై సెప్టెంబర్ 2026లో యునైటెడ్ ఫోరం ఆఫ్ బ్యాంక్ యూనియన్స్ (UFBU) దేశవ్యాప్తంగా నిరసనలు చేపట్టింది. వీటిలో పెన్షన్ ప్రయోజనాలను మెరుగుపరచడం, పాత పెన్షన్ విధానాన్ని (OPS) తిరిగి అమలు చేయడం, పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న వేతన సమస్యలను పరిష్కరించడం వంటి డిమాండ్లు ఉన్నాయి. సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 చివర్లో మూడు రోజుల బ్యాంకు సమ్మెకు పిలుపునిచ్చారు. అయితే, ఇండియన్ బ్యాంక్స్ అసోసియేషన్ ఈ అంశాలపై చర్చించేందుకు అంగీకరించడంతో సమ్మెను వాయిదా వేశారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, ఆర్థిక మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ జారీ చేసినట్లు చెబుతున్న ఒక గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ సోషల్ మీడియాలో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) వైరల్ అవుతోంది. ఇందులో అన్ని ప్రభుత్వ రంగ బ్యాంకులకు ప్రతి శనివారం సెలవు ఉంటుందని, ఈ నిబంధన వెంటనే అమల్లోకి వస్తుందని కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం ప్రకటించినట్లు పేర్కొన్నారు. ఈ పోస్ట్లో చేసిన వాదనను ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ప్రభుత్వ రంగ బ్యాంకులకు ప్రతి శనివారం సెలవు ఉంటుందని ఆర్థిక మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ జారీ చేసిన గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్.

Bellingham unlocks new level and potential to be 'one of the greatest'
- Published
Just a year ago, Jude Bellingham's place in the England squad was up in the air. Now he is being talked about as having the potential to be one of football's "greatest of all time".
The Real Madrid man was left out of Thomas Tuchel's Three Lions squad in October 2025 and his place at the World Cup was called into question, with the German head coach saying Bellingham wouldn't get star treatment.
But Bellingham did of course make the squad for the World Cup and was arguably his team's standout performer, finishing as England's top scorer with seven goals as they reached the semi-finals and finished third.
He has already shown that he is world class with starring performances for club and country, but the way he helped England to dismantle Croatia 7-0 in the Nations League on Saturday looked like someone perhaps reaching a new level.
The 23-year-old was instrumental in Rijeka, scoring as well as registering a hat-trick of assists. He even ended the match wearing the captain's armband as England inflicted the heaviest defeat in Croatia's history.
"Bellingham can go on to be one of the greatest players of all time," former Manchester United and Republic of Ireland midfielder Roy Keane said on ITV after the game.
"At this moment in time, he is an amazing footballer. The package – his running power, his delivery, his goal threat. The way he is progressing as a player, I still think there is a lot more to come from him."
Bellingham, recently voted England's player of the year for the second year in a row, is now "nailed on as the 10" for the future, former England defender Matt Upson told BBC Radio 5 Live.
Keane added: "He has been fantastic in possession, but what he does out of possession lifts all these other players.
"If you have a player that good in your team, who is amazing in possession and he's playing for Real Madrid and doing brilliant things, but his work rate off the ball... that will just inspire other players. He is a huge leader for them."
'Push for next level or other teams will catch up'
England's front four will share praise for the way in which they demolished the Croatian backline.
Record goalscorer Harry Kane scored twice, as did Bukayo Saka, with Anthony Gordon scoring and assisting too.
And Kane will be back in the spotlight on Tuesday when he can equal Peter Shilton's all-time England men's appearance record against the Czech Republic at Wembley.
In moving to 89 goals for his country, the 33-year-old again showed how irreplaceable he is for England, but, when he was rested with 20 minutes to go, it was Bellingham who took the captain's armband.
And that highlighted the younger man's importance as a leader within the squad.
Bellingham was also directly involved in more than two goals in an England game for the first time, and he became the first player to record three assists in a game for the Three Lions since Trent Alexander-Arnold against San Marino in November 2021.
It was Bellingham's performance in front of goal that impressed former England striker Ian Wright.
"When Bellingham is on the pitch, he is always driving forward and going again and again," Wright said.
"He was involved in everything. His athleticism, his technical ability, his intensity. He never lets up, the way he gets in the box, he is always in there unmarked. He is always in there."
Bellingham showed every aspect of his game against Croatia and Tuchel was asked by BBC Sport if he had gone to another level.
"Yes, at the moment it seems like it, and you always need to," Tuchel said.
"It's like you can never stand still. You have to develop and you have to push for the next level, otherwise other teams will catch up."
Tuchel, who said the performance was a way to "move on" after the disappointment of England's World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina, said that he "adjusted some things" following the tournament, giving players, including Bellingham, "a lot of responsibility".
Saka was part of the front four and Bellingham assisted his first goal with a high quality cross.
"He was amazing tonight," Saka said of Bellingham.
"He deserved player of the year and he deserved man of the match tonight too. He was special.
"[I'm] happy to play with him and happy to have him in the England team."

Rachel had been hiking a remote section of the reserve when the wind shifted without warning, turning a controlled burn nearly six miles away into a fast-moving wildfire cutting off her only route back to the trailhead. She had no cell signal, no clear path around the advancing smoke, and less than twenty minutes before the fire line would reach her position on an open grassy ridge with nowhere to shelter.
That's when the bison found her.
A herd of nearly thirty animals, moving away from the fire themselves, suddenly changed direction as they passed her position, slowing and gathering into a tight defensive ring around her exact spot on the ridge, facing outward, the way herds typically only form when protecting newborn calves from predators.
Rachel said she didn't understand what was happening at first, terrified she was now trapped between fire and a wall of two-thousand-pound animals. But the herd held its formation as the fire's smoke rolled over them, and she realized, watching the ash fall around the massive bodies surrounding her, that their sheer size and the churned, trampled earth beneath the herd was creating a wide buffer of bare ground the flames couldn't easily cross.
The fire burned around the herd's position rather than through it. When air support finally spotted the unusual circular formation from above and redirected a rescue team, they found Rachel unharmed at the center, the herd only breaking formation and moving on once the helicopter's rotors got close enough to disperse them.
Wildlife officials say bison herds have never been documented forming protective circles around a human being before, only around their own young. They have no explanation for why this herd made the exception.
(Facebook user "Wonder Paws")
The above image is fake, and the story accompanying it is not true. The image contains numerous signs it was generated using artificial intelligence. There also was no available evidence of bison legitimately protecting a hiker in this manner.
The first sign that the image was artificially generated was visible in the top portion showing the circle of bison. Several of them are facing outward but also appear to have heads on both sides of their bodies. The hiker is also not visible in the top portion. Furthermore, the bison in the lower portion of the image, showing the alleged rescue, appear to be copy-and-pasted versions of the same animal. Some bison in the lower portion also appear to have heads on both sides of their bodies.
The post appears to have first ben shared by a Facebook account that has a history of posting AI-generated material.
The "photograph" was allegedly taken in August 2025, according to the timestamp at the top left. We looked for evidence of news coverage around that time about a rescue involving a woman named Rachel and found no reporting from trustworthy outlets such as The Associated Press and Reuters. The story in the post also did not contain information that would be included in legitimate reports about such an incident, such as the specific location of the wildfire.
The image and accompanying story are an example of AI slop: low-quality content that's easy to create thanks to AI tools. Such content overwhelms social media feeds, leaving users unsure of what's real and what's not.
For further reading, Snopes has covered numerous examples of AI slop.

The Matic is our favorite robot vacuum and robo-mop, and it’s also now the first to escape the FCC’s Roomba ban.
The Matic is the first robovac to get an FCC ban waiver, not that it needs it
Unlike the router companies, Matic is publicly committing to US manufacturing.
Well, sort of — because the Matic wasn’t banned to begin with.
Here’s what’s actually happening: On October 2nd, the FCC added the original Matic, model 4MA0001, and its charging dock model 4DK0008 to its ban waiver list. That allows the FCC to approve these radio products for import, marketing, and sale.
But the Matic doesn’t need a waiver, because its radios were already approved years ago. The FCC’s foreign drone, robot, and router bans only keep future products from getting imported into the United States, not existing ones whose radios have already been approved.
Besides, Matic’s products don’t get FCC approval to begin with — instead, Matic ships them with an off-the-shelf Intel AX210 Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chip that gets its own approval from the FCC. (It’s the same kind of Wi-Fi card you’ll find inside a desktop or laptop computer.) Matic also doesn’t need to worry about an import ban specifically, because Matic assembles its robots right here in Mountain View, California.
A waiver could theoretically help if Matic were to build new products outside the United States and try to import them here, except that the FCC hasn’t granted Matic a blanket approval on a brand of robot, like it did with Asus and Netgear’s routers. Instead, it specifically granted a waiver for the Matic models 4MA0001 and 4DK0008, which, again, have already made it through the FCC.
The waiver might not be completely symbolic. The FCC is currently trying to close lots of the loopholes that currently make its ban impotent, is weighing whether to make manufacturers disclose all the components in their gadgets, and is retroactively cracking down on some companies it sees as flaunting the rules. While Matic assembles its robots in the US, it admits it doesn’t yet source 65 percent of its components from US suppliers, the threshold for it to be seen as Made in the US, and perhaps one of those foreign components could trip it up if not for the waiver.
Even so, Matic already gets its “core compute platform” from Nvidia, co-founder and CEO Mehul Nariyawala tells The Verge, and sources other “critical components” from US companies “whenever possible.”
And unlike some of the other companies where the FCC has mysteriously granted a waiver, Matic is committing to more US manufacturing and onshoring.
“Up till 3 months ago, both our R&D offices and production facilities were in the same office in Mountain View, about 24,000 square feet,” Nariyawala tells The Verge. “We’ve turned that entire facility into production facility and moved our office to Menlo Park.”
He says Matic went from shipping 1,500 robots a year ago to 17,000 now, and is trying to find more and more US suppliers so it can use even fewer foreign parts.
“At the moment we might be the only floor cleaning robot built in America,” he says. “That is becoming one of the key value propositions for our product.”

Getting a student to choose a college is one thing. Getting them to come back for another year is just as important.
Ranging from Ivy League universities to military academies, Business Insider calculated the college with the highest retention rate in each state.
The first-year retention rate shows the proportion of students who return to their studies in the fall for their sophomore year. It's a metric colleges care about because it can indicate higher student satisfaction and strong academic support.
Business Insider compiled each state's winner using provisional fall 2024 data from the Department of Education's Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS).
The retention rate covers full-time, first-time bachelor-seeking students who entered in fall 2023 and measures whether they returned for fall 2024.
The cohort size is adjusted to account for any permitted exclusions, such as a student's death.
Business Insider also limited the data to degree-granting institutions only and set a minimum cohort size of 100 to avoid very small cohorts inflating retention rates.
Because the data is provisional, the figures could be revised and should not be considered final counts.
