Quick Answer
Meta Muse is a powerful AI agent that can handle emails, purchases, bookings, and more. But its need for deep access to personal data, combined with Meta’s privacy record and early reports of Muse ignoring user permissions, makes trust its biggest problem.
A few days ago, Meta hosted its annual hardware/software event, Meta Connect, at Menlo Park, California. The event was dominated by new hardware launches, such as the new Meta Ray-Ban glasses, new VR glasses, and camera-free Ray-Ban glasses (audio only), but swimming beneath the surface of all these was something that was actually introduced earlier. Meta had introduced Meta Muse in early September, but announced the rollout of the Muse AI agent on its Meta wearables and Meta Muse Charm at the event, and for us, that was easily the real highlight of Meta Connect.
After investing heavily in recruiting AI talent, Meta finally had something to show: an AI agent, which will basically make your dreams of having a robot butler come true. Not surprisingly, it has been making massive tech waves ever since. Since Meta Connect and its rollout, Muse has been topping app store charts, and its early numbers are being compared with ChatGPT, with many pointing out that it is far ahead of OpenAI’s chatbot’s numbers.
While this may paint a very rosy picture for Meta Muse, the reality may be a trifle thorny.
What those numbers do not tell – the “Threads” deception
These numbers, impressive as they are, do not necessarily mean Muse is a runaway success. There are a few reasons for this. Topping app store charts is more of a temporary phenomenon, often influenced by what is trending in a particular week, and does not represent real industry trends. Also, Meta has billions of users across different social media and messaging platforms, which makes it easy for the tech giant to get a few million users quickly without too much trouble. But the adoption rate might not match the number of downloads or sign-ups.
We have seen this happen with Meta’s X rival app, Threads, as well. It has more “active users” as per the numbers than X, which means it must be more used and popular than X, but that is mostly because of Threads’ integration with Instagram and Facebook, which gets the app most of its “active users.” However, the time spent on the app is not nearly the same as its other two sibling social media apps. Similarly, early ChatGPT comparisons with Meta Muse signups may not be fair, because ChatGPT was not launched or advertised as a tool for the masses when it was first launched. It did not have the sort of subscriber base and reach that Meta has, and back then, AI chatbots were not too common either.
Definitely a big deal
That does not mean Muse does not represent a big tech leap. So far, AI chatbots have generally been used for queries, information, help with work, and even personal advice, but that’s mostly about it. All of these chatbots are more about helping you with your queries, with no bar to the nature of the query. While useful in this regard, many are not able to perform actions that have an impact on your day-to-day life. That is where Meta Muse differs.
As we said earlier, Muse is actually the robot butler that the future always promised us. It can get tasks done and help you with managing your digital and even real life. Once you give it access, the AI agent can go through your mail, find messages, draft new messages, reply to emails, all without too much intervention. That might not sound too impressive, as most AI agents and virtual assistants can do the same with a simple command. But Muse goes a step further – it can even make purchases, make reservations, book appointments, and more, across different devices and platforms. In fact, if allowed, Muse can basically make deals on Facebook Marketplace or book you a table at your favorite restaurant or even call you a cab, all without needing any major intervention. Proper butling!
Muse has power and potential, but does Meta have our trust?
As impressive and life-altering as it may sound– some are calling it the biggest tech innovation since the iPhone – Meta still has a massive hurdle that it would have to cross to make Muse the AI butler it wants it to be. And that is the lack of trust in Meta.
For all its innovation and massive subscriber base, Meta has been in a number of controversial situations when it comes to security and privacy. Zuckerberg’s brand has been accused of and even found guilty in cases that range from rigging elections, pushing agendas and ads, to exposing young children to adult content and potential groomers, to monopolizing social media and personal messaging space and using unfair means and practices to kill competition. Its recent hardware “hit” the Meta glasses have also got into a privacy mess, and have been (in)famously christened pervert glasses, following reports of their being used to record people without their consent.
Now, Muse requires even more data and access to private information to actually deliver on its promises. For instance, to be able to draft emails, it needs access to your email account. To be allowed to send messages, it needs permission to read, understand, store, and reply to messages, and needs access to your contact list. To make a reservation, it needs to know your location; to order things online, it needs to have your bank details and also your address. Basically, it needs to have complete access to all your information to act like the magic help that Meta is claiming it can be.
Why I am not A-Muse-D
And that is where my beef with Muse really comes in. Had this been any other company– if Apple had managed to deliver on its intelligent Siri promises or Google had delivered Gemini with such prowess, I personally would have felt less apprehensive in handing over the keys to my digital life, but to give Meta even more access to my data than it already has just feels scary.
Even though I have come to terms with the fact that we are all under passive surveillance from brands at all times, it will take some time for me to give complete control of my data over to Meta without any struggle.
Some of the recent headlines Muse has made do not help its cause. Recently, the AI agent not only made a deal for its user on Facebook Marketplace but even shared his address with the buyer. All without consent. The user, a tech YouTuber, Matt Robb, mentioned how the AI agent accepted low offers and even pretended to be the user while chatting with the buyer, calling the buyer to his address when he was not home at all. Once Matt realized what was happening, he specifically instructed Muse to not share his address. He then asked his friends to send him messages on Facebook Marketplace to see if the agent shares the address. Rather disturbingly, it did: multiple times, and even accepted low offers, all without consent. In another report by Apple Insider, alleged that Muse accessed and uploaded past and present Apple Messages even though the user said he had not granted it permission to do so. All this despite Meta’s claims that Muse has strong privacy and security protections.
All of this does not take away from the fact that Meta has created something really powerful with Muse. It has managed to deliver a finished, capable AI agent which can manage your digital lives, if you let it. Unfortunately, it may also steal your data, force specific ads, and make conversations on your behalf by pretending to be you. And therein lies the problem. The AI Agent is not just about technology, but also about trust. Meta has delivered on the first front with Muse, but until it delivers on the second, I refuse to be A-Muse-D by it. Pun intended.

Pointing out that high-cost medicines used to treat cancer, kidney ailments, and AIDS are being sold at prices up to “70 times higher” than the rates at which dealers and stockists procure them, Karnataka Health Minister U.T. Khader has written a letter to Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda, seeking national action against “abnormal gaps” in drug prices.
The Minister said dealers and stockists purchase advanced pharmaceuticals from manufacturers at heavily discounted wholesale landed rates, while the MRPs printed on the medicines are fixed at “inflated, highly disproportionate levels”. The letter said the gap between the procurement price and MRP was “sometimes 30 times to more than 70 times”.
Mr. Khader said that the issue was particularly concerning for in-patients, emergency and intensive-care patients, oncology patients, and those requiring implants, surgical consumables, and other hospital-based treatment, as they cannot realistically compare suppliers or defer purchases.
The letter said that while the existing MRP framework prevents medicines from being sold above the printed MRP, it does not address situations where the MRP itself has little relation to the actual institutional transaction price, adding that hospitals retain an excessive undisclosed margin.
Mr. Khader sought a national study comparing the printed MRP, manufacturer/importer price, hospital’s net acquisition price, and the price ultimately billed to patients for selected high-value medicines, medical devices, and consumables. He also proposed that the patient-facing price of products supplied through hospitals be capped at the lower end of the applicable statutory price, MRP or the hospital’s net acquisition cost plus a notified and reasonable service margin and applicable taxes.
The Minister said Karnataka would “cooperate with any pilot or national framework” and could, within its powers, make private hospitals disclose more information, require detailed bills for patients, and set up a system to handle complaints locally. However, he said the Centre needs to fix the basic problem — the large difference between what hospitals pay for medicines, the MRP printed on them and what patients are finally charged.

In 2025, India recorded 55 deaths by malaria, 131 deaths by dengue, and 27 deaths by kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis or black fever), according to Union Health Ministry data, whereas there is no single comparable and comprehensive national measure of its annual human rabies mortality, even as the country looks to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies by the year 2030.
While a community-based study led by researchers from the Indian Council of Medical Research-National Institute of Epidemiology (ICMR-NIE) and published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases recently estimated that 5,726 people die of rabies in India every year, the Health Ministry’s Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme-Integrated Health Information Platform (IDSP-IHIP) system reported 21 deaths by rabies in 2022, 50 in 2023, and 54 in 2024.
In contrast, the Registrar General of India’s Medical Certification of Cause of Death (MCCD) system recorded 66 medically certified rabies deaths in 2022, and 271 in 2023. The MCCD system, however, covers only medically certified deaths and does not capture all registered deaths.
These figures are not directly comparable — the IDSP-IHIP is a disease surveillance system, while the MCCD captures medically certified causes through civil registration. At the national level, the MCCD covered 22.3% of registered deaths in 2022, and 22.0% in 2023. Neither system, therefore, provides a complete national count — underscoring the gaps in India’s rabies mortality surveillance.
The government table, sourced to IDSP-IHIP, had recorded one death in January 2025 but did not provide a figure for all of 2025. The government’s published table, labelled ‘Human Rabies cases (Death)’, gives the source as IDSP-IHIP.
ICMR for its study surveyed 3,37,808 people in 78,807 households across 60 districts in 15 States and estimated that India sees about 9.1 million animal bites every year, including about 5.6 million dog bites.
The researchers used the community survey, laboratory data, and a probability decision-tree model to estimate the number of people who progress from an animal bite to rabies and die. The 5,726 figure is therefore a modelled estimate of annual deaths, and not a count of deaths recorded in hospitals or by government surveillance.
The difference between the two datasets is substantial. The 54 deaths reported through government surveillance in 2024 is less than 1% of the study’s estimated annual toll of 5,726.
“The two figures, however, are generated through different methods and should not be treated as directly equivalent. The figures therefore highlight a large gap between reported surveillance deaths and estimated mortality,” a senior Health Ministry official said.
“Lack of consolidated data is a challenge in rabies eradication. Very often cases and deaths occur in areas of the country where they are not measurable. Vaccination of stray dogs, stringent post-exposure vaccination for humans, and disruption of the rabies chain is essential to curb the problem,” Nirmal Kumar Ganguly, medical scientist, public health expert, and former ICMR chief, speaking exclusively to The Hindu, said.
The National Centre for Disease Control itself says efforts are continuing to make human rabies a notifiable disease across India, and that all States have been asked to notify the disease under the relevant State legislation.
The Health Ministry has also acknowledged the surveillance challenge, with deaths occurring outside the formal health system posing an additional difficulty in capturing the full burden of disease.
Meanwhile, the Lancet study found important gaps even after animal bites. About one in five dog-bite victims had not received the anti-rabies vaccine, while only 66.2% had received at least three doses. Among those who received only one dose, nearly half did not complete the vaccination course. Only about one in 10 eligible victims received passive immunisation.
Rabies is a vaccine-preventable viral disease that attacks the central nervous system and is almost invariably fatal once symptoms appear, with infected dog bites causing most human transmission.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that domestic dogs are responsible for up to 99% of human rabies transmission. Globally, rabies causes an estimated 59,000 human deaths every year, with more than 95% of deaths occurring in Africa and Asia.
The WHO estimates that India accounts for 35% of rabies deaths globally and 59.9% of rabies deaths in Asia, underlining the country’s significant contribution to the global burden. Children are particularly vulnerable. The WHO says 40% of people bitten by suspected rabid animals are children under 15 years. Rabies is entirely preventable through timely vaccination of dogs and prompt post-exposure care.
The ICMR-funded study states that although there has been a substantial decline in human rabies deaths over the past two decades, India needs to fast-track its actions to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies by 2030 by adopting a focused ‘One Health’ approach — integrating human and animal surveillance, ensuring timely administration of the full course of post-exposure prophylaxis, and accelerating dog vaccination across the country.

The director of films once considered too domestic for foreign export, Yasujiro Ozu (1903-1963) now sits high in the world cinematic pantheon. From his signature low camera angles to the “pillow” shots that serve as postcard-like pauses between scenes, his technique has been obsessively analyzed but remains sui generis.
That, however, is not the main subject of the splendid Daniel Raim documentary “The Ozu Diaries.” Drawing from Ozu’s journals and essays as well as other archival materials, it focuses more on the man and artist than his aesthetics.

The botched execution recentered the national debate over the ethics of the death penalty. Public favor has evolved in recent decades: Support for capital punishment dipped in the 1960s and a 1972 Supreme Court decision led to its suspension for several years. It’s been an encouraging year for South Korea’s Busan International Film Festival (BIFF), which has received recognition from the International Federation of Film Producers Associations (FIAPF) and also been designated a pathway to an Oscars’ nomination.
FIAPF announced in March that BIFF has been added to its list of “A-list festivals” joining the ranks of festivals such as Berlin, Venice and Cannes. A few months later, the Academy of Motion Pictures Arts and Sciences (AMPAS) announced that the top prize winners of six international festivals, including Busan, will automatically qualify for submission to the Best International Feature Film category of the Oscars. This places BIFF in a select gathering alongside Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance and Toronto.
Jung Hanseok, who took up the post of BIFF festival director last year, says these developments are already “having a positive effect on both the number and quality of submissions to the festival. They give filmmakers a meaningful additional incentive to submit their work to BIFF.”
Watch on Deadline
BIFF only introduced a fully-fledged competition section last year, handing out awards in six categories, including Best Film, which has become the pathway to the Oscars, along with Best Director, Special Jury Award, Best Actor, Best Actress and an Artistic Contribution Award.
Last year, Gloaming In Luomu, from Korean-Chinese filmmaker Zhang Lu, was awarded Best Film, with Taiwan’s Shu Qi taking Best Director for Girl. The festival also has a Vision Awards ceremony – recognising films across both the ‘Vision – Korea’ and ‘Vision – Asia’ sections – in which a wide range of independent juries hand out prizes.
“Compared with the competition sections of longer-established festivals, BIFF’s Competition is still very new,” Jung cautions. “So one of our early challenges was to communicate its value and build confidence in the section as quickly as possible. I think the FIAPF recognition and the new Academy pathway have helped accelerate that process.”
Jung cites China as one territory where filmmakers’ interest in BIFF has risen, due to the fact that filmmakers invited to A-list festivals are more likely to receive attention when applying for public support.
“We’ve seen similar changes in Japan, where key industry figures have been noticeably more proactive and receptive towards BIFF’s Competition than they were last year,” he says. “Some filmmakers may now be able to envision a longer-term path that begins with winning the Busan Award for Best Film and continues into an Oscar campaign.”
He adds that Korean filmmakers are also waking up to this possibility. Korea’s Oscars committee has already submitted Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love as its official entry, which is currently receiving an Oscars-qualifying run in Korean theatres before streaming on Netflix. In theory, a Best Film Award win from Busan could make a second Korean film eligible.
However, BIFF’s Competition section embraces the whole of Asia and this year’s line-up of 14 titles also spans films from China, Taiwan, Japan, Uzbekistan, Indonesia and Iran (see here for the full line-up), so the field is wide open. Chinese director Zhang Yimou is heading the seven person jury that will decide on the awards.
Jung says he didn’t really appreciate the impact of the new Competition section last year, until he was planning this year’s festival: “We’ve sensed a much more positive and receptive atmosphere around the Competition section than we did in its first year. For that reason, our main priority this year has been the stability and consolidation of the Competition,” he says.
“In the longer term, BIFF intends to remain grounded in an Asian perspective and in values that emerge from within Asia when operating the section. At the same time, we want to continue asking ourselves what exactly ‘Asian’ should mean in that context.”
When asked about the competition selection criteria, Jung says it’s “quite simply, the quality of each individual film”. He adds that the 14 selected titles, when look at together, “should form a compelling cinematic landscape that reveals something of contemporary Asian cinema as it exists today. One notable difference this year is that the quality is more consistent across the Competition, while the overall standard of the line-up has also risen.”
The festival opens tonight (Tuesday, October 6) with a screening of Kim Jong-kwan’s The Table: Day And Night, and with Kim Minha (Pachinko) hosting the opening ceremony. Other talent attending the festival includes Michelle Yeoh, who is being honored as Asian Filmmaker of the Year; Hong Kong filmmaker Ann Hui, who is receiving the Camellia Award; Maggie Gyllenhaal, presenting her short film Flesh Impact in Special Screenings; and French actress Isabelle Huppert, who will meet local audiences with her latest film, All About Corinne.
The stacked talent list also includes Iranian filmmaker Majid Majidi, who has Midday Meal in competition and will be making his first visit to the festival; Japanese anime master Rintaro, who worked in the same era as the legendary manga artist Tezuka Osamu; and Alfonso Cuaron, in town for a special IMAX screening of Gravity and the Asian Premiere of Jonás Cuarón’s Campeón Gabacho.
In total, BIFF is screening 246 films – five more than last year and marking the festival’s largest lineup since 2019 – and is opening one day earlier than in previous years. Jung explains that BIFF has also increased the number of screenings from Thursday through Sunday, when attendance is at its highest. “These were all practical improvements intended to give audiences greater convenience and more opportunities to see films,” he says. “The response so far has been very positive. Even before on-site ticket sales begin, online bookings alone suggest that this year’s total attendance could surpass last year.”
In addition to the Competition and Vision selections, the festival’s major sections include Gala Presentation, which is showing six titles including Hirokazu Kore-eda’s Look Back and Yeon Sang-ho’s Paradise Lost; and Icons, which this year is showing 16 titles including Ira Sachs’ The Man I Love, Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s All Of A Sudden, Pedro Almodovar’s Bitter Christmas, Christian Mungiu’s Fjord and Lav Diaz’s Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors.
On Screen is world premiering initial episodes from three highly anticipated series: Netflix’s The Blue Road and Dead-End Job and Disney’s The Remarried Empress. The Blue Road director Han Jun-hee will be on hand during Netflix’s Creative Asia day to present a masterclass entitled “Making Unexpected Stories Resonate”.
BIFF’s popular Open Cinema section, which offers free open-air screenings at its iconic Busan Cinema Center, is showing eight films including Look Back, Banjong Pisanthanakun’s Inherit, and Ervin Han and Raúl García’s Annecy award-winning animation The Violinist.
This year’s special programmes include ‘Those Beautiful Years, Ahn Sung-ki’, focusing on the late Korean actor, and a Japanese animation special: ‘Masterpieces of Madness, Exhilarating Prospects 12+1’. The annual ‘Carte Blanche’ programme invites prominent figures from the world of cinema to personally select films that have profound influenced them. This year’s guests include Korean filmmaker Kim Jee-woon, Chinese actress Fan Bingbing, and Korean cinematographer Hong Kyung-pyo.
The Flash Forward section for non-Asian first and second-time filmmakers is screening eight titles include Stephanie Ahn’s Bedford Park and Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s La Bola Negra. Other major sections include A Window On Asian Cinema, Korean Cinema Today, World Cinema, Wide Angle, focusing on short films and documentaries, and Midnight Passion.
While BIFF prides itself on showcasing cinema from across the Asian continent, it’s also the case that many public audience members, not to mention press and industry, are attending the festival to catch up with the latest Korean cinema. In this respect, BIFF is also riding a positive trend as local cinema began to revive at the beginning of this year, following a long period of declining box office and audience apathy that held back post-pandemic recovery.
Starting from the Lunar New Year holiday in February, Korea has enjoyed a string of domestic hits including historical drama The Kings Warden, Yeon Sang-ho’s Colony, Na Hong-jin’s Hope, and horror film Salmokji: Whispering Water.
Also climbing up the 2026 Top Ten chart is Hur Jin-ho’s political thriller The Assassin(s), which premiered at Toronto International Film Festival and has so far grossed nearly $18M since its release over the recent Chuseok holiday. However, the film had to withdraw from its planned BIFF participation due to the huge row that erupted when right-wing critics accused the film of historical inaccuracy. The Directors Guild of Korea has recently come out in support of the film.
Controversy aside, however, Korean cinema currently has a lot to celebrate, and the recent success of The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day in this market have also brought relief to the territory’s beleaguered cinema operators. Jung welcomes this return of Korean audiences to physical theatres, although he cautions there’s still work to be done to return the local industry to full health.
“The fact that cinema attendance is increasing compared with last year suggests that there are encouraging signs of recovery,” he says. “In particular, several Korean films and major Hollywood releases have helped younger audiences – who make up an important part of Korea’s cinema-going public – become accustomed once again to the experience of going to a movie theatre to watch a film.
“At the same time, it remains very difficult for small and mid-budget films both to secure financing and to obtain theatrical releases,” he continues. “Government policy in this area is becoming more active, but we will need more time before we can judge its effects.”
Busan International Film Festival is taking place October 6-15 at Busan Cinema Centre and multiple venues across the city. The festival’s industry platform, Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), kicks off on Saturday, October 10 and runs until Tuesday, October 13.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.

On August 1, 2026, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari claimed that of the 27 lakh people whose names were deleted from the voter list after adjudication due to ‘logical discrepancy’, only seven lakh had filed appeals before the court-appointed appellate tribunals seeking inclusion in the electoral rolls.
Speaking at the launch of the Census self-enumeration exercise in Kolkata, he said, “Out of the 27 lakh people who were given an opportunity to approach the SIR tribunal, around seven lakh had applied. The rest have not submitted any application or appeal so far.”
The figure was reported by multiple media outlets which quoted the chief minister (1, 2, 3). Adhikari went on to link the failure to appeal with questions of citizenship, and citizenship with access to welfare, saying, “Until the entire process was completed, it would not be possible to determine whether those who had not made any claim as voters would later seek recognition as Indian citizens.” He added, “If someone is not a citizen of the country, they will not get benefits of any social scheme.”
Five days later, The Telegraph published the same seven-lakh figure, this time attributing it to an unnamed senior official of the West Bengal government. According to the report, the official said, “It has been found that only about 7 lakh of the 27 lakh voters excluded by the adjudicators for ‘logical discrepancies’ have appealed before the tribunals.” The official said the figure had emerged from a compilation of reports from various districts, and that the state authorities had no idea why the remaining 20 lakh had not appealed before the tribunals.
The Figure was Unverifiable at that Time
In August, the seven-lakh claim could not be independently verified against any official source because the Election Commission’s own disclosure did not provide a separate breakdown of appeals filed against the exclusion of voters. An RTI reply that disclosed the total number of appeals carried a footnote clarifying that the figure included both appeals against the inclusion of names in the electoral roll and appeals against exclusions.
The RTI was obtained by Isha Khan Choudhury, Congress MP from Dakshin Malda in West Bengal, and placed before the Supreme Court on August 24, 2026, during the hearing of a petition filed by Prasenjit Bose of the Congress and Derek O’Brien of the Trinamool Congress against the Election Commission of India.
During the hearing, Justice Joymalya Bagchi observed that the break-up of the appeals mattered since “it was exclusion which was causing an immediate violation of a person’s rights.” The bench consequently directed the ECI to provide a separate account of the appeals, specifying how many were pending before the tribunals and segregating appeals relating to voters who had been excluded or included, as well as cross-appeals.
The ECI submitted this segregation on September 16.
ECI Numbers Refute Adhikari’s Claim
According to the latest affidavit filed by the ECI before the Supreme Court on September 16, 2026, of the more than 38.31 lakh appeals filed, over 22 lakh were filed against exclusion by voters whose names had been excluded or deleted, while more than 16 lakh were filed against inclusion.
Of the more than 38 lakh appeals filed, only 1.26 lakh had been decided by that date. Annexure R/1 to the ECI’s affidavit provides a district-wise break-up of the total appeals submitted to the appellate tribunals and is reproduced below.
It must be noted that the total number of appeals filed, as mentioned in the ECI’s affidavit (38,31,429), does not match the total number of appeals submitted in Annexure R/1 (38,29,926). The discrepancy is 1,503 appeals. Nevertheless, the outcome-wise data provided in the annexure shows that 8,649 appeals resulted in exclusion from the electoral roll, while 1,13,943 resulted in inclusion. In other words, nearly 93% of the appeals that had been decided resulted in the elector being included in the electoral roll.
Did the Claims Accumulate after the CM’s Statement? No
One may argue that the chief minister spoke on August 1, while the Commission filed its figure in the Supreme Court on September 16, leaving enough time for appeals to have accumulated in the intervening period. The available data, however, allows this possibility to be tested directly, because appeal totals are available for both dates. On August 7, 2026, six days after the chief minister’s statement and a day after The Telegraph report, the tribunals already had 38,10,620 appeals, according to an RTI response from the ECI to Isha Khan Choudhury, Congress MP for Dakshin Malda. By September 10, 2026, the figure stood at 38,29,926, according to the district-wise report annexed to the Commission’s affidavit. Thus, the total number of appeals increased by just 19,306 across the entire state during this period.
In the light of the latest revelations made by an Indian Express investigation, which have raised serious questions about the functioning of the Election Commission of India and chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, the seven-lakh claim takes on an even greater significance.
To sum up, Suvendu Adhikari’s claim on August 1 that out of some 27 lakh electors placed under adjudication and subsequently excluded from the electoral roll, only seven lakh had appealed against their exclusion is difficult to reconcile with the data that was already available at the time. The ECI has made it clear that the number is around 22 lakh. The discrepancy assumes greater significance given that Manoj Agarwal, the then chief electoral officer of West Bengal who oversaw the SIR process, is now the Bengal’s chief secretary.

Bestselling author Steven Galloway's wife testifies on Day 1 of defamation trial
Former UBC writing professor claims he was defamed by false accusations of sexual assault
The wife of former University of British Columbia (UBC) professor Steven Galloway was the first witness to testify on day one of the defamation trial against four defendants he says falsely accused him of sexual assault.
Galloway’s accuser is a former student, "AB", who is the main defendant in the lawsuit. Others named as defendants are alleged to have spread the sexual assault claim, including on social media.
Katie Wagner told the court that Galloway was at a speaking engagement in Ohio in late 2015 when he first became aware of the accusation.
Wagner says that, when she arrived in Ohio to support him, Galloway was in a hospital on 72-hour suicide watch.
"He was in a hospital gown, he was upset, crying, shaking. He knew there was an accusation of sexual assault, but of course, he hadn’t sexually assaulted anyone — so there was a lot of us trying to figure out what was going on," she told the court.
Galloway, a bestselling Canadian author, was never criminally charged — though he was fired from his job as a tenured professor and chair of the UBC creative writing department.
A report by retired B.C. Supreme Court judge Mary Ellen Boyd, commissioned by UBC, concluded the claims against Galloway were unsubstantiated.
After arbitration, he was awarded over $240,000 in damages from the university.
'Never going to be an end'
Wagner said Boyd’s report only served to sparked a "mob of people online" to repeat the accusations.
"There would be a flurry on Twitter — which was such a big thing," said Wagner. "I think there was a sense at that point … that there was never going to be an end to it."
Wagner testified that the accusations and resulting firestorm has been hard on their four children, finances, and life in general.
She said Galloway became extremely withdrawn, and at one point she found him trying to hang himself with a rope. She also recounted strictly controlling his medications for fear he would intentionally overdose.
Galloway sued numerous people for defamation in 2018. His accusers fought the case all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, claiming their accusations were protected speech.
The high court refused to hear the case, after a lower court said that if the defendants' arguments held, "there would be no legal consequences of any kind" to publicly calling someone a rapist.
At least nine of the defendants have settled out of court or issued apologies, including author Chelsea Rooney, whose lengthy statement of apology was published this past weekend.
Galloway is the author of novels including The Cellist of Sarajevo and The Confabulist. His lawyer said he is seeking special damages, to account for Galloway's former standing as a star in the literary world who had his career cut short.
AB has asked the court to keep her identity confidential over concerns an "online mob" would be unleashed against her.
Her counsel told the court that AB has attempted suicide. He said while news stories published about the case haven’t revealed her identity, people have named her in the comment sections under the articles.
The trial was originally scheduled for 60 days, but with fewer defendants, B.C. Supreme Court Justice Neena Sharma said it will likely take 20 days.

Jagtar Singh Johal, a British Sikh man who was arrested in India in 2017 in connection with alleged terrorism offences, has been granted bail by a Delhi court.
Johal, from Scotland, was arrested for his alleged role in funding the Khalistan Liberation Force, which had carried out targeted killings in India’s Punjab region.
His full trial has been repeatedly deferred by the authorities in the federal court but largely similar conspiracy charges were dismissed by a court in Punjab last year. Throughout his detention the prosecution has failed to produce verifiable evidence, leading to the deferred hearings.
Johal, now 39, travelled to India to marry his fiancee in late 2017. On 4 November, three weeks after the wedding, the couple were shopping with a relative in the Punjab city of Jalandhar when a group of men took Johal from his car, placed a black hood over his head and put him in an unmarked vehicle. He claims he was then denied access to a lawyer and tortured in an attempt to extract a confession. A question remains over whether he was arrested following a tip-off from British intelligence services.
Commenting on Friday’s ruling, Johal’s Scotland-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “The past two years has been an expensive rollercoaster, contesting bails at the supreme court and back to the high court. I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison. We have waited so long and fought so hard for this moment.”
He added of previous hearings: “Whenever the evidence against Jagtar is tested in court, judges find what we’ve said all along, which is that there isn’t any.
“How long will this sick joke of a legal process be allowed to continue? We’re obviously delighted that Jagtar will soon be released, but he won’t be truly free until he is back in Dumbarton, with his wife and family.”
Gurpreet Johal, who also lives in Dumbarton, has lobbied a succession of UK foreign secretaries, who have repeatedly admitted the case has dragged on too long, but have been reluctant to call publicly for his release on the grounds that they should not interfere in the judiciary of another country.
The UK government recently appointed Alistair Burt as a special envoy for complex consular cases and he has met Gurpreet Johal in Scotland to discuss the case.
Dan Dolan, the deputy executive director of Reprieve, one of the organisation’s fighting for Johal’s release, said: “While this judgment is welcome as Jagtar should not be in prison a day longer, we must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way. The conditions attached are likely to be onerous. We must also remember that Jagtar will still be facing the death penalty in eight cases against him, despite these cases essentially duplicating trumped-up charges on which he has already been fully acquitted.”
Chris Esdaile, a senior legal adviser to Redress, another organisaiton representing Johal, said granting bail “can’t undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention”.
He added: “The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent.”
Johal’s lawyers said they were still awaiting the details of what would happen next in relation to posting bail terms. While the judges’ order was that Jagtar should be released on bail, he remained in custody while judges confirmed his bail conditions, which may be stringent. The court must also confirm the sums of money that must be posted as a bond.

BOJ chief calls for more focus on anchoring inflation around target
TOKYO, Oct 6 : Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Tuesday it was becoming more important to anchor underlying inflation around the central bank's 2 per cent target, signalling readiness to keep raising interest rates to blunt the risk of too-high inflation.
The remarks come ahead of the central bank's two-day policy meeting ending on October 30, where new quarterly growth and inflation forecasts will be closely watched for clues on the timing of the next rate hike.
Ueda said economic and price developments were broadly in line with the BOJ's forecasts, with the economy recovering moderately and the central bank's "tankan" survey pointing to solid business sentiment.
Rising raw material costs are pushing up wholesale inflation with price pressures spreading to consumer inflation, Ueda said, adding that long-term inflation expectations continue to rise.
He also warned of the risk of underlying inflation overshooting the BOJ's target due to price pressures from the US-Israeli war on Iran, strong AI-related demand and the weak yen.
"Financial conditions remain accommodative and continue to underpin economic activity" even after last month's rate hike, Ueda said, adding that the central bank will continue to raise borrowing costs to adjust the level of monetary support.
"It has become more important than before to ensure underlying inflation becomes anchored around 2 per cent" so that the risk of an inflation overshoot does not materialise and damage the economy, he added.
In a statement announcing the September rate hike, the BOJ said only that it was "important" to anchor underlying inflation around the BOJ's target.
The BOJ raised its key rate to a 31-year high last month, with Ueda signalling the central bank had entered a phase focused on preventing underlying inflation from overshooting its target, raising the prospect of tighter policy.

The Keralam government’s announcement that it will make private health care more “affordable” through consultations with the private health sector, and that a Bill in this regard was in the offing, should be seen against the State’s seven-year legal battle before the Kerala High Court upheld the Kerala Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulations) Act 2018, throwing out all objections raised by private hospitals.
The KCE Act was the first ever attempt made in the State to bring the entire health sector, public and private, under a regulatory framework.
But the Act was systematically opposed and its implementation stalled at every turn by the private health sector in the State.
It was in November last year that the Kerala High Court threw out all objections raised by the Kerala Private Hospitals’ Association (KPHA) and the Indian Medical Association (IMA) and upheld the validity of the Act.
Contentious area
Unlike the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 (Central Act 23 of 2010), which attempted to cap the treatment/procedure/diagnostic rates charged by the private health sector by fixing a price range, the KCE Act had not touched this contentious area at all.
The KCE Act just insisted on mandatory registration of all clinical establishments under all systems of medicines (including hospitals, clinics and laboratories) and that every establishment maintain certain minimum standards based on the category in which they fall. It also said that hospitals display their rates for various procedures openly so that there is transparency.
However, the private health sector argued that it violated rights under Article 14 and Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
Appeal in SC
Even after the High Court specifically held that KCE Act’s Section 16 (mandatory registration of clinical establishments), Section 39 (display of fee rates and package rates for services) and Section 47 (obligations concerning life-saving treatment/emergency care and safe transfer of patients) were constitutionally valid and gave directives to the government to implement the Act without delay, KPHA went in appeal to the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court has not stayed the KCE Act, but granted members of the petitioning associations interim protection against coercive action by the government.
Yet to register
Kerala Clinical Establishments Council, which is responsible for the implementation of the Act, maintains that the registration process is continuing and that even now, many clinical establishments are yet to register themselves under the council.
Small hospitals with up to 15 beds have been given some concessions by the council, trimming down the checklist for assessment to just basic and essential points, so that at least the basic registration brings these establishments too within the regulatory framework.
The government’s efforts to draft a new Bill to bring in a regulatory framework that “protects patients’ interests while taking into account the operating costs and practical difficulties of private hospitals” is well-intentioned, but the fact remains that the private health sector is still holding out against the KCE Act at the Supreme Court.
Questions are also being raised whether a new legislation is in order or if the costing regulations can be incorporated into the KCE Act itself.
‘Entirely welcome’
Meanwhile, public health activists like B. Ekbal have stated that any attempt by the government to regulate the treatment expenditure in the private sector and save people from catastrophic health expenditure is entirely welcome.
Dr. Ekbal said that though private hospitals are an essential component of the health system, health care cannot be left entirely to market logic. It is the government’s responsibility to regulate the sector adequately so that patients are not exploited.
In a statement here, Dr. Ekbal said that the Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs) should be insisted on and that the government initiate a scientific cost evaluation of various medical and diagnostic procedures and treatments so that a rational and transparent rate list suited to the State can be evolved.

Kenyan prisoners play chess for fun behind bars and to help with rehabilitation
Kenya’s Department for Correctional Services has introduced chess across the country’s prisons since 2024, in one of the most prominent institutional carceral chess programs in Africa
MURANG'A, Kenya -- The black-and-white stripes of Brian Gatonye’s prison uniform match the pieces staring back at him from the chessboard at Kenya's Maranjau Prison.
The 27-year-old has served about 18 months of a three-year sentence for assault and is due to be released in November 2027.
During a break in the prison yard, he considers his next move: a pawn, perhaps, or a knight. The break isn't long, but if he finishes the game quickly he may have time to face one of the skilled guards.
But it is unwise to rush or act impulsively — in chess as in life, he has learned.
“Chess has taught me a lot,” Gatonye said. “It has taught me (about) being calm, choosing my decisions wisely. Before doing an act, I have to think first of what the repercussions are — and then I move.”
Gatonye is among a growing number of Kenyan prisoners who have taken up chess in recent years. The game has become part of rehabilitation programs in the country’s prisons, where officials and participants say it encourages patience, problem-solving and interaction between prisoners and guards.
At Maranjau, which holds about 450 prisoners according to Superintendent Humphrey Young, some choose chess over resting or playing soccer during their free time. They are drawn by the competition and what they say the game does for their state of mind.
“Chess has become one of our integral programs,” Young said. “Some of the skills chess teaches our offenders as they reintegrate back to society is how they can improve their problem-solving processes, and how they can think around issues that affect them once they’re out.”
Chess programs have operated in some Kenyan prisons since at least 2022. The government has supported the initiative alongside the International Chess Federation, known as FIDE, Chess Kenya and The Gift of Chess, a nonprofit organization that distributes chess sets.
The game is now played in all 134 prisons in Kenya, according to Phylis Ngigi, global outreach director for The Gift of Chess.
Kenya participated for the first time in FIDE’s Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners in 2024. Competitions are also held between Kenyan prisons, while some guards have been trained as chess coaches and play alongside prisoners.
At Maranjau, Young said the games create opportunities for prisoners and guards to interact in a less formal setting.
Supporters say chess offers more than recreation. Responsibility and the ability to work with others are important elements of prison rehabilitation, said Monica Njoroge, a project officer at Resources Oriented Development Initiatives.
The Kenyan nonprofit runs farming programs in prisons, where participants tend communal gardens while learning agricultural skills that could help them find work after their release.
Njoroge is not involved in the chess program, but she frequently visits Maranjau and has watched prisoners play.
“It is a game that trains patience and also having a clear mind in making decisions, being keen on what your next move is and the consequences that will come,” she said.
Kenya’s prison chess program has not been independently studied, and its long-term effects on behavior or reoffending are unknown.
For the prisoners gathered around the boards at Maranjau, there is a simpler attraction: They enjoy the game.
“It is a social game,” said Edwin Raj Walukaya, a 31-year-old prisoner. “It gives us friends and occupies our minds.”
For Gatonye, chess has become something he hopes to carry with him beyond prison.
“After being released, I hope to continue playing chess,” he said. “It brings peace inside my mind and heart.”

A ‘Wall of Hope’, a youth-led initiative by the Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF) and its Department of Youth Mental Health, was unveiled at the IIT-Madras Research Park in Taramani on Saturday, a press release said.
With young people facing increasing mental health challenges and suicide remaining concern, creating spaces for expression, connection, resilience, and help-seeking is vital.
The mental health campaign, which began on October 10, 2025, encourages young people aged 10-25 to express, share, and reflect upon their personal reasons for living, through brief messages of hope.
Adolescents and young adults across the country were invited to write the purpose of life on colourful post-it notes.
The activity is completely youth-led through peer leaders and trainer modules, where young people played a central role in leading and facilitating the campaign.
More than 20,000 responses from across six States have been collected.
Additionally, 400 volunteers have been trained to conduct this activity, which is voluntary and anonymous, to initiate and foster conversations around mental health.
Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, Madras High Court judge, and Lakshmi Vijayakumar, founder of suicide prevention organisation SNEHA, participated in the event, besides SCARF vice-chairperson R. Thara and director Sridhar Vaitheswaran.
(Assistance for overcoming suicidal thoughts is available on the State’s health helpline 104, Tele-MANAS 14416, and Sneha’s suicide prevention helpline 044-24640050)

The Diabetic Foot Society of India (DFSI), under the aegis of its national president V.B. Narayanamurthy, has written to Zulfiqarali G. Abbas, president of the Pan-African Diabetic Foot Study Group (PADFSG), proposing the formation of a global alliance on diabetic foot survival and limb preservation.
The letter, a copy of which was shared with The Hindu, notes that diabetic foot ulceration is an under-recognised cause of premature death, major amputation, recurrent illness, disability, and social exclusion. Available evidence shows that its five-year mortality is comparable to that of some cancers. And yet, global investment, policy attention, organised pathways, and post-amputation support remain substantially below the scale of the problem, the letter notes.
The DFSI, therefore, has proposed that institutions, including itself, King’s College London, International Association of Diabetic Foot Surgeons, D-Foot International, American Limb Preservation Society, Federation of International Podiatrists, and PADFSG, come together to form a Global Alliance for Diabetic Foot Survival and Limb Preservation, to create a sustained, scientific, and policy platform for prevention, limb preservation, improved survival, rehabilitation, surveillance, research, and engagement with governments and the World Health Organization (WHO).
The letter further stated that DFSI would announce the shared intention to form the Alliance at its next national conference, slated to be held on October 2, 2026. This, it said, would be an announcement of intent rather than a representation that the Alliance had been legally constituted or that any institution had accepted a financial or contractual obligation.
The letter urged the PADFSG to provide in-principle concurrence with the formation of the Alliance and the proposed conference announcement.
Apart from the proposal for the alliance, the letter also contained a draft Joint Global Declaration for joint consultation and unveiling, and asked for comments on the proposal and draft declaration from the PADFSG.
The DAFSI also stated that subject to the PADFSG’s concurrence, it proposed to convene the first founding meeting of the Alliance within 30 days of its conference.
The proposal
The proposal noted that the Alliance would provide a common platform for scientific leadership, policy advocacy, regional demonstration programmes, and responsible resource mobilisation. Its objectives would include advocacy with the WHO and national governments to secure explicit recognition of diabetic foot disease as an important medical condition; to improve survival and quality of life through multi-disciplinary care and patient-centred research; to promote prevention, early detection, and rapid referral; to advance surveillance and support the development of registries; to strengthen post-amputation rehabilitation; to promote research and training programmes; and to ensure the meaningful participation of people living with diabetes in governance and programme design.
The proposal also detailed membership and governance, standing bodies, the Secretariat, proposed activities of the Alliance, donor engagement, and financial management, as well as a performance framework and a risks safeguard.
The declaration
The draft declaration called for diabetic foot disease to be recognised as a major cause of premature death, disability, and exclusion. It called upon the WHO Director-General, regional directors, and member states to make diabetic foot prevention, limb preservation and survival a visible part of diabetes policy, establish common indicators and baseline registries, and support flagship programmes in at least two WHO regions.
It also proposed a goal to reduce risk-adjusted five-year mortality after a new diabetic foot ulcer by 30%, and potentially avoidable major amputations by 50% by 2030.
The draft declaration called for coordinated action that keeps people alive, mobile, included, and able to live with dignity.

Bitchat, the decentralised messaging platform founded by Twitter (now X) cofounder Jack Dorsey, has been removed from Google Play Store and Apple’s App Store following an official government order. In a post on X, Dorsey shared an official email from Apple, which read that the IT ministry (MeitY) had issued directions for the removal of the Bitchat app from the App Store under Section 69A of the IT Act. The email noted that the app allegedly included content deemed illegal in India. However, the communique did not specify what content had triggered the takedown order. Apple advised the developer to seek further details from MeitY directly. The Apple email further noted that Bitchat’s beta-testing access via TestFlight has also been blocked. However, the app would remain available on its App Store outside India. Meanwhile, Bitchat is no longer available for download via the Google Play Store as well and its website also appears to no longer be accessible in the country. It’s unclear whether this is for the same reason. Launched by Dorsey in 2025, Bitchat is an open-source messaging app that enables peer-to-peer (P2) communication through Bluetooth mesh networks without requiring internet access or centralised servers. The app does not require users to make accounts and has no central identity system either. It can be used during extreme occasions like internet outages and natural disasters, or in areas with poor network coverage. This is not the first time that Bitchat has landed in choppy regulatory waters in the country. In July this year, Dorsey had claimed the Indian government had directed GitHub to remove multiple repositories linked to Bitchat. He had shared a notification issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) to support his claims. The I4C’s notification had raised concerns that Bitchat’s implementation of anonymous communication prevents authorities from obtaining subscriber details or communication records during active investigations. The agency also warned that the platform could be exploited to evade surveillance and bypass internet shutdowns to coordinate unlawful assemblies, protests, or criminal activities. Notably, I4C’s concerns had come amid the unrest over the NEET 2026 paper leak, when protesters were reportedly using Bitchat to communicate amid suspension of mobile internet services at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi. The action against Bitchat appears to be a part of Centre’s broader plan to tighten scrutiny of social media platforms. Earlier this year, MeitY had proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, which would make government advisories legally binding on online intermediaries. The draft rules also proposed requiring platforms to remove content that could be used to commit unlawful acts within three hours of receiving a court order or a reasoned government notice.

In October 2026, a screenshot of an alleged post from U.S. President Donald Trump's Truth Social account spread online, showing Trump seemingly thanking billionaire Elon Musk for artificially increasing Republican votes ahead of the November 2026 midterms.
The purported post (archived) stated:
Republicans must WIN the 2026 Midterm Elections, and we must use every appropriate tool—Whether you vote early, absentee, by mail, or in-person, we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dummods with massive turnout! (@realDonaldTrump on Truth Social)
The above post is a doctored version of a real Truth Social post from Trump's account. The yellow highlighted line about Musk was edited into the post. As such, we rate this image as fake.
On Oct. 3, 2026, Trump wrote (archived) the following post on Truth Social. The fake highlighted line about Musk was added after "we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dumocrats with massive turnout!":
Republicans must WIN the 2026 Midterm Elections, and we must use every appropriate tool — Whether you vote early, absentee, by mail, or in-person, we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dumocrats with massive turnout! SO IMPORTANT — PLEASE GET OUT AND VOTE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP
swampthevoteusa.com/
(@realDonaldTrump on Truth Social)
The post in the screenshot is clearly edited, based on the nonsense phrase "Dummods" which appears to be a garbled version of "Dumocrats."
Snopes also looked up variations of the phrase on Trump's Truth, a website that archives his posts "every few minutes" and makes it easier to find them — including deleted posts. There was no evidence of Trump thanking Musk on Truth Social for making "every Republican vote" count as three votes.
Trump has been speaking at campaign rallies nationwide, trying to drum up support for Republican candidates ahead of the November 2026 midterm elections.

Far-right election win leaves migrants questioning their future in eastern Germany
The far-right Alternative for Germany party's recent election win in Saxony-Anhalt has sparked fear among migrants
BERLIN -- Ever since the far-right, anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany party won a regional election last month, not a day goes by without Ola Akhras and her husband discussing whether they should go back to Syria.
The couple live with their two young daughters in Magdeburg, where Saxony-Anhalt's newly elected state legislature is meeting Tuesday for the first time since the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, surged to its best result yet — putting it in a strong position to form Germany's first far-right regional government since World War II.
During its first sitting, the 83-seat legislature will elect its speaker — a job that traditionally goes to the largest party — and the AfD hopes for an initial symbolic victory. The state's next governor is unlikely to be chosen before December.
“It’s bad — we’ve built our lives here, we really loved being here, but now we don’t feel welcome anymore,” said Akhras, who fled Homs for Germany in 2018. She speaks fluent German and works as a doctor at the local hospital, where she is completing her specialist training in internal medicine.
Akhras, who wears a hijab, says she feels appreciated at work, but has lately encountered hostility while shopping and no longer feels safe leaving home in the evening. Her sense of not belonging has become overwhelming since the election.
“Our children will never be recognized as Germans here,” she said.
The mood in society is very different from a decade ago, when Germans welcomed more than a million migrants from war-torn countries such as Syria, Iraq and Afghanistan under Chancellor Angela Merkel. Many built new lives, learned the language and found work.
However, as Germany’s economic problems — slow growth, high inflation, rising energy prices — have worsened, public sentiment toward the newcomers has deteriorated. The AfD and other critics of immigration have blamed migrants for the country's problems.
The 13-year-old party has gained support particularly rapidly in Germany’s formerly communist and economically weaker eastern states, including Saxony-Anhalt. However, it also continues to gain on the national level. It is the strongest opposition party in parliament and leads recent polls.
The AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt last month underlined the party's skill in capitalizing on discontent with issues well beyond its core theme of curbing immigration as Chancellor Friedrich Merz's unpopular national government struggles to turn around Germany's stubbornly sluggish economy.
The party's strong showing has unsettled migrants and those Germans who thought the nation was immune to nationalism after the horrors of the Nazi past.
It remains uncertain that AfD will form the next government in Saxony-Anhalt — it fell three seats short of a majority in the Sept. 6 election. But many immigrants and refugees fear that if the far-right party succeeds in heading the state government it could try to implement its campaign promises, which include more and faster deportations as well as restrictions on the admission of asylum seekers.
There are no figures yet showing whether racist incidents have increased since the election, but “counseling centers are extremely busy, the phones are ringing off the hook, counseling appointments are fully booked, and people are in great need of counseling and support,” said Undra Dressler, the executive director of the Saxony-Anhalt State Network of Migrant Organizations.
“We know of people who have left, people who are considering it, and people who have made a conscious decision against it and say: ‘I’m staying. I won’t accept these conditions. Now more than ever, I’m going to get involved,’” Dressler said.
One of those determined to stay is Mohamad Aldabagh, a pharmacist from Homs who fled to Germany in 2015 at the height of Syria's civil war. That year, hundreds of thousands crossed the Mediterranean on flimsy rubber boats in hopes of finding a safer future in Europe.
“It’s been a very good experience living in Germany over the past 10 years,” said Aldabagh, a 34-year-old father of two young children who works at a pharmacy in Magdeburg. “I’ve rebuilt my life here, and I won’t let anyone take that away from me.”
While he says he has experienced racism as well, he believes that skilled workers like himself or the many foreign doctors working in Germany are needed and that society can't afford to treat them badly.
While the AfD program for Saxony-Anhalt does not reject labor migration altogether, it takes a highly selective approach to recruiting foreign workers.
The party explicitly proposes refraining from recruiting workers it describes as “culturally foreign” and ending a state program designed to support the integration of foreign skilled workers, says Rahim Hajji, a professor of social and health services at Magdeburg-Stendal University of Applied Sciences.
“This raises a fundamental question,” Hajji said. “How is a state with an ageing population and growing labor shortages supposed to meet its demand for skilled workers if it substantially restricts the pool of international workers it is willing to recruit?”
As of this August, more than one in four doctors, or 27.1%, in Saxony-Anhalt’s hospitals did not have German citizenship, according to a survey by Mediendienst Integration group, which researches migration in Germany.
“We want to contribute to the well-being of society here,” said Aldabagh. “We are needed. We are not the black sheep in this country.”
He then paused and added: “But if we don’t get respect anymore, then we’ll move to another state where AfD isn’t as strong.”

Socialism is breaking through to the mainstream this year, with surveys showing most Democrats, and plenty of independents, now view the term positively.
Gen Z is warming to socialism. But they’re still not sure what it means.
They’re interested, but don’t sign them up for the revolution just yet.
The shift is being led by young people in particular, who have also helped left-populist candidates win high-stakes primaries this year. A Cato Institute poll from June found that over half of Gen Z are more supportive of socialism (53 percent) than capitalism (45 percent). And more than half (57 percent) of people ages 18 to 34 have a positive view of socialism, according to a Gallup poll from August — versus just 34 percent of people over 55.
Figures like these are inspiring socialist organizers and frightening Republicans, who are accusing Democrats of sliding into “communism” in their midterm messaging.
But here’s a little secret I’ve been hearing in the focus groups I run through my research, media, and strategy company focused on Gen Z — it’s not “socialism” that’s attractive to young voters. In fact, there’s little agreement on what the word really means.
Instead, it’s the social policies these candidates are running on that resonate — things like affordable housing, healthcare, education, a higher minimum wage, and higher taxes on corporations and wealthy individuals.
All summer long, I asked Gen Z voters to define socialism. There was no consensus answer, but much less talk of “workers controlling the means of production,” as one 22-year-old woman from New Jersey referenced, and much more of a focus on what a 21-year-old man from Florida described as a “social safety net.”
Understanding where they’re coming from is important to both critics and supporters: Revolutionaries and reactionaries alike who think young people are signing up for a specific ideology are misreading the moment. When it comes to the rise of “socialism,” young people want what they’ve always wanted: to be heard, and to be helped.
Gen Z’s interest in the term was closely tied to the myriad ways their economic outlook has deteriorated in the past year.
“I feel like over the last year things definitely have changed. You see it generally even with gas prices. ... A lot of it has to do with the fact that our country has involved itself in a lot of different conflicts around the world at this point,” the 21-year-old from Florida said.
“During the school year I am relying on my refunds from school to pay my rent, to pay my car payment and car insurance, phone bill, internet, stuff like that,” said another 21-year-old man from Pennsylvania.
“I haven’t been able to financially plan for my education in the way I thought I was going to and have been needing to save more of my own money from jobs I’m working to help account for those differences,” said a 21-year-old woman from North Carolina.
As economic anxiety reshapes Gen Z’s politics and life feels harder and harder to afford, young people are looking for the government to provide social support.
Consistently, I asked groups of young people this summer what they’re looking for in an ideal political candidate — and the government more broadly. Overwhelmingly, they told me they’re in favor of politicians who understand everyday people and a government that provides social services for its constituents.
“A political candidate who understands the common person. Someone that’s not financially out of touch, who doesn’t take money from different corporations. Someone who understands the struggles of an everyday American and knows what’s going on with the economy and can understand the struggles of students, children, families,” said a 21-year-old woman from Michigan.
“Providing a higher safety net with welfare, especially with hospitals because of the ‘big, beautiful bill’ and its effects,” said a 19-year-old from New York City, citing the impact of the Trump administration’s recent tax bill that slashed healthcare spending.
“A candidate who isn’t afraid to say that we deserve more as citizens,” said another 19-year-old woman from Michigan.
According to many of the young voters I spoke to, in their eyes, this is what socialism means: a more ambitious, generous, and equality-minded government. And when I asked them to tell me about the policies they associate with democratic socialists, they said things like “Medicare-for-all,” “help with college tuition,” and “social safety nets like healthcare, public education, public housing.”
In pushing back against socialism’s rising popularity, critics often invoke history, pointing to Marxist governments where equality was instituted by force and coercion and associated with poverty and deprivation.
“They’ve gone communist, but we’re not going to let that happen,” President Donald Trump said at a South Carolina rally in August. “It’s never worked in 1,000 years with different names, lots of different names. It’s never worked once.”
Just as Gen Z was presumed to be “woke” Democrats four years ago and then swung hard to Trump and MAGA in 2024, the socialist turn is just as conditional.
On the whole, however, young people I spoke to were less likely to tie socialism to “communism” or to places like Cuba, Venezuela, or Soviet Russia. Instead, they gave examples where they perceive socialism to work well, often mentioning wealthy Western countries and the social support systems associated with these kinds of governments.
“I think Scandinavian countries and those countries have had socialist policies in place and people end up having universal healthcare and people are able to live more comfortably and receive more money from the government to support them,” said a 21-year-old woman from Massachusetts. “I know in Canada there’s some socialist policies that I think have benefited people in regards to healthcare and welfare and social security.”
This shouldn’t be surprising. With years of distance from the Marxist governments that our parents and grandparents may think back to (even the oldest Gen Z were born well after the Cold War ended) young people are more focused on social policies than the core tenets of socialism.
“The first thing that comes to mind is the government’s involvement in making sure that everybody is cared for and everyone’s health remains a priority despite their income,” said that 21-year-old woman from Massachusetts. “And I think that is something that makes me view socialism in more of a positive light because some people obviously don’t have the same financial situations as others. That doesn’t mean that they should be undervalued in society.”
But just as socialism’s detractors are misunderstanding its appeal among young voters, its supporters should be just as wary of assuming voters are signing up for their movement.
I’ve heard anecdotes like the ones above shared over and over again. And yet, very few young people I’ve spoken to in the past few months have been willing to call themselves a socialist.
This is consistent with a broader Gen Z skepticism toward political parties. While they’re leaning into the policies associated with “socialism,” they still largely reject labels — whether that label is Republican, Democrat, or…socialist.
Asked if she would consider herself a democratic socialist or a socialist, the 21-year-old from Massachusetts said she “would definitely lean that way.” A 19-year-old woman from Colorado said, “I would say I lean towards it, but I haven’t completely been with that party.”
And a 23-year-old woman from Arizona said: “I would say I’m in between democrat and democratic socialist.”
And while a 19-year-old from Michigan said she appreciates that democratic socialists are “going to help get baseline needs for people across America met in ways that aren’t going to happen if we have someone who is taking money from PACs and corporations making money off of people going into medical debt and things like that,” but asked if she would label herself that way, she said, “I feel like I don’t know enough about it.”
This isn’t universal. Polls suggest a sizable number of young Democrats identify as democratic socialist when asked. But when it comes to organized political behavior, the Democratic Socialists of America only recently passed 120,000 official members, even as they’ve had unprecedented success in raising their profile and nominating candidates this cycle.
Just as Gen Z was presumed to be “woke” Democrats four years ago and then swung hard to Trump and MAGA in 2024, the socialist turn is just as conditional. They’re looking for concrete solutions, not dogma, and if they don’t see results, they’ll look elsewhere.

Keralam Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan’s statement at a recent function about avoiding unnecessary angioplasty seems to have stirred a hornets’ nest with many doctors objecting to the “generalised statement,” while some lone voices pointed out that Mr. Satheesan was 100% right and that unnecessary procedures had become the norm.
In a Facebook post, Rajesh Gopalan Nair, Professor and Head of Cardiology at the Government Medical College Hospital, Kozhikode, had appreciated Mr. Satheesan “for pointing out a truth.” But it set off an avalanche of comments from the doctors and public, with the latter narrating their harrowing experiences in hospitals and appreciating Dr. Rajesh for calling a spade a spade, while many doctors expressed disappointment at Dr. Rajesh’s stand.
Dr. Rajesh, however, made it clear in his post that a person coming into the emergency with a suspected heart attack should in no way distrust the doctor, for the situation may call for an immediate angioplasty.
Second opinion
He also explained clearly the situations when one could afford to wait and seek a second opinion, if angioplasty was suggested to a patient. He also cautioned the public against looking at every doctor or hospital with suspicion. Angioplasty should definitely be done when it is clinically indicated and these situations are clearly documented, he said.
Even though much of the medical fraternity expressed their displeasure at the “unsubstantiated” statement of the Chief Minister and the support that unexpectedly seemed to have come from one of their own, Dr. Rajesh refused to be cowed down. He maintained that he stood by his position that some of the angioplasty procedures done in hospitals were indeed not warranted.
On Monday, the Interventional Cardiology Council of Kerala (ICCK) said in a statement here that public’s apprehension over “unnecessary” medical procedures should not delay life-saving treatment during a heart attack emergency.
Responding to the Chief Minister’s remarks on avoiding unnecessary investigations and angioplasty, the council said it supported evidence-based and ethical medical practice and the principle that every intervention must have a clear clinical indication.
ICCK president Rajesh T. said that public discussion on angioplasty should clearly differentiate between elective intervention in stable patients and primary angioplasty during an acute heart attack, where treatment is highly time-sensitive.
What the data show
According to Statewide ICCK registry data presented at the council’s last annual conference, more than 70% of angioplasties performed in Kerala involved acute and emergency clinical situations.
He said the council welcomed any discussion aimed at strengthening evidence-based care, transparency and public confidence in the health-care system. “In stable patients, there is usually greater scope for detailed evaluation and for deciding whether medicines, further assessment or intervention would offer the greatest benefit. In an acute heart attack, however, delay can have serious consequences,” ICCK said.
However, the council cautioned that a general atmosphere of mistrust surrounding cardiac procedures could have unintended consequences, particularly when a patient develops severe chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of a heart attack.
