'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago
- Published
Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since.
"He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog.
"He used to work out every morning."
Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993.
Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role.
After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began.
That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15.
Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well.
Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.
It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.
In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.
Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.
The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.
It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories.
"My classmates told me that my father sold out his country.
"That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."
In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.
After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.
Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried.
"I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers.
"She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"
Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.
Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home.
"First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."
Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.
All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.
The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.
Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.
At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.
The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.
Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.
Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.
As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."
She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches.
On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present."
One of his favourite songs included the lyrics: "I had a sweater, a blue sweater, that my sister took" - which reminded him of his sister who was also a freedom fighter and had been killed during the war.
She also has memories of her mother loving music - playing and singing hits by Abba, Dolly Parton and Whitney Houston.
Until her father's arrest, Hanna remembers September as being full of hope with its three big Orthodox Christian festivals, including the Geez New Year. Now the month brings her no joy.
Ibrahim Sherifo knows exactly how she feels. Both his parents, who were senior members of the ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), were among the G-15 people arrested 25 years ago.
He was 13 years old at the time
"For me 18 September 2001 is a dark day, but not only for me, it is a dark day for Eritrea and its people, because it is the day when law and democracy was detained," he tells the BBC.
He is now 38 and living in exile in the Netherlands, where he was granted asylum, and is pursuing an MA in political science - following in his father's footsteps.
His dad Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo was the local government minister and de facto deputy president before his detention.
Ibrahim was with his mother, Aster Fissehatsion, staying with her sister when he remembers security agents knocking on the door early in the morning and taking her away in her pyjamas.
Worried about his father, Ibrahim immediately ran to his nearby house but was told he had already been picked up when he had gone out for exercise.
Both Hanna and Ibrahim say they are forever grateful to the friends and family who offered them care and supported them as they grew up without their parents, despite the risks.
They are also proud of what their parents stood for and daring to call for reforms.
"They had conscience and couldn't observe idly while what they fought for what had been hijacked by Isaias and his coterie," says Ibrahim.
"As a family, we should be informed whether they are alive or not," he adds, accusing the government of wanting to erase all memory of the political prisoners.
Hanna also wants the plight of the many others whose relatives have disappeared over the years to be heard too.
Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down"
Human rights groups, including the UN, consider the G-15 prisoners of conscience and have been calling for their release.
President Isaias, now 80, has still not implemented the country's first constitution - approved in 1997 - and remains in power without ever holding an election.
Hanna recalls that on the eve of her father's disappearance, she had a "bad feeling" - and had crept into his bed and tied his legs to her own with string while he slept.
"In the morning he woke up to find he was tied up and to release himself he pulled my legs and I woke up. I begged him not to leave but he assured me that he would return [after his run]."
Describing the years of sorrow since, she says it is like living in the deep sea.
"Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down.
"Sometimes you lose hope and you are out of breath."
Asked what she would say if she could get a message to her parents, she replies: "Don't worry about us.
"Like you survived the struggle through sheer steadfastness, we hope you can pull through this too and return to us."

Siri can index more of your personal data — here's how to limit it
If you’re concerned about Apple’s new digital assistant, here’s how you can restrict its access to your data.
With the release of iOS 27, Apple has finally begun rolling out its long delayed redesign of Siri. You'll need to join a waitlist before you can get Siri AI, but once you gain access to the new digital assistant, you're likely to find it's a significant leap over its predecessor. Engadget's Mat Smith found the new Siri much improved when he tested it on the iOS 27 beta, thanks to its ability to deliver smarter, more personalized responses.
However, there is a downside worth mentioning. Apple partnered with Google to train the new large language models that power Siri AI's features. And as with any AI system, the new Siri requires a great deal of data to work at its best, and that data comes from you(r phone).
How does Siri AI access data from your apps?
The reason Siri AI can provide a more personalized experience is thanks to a framework called App Intents that allows Apple Intelligence tools, including Siri, to access data from the apps on your Apple devices. When you enable Siri AI on your iPhone, iPad or Mac, Spotlight and Siri are unified under a single interface. By default, when you ask Siri a question, it will search through your Apple apps, including Notes and Messages, to pull information that might be relevant to your prompt or query. If a developer has chosen to support App Intents, Siri will be able to scan through their apps too.
Siri AI relies on a combination of on-device models and Apple's Private Cloud Compute (PCC) infrastructure, meaning the assistant will sometimes offload your data to a remote server for processing. Apple says it does not store any data sent to its PCC servers after processing a request, and that it can't even see the data. Still, you might feel uncomfortable about sharing data regardless. Thankfully, there are ways you can control what Siri can index.
Restrict Siri AI's access to content inside your apps
As mentioned, Apple has left it up to developers to decide if Siri AI can access the data people generate inside of their apps. That means as long as they allow iOS 27's Spotlight tool to index the contents of their apps, Siri AI can in turn access and surface that information for you as a user. However, you still have control over the process, and can ultimately decide to restrict Siri from accessing your apps. To do so, follow these steps:
- Open the Settings app.
- Scroll down and tap Apps.
- Select the app you want to restrict Siri from accessing.
- Tap Search.
- Toggle off Show Content in Search.
After you disable Show Content in Search in relation to a particular app, Siri won't pull information from that app, even if you ask it to do so directly. For example, if you disable indexing of Messages, and ask Siri to summarize a series of messages from your friend, the digital assistant will tell you it can't find those messages.
In the Apps settings menu, you may have noticed a collection of options grouped under "Apple Intelligence & Siri." For the purposes of this guide, you can leave those alone; they don't have privacy implications. Instead, they primarily control where iOS might suggest an app for you. For instance, if you disable the "Suggest App" option, you won't see that specific app among the "Siri Suggestions" iOS generates when you access your iPhone's search shade. The "Learn from this App" option sounds nefarious, but it merely allows iOS to see how and when you're using your apps so that it can tailor when it surfaces those apps for you.
On-screen awareness
Even after you restrict Siri's ability to search through your apps, you can still get it to help you with situations requiring contextual knowledge on a more ad-hoc basis. A feature called on-screen awareness allows Siri to read the contents of screenshots and images. This can be useful from an accessibility standpoint, or if you want Siri to summarize a lengthy article or message thread. Just note if you snap a screenshot and ask Siri to interpret it, it might be sent to the company's PCC servers.
Ensure you're not sharing Siri recordings with Apple
By default, Apple won't collect or use the data from your interactions with Siri to train future versions of the virtual assistant. But as part of your iPhone's setup process, you might have accidently opted into sharing your Siri recordings and transcripts with the company. Either way, it's worth checking to confirm your Siri data isn't being used for model training.
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap Privacy & Security.
- Scroll down and select Analytics & Improvements.
- Disable Improve Siri & Dictation if turned on.
Disable Siri AI altogether
One final option worth mentioning is that you can revert to the older version of Siri. This gives you a way to continue using apps like CarPlay with your voice while limiting your privacy exposure. Unintuitively, however, you'll find the option to do this hidden inside the Screen Time section.
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap Screen Time, followed by Content & Privacy Restrictions.
- Enable Content & Privacy Restrictions.
- Tap Siri.
- Under Allowed Siri Version, select Siri Classic.
Alternatively, you can disable Siri entirely by following the steps below.
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap Siri.
- Scroll down and select Turn off Siri.
If you want to restrict any other part of the Apple Intelligence suite, Apple has helpful support page on the topic.

On Sunday night, John Oliver dedicated the majority of his Emmy-winning show “Last Week Tonight” to the Secret Service’s failings in recent years while declining to address the major media news of the week: David Ellison’s newly-formed Skydance Corp. swallowing up Warner Bros. Discovery — which controls Oliver’s network HBO — and merging it with Paramount Skydance to form a mega-company.
So, would his late-night compatriot Jon Stewart give his two cents on the merger during Mondays’ episode of “The Daily Show,” since it’s also a part of Skydance Corp.?
Popular on Variety
Apparently not.
Stewart dedicated the show entirely to AI, first ripping apart AI leaders’ empty promises of job creation, economic prosperity and its ability to cure cancer while admitting that there’s a 10-25% chance it will kill us all. Currently, however, AI is primarily being used for ICE and other surveillance, drone warfare targeting and potential dynamic pricing at places like McDonald’s.
“What are we getting in exchange for this 10-25% chance at extinction?” asked Stewart, adding, “Right now it’s mostly murder, surveillance and surge pricing for the McRib? What a trade! I’m getting the sense that you guys might be full of shit.”
The comedian also pushed back at President Trump allowing these AI companies to self-regulate after his recent fawning AI summit, since the Zuckerberg’s and Musk’s of the world don’t exactly have a sterling track record when it comes to playing it safe. There’s also the matter of how many jobs AI will eliminate. Though AI leaders keep repeating over and over that the technology will lead to newer, different jobs and an economic windfall for everybody, they can’t say what jobs it would create or how it will economically benefit everyday people.
“The view of our self-policing geniuses is that the new world that we are building must continue without regulation or financial limitation because it’s important work carried out by important people,” offered Stewart. “And my guess is: They’ll still have jobs when this is done… Stop lying to us! Claims of universal high income and incredible hobbies isn’t going to paper over how frightening this future can sound.”

Owner, businessman & player: Messi has big plans as a golden era ends
- Published
Lionel Messi is about to play his last match for Argentina.
On what will be his 208th appearance, the country's most-capped player and record goal scorer will bid an emotional farewell in a friendly against Benin at the Monumental in Buenos Aires.
Arguably Argentina's greatest ever player - only Diego Maradona comes close - announced his retirement from the national team on 31 August, six weeks after the World Cup final defeat by Spain, saying he had nothing more to give.
Coach Lionel Scaloni insists that if Messi ever wants to carry on, he can, and there is no embarrassment in changing one's mind. But that chapter seems closed.
His club career though goes on. The contract with Inter Miami runs to the end of the 2028 season, but it is reviewed year by year, and nobody close to him expects him to walk away a day before he has to.
In fact, it is quite likely he will renew it if he feels, mentally and physically, up for it.
Ask the people around him what comes after that and they smile, because Messi has never really planned beyond his next game.
Even so, the shape of what lies ahead is already in front of us. He will stay inside football, because he would struggle to live without it, but his other business interests stretch far outside the game.
- Messi retires from Argentina duty with 'nothing left to give' 
  - Published31 August
- How Messi's decade of dominance almost never happened 
  - Published31 August
An owner who wants to be involved in everything
Messi used to like the idea of being a sporting director or an adviser to the president, close to the decisions without all the travelling and the phone calls.
And asked recently whether he would rather be a coach or an owner, Messi chose owner.
A coach lives and dies by every Saturday and has to worry about far too many things for Messi's liking.
An owner shapes the direction of a club from a little further back. Having said that, he would be an owner who does not stop at approving the appointment of a manager and stepping away. He would want to be involved in everything.
The groundwork is being laid in Spain. UE Cornella, on the edge of Barcelona and in the fifth tier, is the nursery where young players grow. He bought it in April.
CD Eldense, in the second division, announced Messi as its new owner on 1 October, subject to authorisation from the Spanish sports council, the CSD.
Eldense will be the club that leads his football operation, but the target this season is not to get relegated, so former Villarreal boss Javi Calleja got the job with the arrival of the new owner.
The plan is to run both through people he trusts, who will act as a link between Messi and the clubs until the day he can give them his full attention.
For now he follows every Eldense match closely on his computer. After Eldense beat Real Oviedo by four goals to one, his first message as owner was an Instagram post that read "Aupa Deportivo".
The pull of his name has been felt as well. Around a dozen sponsors came forward within a couple of days, some of them brands that had been talking to the previous owners without ever closing a deal, and some that already have a relationship with him.
In Uruguay he and Luis Suarez founded Deportivo LSM in May 2025, and they won promotion to the country's third tier in its first season.
A network of more clubs was discussed at the start. But the sums needed to lift them up the divisions have cooled that idea quickly, and it is not on the table today. Messi's focus is to see whether Eldense can establish itself in La Liga.
There is a link to Miami as well. As part of his contract with Inter Miami, he will have some shares in the club when he retires. A franchise of his own is not part of the plan.
Could he go home to Newell's Old Boys, the club where he played as a child in Rosario? The idea has never been formally discussed.
It may have crossed his mind while drinking mate with Suarez, in the way a return to Barcelona or a spell at Napoli, the club of Maradona, might have.
Nobody close to the player expects it though. Everything is built around Europe and Miami, and the perfect home is waiting for the family in Castelldefels, close to the sea and Barcelona.
- A rivalry that changed football 
  - Published5 June
- Goals, records, tears ... Messi's most iconic moments 
  - Published31 August
A growing business empire and love for youth football
Newell's will still be close, because the club is one of the sixteen academies at this year's Messi Cup.
If owning clubs is one love, youth football is the other, and his regular presence at his son's games and the Messi Cup are the proof.
He puts his money and his time into a tournament for Under-16 academies, which began in 2025 with eight teams.
Last year, the organisers expected him to come to one or two games, perhaps only the final, but to everyone's surprise, he sat through every match on every day.
This year the teams doubled to 16, from 25 October at Inter Miami's facilities in Florida, including Atletico Madrid, Chelsea, Barcelona, Inter Milan, Arsenal, UE Cornella, and others.
Away from the pitch, Messi has built a portfolio that helps explain why Forbes put his net worth at about $1.1bn, external in June, with earnings of around $140m over the previous year split between football and business.
His best known endorsement is the lifetime Adidas deal he signed in 2017.
The most visible piece is MiM Hotels, six boutique properties from Ibiza to Andorra, which Melia has run under a rental agreement since 1 November 2025.
MiM takes its name from Messi and the Majestic hotel group, and runs the hotels inside its Melia Collection.
In Rosario, his family firm invests in Carrasco M, a development of 24 homes by the Parana river, with Ángel Di María's property agency handling the sales.
He is also a partner in the restaurant chain El Club de la Milanesa which plans to open five branches in Catalonia, the first in Castelldefels.
He has a mate collection with the drinkware giants Stanley, the brand's first multi-year deal with an athlete, and he gave his opinion on materials and colours.
The business side began with his father. Jorge Messi, who died in August aged 68, looked after his son's affairs from the start, and some of his early advice led the family into trouble with the tax authorities in Spain.
The company then grew into branches for TV production, marketing, media and commercial partnerships, among others, all well established by the time Jorge fell seriously ill.
Messi trusts the people who run them, some of them with him since his early days at Barcelona, and a thorough filter means he only gets offered and chooses what he is comfortable with.
He sets his own relationship with the business world, and nobody imposes anything on him.
In Miami last November, Messi told the America Business Forum: "Business is something that interests me. I would like to keep learning because I know nothing and I am just starting out."
The portfolio his circle has prepared is already impressive while he finds more football targets to keep the flame alive.

It's been five years since James Bond was on the silver screen in No Time to Die. For fans of the secret agent, the wait has been arduous, made even harder by the fact that Amazon, which now owns the franchise, still hasn't chosen a successor to Daniel Craig, let alone started filming Bond's resurrection.
But if it's seemed like a long haul for fans, just think how it has felt for Omega, which counts on a steady stream of Bond action to regularly inject lots of lovely cash into the company via watch releases linked directly to the films. Omega's last official Bond film tie-in watch was the titanium No Time to Die Seamaster prematurely launched back in 2019, ahead of the film’s then Covid-delayed release in 2021.
Considering that Swatch Group’s net profit collapsed by almost 90 percent to $32 million in 2025 (though, thankfully, things look rosier so far this year), we shouldn't be surprised that Omega isn't bothering to wait for Jeff Bezos to put his white cat down and proceed with world domination. As there's no new Bond or Bond film to work with, Omega has decided to launch 007-themed watches anyway—not just one, but an entire collection totaling six Seamaster Divers.
You can hardly blame the brand. When Omega first strapped a Seamaster to Pierce Brosnan's wrist in 1995's GoldenEye, it reportedly saw a 20-fold sales increase. In 2012, Omega's then-president Stephen Urquhart even told Variety that Omega’s sales “look like a stock market chart” that peaks during promotion of Bond films, then sinks afterward. “The films have had a very marked influence on sales,” Urquhart conceded.
The new “James Bond and Spectre” collection is themed around good and evil, with three watches bearing the “007” symbol of James Bond, and three the octopus-like motif of Spectre, the fictional global terrorist organization in the series.
The six Seamaster Diver 300M watches share the same movement. However, the two non-limited stainless-steel editions are the core pieces, available individually at $8,600 each—one with a blue aluminum dial dedicated to James Bond, and the other black for dastardly Spectre fans. Both come on a brushed mesh bracelet.
The James Bond edition has a grade 5 titanium bezel, while the Spectre edition boasts a black ceramic bezel ring to match the dial's blackened grained finish.
The remaining four Seamasters are split across two limited-edition numbered sets—one dedicated to Bond, the other to Spectre—capped at 77 boxes each. At a cool $89,800 per pair (Omega won't sell them individually), you get one stainless-steel model on a brushed mesh bracelet, and a second in platinum-gold on leather.
Each set comes in a presentation box with an additional NATO strap, strap-changing tool, cuff links, a cord bracelet, a loupe, a leather travel pouch and card holder, and papers. In the James Bond set, the strap keepers are engraved with 007; in the Spectre set, the strap keepers carry the Spectre emblem.
This collection is not the first time Omega has sought to leverage its Bond connection without a film peg. Back in May of this year, Omega unveiled the Seamaster Diver 300M Chronograph “007 First Light,” a new 44-mm chrono tied to 007 First Light, a James Bond game developed by the same studio responsible for the Hitman franchise. Originally designed as an in-game gadget, Omega turned it into a production model.
Back in 2012, there was the Seamaster James Bond 007 50th Anniversary watch with a red number 50 on the bezel. In 2019, there was an On Her Majesty's Secret Service edition Seamaster to mark 50 years of the 1969 film, limited to 7,007 pieces. Then, in 2022, Omega released a Seamaster to coincide with 60 years of Bond movies.

Jim Bakker, the televangelist who built a media empire with former wife Tammy Faye Bakker, has died. He was 86.

“It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening,” read the Instagram post from Monday, October 5.
The statement continued, “For 66 years, Jim gave his life to preaching the Gospel of Jesus Christ. He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry.”

A hot tip to battle performance anxiety? 'Pretend flush' a mistake down the toilet
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
In 2012, psychologist Cindra Kamphoff was running a marathon. Then at Mile 22, her self-doubt started to kick in. She remembers telling herself, "This is dumb. Why am I doing this?"
Life Kit
Beat performance anxiety with these quick tips
But Kamphoff, who works with top athletes on how to overcome performance anxiety — including from the Minnesota Vikings and USA Track & Field — was prepared. She had written positive phrases on her arm that she could read when she needed a boost during the race: "I'm strong, I'm fast, I'm fit, I'm ready."
This is just one of many techniques that Kamphoff shares in The Confidence Habit: 7 Core Practices to Transform Self-Doubt to Self-Belief, published in September. The book offers creative ways to manage fear and negativity — like pretend-flushing your mistakes down the toilet — before, during and after a high-stakes task.
These tools can be applied to any situation, whether it's a race, work presentation or a job interview. The goal is for people to "be their best in the moments that matter most to them," she says.
Kamphoff, who has a PhD in sport and performance psychology, shares four tools you can try today.
Move on quickly with "learn, burn, return"
Maybe you fumble the ball in a big game or forget the lines in your school play and can't stop thinking about it afterward.
If you make a mistake during a high-stakes moment, Kamphoff says it's important to move on quickly.
She suggests a tool she calls "learn, burn, return" to build back your confidence and keep your goals in reach. Try this if you fumble mid-performance, or as a way to reflect after the event.
Learn: Ask yourself, what did you learn? Use this prompt: Next time, I will _____.
Burn: Think of a motion or a cue you can use to remind yourself to move on quickly. Kamphoff says you can snap your fingers, say "that fast" or "you might literally pretend to flush a toilet."
She taught the toilet flush move to former Minnesota Vikings player Adam Thielen, who used it after he fumbled during a playoff game in 2020. He then went on to catch a 43-yard pass over his head that helped the Vikings win the game.
Using the same motion or phrase every time you "burn" helps your brain strengthen new neural pathways when it comes to moving through anxiety, she says.
Return: Now it's time to build yourself back up. Remind yourself, "you got this, you're doing the best that you can," says Kamphoff.
Speak to yourself powerfully
How you talk to yourself matters, Kamphoff says. According to the American Psychological Association, self-affirmations, even in small doses, can have lasting effects on our self-esteem.
When Kamphoff wrote positive messages on her arm to motivate her during her marathon, they worked because she was giving her brain evidence that she could be successful.
As Kamphoff repeated these phrases during her race, her pace picked up. She ended up not only winning the race in her division, but running her last four miles the fastest out of any part of the marathon.
To make what Kamphoff calls a "power phrase," choose a statement that starts with I will, I can or I am. Then ask yourself, How am I at my best? What does that look like? What does that feel like?"
Kamphoff chose phrases that reminded her of her love for running — and that she had trained for hundreds of miles to run the race.
Set gold, silver and bronze goals
Instead of focusing on one perfect outcome, set a range of goals for yourself. Kamphoff recommends creating a "gold, silver and bronze goal," she says.
Let's say you're running the mile in track. Your bronze goal might be running a time you're generally happy with, your silver goal might be to run a personal best, and your gold goal might be to win the race.
This can help decrease anxiety and increase confidence by removing the pressure of one ideal performance and shifting focus to the present moment. Especially because "an outcome is something you can't control," she says.
Fact-check your self-doubt
If you're feeling overcome with negative thoughts right before a job interview or a big test, ask yourself three questions:
- Is that thought true?
- Is that thought serving you?
- What would be a more empowering statement? 
This method is similar to other frameworks, like acceptance commitment therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy. It can pause negative thoughts and help you get back to the present moment.
For example, if you walk into a job interview thinking, "If I don't ace this, I'll never get another job," this exercise can challenge that thought. And it can help you find a more positive, grounded alternative: "Even if I don't get this job, I know I'm capable of success and that there are better opportunities for me."
Remember, she says. Confidence is a choice you get to make.
"You get to decide in the moment, are you going to be confident?" she says. "Many times the action of confidence comes before the feeling, and it's a skill."

The Billboard Hot 100 is widely considered the definitive all-genre singles chart in the US.
Although it was officially launched in 1958, Billboard began using modern airplay and sales data in 1991, allowing for more time-sensitive calculations and accurate rankings.
Well over 1,000 songs have reached the coveted No. 1 spot, but it's far more difficult for a song to debut in the top position; it typically means a much-promoted single has met high expectations, or at least that an artist is supported and beloved by a legion of fans.
Keep reading for a complete list of instant chart-toppers throughout history, listed below in chronological order.
1. "You Are Not Alone" by Michael Jackson
Michael Jackson was the first artist to achieve this feat with "You Are Not Alone," which debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated September 2, 1995.
It was the second single from Jackson's ninth album, "HIStory: Past, Present and Future, Book I."
2. "Fantasy" by Mariah Carey
"Fantasy" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated September 30, 1995. It was the lead single from Mariah Carey's fifth album, "Daydream."
3. "Exhale (Shoop Shoop)" by Whitney Houston
"Exhale (Shoop Shoop)" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated November 25, 1995. It was the lead single from the soundtrack for the film "Waiting to Exhale."
4. "One Sweet Day" by Mariah Carey & Boyz II Men
"One Sweet Day" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated December 2, 1995. It was the second single from Carey's fifth album, "Daydream."
5. "I'll Be Missing You" by Puff Daddy & Faith Evans, featuring 112
"I'll Be Missing You" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated June 14, 1997. It was the second single from Diddy's debut album, "No Way Out," when he was known as Puff Daddy.
6. "Honey" by Mariah Carey
"Honey" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated September 13, 1997. It was the lead single from Carey's sixth album, "Butterfly."
7. "Candle in the Wind 1997/Something About the Way You Look Tonight" by Elton John
"Candle in the Wind 1997/Something About the Way You Look Tonight" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated October 11, 1997. The double A-side single later became the first song ever to be certified diamond.
8. "My Heart Will Go On" by Celine Dion
"My Heart Will Go On" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated February 28, 1998.
The famous ballad was written for the soundtrack of "Titanic" and served as the movie's main romantic theme. It was also released as a single from Dion's fifth English-language album, "Let's Talk About Love."
9. "I Don't Want to Miss a Thing" by Aerosmith
"I Don't Want to Miss a Thing" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated September 5, 1998. It was recorded for the film "Armageddon."
10. "Doo Wop (That Thing)" by Lauryn Hill
"Doo Wop (That Thing)" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated November 14, 1998. It was the lead single from Lauryn Hill's debut album "The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill," which won the Grammy Award for album of the year.
11. "This Is the Night" by Clay Aiken
"This Is the Night" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated June 28, 2003. It was Clay Aiken's debut single after competing on season two of "American Idol."
12. "I Believe" by Fantasia
"I Believe" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated July 10, 2004. It was Fantasia's debut single after winning season three of "American Idol."
13. "Inside Your Heaven" by Carrie Underwood
"Inside Your Heaven" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated July 2, 2005. It was Carrie Underwood's debut single after winning season four of "American Idol."
Underwood made history as the first country artist to have a No. 1 debut on the Billboard Hot 100.
14. "Do I Make You Proud" by Taylor Hicks
"Do I Make You Proud" debuted at No. 1 on the chart dated July 1, 2006. Taylor Hicks first performed the song on the fifth season finale of "American Idol," and it was released as a single shortly after his victory.
15. "3" by Britney Spears

How to add and customize your CarPlay widgets
Personalizing your CarPlay dashboard beyond its apps only takes a few easy steps.
Since Apple added widgets to CarPlay in iOS 26, compatible cars have gotten even closer to being a proper extension of your iPhone. Instead of being limited to navigation, messaging and audio, CarPlay widgets let you view information from many other apps on your phone. Whether you want to check live game scores, manage your smart home or follow the forecast at your destination, a widget makes it simple to do so on the road.
Before diving in, you should know there's a difference between a CarPlay app and a widget. An app like Maps or Spotify is fully optimized for CarPlay and takes up most, if not all, of your display for easier interaction. On the other hand, widgets appear in customizable stacks and provide specific details from the app they represent.
Luckily, customizing your CarPlay experience, including widgets, is straightforward. And even better, iOS 27 expanded the available widget pool beyond what was possible before.
How to start adding widgets to CarPlay
While you're parked or not driving, open the Settings app on your iPhone, then go to General > CarPlay and tap your car. Next, select Widgets. Make sure Show Widgets is enabled, then select Add Widget to browse your options.
You'll see recommended choices at the top, followed by a list of compatible apps on your phone. A given app can offer multiple widgets, so make sure to explore them all. The number of widgets that show at a time changes based on the size of your car's infotainment center.
Removing or rearranging widgets is simple. From the same page, use the handles on the right side to drag items and adjust your layout, or hit the red minus button to remove anything you don't want anymore. Some widgets will show a blue i icon to customize them, such as picking one of your saved locations in the Weather app.
At the bottom of the Settings page, you can also toggle some automation options. Turning on Smart Rotate will change to the most relevant widget in a stack based on factors like the time or your location, while Widget Suggestions will display potentially useful ones even if you haven't manually added them.
To access your widgets while on the road, swipe from left to right and you'll find them on the leftmost page. Swipe up or down on a stack to move through them as needed.
Recommended widgets for CarPlay
Widgets can fill gaps that CarPlay apps aren't able to, so there are lots of ways to put them to use. If you ever feel homesick on long trips, add the Photos widget and select any album to show. Meanwhile, if you take full advantage of Apple HomeKit and are worried that you may have left a lamp on, you can turn it off using a Home widget.
Additional first-party options include Reminders, Weather, Clock and Podcasts. An analog clock looks fancy when you don't need navigation, while Weather can tell you when the sun will set or rise. Apple Sports is also an option for following your favorite teams as you drive.
Many third-party widgets offer unique additions to your dashboard, especially after iOS 27's expansion. You can see what your friends are up to using Instagram stories or add the Amazon widget to check your order status and make sure you're home in time. If you're in need of an AI voice assistant in the car, you can utilize widgets for chatbots like Claude and Gemini.
Some widgets are certainly more useful than others; you likely don't need to check your Duolingo streak or see LinkedIn updates while driving. For best results, stick to widgets that provide easily glanceable, non-distracting info.

FlyDubai attacker intended to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport, investigation finds
Motive behind midair attack aboard FlyDubai plane remains unclear
TEL AVIV, Israel — An ongoing investigation into last week's midair attack on a FlyDubai plane has found that the co-pilot who tried to take control of the flight intended to crash it into Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport, a person familiar with the matter but not authorized to speak publicly told NPR.
The plane was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv and was intending to land at Ben Gurion midmorning on a busy weekday. The co-pilot attacked the plane's captain midflight with an axe and attempted to take control of the plane.
It is believed that the co-pilot likely acted alone, the source said.
Authorities in the United Arab Emirates — which is leading the main investigation into the incident, with help from Israeli officials — and in Israel have deemed the attack an attempted terrorist attack, although the motive is still being investigated.
The commercial flight had 172 people on board, according to the airline, the majority of whom were Israeli. All passengers and crew were safe and accounted for after the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. They were flown to Tel Aviv late Wednesday.
Investigators said that the co-pilot carried out the attack with what's called a crash axe — a lightweight emergency tool stored in the cockpit to break through panels or jammed doors in the event of a crash.
The aviation tracking site Flightradar24 said data shows at one point the plane descended more than 14,000 feet, or nearly 3 miles, in under 30 seconds — way faster than normal.
The pilot was able to open the cockpit door during the attack, and passengers rushed in and subdued the attacker, while another pilot who happened to be on board helped land the plane, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who spoke to the injured pilot as he was recovering in the hospital.
Both the pilot and the co-pilot are alive and have been transferred to the UAE for questioning.
Attacker is an Omani national
The co-pilot is from Oman, according to Israeli officials. Omani and Emirati officials have not confirmed that publicly.
The detail of his nationality is raising questions in Israel about how he was allowed to fly a plane heading to Ben Gurion, as Israel does not allow pilots from countries it doesn't have diplomatic relations with to fly in its airspace. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Fox & Friends that Israel checks the background of pilots flying routes into the country, and that the attacker must have gotten through a "loophole."
Officials from Israel's Ministry of Transportation and security services have traded accusations over the lack of oversight and vetting of the pilot. Meanwhile, several of Netanyahu's political opponents have said the security breach is a failure on the prime minister's part and have called for a larger investigation.
Netanyahu announced late Sunday that there will be a formal examination into the security situation around "foreign civil aviation into Israel," but did not provide further details.
A politically tense time in Israel
National elections in Israel — which will determine whether or not Netanyahu will remain prime minister — are just weeks away. It's the first such national election since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which sparked the war in Gaza.
Polls in Israel show that the race is tight, and analysts say the FlyDubai attack would likely not change Israelis' attitudes on how they will vote.
Netanyahu has been campaigning largely on the idea that he alone can protect Israelis from the external threats that Israel faces, while his opponents have pointed to what they see as major security failures under his leadership — including the Oct. 7 attack.

Jim Bakker’s death was confirmed by his second wife, Lori Bakker, on Monday

Jim Bakker, the televangelist who co-founded a lucrative media empire with his first wife, Tammy Faye, before a high-profile sex scandal and federal fraud convictions brought down his ministry, has died at the age of 86.
His death was confirmed in a statement on Monday by his second wife, Lori Bakker. The cause of death was not immediately disclosed.
"He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry," she said.
Based near the entertainment hub of Branson, Missouri, the couple had produced and hosted "The Jim Bakker Show" in the area since launching it in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020.
Decades prior, it was another evangelical broadcast that elevated Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker to national prominence. Their celebrity status routinely made them subjects of satire on late-night comedy programs and "Saturday Night Live," and their life story inspired the September 2021 feature film "The Eyes of Tammy Faye."
At its peak in the mid-1980s, the couple's religious organization reached up to 13 million viewers each night and operated the Heritage USA Christian theme park and hotel complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina.
Born in Muskegon, Michigan, Bakker studied at North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. After marrying in 1961, the pair left school to begin an itinerant ministry, traveling the country to perform at tent revivals and local churches, with Bakker preaching while his wife sang and played the accordion.
Their efforts caught the interest of televangelist Pat Robertson, leading to a children’s program on his Christian Broadcasting Network in 1965. By 1966, Bakker was hosting the religious talk show "The 700 Club."
Bakker departed CBN in 1972 and established the PTL Satellite Network two years later. Its centerpiece broadcast became "The PTL Club," short for "Praise the Lord."
At its height in the 1980s, the program generated millions of dollars annually from millions of devoted followers.
Filmed largely at their extensive resort south of Charlotte, North Carolina, the show blended guest interviews with Christian musical acts. Bakker delivered encouraging sermons, while Tammy Faye—distinguished by her dramatic mascara—performed music.
The couple’s prominent lifestyle and Tammy Faye’s recognizable appearance made them frequent targets for television comedy.
The ministry collapsed in March 1987 following Bakker’s admission of a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Bakker stepped down from his position, transferring control to pastor Jerry Falwell.
Tammy Faye remained supportive of her husband publicly during the scandal, which came to be viewed by critics as emblematic of 1980s televangelist excess.
Conditions worsened further.
Federal prosecutors indicted Bakker in 1988 on conspiracy, wire fraud, and mail fraud charges tied to PTL financial operations. Following his conviction, he received a 45-year prison term, which was later reduced to eight years.
At a media briefing after the verdict, Tammy Faye addressed reporters by singing the hymn "On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand."
The marriage ended in divorce in 1992 while Bakker remained incarcerated. Tammy Faye later wed building contractor Roe Messner, who had built the Heritage USA property and was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995. She died of colon cancer in 2007.
Paroled in 1994, Bakker married Lori in 1998, and five years later they established "The Jim Bakker Show" on the PTL network.
In June 2021, Bakker and his media company resolved a lawsuit over claims made in early 2020 that a health supplement called Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who purchased or donated to receive the product following claims made during 11 broadcasts.
Bakker had two children with his first wife, and he and Lori adopted five children in 2002.

Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe has earned international attention after The New York Times featured him on its front page, calling him a “rock star” for his aggressive approach to food safety enforcement.
Known for his no-nonsense style of administration, Mundhe has conducted surprise inspections at restaurants, food outlets, warehouses and quick-commerce dark stores across Maharashtra. His inspections have resulted in temporary closures, licence suspensions and action against several well-known food businesses.
NYT Calls Mundhe A ‘Food Safety Celebrity’
The New York Times featured Mundhe on its front page with the headline, “In India, a Food Inspector Is a Rock Star”, accompanied by the strap, “Diners revere him and owners fear him.”
In its detailed report, the newspaper described Mundhe as a “food safety celebrity” and examined how his inspections have transformed him into a recognisable public figure. His actions have also brought greater attention to hygiene standards in restaurants and food businesses.
Mundhe has previously been popularly referred to as “IAS Singham” because of his strict and uncompromising administrative style.
‘Good Governance Is Not About Making Headlines’
Reacting to the international coverage, Mundhe said that the purpose of his work was not to gain publicity but to improve the system and protect consumers.
“Good governance is not about making headlines but about making a difference,” Mundhe said.
He added that food safety was ultimately about safeguarding people, maintaining standards and creating trust between citizens and public institutions.
“When enforcement is fair, fearless and consistent, institutions earn credibility and citizens begin to believe that the system works,” he said, adding that the NYT had captured “one such story from Maharashtra”.
Restaurants, Food Outlets Face FDA Action
Since taking charge as Maharashtra FDA Commissioner earlier this year, Mundhe has overseen a series of inspections targeting restaurants, food manufacturers, warehouses and other establishments.
Several establishments have faced temporary closures or licence-related action following inspections that allegedly uncovered hygiene lapses and food safety violations.
Popular chains including Domino’s and Pizza Hut were among the outlets that faced temporary closure after inspections reportedly found issues such as cockroaches and expired products at their premises.
The FDA’s action has also extended to some of Mumbai’s long-established food businesses, with certain outlets facing brief licence suspensions following inspections.
Why Tukaram Mundhe Has Become Popular
Mundhe’s strict enforcement has made him a controversial figure among some food businesses but a popular one among consumers concerned about hygiene.
Videos and reports of his surprise inspections have circulated widely, turning the FDA commissioner into a familiar face beyond government and administrative circles.
While establishments have faced action for alleged violations, Mundhe’s approach has also resonated with diners who want greater accountability from restaurants and food businesses.

Donald Trump has ordered the rare use of a firing squad for the execution of a former army major who killed 13 people in Texas in 2009.
Former army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan’s method of execution was approved by the president at the recommendation of defence secretary Pete Hegseth, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said.
Hasan opened fire at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009, killing 12 active-duty but unarmed soldiers and a retired serviceman and injured 32 people. He was sentenced to death after being convicted on 45 counts of premeditated murder in 2013 for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the Texas military base.
The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to deploy to Afghanistan. Prosecutors said he was motivated by unwillingness to be sent to Afghanistan and the shooting was in retaliation for America’s wars in the Muslim world.
Hasan was left partially paralysed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police upon his arrest.
Parnell said the "judgment day for Hasan has finally come" and that the date and place of his death would be set by the secretary of the army.
Death by firing squad was one of the forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to the list of permissible methods of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with gas asphyxiation and electrocution. The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which had also proved challenging to carry out for other reasons at times.
Hasan is one of four military inmates awaiting execution, which requires approval from the president and an appellate review.
Hasan's military execution is different from the majority of executions, which are legal in 27 states of America.
Execution by firing squad is rare in the country, with the latest being carried out in March last year in South Carolina.
In 2024, the South Carolina Supreme Court had ruled that firing squad, lethal injection and electric chair were all legal methods of execution. The court noted the firing squad was not cruel because a prisoner would not suffer longer than 15 seconds.
Brad Sigmon became the first person in the state to be executed by firing state and the first across the country in 15 years. Mikal Mahdi was executed in a similar way on 11 April.
In all, at least six people have been executed by firing squad since the country reinstated the death penalty in 1977.
Since 1608, at least 145 civilian prisoners have been executed by shooting, nearly all in the state of Utah, according to the Associated Press.
Hasan will be the first person to face a military firing squad since the end of World War II. His will also be the first military execution, by any method, since 1961.
The last military execution, the Death Penalty Information Center said, was done by hanging, while the last-known execution by a military firing squad was likely carried out "by musketry" in November 1945.
Trump, a supporter of the federal death penalty, reinstated the execution method on his first day back as president in January 2025.
At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The Utah Supreme Court halted the scheduled 5 September 2025 firing-squad execution of death-row inmate Ralph Menzies.
Trump's approval for Hasan’s execution comes as plans by Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week.
Prison personnel botched an attempt to administer a lethal injection, leaving Christa Pike alive but unconscious and hospitalised on life support.
Pike's lawyers had previously urged the Tennessee Department of Correction to consider an alternative to lethal injection such as hanging or firing squad, in anticipation of the trouble executioners would face in establishing a sound intravenous line.
"There’s nothing Donald Trump loves more than the power to kill," Death Penalty Action, a campaign group opposed to capital punishment, said, pointing out that he oversaw more executions during his first term than any president since Franklin D Roosevelt. “Truly, this is just another distraction and a ploy to stem his record-low approval ratings."

On Friday morning, Shivon Zilis, a top executive and lieutenant of Elon Musk at his brain chip implant company Neuralink—as well as mother of four of the 14 children he is known to have fathered—took to his social media platform, X, to announce an abrupt shift in their relationship.
“It’s hard to go from in love to let go in a week with no warning, but that’s just how it is sometimes,” Zilis wrote, sharing a screenshot of the X account @BigTechAlert that showed Musk had unfollowed her there. Zilis’ post continued: “I feel happy that I got to show Elon how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness,” followed by warm praise and best wishes for Musk. “I do hope and pray he and I can be great friends and coparents,” Zilis concluded, leaving some ambiguity as to what exactly changed between them and whether she remains a director of operations and special projects at Neuralink, though it does not appear as if she has left the position.
While this was a strange revelation of a private matter, it seemed hardly out of the ordinary for Musk’s dizzyingly complicated family life. At this point, all four of the women confirmed to have had children with him—Zilis, ex-wife Justine Wilson, Claire Boucher (better known as Grimes), and Ashley St. Clair—have used X to share details of their time with him or push back against his own claims.
Both Wilson and St. Clair participated in filmmaker Alex Gibney’s sprawling new documentary Musk, in theaters nationwide on October 16 and screening at the WIRED World Fair in Miami next month. St. Clair, a former conservative influencer, alleges that she rejected a nondisclosure agreement worth $40 million that would have prevented her from talking about her tumultuous association with Musk. Among an ensemble of tech entrepreneurs, journalists, and former Musk employees, the pair stand out as arguably the most important critical voices in the film, shedding light on Musk’s rise in Silicon Valley as well as his turn toward MAGA extremism during the 2024 election.
At a run time of nearly four hours, Musk sounds like daunting viewing, though once it’s over, you’ll find yourself wondering if it could’ve been a 10-part miniseries. That’s how much ground there is to cover, from the unrealistic ambitions of landing on Mars and the corporate colonization of Texas to the fatal collisions involving “self-driving” Teslas and the annihilation of the US Agency for International Development by the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) at the beginning of Trump’s second term. (WIRED’s reporting is cited in the documentary, which features interviews with global editorial director Katie Drummond and contributing editor Zoë Schiffer.)
Alongside a fast-moving, comprehensive account of Musk’s career as an all-powerful and untouchable oligarch, his former romantic partners provide crucial context about exactly who he is, piecing together a devastating portrait of the type of man to “let go” of a significant other by unfollowing her on social media.
Wilson reflects movingly on the loss of their firstborn to a SIDS-related condition, which is juxtaposed with a Musk post on X in which he wrote that he held their infant son as he died—a comment to which his ex-wife replied, “not that it matters to anyone except me, because it is one of the most sacred and defining moments of my life, but I was the one who was holding him.”
In the film, she also addresses the pain of Musk repeatedly insisting that their transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, was “killed by the woke mind virus,” calling this an unconscionable comment given the actual loss of a child they experienced together. Musk goes on to tell Gibney that right after passing along the message that he would “always love” Wilson, he cut off their daughter’s health insurance and that he has “never tried to repair things” with her.
“He was constantly remarking on the ways he found me lacking,” Wilson says in recounting their marriage. She claims that when she reminded her husband that she was his spouse and not an employee, he told her, “If you were my employee, I would fire you.” Summing up their overall dynamic, she says: “I learned the term gaslighting through my relationship with Elon.”
St. Clair, defiantly outspoken against Musk since revealing in early 2025 that he had fathered a child with her, alleges that her whirlwind affair with the billionaire was a temporary illusion of compatibility that led to a messy and ongoing custody battle. (Musk also covers a custody dispute with Grimes that was eventually settled for undisclosed terms.) St. Clair says in the film that Musk lost interest in her once she was pregnant and claims that he sought to father children with other women. According to The Wall Street Journal, this included cryptocurrency influencer Tiffany Fong, whom he messaged with an offer to give her a child. (Musk did not immediately return a request for comment on this matter. Fong declined to comment publicly on the Journal’s story except to say that she had requested not to be included in the outlet’s reporting.)
“It’s like a Gatling gun of sperm in his DMs,” St. Clair quips. In the film’s interviews, both she and Wilson voice discomfort over their ex’s views on birth rates and ambition to father a “legion” of offspring, with Wilson claiming he regards the mothers of his children as replaceable “breeders.”
Elsewhere in the film, St. Clair covers her allegation that Musk retaliated against her by reducing his financial support for their son, Romulus. And her reluctance to touch on certain issues the filmmakers ask her about seems to serve as something of an answer in its own right. “I’m not at liberty to say,” she responds carefully when asked if she ever witnessed Musk using illegal drugs.
Gibney’s broad account of how Musk wove together a tech empire and his celebrity image through relentless self-mythologizing, then insulated it from government oversight by backing Trump and seizing power within his administration, is an utterly convincing one. But most of the story will be familiar to those who have kept up with Musk headlines for the past decade. What’s truly eye-opening in Musk is the way the women he was once close to talk about what they see as his boundless capacity for cruelty and narcissism.
Is there a world in which Zilis, too, comes forward to share her intimate conversations and correspondence with Musk? That surely depends on whether she has signed any legal documents like those presented to St. Clair. What’s more than evident, however, is that for all his resources, Musk can’t buy the silence of everyone he’s ever known, and if anyone can finally shred his aura of genius inventor-king, it’s the women he’s allowed—however briefly—to share his orbit.

India Mobile Congress begins on Wednesday, PM Modi to inaugurate on October 8
The India Mobile Congress, being held at Yashobhoomi from October 7 to 10, will be themed “Scale Without Boundaries” this year.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi will inaugurate the 10th edition of the India Mobile Congress (IMC) in New Delhi on October 8, with telecom operators, technology companies, policymakers and startups expected to use the four-day event to showcase new technologies and discuss the next phase of connectivity.
The event, being held at Yashobhoomi from October 7 to 10, will be themed “Scale Without Boundaries” this year. The formal inauguration comes on the second day, although the conference programme begins a day earlier, with a line-up of government and industry speakers.
What is lined up?
The opening day on October 7 will feature Lauren Dreyer, vice-president of Starlink Business Operations at SpaceX, alongside Hideo Fuseda, vice-minister for international affairs at Japan’s ministry of internal affairs and communications.
Minister of state for communications Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani, Department of Telecommunications (DoT) Secretary Amit Agrawal and C-DOT chief executive Rajkumar Upadhyay are also scheduled to speak.
Representatives from companies including Qualcomm, GSMA, Ericsson, Jio, Vodafone Idea, Bharti Airtel and Intel are also expected to participate in sessions throughout the day. Discussions will cover areas including next-generation networks, AI, 6G, digital infrastructure and satellite communications.
The second day, October 8, will begin with the formal inauguration by PM Modi. The programme will also feature keynotes from major industry leaders, including Reliance Jio chairman Akash Ambani, Bharti Enterprises founder and chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal and Aditya Birla Group chairman Kumar Mangalam Birla.
The day is also expected to see government announcements, partnerships and discussions around investment and business opportunities in the telecom and digital technology sectors.
The third day will continue with keynote sessions, panel discussions and industry conversations across multiple tracks. The programme includes sessions on 6G, AI-native telecom networks, intelligent RAN, cybersecurity, satellite communications, network APIs, cloud and edge computing, semiconductors and digital infrastructure. GSMA, for instance, has sessions planned on digital trust, satellite communications policy, AI-native telecom networks and the transition from connectivity towards digital infrastructure.
Over four days, an exhibition at Yashobhoomi will run alongside the conference programme, with companies showcasing products, technologies, and live use cases spanning 5G and 6G, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, satellite communications, cybersecurity, advanced manufacturing, and cloud and edge computing.
Focus on deep-tech
Startups will also have a significant presence through the ASPIRE programme, which this year places greater emphasis on deep-tech and frontier technologies, including support for startups to move from prototypes to market opportunities and investment.
The event will also feature international participation and technology demonstrations, with the broader programme spanning policymakers, telecom companies, equipment makers, technology firms, startups and investors.
The 2026 edition is the 10th iteration of IMC, which is jointly organised by the DoT and the Cellular Operators Association of India.

SCO condemns Winnipeg Sun, mayoral-candidate CEO for column questioning deaths at residential schools
Column published days after National Day for Truth and Reconciliation; Kevin Klein disavows responsibility
A column questioning the deaths of children at residential schools has led the Southern Chiefs' Organization to condemn the Winnipeg Sun and express concern that the newspaper's CEO is running for mayor of the Manitoba capital.
On Oct. 4, the Sun published a column entitled "Grave misdirection: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence," suggesting the deaths of Indigenous children at residential schools have been mischaracterized.
"Each death is a tragedy, but none is evidence of an atrocity," the column states, citing as examples the death of one child from bronchitis and another by lightning.
The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation documented the deaths of at least 4,200 Indigenous children over the course of 165 years at Canada's residential schools. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada defined the deaths and widespread abuses within residential schools as cultural genocide.
The publication of the column four days after the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation led to a formal statement of condemnation from the Southern Chiefs' Organization, which represents 33 Anishinaabe and Dakota First Nations in Manitoba.
"Survivors and their families should not be forced, yet again, to prove what happened to them or defend the children who never came home," SCO Grand Chief Jerry Daniels said in a statement. "Thousands of children died while attending residential schools. Children were forcibly removed from their families and Nations, stripped of their languages and cultures, and subjected to systems of abuse, neglect and assimilation.
"These are not allegations or political talking points. They are part of Canada's documented historical record."
The co-author of a book about residential school denialism called the column disgusting because, he said, it perpetuates the notion the deaths of thousands of children who were forcibly removed from their families is less horrific because many died of disease, malnutrition and neglect as opposed to murder.
"A lot of people will say, oh, it was just tuberculosis. Lots of kids died of tuberculosis in the early 20th century," said University of Manitoba history professor Sean Carleton, the co-author of Truth Before Reconciliation: Confronting Residential School Denialism.
"That, in fact, is true, except for the fact that, you know what spreads tuberculosis faster? Overcrowding, poor nutrition. Lack of proper sanitation, overwork. All of these issues that were known to be systemic to the residential school system."
Carleton said the column perpetuates what he describes as far-right misinformation about First Nations making claims about mass graves or clandestine murders.
"This is a distraction tactic. It's an attempt to move the goalposts, to make it extremely difficult for Indigenous nations, to explain the complicated nuanced understanding of what we already know, thanks to church and state records, that at least 4,000 children died in these institutions for a variety of different reasons," he said.
As criticism of the column mounted Sunday, the editor-in-chief of the Klein Group, the company that owns the Winnipeg Sun, dug in her heels. Heather Klein defended the column in a followup entitled "Disagreement is not denial."
The Southern Chiefs' Organization also criticized her husband, Klein Group CEO Kevin Klein, the candidate who is running for Winnipeg mayor.
Daniels called it "deeply concerning" someone seeking public office provided a platform for someone to use residential schools and the deaths of First Nations children as the basis for political commentary.
"Winnipeg is home to a large and vibrant First Nations population. Anyone asking to lead this city has a responsibility to understand the history of residential schools and the ongoing responsibilities of reconciliation," Daniels said.
Kevin Klein said in a statement he is not responsible for the content of the Winnipeg Sun while he runs for mayor.
"From the day I entered the race for mayor, I stepped away from every editorial decision at the Winnipeg Sun, and I have kept that commitment. The paper stands on its own," the mayoral candidate said.
Heather Klein alone is responsible for the content, he said, adding he does not assign stories, edit copy, approve pieces or stop them from running.
"Any suggestion otherwise is reckless and without foundation," he said.
Other mayoral candidates criticize Klein
Several mayoral candidates also criticized the newspaper CEO-turned-candidate.
Mayoral candidate Noah Redden said in a statement there is a difference between upholding freedom of speech and tolerating hate speech.
Redden called residential school denialism inflammatory and said Klein needs to explain to Winnipeg's Indigenous population why his newspaper echoed attacks on residential school survivors.
Incumbent mayoral candidate Scott Gillingham told reporters Sunday he's spoken to enough Indigenous families in Winnipeg to hear first-hand the impact of residential schools.
"What is not deniable in my mind is the impact, the lasting, devastating impact of residential schools on our country," said Gillingham, who attended TRC Day events in an official capacity on Wednesday.
Klein said Friday he did not attend TRC Day events but called the national holiday important.
"Canadians ought to know what took place in the residential school system and what it has meant for Indigenous families and communities ever since," Klein said Sunday in a statement.
"The wrongs of the past should not be forgotten. As a father and a grandfather, I cannot begin to imagine the pain those families carry."

A surge in Russian jet-powered drone strikes on Ukrainian data centers has increasingly disrupted mobile phone and Internet services for thousands of people. Now Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and other government officials are warning of the need for more air defense capabilities, as such telecommunication outages could threaten Ukraine’s digital economy and undermine the country’s ongoing resistance to Russia’s invasion.
The Russian attacks on Ukrainian telecommunication infrastructure have focused on Ukraine’s capital of Kyiv since September 23, according to the nonprofit Reporters Without Borders. Ukraine’s digital transformation ministry reported that 100,000 households in the Kyiv region were temporarily experiencing Internet outages from those initial strikes—and Russia has only intensified its strike campaign against major Ukrainian data centers and mobile phone networks in recent weeks.
“Russian attacks on Ukraine’s telecommunication infrastructure are not new, with strikes and shelling previously damaging fiber optic lines, cell towers, and facilities belonging to mobile network companies,” said Tetiana Gaviuk, analyst for Europe at ACLED, in a post on October 1. “However, the recent concentrated attacks on Kyiv’s data centers and telecom networks stand out because multiple providers and facilities were hit within days, indicating Russia’s increased pressure on Ukraine’s digital infrastructure.”
Such repeated attacks could undermine the telecommunication networks that support Ukraine’s banks, payment systems, and public services, according to warnings from officials and industry figures, as reported by The Guardian.
Russia’s strike campaign
Russia has launched mass missile and drone attacks on Ukraine’s power grid infrastructure, railroad stations, shipping ports, and even residential apartment buildings since the first year of its full-scale invasion in 2022. But such long-range strikes have become even more damaging this year, as they have exhausted Ukraine’s supply of missile interceptors—and Russia has also upgraded many of its one-way attack drones to become faster jet-powered drones that are more difficult to shoot down.
For example, Zelenskyy stated on October 4 that Ukrainian air defenses currently intercept more than 85 percent of conventional Shahed-type drones originally developed by Iran and supplied to Russia. But such interception rates fall to just 50 or 60 percent when dealing with newer and faster jet-powered Shahed drones.

South Korea captain Lee Gi-hyuk has apologised for gloating about avoiding mandatory military service after winning gold at the Asian Games.
His side beat hosts Japan 1-0 in the final and, afterwards, Lee held up his gold medal and triumphantly announced he was "not going to the military".
In a social media post reported by local media,, external the 26-year-old later said he was "deeply sorry to the fans who are currently fulfilling their military duty, as well as to all those who sincerely supported us".
South Korean males are, in most circumstances, required to undertake between 18 and 21 months of active military service before the age of 28.
However, the government rewards Asian Games champions and Olympic medal winners of any colour with a service exemption bar basic training, which lasts less than a month.
Golfer Tom Kim also avoided military service by winning gold at the Asian Games.
Athletes who have previously secured the exemption include former Tottenham footballer Son Heung-min, who served for only three weeks in 2020 having won the Asian Games with his country two years earlier.
"As an adult I should have thought carefully before speaking," added Lee, who was one of the overage players in his country's Under-23 squad and plays for Gangwon FC in South Korea's K League.
"I deeply regret having spoken so carelessly, and I will continue to reflect on my actions.
"I sincerely apologise to all the fans who have supported us wholeheartedly and who are doing their utmost to fulfil their military duty."

Cable lobby groups notified the Federal Communications Commission that they will sue the agency to block its controversial repeal of the National Television Ownership Rule, which limits the number of broadcast TV stations a single company may own.
The cable groups said that larger broadcast TV station groups will have leverage to demand higher retransmission fees from TV providers, resulting in “higher monthly TV bills for consumers.” They said the FCC repeal order “arbitrarily and capriciously ignores the harms that will surely follow from allowing broadcast station groups to exceed the National Cap.”
The cable lobby groups represent top providers Comcast, Charter, and various other cable operators. Top cable companies have also expanded through mergers. Charter completed a purchase of Cox in August after the FCC rejected protests by advocacy groups that said the cable deal “would create unchecked gatekeeper power over Internet distribution” and make it easier for the biggest cable companies to raise prices.
The FCC voted to eliminate the TV ownership rule on August 6, and finally published the repeal order on its website on October 1 after an unusually long delay. The delay may be explained by the FCC shoring up its legal arguments in anticipation of lawsuits because the agency is claiming authority to repeal a limit set by Congress over 20 years ago.
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has said that replacing a strict ownership limit with a “case-by-case review” of each proposed merger will let the agency approve deals that promote the public interest while rejecting deals that do not. Given Carr’s history of threatening to revoke licenses from broadcasters disfavored by President Trump, case-by-case reviews would let Carr influence news coverage of the administration by allowing favored broadcast companies to expand.
Cable lobby petition
The TV ownership rule prohibits any single broadcast station owner from reaching more than 39 percent of all TV households in the US. Congress directed the FCC to set the cap at 39 percent in 2004. On Friday, cable lobby groups submitted a petition asking the FCC to keep the TV ownership cap in place until litigation over the FCC’s authority to repeal the rule is over.
