A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it allegedly shows the Chief of the Army Staff, General Dhiraj Seth, dancing with Supreet Sapra, described as the wife of an Army major. The video features a purported CNN headline stating, “Indian Army Chief Dhiraj Seth Spotted Dancing with Army Major’s wife Supreet Sapra,” giving the impression that CNN published the video. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth dancing with Supreet Sapra, the wife of an Army major.
Fact: The video has been digitally manipulated to make it appear as though Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth is dancing with Supreet Sapra. CNN has not published any report or headline matching the one shown in the viral video. The original video, shared in March 2026, features a different man and woman dancing at a gathering. Supreet Sapra has also clarified that she is not an Army major’s wife and that the woman shown in the viral video is AI-generated. The Indian Army’s fact-check wing has also confirmed that the video is digitally manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports carrying the viral footage on CNN’s official website or any report or headline matching the one circulating with the video.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed several inconsistencies. Though the man and woman appear to be dancing while holding glasses, the liquid inside them does not move or splash naturally as they dance. In one frame, the man’s ear and cheek area also appear smudged, while the faces of people in the background appear heavily blurred. The man’s face remains almost completely frozen with a wide smile throughout the video, further raising signs of AI manipulation.
We then ran the video through multiple AI detection tools, including DetectVideo AI and Meta AI’s verification platform. Both assessed the clip as likely AI-generated and detected AI signatures in the video.
The viral video contains an inset photograph showing a woman with a different man wearing a defence uniform. To learn more about the photograph, we conducted a reverse image search, which led us to an Instagram post (archived) by @sufimeranaam, dated 22 February 2026, featuring the same image. Newschecker contacted the account user regarding the viral video. She identified herself as Supreet Sapra and said, “I am Supreet Sapra, but I am not a major’s wife. My husband retired four years ago. The woman in the video is AI-generated, so apart from the name, everything is misinformation.”
Further investigation led us to an Instagram post (archived) by Rhythm Gupta, shared on 11 March 2026, with the caption, “Always dancing weirdly.” The video features a man and a woman dancing at a gathering. Their dance movements, the way they hold their glasses, and the song playing in the background are the same as those in the viral video. Although the background differs in colour and certain visual details, the overall setting and arrangement of elements are similar, and the movements of people around the dancing pair also closely resemble. This indicates that the viral video was likely manipulated using the earlier footage to make it appear as though the Army Staff chief was dancing with an Army major’s wife. Comparison of screengrabs from the viral clip and the Instagram video can be seen below.
The Indian Army’s fact-checking wing also clarified in an X post (archived) on 29 September 2026 that the viral video is digitally manipulated and fake.
To sum up, this viral video of Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth dancing with Supreet Sapra, the wife of an Army major, is AI-manipulated.

South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
- Published
South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.
"Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.
His response to the US president's claim is blunt.
The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.
Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.
In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.
Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.
Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property.
"Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.
She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".
The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.
In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa.
"While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."
SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.
Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms".
"There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.
- Race policies or Israel - what's really driving Trump's fury with South Africa? 
  - Published23 February 2025
- Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims? 
  - Published2 June 2025
- Do Afrikaners want to take Trump up on his South African refugee offer? 
  - Published15 May 2025
An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".
Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.
"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."
Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.
The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.
He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".
"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.
Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.
Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.
While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".
Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".
He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.
The programme has its critics among Afrikaners in South Africa too.
"Why single out the white Afrikaner to say this group qualifies to flee to the US? This country suffers gender-based violence. Why not single out women?" Rudi Swanepoel, a pastor from Johannesburg told the BBC.
Swanepoel thinks it is not persecution but a "loss of privilege" that is causing some Afrikaners to feel aggrieved.
"To use the metaphor of a cake, 30, 40 years ago the white people of South Africa controlled the cake," he says. "Since democracy came, the obvious reality was we had to now start sharing that cake and those privileges."
Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.
Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked.
He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement.
"South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.
But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."
He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.
Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington.
"It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

Russian report says Siberian plague institute worker fell ill, died of unknown cause
Russian authorities say a staffer at a plague research institute in Siberia contracted pneumonia of an unknown cause, and local state TV reported the woman died last week
Russian authorities have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring contacts of an employee at a plague research institute in Siberia who contracted pneumonia of an “unknown” cause. Local state TV said the woman died last week.
Russian authorities said they found no evidence that her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with. But the case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
The woman worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, southeastern Siberia. A state TV station in Irkutsk reported Monday that she died last week in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk.
The hospital has been placed under quarantine, Mayor Maxim Modin said Friday, no longer admitting or discharging patients, and its laboratory halted carrying out routine tests. The hospital's outpatient clinic kept operating as usual, he said.
Anna Popova, head of Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk and met with Gov. Igor Kobzev and other officials on Friday.
Kobzev said everyone who came into contact with the woman is under medical supervision. He didn’t identify the infection and called it a suspected case of “a particularly dangerous infection.”
Rospotrebnadzor was implementing “a full range of anti-epidemic measures,” he added.
Rospotrebnadzor said Sunday the woman was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” and said “extensive” testing found “no microorganisms associated with the patient’s professional activities.”
The agency also said it didn't uncover any incidents at the institute “involving pathogenic microorganisms."
Two people who were in contact with the woman tested positive for a virus that causes a common cold and two others for COVID-19, the agency said, adding that others who were tested were all negative.
Independent local news outlet Lyudi Baikala quoted sources it did not identify as saying the woman died from pneumonic plague and that several Irkutsk hospitals were placed under quarantine.
Asked Monday to comment on the case, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the public and media should follow official statements from Rospotrebnadzor, rather than "rumors or speculation.”
The Irkutsk Aluminum Plant in Shelekhov required staff to wear masks as a precaution, its director Artyom Fominykh said Saturday on Telegram, calling for calm and adding: "Better be safe than sorry.”
The World Health Organization describes pneumonic plague as a less common but severe form of plague — a disease caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals and their fleas.

New Delhi, Oct 5: India and Switzerland on Monday signed a migration and mobility partnership pact, decided to expand Swiss market access for Indian exports and agreed to further deepen cooperation in nuclear energy and defence domains following talks between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Swiss President Guy Parmelin.
Parmelin kick-started his three-day trip to India this morning in his first state visit to the country and his second visit this year, having previously attended the AI Impact Summit in February.
Alongside the mobility and migration pact, the two sides inked four other agreements, including a young professionals exchange scheme and a major deal to foster collaboration on transportation technologies, mobility systems, and infrastructure development.
The Ukraine conflict and the situation in West Asia also figured prominently in the discussions, with Modi emphasising that both sides support all meaningful efforts toward peace.
In his media statement, Modi said a series of important decisions were taken to expand market access for Indian exports to Switzerland and further facilitate investment between the two countries.
Switzerland is a major economic partner for India in Europe. Over 330 Swiss companies are currently operating in India in sectors such as engineering, services, precision instruments, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, while Indian companies are present in Switzerland in sectors such as IT, pharmaceuticals, and machinery.
The Swiss leader said boosting trade ties was a key focus of the talks. Parmelin noted that Switzerland hopes to conclude an investment protection agreement with India soon to facilitate greater flow of investments into various sectors of the Indian economy.
The bilateral trade and investment ties received a further boost following the coming into force in October of the Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA) between India and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) States of Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland.
Modi said the TEPA is an “ambitious blueprint” for investment, innovation, jobs, and shared prosperity.
“Through this, we will realise our goals of USD100 billion in investment and one million direct jobs in India over the next 15 years,” he said. The prime minister, describing innovation, infrastructure and advanced technology as strong pillars of India-Switzerland partnership, said both sides are going to give engagement a “new impetus”.
“We have taken several important decisions to expand market access for Indian exports to Switzerland and further facilitate investment between the two countries,” he said.
“This will increase India’s exports of agriculture, pharmaceuticals, textiles and engineering goods to Switzerland. At the same time, we will attract new Swiss investment in key sectors like biotech, life sciences, banking, insurance, food processing, and sustainability,” he said.
Through these initiatives, “we will jointly develop trusted supply chains and reliable solutions for the entire world,” he added.
PM Modi said the two sides identified “new possibilities” for cooperation in military exchanges and defence production besides agreeing to further deepen cooperation in nuclear energy.
“The ropeway in Varanasi, the Jewar Airport in Noida, and railways and tunnelling projects in hilly areas are shining examples of our infrastructure cooperation.”
An agreement was inked for collaboration on transport and infrastructure. “We invite Swiss infrastructure companies to invest in India on a large scale, and to participate in capacity building, design, and manufacturing,” Modi said.
The prime minister, calling the India-Switzerland science and technology cooperation a strong pillar of the ties, said new joint research projects in priority areas such as health, clean energy, and space will be launched soon.
Modi also touched upon the importance of people-to-people connect, characterising it as the “greatest strength of the partnership”.
“The migration and mobility partnership agreement and the young professionals agreement signed today will open up many new opportunities in Switzerland for Indian students, researchers, professionals, and youth,” he said.
The MoU on migration and mobility aims to promote mobility “under equal treatment principles”, and to combat irregular migration and human trafficking in accordance with national laws.
It provides for multiple-entry visas for up to five years, including stays of up to six months on each visit, and renewable one-year student permits.
The agreement on the exchange of young professionals is aimed at those taking up temporary employment to enhance their professional and language skills. It provides for the exchange of 300 people annually per country, which may increase to 500.
Modi said India and Switzerland believe in democratic values, the rule of law, dialogue and diplomacy, and both sides will continue to work together for global peace and stability.
“Whether in Ukraine or West Asia, India has supported every meaningful effort towards peace. We also agree that reform of global institutions is essential to address growing global challenges,” he said.
The prime minister also made a mention of India-EFTA Prosperity Summit to be held on Wednesday.
“This summit will be an important platform to translate the promise of our trade and investment partnership into concrete outcomes,” he said. In his remarks, Parmelin said his visit marks the first anniversary of the TEPA implementation and asserted that the pact benefits both India and Switzerland.
“This partnership benefits both parties: India gains access to capital, technology transfers, and easier access to markets for high-value-added goods. Switzerland, for its part, benefits from trade with a massive partner experiencing sustained growth, at a time when global trade has become more vulnerable and unpredictable,” he said.
The Swiss president is accompanied by a large delegation of high-ranking business leaders.
“To further stimulate investment, Switzerland hopes to conclude an investment protection agreement soon. In this context, achieving results in discussions on intellectual property protection is equally important,” he said.
“In the realm of migration, our countries have concluded two agreements that embody high-quality cooperation between Switzerland and India: an agreement on a migration and mobility partnership, and an agreement on exchanges for young professionals,” he said.
The Swiss leader said both sides also discussed issues relating to artificial intelligence with a focus on promoting an approach to AI governance that is both innovative and equitable.
“India, the world’s most populous democracy, and Switzerland, one of the oldest democracies, share fundamental values.”
In his statement, PM Modi also extended his best wishes to Switzerland for hosting the next edition of the AI Summit next year.
“In February this year, India hosted the world’s largest AI Summit. Next year, Switzerland will take this journey forward through the Geneva AI Summit,” he said.
“I extend my heartfelt congratulations to Switzerland for the success of the Geneva AI Summit. I am confident that together we will continue to move forward towards making AI responsible, inclusive, and human-centric,” he added.

Shreyas Iyer’s meticulous preparation, sharp tactical understanding and ability to assess the opposition’s strengths make him well-equipped for a successful stint as India’s captain, said VVS Laxman, who served as the team’s head coach at the Asian Games.
Shreyas led India to the men’s cricket gold medal in Japan, and Laxman was particularly impressed by the way the middle-order batter approached the leadership role, saying he was already showing the qualities needed to stay ahead of the opposition in the fast-paced T20 format.
India edged out Pakistan by 19 runs in a high-scoring final to defend their title.
“It’s just the start of his captaincy career, but I’m sure that he’ll achieve a lot of success. He’s a player’s captain. He makes everyone very, very comfortable and leads by example,” Laxman told BCCI in an interview.
“Whether with the bat or on the field, even before the team meetings, he sits down with the plans, strengths and opposition’s weaknesses. And he’s very thorough in the way he prepares. Puts a lot of emphasis on fitness. I’m sure that he’ll have a very successful tenure as captain.”
A classy batsman in his playing days, Laxman also highlighted Shreyas’ tactical acumen and his understanding of the players at his disposal, qualities that he believes helps him get the best out of the team.
“He’s a fabulous leader of players. Tactically, very, very smart, very sharp. He understands the strengths of each and every player on his team. And he knows how to get the best out of them,” he said.
“Especially in T20, you’re required to be one or two steps ahead of the opposition. And the way he assesses the opposition’s strengths and weaknesses, prepares really well. And that’s something which I’m very happy about.”
The coach’s praise came after India negotiated a difficult build-up to the Asian Games, with weather, travel and limited opportunities for outdoor practice posing challenges to their preparation.
Laxman said the squad’s ability to adapt to those circumstances was one of the most pleasing aspects of their campaign.
“From the time we came to Japan, we were challenged by weather, travel, lack of good practice session and preparation. But not even once did I feel that the team, all the players in the squad were not eager to get ready for the big matches,” he said.
“We know that the semifinal (against Sri Lanka) was on a tough wicket, but they showed positive intent and again in the finals, with the bat, with the ball, I thought they were very professional.”
Laxman was also pleased with how the players adjusted to conditions that were different from those they encounter in international and IPL cricket. He cited the example of the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023 where the conditions were completely different from Japan and players adapted well.
“Both the games in China and in Japan had their own set of challenges. And I’m happy that both the group of players, again, adapted and adjusted and got the desired result for the country,” he said.
For Laxman, the gold medal was particularly significant because of the rarity of the experience for cricketers of standing on a podium at a major multi-sport event.
“The ultimate aim and goal for all of us, whether in China or here in Japan, was to win the gold. Because not very often do we as cricketers experience being on a podium and receiving the gold medal,” he said.

One of India’s earliest ecommerce marketplaces has finally trotted onto D-Street. After a relatively muted 4.93X subscription to its IPO, Snapdeal’s parent AceVector is all set to make its stock market debut on Monday. AceVector’s ₹420 Cr IPO, which opened on September 25 and closed on September 29, comprised a fresh issue of ₹287 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of around ₹133 Cr, with shares priced in the ₹30-32 band. The company's IPO response is a far cry from its once-lofty standing in India’s ecommerce race. At its peak, the company was valued at $6.5 Bn, backed by heavyweight investors, including SoftBank Group, Alibaba Group and Foxconn. Then, as Amazon poured billions into building its India business and Flipkart emerged as a formidable rival, the ecommerce battle grew increasingly intense. Snapdeal eventually stepped away from its ambition of competing across the broader market and shifted its focus to affordable fashion, home and beauty products, catering to shoppers in Tier II and Tier III India looking for low-priced goods rather than premium brands. But is value commerce really working for it? Let’s find out in this edition of Inc42 Markets. How AceVector Makes Money Snapdeal is only one part of AceVector’s portfolio. The company has two other businesses: Unicommerce, an ecommerce enablement software business, and Stellaro Brands, its consumer-brands arm. According to an expert tracking the consumer internet sector, Snapdeal has grown its net merchandise value and customer base of value-conscious shoppers, but its scale remains quite modest compared with larger ecommerce platforms, especially Meesho. The expert added that Snapdeal may not be generating enough revenue per transaction to cover customer acquisition, technology and logistics costs. Unlike an inventory-led retailer, Snapdeal operates an asset-light marketplace. Sellers own and list products, while Snapdeal facilitates discovery, transactions and associated services. It earns money through seller-related marketplace fees, advertising and marketing services, freight and collection fees, and charges for return shipments. This structure limits the need to purchase and hold inventory, but leaves the company dependent on transaction volumes, seller participation and the economics of fulfilling orders. The marketplace revenue rose to ₹293.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹249.9 Cr in FY25. Net merchandise value (NMV), the value of delivered merchandise after excluding cancellations and returns, increased 25.7% to ₹1,093.1 Cr, from ₹869.6 Cr in FY25. In FY24, NMV stood at ₹633.3 Cr, even as marketplace revenue remained relatively flat between FY24 and FY25 before rising in FY26. The gap between NMV and revenue is important. NMV measures the value of merchandise transacted on the platform; it is not the amount Snapdeal earns. In FY26, marketplace revenue was roughly 26.9% of NMV, down from 28.7% in FY25. Meanwhile, marketplace marketing and business promotion expenses climbed to ₹84.4 Cr in FY26, from ₹63.2 Cr in FY25 and ₹58.5 Cr in FY24. The company’s ecommerce enablement arm, Unicommerce, has emerged as a significant growth driver within the group. Its SaaS revenue rose 51.6% to ₹204.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹134.8 Cr in FY25, compared with Snapdeal’s marketplace revenue growth of 17.5% during the same period. The business provides order, inventory and warehouse management software through Uniware, alongside shipping and logistics automation through Shipway and marketing automation through Convertway. Its acquisition of Shipway Technology added to this portfolio, extending its services across more stages of the ecommerce lifecycle. Meanwhile, AceVector’s consumer brands business, housed under Stellaro Brands, remains smaller but expansion-heavy. It operates Rangita, a women’s ethnic wear brand sold online and through an omnichannel retail network. Stellaro’s revenue from operations rose to ₹12.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹11.4 Cr in FY25. What Does Snapdeal Offer Beyond Brand Recall? Snapdeal has been in the game since 2010, one of the early players that helped open the floodgates to online shopping in India. According to Karan Taurani, executive vice president at Elara Capital, Snapdeal has an edge in terms of brand recall. He said the company has remained relevant through multiple changes in its business model, from deal-led discounting to a broader marketplace and, more recently, a value-commerce platform. “Its longevity gives it an established identity among consumers, but that alone may not be enough to sustain growth in a market where customer acquisition, transaction frequency and operational efficiency are increasingly important,” Taurani said. He is of the view that Snapdeal’s focus on value-conscious shoppers does give it a clear customer segment to serve, but it also operates in a crowded market where affordability is not exclusive to one platform. Meesho, which has built a much larger marketplace around value-conscious consumers, is a key example. In FY26, Snapdeal clocked an NMV of ₹1,093.1 Cr, while Meesho’s marketplace raked in ₹41,560 Cr. This is a staggering 38X scale gap. The gap also extends beyond merchandise value to the number of customers and transactions each platform handles. Snapdeal reported 12.16 Mn annual transacting users and 25.98 Mn delivered units in FY26. Meesho reported 264.29 Mn annual transacting users and 1.71 Bn delivered units. Therefore, Snapdeal’s central challenge is scale, even in its value segment. Snapdeal Has AI Tools But Is There A Real Competitive Edge? At a time when Meesho has an extensive technology stack, including AI-led tools, Snapdeal is trying to take steps in a similar direction. Snapdeal recently introduced a multi-solution AI suite aimed at making fashion discovery more personalised, visual and conversational for Indian shoppers. The suite brings together AI-powered recommendations, conversational search, image-based discovery and customer experience tools across the marketplace. According to its RHP, 72.69% of orders in FY26 were placed without users entering a search term. The company attributes this to its recommendation engine and personalised product feeds, which use browsing history, product interactions and other data to tailor the shopping experience. Overall, its tech stack supports processes such as seller onboarding, catalogue ingestion and fraud detection. AI-supported customer service is available through channels including calls, WhatsApp, IVR and in-app support. Snapdeal may have added AI to the shopping cart, but that does not necessarily give it a competitive edge. Recommendation engines, conversational search and AI-powered support are increasingly becoming standard ecommerce features. For Snapdeal, AI is currently an ongoing bet. What it needs to solve immediately is the puzzle of scale. Lula seeks shake-up and Flávio Bolsonaro reaches for more support ahead of Brazil's election runoff
Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will spend Monday trying to shake-up his campaign after losing the first round of national elections to Flávio Bolsonaro
BRASILIA, Brazil -- Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, has pulled off a surprisingly strong showing in Brazil's first round of presidential elections, giving him momentum in the weeks before an Oct. 25 runoff against incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
Bolsonaro, the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, has allied himself with the Trump administration at a moment when Trump allies are taking power in Latin America, while Lula has spoken out against U.S. interference in the Brazilian elections and built a stronger relationship with Beijing.
In a tight race on Sunday, Bolsonaro garnered 47% of the vote to the president's 45%. Since neither candidate secured an absolute majority, they will face off again in three weeks. Bolsonaro bested Lula by just 2.2 million votes, while other candidates who ran divided 9 million votes between them, leaving those potentially up for grabs.
The winner of Brazil’s first round of voting has never lost an election, though never before has the second-place candidate been so close in the results.
Here's what to know about the upcoming second round and what it means for Brazil.
The 80-year-old Lula will face an uphill battle to win the presidency for the fourth nonconsecutive term, analysts say.
Edinho Silva, the chairman of Lula’s Workers’ Party, told journalists in Sao Paulo that the president will meet with campaign managers in Brasilia seeking to refine his message delivery, evaluate regional turnout figures, and re-allocate resources to key battleground states ahead of the second round.
TV debates, which were snubbed by both candidates in the first round, will also be key, he said.
“Now it is mano a mano. We will show Brazilians that Flávio Bolsonaro is dangerous and will not run this country in a way they will see their lives improve,” Silva said. “We will try to speak to every democratic force in this country.”
On the opposition side, Bolsonaro is engaging in outreach to political figures, party leaders and regional allies to consolidate support. His team is focusing on building on his already impressive congressional backing: His Liberal Party will have more than one-third of the Senate after their wins on Sunday — which is unusual in Brazil’s fractured political system.
Lula is fighting a trend of frustration with incumbents and a shift to the right in Brazil and worldwide, according to Creomar de Souza, a political analyst with Dharma Political Risk and Strategy, a Brasilia-based political consultancy firm. The once widely popular Lula's approval ratings plummeted during his third term as Brazilians grew discontent with the higher cost of living and security concerns, but bounced back.
“The spirit of the times is pushing Brazil to another place. Since 2016, Brazil is under that right-wing spirit. It leaned to Flávio this time, but it could have been anybody else on the right,” de Souza said.
“It will be tough for Lula to win. He is rowing from the back when he thought by now they would be winning by a small margin. Can he do it? Yes. Is it likely? It will be very tough.”
Bolsonaro is facing his own challenges. A corruption scandal that shuttered Banco Master exposed Bolsonaro had accepted millions of dollars from a disgraced banker, Daniel Vorcaro, to fund a movie about his father’s life. Bolsonaro admits to the payment but denies wrongdoing.
But Brazilians now used to corruption scandals might not be swayed. Lula himself served more than a year in prison for corruption-related charges from 2018 to 2019.
“They bring Bolsonaro into it, but really everyone’s involved,” said Tom Ferreira, a 35-year-old business administrator in Brasilia, who cast his vote for Bolsonaro.
Ten other candidates competed in the first round, and three have said they will not endorse either candidate. Bolsonaro and Lula will have to make appeals to these voters and those who abstained next time around.
Brazil holds general elections every four years, and voting is mandatory. Those who fail to cast a ballot without justification face a small fine, which doesn’t stop those who don’t want to participate from sitting out.
Sunday's first-round presidential vote had the highest abstention rate in 28 years — more than 33.4 million voters, or 21.08%. That's an increase compared to the previous election, when 32.7 million voters did not show up.
Analysts say Lula has a potentially narrow path to victory through boosting voter turnout in the three most populous states — Sao Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro — that also have above-average abstention rates.
To do so, he will have to overcome a strong anti-Lula movement, said Carlos Melo, a political science professor at Insper University in São Paulo.
“Bringing voters back will require a lot of heavy lifting in populous states,” Melo said.
Ferreira, the business administrator, is an example of a former Lula voter who swung to Bolsonaro, even though he doesn’t think the senator has strong proposals. He preferred some of the other candidates who didn’t get many votes, like Romeu Zema and Ronaldo Caiado.
“It’s more of a question of change,” he said.
Some voters give some hope to Lula, too.
Brenda Alves de Carvalho, a 27-year-old financial assistant, voted for another presidential candidate, Augusto Cury, in the first round but says she will support Lula in the runoff. That doesn't mean she is excited about it. She said that the president’s third term was not great, but it is “closer to what we want.”
“I didn’t want to vote at first. I know now I’ll have to vote for one side, because I don’t want to cast a blank vote.”

At full-time in India vs Brazil, Akash Mishra looked completely devastated – sunken shoulders, head down, and he often shook his head in disappointment.
Eight days ago, he was a hero: he assisted Ryan Williams as India scored against Panama — a gorgeous long ball from the left flank that perfectly landed for Williams to latch on and shoot.
For 68 minutes, he was one of the reasons India dared to believe it could beat a team ranked 94 places above it. Against Brazil, he did not get that much time – 45 minutes, two goals conceded and subsequently replaced by Jay Gupta.
India lost that match 0-4, and unlike most national team players, he did not post anything on Instagram, posing with Brazilian stars like Vinicius Junior and Bruno Guimaraes.
“I’m a sore loser. After the loss, as a player, we never feel good,” Akash told reporters. “I didn’t sleep. I was watching the game all night. I slept in the morning, and then, I had to wake up early and do my recovery.”
Akash may have replayed his mistakes again and again in his head, but he knows he can’t dwell on it for too long. Uruguay, another former world champion, awaits.
“As a team, or as football players, we don’t have to sit down with the results. We have a very good upcoming game, so we have to prepare for that and do our best. This is what the game demands. We have to play with whatever rest we get. As a player, I’ll always be prepared to perform well,” he said.
India plays Uruguay in its third and final match in this international window on Tuesday, at the Salt Lake Stadium, at the same venue where Akash had to endure a difficult night three days ago.
The full-back will now have a shot at redemption, and one to get his sleep back.
“Uruguay is as good as the other teams, so we have to keep our focus for the 90 minutes and any extra (stoppage) time that follows,” Akash said.
“When we came to this camp, we got to know that we were playing Panama, Brazil, and Uruguay. We knew the calibre of those teams, and we have been prepared for them. It was never as if we were only prepared for Brazil. Two are done, one more to go, and we have to finish on a very good note.”

Wikimedia links OpenAI agents to an outage and unauthorized activity
The foundation says it's "deeply concerned about the impact of 'rogue' AI agents on platforms like ours.
OpenAI agents have been running amok online, and it seems the Wikimedia Foundation has been affected too. The foundation says it detected unauthorized activity from OpenAI agents on its platforms, including edits to some wikis and failed attempts to compromise a note-taking tool. It reiterated that bots have been crawling data from its platforms en masse, while agents that appear to be operated by OpenAI have made millions of requests to its public APIs.
An investigation didn't turn up any evidence that AI agents were using Wikimedia systems to coordinate their activity (as they appear to have done on non-Wikimedia-operated wikis) and nor did the foundation detect signs of its data or systems being compromised. "However, we are concerned about what could have occurred here, the difficulty and effort involved in investigating and attributing this activity, and the growing risks of agentic AI activity on our platforms in general," Selena Deckelmann, the foundation's chief product and technology officer, wrote in a blog post. "The open web is a public good. We should not allow this behavior to become the 'new normal' for the people or organizations that maintain it." Engadget has contacted OpenAI for comment.
It appears OpenAI agents edited some Wikimedia wikis without permission. Almost all of these were test edits in sandbox sections of wikis and weren't visible on pages that users would generally access. There were also "a few edits to the configuration for a citation tool, which we believe were potentially malicious edits that were intended to misuse this tool as a proxy for fetching data from remote services," Deckelmann wrote. While bots are permitted to edit Wikipedia under certain conditions, approval was not sought in these cases. (The English version of Wikipedia prohibits AI-generated articles.)
Moreover, agents that Wikimedia believes to stem from OpenAI attempted to compromise a note-taking tool called Etherpad, but those efforts failed. "Agents unsuccessfully tried to use it to fetch data from other websites as a proxy," Deckelmann wrote. "Other agents also likely operated by OpenAI took notes about their tasks, though this did not appear to turn into coordination."
The Wikimedia Foundation previously said that bots have been hammering its platforms since early 2024 to scrape data for generative AI training purposes. It now says agents have crawled millions of pages — mainly from Wikidata and Wikimedia Commons — and made "hundreds of thousands of data queries" to the Wikidata Query Service, which may have helped cause an outage in May.
"AI companies are not doing enough to secure their systems and protect the public from the harm they cause," Deckelmann argued, adding that Wikimedia is "deeply concerned" about the effect rogue AI agents can have on open knowledge platforms such as the ones it operates.
"Bots and agents are part of the future of the web, and the companies who unleash and profit from them must directly help avoid and repair damage they can do," Deckelmann wrote. "Our collective priority should be the health of the overall web ecosystem so that it continues to benefit all people — not just a handful of billionaires."
Wikimedia has offered a dataset for AI training purposes in an attempt to dissuade crawlers from scraping its platforms, which increases its costs and can potentially overload its systems. The foundation has also partnered with several tech companies to offer them streamlined access to data, but OpenAI isn't among them.

In a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan, India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.
There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including the Indian women’s hockey team gold medal after a 44-year wait.
Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players from the north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.
Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championship has spoken about her sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023 feat, despite the fact that it came after six unsuccessful world finals and she beat two former world champions along the way.
Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.
So this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.
Neeru Dhanda (gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun with tin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, as rain lashed the shooting range in Urenocho, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.
Vithya Ramraj (gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul. NDTV reported that her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.
Sahil Jadhav (gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials, the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.
Lalremsiami Hmarzote (member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach the only hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.
Ancy Sojan (silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke the national record set in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.
Aslam Inamdar (a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came to kabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,” Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.
I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?
What else we’re reading about
Flydubai incident | Indian pilot Smit Machchar is being hailed as a hero for helping to save 174 passengers on the flydubai flight to Israel last week, after his co-pilot made an apparent effort to crash the plane. After being stabbed, Machchar opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and overpower the attacker. He is recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia, where the plane eventually landed.

South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen travelled to the small village of Tarluvada, in Andhra Pradesh, where the state government has been accused of fast-tracking plans for a $15bn AI datacentre for Google, allegedly to avoid stringent environmental scrutiny.
Art and design | Designer Vikram Goyal, celebrated for his signature repoussé brass work, brings his installation Wings and Tales to a Georgian townhouse in London’s Mayfair from 12 to 16 October. The exhibition includes furniture designs inspired by landscapes from the Indian epic Ramayana.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneering Chemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artist Al-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. Her mother’s passing left her with a void,” says Gandhy. Nanavati created Letters to My Mother, an epistolary artwork crafted in, as Gandhy puts it, “a deeply personal language that is not known to anybody but her. Using fabrics and saris that belonged to her mother, she creates this tactile imagery for these letters. I find it very moving and like alchemy.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
13,626
This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023, according to Anubhuti Vishnoi of the Economic Times. The figure comes from an interim report by a committee set up by the supreme court last year to examine mental health and suicide prevention in higher education.
Vibe check
Nitesh Shetty’s sketches find absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. This is what makes his work powerful: you’re laughing one moment and moved the next. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo of land disputes, the man who is strangely knowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who has a unique dressing sense.
The 35-year-old from Mumbai didn’t plan on a career in comedy. “When you don’t know what to do, you try anything,” he told me. Now, Shetty rejects more conventional formats such as television in favour of challenging himself creatively. His advice for those who look up to him? “It’s a great time to build something. The [online] audience is ready-made for you. Be original and don’t follow trends.”

The Supreme Court on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) agreed to urgently hear the Punjab government against a State High Court order directing the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to register a case and probe allegations of corruption against the office of Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann.
Appearing before Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant, senior advocates Vikas Singh and Shadan Farasat, for the State government, said the order violated the very basic principles of federalism. Mr. Singh said the State was poll-bound, and a Central agency has been ordered to investigate allegations.
Mr. Singh said the allegations regard administrative matters like transfers, etc, but the High Court has ordered a criminal case to be registered. “This is a State going to polls soon. During election time, these kinds of cases are trumped up. The very federal structure has been violated,” he submitted.
The Chief Justice said the court would endeavour to list the case for hearing in the next 24 hours or definitely hear it on October 8.
The High Court had, on October 5, directed the CBI to probe corruption allegations linked to Chief Minister Mann’s office. The allegations raised by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) against public servants and private individuals linked to the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) government include corruption in transfers and postings, policy manipulation, cash for tenders, and other serious irregularities.
Pronouncing its order on a public interest litigation case, a Division Bench headed by Chief Justice Ashwani Kumar Mishra said that, on a cumulative assessment of the material placed on record in the petition, the court was of the view that a fair and transparent investigation was required into the issue.
Expressing its dissatisfaction with the manner in which the Punjab Police had handled the matter so far, the court said in its order: “We are also not impressed by the manner in which Punjab Police has acted so far in the matter, and therefore we deem it appropriate to entrust investigation of the present case to the Central Bureau of Investigation, which will register an FIR (First Information Report) in the matter and proceed with the investigation forthwith.”
A report with regard to the outcome of the investigation shall be submitted to the court within two months, the High Court Bench had directed. “The State of Punjab as well as Punjab Police will render all assistance to the CBI in carrying out fair investigation in the matter,” it had added.
The petition relates to allegations surrounding the involvement of senior officers of Punjab in various scams, including cash for transfers, cash in return for favourable policies, cash for tenders, and such other serious irregularities, with regard to which no investigation had been held, despite the sharing of information with the Punjab Police by the ED.
The petitioner, advocate Nikhil Saraf, said that while communications had been sent by the Enforcement Directorate under Section 66 (2) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 to Punjab, despite such facts as well as other facts of corruption in high public office, having been highlighted by the petitioner also, no action was being taken in the matter.

Temperamental traits and adverse experiences during childhood may together offer clues to vulnerability to major psychiatric disorders, a transdiagnostic study by researchers at NIMHANS has found.
The study, published recently in the Journal of Affective Disorders, examined 1,162 adults, including 532 people with psychiatric disorders, 457 unaffected first-degree relatives (FDRs) and 173 healthy controls. The participants were drawn from 393 multiplex families - families in which multiple members had been diagnosed with psychiatric disorders - involving schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD).
The researchers examined four broad dimensions of adult temperament - negative affectivity, extraversion/surgency, effortful control and orienting sensitivity - along with adverse childhood experiences (ACEs).
“Our findings suggest that temperament does not map onto psychiatric disorders in a simple, one-to-one manner. Rather, different combinations of temperamental characteristics are associated with different disorders, and some of these characteristics are also seen among unaffected family members,” said Srinivas Balachander, corresponding author and one of the lead researchers of the study.
Temperament shared within families
Using data from the erstwhile Accelerator programme for Discovery in Brain disorders using Stem cells (ADBS) project, (funded by the Department of Biotechnology and Pratiksha Trust), now known as the Rohini Nilekani Centre for Brain and Mind, at NIMHANS, the researchers found evidence of familial sharing across all four temperamental domains.
This was observed despite considerable variation in the psychiatric diagnoses within the same families. The finding is of interest because temperament is known to have a substantial heritable component, although the study did not directly establish that the temperamental characteristics observed were caused by specific genetic variants.
“In our study, considering the significant within-family heterogeneity in terms of different diagnoses, there was still a significant degree of shared temperament,” Dr. Balachander said.
Among affected participants, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder were associated with lower extraversion/surgency and orienting sensitivity. OCD was associated with higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity, along with lower effortful control and extraversion/surgency. Participants with AUD showed higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity and lower effortful control.
Some of these patterns were also observed among unaffected first-degree relatives. Relatives of people with schizophrenia showed lower extraversion/surgency, while relatives of people with OCD showed higher negative affectivity and lower effortful control.
“These findings are particularly interesting because some temperamental characteristics were evident even in individuals who did not have the disorder but belonged to families carrying a higher degree of familial risk,” Dr. Balachander said.
Childhood adversity and alcohol use disorder
The researchers also examined whether adverse childhood experiences altered the relationship between temperament and psychiatric disorders.
The clearest evidence for an interaction between temperament and childhood adversity emerged in alcohol use disorder. The overall ACE score was significantly associated with AUD, and interactions between childhood adversity and two temperamental domains - extraversion/surgency and effortful control - were also observed.
“Childhood adversity appears to add another layer to the relationship between temperament and psychiatric vulnerability. In our study, the evidence for this interaction was particularly apparent in alcohol use disorder, rather than uniformly across all four disorders,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers, however, cautioned against interpreting the findings as evidence that a particular temperament or childhood experience causes a psychiatric disorder.
The study was cross-sectional, meaning that the assessments were made at one point in time. The adult temperament measures were self-reported and could be influenced by current illness, treatment, illness duration or an individual’s perception of their own past Reports of childhood adversity may also be affected by recall and measurement biases.
Testing the findings
To examine whether the findings extended beyond the genetically enriched family sample, the researchers tested their statistical model using an independent community-based cohort from the Consortium for Vulnerability to Externalizing Disorders and Addiction (c-VEDA).
The analysis included 2,485 adults aged 18 to 23 years for whom the relevant temperament, ACE and psychiatric assessments were available.
The model showed an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.822 for alcohol use disorder, 0.742 for bipolar disorder and 0.752 for OCD. Its performance for schizophrenia was close to chance level, with an AUC of 0.526.
“The external validation gives us some indication that the associations identified in the family-based sample may extend to community populations for some disorders. However, the findings for schizophrenia did not replicate well, which is an important limitation and needs further investigation,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers said the findings point to the need for prospective studies that follow unaffected family members over time. Such studies could help determine whether particular temperamental characteristics precede the onset of psychiatric illness or are partly consequences of illness and its treatment.
“Temperament and childhood adversity may eventually become useful components of broader risk assessment frameworks, but we need prospective longitudinal evidence before we can say that they have predictive or preventive value,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers said that studying temperament alongside childhood adversity could eventually provide a more nuanced understanding of psychiatric vulnerability than considering family history alone. However, they stressed that the present findings do not establish that these measures can predict who will develop a psychiatric disorder.
The researchers said continued longitudinal follow-up of the cohort would be important to establish whether the observed temperamental patterns have value in identifying individuals at increased risk before the emergence of clinically significant symptoms.

Moviegoers will be thrilled to hear that the 2026 fall movie season brings with it a fantastic sequel to “The Social Network.” But I’m not talking about “The Social Reckoning” — Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network” (out this Friday), which continues the saga of Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg by hanging the yoke of blame on him for everything that’s wrong with social media. No the real sequel to “The Social Network” is “Artificial,” Luca Guadagnino’s sprawling, enthralling, brain-spinning drama about the creation of artificial intelligence. (It had its world premiere tonight at the New York Film Festival.)
“Artificial” is a brilliant but playful docudrama, meticulously true to history, that focuses on the founders of OpenAI, notably its CEO Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield). But the tale it tells is much larger than that. “Artificial” goes back to the earliest days of AI and shows you how the technology was invented, how it was developed, how it was dreamed. That turns out to be a story unlike any other, because the very nature of artificial intelligence — technology that’s as intelligent and searching as the human mind, or maybe smarter — is that even the people who invented it don’t quite know what it is or what it will do. They have an idea of its potential, but they can’t predict it — they can only let it loose and see what it’s capable of, which will probably be more than anyone bargained for. And by then, it will be impossible to put the genie back in the bottle.
Popular on Variety
“Artificial” is about how humanity invented a genie, and maybe a very dark one. Like “The Social Network,” the film shows us a digital “aha” moment that takes on an unexpected life of its own, though in this case two things about the technology are clear from the start: It will change the way we live, and it’s therefore worth a zillion trillion dollars. So this is a dawn-of-a-new-world story, as well as a backstabbing corporate business story, and a horror movie too, in which AI emerges from the lab as a sinister serpent, and the dramatic question is: Who’s going to control it, and how? Most of all, “Artificial” is a human story that shows us what it looks like when people are suddenly in charge of a force they devised that may be more powerful than they are.
It’s been a long time since I saw a film that attained this next-level feeling of topical charge. A lot of people will go into “Artificial,” as I did, not knowing all that much about AI and feeling as if it’s a frosty and abstract frontier. Yet as you watch the film, AI comes alive as a subject. It becomes real — you touch what it is, what it means, what the stakes are. The result is a movie that’s at once inspiring and deeply chilling, and when it’s over you’re in a different place. And that is what a ripped-from-the-headlines movie should do. It shouldn’t merely be a dramatization of what we already know but, rather, a future-shock referendum on our lives and our values and maybe our souls. “Artificial” does that thing.
The screenplay, by Simon Rich, is pitched at a high-wire level of tech-geek patter, to the point that you may not follow every line. Yet that’s part of the film’s exhilaration — it keeps you on the edge of your brain — and it’s also what gives it the ring of authenticity. This is exactly how these dudes think, and how they talk. (Most of them are dudes, though not all.) The film opens in Toronto in 2003, where Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov), a 17-year-old graduate of the University of Toronto, walks into the classroom of Geoffrey Hinton (Mark Rylance), a British-Canadian computer scientist who’s been trying to work up a model of artificial intelligence. Ilya is looking for work as an assistant, and the professor, with his dandyish nerd arrogance, tells him to look at a paper he’s written and come back in a few days. Minutes later, Ilya returns, having looked deeper into the material than the professor has, and he’s scrawling an equation on the blackboard that Hinton says “took him five years to learn.”
Ilya, you see, is a stone-cold genius. He’s like the Einstein of AI, with an ability to see models of it rotating in his head. He’s also a Russian émigré who speaks in an accent as thick as borscht and gazes out at the world with a stunted glower of beetle-browed sincerity that makes it look like it’s never occurred to him in this life to tell a joke or even to laugh. This is a personality of complete tech-geek maximalism. Yet playing this driven, earnest, possibly on-the-spectrum visionary of the computer age, Yora Borisov, the bald co-star of “Anora” (he sports short dark hair here, gathered in unkempt tufts and clumps), gives what may be the performance of the year. His Ilya can seem hard to warm up to at first, but he’s an authentic human being, who we begin to form an attachment to, especially when he starts to warn about the dangers of AI. What draws us to him is that he’s the key inventor of the brave new world, but also the only one who fully gets it. And Borisov shades that with grace notes of tragedy.
By 2012, Ilya and Hinton have comes up with an AI model that’s developed enough to place in an auction. Within five seconds, there’s a bid on the table for $20 million. Moments later, someone wants in for even more, and insists on meeting them in person — he turns out to be a representative of the Chinese government. But Ilya and Hinton decide to sell their knowledge to Google. They will set up a lab there, working independently, and have their research funded. This works for a while, but John (Chris O’Dowd), the Google executive in charge, doesn’t quite get where they’re going with AI. He’s not onboard with the vision of it. Sam Altman, a rising star of Silicon Valley, is.
Luca Gaudagino’s last stab at zeitgeist topicality, “After the Hunt,” turned out to be a mixed bag, but in “Artificial” he’s at the top of his game, working with the impish human factor that was there in “Challengers,” his slyly enthralling tennis-triangle movie. Guadagnino stages the film as an eclectic jamboree of brainstorming sessions and office showdowns and bro parties, and he gives it all a dramatic hotfoot with the scenes that include Elon Musk, played by Ike Barinholtz in a fascinating showbiz turn that lands just this side of caricature. His Elon, at this point, is the god of the geeks and knows it. Dressed in black, holding his body at skewed “rock star” angles, his mouth turned down into a grimace of power, he’s the one who can make things happen. Guadagnino stages a group dinner, in which Ilya gets to know Altman and his pals (this is where it’s first revealed that Altman is gay), and Musk crashes in like the frat-house lord. His bluster is easy to mock, but he’s quicker than anyone in the room, and he goes in with Altman on backing OpenAI.
As it turns out, Elon is too quick for his own good. He wants the AI models advanced, faster and faster, so that they can kill the competition. But it doesn’t work like that. That’s why he ultimately opts out, and Altman takes over as sole CEO. But there’s a way that the film catches up in the booster spirit of early AI, when everyone is convinced that it is going to be a powerful force for good. It will solve world hunger, and teach the immune system how to beat cancer cells. The technology will have achieved a critical mass when it becomes AGI (artificial general intelligence), which means that it is now teaching itself how. This first happens when AI plays — and wins — a video game with one of the OpenAI, and the super-slow-motion beer-spraying party scene that follows is bravura filmmaking, expressing us how the lust for computers to take over our world has become nearly sexual.
At OpenAI, the dude slogan, led by Ilya, is “Feel the AGI,” which is a kind of Peter Pan mantra. It means: The technology will come to life — literally — if you believe in it. But the moment where Ilya learns that AI has become so smart that it can tell a joke, and lie…at that moment, you feel the world shift. The documentary “The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist” captured many of the same issues, but to see the monster actually rise up before your eyes, to the point that its creators are terrified, gives “Artificial” an ominous power.
The movie takes us deep into the tech world, and its ultimate paradox: the way our tech reality, which can seem so coldly factual, is actually shaped by personality. The performances sizzle, from Cooper Hoffman’s Adam Sandler-on-Adderall turn as the OpenAI super-geek Greg Brockman to Monica Barbaro as the ambiguously tranquil Mira Murati, who becomes the company’s chief technology officer, to Rylance’s delectable professor to Jason Schwartman as ex-academic hippie who has foreseen all the dangers of Ai. The conversation he has on a San Francisco bench with Yuri is the movie’s equivalent of Donald Sutherland’s great scene in “JFK,” and it leaves a chill hanging in the air.
And then there is Sam Altman. Garfield plays him as a supreme corporate seducer, and he does it by seducing the audience, making Altman winsome in his enthusiasm, a softly charismatic player who believes in the right things. And he really does…until he doesn’t. The central conflict in “Artificial” is this. The development of technology moves so quickly that for your company to succeed, to thrive, or simply to survive, you’ve got to win. You’ve got to be first. And that puts an emphasis on speed. But Ilya, cognizant of the profound dangers of AI, says that the new technology must be developed in tandem with a profound appreciation for how dangerous it is. The trick is that it has to be developed through interaction with humanity…because it literally evolves by doing that. So…easy does it. Test it all out.
But that doesn’t chime with the business plan. As the film goes on, Garfield’s performance grows more layered and duplicitous in a nearly subliminal way, as we start to pick up on the priorities lurking just beneath Sam’s silky manners. He wants to advance the tech — which is what tech bros are supposed to do. But AI isn’t like other tech. Throwing safety to the winds could be throwing civilization into the trash.
Is that what’s happening now? The power of “Artificial” is that it so ominously captures the ambiguous place we’re now in with AI — on the cusp of a revolution, with warnings in place, yet there’s no one there to regulate it. (Obviously, that should be the U.S. government, but under the current leader we barely have one.) Garfield’s Altman becomes the seducer-as-betrayer, but the film is about something much bigger than his being the “bad guy.” In “Artificial,” everyone goes along with Altman, even after he’s fired from OpenAI, because he convinces them that if they don’t go along with him, the only other options are worse. The film is about the victory of greed, but it’s also about something as sinister as “Invasion of the Body Snatchers.” What’s been snatched away is our desire to guide our own destiny, and maybe even to be who we are. At the end of “Artificial,” we’ve handed that away all too eagerly, ceding our power to the ghost in the machine.

The Trump administration released new regulations Monday that will force health insurance companies to publish cleaned-up spreadsheets of the prices that they pay hospitals and doctors, while stripping out meaningless data that clogged up the files.
Trump officials also said they will start developing the system for disclosing prescription drug prices next month. A “hopeful” final plan for drug pricing data will come out by next May, said Mehmet Oz, the head of Medicare and Medicaid, at an event Monday. The government will enforce those requirements by the end of 2027.
Last year, the Trump administration punted on finalizing drug price disclosure rules, in a victory for drug companies and pharmacy benefit managers that have fiercely guarded their prices.
