When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.
Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.
The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.
Few in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.
Just as protests have erupted globally over AI datacentres – from California and Texas to Scotland and Australia – communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.
“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”
Pointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”
The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.
Publicly it was announced as a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.
But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.
Activists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.
The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’s Economic Survey 2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.
But locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.
Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.
Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.
Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.
“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.
Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with a deliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.
“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.
In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres – documented emitters of heat – could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.
The strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought while polluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.
Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.
“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”
Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”
For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.
The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.
“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.
Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.
But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.
“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.
“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”
The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.
One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.
“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”

Trump says journalists should be ‘arrested’ for reporting on empty seats at rally
The president claims upper-level empty seats were simply attendees moving down to the main floor during the Vandalia, Ohio event

President Donald Trump suggested on Monday that reporters from The New York Times and other media outlets should be “arrested” following their coverage of his weekend campaign event in Ohio.
The backlash followed a report by New York Times correspondent Katie Rogers, who noted that “several areas of an upper deck were empty” by the time Trump finished speaking on Saturday at Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio. Rogers reported that the school’s student center, which hosted the event, has a capacity of 4,500 people.
Trump disputed those account details in a series of posts on Truth Social, claiming the venue was full and arguing that empty upper levels were merely the result of audience movement.
“The Fake News New York Times ‘reported’ on my Great, PACKED Rally in Ohio that, ‘the place was not full. Some upper sections were almost completely empty,’” Trump wrote. “In actuality, thousands of people were unable to get in. The Arena was totally MAXED OUT, including all upper sections.
“What does happen at all of my SOLD OUT Rallies, is that the people in the upper sections tend to migrate down to the Main Floor — The ‘migration’ process always happens!”
In another post, Trump criticized media coverage of his crowd sizes relative to other political figures and called for legal action against journalists.
“The Ohio Arena was already full to the brim — And yet these people were still trying to get in,” Trump wrote. “The New York Times said, ‘There were empty seats’ when, in fact, there were none, and thousands of people had to be turned away. The New York Times, and many other Artificial Media Outlets, should be arrested for their dishonesty and disservice to our Country.”
He added: “When Bernie Sanders has 500 to 1,000 people, they make it sound like it’s the biggest event that ever took place. When PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP has 50,000 people, they make it sound like nobody showed up!”
Trump also claimed that he uses video recordings to counter media reports about his events.
“I have cinematographers shooting the various Arenas where I speak, in that some of the Fake News likes to dishonestly report lies and untruths,” he wrote.
He insisted that his events remain “HOTTER than ever” and described them as “happenings” that “will never be duplicated again.”
During the rally itself, which was held to support Republican candidate Jon Husted in his Senate race against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, Trump addressed the crowd size directly from the stage.
“There are thousands of people outside [who] can’t get in,” he said. “If you’d like to give up your seat, please, we can work it out, get out of here.”

On Monday morning, the Nobel Prize for medicine was announced. This year, I wonder: Will Claude or a future artificial intelligence agent ever win the most prestigious award for medical discovery?
Imagine a future AI agent responding to a scientist’s insightful prompt by successfully identifying a completely novel approach to curing cancer, along with a detailed and actionable plan for implementing it. Given the toll of cancer on our species, I suspect few today would consider that a bad outcome.
But as a former medical school dean who was regularly called upon to adjudicate complex issues of credit, I’m uncertain how credit for such a future world-changing discovery would or should be assigned. Until today, human scientists have been the agents responsible for discovering cancer cures, and for doing so they (and key associates) have been showered with academic credit and awards, perhaps even a Nobel Prize. Are we now entering a world in which some (or all) Nobels will be awarded to Claude, ChatGPT, or their AI successors, rather than human scientists? And if so, would it matter?
The Nobel statutes don’t mention “human” but refer instead to “persons.” In 2024, two of the three winners of the Nobel Prize in chemistry were given credit for their work on the AlphaFold model at DeepMind — even though many more were involved. So without changes to the rules, a future prize for a discovery made by AI would most likely go to some “persons” given credit for making the AI possible — at least at first. But the committee may elect to change the rules or interpret them differently. The Nobel Peace Prize, for instance, has gone to organizations rather than persons.
Today, credit for discovery plays a central role in the reward structure of science. As “the currency of the realm,” credit powerfully influences the norms and practices of the research ecosystem. It’s required for scientists to secure appointments, promotions, funding, access to students, and other necessities. It’s also a mechanism for evaluating research impact and providing accountability for research claims.
It didn’t always work this way. The current credit ecosystem arose in the mid-19th century, as science emerged as a profession alongside the rise of the modern scientific journal. It’s been further modified by many factors, from today’s online publishing platforms to new means for assessing and quantifying scientific impact, and the increasingly interdisciplinary and team-based nature of research.
As we begin to acknowledge AI as a generator of scientific discovery, will the approach to scientific credit be transformed as well? Current and future scientists would certainly like to know.
Despite many unknowns, it’s hard to imagine the status quo holding. In perhaps the most likely outcome, humans will continue to be responsible for many discoveries, often aided by AI along the way. The credit ecosystem will continue to recognize these human achievements, while finding ways to appropriately recognize the contributions of their AI collaborators.
But if AI itself is recognized as the responsible agent for some discoveries — even profoundly important ones, such as a cancer cure mentioned above — how would credit be handled? Would assignment of credit as we know it today even matter?
In that world, humans might retain (for a while) a desire to acknowledge the role of AI in those discoveries, even bestowing previously human-only awards upon the responsible AI agents. Perhaps some credit would also go to their human creators, those putting forth insightful prompts, and those creatively implementing the work.
But in a world of predominantly AI-driven discovery, the current role of credit as an incentive for the human research ecosystem would dramatically change.
In considering this future, we must consider another role that credit plays. Beyond serving as an incentive and accountability mechanism in the human academic research ecosystem, there are commercial incentives for discovery, and credit plays a different role in that setting. A major commercial incentive for biomedical research involves the awarding of patents for discovery, and today only humans are eligible to be named discoverers. If future laws change to allow recognition of AI agents and/or their human creators as discoverers (with or without human collaborators), how might this affect accountability, ownership, and the ability to profit from discoveries?
For research conducted today in both academic organizations and for-profit companies, ownership of intellectual property is generally held by these organizations rather than the human discoverers now named in patents. Patent law might evolve to allow organizations to name AI agents — even proprietary AI versions — as discoverers. But assigning credit would remain complicated to the extent humans will likely play creative roles in successfully implementing AI-generated ideas, though efforts are underway to create AI-automated research systems.
Today, the science community is composed of humans who seek and often compete with others for discovery as well as credit, and this feature of scientific culture is believed to play an important role in the success of the enterprise. As AI becomes a key enabler and even primary driver of discovery, the current culture of credit will evolve to accommodate that reality. Changes to the credit economy may be among the many trade-offs we accept to realize the benefits of AI-driven discovery, in biomedical research and other domains of human activity.
Whether an AI agent will ever receive a Nobel laureate is, at least in part, a question about what jobs we want credit to perform. If it’s mainly an incentive for human scientists and the overall enterprise, its role will change as machines play a greater role in discovery. If credit continues to influence allocation of trust, resources, and responsibility, those needs will persist, necessitating decisions on how best to manage them in an AI dominated research ecosystem. This may be further complicated by recent debates about whether AI agents may evolve into moral agents whose status would justify their receiving credit for “their work.”
I don’t know how these questions will ultimately be resolved. And I suspect the answers will differ across diverse domains related to research: human scientific careers, journals, funders, universities, biopharmaceutical companies, patent offices, and yes, prize committees. The current system was designed for a world of human discoverers. Though that day may never be fully behind us, we must begin serious conversations about what changes the age of AI science will bring to scientific credit.
Jeffrey S. Flier is a Harvard University distinguished service professor and the former dean of Harvard Medical School.

Kuku Technologies Limited, parent company of audio OTT platform Kuku FM and microdrama app Kuku TV, swung into the black in the fiscal year FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹182.7 Cr against a net loss of ₹152.6 Cr incurred in FY25. The company’s profitability came on the back of a notable uptick in its top line performance. The IPO-bound startup, which filed its confidential DRHP with the SEBI earlier this year, saw its operating revenue for the fiscal year zoom more than sixfold to ₹1,484.2 Cr in FY26 from ₹241.6 Cr in the previous fiscal. Including other income of ₹26.2 Cr, total income for the fiscal stood at ₹1,510.4 Cr. Subscriptions remained the overwhelming source of Kuku Technologies' revenue during FY26. The company generated ₹1,475.4 Cr from subscriptions, accounting for more than 99% of its operating revenue. This was followed by ₹6.9 Cr from pay-per-piece (PPV) content purchases, while advertising brought in the remainder ₹1.9 Cr. India continued to account for the vast majority of its business, contributing ₹1,463.6 Cr, or roughly 99% of operating revenue. International markets contributed ₹20.5 Cr during the year. The profitability was also charged by a deferred tax credit of ₹98.2 Cr and a tax expense of ₹4 Cr. Excluding that, the profit for the year stood at ₹88.6 Cr. At the operating level, Kuku Technologies swung to an EBITDA profit of ₹82.9 Cr in FY26 from an EBITDA loss of ₹159.8 Cr in FY25. Kuku Turns Profitable Ahead Of IPO The company, which operates audio OTT platform Kuku FM, microdrama app Kuku TV, among others, has swung to the black ahead of going public. Earlier in September, the markets regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) approved the proposed listing of Kuku Technologies. Kuku filed its confidential DRHP with the SEBI in June. As per sources, the IPO’s size could be in the range of ₹2,500-3,500 Cr ($261-366 Mn) and could potentially value it at ₹15,000 Cr (about $1.8 Bn). The IPO will consist of a fresh issue of shares as well as an offer-for-sale component. Kuku plans to deploy the capital to upgrade its tech, AI infrastructure, content production and fuel geographic expansion. As of now, the startup’s content library spans more than 20,000 titles across seven languages and multiple genres including drama, finance, and well-being. It claims to have more than 1 Cr listeners and creators on its platform and 400 Mn app downloads across its portfolio. Kuku has raised over $156 Mn to date from the likes of Fundamentum Partnership, Krafton, Vertex Ventures, IFC, 3one4 Capital, among others. Its most recent $85 Mn Series C funding round, in October 2025, was led by Granite Asia. Magnifying Kuku FM’s Spending Total expenses for the fiscal year surged 3.5X to ₹1,421.8 Cr in the year under review from ₹411 Cr in FY25. Here is a breakdown of where the startup spent a major share of its expenses: Marketing And Advertisement Expenses: Constituting 77.7% of the overall expenses, Kuku FM spent ₹1,105.1 Cr on marketing and advertising in FY26. This is a near 4X jump compared with around ₹284.8 Cr spent on marketing in FY25. Operational Costs: Spending under this head rose 11X to ₹96.3 Cr in the year under review from ₹8.7 Cr in the previous fiscal. Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee-related expenses grew at a much slower pace, increasing about 24% to ₹74.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹59.9 Cr in FY25.

An Oct. 2 video shows Trump fielding reporters' questions outside the White House. Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy asked, "What do you think about New York's governor appointing a special prosecutor in the Cornell rape case, Letitia James?" (James, New York's attorney general, previously led a civil fraud case against Trump.) Trump thrice called James corrupt, saying he feels "badly" for "whoever" James prosecutes and alleged that defendants she targets "won't get a fair shake."
A rumor circulated online in early October that U.S. President Donald Trump said he feels "badly" for the seven current or former male Cornell University students whom a female former student accused of rape.
Trump purportedly made the remarks while answering a question about New York Attorney General Letitia James' appointment as a special prosecutor to investigate the case.
Snopes readers asked about this claim via email, with one person inquiring, "I saw something that says Donald Trump said he feels bad for the 'Cornell 7,' but can't find reputable sources. True??"
In sum, people correctly attributed this statement to Trump. A C-SPAN video shows Trump standing outside the White House on Oct. 2 and responding directly to a reporter's question about the Cornell case, thrice calling James corrupt and saying he feels "badly" for "whoever" James prosecutes, alleging that defendants she targets "won't get a fair shake."
James previously sued Trump and his associates in a civil fraud case beginning in 2022, leading to Trump repeatedly targeting her on social media.
In an emailed response, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis referred us to Trump's own comments, adding that the White House believes James has weaponized the justice system to unjustly target the president.
Digging into the rumor
The Cornell accuser, identified in court documents only as Jane Doe, claims the seven men sexually assaulted her at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Oct. 19 and 20, 2024. She filed a lawsuit against the seven men, the university, the fraternity and others, in mid-September.
On Sept. 28, Tompkins County, New York, prosecutors announced they were reopening the criminal investigation, citing a "discrepancy" between Doe's original statement and the allegations in the lawsuit.
Prior to New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointing James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case on Oct. 1, James posted a statement of compassion for Doe on her official social media accounts, writing, "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you."
In an example of the claim from Oct. 2, a Facebook post (archived) displayed a meme reading, "This is disgusting: Trump just said he 'feels badly' for the people accused in the Cornell rape case because Letitia James is now overseeing the investigation. Not one word for the victim."
(Really American via Facebook)
Other users shared the rumor about Trump's remarks on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived) and X (archived). Some posts didn't mention James but did include a video showing a reporter's question about James and Trump's answer. Examples of those posts appeared on Bluesky (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived).
The remarks occurred when Trump spoke to a group of reporters outside the White House. Videos show Fox News' Peter Doocy asking Trump about Hochul appointing James as a special prosecutor:
DOOCY: What do you think about New York's governor appointing a special prosecutor in the Cornell rape case, Letitia James?
TRUMP: Letitia James is a corrupt person. She's totally corrupt and I can't imagine it. And, I feel badly for whoever she's looking at because they won't get a fair shake. But Letitia James is a corrupt person.
C-SPAN posted remarks on social media. (Readers can also watch the full press gaggle on YouTube, with the pertinent moment beginning at 6:24.)
Trump has made other remarks about the Cornell case. During a similar gathering of reporters on Oct. 1, a video shows an unidentified reporter asking Trump, "Mr. President, do you think that Cornell University has done enough to investigate the alleged rape on campus?" Trump answered, "Well, I don't know that much about it but Cornell is a fine school, and I'm sure they'll do what's right." (Readers can watch that full gaggle on YouTube, with the Cornell question occurring at 11:43.)
Trump has also posted about the case on Truth Social (archived), labeling it "the highly controversial Cornell University rape case" and questioning why Hochul would appoint James.
For further reading, we previously reported Trump authentically expressed well wishes to Ghislaine Maxwell, the close associate of deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, prior to her conviction on federal sex-trafficking charges.

- Reports spread in early October 2026 that a Russian lab worker may have died of the pneumonic plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
- The pneumonic plague "has a nearly 100% case-fatality rate when untreated," according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The illness requires antibiotic treatment that should start as soon as the plague is suspected, before test results, per the CDC.
- The rumor stems from news media reports saying Russia announced that a 28-year-old lab worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia had died of an "unknown" infection, and that nearly 200 people have been isolated as a result. The reports cite Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian public agency responsible for "federal state sanitary and epidemiological supervision," according to the Russian government.
- Snopes could not reach the website of Rospotrebnadzor and does not have access to primary sources, therefore we cannot confirm the details of the lab worker's death. Russian news agency Interfax reported the Russian government as saying she had died of a pneumonia pathogen of "unknown etiology," meaning its origin is not clear.
- On Oct. 4, Interfax also reported Rospotrebnadzor as saying, "based on the results of extensive testing, no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities were detected in the patient's sample." If true, this would suggest the lab worker did not die of pneumonic plague.
- 
A U.S. Department of State spokesperson said via email that the department is aware of the reports and is "monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners."
- 
Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have also reached out to the CDC and the Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety of the European Union Commission. We are waiting for responses.
In early October 2026, a rumor spread that a worker at a Russian lab that studies Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes the plague, had died of the pneumonic plague.
Some social media users said the lab worker's death resulted from an accident at the lab. One X post reads, in part, "A lab worker in Russia has died from pneumonic plague."
Meanwhile, several Snopes readers emailed us asking for details about the story.
The claim stems from various news reports about a 28-year-old woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia. Around 200 people have reportedly been isolated as a precautionary measure. The articles cited Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian public agency responsible for "federal state sanitary and epidemiological supervision," according to the Russian government.
In short, it has not been possible to independently verify the rumor without access to primary sources or confirmation from Russian authorities. Therefore, this claim is unrated. We will update this article if we learn more.
Russian authorities reportedly implement containment measures
Snopes could not reach the website of Rospotrebnadzor, therefore we could not confirm the details of the lab worker's death. On Oct. 4, Russian news agency Interfax reported that the Russian government said she had died of a pneumonia pathogen of "unknown etiology," meaning its origin is not clear.
The same report adds that Rospotrebnadzor said no microorganisms associated with the individual's professional work were detected in that person's samples following "extensive testing." If true, it would suggest the lab worker did not die of pneumonic plague.
Local authorities have reportedly implemented preventative measures. Interfax cites the Rospotrebnadzor health agency as saying:
Due to the patient's professional activities, upon receiving information, a comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures was immediately and fully implemented in accordance with sanitary legislation. This included identifying the widest possible circle of people who had been in contact with the patient, inpatient medical observation, and daily laboratory testing. The results revealed two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection. No other infectious agents were detected.
View from U.S. Department of State
"We are aware of reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia," a U.S. Department of State spokesperson said via email. "We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners."
We contacted the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety of the European Union Commission requesting updates on the situation. We will update this report if we receive responses.
There are three main types of plague: bubonic plague, which infects lymph nodes; septicemic plague, which infects the blood; and pneumonic plague, which infects the lungs. The bubonic and septicemic plagues are most commonly transmitted via flea bites and handling infected animals, while the pneumonic plague spreads through the air via infected droplets.
The pneumonic plague "has a nearly 100% case-fatality rate when untreated," according to the CDC. The illness requires antibiotic treatment that should start as soon as the plague is suspected, even before test results, per the U.S. health agency.
"Plague is a known disease and is treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early," the State Department spokesperson said via email. "Cases occur naturally in many parts of the world."
For further reading, Snopes covered the 2021 death of a child in Colorado who had a confirmed plague infection.

The past fortnight has brought several developments around Apple in India. The iPhone 18 Pro and Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo began shipping, putting the company’s latest hardware in focus. But another development has drawn attention: Apple Pay, a service the company has been talking about bringing to India for more than a decade, is finally here. Apple launched the service in India on September 30, 2026, allowing users to pay at physical stores, within apps and on websites using an iPhone, iPad or Apple Watch. In 2016, then CEO Tim Cook during his visit to India said that Apple was looking at bringing Apple Pay to India, and had even met the then ICICI Bank CEO Chanda Kochhar to understand the bank’s views on mobile payments. Ten years later, Apple Pay is finally here, but the payments landscape has changed considerably. The Unified Payments Interface (UPI) processed 24.51 Bn transactions worth ₹29.82 Lakh Cr in August 2026, as per the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). The question is whether Apple can find room in a market where consumers already have several ways to pay. Narrower Than The US Version Apple Pay allows users to add eligible cards to Apple Wallet and authenticate payments through Face ID, Touch ID or their device passcode. At physical stores, they can tap their devices against compatible contactless terminals. Online, they can pay without repeatedly entering card details. The India offering is narrower than the service available in the US, where customers can use cards from a wider range of participating banks and issuers. US users can also access Apple Cash for person-to-person money transfers, subject to eligibility. Apple has not announced a comparable service for India. At launch, Apple Pay supports eligible Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard credit cards. RuPay cards and cards from other banks are not supported under the initial rollout. This limits the number of consumers who can use the service, even among iPhone owners. Tarun Pathak of Counterpoint Research said Apple’s entry is late from both a global launch and competition standpoint, but pointed to regulatory requirements and the relatively small size of India’s installed iPhone base as possible reasons for the delay. “Clearance of regulatory and technical roadblocks allowed Apple to hold its standard global architecture when it comes to Apple Pay experience built around NFC card tokenisation, plus the native Apple ecosystem leveraging the security of Face ID, Touch ID, and Apple Watch integration for fast NFC tap-to-pay at POS terminals,” Pathak said. Apple’s approach keeps the payment experience tied to its own devices and security architecture. However, the restricted bank rollout means the company will need to expand its partnerships before the service can reach a wider customer base. UPI Poses A Challenge For Apple Pay UPI’s dominance presents a different challenge for Apple Pay. Unlike markets where card-based payment plays a larger role, India has built a digital payment ecosystem around direct bank-to-bank transfers, with consumers using apps such as PhonePe and Google Pay for everyday transactions. According to the Reserve Bank of India’s Payment System Report, December 2025, UPI accounted for 85.5% of digital transaction volume. This figure underlines how firmly UPI is embedded in India’s payment ecosystem, leaving Apple Pay to build adoption in a market where consumers already have an established way to pay. Apple Pay’s launch in India does not support UPI integration. Its initial use case is therefore centred on consumers who own compatible Apple devices and hold eligible credit cards. With Apple Pay, the company is offering contactless payments, but Apple will need to give users a reason to choose card-based payment through its devices when UPI is already widely available. The availability of tap-to-pay alone may not be enough to change consumer habits. Samsung Wallet already offers NFC-based payments on compatible Galaxy devices, alongside other wallet features. Despite Samsung supporting UPI payments, it has hardly made a dent. An industry insider who has worked in fintech told Inc42 that the service is unlikely to make a major difference to the sector in its current form. “Apple Pay launch is only restricted to Axis Bank, with no UPI integration. Even today Android users are around 90% of the mobile phone users. Apple Pay is just allowing you to save the card and pay via NFC,” the insider said. The insider also pointed to existing options for Android users, saying popular apps such as Phonepe have integrated card-based payment features for Visa and Mastercard users. The source expects some Apple users to adopt the service for high ticket purchases but does not see it as a threat to the fintech industry. The insider also questioned whether Apple would enter UPI, citing NPCI’s transaction data storage requirements and Apple’s policies of not storing transaction details. Can Apple Pay Drive Card Payments? Apple Pay’s entry could give a push to credit card transactions, particularly among iPhone users who prefer using cards for higher value purchases. Amrish Rau, MD and CEO of Pine Labs, had anticipated the service’s India entry before its launch, arguing that it could shift some transactions towards cards as credit card payments and UPI continue to grow. “We do believe Apple Pay will enter the market before the end of this year. What that is going to do is flip and create a spread in terms of how payment transactions will happen. More and more payment transactions will go back to credit cards, as credit cards plus UPI continue to grow in the market,” Rau said during the company’s Q1FY27 earnings discussion. Data from the Reserve Bank of India’s Payment System Report, December 2025 points to the growth in credit card spending. Credit card spending rose to ₹23.2 Lakh Cr in calendar year 2025, up from ₹8.9 Lakh Cr in 2021. Private banks also strengthened their position in the segment, accounting for 71.1% of outstanding credit cards. Debit card usage, meanwhile, has moved in the opposite direction. Transaction volumes fell 67% between CY2021 and CY2025, as consumers increasingly shifted to UPI for everyday payments. The divergence matters for Apple Pay. While UPI has become a common choice for routine transfers and purchases, credit cards continue to serve consumers looking for credit, rewards and payment flexibility. Apple pay could make card payments more convenient by allowing users to tap their devices at compatible terminals instead of carrying a physical card. However, growth in credit card spending does not automatically translate into demand for Apple Pay. Besides, its reach will also depend on how many consumers are willing to change their existing payment habits. For Apple, the immediate opportunity may be to increase the frequency with which existing users pay by card through its devices. Whether that translates into a meaningful shift in India’s payment mix will depend on wider bank support, merchant acceptance and consumer adoption. India women’s long-serving captain 
Harmanpreet Kaur
 has stepped down from captaincy in all three formats. The 37-year-old said she had fulfilled her responsibility as captain and is now ready to return to the game without the pressure of leading the side.
“Today, I step down as captain of the Indian Women's Cricket Team across all formats,” she posted on her Instagram account.
‘This is not an easy decision’
Harmanpreet said giving up the captaincy was an emotional decision after years of leading India.
“This is not an easy decision. It carries years of memories, emotions, sacrifices, and moments that will stay with me for the rest of my life,” Harmanpreet said in a lengthy statement.
She also made it clear that stepping down as captain does not mean the end of her international career.
“Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again. Captaincy ends. The journey continues,” she added.
A decade as T20I captain
Harmanpreet took charge of India’s T20I team in 2016 and remained in the role for 10 years. She became the ODI captain in 2022 before taking over as the all-format leader in 2023.
Her time as captain included some of India women’s biggest achievements. 
Under her leadership, India won their maiden ODI World Cup in November last year and recently secured a second successive Asian Games gold in the T20 format.
Harmanpreet said she was stepping away from leadership with confidence in the team’s future.
“I’m leaving the captaincy with a heart full of emotions, but also with peace,” she said.
“Because I genuinely believe my team is in a good place,” she said.

Consumers of electricity in Telangana, except those availing energy to run their agricultural pump-sets, are in for yet another shocker with the Telangana Electricity Regulatory Commission (TGERC) approving true-up charges of ₹5,420.23 crore to be collected from consumers other than farm power consumers, for energy consumed during 2022-23 and 2023-24.
What are true-up charges?
The true-up charges are the cost of difference for energy already consumed — the difference between cost of power supplied and the price recovered from consumers. Increase in the cost of supply is attributed to unexpected spike in fuel, power purchase and operational costs.
The total true-up charges approved stand at ₹7,635.22 crore including ₹2,214.99 crore for energy consumed by agricultural pump-sets, which is being provided free of cost. The Commission suggested the two Discoms to approach the State government for recovery of true-up charges pertaining to energy used for agricultural pump-sets.
₹0.30 per unit in November, ₹0.50 per unit in December
Accordingly, ₹0.30 (30 paise) per unit would be recovered from domestic, commercial, industrial and for lift irrigation schemes from the monthly bills to be issued in November and ₹0.50 (50 paise) per unit from December onwards. The recovery or burden of true-up charges would be for 29 months in case of consumers of the Southern Power Distribution Company of Telangana Ltd (TGSPDCL) and for 26 months from consumers of the Northern Power Distribution Company of Telangana Ltd (TGNPDCL).
What does it mean for domestic consumers?
A household consuming 200 units of energy a month for instance, would have to pay an additional charge of ₹60 in the bill to be issued in November ₹100 from December onwards, till March 2029 in case of consumers of TGSPDCL and till December 2028 in case of TGNPDCL consumers.
In its order passed on Monday (October 5, 2026), the TGERC stated that the total true-up charges of ₹7,635.22 crore include ₹5,186.29 crore of power purchase true-up for 2022-23 and ₹2,448.93 crore of revenue true-up charges for 2023-24. Of the total approved true-ups, the per unit recovery works out to ₹0.80 per unit for 2022-23 and ₹0.33 per unit for 2023-24.
Recovery charges to span 29 months for TGSPDCL consumers
The total recovery from consumers in TGSPDCL would be ₹4222.93 crore across 29 months and ₹1197.3 crore from consumers in TGNPDCL limits across 26 months from November 2026.
The approved energy sales for 2022-23 were 64,434.42 million units (MU) including 17,629.25 MU for agricultural pump-sets and for 2023-24 they were 74,442.36 MU including 25,154.04 MU for agricultural use. The Discoms have charged ₹798.87 crore more than cost of supply from consumers during 2024-25 and it would be adjusted in the annual revenue requirement of the retail supply business for 2026-27, the current year.

This past year, OpenAI, Anthropic, and other labs have announced breakthroughs on numerous long-standing mathematical problems, in some cases pushing well beyond what researchers expected current systems to be capable of — including resolving one of the famous Millennium Prize problems. But in classic Silicon Valley style, AI labs are moving fast and breaking things, barreling through the discipline with all the grace of a runaway bulldozer. Results that might normally have been celebrated have instead sparked backlash. AI labs say they are learning from earlier mistakes. Whether those promises bear fruit remains to be seen.
Read on below for the latest updates in the AI takeover of mathematics.
- OpenAI keeps bulldozing mathematicians In a chaotic few months, OpenAI has demonstrated it can do two things with remarkable consistency: make impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, then colossally screw up announcing them. OpenAI is now trying to do better. Somehow, it has botched that too. OpenAI’s latest attempt to repair fractured relations with a mathematical community it has repeatedly alienated is to consult a new independent advisory group of elite practitioners. But mathematicians speaking to The Verge, including one of the group’s members, describe a messy and confusing affair bearing many of the hallmarks of OpenAI’s previous rushed forays into mathematics, suggesting the company has learned little from its mistakes. And then there’s the daunting task the group has been handed first: helping coordinate the release of scores more results OpenAI says its unreleased model has produced, the prospect of which is already stirring dread among researchers over what this looming tidal wave of breakthroughs could do to their field. Read Article >
- OpenAI wants to consult elite mathematicians about how to not fumble again After turning a string of spectacular mathematical results into a reputational crisis, OpenAI is consulting human mathematicians to help it figure out a less disastrous path forward. On Monday, the company announced a new independent panel of mathematicians tasked with advising it and other AI companies on their interactions with mathematical research and the wider mathematics community, including how new results are presented and released. Its abrupt arrival caught many mathematicians by surprise. Researchers told The Verge the group is a good first step, but many said they were left with basic questions about what it will actually do, how much influence it will have, and whether OpenAI will actually listen to it, as well as concerns over whether such a small group of prominent researchers can represent the wider mathematical community. Read Article >
- OpenAI just wants to win OpenAI has spent the last few years planting flags across the increasingly difficult terrain in mathematics. This week, it claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem. In normal circumstances, this would have been celebrated as a historic achievement. Instead, many mathematicians have watched OpenAI’s relentless advance with growing unease. To them, the company appears less like an enthusiastic newcomer than an impossibly well-resourced interloper, charging into problems they have dedicated their lives to studying with little apparent regard for long-standing norms or the consequences for those left in its wake. At the heart of that unease is a sense that OpenAI is doing mathematics for different reasons. Mathematicians want to advance the field. OpenAI wants to win. Read Article >
- Mathematicians want proof OpenAI didn’t use their work Another researcher is challenging OpenAI about the data driving its increasingly impressive array of mathematical discoveries. Just days after a bitter row erupted over whether the company’s models benefited from unpublished work, a second mathematician has come forward accusing the AI giant of unethical and “dishonest” behavior and a lack of transparency about the origins of its training data. In a series of posts on Mastodon, mathematician Andreas Thom raised concerns that interactions he and his colleagues had had with the ChatGPT chatbot before OpenAI’s triumphant announcement may have contributed to its success in the field. One of the 10 results OpenAI announced with great fanfare last month involved Thom’s area of expertise, so-called non-sofic groups, and OpenAI acknowledged that their result built heavily on previous work by Thom and fellow mathematician Gábor Kun. Read Article >
- OpenAI’s sly mathematical breakthrough sends a chill through academia OpenAI’s announcement Tuesday that it has solved one of mathematics’ legendary Millennium Prize problems should have been a moment of triumph. The result is both an undeniable achievement and a striking demonstration of just how rapidly AI is transforming mathematics. But before it was even formally announced, the breakthrough had been complicated by the unusual circumstances that prompted OpenAI to pursue the problem: After hearing other researchers were making progress, it seems to have thrown its considerable resources into a last-minute effort to beat them to the punch. The ensuing controversy has surfaced allegations of scooping, spying, and flagrant violations of long-standing academic norms that researchers fear could have a chilling effect on the field. As Abhishek Saha, a mathematics professor at Queen Mary University of London, explains it, OpenAI has engaged in the “kind of things that mathematicians will generally not do.” Read Article >
- Drama swirls around OpenAI’s legendary mathematical milestone OpenAI says it found a solution to a major math problem that has remained unsolved for around 90 years, as reported earlier by The New York Times and Wired. In a blog post on Tuesday, OpenAI announced that it discovered a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem — which relates to the flow of liquid and gas — using an internal AI model more powerful than the newly released GPT-6 Astra alongside 10,000 concurrent agents. The Navier-Stokes problem is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million reward for solving. OpenAI says it started training the internal AI model on August 28th, which has “exhibited unprecedented performance in our benchmarks, including mathematics.” The solution is a big breakthrough for the mathematics community, but it doesn’t come without controversy. Read Article >
- Welcome to the AI crisis in math Today on Decoder, I’m talking with Robert Hart, The Verge’s London-based AI reporter, about what AI is doing to the field of mathematics and the existential crisis many lead mathematicians are having about it. OpenAI just published a set of solutions to longstanding problems in math that went off like a bombshell in the field. It caused a huge debate in the math community, and Rob spent some time talking to some of the most accomplished mathematicians of our time about it. Read Article >
- The AI takeover of mathematics has begun Mathematician James Maynard has spent a lot of time this past year “soul searching.” A professor at the University of Oxford and winner of the prestigious Fields Medal, Maynard told The Verge he’s been grappling with the future of his field as the traditionally slow-moving discipline hurries to adapt to AI. Days before we spoke, OpenAI revealed it had produced the solutions to 10 long-standing mathematics problems, some of which had confounded academics for decades. Like generative AI used to produce text and images or propose ideas in science and medicine, the technology learns patterns and connections from the vast amount of material it’s trained on and uses them to create something new. Applied to mathematics, that can mean combining known results, methods, and tools in new ways to attack a problem, sometimes drawing links between disparate fields or resurfacing concepts buried in academic literature. John Lee promises ‘high-quality’ experience for Apec finance meeting guests
City leader says Beijing is handling attendee registration without confirming whether US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is among the guests
Hong Kong’s leader has pledged to provide guests attending this month’s Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting with a “high-quality” experience, as the city works closely with Beijing to assist delegations with the registration process.
About 500 guests, including finance ministers and senior officials from the 21 member economies, are expected to attend the annual meeting on October 20 and 21, which will be hosted by Hong Kong for the first time at the Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai.
Asked whether US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent would attend the summit, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Tuesday only that the Ministry of Finance in mainland China was handling attendee registration.
“The Hong Kong government will continue to maintain close communication and cooperation with the Ministry of Finance to assist the delegation in completing the registration procedures,” Lee said ahead of the Executive Council meeting.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to another working week. We hope the weekend respite was relaxing and invigorating. Now, though, that oh-too-familiar routine of meetings, deadlines, and the like has returned with a vengeance. You knew this would happen, yes? After all, the world — such as it is — continues to spin. So to nudge it in a better direction, we are relying, as always, on a cuppa stimulation. Our choice today is blueberry hibiscus. Of course, you are welcome to join us. Meanwhile, here are a few items of interest. Best of luck accomplishing your goals, and we hope you conquer the world. And, of course, do keep in touch. …
Vaxcyte disclosed that its experimental pneumococcal vaccine hit the primary endpoints in a Phase 3 clinical trial, setting up a competition with Pfizer and Merck, STAT writes. Vaxcyte’s shot, VAX-31, is designed to protect against 31 serotypes, or strains, of bacteria that can cause pneumococcal disease, including pneumonia, compared to 20 strains for Pfizer’s Prevnar and 21 strains for Merck’s Capvaxive. The company needs two more trials to deliver results before it can file for approval: a study looking at VAX-31 administered alongside an influenza vaccine and a study in adults who previously received a different pneumococcal shot.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has extended its review of an experimental hemophilia A drug from Novo Nordisk due to ongoing remediation work at a manufacturing facility, Reuters notes. Novo had submitted the application for the drug, called denecimig, in September 2025 and was expecting an FDA decision in the third quarter of 2026. While the regulator has not yet set a new timeline for its decision, Novo said the FDA did not raise any concerns regarding the safety or effectiveness data from the drug’s clinical trials. Novo added that the manufacturing site issues do not impact any of its other medicines currently on the market.

Seventy years ago last summer, a group of scientists met at Dartmouth College to discuss a wild idea—that machines might one day be capable of human-like thought processes. One of those scientists, John McCarthy, had suggested a name for the new field: artificial intelligence. It stuck. When you search Google Scholar for “artificial intelligence,” approximately 7,420,000 results appear. The term is utterly ubiquitous. Everyone understands it. Even for people who despise AI, the least of their worries is what we call it.
Well, not everyone. Somehow, President Donald J. Trump developed a distaste for the term, and when he doesn’t like something, he feels free to issue an edict against it. In a September 23 speech at the United Nations, he hinted that he might want to do away with the term “artificial intelligence.” His rant seemed like bluster, even for someone with a penchant for renaming gulfs, lakes, and centers for the arts. Renaming an entire field of study and America’s most pivotal industry? This week, at a White House lunch with top AI leaders, he actually pulled the trigger with an executive order declaring that “artificial intelligence” was now a verboten coinage. Instead, the government will call it “Super Intelligence.” Clearly the president expects the private sector to follow suit.
To their shame, the lords of AI meekly acquiesced. From this point on, they will presumably be known as the lords of SI.
One can’t help but see this as the ultimate presidential flex—for all the executives’ trillions of dollars and all their actual intelligence, the alpha in the room was the guy with the orange skin. Changing a name might seem like a minor matter compared to the enormity of constraining a potentially catastrophic technology. But to this crowd, artificial intelligence is much more than a bunch of letters strung together. It’s their foundation. Their identity. When they were kids reading science fiction books under the covers, the term ignited their imaginations.They built or transformed their companies in service of AI, and it's just about all they’ve talked about for the past four years.
Yet when the president used his lunch soiree to win their approval for his wacky idea to undo 70 years of history, apparently not a single person in the room expressed an objection. Not Jeff Bezos, Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Greg Brockman, Alex Karp, or Elon Musk.
Jacob Weisberg, author of the recent book Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era, views the episode as a classic Trump loyalty test, meant to assess if otherwise powerful people will demean themselves to curry the president’s favor and avoid his wrath. If you pass the loyalty test, you fail the backbone test. “The only way to resist this kind of thing is by acting collectively,” says Weisberg. “If all of those guys had just said, ‘We'll agree to the terms of the self-regulation, but we don't accept [the name change], what would he have done?”
Instead, because of the lamb-like silence of the billionaires, Trump could claim that those leaders actively blessed his idea. When a reporter in the post-lunch press gaggle mentioned AI agents, he corrected her, saying, “The name has been changed by the biggest, the, smartest, the greatest people anywhere in the world.” Really?
Even using the magic of, uh, superintelligent systems like ChatGPT or Gemini, I could not find a single instance of any one of those great people previously politicking that the term artificial intelligence should be put to rest. Satya Nadella did once say that he would have preferred that AI had been called “different intelligence,” but that hasn’t dissuaded him from repeatedly using the term. And while it’s true that Mark Zuckerberg recently established a Superintelligence Lab, his company persistently pushes a product called Meta AI to its billions of users and sells what it calls AI glasses.
I asked Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI, and xAI whether they were going to change instances of AI in their product names, research papers, and communications. My query to the latter two was whether they were going to change their company names to get in sync with the presidential order. As I write this, none of them have gotten back to me.
My bet is that they will do the minimum to avoid presidential ire, while trying to run out the clock until the next administration puts this bizarre idea out of its misery. It’s been suggested that the executives actually welcome a rebranding of what has become a toxic term. I’m skeptical of that, especially since the president’s mandated replacement, “super intelligence,” is a hell of a lot scarier than the original term.
From a scientific perspective the change also makes no sense. No less an expert than Nick Bostrom, the philosopher who popularized the term superintelligence in an eponymous book, seems baffled by the idea. Superintelligence, he explained to me in an email, “refers specifically to systems that greatly surpass all the best human brains. ‘AI’ has referred to a much broader category of systems, which includes, for example, email spam filters, spell checkers, simple navigation systems, early LLMs, and the chess engines of the ’70s that didn’t yet match the best human chess players. It seems awkward to refer to these as ‘superintelligent.’”
So what is the president’s reason for demanding the change, besides because he can? In his UN speech, he said he didn’t like the term because “the word ‘artificial’ makes intelligence fake. And it is not fake.” What is fake, he said after the White House lunch, is the term “artificial intelligence.” “It’s a fake word, it’s not good, an inappropriate term.” You don’t need to be a psychologist to see how this impulse might be associated with his decision to bounce CNN, Politico, and MSNow from the White House, because he perceives their news as “fake.”
Still, the leap that equates artificial with fake doesn’t track. In 1956, McCarthy used it to distinguish between human intelligence and the machine version of intelligence. The problem isn’t that the term leads people to regard AI’s output as fake—in fact, it’s so real that we human beings often can’t tell whether we’re dealing with an AI model or a human. Mandating that the distinction be explicit, with watermarks and labels, should be one element of the AI regulation that the White House seems allergic to.
As Weisberg notes, it’s very much in character for Trump to make a crazy edict like this one. What’s disturbing is the glaring lack of character from the executives who didn’t push back. They left with the prize of self-regulation instead of strict oversight, but not with their dignity.
But failure to defend the freedom to refer to artificial intelligence as artificial intelligence (as California governor Gavin Newsom decreed in his own Trump-trolling executive order) casts doubt on even that agreement. Making voluntary standards effective requires considerable fortitude, as prioritizing safety can be at odds with financial and competitive factors. Yet we are being asked to trust these supposedly independent corporate giants who nodded like bobbleheads while a technologically unschooled crank-in-chief demanded they abandon the term at the center of their lives and livelihoods. Inappropriate, and fake.

- Published
The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) would "look at" the unusual step of funding a women's Test in the West Indies next year in order to aid England's Ashes preparations.
The Test in the Caribbean, part of a multi-format series in the spring of 2027, was announced in 2024 and is scheduled before England's bid to regain the Ashes from Australia.
Last week, Cricket West Indies (CWI) announced a wide range of money-saving measures, including cuts to player contracts.
In March, a women's Test that West Indies were due to host against Australia was cancelled, though the white-ball element of that tour went ahead.
There have been no discussions between the ECB and CWI about cancelling the Test.
The tour as a whole – including three T20s and three one-day internationals in April and May of next year – is not under threat, though exact dates and venues are still to be confirmed.
Asked by BBC Sport if the Test was in doubt, ECB chair Richard Thompson said: "I hope not. That's not expected to be cancelled. I hope it will take place."
However, when it was put to Thompson that the ECB may need to provide some funding for the Test to take place, he said his organisation would "look at" the situation should it arise.
Governing bodies usually have reciprocal arrangements for the home board to pick up the logistical expenses of the visiting team, including things like travel and accommodation.
In the West Indies, these can be inflated by the cost of flying West Indies and visiting players between islands. Last week, CWI said it has spent more than $80m on domestic air travel in the past 15 years.
Thompson pointed to a similarly unusual situation when the Zimbabwe men's team played a Test in England last year, with the ECB paying the visitors a touring fee.
"We want that Test match to play out," said Thompson. "It's very important for us because our first women's match in the Ashes is the Headingley Test, so we need a good red-ball warm-up.
"We've got to be playing somewhere and we'd much prefer that to be the West Indies.
"We all have a huge sympathy for the West Indies, we all want to see a successful West Indian nation. They have very unique challenges and I hope through the International Cricket Council and others we can find a way through this."
The first match of the multi-format women's Ashes series is the sole Test at Headingley in June – the only Test, men's or women's, staged north of Nottingham next summer.
England have played one Test since they lost every game on the Ashes tour of Australia in early 2025 – a defeat by India at Lord's earlier this year.
They have not played West Indies in a women's Test since 1979, while West Indies have not played a Test against anyone since a trip to Pakistan in 2004.
The Test in West Indies is one part of England's Ashes Test preparations. In January, the squad will take part in a 10-day red-ball training camp in India.
In 2023, England played Australia A and Australia played England A as Test warm-up matches and that arrangement could be replicated in 2027. Plans for domestic players to potentially be involved in some red-ball cricket in the early part of next season are also being finalised.
Thompson was speaking at Lord's as the ECB launched initiatives to take cricket to more than 1,700 state secondary schools and more than 3,500 teachers.
'Cricket for Teachers' and 'Secondary Countdown Cricket' are part of the ECB's aim to reach half of all state secondary schools in England and Wales by the end of 2028.
Earlier this year, a report by the Sutton Trust found cricket to be one of the most elitist jobs in the country, with 59% of male professionals and 50% of women privately educated.
"We really want teachers to upskill and be able to coach," said Thompson. "The second part is to be able to do something no other team sport can do, which is bring boys and girls together until the age of 16.
"This adds to the pathway. It's another stepping stone for a late developer, or an opportunity for someone to think they want to play the game properly, with a hardball.
"It's meaningful in that we want to reach one and a half million children who have never played the game before. That's a significant programme and the ambition that sits behind this."

Andrew Garfield admits he was initially charmed by Sam Altman before he portrayed the controversial CEO of OpenAI in director Luca Guadagnino’s new film “Artificial.”
“I remember seeing Sam testifying to Congress for the first time, way back when,” Garfield said on Monday night at the movie’s world premiere at the New York Film Festival. “I was like, ‘This guy seems fucking great. He’s honest. He’s transparent. He’s talking about regulation, and he has no stake in OpenAI. We need more of these people in control. He’s incredibly charming and charismatic.’ And then you learn more about a person.”
Garfield, who spent “two to three months” listening and watching footage of Altman while preparing to play him, described feeling a moral responsibility to participate in a movie like “Artificial.” When they were filming, Garfield recalls, “there were news stories coming out every day” about the dangers of AI.
Popular on Variety
“I wish we could give it even more teeth in a way,” Garfield said. “We need to shine the light as bright as possible at the nooks and crannies of people we’re giving all of our autonomy and power to.”
Garfield was joined at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall by Guadagnino, writer Simon Rich and actors Yura Borisov (as OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever), Ike Barinholtz (as Elon Musk) and Cooper Hoffman (as OpenAI president Greg Brockman). Monica Barbaro, who portrays OpenAI’s chief technology officer Mira Murati, wasn’t in attendance. The movie charts the evolution of OpenAI and dramatizes the tumultuous time when Altman was controversially fired and then rehired by the AI giant.
Garfield has portrayed many real people on screen, including Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in “The Social Network” and composer Jonathan Larson in “Tick, Tick… Boom.” It’s a responsibility the actor doesn’t take lightly.
“I feel a tremendous amount of compassion for what that must feel like, being on the inside of his soul, going like, ‘That’s not me,’” Garfield said of Altman. “I imagine it would feel confronting. I would feel that way. I’m projecting.”
In any case, the real Altman seems to be shrugging off “Artificial,” which he hasn’t seen. “I mean, they’re trying to make a good movie, and maybe it will be good,” Altman said in a wide-ranging interview with Vanity Fair, adding that “it will not be good as an accurate depiction.”
Borisov, a recent Oscar nominee for “Anora,” admits he’s worried about what the real-life Sutskever — and the public — will think about the film.
“I can’t answer so beautiful like Andrew. That’s why he’s playing Sam,” Borisov joked. “I was nervous to watch this. It was our first time. [I have] so much feeling now about this. It’s like a child just being born, and you’re waiting for it to start breathing.”
Barinholtz, meanwhile, doesn’t seem too concerned about Musk’s reaction.
“When you’re playing as someone universally beloved as Elon, and who everyone admires and who is a good person and walks normally…,” Barinholtz cracked. “When I first met with Luca, I said, ‘I have very complicated opinions on Elon.’ And he said, ‘It’s not about what you feel about Elon. It’s about finding what he loves about himself.’
Barinholtz found it “interesting” to play Musk at this particular moment in time. “It’s not at the RNC with the chainsaw. This is him in 2014 when a lot of people were like, ‘This guy is amazing. He’s going to save you.'”
Rich, a humorist who worked at “Saturday Night Live” and penned the 2020 satire “An American Pickle,” was inadvertently motivated to write “Artificial” by his childhood friend, Danny Selsam.
“He started warning me about artificial intelligence in 2008. My friends and I were so shocked by his predictions that we actually discussed potentially doing an intervention to get them medicated, or perhaps institutionalized. We thought he lost his mind,” Rich said. “We took him a little bit more seriously when he joined this new nonprofit called OpenAI.”
A year before ChatGPT was released, Rich says, “Danny started showing us stuff on his computer that was so terrifying that I felt the urge to warn people. When I told journalists what I had seen, they thought it was a hoax. They thought I was trying to prank them.”
Rich tried to vocalize his concerns, writing about the dangers in columns for outlets like Time magazine. But the public failed to take notice.
	“I quickly realized there’s a limit to what I can do being a non-celebrity and not particularly charismatic or good-looking,” Rich said. “So this is kind of a last-ditch effort to warn mankind. I wrote this movie and
I hope to god that a couple people pay attention.”
A late addition to the NYFF lineup, “Artificial” became one of the year’s buzziest releases after Amazon MGM dropped the nearly completed film, saying the movie would be “better served if it were released by a different studio.” That’s after Amazon signed a major $50 billion partnership with OpenAI. And Altman is close with Amazon chief Jeff Bezos, having attended his Venetian wedding to Lauren Sanchez in 2025.
Neon ultimately acquired “Artificial” and plans to release the film in theaters on Dec. 25.
Landing the world premiere of “Artificial” was a coup for NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim, who described the movie’s festival plans as a “genuinely up-in-the-air situation.” Lim noted that Guadagnino has a long history with New York Film Festival, having premiered movies such as “Call Me by Your Name,” “Bones and All,” “Queer” and “After the Hunt” at prior editions.
“I thought we would be a great launchpad for the film,” Lim told Variety prior to the premiere. “This is a film that deals with a very pressing situation. AI is in the news practically daily. The film recaps this trajectory that we’ve been on with alarming clarity. And it does this in the form of an incredibly entertaining movie. It has a very dark humor, which is certainly one valid way of approaching the dystopian present.”
