This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Oliver Kharraz, the 53-year-old CEO and cofounder of Zocdoc, based in New York City. It's been edited for length and clarity.
I grew up in Germany and attended college in Munich. I got an MD and a doctorate in neuroscience. I became the most recent doctor in a 300-year family tradition, and previously practiced clinically.
During college, I built my first company. I provided internet access to a few local companies and offered data storage and remote access solutions. I had the choice to either drop out of college and make it internet-ready or sell it. I sold it in 1994.
I then spent seven years at McKinsey as an associate principal, which was great training for me — it was sort of a prelude to some of the things I had to do at Zocdoc later. I worked at the Munich office, then transferred to the New York office in 2004.
I started Zocdoc, an online service that lets people find and book in-person or telehealth appointments for medical or dental care, in 2007 with two cofounders, one of whom I met at McKinsey. We were in the process of starting several companies and discussing our personal experiences with the healthcare system. As we talked, it became clear to us that this was a better opportunity than what we were pursuing separately.
I became the CEO in November 2015. Here's a typical day in my life.
I wake up naturally at 4:30 a.m. after four to five hours of sleep
I've always been an early riser and feel most productive in the hours before sunrise.
I grab my phone and look at the company numbers. I have several reports that the system automatically sends, so they're waiting in my inbox. I look at our KPIs, and if something looks off, I might shoot off a couple of questions to the team. I frequently send those out with an 8 a.m. timer, so people don't get scared about why the CEO sends emails in the middle of the night.
I then read for half an hour, a mix of history, biography, philosophy, and health industry news.
I then exercise for 30 minutes
This is a newer addition to my routine, despite my medical background. At my age, I try to alternate between cardio and weights and aim to keep my pulse consistently above 140.
After working out, I take a long shower to think and brainstorm
Once a week, I dedicate this shower session to imagining a hypothetical competitor to Zocdoc and how they would try to put us out of business. This mental exercise is key to staying ahead of threats.
I find that setting aside time in the shower to process the information I've taken in over the last 24 hours is helpful. I take long, warm showers, nearly in sensory-deprivation mode. I think the main job of the CEO is to be a bit of an oracle, predicting the future.
After my long shower, I enjoy family time with my wife and daughters over breakfast
I would say I make breakfast half the time, and my wife makes it the other half. I'm increasingly skipping carbs and choosing Greek yogurt, nuts, seeds, and maybe some berries. The rest of the family still eats bread, and so there's bread, butter, honey, jam, and eggs.
I then drive my twin teen daughters to school and deliver my own dad podcast filled with family history and important lessons. I do what I can to give them a frame of reference for the very complicated world around them, values, an understanding of incentives, and how to get things done.
Depending on traffic, it takes 15 to 20 minutes to get to the office after dropping my kids off at school
I live in Brooklyn and drive to the Zocdoc office in SoHo. I go into the office five days a week because it's important to me to be in person.
When I arrive at the office, my calendar is stacked with 10 hours of back-to-back meetings and work blocks, all aimed at Zocdoc's next stage — planning up to five years into the future, managing risk, creating a bigger moat, and always keeping the company three steps ahead (thanks to my shower sessions).
I have a weekly meeting with a core group of lieutenants to review macro updates on the company. I then have one-on-ones with a lot of my leadership team. I also have office hours where anyone can book time with me and chat about any topic.
One of my philosophies is that while I'm working, I keep my office door open, so anyone is welcome to walk in and chat to me about whatever they think I should know.
I sometimes get around to a formal lunch, but I'm not consistent
If I do have lunch, I mostly eat a few hard-boiled eggs and some Sriracha. It's quick, gives me a set number of calories, and is high in protein.
After lunch, I have more meetings, but I spend a good chunk of time external-facing, talking to customers. I also speak to regulators, investors, and prospective partners.
I use AI extensively and believe that leaders who ask their teams to use it should lead by example and use it themselves first. I created an AI Chief of Staff to handle rote work, challenge my thinking, explore ideas, and surface second-order effects.
A common AI prompt I use is: "Argue the opposite side and tell me what I'm missing." On the personal side, I've also been using AI to build tools that take more admin off my family's plate.
I leave the office anywhere between 7 p.m. and 10 p.m
On the drive home, I listen to news and audiobooks at 1.5x to 3x speed. Although I drive to work, I take the subway throughout the day to and from external meetings as needed.
I have dinner with the family and spend some time with the kids. A point of pride for me is that my kids still love it when I help with their homework, even though they're teenagers and know everything.
My mother-in-law lived with us for 13 years. She was excellent for the family's nutrition, and she had her repertoire, so we mostly ate that. More recently, we've gone a lot broader and mixed up our diet. We go out to eat on weekends, and we're all foodies.
After the kids go to bed, my wife and I spend time together. We'll watch some TV and enjoy "Only Murders in the Building", "South Park," "Succession," and "Industry." Sometimes we watch movies as well.
My wife and I say goodnight at 10 p.m., and then I go to sleep.
I try to minimize work on the weekends, but I do work
My theory is I belong to Zocdoc from 4 a.m. on Monday until 10 p.m. on Friday, and then I belong to my family. It's not to say there aren't the occasional work trips, meetings, or calls on the weekends, but I try to minimize them.
We spend a lot of time together as a family on the weekend. I enjoy reading philosophy and history for fun. I also enjoy fishing.

WASHINGTON — Stem cell entrepreneur Chuck Meeker is bullish about his industry’s prospects with the Food and Drug Administration nowadays.
“If I were a betting man, I would say before the end of the year we have a series of FDA roundtables happening,” Meeker told STAT at PepMed 2026, a conference for regenerative health businesses held by the American Academy of Peptide Medicine. (The FDA declined to say whether such events were imminent.)
That stem cells made an appearance at a conference centered on peptides isn’t a coincidence. Peptides and stem cells are two peas in the pod of regenerative medicine, which focuses on therapies that claim to trigger the body’s natural healing mechanisms. But while compounded peptides are having a bit of a moment with the FDA, commercially available, unapproved stem cell therapies have remained a black sheep for the agency.
Meeker and others at PepMed told STAT they believe that’s about to change. The stem cell industry sees the FDA’s tentative embrace of peptides as its chance to get a foot in the door — and bring stem cells from the grey market to millions of Americans.

Northern Ireland vs Georgia; UEFA Nations League Group B2
Northern Ireland vs Georgia. UEFA Nations League Group B2.
Clearer Twist National Stadium at Windsor Park.
Northern Ireland 0-0 Georgia: Liverpool's Giorgi Mamardashvili saves late Isaac Price penalty in Nations League stalemate
Match report from the UEFA Nations League Group B2 match between Northern Ireland and Georgia at Windsor Park; Liverpool goalkeeper Giorgi Mamardashvili saves Isaac Price's late penalty in stalemate
Monday 5 October 2026 22:04, UK
Isaac Price missed a late penalty as Northern Ireland were held to a goalless draw by Georgia which nevertheless keeps them top of their Nations League group.
Liverpool goalkeeper Giorgi Mamardashvili guessed right to keep out Price's 84th-minute spot-kick after a combination of Nodar Lominadze and Saba Sazonov fouled Ruairi McConville as he sent a header against the crossbar during a goalmouth scramble.
Jamie Donley and Josh Magennis also brought saves out of Mamardashvili and Tom Atcheson felt he had should have had a first-half penalty, but Northern Ireland were held to a stalemate for the second time in a week at Windsor Park.
Georgia, still yet to score in this season's Nations League, responded to their 1-0 loss to Northern Ireland in Tbilisi 11 days ago by sacking Willy Sagnol, but Ramaz Svanadze is still awaiting his first win in charge despite Khvicha Kvaratskhelia showing flashes of his brilliance in the second half.
Northern Ireland started the night as the only side yet to concede in this season's Nations League, and Pierce Charles made big saves from Zuriko Davitashvili and Giorgi Tsitaishvili to make it four competitive clean sheets in a row for the first time since 2017.
The 21-year-old goalkeeper's seventh clean sheet in nine competitive appearances ensured Michael O'Neill's side remain top of Group B2 by a single point from Hungary.
Northern Ireland's confidence showed in their positive early intent but it took time to wear down a Georgia side who stubbornly defended their box.
McConville was first to test Mamardashvili as he met Justin Devenny's cross but his header was pushed to safety.
With the Northern Ireland fans singing 'Who are you?' at Ballon d'Or nominee Kvaratskhelia the visitors fashioned the clearest chance yet as Davitashvili wriggled free and hit a powerful strike that brought an excellent save from Pierce Charles.
Northern Ireland were soon back in the ascendancy, and when Trai Hume's long throw was allowed to bounce in the box, an improvised looping effort from Donley had Mamardashvili scrambling back.
Patrick Kelly then charged into the box but made the wrong choice in trying to find Donley as his cross was picked off, and Atcheson could not believe he was the one penalised in a clash with Sazonov but the decision was confirmed by a VAR check.
Northern Ireland struggled to replicate that fluidity after the break with some loose passing, and there was a further blow just after the hour when Ethan Galbraith, full of ideas on his return to the side after welcoming a baby boy, hobbled off.
Georgia were growing in confidence, and Pierce Charles did well to gather a deflected strike from Tsitaishvili before Kvaratskhelia blazed over.
It ended chaotically. When Shea Charles won the ball on the edge of the box it ran for Magennis who forced the save from Mamardashvili.
From the resulting corner, McConville got up but took a boot in the face Lominadze and a shove from Sazonov, with Austrian referee Sebastian Gishamer awarding the penalty after being sent to the screen.
Price, who scored his first goal in 10 internationals against Ukraine on Friday, stepped up but it was a comfortable save for the Georgia goalkeeper.
With almost the last kick of the game, Georgia appealed in vain for a penalty after Callum Marshall collided with Sazonov in the corner of the Northern Ireland box.

Editor’s note, October 4, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave. The one below was originally published last year.
When does trying to have a healthier baby become eugenics-y?
New genetic testing offers us the chance to create superbabies. It can come with unintended consequences.
This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. Submit your own question here.
My partner and I did IVF recently and luckily we ended up with several embryos. One of those will be implanted in me so I hopefully get pregnant. But which one?
My fertility clinic is encouraging me to do PGT-A testing, which would screen for things like Down syndrome and would also let me see the sex of each embryo so I could potentially choose whichever I want. (And to be honest, I really want a girl!) I’m also hearing about these new companies that can test embryos for all kinds of things — like how smart the kid might be, how tall they’ll get, and whether they’ll have a lower chance of getting breast cancer, diabetes, mental illness, stuff like that.
I don’t know how to feel about any of this. On the one hand, it feels weirdly eugenics-y to do so much tinkering with embryos, and I can’t help feeling a little pressured into overmedicalizing everything with these expensive tests. But then again, if I could do something to make my baby healthier and happier, don’t I kind of have to do everything in my power? What does a parent owe their child?
Dear Expecting,
This is such an exciting — and also confusing — time. You’re about to have your first kid, and that comes with all sorts of fears and insecurities and hopes and dreams. You want to do the right thing — no, the best thing! — for your child. It’s a beautiful impulse. Unfortunately, it makes it easy for companies to prey on you.
So let me walk you through what these companies can and can’t really provide. After we talk about the science, we can talk about the ethics.
The simpler test you mentioned, PGT-A, has been around since the 1990s. It can indeed screen for conditions like Down syndrome and let you see the sex of each embryo. Mind you, that doesn’t predict what gender your child will ultimately end up identifying with — more on that soon.
The newer testing you mentioned is called polygenic testing. The conditions it screens for are complex ones, influenced by thousands of genes. We’re talking about everything from breast cancer to depression. Some companies even offer screenings not for disease prevention, but for genetic enhancement — so you can select for a taller kid or a kid with higher IQ.
Polygenic testing companies claim to predict each embryo’s risk for each condition, and the potential reduction of risk you’ll get if you choose one embryo over another. As the statistical geneticist Sasha Gusev explains, it’s very, very easy to be misled by this claim. If the company claims to lower absolute risk of Type 2 diabetes by 12 percent, you might think this means, “The chance of my kid ever developing diabetes just went down by 12 percent — great!” But really what it means is that, all else equal, a kid who would’ve developed diabetes is likely now at the high end of pre-diabetes instead, or just develops diabetes a few years later. The same holds true for other conditions, like breast cancer. Sure, if your kid is going to develop diabetes or breast cancer, you’d rather they develop it later — but it’s not the bill of perfect health customers might imagine.
“Typical risk reduction estimates tend to exploit statistical assumptions to overstate their benefits and lead to confusion,” Gusev writes.

It’s also important to note that there’s a difference between a physical disease like cancer, which is straightforwardly and universally negative, and a complex mental health condition like depression. For one thing, polygenic scores don’t perform as well in psychiatry, as the psychologist Eric Turkheimer notes. Plus, most mental health conditions come in mild to moderate to severe forms, and it’s not clear that we should want to get rid of mild or moderate manifestations.
“Sure, it would be nice if no one ever got depressed, but what would that actually mean?” Turkheimer writes. “People are going to be sad, and the most modern models of psychiatric disorders view most of them as extremes on continuous dimensions of normal behavior. I don’t think we want some kind of genetic version of Soma.”
To give a personal example: I have generalized anxiety with some obsessive tendencies. Is that a major pain in the butt sometimes? You bet. But if I could wave a magic wand and get rid of it, would I? No. In my experience, this trait is linked to another trait I deeply value: my creativity. The same thing that propels me down rabbit holes of worry also propels me down rabbit holes of getting super curious about some topic, researching it into the wee hours of the morning, and then writing a novel or children’s book about it.
That brings me to one other scientific issue: pleiotropy. It’s a fancy term for a simple truth, which is that genes can have an effect on more than one trait. When it comes to behavioral polygenic testing, we actually know very little about which genes cause what — a gene that’s correlated with depression or anxiety may also be correlated with a bunch of other things. So, if everyone were to start selecting embryos to try to protect their kids from depression or anxiety, what would happen? We don’t know!
Pleiotropy is a scientific issue, but it’s also a moral issue, because in trying to protect your kid from a negative outcome, you could also be accidentally barring them from a positive one.
And that’s just the tip of the moral iceberg.
Another issue is the potential psychological harm that can result from commodifying our kids — treating them like consumer objects with selectable parts. Let’s say you use polygenic testing to try to select for high IQ. Even if the company’s predictor is right 80 percent of the time, that means it’s wrong 20 percent of the time. What happens if it’s wrong about your kid, and they end up with a low IQ instead of a high one? How will your kid feel? Unless you hide the truth from them, they’ll know that they are not what you wanted, that they failed to live up to the vision you went out of your way to chase.
The same goes for sex selection via good old PGT-A. I know you really want a girl. But what would happen if you select for a girl, and then your child grows up and turns out to be trans? They may feel an extra sense that they’re letting you down by not conforming to the gender expectations you had for them.
Then there are the ethical questions around unequal access. Polygenic testing isn’t cheap. (One company, Orchid, charges $2,500 per screened embryo. Test 10 embryos and that’ll cost you $25,000.) So, at least in the short term, that raises the specter of entrenching a caste system, where the gap between rich and poor expands dramatically as the rich get smarter and stronger.
Technologies tend to get cheaper over time, so maybe everyone will ultimately be able to afford polygenic testing. But that raises another problem: implicit coercion. If more and more of us make ourselves smarter and stronger, we may create a society in which everyone feels pressure to alter their child’s biology — even if they don’t want to. To refuse embryo selection would mean to put a child at a huge professional disadvantage, or to face moral condemnation for making “suboptimal” kids when optimization is possible. Society may no longer offer health insurance benefits or accommodations for kids with disabilities (or even non-enhanced IQ), reasoning that “it was the parents’ choice.”
Some philosophers, like Julian Savalescu, already argue that parents have a “moral obligation to create children with the best chance of the best life.” Polygenic testing companies love that argument; Orchid founder Noor Siddiqui tells parents that “the responsible decision” is to “protect their children” from disease, using language like, “What if you could have stopped it...but chose not to?” And we generally live in a culture that’s obsessed with optimization.
So it’s no wonder that you find yourself asking, “If I could do something to make my baby healthier and happier, don’t I kind of have to do everything in my power?”
It’s a view that will be very appealing to utilitarians, who believe the right action is the action that maximizes well-being or happiness. But maximizing principles can be dangerous. If we’re laser-focused on maximizing one value, however noble it may be, that can lead us to overlook a host of other important values. Think about diversity, for example; polygenic testing could lead to a less diverse world.
And it’s not even clear how to maximize well-being given that each embryo will have some downsides: How would you choose between one embryo with a slightly elevated risk for schizophrenia, another with a moderately elevated risk for cancer, and a third with a high risk for Alzheimer’s? You’d have to decide how to rank the importance of each condition, which would require a dizzying bit of moral math: How much weight do you put on the longevity associated with each condition, how much on patient-reported quality of life for each condition, and how much on your own ability to cope with each — and society’s ability (which will change over the years)? Plus, even if the screening does end up optimizing life for your individual child, it could have negative effects on the population level, for the reasons we covered above.
As the Nobel laureate Herbert Simon pointed out, many problems contain way more variables and way too much uncertainty for maximizing along a single axis to be feasible or even desirable. So it often makes sense to just go with an option that’s “good enough.” He coined the term “satisficing” — a portmanteau of “satisfying” and “sufficing” — to describe opting for this good enough choice.
What would satisficing look like in the context of embryos? If there’s a very serious condition that runs in your family — like Tay-Sachs or the BRCA mutation that markedly increases cancer risk — then I do think there’s a strong case for screening for that. These conditions are debilitating and can lead to early death. Nobody wants them. Genetic testing that lets us prevent them is an awesome gift.
Then there are conditions that can include suffering, like autism, but can also be very compatible with a happy life. Mental health conditions in particular are heavily socially constructed — a lot of the associated suffering comes about because society constructs a certain biological reality as a problem and doesn’t support the people who have it. In these cases, if you want to give your child a “good enough” or even “optimized” life, remember that you don’t have to achieve that by biological means; working to change the social environment can be just as important, and it doesn’t carry the societal risks associated with polygenic testing.
Ultimately, when considering what counts as a “good enough” life, each parent will draw the line in a slightly different place. And there’s a part of that that can’t be boiled down to objective facts about disease, because this is also about how well-resourced the parent feels — emotionally, socially, and financially — to deal with a certain condition. What feels manageable to one parent may feel crushingly hard to another.
So, I can’t tell you exactly which screenings to do and which to forgo. What I do want to tell you is to resist being bullied or shamed by others, especially those with a profit incentive to push you in a certain direction.
As the epidemiologist Abby Lippman has noted, genetic testing is supposed to offer parents more choice, but it too often has the opposite effect. When someone like Orchid’s Siddiqui says about a disease, “What if you could have stopped it...but chose not to?” — well, that language preys on parents’ worst fears and insecurities. It holds parents hostage while pretending to be giving them more autonomy.
You are nobody’s hostage. You are a moral agent free to look at the many different relevant factors, weigh them all in the balance, and then make the choice that works well enough for your family.
Bonus: What I’m reading
- Silicon Valley is obsessed with IQ, so it’s no surprise that tech execs there are using polygenic testing in hopes of creating supersmart babies. This article shows the kind of mental pretzels customers get into when trying to figure out whether to select the embryo with the highest predicted IQ or that with the lowest risk of disorders. One couple asks: “How much additional risk of ADHD cancels out against 10 extra IQ points?”
- Rereading “The Last Children of Down Syndrome,” Sarah Zhang’s 2020 Atlantic feature on prenatal testing, it struck me that when people think “prenatal testing,” Down syndrome is often the first condition that comes to mind, even though it’s not the most severe or straightforwardly negative (it’s compatible with a happy life). It’s just that Down syndrome was easy to test for, so we started testing for it early. I wonder if that built up the condition as a bogeyman in the expectant parent’s imagination — if the fact that we could screen for it shaped the public’s perception of Down syndrome as something that should be screened for and potentially screened out.
- One trait that many people assume we should select for is a great memory. But I highly recommend the short story “Funes the Memorious” by Jorge Luis Borges. It’s a reminder that having too good a memory is not always a benefit.

The story so far: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has warned against the indiscriminate, repeated, or prolonged use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and antibiotics, linking inappropriate use to avoidable renal complications and chronic kidney disease (CKD).
In its September 21 circular, it also reminded doctors, pharmacists, hospitals, and the public that these medicines are subject to prescription and other regulatory safeguards.
What does the latest directive mean?
The CDSCO circular is, in significant part, a reminder that existing rules already require medical supervision for these medicines and doesn’t amount to any new ban on painkillers or antibiotics.
Most NSAIDs are classified under Schedule H of the Drugs Rules, 1945. Most antibiotics are under Schedule H1. These medicines are therefore not meant to be sold at retail without a prescription from a Registered Medical Practitioner.
Schedule H1 medicines also carry a specific warning that they should be taken only on and according to medical advice.
The regulator has asked the public not to take NSAIDs or antibiotics indiscriminately, repeatedly or for prolonged periods without medical advice.
“Antibiotics should not be self-medicated or used for illnesses where they are not clinically indicated,” it said.
Also, doctors have been asked to prescribe them only when clinically justified, in the appropriate dose and for the appropriate duration, and to follow antimicrobial stewardship principles. Pharmacies, hospitals, and healthcare institutions have also been put on notice.
The kidney warning is particularly relevant to NSAIDs. These drugs can reduce blood flow to the kidneys and are associated with acute kidney injury, particularly among people who already have kidney disease, diabetes, or hypertension. Longer-term use has also been associated with CKD occurrence or progression.
Importantly, the warning does not mean that all painkillers or antibiotics are inherently unsafe. The concern is inappropriate selection, dose, duration, and unsupervised use.
How extensive is antibiotic misuse?
There is no single national figure that captures all inappropriate antibiotic use in India. Available studies, however, show that self-medication remains a significant problem.
A systematic review covering 66 Indian studies and nearly 30,000 participants estimated overall self-medication at 64.4%, although this included medicines generally and not antibiotics alone. Analgesics, antipyretics, antibiotics, and cough remedies were among the commonly self-medicated drug categories.
A community study from South-East Delhi found that 35% of 200 participants reported antibiotic self-medication. Fever, cold, and flu were common reasons, while pharmacies were the main source of antibiotics.
While these studies cannot be interpreted as a national prevalence estimate and represent different populations and locations, together they illustrate why prescription enforcement and antibiotic stewardship remain concerns.
What does antibiotic misuse do?
Antibiotics work against bacterial infections. They do not treat viral illnesses such as most common colds and influenza.
When antibiotics are used unnecessarily, incorrectly or for an inappropriate duration, bacteria can be exposed to the drug without being eliminated. Resistant organisms can then survive and multiply. This contributes to antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
The consequences extend beyond the individual who takes the antibiotic. Resistant organisms can spread to other people and through healthcare and environmental pathways.
WHO estimates that bacterial AMR was associated with more than 4.7 million deaths globally in 2021. In 2023, approximately one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections globally was resistant to antibiotics. WHO says misuse and overuse of antimicrobials are important drivers of the problem.
What does WHO say about antibiotic use?
WHO has increasingly moved towards antimicrobial stewardship — ensuring that antimicrobials are used only when necessary and that the right drug, dose and duration are selected.
Its AWaRe classification divides antibiotics into three groups: Access, Watch and Reserve. Access antibiotics are generally preferred for common infections because they have a narrower spectrum and lower resistance potential. Watch antibiotics have greater resistance potential and therefore require more careful use. Reserve antibiotics are intended for infections caused by multidrug-resistant organisms when other options are inadequate.
WHO’s analysis of 2022 antibiotic-use data found that only about one in three reporting countries/territories/areas met the target of having at least 70% of antibiotic consumption from the Access group. WHO has called for stewardship policies to reduce unnecessary antibiotic use and encourage Access antibiotics when they are clinically appropriate.
WHO’s 2025 global AMR surveillance report, based on more than 23 million laboratory-confirmed cases reported by countries, also underlines the continuing global burden of resistance and the need for better surveillance.
Which drugs are commonly misused, and who is most vulnerable?
NSAIDs are among the medicines of concern because they are widely used for headaches, fever, body pain, arthritis, dental pain, and other painful conditions.
Common NSAIDs include ibuprofen, diclofenac, naproxen, and similar anti-inflammatory painkillers. Their risks become more important with prolonged or high-dose use and in people with kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, dehydration or other risk factors.
Indian pharmacovigilance data, although based on reported adverse events rather than population prevalence, provide an important signal: in one analysis of NSAID-associated CKD reports, 82% of cases were among people aged 40–80 years, with diclofenac implicated in 43% of the reports.
For antibiotics, children are an important vulnerable group, largely because parents or caregivers may administer medicines based on previous prescriptions or advice from pharmacies and family members. The recent Indian meta-analysis found substantial antibiotic self-medication among children.
Older adults and people with chronic diseases also require particular caution because kidney function may already be reduced and multiple medicines may be involved.
What measures is the government bringing in?
India has been working on AMR for more than a decade. The National Programme on AMR Containment was launched in 2013, with surveillance, monitoring of antimicrobial consumption, infection prevention and control, and promotion of rational antimicrobial use among its objectives.
India launched its National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance 2.0 (NAP-AMR 2025–2029) in November 2025. It adopts a One Health approach, bringing human health together with animal, agricultural, and environmental sectors. It includes surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention and control, research and monitoring.
The government has also used the Drugs Rules to control antibiotic sales. Schedule H1 requires records of the supply of listed medicines, including details of the prescriber and patient, with records maintained for three years.
There is also a recent regulatory development in August 2026, when CDSCO issued a draft notification proposing four additional drugs for inclusion in Schedule H1.
Why have rules not worked so far?
The central difficulty is that regulation has existed for years, but implementation has been uneven.
India’s NAP-AMR documentation itself records earlier CDSCO awareness and enforcement drives concerning Schedule H and H1 medicines, including restrictions on selling antimicrobials without prescriptions. Yet studies continue to document antibiotic self-medication and access through pharmacies.
Similarly, antimicrobial stewardship programmes have been part of India’s AMR strategy since the first National Action Plan. The 2017–2021 plan called for stewardship programmes, treatment guidelines, multidisciplinary stewardship committees, and training.
The continuing problem, therefore, is less about the absence of rules and more about translating those rules into routine practice — ensuring that prescriptions are actually required at the point of sale, that doctors prescribe antibiotics appropriately, that patients do not demand or reuse medicines, and that hospitals monitor antibiotic consumption.

Drishyam The Conclusion has emerged as a monstrous blockbuster, and a large part of the credit goes to its formidable writing team. Aamil Keeyan Khan has penned the dialogues and is also one of the screenplay writers, along with Parveez Shaikh and director Abhishek Pathak. In an exclusive interview with Bollywood Hungama, Aamil Keeyan Khan opened up about the challenge of writing the third and final chapter of the Drishyam series, living up to the massive expectations surrounding the franchise, cracking its all-important climax and a lot more.
EXCLUSIVE: Drishyam The Conclusion writer Aamil Keeyan Khan reveals why Christopher Pinto dies on November 18 and the surprising Drishyam 2 connection; decodes the climax: “Vijay Salgaonkar ne kya kiya isn’t the problem, kaise kiya gives audience the high”
How has your life been since the release of Drishyam The Conclusion?
My phone hasn’t stopped ringing. I knew the film would do well, but I didn’t expect the response to be so overwhelmingly positive. I haven’t seen such a reaction before. So, it's very elating.
The grave of Christopher Pinto plays a crucial role in the film. He died on November 18. That’s incidentally your birthday! Drishyam 2 was also released on the same day...
(Laughs) Yes. It was a call taken by the direction team, since the previous Drishyam had been released on November 18. In fact, Christopher Pinto’s birth date should actually have been July 1 instead of July 2. Had that happened, he would have shared his birthday with Abhishek!
Abhishek Pathak said that he started writing the film from the climax. What was the writing process like? 
With each part, it becomes even more difficult to surprise the audience because they are coming in with huge expectations. During the release of the first part, viewers didn’t know what to expect. The expectations were there for the second part, but with the third part, the audience is aware that Vijay will now have certain tricks up his sleeve. That made it difficult. Also, given the humongous popularity that the first two parts have enjoyed, the pressure was immense as to how crack an ending that really works.
First and foremost, we had to figure out the beginning and the end, that is, Vijay fasega kaise aur usme se niklega kaise! That was a time-consuming, yet very satisfying process.
Which was the most difficult scene to crack?
That would be the climax, especially the last 30-40 minutes. In the Drishyam series, Vijay ne kya kiya is never the problem. Kaise kiya is what gives the audience a high. Viewers have a strong connection with Vijay Salgaonkar. They know ki kuch toh kar lega yeh. Kya karega aur kaise karega is the fun part.
Since the pressure was so immense, the biggest challenge was figuring out how to land the reveal - kis order mein revelations aayenge aur kaise aayenge. Once you know what he has done and what he hasn’t done, the question is how you layer all of it in the screenplay for maximum impact. Abhishek, Parveez Shaikh and I brainstormed a lot about that.
Interestingly, the monologue that came towards the end was one of the first things I wrote. We had gone to Goa to work on the film and were still figuring out how to approach the screenplay. I wrote the monologue to get a sense of the direction we wanted to take. Abhishek liked it, and after that, we kept discussing whether it should remain in the film or be dropped. Eventually, we decided to retain it.
Pav Bhaji has become synonymous with the Drishyam series. Audiences almost expect someone to mention the dish, and this time, it’s Gaitonde (Kamlesh Sawant) who does so, leading to a lot of laughs. What was the thought process behind organically weaving the Pav Bhaji reference into the film?
That was Abhishek’s idea. Drishyam has a very strong pop-culture recall, and the Pav Bhaji memes are shared every year without fail on October 2. Abhishek asked me if there was a way we could weave that reference into the script. That’s where the idea came from, and with a twisted character like Gaitonde, it was quite easy to make him mouth that dialogue.
You have a cameo in the film (he’s the one who enters the green room and informs Raghu Nayak that Rajveer Singh Tomar is waiting to see him). Did the makers ask you to make the special appearance, or was it your wish to be on screen?
I’ve always had the desire to act. In fact, I came to Mumbai to become an actor. What happened was that the actor who was supposed to play this part couldn’t make it that day. So, I was asked, ‘Yeh scene karega?’ I immediately said, ‘Of course!’
Dr Sharad Bhutadiya, who plays Martin Uncle, was missing this time. Were there any scenes featuring him that were eventually removed, or was he never a part of the third film?
No, he wasn’t a part of it. While we were writing the film, Abhishek was very clear that he didn’t want any scenes that had no bearing on the main plot. Initially, a few scenes were supposed to be set at Martin’s Café, but we eventually shifted them to other locations. As a result, it didn’t make sense to force Martin Uncle into the story just for the sake of having him there.
The Drishyam series comes to and. How do you feel?
I feel as relieved as Sam – now I can be at peace (laughs)! On a serious note, it's nice that the audience has responded so positively to it. But the story is complete here, and we should not even attempt to move forward. You should know when to leave the ring. So, it’s the correct decision. Also, from the start, we felt that if we write it with the intention of concluding the series, we will give it our all. Hence, we haven’t left any open endings. There’s a lot of chatter on the internet ki yeh kar sakte the aur woh kar sakte the. But if somebody sat down and debated with me, I can prove why it can’t be done and why this is the end of it.
You have written many of Ajay Devgn films in recent times and played a big role in his success…
On the contrary, he has played a big role in my success. Ajay sir, along with the teams at Devgn Films and Panorama Studios, has been like family to me. They have treated me with a lot of warmth and kindness. Working with them feels almost like working on a home production (smiles). I hope I get to collaborate with Ajay sir on many more films. When you get to work with a great artist and a wonderful human being, who also happens to be a massive star, it’s a jackpot.
The fact that Kumar Mangat Pathak, Rohit Shetty and even you have worked with him repeatedly says a lot about the kind of person he is...
Absolutely. You can see the loyalty that people around him have towards him. There are many actors who are stars, but not all of them inspire that kind of loyalty and genuine affection. Ajay sir does, and that says a lot about the person he is.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

The Best E-Readers That Aren’t a Kindle
Featured in this article
There are no fewer than 10 e-readers in my house at any given time, and I wouldn't have it any other way.
While nothing replaces the feel of a physical book, I usually reach for one of my e-readers as part of my nighttime routine. To me, these tablets are the easiest way to read because they grant immediate access to whatever is in my TBR pile at a given time. Whether it's a library book through the Libby app or a series I'm buying up because I can't wait any longer for a copy to be available, whatever I want to read, I can access it immediately on my e-reader.
It’s also convenient that e-readers (short for “ebook readers”) can store thousands of books at a time. These slim devices use E Ink screens to give text a paperlike appearance. They’re also designed to strain your eyes less than other digital devices, like your phone or computer screen.
And while many strongly associate Kindle with e-reader, you don't have to turn to Amazon for the best device. In fact, my all-around favorite isn't a Kindle at all, and there are plenty of other models to shop from that let you steer clear of the tech behemoth and its recent price increases. These are all my favorite e-readers that won't require you to support Amazon to enjoy the experience.
Updated October 2026: I've moved all Kindle recommendations (and details about the newly announced Kindles) out of our top picks to focus entirely on non-Amazon e-readers. There are also new sections for what I'm testing next and e-reader accessories compatible with my picks.

Honorable Mentions
Below, find a few more e-readers I like but don't necessarily love as much as my top picks.
Boox Go 7 ($270) and Boox Go Color 7 ($290): Boox is known for its wide range of e-paper tablets, including the Boox Go 6 (Gen II) I recommend above. If you're looking for something a little larger with a similar Android-based experience, the Go 7 and Go Color 7 are both solid choices. There are page-turner buttons, and it's a nice square shape that's easy to hold and use. If you, like me, don't use color features a ton, it's worth saving the extra money on the black-and-white model. Regardless, it's great that the price difference between the two models isn't steep.
Boox Palma 2 for $250: This is a fun, pocket-sized device, with fingerprint recognition, a faster CPU, and a newer version of Android than previous models. Former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So loved using it with the Kindle app, but she wishes it cost less. Boox recently announced the Palma 3 is coming out (though it doesn't have a confirmed launch date) which explains why it's been unavailable for so long. The Palma 3 is next on my testing list, but if you want a similar device you can purchase now, the Boox Palma 2 Pro ($400) is available with a higher price tag, but color screen.
Nook GlowLight 4 Plus for $200: The 4 Plus is the only waterproof Nook in the lineup, and it has the biggest screen at 7.8 inches, along with 32 GB of storage. It also has physical page-turn buttons and a headphone jack for listening to audiobooks (you can also connect wireless earbuds via Bluetooth). Unfortunately, it was often slower than my Kindle and tended to freeze. While the large library has cheap and even free ebooks, it's not as good of a selection as Kindle Unlimited. The process of getting a book from the library on a Nook is also frustrating. You'll need to download either Adobe Digital Editions or Android File Transfer before physically connecting the device to your computer and then transferring the files.
Nook 9-inch Lenovo Tablet for $150: If you mainly read cookbooks or other color-intensive materials, and you want a dedicated reader, you might want to consider this affordable tablet from Nook and Lenovo, which has the Nook app built in. It's a tablet rather than an e-paper device like the rest of the gadgets in this guide, so you'll lose the E Ink screen and the distraction-free nature of an e-reader. Xteink X4 for $69 and X3 for $69: These are similar to the Xteink X4 Pro above when it comes to the app and basic capabilities, but you'll lose out on the touchscreen, home button, and front light. The X3 is super small, with just a 3.7-inch screen that fits on the back of my iPhone 16 Pro, and it has stronger magnets to put itself into place. What I’m Testing Next
There have been several new e-readers announced, mainly new models from Boox like the Palma 3 and Picco, that I'll be reading my latest books on this fall, which will include R.F. Kuang's Babel and the latest ACOTAR book, along with an alarmingly long list of suspended holds in my Libby app that I really need to work on. Here's what I'll be testing next:
Boox Palma 3 for $320: Boox's popular Palma devices are made to be mobile e-paper screens, and are a popular choice as a smaller e-reader. The new Palma 3 has been announced after months of the Palma 2 being out of stock, and it promises a 6.13-inch screen, dual-tone front light, a rear camera, dual microphones, and a customizable smart button. There's no timeline yet for its launch, but I'm hoping we see it available before the end of the year.
Boox Picco for $100: This miniature e-reader will have a tiny 3.97-inch screen and be Boox's smallest e-reader to date. Boox says it's the first of its Tiles ecosystem, so I'm keeping an eye out for more launches within that line. The Picco is currently available for preorder and is due to ship in October.
Boox Note Mini C for $550: When Boox announced the Palma 3, it also announced its new e-paper tablet, the Boox Note Air6 C, and a miniaturized version, the Boox Note Mini C. There are now aluminum-backed versions of all three, though the Paperwhite and Colorsoft have it as part of the higher-end Signature Edition that comes with a few more features. I'll be testing and will add my top pick to this guide for reference, but this guide will focus more on non-Kindle e-readers going forward.
What If I Want a Kindle?
Maybe you've read this guide and decided a Kindle is best for you. That's fine! Kindle is my longest-used ecosystem and it's plenty convenient, especially if you already have ebooks purchased through Amazon. While I have an entire guide dedicated to shopping for a Kindle, here's a quick overview of my top picks (and other models you might spot).
Also, Kindle does have new versions of the base Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, Kindle Colorsoft, and its Kids versions of each model coming out. You might want to wait and see if you prefer the newest versions to these, and I'll be testing them soon to see how they compare to past Kindles and other e-readers. Kindle also raised the prices of most of its e-readers at the end of August, and the new models match that pricing.
Kindle Colorsoft Signature for $320 and Kindle Colorsoft ($290): The Kindle Colorsoft Signature is Amazon's first Kindle with a color screen. I do like the Colorsoft if you read books with illustrations or heavily annotate your e-books, but the Kobo devices I recommend can do the same thing for cheaper.
Kindle Scribe (3rd Gen, 2025) for $500 and Kindle Scribe Colorsoft for $630: The latest Kindle Scribe arrived in December 2025 with a color version. It also has a new exterior design that does away with the single thicker side and standardizes bezels and frames across all sizes, and a lot of AI features. The older Kindle Scribe (2nd Gen) is still my preferred option if you want a Kindle e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.
Kindle Scribe Without Front Light for $430: This is the third and final installment of Amazon's latest generation of Kindle Scribes. Great E-Reader Accessories
Looking to jazz up your new e-reader? Here are some of my favorite accessories to pair with my favorite non-Kindle e-readers. FAQs
How Do You Get Ebooks?
Ebooks can be cheap, but as with regular books, the cost can add up if you're a big reader. To keep costs low, take advantage of your library card and check out ebooks instantly from the comfort of your home. We have a detailed guide that explains How to Get Free Kindle Books With Your Library Card, but the short version is that most libraries distribute books via OverDrive. You can access these books a few ways: through Kindle or directly from OverDrive with a Kobo, or you can download the Libby app. These ebooks are automatically removed from your device and returned to the library when they're due.
Each e-reader's own book service varies in quality. My favorite is Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month, which includes millions of titles, including audiobooks and magazines. Amazon's Prime Reading also offers a handful of free books every month, which is good to know if you already have a Prime account. You can even lend books to friends and family for a short while (or have them share a book with you). For more details on each option, check out our guide to the Best Ebook Subscription Services here.
What File Formats Do E-Readers Support?
The most widely used format is EPUB, which works natively with all the e-readers in this guide except for Kindle—technically. You can still upload EPUB files to your Kindle, but you'll have to use the “Send to Kindle” feature (through Amazon, your email, or the Kindle app) to convert it to Amazon's proprietary format called AZW. (Newer Kindles support AZW3 and KFX, specifically). Other formats that will work with these e-readers include PDF, TXT, HTML, DOC, and DOCX.
Can I Install Apps on an E-Reader?
Kindle, Kobo, and Nook all use proprietary operating systems that don't allow you to install third-party apps. The Boox, on the other hand, runs Android (mainly Android 11 and newer). That means you can use it to download any apps available in the Google Play Store or side-load apps from your computer.
Do You Need an E-Reader? What About a Phone or Tablet?
You don't have to buy a separate device to read ebooks. Smartphones and tablets are perfect for this purpose. You can use Amazon's Kindle app to read ebooks (iOS, Android) and download OverDrive's Libby app (iOS, Android) for library-book access. However, the E Ink screens found in e-readers are just nicer to look at. I also like that these devices are one-trick ponies; there are no distracting notifications or social media feeds ripe for doomscrolling.
If you'd still rather have one smart device you can use for reading and other purposes, take a look at our Best Tablets and Best iPads guides for recommendations.
What About a Digital Notebook?
I've tried just about every digital notebook on the market; these devices are designed for handwritten notes on an E Ink screen. E-readers with that capability usually still prioritize reading, though there are plenty of models I like that can do both. The Kobo Libra Colour is my favorite option for annotating books, and it can double as a small digital notebook. If you want a larger option, check out my full guide to every digital notebook I've tested.
How Do I Test E-Readers?
The most important step I take when testing e-readers is to read on them! I spend hours reading books acquired in a variety of formats, including books I purchased directly from each brand's store, downloaded from local libraries via OverDrive/Libby, and PDFs acquired for free from God knows where.
In the process, I evaluate battery life, brightness, performance lag, screen responsiveness, and text sharpness. I check for extra tools, like whether the tablet in question accommodates accessories like a stylus. I also note features like waterproofing, annotation capability, and access to exclusive subscription services.

Quick Answer
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 is a powerful 2-in-1 Windows tablet for creators, with a sharp 3K OLED display, strong Snapdragon X2 Elite performance, excellent battery life, and full desktop apps. However, its high price, weak touch experience, and some ARM app limits hold it back.
People still debate why the tablet category exists. Some people believe they can replace laptops, while others see them as glorified smartphones with bigger screens.
I agree with both statements, as tablets are extremely portable. They are thinner, lighter, and easy to carry anywhere, and they can also convert into a laptop on the go, with the added advantage of a stylus for note-taking, sketching, or even marking up PDF files. Not to mention, they’re also great for watching movies and other entertainment.
But they are extremely limited in software capabilities despite hardware that can run fully native desktop applications. But Apple’s software limitations are also a deal-breaker for many. On the other hand, it runs the full Windows 11 OS on tablets without limitations. But it isn’t optimized for tablets.
For most people, or for creative work, the iPad is the first choice. But I recently got a chance to review the ASUS ProArt PZ14, which is a 2-in-1, tablet-first Windows device designed for creative work that is portable and offers an excellent OLED screen, solid performance, solid battery life, and is capable of running fully native applications, and comes with a keyboard and a pen out of the box for all your creative work and note-taking. I have been using the ASUS ProArt PZ14 for the past two weeks. In this detailed review, you will find out whether the ASUS ProArt PZ14 breaks tradition by doing things differently. Or is it just another tablet in the debate? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Design and Build: Lightweight and practical, but the design is an acquired taste
ASUS ProArt PZ14 is a tablet-first Windows PC. The keyboard detaches completely from the tablet, and all components, including the processor, sit on the back of the display.
As a result, it carries all the weight. ASUS includes a magnetic case in the box that you can attach to the back of the tablet to use as a stand and to hold the ASUS Pen 3.0. I wouldn’t recommend attaching it without the case because, while you’re holding the tablet, the magnets are not strong, and it can easily fall off, which it did. But hopefully, thanks to the build, it survived accidental falls.
Thanks to the matte finish, the back of the tablet isn’t a fingerprint magnet either, but stains are visible if you look at it a certain way, and they wipe off easily with any standard cloth.
An ASUS design choice on the back can be a hit or a miss depending on your perception. Right off the bat, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 doesn’t look like a tablet. It felt like a very niche tablet designed for a specific purpose. It has a single rear camera. Thankfully, there is no bump, and it comes with a lot of stickers, which indicates it is more than just a tablet.
You get ProArt branding at the top in the center. Overall, the fit and finish are solid, but the looks can be hit or miss based on your perception. I wish it looked more like a tablet.
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 comes with dual speakers, with one on each side The power button is on the top in landscape and on the right in portrait, which is convenient for landscape use but less convenient in portrait.
And you can find the volume-down and volume-up keys on the right as well, making it easy to control with your right hand. The SD Express 7.0 card reader and two USB4 Type-C ports are on the left side.
The look changes entirely from the front. It comes with a 14-inch 3K OLED display with a 144Hz refresh rate and minimal bezels, similar to the iPad Pro, but wider overall. At the top, you get an 8MP IR front camera with no privacy shutter.
The tablet weighs just 790 grams, making it lightweight and easy to use, but the larger display is hard to hold for long periods when using it as a tablet. The tablet has rounded corners on the back, which make it easy to hold for long periods, and the textured finish on the front half provides better grip. The matte finish makes it less slippery.
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 also has an IP52 rating. ASUS officially claims that it is tested to MIL-STD-810Hstandards . So you have the military standard, but don’t drop-test it like other laptops.
When I first held the ASUS ProArt PZ14, the back finish felt like plastic. However, ASUS claims the chassis uses an aluminum alloy. The sides feel very solid.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Display: A gorgeous 3K OLED made for creators
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 display is one of the best-looking, and if there is one reason to choose this tablet, it’s this display. Whether you are a business user, a graphic designer, or someone who wants to casually watch movies and play games, it delivers a great viewing experience.
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 comes with a 14-inch 3K OLED display. It comes with a 144Hz refresh rate for a smooth experience. The 14-inch display is a sweet spot. On your desk and used with the keyboard, it is a sweet spot and a perfect middle ground between the 13.6-inch and 15-inch laptops, but it feels very large in hand when you hold it and use it as a tablet.
The OLED display is one of the best I have seen on a tablet, matching premium, high-quality displays with 100% DCI-P3 color gamut and PANTONE validation. The blacks look deeper, and colors are represented very accurately, making it a good choice for designers and photographers who want to edit images accurately. The touch response is also fast, but Windows is the one to blame. It makes interactions less convenient, which I will cover more in the OS section.
The display also supports a stylus. ASUS includes the ASUS Pen 3.0 out of the box. Writing and drawing on the display feels faster and more fluid. But because of the glass finish, it feels slippery while taking notes. You can apply a matte-finish screen protector for a better typing and note-taking experience on this tablet. After the iPad Pro, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 provided the best note-taking experience, even better than the Apple Pencil in some cases.
ASUS, being extra generous, added the pencil-scribble sound while taking notes. Well, thank you, ASUS, for looking at those tiny details to enhance the user experience. But it sounds so artificial.
Next, this 16:10 aspect ratio is perfect for watching content. I watched three episodes of Better Call Saul (season 4) on Netflix, and the experience was better on the ASUS ProArt PZ14 than on my iPad Pro.
With 3K resolution and 243 pixels per inch, it is also one of the sharper displays. It looks sharp even when you zoom in on minor editing details.
However, if you often read web pages, blogs, or docs on this tablet, while it looks fine when using it in laptop mode, as soon as you pick it up and use it as a tablet, you are holding a massive tablet, and 16:10 feels very wide when you put it close to your eyes, which means you need to move your head to read the text. Also, portrait mode isn’t appealing either, with that 14-inch massive screen making it hard to read and scroll. With this large form factor, using it with a single hand is almost impossible. You can try if you want.
Overall, the display is one of the ASUS ProArt PZ14’s biggest strengths. Whether you’re watching content, editing, or designing, everything looks incredible on this massive screen.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Keyboard and Trackpad: Laptop-like typing, but better suited for a desk
ASUS also provides a keyboard out of the box. Unlike with the iPads, which you need to buy separately and are also expensive. Fortunately, the typing experience is as good as on thin-and-light laptops. However, if you’re used to mechanical keyboards or longer key travel, you might find it hard to type at first, but you can eventually get used to it.
Also, there are a few things that you need to know: the keyboard completely detaches from the tablet, which means it doesn’t have a hinge that holds the display and keyboard together. A small magnetic attachment on the bottom of the tablet connects to the keyboard.
You can just hover the tablet over the keyboard, and it attaches magnetically. However, the magnet isn’t as strong, so it can also detach easily. And since there is no strong hinge holding the keyboard and tablet together, you cannot place it on your lap and type on uneven surfaces, where the tablet takes the full weight and could tip back.
Fortunately, ASUS also included a full touchpad, and again, it’s almost like using the touchpad on a regular thin-and-light laptop. The speakers are very loud. They have rich sound. There is no headphone jack.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Specs and Performance: Snapdragon X2 Elite delivers plenty of power
Under the hood, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 runs on the Snapdragon X2 Elite X2E-88-100 processor. My variant has 32GB of LPDDR5X RAM and a 1TB M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD. That’s a large configuration by current standards.
Qualcomm is trying too hard to become a name for its PC processors after it conquered Android phones. The processor offers very solid performance. Tasks feel faster, and it compares with some of the best in the industry right now, including the Intel Core Ultra 7 series and Ryzen AI Max+, among others. In comparison, in Geekbench single- and multicore scores, Snapdragon X2 Elite has produced very good numbers.
You can see the benchmarks of the ASUS ProART PZ14 from third-party testers.
The tablet also offers a dedicated performance mode that provides extra power when needed. This results in smooth day-to-day performance; whether it’s opening apps, touch interactions, gaming, or uploading files, everything feels smoother on this tablet
The built-in SD Express 7.0 card reader delivers strong sequential read and write rates, including 730 MB/s sequential read speeds. So if you are a creator who copies videos and files to and from the tablet, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 won’t consume your time.
However, while the processor is solid in CPU performance, the GPU is still weaker on Snapdragon processors, and the same is true of the Snapdragon X2 Elite. It comes with an integrated Qualcomm Adreno GPU. That performs decently; however, it’s not as good as Radeon or Intel Arc GPUs.
Because of this, it might not excel at higher-end applications or even gaming. It can offer decent performance, but not top-tier.
While the GPU might not be the most powerful, the NPU performance is significantly better. The Snapdragon X2 Elite includes a Qualcomm Hexagon NPU rated up to 80 TOPS. This lets you offload a few AI tasks locally for better performance. For instance, if you are a creator, you can run AI models locally.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 also comes with a fan. Under load, the tablet tends to get a bit warmer, and the fan kicks in.
Overall performance is impressive for such a thin and light device. Daily use, such as browsing the web, watching movies and shows, and running a few high-end software applications, feels faster and handles every task without breaking a sweat.
Moreover, while compatibility with popular ARM apps on Windows has improved over the years since Qualcomm announced Snapdragon X Elite, some older programs and plug-ins still aren’t natively compatible with Windows on ARM, and some run via x86 emulation.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Battery Life: Easily lasts an entire workday
The battery life is incredible on this tablet, and Windows on ARM has already proved it. The ASUS ProArt PZ14 comes with a 75Wh four-cell lithium-ion battery. ASUS also offers a 68W USB-C charger in the box.
Even in performance and non-performance modes, battery life stays consistent. On average, I got around 12 to 14 hours of battery life with light to medium use and about 10-11 hours with heavy use, including gaming. With light use, just using the browser, I even got two days of battery life.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Windows 11 Experience: Full desktop software, but a poor tablet interface
Now let’s address the elephant in the room: Windows 11. I would say having Windows 11 is both the biggest strength and also the biggest weakness of this tablet. The ASUS ProArt PZ14 ships with Windows 11 or Windows 11 Pro out of the box, depending on the configuration. My unit comes with Windows 11 Home.
No matter which version you are on, Windows 11 isn’t optimized for the touch interface. In Windows 11 touch mode, it feels like a desktop and has very small buttons, menus, and toolbars.
If you primarily want to use the ASUS ProArt PZ14 as a tablet, and you’re used to iPad Pro-type interaction, you will definitely find it hard to use day-to-day. Fortunately, using the pen minimizes this. However, if you primarily use your hands, keep that in mind.
Also, this tablet has a core Windows problem. The biggest problem is the annoying Windows updates. They are still an issue even after Microsoft promised to reduce those interruptions. Unfortunately, I haven’t been able to set up the tablet from scratch because it’s a pre-owned unit, and someone else has already set it up for me, so I was saved from dealing with lengthy setup processes.
Another big limitation of Windows running on ARM is limited app support. While app support has improved significantly since I first reviewed the Snapdragon X Elite laptop, most popular applications are now natively available on Windows on ARM, but a few legacy applications still use Prism emulation, which affects performance and misses core features. However, if you mainly want to use it as a creator tablet, most creator apps are natively available on Windows, and a few games are also natively supported on Windows on ARM.
But the biggest advantage is that, since it runs on Windows, you can run full desktop-level software without any limitations. You can multitask with multiple windows. If you want better multitasking and portability at the same time, this is something you should get.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Ports and Connectivity: USB4 and SD Express are useful, but some ports are missing
Despite its tablet form factor, ASUS has included decent port support on the ASUS ProArt PZ14. It comes with two USB 4.0 Gen 3 Type-C ports that support up to 40 Gbps, which can be used to connect external SSDs, docks, and even an external monitor.
It also includes an SD Express 7.0 card reader, which is excellent for transferring video and photos from your cameras. There’s no HDMI port, which I miss, but you can easily work around it with external peripherals. The camera quality is also good, much better than the webcam quality on other ASUS laptops I have tested. The rear camera is also decent in good lighting, which you can use to scan documents quickly. The tablet also supports Wi-Fi 7 or Bluetooth 6.0.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Verdict: A powerful Windows tablet for creators on the go
So, that is everything that you need to know about ASUS ProArt PZ14. With its excellent display, tablet-first design, portability, battery life, and solid performance, it is a great pick for anyone who wants a powerful tablet on the go.
The 3K OLED display also makes it a great option for entertainment whenever you want to watch content or even play games. Overall, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 is a great option for a creator-first experience and for anyone who values portability and wants an all-in-one tablet that can replace a conventional laptop and a tablet at home. However, the tablet costs Rs 2,69,990 for 32GB LPDDR5X RAM. It is expensive.

Srinagar, Oct 5: Vice Chairman (VC), Jammu and Kashmir Lake Conservation and Management Authority (JKLCMA), Khurshid Ahmad Shah, today conducted an extensive inspection of the Dole Demb area to review the existing condition of the water body and its surrounding areas and assess the scope for beautification and development of the site.
The Vice Chairman was accompanied by the Superintending Engineer, Collector Land Acquisition, FA&CAO, Executive Engineers of Lake Division 1st and Lake Division 2nd, Technical Officer, Assistant Executive Engineers, Junior Engineers, and other officers and officials of the Authority.
Emphasising the importance of developing the site in a planned and sustainable manner, the Vice Chairman directed that the beautification proposal should incorporate modern landscaping, suitable plantation, improved pathways, aesthetic features, and other necessary amenities. He stressed that the area should be developed as a state of the art public space while maintaining the ecological character of the water body. He observed that the development of Dole Demb would also contribute towards enhancing the overall tourism potential of the area and attract more visitors to Dal Lake.
The Vice Chairman directed the concerned officers to immediately undertake bush cutting along the site and carry out other necessary site clearance works to improve the overall appearance and accessibility of the area, so that further dredging and restoration works in the Dole Demb area can be taken up. He further instructed the Engineering Wing to prepare detailed estimates for the proposed beautification and development works at Dole Demb.
The Vice Chairman further directed the concerned officers to ensure close coordination among the Engineering, Revenue, and field wings so that the proposed works are planned and executed in a time bound manner. He emphasised that the development should focus on environmental improvement while enhancing the visual appeal and overall utility of the area for tourism.
Reiterating the Authority’s commitment towards the conservation and beautification of water bodies and their surrounding areas, the Vice Chairman stated that LCMA will continue to undertake integrated conservation, restoration, and development measures to improve urban water bodies and create clean, attractive, and environmentally sustainable spaces for the public and tourists. He emphasised that such initiatives would also contribute towards strengthening the tourism potential of Dal Lake and its adjoining areas.
