'I reduced my running because of urine leaks' – Commonwealth finalist Korir
- Published
Naomi Korir's career on the track reached a high point in August when she finished fifth in the final of the mile at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
But things could have been very different for the Kenyan middle-distance runner.
The 28-year-old was born with fistula, a medical condition in which abnormal openings develop between organs and can lead to uncontrolled leakage of urine or faeces.
While Korir loved athletics as a child, it initially forced her to rethink any plans to be a runner.
"I played most of the sports activities: football, netball, athletics, even rugby," she said.
"But it was difficult because [of] the training, and the urine is flowing continuously. It's bad.
"I reduced my running to shorter distances to reduce the leaking.
"I began doing 100m hurdles."
Despite the challenges, Korir's love of sport also offered a form of escape and belonging.
"I could do it because I loved it," she explained.
"Because most of the people could avoid me, I did a lot of activities just to pass time and not to feel that I'm excluded."
Three surgeries and a second chance
The charity Doctors Without Borders estimates that 500,000 women live with fistula globally.
Some develop a fistula after childbirth while for others, like Korir, it is congenital.
Access to good obstetrics, or to simple surgery, means that the condition has all but disappeared in some countries, but it remains a problem in sub-Saharan Africa, where high quality medical care can be hard to access.
Korir was born with genitourinary tract fistula - an opening between bladder and vagina which caused her urine leakage.
Surgery was required, but her first two operations failed to solve the problem.
In August 2013, a third operation finally brought relief for the then 13-year-old.
The procedure was carried out in her home town Eldoret by the Gynocare Hospital, which specialises in fistula, obstetrics and reproductive health.
"It's a difficult condition to live with every day," Gynocare director Caroline Mabeya told BBC Sport Africa when discussing the stigma and isolation women with the condition suffer.
"They are ostracised in the society. That's the psychological torture that they face with the fistula."
The hospital has treated patients from across East Africa since opening its doors in 2011. Its work extends beyond surgery, with a post-operation programme designed to help women rebuild their confidence.
"We offer free treatment for these women at Gynocare because most of them are very poor," Mabeya explained.
"When they come into the facility, they are crushed, they have low esteem. So, there's a huge amount of effort that is put in to make them at least be strong enough to be reintegrated and get back into the community."
'A champion in sport'
For Korir, successful surgery offered a second chance, both on the track and in the classroom.
As well as allowing her to run properly again, she continued her education through Gynocare's Beyond Fistula programme.
"I have a family in GynoCare, a fistula home," she said.
"That is where I schooled after my surgery until I finished my secondary level."
In 2019, Korir began competing professionally and two years later was part of the Kenyan duo which claimed a silver medal in the 2x2x400m mixed relay alongside her partner Ferguson Rotich at the World Relays in Poland.
A year later she went one better, bagging gold as part of Kenya's 4x400m relay team at the African Championships in Mauritius.
The mile at this year's Commonwealth Games was her first appearance in major global final.
"I'm giving hope to young women maybe who have lost hope," she said of her achievements.
"They need to come back again in living and enjoying life."
Mabeya says Korir's transformation makes her a powerful example to the women currently receiving support at Gynocare.
"She makes them realise that you can actually pull yourself out of these struggles and still make it in life and succeed.
"Naomi actually is one of those patients that inspires us to continue working very hard, because we struggle with this condition and these women. The work is not easy."
As a young girl, Korir sang in church and played the keyboard, convinced that music was a more likely career than athletics.
"But now I'm in different career and I'm so happy," she beamed.
And with the World Championships in Beijing next year and the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, Korir believes there is another chapter to write.
"I know I'm a champion in life, because conquering fistula alone is being a champion.
"Now I'm looking forward to be a champion in sport."

Instagram is toying with a read-only mode for Plus subscribers
That’s a nicer name than ‘stalker mode.’
Instagram is internally developing a possible new feature that seems tailor-made to allow for nefarious behavior. Leaker and reverse engineer Alessando Paluzzi posted on X with the discovery of an Instagram feature billed as "read-only mode." According to the uncovered screenshots, this option allows for a session where "you can't like, comment, message, follow or view stories" on the social network, which would allow a user to browse the platform without leaving any type of paper trail about what they were viewing. It appears to be a concept for Instagram Plus accounts from the images shared.
A spokesperson from Instagram told Engadget that read-only mode "is an internal only exploration, not testing externally at all." So this feature is far from launching if it ever does, and tech platforms will regularly try out features that never see the light of day for users. But it also doesn't suggest whether there's any acknowledgement internally that this type of reduced visibility could be used for stalking or other criminal purposes. Hopefully the team can sufficiently address those safety concerns before any potential external tests or launch.

A military aircraft carrying 25 passengers and seven crew members has crashed in southern Nigeria, triggering a frantic search and rescue operation, according to authorities.
There was no immediate information on casualties.
Nigeria’s Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo said in a statement that the aircraft was on a routine mission to Lagos when it crashed in the Igbokoda area of Ondo state.
The Nigerian Air Force identified the aircraft as an ATR-42. It was not immediately clear to what extent the aircraft was damaged.
“Search and rescue operations, in coordination with relevant authorities and emergency response agencies, are currently ongoing,” air force spokesperson Ehimen Ejodame said.
Locals told The Associated Press that the aircraft crashed near a river and that part of it was sinking in the water.
“We heard something like a thunder strike,” said Akinbulejo Pius, a witness. “The plane cleared some trees. We found some body parts, some clothes and shoes.”
Mr Keyamo said the aircraft first disappeared from radar at around 9 am local time, and that it was found to have crashed close to a naval base.
The Nigerian military has in the past used the ATR-42 for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), alongside for transporting personnel and supplies.
Writing on X, Mr Keyamo said: “I regret to inform the general public that Air Traffic Controllers have informed me of the disappearance of a military aircraft with tail number NGR 931, enroute Lagos from Benin at 0913 hours earlier today. All efforts to raise the aircraft on radio proved abortive.
“Subsequently information however confirmed that the military aircraft has crashed close to the Naval Base in Igbokoda, Ondo State. The wreckage has been located and search and rescue operations are ongoing.
“Preliminary information suggests that there were 25 passengers and 7 crew members on board.
“Whilst the control and regulation of military aircraft are completely outside the authority of the Ministry of Aviation, and Civil Aviation Authority, I have just spoken to the Chief of Air Staff, Air Marshal Sunday Kelvin Aneke and pledged our total cooperation and assistance in the search and rescue efforts ongoing.
“Further information on this unfortunate incident will be made available subsequently.”

Mini PC vs. laptop: Which is better for your home office?
A laptop can become a desktop with one cable, making the home-office choice less obvious than it looks.
I own both a mini PC and a laptop, and I prefer to have the mini PC on my desk. It doesn't take up much space and fades into a setup that revolves around the monitor, keyboard and mouse I actually use. The small box becomes a part of the office and an organized desk.
However, a laptop can do the same. Plug one into a big screen via HDMI, throw in a wireless keyboard and mouse, and the basic experience is pretty close. This can get even better with a compatible USB-C or Thunderbolt dock to manage displays, peripherals, networking and charging all in one. When both computers are set up at a desk, the gap between them becomes tiny.
What you're paying for and whether the computer needs to leave that desk are the more important questions.
Mini PCs are often closer to laptops than desktops
While their name implies a desktop PC that's been hit with a shrink ray, there are plenty of mini PCs based on hardware that would be perfectly normal in a laptop. For instance, the ASUS NUC 15 Pro supports Intel's Core Ultra 7 265H (a mobile processor), along with SO-DIMM memory and M.2 SSD storage.
There's a practical explanation for that. When you're attempting to fit a whole computer into a box that's small enough to fit behind a monitor, laptop components are quite convenient. But similar parts don't guarantee identical performance. Cooling, firmware and manufacturer-set power limits all have an impact on what a processor can sustain, especially when you put it to work for more than a quick benchmark. Thus, two machines with the same CPU name can still behave differently.
Upgradeability varies too, which is one of the main downsides of a mini PC. The NUC 15 Pro offers two SO-DIMM slots and two M.2 storage slots on supported configurations, offering greater flexibility for memory and storage upgrades than some thin laptops with soldered memory. Not all configurations include memory or storage from ASUS, however.
That last detail is important for fair price comparisons. When you start adding RAM, an SSD and perhaps an operating system to the list of items, a bargain-looking barebones mini PC can turn into less of a value.
The same reality check applies to graphics. Integrated graphics are just fine for email, office apps, video calls and browser-intensive tasks. If you're doing demanding video editing, 3D work or any other GPU-intensive task, don't assume that the small desktop box has more graphics power than a laptop.
A docked laptop makes this a much tougher choice
A mini PC has straightforward appeal compared to a laptop: you're buying the computer without the built-in screen, battery, keyboard and trackpad that may go unused for the majority of its lifespan. That's largely why I enjoy mine. I prefer to have a machine that's part of the workspace and always available. But a laptop has a pretty good response to that argument, and it's a single cable.
With a compatible docking station, a laptop can connect to external displays, Ethernet, a keyboard, mouse and other USB devices simultaneously. Supported models can also be powered from the same dock (specific capabilities vary by laptop and dock). Close the lid, tuck the machine into a stand and your day-to-day setup can feel like one built around a mini PC.
The difference is evident when you have to travel. Unplug the laptop and the same computer comes with you, including your local files, apps, browser sessions and settings. There's only one machine to maintain — no need to wonder which computer has the document you definitely saved five minutes before a meeting.
But that doesn't mean a laptop is the obvious home-office option. Mini PCs can be compact, flexible and even more cost-effective if your computer doesn't move around much and you already have a monitor and peripherals. If you're a frequent traveler, work in various locations or want to keep everything on one machine, a docked laptop might be the better choice.

A purported Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping (here & here) claims that the Rajasthan High Court has given a judgment that provides for six months of imprisonment and a ₹50,000 fine for any candidate who fails to secure at least 100 votes in the Sarpanch elections. Let us verify the authenticity of the claim made in this post.
Claim: A Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping claims the Rajasthan High Court has ordered a six-month jail term and a ₹50,000 fine for Sarpanch candidates securing under 100 votes.
Fact: The viral newspaper clipping is an AI-generated fake image. The Rajasthan High Court has given no such judgment, Dainik Jagran published no such report, and Indian electoral laws contain no provision imposing jail time or fines for low vote counts. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
First, an initial search confirmed that the Rajasthan High Court has not issued any such judgment regarding low vote counts in Panchayat elections. Additionally, we found no news reports published by Dainik Jagran corroborating this matter. Moreover, no such law, Court order, or judicial mandate exists under the Election Commission of India or Indian electoral statutes (such as the Representation of the People Act, 1951) penalising candidates with imprisonment or fines purely for receiving a low vote count. Under current election rules, the only major consequence for a poor electoral performance is the forfeiture of the security deposit, which applies if an unelected candidate fails to secure more than one-sixth of the valid votes polled.
Further, we ran the viral newspaper clipping through the OpenAI content detection tool, which confirmed that the clipping is an AI-generated image created using OpenAI tools. Earlier, we debunked a similarly fabricated clipping that falsely claimed a woman gave birth to puppies in the United States.
To sum it up, the viral newspaper clipping is a fabricated AI-generated image, and there is no legal provision or court order mandating jail time or fines for securing low votes in a Sarpanch election.

A US marine stationed on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa is accused of murdering a Japanese woman and has been arrested on suspicion of murder, police said on Sunday.
The suspect allegedly “killed [a] 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha and stole her wallet” as well as her backpack, local police told news media outlets.
Citing police, NBC News reported that the suspect charged in the case was identified Lance Cpl Devin Jacob Ballard, 20. Anna Yagi was identified as the victim.
Ballard denied the allegations, police said, according to NBC.
Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving accidents by US personnel have long sparked protests on Okinawa. The island bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of US military facilities in Japan.
US ambassador George Glass posted on social media that he had spoken with Japan’s foreign ministry and Okinawa’s governor, offering “sincere condolences to the victim’s family” and pledging cooperation into the investigation of her death.
The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said Japan had lodged a protest with US authorities and called the crime “exceptionally brutal and vicious”.
The government has urged the US “to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among US military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes,” Takaichi said.
Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.
Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station where he was arrested, NHK reported.
“We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened,” Yagi’s brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper. “My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter.”
The US has about 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
Crimes committed by US personnel in Japan have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
“Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen,” Japan’s defense minister Shinjiro Koizumi said.
In June 2025, a Japanese court sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton – then 22 – to seven years in prison after being convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
Earlier, in 2017, former US marine and civilian military base worker Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, US forces in Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated American marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.
According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since Okinawa was returned to Japan from the US in 1972 after the second world war.
The number of arrests in a year hit 80 in 2024, the highest in 20 years.

Tamil Nadu is recording around 200 cases of dengue a day. Fresh cases are being reported in places including Chennai and its neighbouring districts and cities such as Coimbatore and Madurai.
Officials of the Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine said the caseload remained steady and was not at outbreak proportions. A. Somasundaram, Director of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said cases had not risen exponentially, with the numbers remaining broadly steady. “We are seeing nearly 200 cases a day. The numbers are not doubling or tripling, which usually happens in an outbreak. Right now, there is a static trend in the number of dengue cases, and we are expecting the cases to decline soon,” he said.
Cases are being reported across cities including the Chennai belt (Tiruvallur and Kancheepuram), Coimbatore, and Madurai. This could partly be due to a “natural bias” with these areas having more hospitals and testing facilities, Dr. Somasundaram said.
“We have specifically instructed staff to increase the number of tests for dengue for better surveillance and patient management. This is so we don’t miss a case, and when samples are tested, we can identify pockets of cases or clusters, which are likely to bring about an outbreak,” he said. There are over 4,500 government and private laboratories in the State, he added.
Surveillance measures to identify Aedes mosquito breeding pools are continuing, but the number of pools detected has started to decline as a result of source reduction measures. The mosquito density is slowly coming down, the official said. About 25,000 Domestic Breeding Checkers (DBC) have been engaged across the State, with 20 persons covering one block.
Dr. Somasundaram said while preventive measures had been intensified, they had been holding daily monitoring meetings with District Health Officers via video conferencing. “We are analysing the case trend, whether increase or decrease or static, and number of laboratory tests conducted. We are also monitoring fever triaging, patient management, and discharge policy. Patients are being categorised as having mild, moderate, or severe symptoms and treated appropriately. Right now, the severity of infections is less. Fogging operations and source reduction measures, along with work taken up by DBCs, are being supervised. We are also looking at creating awareness among the public,” he said.
With October and November being crucial months, he said, there could be intermittent or heavy rain and people should ensure that their household environment is clean. “Avoid storing water unnecessarily. If you have too, keep containers closed properly,” he added.

While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.
Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.
When Ars Technica talked to Nvidia’s Andrew Bell earlier this year, he framed the Shield as a passion project, but it looks like passion projects still have to pay the bills at Nvidia. In that interview, Bell explained that Nvidia still actively manufactures the Shield and sells every unit it makes. Without a stockpile of pre-AI hardware to sell, new Shield TV units are subject to the same supply chain constraints as today’s smartphones and computers.
Nvidia isn’t a victim here, though. As a key player in AI hyper scaling, the company is more responsible than most for the sky-high cost of components. It has also become one of the most valuable firms in the world thanks to its market-leading AI accelerators and GPUs. As a consequence, we’re seeing new products launch at higher prices than their predecessors, and many end up getting more expensive during their lifetimes. Game consoles have been particularly affected, with Nintendo, Microsoft, and Sony all bumping the prices of their current-gen hardware. The PS5 Pro, for example, has gone from $699.99 at launch in 2024 to $899.99 today.
Stock of the Shield TV Pro has been slim for the last few months, probably because it became too expensive to manufacture new units with component prices rising so quickly. At $300, it will make sense for Nvidia to churn out more devices. However, this higher price will cause an already niche set-top box to be even less appealing to people who just want to stream Netflix.
Unless you need the Shield’s extensive codec support or Plex server capability, it makes more sense to get a cheaper streamer. The Shield is still out of stock on Nvidia’s store, but it’s available at the new price from Best Buy.

India, Switzerland sign 5 pacts as PM Modi, President Guy Parmelin discuss trade, defence and nuclear energy
India and Switzerland signed agreements covering migration and mobility, young professionals, transportation, research, and innovation and technology transfer.
India and Switzerland on Monday concluded two agreements on the mobility of professionals and agreed to expand access for Indian exports to Swiss markets as Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Guy Parmelin explored ways to enhance cooperation in defence and nuclear energy.
Parmelin is accompanied by a high-level business delegation and his visit coincides with the first anniversary of the coming into force of the Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA) that India signed with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), a bloc that includes Switzerland, Iceland, Norway and Liechtenstein.
Modi described TEPA, India's first trade deal with any European economic bloc, as an ambitious blueprint for investment, innovation, and jobs that envisages $100 billion in investments and the creation of one million jobs in India over 15 years by the four countries.
“We have taken several important decisions to expand market access for Indian exports to Switzerland and further facilitate investment between the two countries,” Modi said at a joint media interaction with Parmelin.
These measures will increase India's exports in agriculture, pharmaceuticals, textiles and engineering goods, and attract new Swiss investments in biotech, life sciences, banking, insurance, food processing and sustainability.
India, Switzerland sign mobility agreements
The two sides signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) for a migration and mobility partnership, which will develop cooperation in this field “under equal treatment principles” and prevent irregular migration and human trafficking. It also provides for multiple-entry visas for up to five years, including stays of up to six months on each visit, and renewable one-year student permits.
A second agreement will govern the exchange of young professionals taking up temporary employment in the other country to enhance their professional and language skills within their field. This covers the exchange of 300 people annually per country, and the figure may be increased to 500, and a timeline of 30 to 90 days for verification of nationality and residency status.
Modi flags defence, nuclear energy cooperation
Modi said innovation, infrastructure and advanced technology are strong pillars of the bilateral partnership and the new initiatives will help the joint development of trusted supply chains and reliable solutions for the world.
“Today, we identified new possibilities for cooperation in military exchanges and defence production. We also agreed to further deepen cooperation in nuclear energy,” Modi said, speaking in Hindi.
Parmelin described the partnership as mutually beneficial. India will gain access to capital and technology transfers as well as easier access to markets for high-value-added goods, while Switzerland will benefit from trade “with a massive partner experiencing sustained growth, at a time when global trade has become more exposed and unpredictable”, he said, speaking in French.
Switzerland seeks investment protection pact
However, Parmelin emphasised the importance of quickly concluding an agreement on investment protection to stimulate investment.
“In this context, it is equally important to achieve results in discussions on the protection of intellectual property,” he said.
Modi also invited Swiss infrastructure companies to invest in India on a large scale and participate in capacity building, design and manufacturing. He said the two sides will launch new joint research projects in priority areas such as health, clean energy and space.
Parmelin added that both sides aim to promote an AI governance model that is innovative and equitable. “We are living through very difficult times. It is all the more essential to create win-win situations at the international level,” he said.
Five agreements signed
The two sides signed three more agreements – an MoU on collaboration in transportation technologies, mobility systems and infrastructure that will promote cooperation in sustainable infrastructure, electric vehicles, ropeways and tunnels, a letter of intent to promote long-term cooperation between the Indian and Swiss research communities, and an implementation arrangement for cooperation in innovation, technology transfer and entrepreneurship.
Ukraine, West Asia conflicts discussed
International and regional issues, including the conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, figured in the talks between the two leaders. Modi said both sides believe in dialogue and diplomacy and work for global peace and stability. “Whether in Ukraine or West Asia, India has supported every meaningful effort towards peace,” he said.
Sibi George, secretary (West) in the external affairs ministry, told a media briefing that India and the EFTA bloc had agreed to set up a special group to discuss all issues related to trade and investment and to address constraints.
Switzerland is India's largest trading partner in EFTA and its 15th largest trade partner overall, with two-way trade worth $25 billion. About 340 Swiss companies have operations in India and have invested $11 billion in areas such as pharmaceuticals, chemicals, precision engineering and advanced technology
Switzerland is home to almost 30,000 Indians, including students and professionals actives in areas such as financial services, engineering, IT and pharmaceuticals.

An explosive and newly partially unsealed court filing alleges that the US Department of Homeland Security built up dossiers on ICE observers—including their photos, license plate numbers, and other information—and stored them in a system called the Investigative Case Management database, which was built by Palantir.
Palantir did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for DHS calls the case “meritless” and says that “the underlying lawsuit is based on the lie that there is a database of ‘domestic terrorists’ run by DHS.”
Plaintiffs allege in the filing, which is heavily based on documents produced by the government and depositions of DHS agents, that agents had a practice of intimidating protesters and observers. They did this, the filing says, by doing drive-bys of the observers’ homes and, in the case of at least one observer, requiring that she be referred to secondary inspection any time she tries to cross the border until at least January 2027.
"The government is treating people who exercise their First Amendment rights and seek to hold it accountable as criminal suspects, and that's what we're asking the court to stop,” says JoAnna Suriani, an attorney at Protect Democracy who is representing ICE observers in the case.
The filing focuses on agents’ conduct during “Operation Catch of the Day,” an immigration enforcement surge in Maine this past January. It is part of a proposed class action brought in federal court in Maine by four observers: Elinor Hilton, Colleen Fagan, Polyxenia Pantos, and Carlyn Williams. It was filed under seal in September, and a redacted version was made public Friday.
In particular, it describes how one DHS agent, referred to as “Agent J.C.” in the filing, used the Investigative Case Management (ICM) database, which the government describes as the case management system the ICE component Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) uses to document its investigations, to flag observers.
According to the filings, J.C. created ICM records on at least six observers; the government puts the number of people at eight. He labeled two people he filmed at a Home Depot parking lot with “Threat to Law Enforcement, Professional Protestor,” according to the filing, and sent photos of them and others to a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer so he could run a facial recognition search on them using an app called Mobile Query.
On January 20, Pantos briefly watched and photographed an arrest in Portland, Maine, standing a few car lengths away beside their spouse's car. Hours later, per the filing, J.C. ran the car's plate and pulled a report on the owner—Williams—from Accurint, a LexisNexis database for law enforcement, which listed her address, phone numbers, and cohabitants. J.C. then allegedly circulated her photo to his team, asking, “Was this the protestor.” Another agent, per the filing, replied that it didn’t match the woman he had dealt with at the scene; J.C. then told colleagues he was "adding them in ICM now."
According to the legal filing, that afternoon, J.C. called Williams on her cell phone, identifying himself only as "the Department of Homeland Security." According to Williams, he told her she "should encourage" her spouse, Pantos, "not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist." J.C. testified in a deposition that he warned Williams she would be arrested if she “continue[d] to do this.” Government attorneys asserted in a court filing that he denied referencing a “domestic terrorism watchlist.”
According to documents produced by the government, Williams’ ICM record says that she was the registered owner of a vehicle used to “interrupt ICE arrests” and that her driver’s license photo matched a video of "aggressive woman [who] interject[ed] herself into an arrest." According to a 2016 DHS privacy assessment, ICM automatically shares the subject records agents create with CBP’s TECS system, where they act as "lookout records" for screening travelers at the border.
ICM is the system used by HSI agents to create and track case files. ICE awarded Palantir the contract to build ICM in 2014, and the system is built on the company’s Gotham software, which ICE says was customized specifically for operational needs. In 2022, ICE awarded Palantir a new five-year ICM support contract initially valued at up to about $96 million. In 2025, the agency added nearly $30 million to that contract to develop a new platform called “ImmigrationOS.”
Todd Lyons, the former acting director of ICE, wrote in an April letter to Rep. Maxwell Frost, the Florida Democrat, that ICE “does not maintain any kind of database of U.S. citizens protesting ICE activities.” He also said DHS isn’t keeping a “separate, standalone database” of people it hasn’t arrested or detained.
The government’s motion to dismiss argues that these were isolated incidents and that DHS policy prohibits this conduct. It says J.C. made records on people he believed were “potential threats to law enforcement” and “did not attempt to nominate any individuals to the terrorist watchlist.”
Attorneys for the observers say that DHS’s efforts have had a chilling effect on their First Amendment rights. According to the motion, Pantos stopped all ICE observation work after J.C.’s phone call to Williams, who briefly continued to observe ICE activity and then stopped all together too.
The observers are asking the court to order that Williams’ records be archived, to bar DHS from using the information it collected about the plaintiffs against them, and to prohibit agents in Maine from threatening observers with watchlists or following them to their homes.

The story so far
The groundwater resources of Kerala have been under severe stress due to changes in rainfall pattern following climate change, high population density as well the fact that approximately 62% of the population relies on groundwater from an estimated 6.5 million open wells for their domestic needs. The State’s fragmented wastewater management system and the unscientific construction of septic tanks and pit latrines at homes close to shallow and open wells have resulted in persistent faecal contamination of ground water in the State, which has been documented by several studies.
A 2024 study in the Journal of Environmental Management reported that 7.4% of the State’s population could be making do with poor quality of groundwater and estimated that 0.59 million people in 252 local self government bodies in the State could be continuously exposing themselves to health risks from consuming ground water from wells which may not be chlorinated regularly.
And the latest report on E.coli contamination comes from Pala, where a water quality assessment conducted in flood-affected areas along the Meenachil river detected E. coli bacteria in 67% of the samples, raising concerns over the safety of drinking water sources in and around Pala.
Researchers attributed the spike in bacterial contamination to the recent floods, which may have allowed contaminated surface water to enter water sources.
How is contamination taking place?
It is a dangerous combination of high population density, unplanned urbanisation with hundreds of septic tanks and wells sitting close to each other in small plots and the State’s natural hydrogeological features that allow surface pollutants to reach the water table quickly. In recent years, unpredictable and heavy rainfall has been adding to the State’s woes, as oversaturation of the soil and the overflow of drainage systems can quickly allow pollution and microbial contamination to infiltrate ground water.
Environmental scientists explain that groundwater is drawn mostly from shallow, unconfined aquifers, which are recharged directly by rainfall and surface infiltration. In most areas the local water table might be sitting just below the level of the river bed and it naturally leaks water downwards to recharge the underlying unconfined aquifers. If rivers are polluted, then all groundwater resources in the surrounding area would also be carrying the same pollutant.
What is the extent of groundwater contamination in Keralam?
A community-level GIS study of 449 households in an urban area of Thiruvananthapuram in 2018 had reported that most of the wells were in an intermediate-high contamination risk state, with more than 77% of wells having a septic tank within 7.5 m radius. Coliform contamination was prevalent in 73% of wells, and the groundwater was predominantly acidic with a mean of 5.4, rendering it unfit for drinking.
This picture could be true for the rest of the State also. Because of the State’s unique geography and highly dispersed, continuous rural-urban settlement pattern, just about 5-6% of major urban zones are connected to a centralised pipe-based sewerage network system. The State’s sanitation strategy relies heavily on onsite sanitation systems, with individual household septic tanks and soak pits for sewage disposal.
Unscientific construction of these household sanitation systems has rendered much of the groundwater resources unsafe for human consumption, unless properly treated.
What are the health impacts?
Safe drinking water is one of the crucial social determinants of health. It is thus unfortunate that a State which has made enviable strides in developing its public health sector has paid little attention to ensuring that people have access to safe drinking water. While people in urban areas have to a large extent, access to treated water supply, in many rural areas of the State serviced by local small water supply schemes, water distribution lines often run close to sewerage lines and even small breaks in the pipelines can lead to the contamination of drinking water
Recurrent outbreaks of water-borne diseases like Hepatitis A, Shigellosis and norovirus outbreaks have been the bane of the State in recent years, especially in the northern districts of the State, indicating the scale and impact of groundwater contamination. Hepatitis A in particular has been taking a heavy toll on the State since the last three years, with significant mortality and in many instances, leaving people with severe morbidities
Epidemiological studies conducted by the ICMR and Health department into amoebic meningoencephalitis, which has emerged as a significant public health problem in Keralam in recent times, has traced the infection to the use of non-chlorinated well water which has high concentration of E.coli, in which free-living amoeba thrive
What is the sewerage infrastructure status?
To modernise sewerage infrastructure, the State is executing projects under the AMRUT 2.0 Mission, a Central initiative aimed at ensuring universal access to safe water and reliable sewerage connections across urban areas. The CAG’s 2025 report stated that at the closure of the AMRUT Mission (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation), Kerala’s overall achievement was just 11.25% and only 0.13% households got sewerage connections.
Keralam’s geography, population density, lack of vast tracts of uninhabited land means that many proposed treatment plants end up being close to residential areas, which triggered huge public protests. Such protests led to the cancellation of multiple approved septage treatment plant projects in many parts of the State. There are also reports about the State’s financial crunch affecting project payments leading to delays in implementation

Anantnag, Oct 5: The MSME Development and Facilitation Office (MSME-DFO), Srinagar, in collaboration with the District Industries Centre (DIC), Anantnag, today commenced a five-day Management Development Programme (MDP) on “Business Marketing Management” for entrepreneurs from the manufacturing and service sectors.
The programme aims to equip Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) with contemporary marketing knowledge and practical tools to expand their market reach, strengthen business operations and compete effectively in a changing business environment.
Prof. Parvez Ahmad Mir, Head, CIED, IUST, attended the inaugural session as the Chief Guest, while the General Manager, DIC Anantnag, presided as the Guest of Honour.
Addressing the participants, Prof. Mir discussed emerging marketing trends and opportunities for MSMEs, stressing the need for enterprises to adopt innovative marketing strategies, leverage technology and build competitive capabilities to contribute effectively to economic growth and employment generation.
The General Manager, DIC Anantnag, welcomed the initiative and termed such programmes a timely step towards strengthening the industrial sector. She emphasised the importance of capacity building and continuous learning to help entrepreneurs respond effectively to changing market requirements.
Assistant Director, MSME-DFO Srinagar, Saheel Alaqband, in his keynote address, highlighted the significance of the five-day programme in strengthening the managerial and marketing capabilities of MSME entrepreneurs. He also thanked the DIC Anantnag for its support and cooperation in organising the programme.
The programme is being attended by 25 entrepreneurs from manufacturing-based MSMEs operating in the industrial estates of Anantnag. During the programme, participants will be exposed to various aspects of business development and enterprise growth, including Intellectual Property Rights (IPR), AI-enabled marketing, contemporary marketing strategies and major MSME schemes and initiatives.
The programme is expected to help participating entrepreneurs improve their market presence, adopt modern business practices and enhance the competitiveness of their enterprises.

The UK has threatened to expel one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat forced to leave Israel as a result of Israel’s decision to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.
This could mean as many as 27 Israeli diplomats being expelled from the UK, a step that would arguably mark the lowest point in British-Israeli diplomatic relations since the formation of the state of Israel.
The mass expulsion threat – more reminiscent of British-Russian diplomatic relations – was first reported by the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials. The UK Foreign Office said it would not comment on speculation, rather than denying the report outright.
Israel has threatened to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem in protest at the UK decision to ban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and to impose sanctions on British firms that aid, support or facilitate the construction of further illegal settlements.
The Foreign Office has been advised informally by the former UK attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel is acting unlawfully if it closes the consulate on the basis it is sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.
Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, has said that Britain’s decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused Britain’s ruling Labour party of being hostile towards the country.
The consulate, which Israel’s foreign ministry has said will close on Thursday, is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza. It is located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East Jerusalem.
An Israeli diplomatic source said: “There is no reason for us to respond to speculation about decisions that other countries may or may not take in the future.
“We have already demonstrated that any step taken against Israel will be met with an appropriate response, and that will continue to be the case.”
The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Jerusalem last week in an effort to persuade the Israeli government to rescind or defer the closure of the consulate but the talks failed.
It has been reported that Powell opposed the decision of the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, to press ahead with the settlement trade ban decision, fearing that it might play to the advantage of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, in the national election on 27 October as he seeks to bolster his case that only his brand of leadership can bring Israel security. There is no evidence yet that the UK decision has featured in the campaign, but tit-for-tat expulsions of diplomats may raise its profile.
The incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this.
Diplomats from other western countries have been very worried about the closure setting a precedent, and suggest that Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it has implications beyond the immediate dispute.
Shutting down the consulate involves Israel claiming authority in Jerusalem that it does not have under international law, so it is effectively a challenge to the status quo.
“We are all concerned because if this (closure of the consulate) goes ahead it would be an incredibly damaging precedent for the status of missions in Jerusalem, which are monitoring the status quo,” said one western diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity.
“It would be inconceivable for the British government to accept (the closure) because they don’t recognise the authority of the Israeli government over Jerusalem under international law. Particularly as Israel is taking this step over British measures which are simply applying international law.”
Israel has also said it is to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine, in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine. The decision also in effect bars them from Israel-controlled East Jerusalem.
France and Canada, which also joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.
Miliband received a very warm reception at the UK Labour party conference last week during a speech in which he highlighted his decision to get tough with Israel over illegal settlements.
UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza begun by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis as the UK became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the death of thousands of Palestinians in a bid to render Hamas inoperative, a task both the Conservative and Labour governments thought was unachievable through his methods.
The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel as a result and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds that he believes this is a matter for international courts alone to determine.

Indian consumer companies are seeing demand hold up in the September quarter, but investors are watching margins, underlying consumption and rural demand as input costs remain a concern.
Early quarterly updates point to continued growth across consumer businesses, although a later festive calendar is expected to shift a significant part of demand into the December quarter. This comes as India’s headline inflation rate (CPI) rose to 4.82% in August 2026, the highest since December 2024, from 4.45% in the previous month.
“Amid sustained inflationary pressure, the need for price hikes is rising, potentially impacting volumes ahead,” said analysts at HDFC Securities in a 5 October report. “As companies attempt to balance growth and margins, we expect earnings stress to persist.”
Demand holds
For Marico, the maker of Parachute and Saffola, domestic underlying volume growth reached double digits in the September quarter.
“Domestic demand remained resilient during the quarter, even as the operating environment stayed volatile through the period,” the company said in a quarterly filing on Monday.
Marico’s value-added hair oils business recorded growth in the twenties for the sixth consecutive quarter, while volumes of Saffola oils declined as the company prioritised profitability and reduced supplies of some variants.
Copra prices remained about 35% below their peak, supporting Marico's gross margins.
“We forecast volumes to grow ~10% YoY led by Parachute, where volumes are expected to grow ~14% YoY—21-quarter high (~10% YoY in Q1FY27), reflecting a second consecutive quarter of market share gain in our view,” analysts at Nuvama Institutional Equities said in a report on Tuesday.
AWL Agri Business, meanwhile, is seeing a broad-based expansion beyond its traditional edible oils business.
The company delivered 12% year-on-year volume growth and 24% revenue growth during the quarter. Food and FMCG revenue rose 33%, crossing ₹2,000 crore for the first time in a quarter. The traditional edible-oil business was more subdued, with volumes growing 3%.
Costs bite
The cost environment will be another variable. Godrej Consumer Products Ltd said it would report “high-teens revenue growth, high-single-digit underlying volume growth and double-digit Ebitda growth” in the quarter.
However, the company is watchful of raw material prices. “Input cost pressures intensified during the quarter,” the company said on Monday.
“We are responding through a combination of calibrated pricing actions, cost-saving initiatives, supply-chain efficiencies, and disciplined cost management,” GCPL said.
Dabur also flagged pressure on margins. “Operating margins were impacted by inflationary pressures during the quarter; partly offset by calibrated price increases and ongoing cost-saving initiatives," Dabur said in its quarterly update on Tuesday. It expects revenues to record double-digit growth in Q2.
Sugar prices have also corrected sharply, down 21% from the peak, after a sharp 16% run-up in August.
Brent crude prices also hover around $100 a barrel due to geopolitical uncertainties, driving higher packaging costs across consumer companies and increasing raw material costs for detergent makers.
Nykaa offers a different picture, with both its beauty and fashion businesses growing at a rapid pace. Nykaa's like-for-like store sales growth was the strongest in six quarters.
Retail lags
Value retailers had a tougher time.
V2 Retail, the value-fashion retailer, reported 0.5% same-store sales growth because Navratri and Durga Puja fell in the September quarter last year and will fall in October this year, the company said.
The timing difference is particularly important for retailers. “With the festive season ahead, we are well-positioned to capture the demand uplift in Q3 while sustaining our long-term growth,” V2 Retail said.
The seasonal change also matters for Avenue Supermarts, the operator of DMart. The company reported standalone revenue from operations of ₹19,206 crore for the September quarter.
Investors were unimpressed. V2 Retail’s share price tanked 19% to hit a 52-week low after the update, while shares of DMart slipped up to 4% on Monday.
The inherent challenges of listed players become visible in such instances.
“We are not very bullish about listed large players and in all of these consumption categories. The future is going to be around the smaller players who will innovate more, who will spend more on new products, who will come out with more experiences,” said Anand Ramanathan, partner & consumer industry leader, Deloitte India.
Rural watch
Companies have implemented major price hikes in recent months.
“We would be cautious about assuming a full margin recovery in Q3 if raw-material inflation persists,” said Ronak Shah, consumer-sector analyst at Equirus Securities.
Shah expects companies to maintain prices during the festive period. “If input costs remain elevated, we would expect further price increases around October-end/November,” Shah said.
Rural demand will also be a key monitorable, given its importance to volume growth. The Union government has declared drought in five states so far and assessed 6.11 lakh hectares of cropland as having been affected by extreme rains and floods, Union agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said on 29 September.
Companies have not yet sounded the alarm on rural demand, as irrigation facilities have developed in recent years.

Relative humidity is a simple concept as weather phenomena go – but it has significant, far-reaching consequences for how we must take care of ourselves on a hot or wet day.
Letting the wind flow freely is the secret to cooling our cities
Humidity is the amount of moisture in the air around us, and there are three ways to track it. The most common of them is absolute humidity: the mass of water vapour in a given volume of the air and water vapour mixture, expressed as kg/m3. The second is specific humidity, equal to the mass of the moisture divided by the mass of air. It is expressed as a dimensionless number (but sometimes also as grams per kilogram, among other similar units.)
The third way is relative humidity: it is important because it factors in the amount of vapour that air can hold at different temperatures. Determining its value is a bit more complicated: it is the vapour density of the air divided by the saturation vapour density at the dry-bulb temperature.
Why does relative humidity matter?
On a hot day, our body uses sweat to cool itself. Sweat is released via our skin to the surface. There, the liquid evaporates. When water changes phase from liquid to vapour, it absorbs heat from the surface on which it lies. So when sweat evaporates, it absorbs heat from the skin, cooling it.
The higher the relative humidity of air, the more it is filled with moisture. When air already contains a lot of moisture, it won’t easily accept more. This means that the sweat on your skin can’t evaporate. At the same time, the body keeps sweating because it is still expecting to cool itself.
As a result, if the relative humidity is high, you can sweat on a hot day even when you are sitting still – while your body also keeps accumulating heat. This can quickly become dangerous.
A relative humidity of 30-60% is generally considered to be comfortable. Environments that have lower levels than this typically use humidifiers to increase the humidity. When the level is higher, a fan will help move the air around you and help sweat evaporate better.
In both cases, drinking water is important.
What does relative humidity imply physically?
Warmer air can hold more moisture than cooler air. So at the same absolute humidity, the relative humidity of warmer air will be lower than that of cooler air. It is like saying two vessels can hold the same amount of water – just that the bigger vessel will be less full than the smaller vessel.
This is why, for example, while Chennai had an absolute humidity of 70% at 2.30 pm on April 23, its relative humidity was lower, around 60%, because it had an ambient temperature of 32 C.
The change in the capacity for moisture as the air warms is also non-linear, meaning it doesn’t increase by the same amount as the air warms. For example, the difference as it warms over 20º C from -20º C to 0º C is small, but there is an enormous improvement in its vapour-carrying capacity as it warms over 20º C from 30º C to 50º C.
How do you measure relative humidity?
There are a few ways to measure relative humidity. One is to conduct a simple experiment with household items; another is to use maths; a third is to use an app or device.
Experiment
For the experiment, you need two mercury thermometers, some cotton, rubber bands, and access to cold water.
First, make sure both thermometers show the same reading, say, under a fan. Next, soak some cotton in cold water and wrap it around the bulb of one of the thermometers with a rubber band. Hold this thermometer under the fan, such that water from the cotton evaporates, and record the thermometer reading after five minutes. Hold up the other thermometer in the air and record its reading after five minutes. You will thus have the wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperatures, respectively.
Next, subtract the wet-bulb temperature from the dry-bulb temperature to get the temperature difference. Finally, use the relative humidity chart (see below) to get the relative humidity value. For example, if the difference was 6 C and the dry-bulb temperature was 28 C, the relative humidity would have been 59%.
A psychrometer is a device that has two such thermometers plus a chart to get the final reading. Modern, electronic psychrometers can calculate the relative humidity directly.
For a rough sense, the lower the wet-bulb temperature, the drier the air is, and the less relatively humid it is.
Mathematics
There are two mathematical ways (among others) to estimate the relative humidity, one simpler and one a bit more involved.
The first way is to divide the actual vapour pressure by the saturated vapour pressure. The vapour pressure is the amount of moisture that air contains. The ‘saturated’ value is the maximum possible amount. The formula (below) requires the dew point (Td), which you can obtain from a weather website.
RH = (e/es)*100
e = 6.11 x 10((7.5 x Td)/(237.3 + Td))
For es, use the same formula but replace Td with T, the actual temperature.
The second way is to calculate relative humidity starting from the specific humidity, pressure and temperature, using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
App
If you prefer software: Search for “hygrometer” in your phone’s app store to locate some options. (A hygrometer is an instrument that measures humidity.) Note that the app will only work if your phone has a sensor that can sense humidity.
If you like hardware, psychrometers and devices called hygrometers are available in physical as well as online stores.
Why does the wet-bulb temperature matter?
This said, a more direct way to understand the implications of the relative humidity for your wellbeing is in the form of the wet-bulb temperature (a.k.a. the adiabatic saturation temperature). It is the lowest temperature a surface – like your skin – can reach when water evaporates from it. The wet-bulb temperature is equal to the dry-bulb temperature when the relative humidity is 100%.
A wet-bulb temperature in an environment of 32-35º C or higher can be quickly lethal, even if you are not doing any physical activity or are in the shade. (At least one study has shown that even a wet-bulb temperature of more than 29º C can be dangerous.)
The climate crisis is rendering heatwaves more common, more frequent, more spread out, and more potent over the Indian subcontinent. As a study published in May 2022 put it:
“Whether today’s most impactful heatwaves could have occurred in a pre-industrial climate, traditionally a central focus of attribution research, is fast becoming an obsolete question. The next frontier for attribution science is to inform adaptation decision-making in the face of unprecedented future heat.”
One way to adapt is to keep an eye on the relative humidity, drink lots of water, and cool yourself.
- Humidity is the amount of moisture in the air around us, and there are three ways to track it. The most common of them is absolute humidity: the mass of water vapour in a given volume of the air and water vapour mixture, expressed as kg/m3.
- The higher the relative humidity of air, the more it is filled with moisture. When air already contains a lot of moisture, it won’t easily accept more.
- A wet-bulb temperature in an environment of 32-35º C or higher can be quickly lethal, even if you are not doing any physical activity or are in the shade. (At least one study has shown that even a wet-bulb temperature of more than 29º C can be dangerous.)
