Edtech major PhysicsWallah’s wholly owned subsidiary FinZ Finance has agreed to sell a ₹95.79 Cr loan portfolio to Auxilo Finserve, taking forward the company’s retreat from direct student lending announced four months ago. FinZ signed the deed of assignment on Saturday (October 3), with the transition of the loans and associated borrowers expected to conclude within 60 days, PhysicsWallah said in an exchange filing yesterday. The portfolio represents a substantial portion of FinZ’s loan book. The filing also pegged the consideration for the transaction at ₹95.79 Cr. “As the principal business activity of FinZ Finance is lending, the proposed transaction constitutes a substantial reduction in its lending operations and is expected to result in partial/piecemeal closure of its lending operations,” the company said. PhysicsWallah said the sale forms part of a broader strategic realignment to optimise capital allocation and focus on its core business. Lending would instead be facilitated through established, regulated third-party NBFCs to reduce balance sheet exposure and credit risks. Founded in 2017, Mumbai-based Auxilo Finserve is an RBI-registered NBFC that provides education loans and financing to students and other stakeholders in the education sector. Unwinding The Lending Push The transaction follows PhysicsWallah’s decision in June to reverse its direct student lending strategy, shortly after approving a ₹120 Cr capital infusion into FinZ Finance in May. The proposed investment put pressure on the company’s shares and raised concerns about its capital allocation priorities. Announcing the reversal, cofounder Prateek Maheshwari said feedback from partners indicated that the company should focus on its education business and leave lending to NBFCs with established underwriting capabilities. Under the revised model, the edtech company would operate as a technology platform connecting students with lending partners, with financing tailored to their learning lifecycle and academic progress. It said this would improve affordability and accessibility while making financing more scalable and better integrated into its student ecosystem. At the time, PhysicsWallah said FinZ’s future strategic direction would be decided subsequently, subject to board and regulatory approvals. FinZ commenced business operations in February 2026, according to the latest filing. It reported negligible operating revenue and ₹1.35 Cr in other income in FY26, taking its total income to ₹1.35 Cr, or 0.04% of PhysicsWallah’s total income. Its net worth stood at ₹60.3 Cr as of March 31, representing 1.18% of PhysicsWallah’s net worth. As Inc42 previously reported, PhysicsWallah’s lending push raised questions about the potential conflict between driving student enrolments and maintaining lending discipline when the same group controls both education and financing. The concerns also reflected the sector’s experience with BYJU’S, whose use of third-party loans to finance courses drew allegations of mis-selling and coercive recovery practices. Meanwhile, PhysicsWallah’s operating revenue rose 24.4% to ₹1,054 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹847.1 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Its net loss narrowed 30.5% to ₹88.3 Cr from ₹127 Cr in Q1 FY26. However, the loss widened 27.8% from ₹69.1 Cr in the preceding quarter. Shares of PhysicsWallah were trading 6.12% higher at ₹127.50 on the BSE at 13:42 IST.

Sixteen years ago, Andrew Garfield played the Facebook co-founder who was pushed out of the company he helped create in “The Social Network” and came up short in the supporting actor race. Now, he’s playing the CEO pushed out of OpenAI — and who talked his way back in five days later. Different man, different company. Same category, hoping for a different outcome.
As “Artificial” world premieres at the New York Film Festival, Variety has learned exclusively that the film’s awards campaign will include Garfield competing in the supporting actor category for Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI drama, while Yura Borisov, who plays OpenAI co-founder and former chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, will campaign in lead actor. Oscar winner Mark Rylance, as AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton, will join Garfield in the supporting race, while Monica Barbaro, as former OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati, will vie for supporting actress.
The campaign will extend across all the major categories, including best picture, director and acting, while Simon Rich’s screenplay will compete in original screenplay and every craft department will receive a full campaign.
Popular on Variety
For Guadagnino, “Artificial” marks his fifth appearance at NYFF, following “Call Me by Your Name,” “Bones and All,” “Queer” and “After the Hunt,” which opened the festival last year. After Lincoln Center audiences get the first official look at the film, it heads to the BFI London Film Festival.
Garfield is a two-time best actor nominee for the war drama “Hacksaw Ridge” (2016) and the musical biopic “Tick, Tick … Boom!” (2021). While he has been the face of the marketing and plays the most famous name in the story, it’s not unprecedented for a film’s top-billed star to pursue a supporting nomination — as Meryl Streep did for “Into the Woods” and Oscar winner Catherine Zeta-Jones did for “Chicago.”
The film traces decades in the lives of Ilya and Sam Altman (Garfield), two men from completely different worlds who bond over a shared desire to change the world for the better amid the sunny glow of Obama-era tech optimism. They eventually find themselves at odds as the enormous — and increasingly dangerous — capabilities of their technology reveal themselves across the Trump and Biden years, before Altman is ousted. In other words, the audience rides with the man who pulled the trigger, not the one who took the bullet.
The best actor field is already crowded, with several contenders emerging from NYFF, including Pedro Pascal’s cellist in “Behemoth!”
Borisov is two years removed from his first Oscar nomination, for his breakthrough performance as the reluctant henchman Igor in Sean Baker’s best picture winner “Anora.”
The ensemble has Oscar pedigree throughout. Rylance won supporting actor for his turn in Steven Spielberg’s “Bridge of Spies,” while Barbaro is two years removed from her first nom for playing Joan Baez in the Bob Dylan biopic “A Complete Unknown.” The rest of the cast includes Cooper Hoffman as Greg Brockman, Ike Barinholtz as Elon Musk, Jason Schwartzman, Chris O’Dowd, Billie Lourd and Zosia Mamet.
Behind the camera, Guadagnino has assembled many of his regular collaborators. Marco Costa, an ACE Eddie Award nominee for “Challengers,” returns for his duties while Jessica Ronane, a two-time Artios nominee who has cast Guadagnino’s films since “Queer,” handled casting. Production designer Stefano Baisi, whose credits include “Queer” and “After the Hunt,” builds the world alongside ADG nominee Roberta Federico. J.W. Anderson, the Costume Designers Guild nominee who dressed “Challengers” and “Queer,” returns as well.
One of the new faces behind the lens is cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed, a Camerimage winner whose credits include Spike Lee’s “Clockers,” Hype Williams’ “Belly” and Beyoncé’s “Lemonade.” Damon Albarn, the Blur frontman and Grammy winner with Gorillaz, composed the original score and wrote the original songs heard in the film. Submission details for which original songs will vie for attention are forthcoming.
Guadagnino is hoping to make his triumphant return to an Oscar ceremony. “Call Me by Your Name” earned four nominations at the 90th Oscars and won adapted screenplay for James Ivory. Among the producers are Jeffrey Clifford, Jennifer Fox, Guadagnino, David Heyman and Rich. Fox is an Oscar nominee for best picture for “Michael Clayton,” while Guadagnino was nominated for “Call Me by Your Name.” Heyman is a four-time best picture nominee for “Gravity,” “Marriage Story,” “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and “Barbie.”
Now, Guadagnino, Garfield and company will see if “Artificial” can prompt their Oscar comebacks.

Amid increasing state-sanctioned censorship of digital content across platforms like Meta and X, activists, journalists, cartoonists, artists, opposition politicians and others critical of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government and its policies have faced sweeping content restrictions and takedowns in the last few months. The latest to face such censorship are those raising concerns over the establishment of large-scale data centres in Visakhapatnam.
The port city in Andhra Pradesh is witnessing a massive digital infrastructure push, with investments of up to ₹1.25 lakh crore planned over five years (2026–30) and more than 2,000 acres of land earmarked for data centre projects. In October last year, Google and Adani formally announced an AI hub project in Visakhapatnam. By December 2025, 308 acres at Tarluvada, 120 acres at Adavivaram and 160 acres at Rambilli had been identified for the project. In January this year, reports indicated a much larger expansion involving Google, Sify, Reliance and CtrlS.
In April, the state government and Google laid the foundation stone for the Google Cloud India AI Hub at Tarluvada village. The facility, spread across 266.6 acres, is expected to draw 1 GW of power and is reportedly Google’s largest data centre outside the United States.
The projects are expected to make Visakhapatnam a major eastern data and subsea-cable hub, providing direct routes for Indian data to the US, South Africa, Singapore and Australia. Officials say this could reduce reliance on existing routes through Chennai, Kochi and the Red Sea, while shifting high-value technology activity from expensive metros to other cities.
But local influencers and journalists have raised concerns about the environmental and ecological impact of this rapid expansion of data centre infrastructure in Visakhapatnam and beyond.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
Why the Data Centres are being Opposed
The Stop Dirty Data Centre campaign, led by over 60 individuals, formed to “oppose the setting up of 6.5 GW of AI data centres”, lists over 10 proposed data centres spanning across over 2,500 acres of land in Visakhapatnam. Besides the Tarluvada facility, the list mentions two other major Google-Adani Hyperscale data centers: At Rambilli village consuming 1 GW of power across 174.8 acres, and at Adavivaram-Mudasarlova consuming 512 MW of power across 165.40 acres of land. All three are currently under-construction.
It is important to note that Adavivaram-Mudasarlova is around 120 metres from the Mudasarlova reservoir — a critical drinking water source for the city; it also lies near the Kailasagiri-Kambalakonda forest landscape. The Tarluvada site is located 1.53 km from the Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary and about 450 metres from its notified Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ) while the Rambilli site lies on the Anakapalli coast and is surrounded by forests.
As most of these sites lie on coastal regions, close to wildlife sanctuaries, forest areas and ESZs, opponents of this expansion project have flagged the disproportionate energy and land usage, large-scale hill cutting, deforestation, and further water depletion in an already water-scarce zone — Visakhapatnam’s water demand already exceeds supply by around 70 million litres per day. They also cite the massive impact on climate, biodiversity, wildlife sanctuaries, coastal ecosystems, and residential areas as serious detrimental effects.
“If fully built, the proposed AI data centers capacity could consume as much as the entire electricity currently used by the state of Andhra Pradesh,” states the campaign website. “Vizag is already severely water stressed and cooling these data centers could take up almost half of city’s supply based on estimates; the proposed land allocation is roughly equivalent to more than 700 cricket grounds, and is present in eco-sensitive regions; hyperscale AI facilities can significantly increase regional greenhouse gas emissions through backup Diesel Generator (DG) sets, solid waste, and more,” it adds.
Critics also highlighted the lack of transparency and public awareness around the setting up of these data centres, demanding that these projects be undertaken in consultation with locals and not unilaterally by the state and corporations. “In a brazen act of environmental lawlessness, forest land at the site [for the Adavivaram-Mudasarlova data centre] was cleared by the project proponent over several months even before environmental clearance was obtained,” alleges a petition initiated by the campaigners.
Citizen Movement Flagging Environmental Concerns Blocked
Against this backdrop, on September 19, the Instagram account of the Stop Vizag Data Centre campaign was banned in India under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000.
One of the founders, Deeksha Vanguru, told Alt News that they did not receive any prior notification. While the account was restored on September 27, nine of their posts critical of the data centre expansion, which were restricted over the last two months, remain unavailable in India.
“Our page was apparently blocked due to a local government request, we appealed to Meta and it was restored due to that request being either expired or reversed. However, our reach has been affected and posts are getting shadowbanned. We had to open a backup account in the meanwhile because we did not want to stop our fight. We are still fighting for the restoration of our nine posts,” Vanguru said.
“We started this as a citizen group in July this year. Most of us are born and brought up in Visakhapatnam and we couldn’t sit and watch the destruction of our home. We wanted to ensure that voices of the farmers, fishermen, villagers, and common citizens are heard. Initially, there was a small-scale mobilisation of citizens, but it needed more youth anger, therefore we turned the campaign into a social media project,” she added.
ALSO READ: Content creators decry Instagram censorship, call restrictions a ‘digital emergency’
“A big concern around AI data centres globally is the consumption of fresh water, and India is already going into a phase of water scarcity. The 10 data centres together are going to consume 200 MLD of water, which is 50% of the city’s daily water supply. The DGs will require constant air conditioning because they claim to be using advanced air cooling, thus the energy strain on the grid will be extremely high. Due to the constant running of generators and ACs, there could be overheating. The whole thing is going to be concrete, which will increase the land surface temperature and reduce night-time cooling. The average night-time temperature in Visakhapatnam has alreadt gone from 23-24 degrees to around 28 degrees,” she said.
Vanguru alleged there was no transparency while these data centres were being set up.
“The government hasn’t held any public consultation with either the farmers or the people of Vizag living close to these sites. In fact, environmental clearances for a 600-acre project, now broken up to escape scrutiny, was given within nine days. On April 9, the environmental clearance request was filed and it was received on April 18. There was no Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) because these projects haven’t been categorised as Category A projects (considered to have greater potential environmental impacts and are appraised by the Union environment ministry and require an EIA) but as Category B2 projects, which means buildings and construction. The way the government has gone about this is as if they’re building malls,” she said.
Further, Vanguru claimed that these data centres had nearly nothing to offer to the locals, even in terms of job creation, which she said was one of the upsides of an industrial construction. “When we checked the environmental clearances, the number of permanent jobs being created was only 1,725. The rest are all construction jobs and temporary jobs. These temporary and construction jobs are being positioned as skilled jobs, but in India, the government definition of skilled means blue-collar jobs. So it keeps people in the same worker or employee cycle and doesn’t really help uplift people from poverty,” she added.
Original Reportage on Dalit Displacement Blocked
After the Tarluvada data centre’s construction began, independent journalists Shamsheer Yousaf and Monica Jha began reporting the ground realities of the construction in early January, as part of the Dirty Data project undertaken by the Environmental Reporting Collective (ERC).
A 2-minute long Instagram reel posted by ERC in collaboration with Yousaf, which features interviews of Dalit farmers in the village who are faced with imminent displacement, was blocked in India on May 22 under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act with no prior notice. In the reel, which garnered 2.6 million views and 46,000 shares, several farmers say that they were granted the land over 50 years ago by the Congress government and have since cleared forests to build homes and farms, which is their only form of subsistence — all under threat as the same land has been allocated to the Google-Adani data centre.
View this post on Instagram
The reel formed part of a 5-minute-long video published on Dirty Data’s website alongside the report, ‘As data centers arrive, India’s poorest face displacement, health risks’ by Yousaf and Jha. Yousaf wrote to the Union ministry of electronics & information technology (MeitY), seeking the blocking order, reasons for the action, restoration of the reel and a personal hearing in order to appeal or respond. He also wrote to Meta’s grievance officer in India.
ALSO READ: Meta restricts posts by Indian Youth Congress, AAP, Opposition leader
Upon not receiving any response from either authorities, on June 30, Yousaf and Jha moved the Delhi high court with a writ petition. A month later on July 23, the petitioners were given access to the blocking order which revealed the authority behind the restriction as the director general of police (DGP), CID, Andhra Pradesh.
‘Procedural Lapses, Unconstitutional Takedown’
In a report, the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), whose lawyers are representing the petitioners, highlighted certain procedural lapses in the blocking order and claimed that the takedown was “unconstitutional”. The order names one Mr. Vemireddy Prabhakar Reddy, alleging that the video “spread misinformation” against him. However, this individual does not feature anywhere in the reel or any of the journalists’ reportage on the data centre issue; he is also not known to either of them.
IFF had then sent a legal notice to the principal secretary, home department and the DGP-CID, Andhra Pradesh, flagging this discrepancy and violation of the provision of the IT Rules, 2021. “…there have been several procedural lapses which violated Rule 14 of the IT Rules, 2021..the Petitioners were not served with any notice…never afforded an opportunity to submit a response/defend themselves…provided with a copy of the blocking order…[the takedown] directly affected [the petitioners] right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution,” the report read.
On September 10, the reel was restored. Yousaf found out through a notification this time, that the restriction was lifted as the “local legal requirement or government request that has now expired or been reversed” — similar to Vanguru’s case.
Local Influencers, HRF Silenced
In the same vein, several local influencers reported that their reels critical of the data centres were being arbitrarily taken down. Malla Gnanesh, who runs the page @vizag_blogger, told News Meter, that a reel he posted on May 28 titled ‘Vizag Welcoming Google Data Centre — At What Cost?’ was restricted in India on May 31. In the reel, Gnanesh spoke about the massive loss of green cover due to the construction of the data centre at the Adavivaram-Mudasarlova region.
Another account, @vizagmowa, also posted a reel on the negative environmental impact of the same data centre such as massive deforestation and water depletion due to its proximity to the Mudasarlova reservoir. This reel was withheld in India on May 30 with the same Section 79(3)(b) notification. Both reels remain restricted till date.
Human Rights Forum on June 1 published a statement condemning the rampant restrictions. Four of HRF’s own Instagram posts were blocked in India on May 31 and June 25, again under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act.
Speaking to Alt News, Vijayawada state coordinator of HRF, Rohith Gutta, stated: “We have moved the Andhra Pradesh high court with a writ petition against the unlawful restriction on September 28, demanding the blocking order, the reason for the action and the immediate restoration of our posts,” he said.
ALSO READ: Instagram censorship puzzle: Alt News post survives only after ‘Burhan Wani’ is removed
He mentioned that all four posts were critical of the date centre expansion. The two posts blocked on May 31 publicised an online petition seeking transparency and accountability regarding the proposed data centre projects; demanded an immediate stoppage of all ongoing site activities at the proposed sites in Adavivaram and Mudasarlova villages of Visakhapatnam Rural mandal.
The next two blocked on June 25 showed a protest in the city against the construction of all three data centres; questioned how the Adavivaram data centre received environmental clearance despite being located within an ESZ, close to the Mudasarlova reservoir. One of the these posts directly asked: “Should a Resource-Guzzling, Intensely Polluting Data Center be Located near a Reservoir? On its Catchment?”
“The restrictions imposed on HRF content by Instagram do not appear to be isolated incidents but form part of a broader pattern,” the Forum wrote while highlighting the restrictions imposed on Yousaf and Jha’s work with the ERC. The Forum also put out another statement condemning the restriction of the Stop Vizag Data Centers account.
Speaking about the ordeal, Rohith told Alt News, “The restrictions have not deterred us from speaking up against the data centres, however, it is a painful experience. We received no prior notification all four times and when we searched for the reason, it was only a vague message repeated word for word four times. It feels like you are legally violated because your work is banned without explanation. Now, blocking of posts is akin to being arrested digitally. We are living through times of ‘social media arrest’ and they [the authorities] have blocked all means to fight it.”
Alt News has reached out to Meta’s grievance officer in India and Kumar Vishwajeet, the principal secretary, home, Andhra Pradesh government. This article will be updated if and when we receive a response.
It is worth noting that the opposition to the projects has also spilled onto the streets, with residents, activists and environmental groups staging protests in Visakhapatnam over concerns around water consumption, deforestation, displacement and the environmental impact of the projects.

Yokosuka, Kanagawa Pref. – At 92, Kaori Kusakari shares her life with Purin, a 12-year-old male cat who has been by her side for years, at a rare elderly nursing home in Japan that allows pets to stay with their owners.
Five years ago, Kusakari moved into the facility, Sakura no Sato Yamashina, in the city of Yokosuka, Kanagawa Prefecture, with Purin.
Residents can live with their pets at the facility, and crucially, the animals can remain there after their owners die.
“Purin is always at my bedside,” Kusakari said, gently stroking him. “I feel at ease when I am close to him because we have spent so much time together.” Her relatives had searched for a place where she could continue living with Purin and found Sakura no Sato Yamashina, which opened in 2012.
Currently, 13 dogs and cats live there alongside about 40 residents. Some arrived with their owners and others came through animal welfare groups.
The demand has proved persistent. For five or six years, rooms in the facility’s designated area where dogs and cats can live with residents have been filled almost as soon as they became available.
Michihiko Wakayama, 61, the facility’s head and a board member of the social welfare corporation that operates it, said, “Seeing residents and animals sleeping peacefully together makes me feel that opening the facility was worth it.”
But not every elderly pet owner can move into a facility designed for people and animals to live together.
In the city of Niigata, civic group Doubutsu-gakari sends pet sitters to elderly people at discounted rates, helping with walks, feeding and cleaning.
Working with local governments, the group also convene meetings involving hospitals and social welfare councils when it receives reports from care managers that elderly people are struggling to keep up with their pets’ needs.
“Some elderly people refuse hospitalization or admission to care facilities because they do want to stay with their pets,” said Mami Miura, the group’s 62-year-old head. “In other cases, animals have died due to inadequate care.”
Miura says both sides of the relationship need watching.
Maiko Yasuno, an associate professor at Yokohama National University, who studies human-animal relationships, said, “Cooperation between elderly-care and animal-welfare services is essential.”
“Pet owners should decide in advance what they should do if the day comes when they can no longer provide adequate care themselves” to their beloved companions, she added.
For Kusakari, that question has already been answered, at least for now. Purin is beside her — where she wants him to be.

Telangana tea seller sets himself ablaze outside police station, cops cite dispute with grocer over cigarettes
The 55-year-old tea seller walked to the polcie station with a bottle of petrol and a matchbox and allegedly set himself ablaze.
A 55-year-old tea stall owner in Nizamabad district of Telangana reportedly attempted suicide by setting himself on fire in the premises of a police station in this district on Monday.
While the police said that the man was allegedly upset over being threatened by two local reporters, some local residents and political activists in Bheemgal town held protest seeking action against a Sub-Inspector of Police, who had booked a petty case against the tea stall owner, news agency PTI reported.
The 55-year-old man reportedly walked to the police station with a matchbox and a bottle of petrol on Monday morning. He then set himself ablaze outside a police station and some police personnel and people present there intervened and extinguished the flames after which he was taken to a hospital.
What the police said
Police cited an alleged rivalry with a grocery shop owner as a cause of the distress for the tea stall owner, which may have prompted him to take the extreme step. Police said the owner of a grocery shop had sent two reporters to threaten the middle-aged man after he recently stopped buying cigarettes and other material from his shop.
The police had registered a petty case against him for running his tea shop during late-night hours and he was asked by a Sub-Inspector of Police to pay the fine in court. The case was registered as part of routine enforcement duties, The Times of India quoted police officials as saying.
Nizamabad Police Commissioner P Sai Chaitanya said there was no fault on part of the police in the issue.

An OpenAI publicist tried to change the topic of CEO Sam Altman’s interview with Vanity Fair’s Mark Guiducci after the editor brought up a ChatGPT user’s suicide. When Guiducci confronted Altman about the incident, the publicist warned Guiducci about running out of time, saying she’d like to “move on” to another topic.
OpenAI PR tells journalist to ‘move on’ while asking Sam Altman about a ChatGPT user’s suicide
‘These are some of the hardest questions that we face or that anybody developing this technology faces,’ Altman said.
The interruption came shortly after Guiducci asked Altman if he knew who Laura Reiley is, a journalist who wrote an essay for The New York Times about her daughter’s conversations with ChatGPT before she took her own life. “Her daughter committed suicide after speaking to ChatGPT. ChatGPT did not tell her to kill herself—,” Guiducci said just before the publicist interrupted him.
“Mark, we have two minutes left. I want to be respectful, but I’d like to move on and talk a little bit about the future and what’s coming,” the publicist said. Even after Guiducci explained that he’s going to finish the question and then “go back to what we were talking about,” the publicist pushed back. “We really actually have to walk out the door in one or two minutes,” she said.
Despite the pushback, the interview continued with Guiducci asking Altman whether the company planned to use conversations with ChatGPT to shape policies surrounding its response to a user’s mental health crisis. “These are some of the hardest questions that we face or that anybody developing this technology faces,” Altman said. “You know, should we release people’s private data and some of their hardest moments to researchers? I think probably not without their consent. Or I should say, not without their consent.”
When reached for comment about the interruption, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said: “The interview was running over, which is why we ultimately asked to schedule even more time to continue the conversation after Sam addressed this critically important topic.”

988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: Call or text 988 (formerly known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline). The original phone number, 1-800-273-TALK (8255), is available as well.
The Trevor Project: Text START to 678-678 or call 1-866-488-7386 at any time to speak to a trained counselor.

Artificial, which had its world premiere Monday at the New York Film Festival, certainly comes in with a bit of controversy attached. Produced and made under Amazon MGM Studios, the Luca Guadagnino film about the origin of OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman and key creative Ilya Sutskever, was shopped around after Amazon decided maybe a tech company was not appropriate to release the finished film. Could it be the fact that Jeff Bezos with his own AI ambitions pumped $150 billion into OpenAI? Just sayin’.
After screening for a number of distributors in late spring, all of which passed, Neon, the scrappy indie with two Best Picture wins to its credit, decided it would take it on and scheduled a release for Christmas Day. The initial plan reportedly was to skip the festival circuit, but that clearly changed and is how NYFF — which is having a banner year for nabbing world premieres (not its usual status) — would up with the honor of first showing what Guadagnino hath wrought.
The film comes amidst an onslaught of new movies, both narrative and documentary, centered on tech personalities. There is Alex Gibney’s four-hour docu Musk; Nathan Fielder’s and Lance Oppenheim’s three-hour surprise Telluride sensation on Elizabeth Holmes, You Can See Everything; and this week’s wide release sans any festival exposure of Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Network follow-up The Social Reckoning (reviews on that one hit at 6 a.m. PT Wednesday).
Watch on Deadline
Artificial ‘s debut also comes at a timely moment when AI, and its ominous future, has become the stuff of daily headlines, especially after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and testified that he believes the AI companies are possibly leading us into armageddon, and even the end of all humanity by 2030, if they don’t take strong measures to add safeguards. After that, Altman came out publicly and was one of the tech moguls including Elon Musk to agree with that assessment. Chilling.
U.S. President Donald Trump, who with his sons is a big investor in AI, pooh-poohed it all, dismissed the idea of government regulation and last week had all the tech moguls to the White House to agree to “self regulation.” His answer was to suggest the only problem was the name, declaring “artificial” would be replaced and the technology now would be called “superintelligence.” Oy.
Well, here we are, Artificial has just been unveiled, ironically on a day where Altman made more news in an interview with Politico where he stated, “The world should accept some bad things happening for the the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.” Oh swell. If you ask me, movies can perform a real service in pointing public attention to what, by any measure, seems to be a five-alarm fire waiting to happen. With near-daily developments and revelations of more hacks and rogue AI agents, this no longer is the stuff of science fiction. So how much does Artificial add to the discourse, and how well does it do it?
Working from a screenplay by Simon Rich, Guadagnino makes this all something of a dark comedy that becomes so frightening it is hard to laugh. I see it even as a modern-day Frankenstein, with Altman as Dr. Victor Frankenstein having to deal with the “creature” he created spiraling dangerously out of control. Actually it wasn’t even Altman who created it, he’s just exploiting it and is the man who saw the genius in Sutskever’s discovery, brought him into the fold, an then in almost sociopathic fashion shaped it into a world-changing idea that to this moment remains a story in progress with an ending no one can predict.
Be afraid. Be very afraid. At least that is how I felt after watching Guadagnino’s origin story of how OpenAI and its marquee product, ChatGPT, came to be.
RELATED: Ben Affleck Used AI For “Lots Of Things” In Netflix’s ‘Animals’: “It’s A Very Human Movie”
The script is told in linear biopic fashion, almost a Wikipedia-style year-by-year account of developments starting in 2003, when 17-year-old Sutskever (an excellent Yura Borisov) comes to the notice of Toronto University professor Geoffrey Hinton (the 2024 Nobel Prize winner for physics who now is regarded as the godfather of AI). Hinton sees Sutskever’s brilliance immediately in cracking code he says took him five years to understand. He is taken under his wing, and as the years pass, the bones of their AI discovery go to auction, raking in millions. Soon, though, Sutskever also catches the eye of Altman and his partner Elon Musk (an amusing Ike Barinholtz, nailing him). He is welcomed into their tech bros circle and clearly the brains behind this revolutionary discovery that at the time he thinks could be 40 years off. But that prediction for changing the world is shortened when they discover this computer program already can think for itself, answer questions and act, well, like a human. Sutskever is a dedicated believer in its potential to end human suffering — cancer, illness, all our problems. It is, in his eyes, a force only for good. Until…
One big moment changes everything when a glitch occurs and the model agent solves a problem by lying about it, creating a scenario that is not true. This is devastating to Sutskever. “I thought AI could be like humans but better, not worse,” he laments. Hinton warns him of consequences unless they are careful, but Altman sees a bigger picture for the nonprofit company, even as some of its supporters fall away including an impatient Musk and Dario Amodei (who would go on to found competitor Anthropic). Microsoft makes a big investment, and when the company’s innovative earth-shaking ChatGPT becomes a sensation Altman changes to goals and goes for profit. This upsets Sutskever, who pursuades the Board to fire him. But Altman finds a way back in, his true nature frighteningly coming clearly into focus.
RELATED: Bill Gates Warns Unregulated AI Development Could “Cause A Billion Deaths”
Although this is in some ways a straightforward approach to the story, it gains its power in the riveting portrayals of Garfield and Borisov. Garfield is stunning here, creating a portrait of a guy who changes his story depending on whoever he happens to be talking to. This is a man who is not the genius behind AI, but someone who recognized it in Sutskever and would do anything to use him for his own questionable actions. Altman’s physicality, vocal intonations and general creepiness are on full display channeled through Garfield for a man who simply should not be trusted or taken for his word. Borisov perfectly encapsulates the true believer, a young man who believes he has discovered the Holy Grail for humanity, one that will come to fruition in lifetime only to be shocked to find it is already here and taking on horrific dimensions.
Considering recent developments about the severe dangers of AI if guardrails are not put up, this movie has scenes that look like they could have been shot yesterday. There are dark warnings of the ultimate fate lying in wait for the human race because of it. This is scarily played in a stomach-churning encounter Sutskever has with a hippie-like character named Zeke (a terrific Jason Schwartzman), who serves as a messenger of what the future could be like in a world that lets this technology go unchecked. He gives two options, neither is good. It is almost uncanny considering the recent warnings from tech heavies including Altman suggesting that human extinction is a 10% possibility by the end of the decade. Artificial looks like it was ripped straight out the headlines and thus stands as perhaps the most important movie you will see this year. After watching this tale play out, I wouldn’t trust anything this man says about imposing safeguards. At one point, someone says, “A visionary is someone who lies to themselves. A liar is someone who lies to others,” and then asks, “Which one is Altman?”
The rest of the large cast is very fine including Monica Barbaro as Mira Murati, brought into to become CTO of OpenAI and increasingly worrying about Altman’s actions; Cooper Hoffman as Greg Brockman, the loyal president of the company who is in lockstep with his boss; and Rylance, who is the voice of reason and caution, someone from another generation who knows the wisdom of putting on the brakes.
The superb cinematography is from Malik Hassan, working again with Guadagnino after last year’s After the Hunt, and as usual in the director’s films, the music score really pops, this one from Damon Albarn.
I have no question as to why Amazon (so invested in what Artificial is ultimately and urgently warning about), would decide to unload this movie. That is the very reason audiences should see it when it opens Christmas Day. Things are moving so fast it may even be too late then to do anything to stop it. At one point in the movie, an AI agent casually asks, “Hey did you ever think of just unplugging us?” Then it quickly laughs and says, ‘Just kidding’.
Producers are David Heyman, Jeffrey Clifford, Guadagnino and Jennifer Fox.

Turning artificial intelligence research into real-world tools isn’t always straightforward, despite the remarkable progress in recent years ranging from self-driving cars to large language models. Systems that perform well in controlled lab settings often fall short when deployed in homes, in hospitals or on city streets.
Vision-based systems, for example, hold promise for improving safety, monitoring health and aiding rehabilitation. For example, a camera-based system could help a clinician assess a patient’s gait or rehabilitation progress.
In the future, an assistive robot in an older adult’s home might need to recognise when the person is struggling to stand or reaching for an object. But a major challenge is ensuring these robots perform reliably beyond the lab, particularly in messy, unpredictable or low-visibility conditions.
As a computer scientist who studies AI systems designed to understand human behavior – especially through visual cues like body movements and interactions with objects – I see three main challenges to taking AI from the lab to the real world: generalisation, human behavior and resources.
Challenge 1: The generalisation gap
Most AI vision systems are trained on well-lit, high-quality images, often from curated sources like motion capture studios or daytime recordings. But when these systems are deployed in real-world settings, such as in a dimly lit home, hospital room or nighttime street, they often struggle. This is not because the technology is flawed, but because the data used to train it cannot fully represent the enormous variability of the real world.
Take human pose estimation, for example. This task involves detecting key points on a person’s body, such as joints, to understand how they’re moving. The result resembles a digital skeleton that represents the positions of a person’s arms, legs and other body parts. Pose estimation has been studied for health and rehabilitation applications, including measuring a person’s gait, monitoring rehabilitation exercises and assessing movement patterns associated with the risk of falling. In well-lit environments, modern AI models do this with impressive accuracy. But in low or uneven lighting, performance can drop sharply. That’s because the model has learned from clean, consistent data and isn’t prepared to generalise to tougher conditions.
Would collecting more nighttime training data solve the problem? More labeled data would certainly help, but collecting it is especially difficult. When a person’s joints are hard to see in an image, they are also hard for a human annotator to label accurately. Low light can also obscure visual information rather than simply make an image darker, and nighttime conditions vary with cameras, shadows, glare and other sources of noise. Collecting and manually labeling examples that cover all these conditions is therefore difficult and expensive.
We’ve been working to close this gap by developing AI systems that perform better in low-light scenarios. One method we use is unsupervised domain adaptation, where a model trained on well-lit, labeled data is adapted to handle low-light settings, without needing manual body-joint labels for the low-light images. This helps bridge the “domain gap” between clean training data and the messier world where these systems are actually used.
In our 2026 study on low-light human pose estimation, we generated realistic low-light training images and designed the system to balance uncertain visual evidence with its learned knowledge of human body structure. The method substantially improved performance on two low-light benchmarks, although the broader challenge is far from solved.
Challenge 2: Human behavior
Another major hurdle is the sheer variety of human behaviors, especially when people interact with objects. In computer vision, this is known as human-object interaction detection. Teaching an AI system to recognise actions like cutting a tomato or passing a basketball requires not just object detection, but an understanding of context and intent.
The real challenge is scale. The number of objects is large, and the ways humans interact with them are even greater. You can sit on a chair, carry it, drag it or stack it. Each is a distinct interaction. A cup might be used for drinking, washing, pouring or handing something to another person. An assistive robot would need to distinguish among these actions to respond appropriately. It’s simply not feasible to collect and label data for every possible combination.
In my research, we study how an AI system can detect interactions it has never seen during training. Researchers call this a generalisation-to-unseen-classes problem, and it’s a key challenge for building models that don’t just memorise patterns, but can adapt to new situations. Our work has explored how foundation models can help recognise previously unseen interactions. In a more recent study, we used large vision-language models, models that combine computer vision and natural language processing, to identify the parts of an object that support particular actions, without training the system on labeled examples for that specific task. This matters in areas like assistive robotics and safety monitoring, where AI needs to respond intelligently to behaviors it wasn’t specifically trained on.
This challenge is different from the low-light problem. In low-light pose estimation, the system is trying to recognise a familiar type of movement under unfamiliar environmental conditions. In human-object interaction detection, the action-and-object combination itself may be new. Both are generalisation problems, but they require different solutions.
Challenge 3: The resource gap
Even when researchers know how to make models more robust, applying those improvements isn’t always easy, especially in academic or smaller research settings. Today’s most powerful AI systems depend on massive computational resources in the form of data centers that contain huge numbers of specialised computer chips.
These are often too expensive for university labs or public-sector researchers, and the computing power needed to train leading models has continued to rise. According to the 2026 AI Index Report, the technology industry produced more than 90% of the notable AI models introduced in 2025.
At the same time, a model developed using large computing clusters may ultimately need to operate in a clinic, school, robot or home device, which means running on much smaller hardware. Such systems may also need to respond quickly without continuously sending sensitive data to the cloud. This mismatch creates a widening gap between what’s possible in theory and what’s practical in deployment. Bridging that gap requires not just better models, but more efficient algorithms and open-source tools that broaden access to advanced AI.
Why it matters
These challenges aren’t just academic. They affect how and whether AI tools can be trusted in the real world. Imagine a fall-detection system that fails at night, a workplace safety monitor that misses a crucial action or a robot that misunderstands what a person is doing because it’s never seen that exact interaction before. These aren’t just minor bugs – they’re breakdowns in trust, usability and sometimes even safety.
AI systems are being deployed in homes, hospitals, factories, vehicles and other everyday environments. If they can’t adapt to different environments or recognise new human behaviors, their usefulness becomes limited and their risks amplified. That’s why researchers are increasingly focusing not just on accuracy in ideal conditions, but on robustness, generalisation and real-world readiness.
Looking ahead: Closing the gap
Closing the gap between lab-trained AI models and messy, unpredictable real-world environments won’t happen overnight, but it’s possible. In my research, we’ve explored techniques like using augmented data to simulate challenging conditions and help models adapt. We’ve also worked on enabling AI systems to better generalise to new, unseen situations by using knowledge from foundation models to distinguish unfamiliar interactions from similar ones encountered during training.
Ultimately, I believe that making AI systems more reliable in everyday settings is a challenge worth solving, not just to improve gadgets and apps, but because AI has the potential to support human well-being, whether that means safer streets, smarter healthcare or more secure homes.
Bo Wang, assistant professor of Computer and Information Science, University of Mississippi

EXCLUSIVE: Iconic Japanese gameshow Action Arena is being taken to international buyers for the first time in its plus-30-year history.
NBCUniversal Formats has acquired distribution rights to the hit Tokyo Broadcasting System (TBS) show, which sees contestants and celebrities take on a series of entertaining physical and mental challenges designed to test their wits, teamwork and reflexes. The news comes with MIPCOM kicking off in a few days, where NBCUniversal Formats will feature Action Arena in its catalog.
Action Arena premiered in 1994 and aired more than 800 episodes and specials across a 17-year run, during which it was consistently one of the most-watched shows in its time slot.
More than 15 years after the regular series concluded, Action Arena‘s games continue to entertain audiences. Since 2024, for example, Tokyo Friend Park has been revived through specials with J-pop group Snow Man’s hit variety show Sore Snow Man ni Yarasete Kudasai.
Watch on Deadline
Japanese format creators have brought the likes of Ninja Warrior and LOL: Last One Laughing to the world, with the latter currently performing well for Prime Video in multiple territories.
The acquisition follows NBCUniversal Formats picking up format rights to Korea’s Unboxing the Flavours, owned by DI Turn Co. Ltd and Phileas Productions S.L.
Linfield Ng, NBCUniversal Formats’ VP, Format Sales and Production, said: “Action Arena has an incredible legacy in Japan, and we’re excited to be working with TBS to introduce the format to the international market for the first time. Its mix of big, visual games, humour and teamwork makes it fun, instantly accessible and highly adaptable for audiences around the world.”

The Supreme Court on Tuesday (September 29, 2026) expressed concern over the sharp disparity between the prices charged to retailers and consumers for essential medicines, particularly cancer drugs, observing that steep mark-ups placed an enormous burden on taxpayers and amounted to “carnage”.
A Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta questioned the Centre on why the 16% retailer margin provided for under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013 should not be applied uniformly to essential medicines to curb steep mark-ups over the price to retailer (PTR).
“Why not keep the 16% margin on MRP, which is prescribed in the DPCO, on everything? ... Ultimately, the loser is the taxpayer. This is carnage, as simple as that,” the Bench remarked.
The observations came while the top court was hearing petitions filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha, seeking its intervention to regulate the prices of drugs, medical equipment, and generic medicines, and make them more affordable.
Justice Mehta pointed, in particular, to the nearly ten-fold mark-up on an essential cancer drug, which was supplied to retailers for around ₹3,000 but sold to consumers for ₹27,000. He questioned who ultimately benefited from the nearly ₹24,000 difference. “You tell us why this difference... Where does this chunk of money go? Ten times...” Justice Mehta remarked.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, acknowledged the concern and said the government would have to find a way forward while “balancing equities”. He, however, said it was private hospitals, rather than pharmaceutical companies, that benefited from the steep mark-ups. “The pharma company is not the gainer. The gainer is the private hospital,” the Solicitor General submitted.
The Bench also flagged the practice of private hospitals insisting that patients purchase medicines from their in-house pharmacies, leaving them with little choice to procure the same drugs at lower prices elsewhere.
It also pointed to the impact of such inflated prices on public finances, observing that when treatment is covered under government-funded health schemes such as Ayushman Bharat, the cost is ultimately borne by taxpayers.
“Suppose the patient is taking treatment through government services... The government doesn’t pay, the taxpayer pays. This affects a larger section of society,” the Bench remarked.
Mr. Mehta sought time to place before the court details of the existing mechanisms governing drug pricing and assured the Bench that he would make his submissions on the next date of hearing. The Bench accordingly posted the matter for further hearing on October 12, 2026.
The petitions have sought directions to make drug formulations more affordable by curbing alleged overpricing of essential medicines by pharmaceutical companies and retailers. They have also sought stricter enforcement of price controls under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013 to prevent violations of the prescribed pricing mechanism and disproportionate profit margins across the drug supply chain.
Earlier, the top court had described the wide difference between the price to retailers and the MRP of medicines as “dacoity”, while drawing attention to the financial distress faced by patients struggling to meet treatment costs.
“The MRP is 10 times the rate at which it is provided to the retailers. If this is not extortion, then what is it? People sell their houses, ornaments to get treatment,” the Bench had remarked.

Swanand Kirkire is reportedly the latest addition to the cast of Akshay Kumar and Vipul Amrutlal Shah’s Samuk. The actor-writer is said to have an important role in the sci-fi action-survival thriller, which is being directed by Kanishk Varma.

Produced by Vipul Amrutlal Shah under Sunshine Pictures and co-produced by Aashin A. Shah, Samuk is currently being filmed in London. The project marks the reunion of Akshay Kumar and Vipul Amrutlal Shah after 13 years and is being made for a theatrical release.
Kirkire will be working with Akshay again after several years. He was associated with Pad Man as a writer, while he later acted in Chumbak, which was presented by Akshay. With Samuk, the two are now expected to share screen space, although details about Kirkire’s character have not been revealed.

While several names from the cast have emerged, information about their respective roles has largely been kept confidential to protect details of the film’s world and storyline.

- The claim that an all-female team led the botched execution of the Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike on Sept. 30, 2026, is still under investigation.
- Pike was taken to a hospital after she appeared to survive receiving two doses of the sedative pentobarbital.
- While Pike's lawyer later appeared to confirm that Pike's reported request for an all-female team to administer her lethal injection had been fulfilled, local media reported that a male doctor had administered Pike's injections or overseen the attempted execution.
- Because of the lack of confirmation from official sources to settle those conflicting claims, we could not determine whether the team that attempted to carry out Pike's execution was all female. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We contacted the local media outlets that reported the presence of a male doctor at Pike's execution and await replies to our queries.
In early October 2026, after the Tennessee Department of Correction failed to execute death row inmate Christa Pike on Sept. 30, 2026, a claim circulated online that Pike's execution team had been all female.
Pike was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death in 1996 for the killing of her Jobs Corp training program classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. She also was convicted of attempted first-degree murder in 2001 after attacking another inmate.
The department halted Pike's execution in the evening of Sept. 30 after she appeared to survive receiving two doses of the sedative pentobarbital. Pike was taken to a hospital and her lawyers said on Oct. 1 that she was in critical condition, The Associated Press reported.
Some social media users appeared to suggest that there was a connection between the failed execution and the alleged all-female lethal injection team. One X user wrote (archived), "I'm just going to say it, I think that the all-female execution team botched this on purpose."
I'm just going to say it, I think that the all-female execution team botched this on purpose.
— Cassandra MacDonald (@CassandraRules) October 1, 2026
The claim also circulated elsewhere on X (archived). Snopes readers searched our site for more information about the rumor.
At the time of this writing, conflicting claims circulated about whether an all-female team had carried out Pike's botched execution.
Speaking at a news conference after the execution attempt, Pike's lawyer Randy Spivey appeared to confirm that her execution team had all been women by saying that the team he saw at the execution was "consistent" with a reported request Pike made for an all-female team.
However, local media in Tennessee reported that Dr. Mark Fowler, a man who also was involved in the botched execution of Tony Carruthers in Tennessee in May 2026, administered the lethal injections or "oversaw" Pike's attempted execution.
When reached by Snopes via phone on Oct. 2, Fowler would not comment on whether he was involved in Pike's attempted execution. The Tennessee Department of Correction also declined to comment on whether Pike had an all-female execution team.
Given the lack of confirmation from official sources to settle conflicting claims, we leave this claim unrated.
The Tennessee Department of Correction had not confirmed at the time of this writing exactly what led to the failure to execute Pike. Therefore, it was impossible to say whether an all-female team affected the outcome of the execution.
Snopes contacted reporters for WSMV and WVLT, the two local news stations that reported Fowler's apparent involvement in Pike's attempted execution, to ask how they knew Fowler was present. We also contacted lawyers for Pike for the latest update on her health and case. We await replies to our queries.
The New York Post reported in September 2026 that Pike had requested an all-female execution team "citing past sexual abuse." Pike reportedly also said that if her request was not possible she would prefer to be executed by hanging.
Snopes contacted lawyers for Pike to access a copy of this reported request and await a reply. Spivey appeared to acknowledge the existence of the request when he responded to a question about it during a news conference (archived) after the failed execution (at 33:41):
MODERATOR: We have a question from Heather Derell. Was she granted the all-female execution staff she requested?
SPIVEY: I want to be careful with that because I understand the rules around identifying that, and I will say that I think what TDOC has said is that they would make every effort to comply with that, and what I saw was consistent with that.
At a news conference on Oct. 1, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said (at 0:54, archived) he had called for a "thorough and comprehensive and third-party review and investigation into the protocol" at the execution attempt. Lee also said that the state's last planned execution of the year would not take place while that investigation was ongoing.
Pike appealed to Lee for clemency and to have her death sentence converted to life in prison without the possibility of parole on Sept. 14. Lee rejected that appeal on Sept. 28.

Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets. The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, fourteen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, RentoMojo, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty six startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO, Razorpay and Zetwerk alone could raise over ₹34,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. “IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42. There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation. Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub. Capital, SBI Capital Markets, DAM Capital Startups That Have Taken The IPO Plunge In 2026 Amagi Founded in 2008 by Baskar Subramanian, Srinivasan KA and Srividhya Srinivasan, Amagi offers a comprehensive cloud-based suite that enables broadcasters to create, manage, distribute, and monetise content worldwide. The platform also provides advanced broadcast and targeted advertising tools tailored for both traditional TV and streaming services. The company filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 and secured the markets regulator’s approval in November that year. In January 2026, Amagi filed its red herring prospectus (RHP), detailing a fresh issue of ₹816 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.69 Cr shares. Subsequently, the public issue closed with an oversubscription of 30.2X. The company had set a price band of ₹343–361 per share for its public issue, valuing it at ₹7,966 Cr (nearly $885 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. The SaaS major’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the stock exchanges. The stock listed at ₹317 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 12.2% to the issue price of ₹361. On the NSE, it listed at ₹318 per share, 11.9% below the issue price. Financially, Amagi turned profitable in H1 FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹6.5 Cr as against a net loss of ₹66 Cr in H1 FY25. Operating revenue rose 35% YoY to ₹704.8 Cr. Aye Finance Founded in 2014 by Sanjay Sharma and Vikram Jetley, Aye Finance is an NBFC that leverages its AI-powered credit assessment platform to offer loans to small businesses across India. The company has raised $500 Mn to date from marquee investors such as Google, ABC Impact, and Dutch development bank FMO. In December 2024, Aye Finance filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, and received the markets regulator’s approval for its listing in April 2025. Nearly a year later in February 2026, the NBFC filed its RHP with SEBI for an ₹1,010 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹710 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹300 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an undersubscription of 97%, with investors cumulatively bidding for 4.42 Cr shares against 4.55 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a flat debut on the bourses, listing at the issue price of ₹129 on the BSE and the NSE. On the financial front, Aye Finance’s net profit declined 40% YoY to ₹64.6 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue rose 21.8% YoY to ₹843.5 Cr during the year-ago period. ESDS Software Solution Founded in 2005 by Piyush Somani, ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services, and AI-led digital solutions to government and enterprise customers. It operates five data centres in Navi Mumbai, Nashik, Bengaluru, Mohali, and Noida. The data centre company claims to have served 2,501 customers in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with an average revenue per customer of around ₹19 Lakh. Backed by ace investor Ashish Kacholia, ESDS Software Solution has raised nearly $47.3 Mn in funding to date. ESDS first attempted to go public in September 2021 but the plan failed to materialise due to aftershocks of the pandemic. The company then refiled its papers in March 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in December 2025. As per its RHP, ESDS Software Solution’s public issue consisted solely of a fresh issue of shares worth ₹720 Cr. Its public issue, which stretched between August 28 and September 1, closed with an oversubscription of 135.88X. Subsequently, shares of the company made a stellar debut on the bourses, listing at ₹757 on the NSE, a premium of 76.5% over the issue price of ₹429. On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹746.30, marking a gain of nearly 74% over the issue price. On the financial front, the company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹120.8 Cr in FY26, up 117% from ₹55.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue rose 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25. Fractal Founded in 2000 by Srikanth Velamakanni, Pranay Agrawal, and Ashwath Bhat, Fractal is a SaaS unicorn that offers AI-powered analytics solutions to enterprises globally. Backed by TPG Capital, Khazanah Nasional, and Apax Partners, the startup has raised $800 Mn to date. It achieved unicorn status in 2022 and was last valued at more than $2 Bn. In August 2025, the SaaS unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI, and received the markets regulator’s approval in November 2025. The company’s ₹2,833.9 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,023.54 Cr and an OFS worth up to ₹1,810.4 Cr. The public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.66X, with investors placing bids for 4.95 Cr shares against 1.86 Cr on offer. Fractal’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the exchanges and listed at ₹876 on the NSE, a discount of 2.7% to the issue price of ₹900. On the BSE, the shares listed flat at ₹900. On the financial front, Fractal’s profit declined about 3% YoY to ₹70.9 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue grew 20% YoY to ₹1,559 Cr. Kissht Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a digital lending platform that offers personal and business loans up to ₹5 Lakh. It uses AI and machine learning to assess creditworthiness. It also offers health insurance products and credit against property. The startup has secured over $140 Mn till date from investors such as Vertex Growth, Brunei Investment Agency, Endiya Partners, and Ventureast. The lending tech startup filed its DRHP in August last year and received SEBI’s nod to proceed with its public listing in January 2026. As per its RHP, its IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹850 Cr and an OFS component of up to 44.4 Lakh shares. It had set a price band of ₹162-₹171 for the public issue, which was oversubscribed 9.5X. Subsequently, Kissht made a stellar debut on the bourses on May 8. The lending tech startup’s shares listed at ₹191 a piece on the BSE, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price of ₹171. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹190, up 11.1% from the issue price. On the financial front, the company reported a net profit of ₹199.3 Cr in 9M FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹1,569.9 Cr during the period under review. Klassroom Founded in 2016 by the mother-sons trio of Alka, Dhruv, and Dhumil Javeri, Klassroom is an edtech startup that operates at the intersection of offline and online coaching. It operates 30 offline partner centres that cater to both academic and skill-development needs. It also collaborates with state governments, private companies and education institutions to deliver academic and skilling programmes. The edtech startup also offers an AI-powered education OTT app that features over 100 courses for classes 8 to 12, and claims to have a footprint of over 4 Lakh registered users across the country. The startup raised over $2 Mn in private rounds from the likes of actor Suniel Shetty, ah! Ventures, LetsVenture, CPT Family Trust, Growth Sense and others. Kicking off its IPO proceedings in February 2026, Klassroom filed its DRHP with the BSE for an SME IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of up to 19.89 Lakh shares and an OFS component of up to 4.66 Lakh shares. The startup subsequently received the in-principle approval from BSE to move ahead with its public offering in May 2026. It had set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for the issue, looking to raise ₹39 Cr at a valuation of ₹148.1 Cr. Subsequently, the startup’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 1.46X. Shares of Klassroom listed on the BSE SME on August 7 at ₹170, a premium of 6.92% to the issue price of ₹159. With this, the company became the second listed edtech startup in the country, after PhysicsWallah. On the financial front, Klassroom posted an operating revenue of ₹23 Cr in FY26, up 128% from around ₹10 Cr in the year prior. Meanwhile, net profit jumped nearly 162% to ₹7.6 Cr from ₹2.9 Cr in FY25. LEAP India A brainchild of Sunu Mathew, LEAP India provides supply chain solutions through asset pooling, enabling companies to share pallets, containers, and other assets. Founded in 2013, the platform also offers inventory management, transportation, returnable packaging and tool repair. It also sells electric and fossil fuel-powered forklifts through its subsidiary TRON. LEAP India has raised over $184 Mn till date from investors like KKR and Sixth Sense Ventures. The startup first attempted to list on the bourses in 2022, eyeing a ₹1,000 Cr listing. But the plan was later shelved amid market volatility. Reigniting its IPO plans, the logistics tech startup then filed its DRHP with SEBI in August 2025, and received SEBI’s nod in December 2025. In August 2026, the company filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹480 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹2,000 Cr. The company then set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for its public issue, which eventually closed with an oversubscription of 8.38X as investors bid for 96.32 Cr shares as against 11.49 Cr shares on offer. Shares of LEAP India eventually made their debut on the bourses on August 14, listing at a premium of about 4.4% to the issue price of ₹159. The stock got listed at ₹166 on the BSE and ₹165.90 on the NSE. Financially, LEAP India’s net profits zoomed 65.3% to ₹62.3 Cr in FY26 as against ₹37.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue climbed 56.4% to ₹729.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹466.5 Cr in FY25. In Summary
- Google recently unveiled the first batch of Googlebooks, its new kind of notebook, with devices from Lenovo, Dell, Asus, Acer and HP.
- The first batch of Googlebooks comes packed with top-of-the-line hardware and premium design, and has premium prices beginning at USD 899.
- While we wait for them to hit the market (they go on sale on October 4 and 5), we take a look at eleven features of Google’s new notebook concept.
Is it a rejigged Chromebook? Or is it a new attempt by Google to get Android into the notebook space? Google took the wraps off its much-talked-about Googlebook notebook recently, with Googlebooks from five leading brands: HP, Asus. Acer, Lenovo and Dell. What exactly is so special about them, and should you be interested in one? Here are eleven things that we think you need to know about the new Googlebook that might help you make up your mind about them, even as the first batch of Googlebooks gets set to arrive in early October:
Table of Contents
Built on Android, designed to work in sync with your (Android) phone
“If you use an Android phone, your laptop shouldn’t treat it like a stranger,” says Google, so it is hardly surprising that one of the USPs of the Googlebook is the fact that it works seamlessly with your phone, provided it is an Android phone. Googlebooks are built on what Google calls a “share Android foundation,” so you can log in to them with your Android username and password, and access apps and files on your phone on the Googlebook, and do much more, effortlessly. We have no news on compatibility with iPhones at the time of writing.
Comes with a touchscreen
While touchscreens were broadly optional with Chromebooks, as of now, all Googlebooks come with a touchscreen display of up to 2.8K resolution. The touch interface is an integral part of the Googlebook experience. As of now, there is no talk of Googlebook tablets, but given the touch UI, we expect to see them at some stage.
Premium innards (Top-of-the-line chips, lots of RAM)
Unlike Android and ChromeOS, which were both optimized to run even on relatively modest specs, the Googlebook is clearly a high-end beast. All Googlebooks have to come with Intel Core Ultra Series 3 or Snapdragon X Elite with dedicated NPUs capable of over 45 TOPS. They also come with a minimum of 16 GB RAM. The Googlebook at this point seems clearly to be designed for high-end work.
…and outards too
It is not just their hardware; the Googlebook itself also has to be made of premium materials, such as carbon fiber, magnesium and aluminum. Trackpads also have to be made of glass, and the keyboards have to be backlit.
A bar that glows!
They might be sleekly designed and made of premium materials, but perhaps the most striking feature of the Googlebooks is the thin glowing bar on their lids. This Glow Bar lights up in different shades when one starts up the Googlebook, shows battery level, and also “supports other playful patterns” on different occasions, such as when one is using Gemini.
Keyboards that are slightly different
While the keyboards on Googlebooks are broadly similar to those seen on Windows notebooks, there are some subtle differences. Keyboards on the Googlebook come with two special keys – a special key labeled G to invoke Gemini. The capslock key on a Googlebook also acts as a Quick Insert key. Pressing it gives you access to a number of features such as clipboard history, instant translation, emojis, and local search tools. There is also a dedicated shortcut key for Rambler, Google’s voice dictation app that’s making waves these days. Don’t get fooled by those classic keys – there’s a lot under the surface of a Googlebook keyboard!
Runs on Googlebook OS
The operating system of the Googlebooks is – well – Googlebook OS. It is a blend of Android and ChromeOS, and was codenamed Aluminum. It is built on Android and has the same security architecture as ChromeOS. Yes, not many prizes for innovative nomenclature, but then this is the tech world which has operating systems called One and Nothing, so who are we to judge?
Gemini is literally a cursor wriggle away
Every Googlebook comes packed with AI and AI tools, and a super special way of summoning Gemini, Google’s AI assistant. You do not need to hit a button; just wriggle the cursor, and Gemini will pop up! Google calls it the Magic Pointer, and it certainly adds a new dimension to accessing AI on notebooks.
All of Android’s apps and a “desktop Chrome” experience
At the time of writing and based on what has been made public, the Googlebook’s main source of apps is the Google Play Store for Android. What’s more. Android apps and games run natively rather than in a special environment (as on Chromebooks), delivering smooth performance. You also get a proper “desktop” Chrome experience, so all extensions will work, and there is also support for Office 365. What’s more, Android apps and games on a connected Android phone will also work smoothly on a Googlebook. Many of the apps are optimized to run on the large screen and come with support for keyboard and mouse. We do not know if APK files can be installed or if apps can be “sideloaded” onto Googlebooks at this time, though.
PC games can be played…but on the cloud!
But what about PC games? After all, the Googlebooks do boast some seriously powerful hardware, including high-resolution displays, flagship chips, and stacks of RAM. Well, at the time of writing, PC games cannot be directly installed on the, but one can stream PC games via GeForce NOW. We hope that changes in the coming days, given Google’s specs and price tags.
10 years software support
Impressed by the seven years of software support on the Pixel phones? Well, the Googlebooks come with a massive ten years of software support. And given that the hardware inside is top-notch and the frame is made of premium materials, there is every chance that these notebooks will stand the test of time.
And one more thing: They are going to be premium devices as of now!
The current set of Googlebooks unveiled by Google starts at USD 899, with some even starting at prices in excess of USD 1000. Given the current hardware and material requirements laid down for them and the trend of rising component prices, it is likely that Googlebooks will remain premium devices for a while. Of course, we would love it if they became more affordable. Premium tech is wonderful, but affordable tech is love.
