Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel are the joint recipients of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, Sweden announced on Monday.
Deisseroth, a professor at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, Hegemann, a professor at Humboldt University in Berlin and Nagel, a professor at the University of Würzburg, Germany, developed a method that uses light, combined with genetic modifications of neurons, to switch on or off individual cells in a living brain. This makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behavior in the brain, and is being studied as a treatment for disease.
The work started in the early 2000s, when Hegemann and Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, a light-sensitive algal protein that allowed a single-cell alga to swim toward light. They found that this protein worked in any cell they injected it in.
Deisseroth then introduced the gene for the protein into nerve cells from rats, becoming able to trigger a nerve signal in the living brain with blue light.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine.
The committee was able to reach all three winners, starting with Deisseroth, who was “definitely asleep, but he woke up”, said Thomas Perlmann, the sSecretary for the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine. “All three said the same thing, that they thought it was absolutely wonderful to receive the prize with the other two; they called them ‘my friends,’” he said.  
There have been 235 award winners since the first medicine prize was awarded in 1901, of which 14 have been women. The youngest recipient was 31, the oldest 87. 
The award has been given 117 times: 40 times to a single individual, and has been shared among two winners 36 times, and among three (the maximum allowed by the Nobel statute) 41 times.
The winner will receive 12 million Swedish Kronor (SEK), or roughly $1.2 million.

UpdateSeparatists win Quebec election in fresh test for Canada’s Carney

Separatists won provincial elections in Quebec Monday, with a promise to hold a vote on leaving Canada after US President Donald Trump leaves office, testing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s message of national unity.
Public broadcaster CBC and private outlets predicted the Parti Quebecois would form the next government in Canada’s French-speaking province, but it was not yet clear if they would control a legislative majority.

President Donald Trump has brought his close aide, Natalie Harp, on stage at a rally in Nebraska to sign an executive order in a desperate attempt to reduce diesel costs ahead of the crucial midterm elections.
In Grand Island Monday night, Trump asked Harp — known as the “Human Printer” for giving the president physical copies of social media posts and news clippings while on the go — to bring him the executive order that will allow anyone to purchase tax-free red-dyed diesel.
Harp walked on stage and handed Trump the executive order, which he signed in front of his supporters. When he was done, he threw his pen into the crowd as they chanted, “Trump, Trump, Trump.”
He then handed the executive order back to Harp and said, “She reminds me of The Price Is Right,” referring to the game show where an announcer asks contestants to “come on down” to the stage.
“This perfect person comes up, hands it, walks off,” Trump said, seemingly comparing Harp to a model who shows off the prizes on The Price Is Right. “We should go on television with this show. Right?”
Harp’s unusually personal relationship with the president has drawn scrutiny in recent weeks afterThe Washington Post reported that she was one of the select few who got to ride with Trump during a secret escape from Air Force One while they were leaving the NATO summit in Turkey amid a potential assassination threat from Iran.
Marc Beckman, senior advisor to Melania Trump, dismissed any rumors that her husband’s relationship with Harp was inappropriate, telling conservative media personality Stella Escobedo on her YouTube show earlier this month that the “liberal media” was “attacking this hardworking, very talented, very intelligent person in Natalie Harp.”
Trump announced the new executive order in Nebraska, where farmers and ranchers have been hit hard by record diesel prices. Red-dyed diesel is commonly used in farming, construction and other industries.
Trump will also urge states to increase the availability of dyed diesel and order the Treasury Department to review federal diesel taxes, according to Politico. The new executive order comes as new polls show Democratic gubernatorial candidates surging in four traditional Republican strongholds.
The White House didn't immediately respond to an inquiry from The Independent.
Trump's announcement came after he said Friday that he wouldn't impose a diesel export ban because the U.S. and other leading industrialized nations, known as the Group of Seven, had agreed to release stockpiled diesel.
"Europe has a lot of diesel, and they’re going to be making a major world contribution, and so are we," Trump said.
Monday's national average price for diesel was $6.32 a gallon, down from the record high of $6.53 on September 22, according to AAA.
Trump appeared Monday at the Nebraska State Fair with Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, who faces Democratic Party-backed independent challenger Dan Osborn.
Two recent polls showed the candidates jockeying for the lead in a state that Trump won by more than 20 percentage points in 2024.
Other polls show Democratic candidates ahead of Republicans running for governor in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas, even though none of those ruby-red states has been led by a Democrat in at least two decades.
And the Silver Bulletin polling-analysis website said Monday that the Democratic edge in the so-called generic congressional ballot had risen to 8.9 percentage points, marking a new high for this year’s election cycle, and that with adjustment for likely voters, that lead increases to 9.6 percentage points.
Patrick De Haan, chief petroleum analyst for the GasBuddy price-tracking website, said on social media last week that expanding access to red-dyed diesel could save some drivers about 60 cents a gallon, but noted that “farmers already use dyed diesel and are still paying record prices.”
“Taxes aren't the problem, supply is,” De Haan wrote.
The global availability of diesel has been pinched by Trump's war against Iran, now in its eighth month, as well as Ukraine's targeting of Russian refineries as it continues to battle the full-scale invasion that Russian President Vladimir Putin launched in February 2022.
Shuting Pomerleau, director of energy and environmental policy at the center-right American Action Forum think tank, responded to Haan's post by saying, "There are no effective ways to quickly bring down the diesel prices."
"It's like using a bucket to empty a river," she added.
As of Friday, 10 states that account for about one-third of all diesel sales in the U.S. had already taken steps to increase the availability of dyed diesel, Politico said, citing analysis by the independent ClearView Energy Partners research company.
Denton Cinquegrana, chief oil analyst for Dow Jones Energy, told Politico that suspending fuel taxes could provide short-term relief with long-term consequences.
“When you’re not collecting taxes, you’re just kicking the can down the road, because you have to fix roads and stuff like that,” Cinquegrana said.

Russia hosts consultations on Afghanistan, including with a Taliban delegation
Russia has hosted consultations on Afghanistan that included a delegation of the country's ruling Taliban government along with officials from China, India, Iran, Pakistan and other nations
MOSCOW -- Russia on Monday hosted a round of consultations on Afghanistan that included a delegation of the country's ruling Taliban government, along with representatives of China, India, Iran, Pakistan and other nations.
Welcoming the Taliban's Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi to Moscow, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov congratulated him on "the fifth anniversary of Afghanistan’s liberation from the NATO contingent.”
“Five years is a short time to overcome the consequences of many decades of occupation, yet your government’s achievements are evident, and we welcome them,” Lavrov said. He hailed the Taliban's successes in combating the Islamic State group and other extremists, and efforts to eradicate drug trafficking.
Since the Taliban took control of Afghanistan in August 2021 after the pullback of U.S. and NATO forces, they have sought international recognition while also enforcing their strict interpretation of Islamic law.
In July 2025, Russia became the first country to recognize the Taliban’s government after removing the group from its list of outlawed organizations.
Speaking during Monday’s talks, Lavrov said that “the powerful military machine of the United States and their NATO allies was broken by the fighting spirit and resilience of the Afghans.”
The former Soviet Union fought a 10-year war in Afghanistan that ended with Moscow withdrawing its troops in 1989. During the past decade, Moscow has sought to bolster its influence in the region by hosting regular consultations on Afghanistan involving senior representatives of the Taliban and neighboring nations.
Lavrov noted that the Taliban's “successes in the fight against narcotics and terrorism are to a significant extent linked to the ongoing military-technical cooperation between our countries.”
Russia's top diplomat reaffirmed that Moscow views the deployment of any NATO military infrastructure on the territory of Afghanistan and neighboring countries as “categorically unacceptable."
“Historical experience shows that such a presence is fraught with destabilization and escalating conflict,” Lavrov said.
He emphasized that Russia will continue to provide humanitarian assistance to Afghanistan.
Officials from China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan also took part in the talks.
Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, said that Moscow was ready to help defuse tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan.
Cross-border fighting between Afghanistan and Pakistan has continued for months despite international mediation efforts.
“Russia stands ready to help end this conflict using all possible means and acting independently or together with other partners if both parties ask for it,” Kabulov told reporters.
While Russia was the first country to recognize the Taliban administration, the group had engaged in high-level talks with many nations and established some diplomatic ties with countries including China and the United Arab Emirates.
Still, the Taliban government has been relatively isolated on the world stage, largely over its restrictions on women.

The Best Power Banks for Keeping All Your Devices Charged
Featured in this article
I hate running out of power. Everybody does. While our gadgets have advanced in many ways, battery technology has been slow to improve. That’s why you’re looking to buy a power bank. A good portable charger is a handy backup that can keep your smartphone, tablet, and maybe even your laptop going for longer. I’ve been testing power banks for years. I’ve tested more than 100 portable chargers. But you only really need one or two.
Most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options. Read the Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks for more magnetic wireless chargers, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations for more power.
Updated October 2026: I added power banks from Pisen, Belkin, Wolfbox, and UGreen, removed some older devices, and updated prices.
Other Portable Chargers I Tested
There are so many portable chargers out there. Here are a few more I like that just missed out on a place above for one reason or another. We also have separate guides for the Best Laptop Power Banks, Best MagSafe Power Banks, and Best Portable Power Stations.
Don’t Bother With These Power Banks
These portable chargers I tested aren’t necessarily terrible, but you can do better.
UGreen MagFlow Pro for $100: I actually quite like this magnetic, wireless charging power bank (Qi2 25W) with its Matrix-style screen that animates to show charging status. But considering the 10,000-mAh capacity, the price is absolutely bonkers. The marketing talks up its cooling properties, but it got very warm when I used it. The attached USB-C cable (45W) is annoyingly obtrusive when it was stuck to the back of my iPhone too.
OnePlus Slim Magnetic Power Bank for $70: Sleek in silver-gray aluminum with a chamfered edge, this power bank looks lovely, but the 5,000-mAh capacity is just over half that after inefficiency takes a bite.
Iniu Portable Charger for $21: It’s very small for a 10,000-mAh capacity. You can charge at up to 45 watts from either of the USB-C ports or 18 watts from the USB-A, but recharging is slow, it fell short of the stated capacity, and the display sometimes failed to update correctly.
FansDreams MChaos for $46: I love the idea of a wearable power bank, and this one comes in lime green with a carabiner that makes it easy to attach to a bag, but recharging is slow, and you’ll be lucky to get one full charge for your phone. It's also currently sold out.
iWalk Portable Charger for $27: The 4,800-mAh capacity won’t come close to fully refilling your device, but it's tiny enough to keep in a bag at all times.
What Features Should I Look for in Power Banks?
There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.
The capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get depends on the cable you use, the device you’re charging, and the charging method. (Qi wireless charging is less efficient.) You will never get the maximum capacity from any power bank. You can generally expect to get between 60 and 80 percent after energy loss through heat and conversion. Some manufacturers list a “Rated Capacity” that’s lower than the overall capacity to give you an indication of what to expect in real-world use. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for devices.
The charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. Many smartphones, including Apple’s iPhones, support the power delivery standard, meaning you can use higher-power power banks to recharge the device with no issues. A few phones, such as Samsung’s Galaxy S range, support a supplementary PD protocol called PPS (Programmable Power Supply) that goes up to 45 watts. Many phones also support Qualcomm’s proprietary Quick Charge (QC) standard. There are also other proprietary fast-charging standards, but you won’t generally find power banks that support them unless they come from the smartphone manufacturer.
Your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. The Nimble, GoalZero, Biolite, Mophie, Zendure, and Sharge portable chargers listed support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. Monoprice does not support pass-through charging either. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.
Can I Take a Power Bank on a Plane?
It’s safe to fly with a power bank, but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours (WH). If your power bank has a larger capacity than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.
Some airlines introduced stricter rules in 2025, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have on board.
Why You Should Avoid Cheap Power Banks
Many years ago, the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 gained notoriety when its batteries caught fire in a series of incidents. There’s been a steady stream of similar, though isolated, incidents ever since. Despite the high-profile coverage of batteries gone wrong, however, the vast majority of lithium-ion batteries are safe.
The chemical reaction that occurs inside a lithium-ion cell is complex, but as in any battery, there’s a negative and a positive electrode. In lithium batteries, the negative is a lithium-carbon compound, and the positive is cobalt oxide (though many battery makers are moving away from cobalt). These two compounds cause a reaction that is safe when controlled and delivers energy to your devices. When the reaction gets out of control, though, you end up with earbuds melting in your ears. What changes a safe reaction to an uncontrolled reaction can be any number of things: excess heat, physical damage during use, physical damage during manufacture, or using the wrong charger.
The three basic rules that have kept me safe through testing dozens and dozens of batteries are these:
- Avoid cheap cords, chargers, and outlet adapters;
- Make sure batteries aren't exposed to excessive heat (above 110 degrees Fahrenheit);
- Regularly inspect batteries for signs of damage.
Avoiding cheap wall-outlet adapters, cords, and chargers is the most important rule. These are your most likely source of problems. Those chargers you see on Amazon for $20 cheaper than the competition? Not worth it. They probably got the price down by skimping on insulation, leaving out power-management tools, and ignoring the basics of electrical safety. Price alone is no guarantee of safety, either. Buy from reputable companies and brands.
Then there’s heat. Too much of it can cause all manner of problems, both in terms of discharge and safety. Avoid heat, and pay attention to your batteries when they’re charging. If your device gets overly hot when charging, this can be a sign of problems. Similarly, beware of any swollen, bulging, or otherwise misshapen batteries.
Why Is My Power Bank Charging Slowly?
I’ve explained charging rates and capacity above, but several factors can cause charging speed to be slower than expected. The rate is determined by the device being charged, so your phone will request a certain wattage, which changes depending on how full its battery is, on-device settings, and the battery temperature.
All devices charge more slowly when they are completely empty, when the battery approaches full, and when it overheats. The cable you use will also have a maximum charging rate, and so will different ports on the power bank. Wireless charging is more convenient, but also slower than wired charging.
How We Test Power Banks
I’ve been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test phone (currently an iPhone 16). I’ll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL and Samsung Galaxy S24+ to test charging speeds, and whatever else I have in. For larger-capacity power banks, I test-charge an iPad Mini and a MacBook Air. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.
Aside from these standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it’s not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.
How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?
I often scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown new brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to those companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would go against WIRED’s editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision on ranking.
There are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to known, reputable brands, but there’s always room for something new if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.

Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls.
The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC.
Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.
Writing in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, Dr Roselyn Campbell, author of the study from Purdue University in the US, notes: “While Aha, the first ruler of the First Dynasty, seems to have only had a few subsidiary burials, his successors included hundreds of subsidiary graves around their tombs and enclosures.”
The graves of the retainers were excavated in the 1920s by the English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who believed them to be an example of human sacrifice – a view some later experts agreed with.
But there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died.
Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge.
“This question of whether or not retainer sacrifice was practised in Egypt has been debated for over a century, but this is the first study to examine the human remains from the tombs themselves,” Campbell told the Guardian.
Campbell reports that 18 of the skulls showed signs of potentially lethal trauma such as fractures and – in one case – a chopping injury to the eye.
Campbell believs Petrie may have seen the skull fractures but did not realise they were injuries that occurred around the time of death, rather than arising as a result of later damage.
The fractures, she adds, are unlikely to have been caused by a mace – a weapon often depicted in ancient Egyptian art as being used by a victorious king to smite his enemies. Instead they are more likely to have been caused by flat, wide objects made of wood or antler.
“For the crania without trauma, we cannot be certain they were sacrificed. It’s quite possible that some of the retainers were sacrificed, while others were not,” she said. “With such a small sample size of the original burial population, we simply can’t see the full extent of these funerary rituals, nor can we be sure that this sample is truly representative of all the retainers.”
Campbell noted the number of subsidiary graves tapered off quickly and seems to have disappeared with the beginning of the Second Dynasty.
Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, said while the idea of retainer sacrifice was not totally new, “this paper is one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains”.
She added: “The practice was short-lived, with people being replaced by statuettes. Possibly some or all retainers felt that this was a boon and that they would enjoy an eternal life in the service of the god-king, though they might also have resented it, been terrified, and tried to escape this fate.”
Dr Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University, Alabama, said similar sacrifices had occurred across different cultures and times, adding that not everyone at the Egyptian site may have been compliant.
“If you really think about what those scenes would have looked like, it would have been very gruesome,” she said. While noting that the study only involved a small number of skulls from the burial site, “the idea that some of the people may have been violently killed, I think, is something that in reality we might expect”, she said.

Voters in Quebec are going to the polls in provincial elections which will probably result in victory for a party that has promised to hold a referendum on independence from Canada within the next two years.
If polls are correct, the Parti Québécois (PQ) will form the government of the province of roughly nine million, the first time that the separatist movement will have gained power in the French-speaking region for more than a decade.
A PQ victory in Monday’s election would also be likely to trigger a return to pitched battles over questions of language and identity between Quebec and the federal government.
Long considered a declining force in Quebec politics, the PQ owes its resurgence to party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon. The 49-year-old Oxford-educated lawyer and polyglot has positioned himself as a TikToking gen-X rebuttal to François Legault, Quebec’s long-serving Premier until he resigned early this year.
Analysts say that St-Pierre Plamondon’s electoral success is not because he is a separatist – the majority of voters do not support an independent Quebec – but because of his rightwing take on red-meat identity issues.
He has blamed immigrants for Quebec’s overflowing schools, increased crime and skyrocketing housing prices, while promising to slash immigration levels and ban “conspicuous” religious symbols from the bodies of teachers and their students. He has derided his critics from the leftist Quebec Solidaire party as “woke”, and has taken to repeating the talking points of hard-right columnists.
Many in the province agree with St-Pierre Plamondon’s rhetoric, even though it strays from PQ’s social democratic roots, according to radio host Patrick Lagacé. “Most Quebecers traditionally see themselves as being on the left. Increasingly, though, they are on the right when it comes to social issues like systemic racism and accommodation of religious behaviour. They’ve hardened on these issues, and don’t see themselves in the left’s recent fixation on identity issues,” Lagacé said.
The biggest drag on St-Pierre Plamondon’s popularity has been his oft-repeated promise to hold a referendum during the first mandate of a PQ government. An overwhelming majority of Quebecers don’t want such a thing any time soon – particularly with Canada locked in a trade war with the US. The province mostly voted for Liberal leader Mark Carney over the separatist Bloc Québécois in last year’s federal election, expressly because of Carney’s “elbows up” posturing against the Trump administration.
But for the PQ, Donald Trump was at first a curse, then a gift. Early in the campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon said he wouldn’t hold a referendum as long as Trump was in power, defusing the issue and allowing St-Pierre Plamondon to concentrate on attacking immigration and immigrants.
The party has also benefited from a four-way race for the right-leaning nationalist vote beyond the reliably Liberal fiefdom of Montreal – particularly around Quebec city, where the upstart Parti Conservateur du Québec has made significant inroads. “The Parti Québécois is benefiting from a massive vote split because those who don’t like the PQ don’t agree on who to vote for,” said poll analyst Philippe Fournier.
Though the PQ will probably form the next provincial government, it remains unclear what sort of mandate it will have. Polls have the party hovering at roughly 30%, somewhat below the likely threshold for a majority government.
In any case, St-Pierre Plamondon is laying the groundwork for confrontation with the federal government. He has mused about defunding the office of Quebec’s lieutenant-governor (the British Crown’s representative in the province) and promised to introduce a law to abolish the province’s ties with the monarchy, which separatists see as the ultimate symbol of oppression of Canada’s French minority.
St-Pierre Plamondon also tore into Carney, after the prime minister said the government will probably increase immigration rates in the country. Doing so, St-Pierre Plamondon said, was an “abuse of power” that would have further nefarious effects on French-language services in Quebec.
For a man who trades on his relative youthfulness, St-Pierre Plamondon’s attacks on the monarchy have the whiff of anachronism – the kind of thing the PQ did in its 1970-era heyday.
Attacking the federal government is similarly outdated, and potentially risky for St-Pierre Plamondon. Carney remains popular in Quebec, and is likely to remain so, at least until the existential threat of Trump recedes.

UFC CEO Dana White said the dream of flexible hours is a trap for aspiring entrepreneurs.
Speaking to Steve Bartlett on Monday's episode of "The Diary of a CEO" podcast, White spoke about why he doesn't believe that a successful business could be built by working from home.
"It's impossible. You can't do it. I'm in the office from 8:30 in the morning, and I don't leave the office till 7, 8, 9, 10 sometimes," White said.
Even on days when his schedule was fully planned, spontaneous conversations with colleagues could surface new issues, spark ideas, and change the course of his day.
"A lot of good ideas come from everybody being at work," White added.
White said entrepreneurship is a poor fit for anyone whose priority is protecting their free time, because business demands can arise at any time.
"There is no such thing as a day off when you run your own business. There are no birthdays, there's no Christmas, there's no Thanksgiving," White said.
Running a business means dealing with a fresh set of problems every day, "but when you like what you do, it's fun," he added.
White said he believed many young people have the wrong idea about what entrepreneurship involves.
"'You know, I'd really like to work for myself, and own my own business because I'd love to plan my schedule.' Oh, you're going the wrong way," White said. "What you need to do is find a 9-to-5 job where you have weekends and holidays off. That's your move."
White has pushed back on the idea that entrepreneurship offers an easier, more flexible life in past interviews.
He said in a March 2024 appearance on the "Lex Fridman Podcast" that he works "just as hard now" as he did when he was starting out.
In a May 2024 appearance on the "In Search of Excellence" podcast, White said that entrepreneurs who want their businesses to succeed must be prepared to become "a slave" to the company in the early years.
Other business leaders have also pushed back on remote work.
Skims cofounder Emma Grede, for example, has said that working from home is "career suicide." Jason Lemkin — also known as the "Godfather of SaaS" — has said that he's only interested in investing in "small, high paid teams that work in the office over six days a week."

The iconic Arthur Read made his TV debut 30 years ago
This is part of a special series in which NPR looks back at its coverage of major news stories from the past.
Which long-running cartoon features this protagonist: he's got round ears, an iconic yellow sweater, and a snarky little sister?
If you immediately pictured an animated, 8-year-old aardvark, you've likely heard of Arthur Read, a character who made his TV debut 30 years ago on Oct. 7, 1996.
But before the bespectacled third-grader made his way onto our screens and into our hearts, Arthur's first home was in the world of books.
Here's a look at the beginnings of Arthur.
A Bedtime Story
The author of the Arthur books is Marc Brown, a writer and illustrator who was raised in Erie, Pa.
Although Brown was interested in art from a young age, after graduating from the Cleveland Institute of Art in 1968, he pursued a string of different jobs working as everything from truck driver to to short-order cook to assistant professor.
Brown says he got the inspiration for Arthur when his son Tolon asked for a bedtime story about a "weird" animal. The first weird animal that came to mind? An aardvark. From there, Brown wrote and illustrated his first picture book depicting an aardvark named Arthur. This animal, with its long anteater snout and small ears, starred in Arthur's Nose, published in 1976.
While working on the next book, Brown made a pivotal change to the character's design. The second book titled, Arthur's Eyes, featured Arthur getting a new pair of glasses. As Brown drew the glasses, he realized there was a problem.
Speaking to NPR's Linda Wertheimer in 1997, Brown said, "I was drawing Arthur, and I wanted him to face the viewer in the book. And I could not show his mouth because his — his nose was so long. And so I shortened it a little bit. And I thought to myself, gee, if there are two books about Arthur, well there might be a third book. Now how do you really want this character to look?"
So Brown spent more time redesigning Arthur's visage, making his face "a little rounder" and "a little more lovable looking." The result, Brown said, made Arthur "more human-like." As Brown published and sold more Arthur books, he was able to make a living writing books. Though they were not an immediate commercial success, Brown's picture books resonated with families, including Carol Greenwald's.
Like Brown, Greenwald was no stranger to bedtime story pleas from her two children. When her son was 3 years old, their neighbor gave them an Arthur picture book. After reading it a few times, Greenwald realized it was unique.
"After reading it for the seventh time," Greenwald told NPR in 1997, "I realized I wasn't tearing my hair out … There are so many books you read to your kids that they love to read, and you read them over and over again, and it makes you feel like you want to scream. But this particular book was not making me feel that way."
Greenwald also said she liked the way Arthur dealt with problems involving school, personal relationships and activities like reading. As a TV producer at the Boston-based public media station GBH, Greenwald raised the idea with her colleagues in the early '90s.
"We have a lot of research that tells us that a kid who watches a TV show based on a book is more likely to want to read that book, is more likely to want to read other books, and is even more likely to go to the library."
From books to television
Although Greenwald believed Arthur was ready to make his public television debut, Brown was less sure. Brown said he was hesitant to allow Arthur to make the multimedia leap, stating that he wanted to keep "control of the character."
But GBH's offer and the subsequent jump in book sales made Brown reconsider.
“I went from, you know, maybe selling two million books over a period of several years to selling two million books in a month,” Brown said. “And to me, that happening is just unimaginable…”
He worked closely with the show's writers and artists to preserve the essential little kid that is Arthur.
Produced by GBH and the Montreal-based animation studio Cinar, the first episode of the series premiered on PBS Kids on Oct. 7, 1996. Its storyline draws directly from the second picture book, "Arthur's Eyes," as Arthur "re-tells" the story of wearing glasses to school for the first time.
The premiere also brought the rest of the Elwood City animal community to life with sound and emotion. Every character is an animal, from Arthur's aardvark parents and sister D.W. (short for Dora Winifred) to the students in Mr. Ratburn's Lakewood Elementary class, including an athletic chimpanzee named Francine and Arthur's best friend, a bunny named Buster. One of the show's underlying themes of getting along with others in your community is present even in its joyful, reggae theme song, "Believe In Yourself" by Ziggy Marley and the Melody Makers as Arthur bops around Elwood City, interacting with family, friends, and trusted neighbors.
Shortly after the series premiere, Brown was asked whether Arthur would remain in third grade or be allowed the opportunity to grow.
“I don't think of Arthur as ever leaving third grade," Brown said. "I sort of think of Arthur as having this portrait in the attic that's aging. (laughs) But Arthur will stay forever in third grade.”
The legacy of a wonderful kind of day
True to his word, Arthur and his friends remained third-graders throughout the entire series' 25 seasons. As reported by the Los Angeles Times in 2022, Arthur aired over 250 episodes and seven television specials. The critically acclaimed series also won four Daytime Emmy Awards for outstanding children's animated program and one Peabody Award.
Although Arthur began as the star, the series evolved to focus on a diverse cast of other characters and their lives as they navigated relatable milestones for 8-year-olds such as developing asthma, learning with dyslexia, and living with diabetes. The principles of believing in yourself, valuing family and friendship, and loving reading carried from season to season.
But not all the characters' stories were celebrated. In 2019, Alabama Public Television refused to air an episode featuring a same-sex wedding between Arthur's teacher, Mr. Ratburn, and his partner, Patrick. As reported by the New York Times in 2006, when an episode of the spinoff "Postcards from Buster" featured a Vermont family with two moms, then-Secretary of Education Margaret Spellings wrote a letter to the then-president and CEO of PBS, Pat Mitchell, reminding her that the show received funding from the Department of Education. She added, "Many parents would not want their young children exposed to the life-styles portrayed in this episode."
When speaking to NPR in 2022, Brown said, "We, as adults, owe children the truth. They're trying to make a foundation on which they can build their lives, and if there isn't truth in that foundation, things get pretty shaky."
For 26 years, Arthur helped families build a foundation of truth and belonging with the animated, animal residents of Elwood City. The series finale titled, "All Grown Up," aired on Feb. 21, 2022. The characters were no longer children, but adults, each aged up 20 years and settled into their respective careers. And of course, Arthur became an author of graphic novels.

A satellite image from Tuesday morning shows Typhoon Choi-wan off the coast Japan's main island of Honshu. The storm is forecst to move northeast and will not make landfall in Japan. Typhoon Nolo and Tropical Storm Koguma are also visible.
| Japan Meteorological Agency
Three storms are churning simultaneously across the western Pacific, an unusual October clustering that’s generating high waves around parts of Japan.
Typhoon Choi-wan, Typhoon Nolo and Tropical Storm Koguma were all active on Tuesday, marking the first time in five years that three systems have existed at the same time in the month of October, according to the Japan Weather Association (JWA).
The three storms are at different stages of development and are spread across a wide swath of the Pacific.

The NFL has suspended a line judge for two games for swearing at Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride.

What are the limitations of using a USB-C to HDMI adapter?
An adapter can bridge the gap when your ports don't match, but you have to check for weak links along the chain.
Although USB-C cables are capable of high-speed data transfers and faster charging, the shift to them has created its own connectivity issues. If your laptop lacks an HDMI output and your display doesn't have a USB-C input, you might consider a USB-C to HDMI adapter for connecting your device to a TV, monitor or projector. While these adapters can help with mismatched ports, they aren't always a perfect solution. They might fail to send high-resolution video or simply display a blank screen.
These issues usually come down to the type of cables, ports and adapter you're using. Importantly, not all USB-C ports support video, with some only capable of charging your device and conducting data transfers. Moreover, the type of HDMI adapter and cable you use determines the maximum resolution and refresh rate of the output.
For permanent setups, top-rated USB-C hubs are often the best option. Or instead of an adapter, you might get a single USB-C to HDMI cable. The advice below will largely apply to all three options.
From USB-C to HDMI
Think of these connections as a relay, with your ports, cables and adapters all running the same signal between your device and display. Your device's USB-C port transmits a video signal through the HDMI adapter, where it is converted into an HDMI signal your display can read. Then, it's handed off to your HDMI cable, which carries it to the finish line of your TV or other display.
The quality of this connection is determined by the weakest link in the chain. With an incompatible port, old cable or overheating cheap adapter, the entire setup suffers.
Let's start with your USB-C port. USB-C ports can only carry video outputs if they support DisplayPort Alternate Mode, which uses the same DisplayPort digital display interface you might know from video cards. Which level of DP Alt Mode your USB-C supports impacts your video quality. DisplayPort 1.4 signals can reach 8K resolutions at a 60 Hz refresh rate, though 8K displays are so expensive that they're barely in use yet. DisplayPort 1.2 can achieve 4K resolution at 60Hz.
DP Alt Mode is an optional feature that manufacturers can add to standard USB-C ports. The Thunderbolt standard uses the same USB-C connection, but comes with guaranteed standards of data transfer rates (depending on the generation) and includes video output. Check the manual or online spec page to confirm a port's capabilities.
Even if your USB-C port can use DP Alt Mode, a basic USB-C charging cable won't transmit video signals; you need a fully-featured cable. If the receiving device doesn't have a USB-C port for video input, you'll need a specialized USB-C to HDMI cable adapter with a chip that converts your DP Alt Mode or Thunderbolt signal into an HDMI signal. The quality of this connection depends on the type of HDMI signal the cable and adapter are compatible with.
Ideally, your laptop will have at least two USB-C ports so you can charge with one while powering a display with the other.
A guide to HDMI signals
Not all HDMI signals are created equal. Since its introduction in 2002, the HDMI standard has gone through several iterations that each pack more bandwidth to allow for higher resolutions and faster refresh rates. Your connection will be limited to the oldest generation supported by either port, the cable or adapter.
While HDMI 2.2 has been approved, it's not really in use yet. Thus, the highest-quality option that's widely available is HDMI 2.1. Also known as Ultra High Speed, this generation of HDMI is more efficient than its earlier counterparts, capable of carrying up to 48 Gbps bandwidth. An HDMI 2.1 connection delivers 8K resolution at 60Hz and 4K resolution at 120Hz. Its other features include support for variable refresh rates, wider HDR signal compatibility and eARC support with enough audio punch to handle Dolby Atmos and DTS:X.
A tier lower are HDMI 2.0 cables and adapters. They're still capable of 4K resolution, albeit at a refresh rate of 60Hz. HDMI 2.0 adapters and cables should meet most streaming needs. The biggest limitation compared to its 2.1 successor is the noticeably lower bandwidth of 18 Gbps, making them not ideal for high-end gaming.
Avoid using earlier-gen HDMI adapters and cables, as they'll noticeably drop your signal quality below current standards. HDMI 1.4 can still reach 4K resolution, but at a diminished 30Hz refresh rate. Unless you've been holding onto a very old adapter, these won't be an issue.

) India is among the top countries with 90% of the world's chewing tobacco-related health burden, and South Asia is the "epicentre" of chewing tobacco, according to new research published in The Lancet Global Health journal.
Researchers estimated that chewing tobacco contributed to 251,000 deaths globally in 2023 -- there were 241 million chewing tobacco users globally, with use peaking among individuals 60 to 64 years old, they said.
The analysis, part of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 (GBD 2023) and covering 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023, distinguishes the burden of chewing tobacco from that of other forms of smokeless tobacco, the team said.
"Chewing tobacco is not a uniform public health problem, and our findings show that a relatively small number of countries bear an overwhelming share of its health burden," lead author Gabriela Gil, research scientist at Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), University of Washington, US, said.
"Understanding how patterns of use differ within these populations is critical to designing more effective prevention and tobacco control strategies," Gil said.
The researchers said despite decades of progress in tobacco control, the global prevalence of chewing tobacco use has remained relatively unchanged. Stroke and lip and oral cavity cancer were found to comprise much of the health loss attributable to chewing tobacco use globally.
South Asia had the highest concentration of chewing tobacco use, with 14.6% of people aged 15 years and above chewing tobacco products in 2023.
The region accounted for 2,10,000 chewing tobacco-related deaths -- about 84% of the global total, the study estimated.
However, more than 90% of chewing tobacco-related deaths and disability burden among men was found to occur in 10 countries, including India, Bangladesh, China, Pakistan and the US.
Among women, more than 90% of the burden was concentrated in countries, including India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Indonesia, Myanmar and China.
The researchers said the figures reflect total deaths and disability, meaning countries with larger populations may account for a greater share of the burden even if their rates are not the highest.
Patterns of chewing tobacco use also varied substantially by age and sex.
"These findings show why chewing tobacco control cannot take a one-size-fits-all approach," senior author Emmanuela Gakidou, professor in the department of health metrics sciences at IHME, said.
"Prevention and cessation strategies need to reflect how patterns of use differ by country, age, and sex, as well as the cultural and social factors that shape tobacco use in each setting," Gakidou said. PTI KRS

New Delhi, Oct 06: INDIA bloc MPs, including Leaders of Opposition Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi, on Tuesday marched from Parliament House complex towards the Election Commission but were stopped by police on Parliament Street, where they sat on a dharna demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
The MPs were stopped in front of the NITI Aayog office, on the stretch between NITI Aayog and Akashvani Bhavan leading towards the Election Commission headquarters.
After being prevented from proceeding further, they sat on the road in protest. Opposition MPs carried cutouts depicting Kumar in an RSS uniform and raised slogans, including “BJP hai CEC hai”, “Vote chor, gaddi chhod” and “Democracy not for sale”.
In a post on X, Gandhi posted, “Gyanesh it's done bro. Time to resign".
TMC leaders Abhishek Banerjee, Derek O Brien, Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, SP chief Akhilesh Yadav and CPI (M) leader John Brittas were among those who took part in the march.
Heavy security deployment and barricading had been put in place in and around Parliament and the Election Commission headquarters ahead of the march.
Security personnel were stationed in the area much before the MPs began arriving. The MPs gathered at Parliament's Makar Dwar before setting off towards Nirvachan Sadan, the Election Commission headquarters.
Ahead of the march, opposition MPs questioned the security arrangements and stepped up their demand for Kumar's resignation, citing the Supreme Court's observations on changes to Form 6, the statutory application for enrolment as a voter. Congress MP Imran Masood accused Kumar of eroding public trust in the Election Commission.
"Across the country, the institution that Gyanesh Kumar headed was an institution the entire country trusted, an institution the entire country took pride in and felt proud of. Questions were never raised over its impartiality. One person has broken that trust," he told PTI Videos.
"And an entire nexus is working together. We will question Gyanesh Kumar, and the BJP chief ministers will start giving the answers," he alleged.
CPI MP P Sandosh Kumar said the Supreme Court's observations on Monday had strengthened the opposition's objections to the additional declaration attached to Form 6 during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
"On September 26, there was a press statement by the Commission and it was stated that the entire process related to Form 6 has been ratified by the Supreme Court. Whereas it has been proven that it is an entirely misleading statement," he alleged. Calling the CEC a "Cheating Election Commissioner", the CPI leader said opposition parties had been agitating against the provisions since 2025 and would intensify their movement.
Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut questioned the scale of security deployment ahead of the march, saying the MPs intended to proceed peacefully.
"We are MPs. We are members of Parliament. We are also citizens of this country. Why is there a need to deploy such a large force to stop us? We will walk and go. We are unarmed," he said.
Raut claimed that Border Security Force and CISF personnel had been deployed and security outside ministers' residences increased.
Accusing Kumar of misleading the public over the Supreme Court's position on Form 6, he said the CEC had "no moral right" to continue in office.
The Supreme Court on Monday said it had not approved any modified version of Form 6 and would examine the Election Commission's records to ascertain whether changes had been made and who had authorised them.
The observations were made while hearing a petition challenging alleged unilateral decisions by Kumar.
In its September 26 statement, the Commission had said the declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR had been upheld by the Supreme Court, while forms prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, would be used outside the SIR period.
The protest comes amid an opposition campaign over alleged irregularities in the SIR exercise and reports of differences within the three-member Commission. The poll body has rejected suggestions of a split and maintained that decisions relating to SIR were taken unanimously.

Anyone with ovaries who lives long enough will experience menopause. While menopause is a natural transition in midlife, it can strongly affect a person’s quality of life and their current and future risk of heart disease, osteoporosis and other issues. So you might think that whether someone is experiencing or has gone through menopause would be noted in their medical records.
But when we and our colleagues examined the electronic medical records of almost 240,000 women, only 12% included mention of menopause, even though more than half the women reported separately that they were experiencing this transition. Our findings, published in the journal Menopause, reveal a major gap in how clinicians capture basic information about women’s health.
The menopausal women we examined are from a broader group of 400,000 who participated in the All of Us Research Program, a nationwide study run by the National Institutes of Health to compile a wide range of health data from at least 1 million Americans. We looked at how information about menopause was included in electronic health records and how this information differed by demographics, such as age, education, race and income.
Because study participants filled out health surveys upon enrolling, we could track discrepancies between their own reports of menopause and what was in their medical records. Age at menopause and symptoms, such as hot flashes or sleep disturbances, were also largely missing from the medical records and survey.
Missing links
Many aspects of menopause, and the diversity in women’s experiences with it, remain poorly understood.
For example, when menopause begins, as well as how disruptive its symptoms are, can vary greatly. Some women experience extreme hot flashes, sleep disruptions and brain fog, while others do not. One woman may go through natural menopause at age 45, and another at 54. Both ages would be considered normal, but that timing can affect current and future health in distinct ways.
Electronic medical records offer an unmatched opportunity to investigate these knowledge gaps, enabling researchers to study the experience of hundreds of thousands or even millions of people using routinely collected data.
Such large-scale studies may shed light on how menopause symptoms change over time and who is more likely to experience them; how markers of heart disease, bone health or mental health track with menopause; how social determinants of health, such as ethnicity and access to healthcare, affect someone’s lived experience of menopause; and countless other unanswered questions.
Closing the data gap
Our study is not the first to point out how inconsistently menopause status and symptoms are recorded in healthcare settings and electronic health records. But it systematically highlights the enormity of the gap, showing that menopause is often not even recorded at all.
It’s not clear why menopause is so rarely documented in electronic health records. It may be because menopause is not a disease, so it does not generally occur to clinicians to note it as a diagnostic code. It may feel obvious or irrelevant to diagnose or measure. It’s possible that patients themselves often don’t bring it up unless their symptoms are severe. Healthcare providers routinely ask middle-aged patients about their reproductive health – for example, when they had their last menstrual period – but this information rarely ends up getting documented in the electronic health record.
As we see it, not capturing this information is a colossal missed opportunity to drive vital research and improve personalized healthcare. Our team is developing a short, simple questionnaire about menopause status and symptoms for patients to fill out as they check in for medical appointments. These responses could then be added to their medical records for use by both their healthcare team and researchers. We are also developing a computer-based approach to infer menopause-related information from other data in a woman’s health record or genetics.
Finally, we are exploring the All of Us dataset to identify systematic differences – for example, in patients’ cultural background or income level, specific health system practices, urban versus rural settings – that might be linked with whether menopause data gets recorded in medical records. These associations can point to targeted ways to encourage its collection.
It’s impossible to research, and treat, what’s not measured. Capturing the menopause transition is an essential step to improving healthcare for women in midlife.
Audrey Hendricks, University of Colorado Anschutz and Nanette Santoro, University of Colorado Anschutz

Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
- Published
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.
Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.
There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.
This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.
Why has fighting broken out now?
It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.
The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.
This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.
This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.
Who are the TPLF?
For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.
It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.
At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.
When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.
Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.
The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.
An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022.
Why has the peace deal faltered?
There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.
The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.
Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.
When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.
The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.
For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.
The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.
But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.
This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.
Who is backing the TPLF?
A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.
Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.
Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.
So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.
TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.
Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.
What is the government's position?
As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.
It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.
During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.
Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports.
Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.
What do we know about the bombing in Tigray?
Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.
The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.
Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.
This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.
The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.
What is being done to stop the fighting?
The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.
It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.
The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.
The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.
The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.
Could the fighting spread?
Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.
The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.
The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.
There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.
The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.
The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.

The recent success of a late-stage mRNA cancer vaccine, showing the drug stopped the return of melanoma, has boosted hopes that the approach can be successfully harnessed to attack other cancers.
The question now is which ones — and whether mRNA is up to the task.
Merck and Moderna reported in August that adding their mRNA cancer vaccine to an existing treatment slowed the return and spread of melanoma. The field had been waiting “with bated breath” for the news on the drug, called intismeran autogene, said Karen Knudsen, the CEO of the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, the research organization founded by tech entrepreneur Sean Parker. The results suggested that the idea of using messenger RNA to train the immune system to attack cancer cells — an approach first devised decades ago — was ripe for further drug development.

Mumbai: The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has intensified its statewide food safety drive ahead of the festive season, with several food outlets and restaurants losing their food licences.
According to reports, the FDA has taken action against eight food establishments in Mumbai and the Konkan region. Following the serious hygiene lapses, the FDA has cancelled and suspended eight establishments' licences.
FDA acts against Mumbai establishments
The FDA, led by Tukaram Mundhe, has suspended the licences of Cafe Sultan in Kalina, Lo Fresh Food in Marol, Country Club and Suraj Lama Momos in Andheri West, and Cafe Pakeezah in Santacruz West, reported NDTV Profit.
The report further states that licences of Blinkit in Vile Parle, Copenhagen Hospitality in Vile Parle and Eatclubs in Bandra West were cancelled.
The strong actions by the FDA followed after food safety officers found severe lapses in storing food, along with a lack of cleanliness and sanitation at the sites.
Inspections in other parts of Maharashtra
The FDA also launched a crackdown in other parts of the state between October 1 and 5.
In the Konkan region, officials seized prohibited food stock worth Rs 2.18 crore from six establishments following inspections, NDTV Profit reported.
The action also resulted in six FIRs, 14 arrests, the sealing of two establishments and the seizure of four vehicles valued at Rs 67 lakh.
The officials even carried out inspections at food establishments in Pune, Nashik and Akola. In Pune, following the FDA inspection at seven establishments, prohibited food items worth nearly Rs 1.38 lakh were seized. Further, seven FIRs were filed, and nearly 10 people were arrested, while four establishments were sealed off.
Similar actions were also taken in Nashik, where prohibited food items worth Rs 3.30 lakh were seized, two FIRs were registered, and two people were arrested.
Sweets seized in Akola
In Akola, the FDA seized 1,900 kg of sweets worth Rs 5.72 lakh that were allegedly being transported in unhygienic conditions.
The regulator said it would continue strict action against establishments involved in the manufacture, storage, transport and sale of unsafe, adulterated, substandard, expired or prohibited food items.

Common mistakes you should avoid when using foldable phones
Your phone can fold in half, but your keys shouldn’t join it.
The most common mistake you should avoid when using foldable phones is dropping them. But that's common knowledge and doesn't make for a very exciting discussion. You're probably thinking about the inside foldable screen, where the most common way to damage it is closing it on something that shouldn't be there. Samsung's foldable care page warns that cards, coins or keys can scratch or even puncture a Galaxy foldable's inner display.
That seems straightforward enough; just make sure your car keys aren't sitting on top of your phone when you try to close it. But if you work a particularly dirty job or live near the beach, that complicates matters. You can't always spot dirt easily, and beach sand will find its way into absolutely anything.
Keep in mind that not all foldables are on equal footing. Some foldable screens are a bit softer and weaker than others. The Galaxy Z Fold8 and Fold8 Ultra, for instance, have an IP48 rating, whereas the new iPhone Duo boasts an IP68. The first digit describes the degree of protection against solid objects; a 4 means objects 1mm thick or larger can't enter, while 6 indicates a dust-tight device.
Treat the inner screen with care
A foldable's inner screen is far from a conventional slab-phone display. It has to fold, after all, so don't assume you can press on it as firmly as you would on a standard phone's outer glass. That includes actions you've probably done without thinking, like scratching a speck from the screen with your nail.
Another mistake is peeling off a factory-applied inner screen film because it looks like disposable shipping protection. This was surprisingly easy to do early on, but now the edges are tucked in and better hidden. Samsung highly recommends leaving these protective layers alone. On the flipside, don't stick an unapproved screen protector over a foldable display. These phones aren't like their slab cousins, so any old screen protector won't do. Only use a protector or stylus the manufacturer specifically lists as compatible with that model.
You don't have to baby a foldable phone, though it may seem that way coming from a traditional smartphone. These precautions just require you to be a little more particular when handling the folding screen. Avoid any concentrated force or closing it on anything other than open air.
What is the lifespan of a foldable phone?
There is no specific lifespan for foldables, though there are suggestions and indicators. For instance, we know that manufacturers test the hinges and screens by folding the phones between 200,000 and 500,000 times. If you open your phone 100 times a day, that would be 5 to 10 years.
However, that's not a guarantee. Samsung claimed the Galaxy Z Fold7's display remained functional after 500,000 folds in lab testing. Sounds pretty reassuring, but a controlled test doesn't mean the Fold7 would survive that many opens and closes throughout your daily life. In the past, Samsung's claim of 200,000 folds on the original Galaxy Fold fell short. When you hear figures tossed around, treat them as general benchmarks and marketing numbers.
Besides, it's far more useful to check for dirt before you close the phone than to count your folds each day. Don't push heavily on the display or use the wrong stylus. Use a soft cloth to clean marks on the screen instead of digging at them with your fingernail. And while the IP68 rating sounds great, Apple notes that the iPhone Duo's water and dust resistance may diminish with normal wear. Nothing lasts forever, but wear increases faster when moving parts are involved.

Mamata Banerjee sends notice to SSKM Hospital for allegedly leaking her medical reports
This comes days after Adhikari said that Banerjee faked her leg injury while releasing a five-year-old medical report
Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee served a legal notice to the Institute of Post Graduate Medical Education & Research (IPGMER) authorities in Kolkata seeking an explanation on how the medical reports of her leg injury ahead of the 2021 state assembly elections reached present CM Suvendu Adhikari.
This comes days after Adhikari said that Banerjee faked her leg injury while releasing a five-year-old medical report which purportedly said that there was “no evidence of fracture/dislocation” on Banerjee’s leg.
“You are called upon to inform me or my client that whether any medical records pertaining to my client has been at all placed before the chief minister (Adhikari) and if so placed, then kindly intimate or my client the due process of law adopted by the department of radio-diagnosis while placing the said records before the chief minister,” the notice sent by Arka Kumar Nag, Banerjee’s counsel, read.
On March 10, 2021, hours after filing her nomination from the high-profile seat of Nandigram where she contested against her protégé-turned-rival Adhikari, Banerjee alleged that unidentified men attacked her. The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) started a probe into the incident then.
She claimed to have fractured her leg and campaigned over the next two months, even holding a road show on a wheelchair with a plastered left leg. Even though the Trinamool Congress (TMC) won the assembly elections, Banerjee lost to Adhikari in Nandigram.
“The findings of the department of radio-diagnosis in the Bangur Institute of Neuro-Sciences at IPGMER (popularly known as SSKM hospital) on March 11, 2021 stated that there was no evidence of fracture or dislocation,” Adhikari told reporters at the state secretariat on Saturday.
The legal notice was sent to the Manimoy Bandyopadhyay, director of IPGMER and two other senior officials of the hospital.
“If it is identified that no due procedure of law was followed while placing the medial records of my client before the chief minister (Adhikari), then it shall be the legal liability of your office to initiate necessary steps in accordance with law against politically motivated officers of your institution involved in causing such delinquency and breach,” the notice stated.
Bandyopadhyay, refused to respond to calls and messages sent to him.
“She is committing a mistake. I asked the authorities to send me the notice through the state health department. She had ordered a CID probe into the incident. I would ask her not to dig further. If I make the X-Ray plates and MRI reports she would not be able to come out of her house. The documents were not with the SSKM hospital authorities. If needed I would reveal from where I got the documents,” Adhikari told media at the state secretariat on Monday.

SC refuses to restrain Gyanesh Kumar, says can't pass order based on news report
The SC bench made it clear that any decision found to have been taken contrary to the statutory requirements governing the ECI could subsequently be injuncted.
The Supreme Court on Monday declined to pass any interim order restraining chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar from functioning over allegations that he took several decisions unilaterally despite objections from the two other election commissioners (ECs), saying it could not proceed on “assumptions” without first verifying the facts.
A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued notices to the Election Commission of India (ECI), the Union government, the CEC and the two ECs on a petition filed by social activist Rakesh Kumar Singh. Track Gyanesh Kumar news live updates here.
The bench, however, made it clear that any decision found to have been taken contrary to the statutory requirements governing the functioning of the poll panel could subsequently be injuncted.
Senior advocate Vikas Singh, appearing for the petitioner, sought the immediate suspension of Kumar. Alternatively, he urged the court to direct the Election Commission to take only unanimous decisions until the next hearing.
Singh relied on the 1993 amendments to the election law to contend that, as far as possible, decisions of the Commission were required to be taken unanimously. He also referred to the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, particularly Section 18, which provides for majority decision-making in case of a difference of opinion.
“There is a distinction. The unanimity relates to transaction of business and allocation of work, while functioning can be by majority,” Singh submitted.
The bench, however, questioned him on what had changed from the 1993 legal position.
