Flávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, leaving progressive voters reeling.
The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.
“Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now.”
The far-right surge was a triumph – albeit an incomplete one – for the Bolsonaro clan and its 71-year-old patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro.
The disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, saw four relatives elected to congress. His 44-year-old wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won a seat in the senate, as did his second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, who is 43. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, 28-year-old Jair Renan Bolsonaro, and the ex-president’s 62-year-old brother, Renato Bolsonaro, both won seats in the lower house of congress.
Across Latin America’s biggest democracy, key congressional and gubernatorial races were also won by staunch Bolsonaristas including Tarcísio de Freitas, who was re-elected as the governor of São Paulo state, and Sérgio Moro, who was elected governor of the southern state of Paraná. Both men were ministers during Bolsonaro’s 2018-22 government.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) will now boast the largest caucus in the senate with 28 of its 81 seats. Combined with the seats of other hard-right parties, that number rises to 43, giving the movement an upper house majority.
Meanwhile, pro-Lula senate candidates, including the former environment minister Marina Silva, the leftwing veteran Benedita da Silva, and the centrist former planning minister Simone Tebet, suffered bitter defeats.
Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, two young Bolsonarista social media warriors, became the best-voted congresspeople in Brazilian history, securing more than 3m votes.
“We are experiencing a revolution … The far right is growing in a very consistent way, election after election,” said Lago, calling the election the worst for progressive and moderate centrist parties since the late 80s.
Lago believed Lula had managed to interrupt the advance of Bolsonaro’s populist movement in 2022, thanks to positive voter memories of his first two terms, from 2002 to 2010. Back then, a global commodities boom allowed Brazil’s first working-class president to fund major social welfare programmes that helped millions escape poverty. “But it was just an interregnum,” Lago said.
Control of the senate should allow pro-Bolsonaro politicians to approve an amnesty for their movement’s charismatic leader, allowing the former president to emerge from the Brasília mansion where he is living under house arrest and reassert his leadership of the far right.
“I think he will be freed and I think he will be very important during Flávio Bolsonaro’s [presidency],” said Lago. “Flávio will be running the country and [Jair] Bolsonaro will be doing what he has always done: leading the revolution.”
The senate majority may also help Bolsonaro’s third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, return from self-imposed exile in the US. The 42-year-old, who has close ties to Donald Trump’s Maga movement, was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison earlier this year for coercion – the result of his lobbying the Trump administration to interfere in his father’s coup trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.
Trump, who has been accused of trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour, has yet to comment on Sunday’s result, although writing on his Truth Social network, he praised the speed of the vote count. But the US president will be delighted by the strong rightwing showing, a major boost to his attempt to expand the conservative “orange wave” sweeping Latin America to its biggest democracy and economy. Recent years have seen a succession of pro-Trump presidents win power in the region, from Costa Rica, Honduras and El Salvador to Chile and Colombia.
One of Trump’s most enthusiastic regional cheerleaders, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, celebrated Bolsonaro’s “historic” victory against “the communist Lula”. “The American continent belongs to citizens who want to live in freedom,” Milei wrote on X.
The prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, wished Bolsonaro “good luck in the final” and celebrated his “great victory”. He wrote on X: “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.”
Speaking after Sunday’s result was confirmed, Lula put a brave face on what analysts called a catastrophic night for the left. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil,” he said, vowing to expose his rival’s “dark past”, which involves well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld and corruption allegations, which Bolsonaro has denied.
But the mood at Lula’s post-election event was reportedly funereal and Bolsonaro goes into the second round as the firm favourite. He is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates – Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema – who, between them, won more than 5.5m votes.
Santos quickly announced he would endorse neither candidate, considering both Lula and Bolsonaro to be “crooks”. Zema has vowed to vote against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) in the runoff, while Caiado has yet to declare his intentions.
Lula’s best hope may be convincing some of the record 33 million Brazilians who did not vote to turn out next time. “He will need to mobilise these apathetic voters who, in a sense, have already abandoned politics, which will be an extremely difficult task,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right.
Rocha has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters and identified “a great deal of voter apathy, especially among those who are not aligned with Bolsonarismo, and who could potentially vote for Lula”.
Although Flávio Bolsonaro has held political office for more than 20 years, “for undecided voters, his main positive characteristic is this idea of ‘renewal’, despite his possible involvement in corruption and with paramilitary groups,” Rocha added.
Lago believed only a dramatic shift from Lula’s campaign – such as changing the candidate, or a severe scandal involving Bolsonaro – could change the election’s outcome. But he was doubtful that would occur.

In a first, cheetahs to roam in tiger territory at Veerangana Durgavati Tiger Reserve
Madhya Pradesh has 60 cheetahs, 57 at Kuno National Park, where they were first translocated from African countries four years ago.
The Madhya Pradesh forest department will shift cheetahs to the Veerangana Durgavati Tiger Reserve (VDTR), home of 30 tigers, making it a first attempt of cheetah-tiger co-existence.
“The forest department has sought permission from the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) to chief cheetahs,” said L Krishnamurthy, additional principal chief conservator of forest (APCCF) (wildlife).
Madhya Pradesh has 60 cheetahs, 57 at Kuno National Park, where they were first translocated from African countries four years ago, and three Kuno big cats at Gandhi Sagar Wildlife Sanctuary. VDTR will become the third home for cheetahs in the state.
A South Africa cheetah expert said it would be a “learning” experience for cheetahs also.
“In South Africa, tigers are living with cheetahs at private reserves only. They are not together in wild. This would be a good experiment to see all three carnivores including cheetah, leopard and tigers together. It would be a learning for cheetahs as well,” said a cheetah expert, who refused to be named.
Susan E Yannetti, who is associated with the Metapopulation Initiative, said, “The last time cheetahs and tigers had a chance to coexist was probably close to one hundred years ago in India, when they were in significant numbers. But it will be interesting to know how they do get along. A cheetah is certainly no match for a tiger. Likely, the cheetah’s flight instinct would kick in, and it would run rather than fight, if challenged.”
Cheetah expert and former Wildlife Institute dean, YV Jhala, who led the team during the translocation of cheetahs to India, said it was a positive step.
"Of course, initially we will lose some cheetahs to tigers, but cheetahs are very intelligent animals. They can sense and move away from tigers. For the expansion of the project, it is very necessary that they adapt to live with other carnivores, including tigers," he said.
"However, they should not live in bomas. It has now been four years; it is time to leave cheetahs in open spaces and allow them to live freely. Free ranging cheetahs are possible only after restoring safe habitats and prey and this is the real test for the project’s success.," he added.
VDTR field director Rajneesh Singh said there is ample historical evidence of cheetahs, tigers and leopards coexisting.
"Earlier, Asiatic cheetahs used to live with tigers and leopards here. Their prey base is totally different. Cheetahs hunt baby nilgais and deer, chitals and black bucks, while there is no such limitation for tigers," Singh said.
"Cheetahs most live in open grasslands while tigers prefer dense forests. As the area of VDTR is very large, there will be very little chance of conflict," he added.
The two cheetahs from Kuno will kept in two bomas. In total, four quarantine compartments and five soft-release enclosures have been prepared across 439 hectares, he said.
Spread over 2,300 sq km, VDTR is home to around 30 tigers. This will also be the first time in India that cheetahs will roam in rocky terrain.
African Cheetahs were translocated for first time in India in September 2022. As many as eight cheetahs from Namibia, 12 from South Africa and nine cheetahs from Botswana were translocated.

Australia’s conservative Liberal-National Coalition has unveiled plans to drastically lower temporary and humanitarian visa numbers while prioritising skilled workers, in a move described by the party as the largest reduction in immigration in the country's history.
Under the proposed policy, temporary visas would be reduced by 650,000 across a four-year period, bringing annual net overseas migration down to 100,000 for two years, roughly a third of its current rate.
The sweeping proposal comes amid growing anti-immigration sentiment across Australia, driven by high living costs and housing shortages. The Coalition has faced intensified pressure from the far-right, anti-immigration One Nation party, which recently outpolled it in surveys after pledging to decrease temporary migration by 750,000 over three years.
"What we’re proposing today is the biggest cut to immigration in the history of this country. It will be putting Australia first and it will be putting our national interest first,” opposition leader Angus Taylor told a press conference on Tuesday.
"The net overseas migration numbers will be 100,000 year one, 100,000 year two, going to 160,000 in year four. That’ll take pressure off roads, off schools, off infrastructure, off houses, and that will ensure that our country has the breathing space it needs."
Under the Coalition's framework, humanitarian visa allocations would be halved to 10,000.
International student enrolments would be limited to 240,000, alongside the elimination of Australia's temporary graduate visa programme allowing post-graduation study and work. However, the Coalition promised to expand temporary skilled visas by 100,000 and also clear a backlog of construction worker applications.
"We have also seen under Labor a shift away from skilled migration to mass migration. We’ll reverse that shift," Mr Taylor added.
The plan represents a sharper reduction than the target set by the centre-left Labor government last month, which sought to bring annual net migration down to 225,000 by 2028.
Migration surged after Australia reopened its borders in February 2022 following over two years of Covid closures, largely driven by international students, backpackers and temporary workers. Intake has nevertheless dropped over the past two years, with net overseas migration standing at 306,000 in the year to 30 June 2025.
Australia's next general election is not due until 2028.

How Evans defied history to join rallying greats
- Published
For what must have felt like an eternity, Elfyn Evans feared history was repeating itself yet again.
At 3.05pm local time in Sardinia on Sunday, Evans could only stand and watch as another world rally title looked to be slipping from his grasp.
Evans was preparing in his head yet another runners-up speech - it would be his sixth - as he waited for Oliver Solberg to cross the finish line and be crowned world champion.
How could this be happening again?
Of the five previous times he had been championship runner-up, three had been decided on the final day and twice after he had taken a lead into the final event.
But at 3.06pm, for once the motor-racing gods were on his side.
With just two turns to go on the final stage of the final round and with victory in sight, Solberg somehow careered off the track into the Sardinian sand to hand Evans his first world title.
In the most dramatic of finishes, the 37-year-old from north Wales became the first British winner of the World Rally Championship (WRC) in 25 years.
Only two British men had taken the title since the WRC's 1977 inception, matching the exploits of legendary pair Colin McRae (1995) and Richard Burns (2001).
Louise Aitken-Walker was Britain's first world champion when WRC ran a women's version in 1990.
"It wouldn't by my proudest way of winning it, but it's job done," said Evans.
"It's been a difficult weekend. I felt on Friday things were slipping away. We were a bit powerless with the road position we had and Oliver was flying."
His experienced co-driver Scott Martin revealed Evans was already apologising for his stage performance as they waited for Solberg to finish.
"I've said all week that until we arrived at the beach after that last stage it was never over. How true that turned out to be," said Martin.
Evans and Martin have been consistent performers throughout the 2026 championship, through the streets of Monaco, the ice and snow of Sweden, the flowing roads of Chile, and the punishing, sun-baked gravel tracks of southern Europe.
Despite winning only two of the previous 12 events, the pair took a 21-point lead into the final race at Rally Italia Sardegna.
Solberg, whose father Petter won the 2003 title, was around one kilometre from glory only to suffer motorsport's version of Devon Loch.
"The lead up to this event gave us a bit of a buffer and we just about managed to hold on at the end. It was an incredible finish," said Evans.
"I feel for [Solberg] after he came so close and lost at the last moment. I've been in a similar situation and it will be tough for him for a few days, but he's shown he's one to watch for the future."
Born to drive
Evans, like Solberg, is also from fine rally driving stock. His father Gwyndaf was British champion, as well as runner-up four times, but the ruddy-cheeked farmer never got the break to complete on the world stage.
The curse of finishing second passed down to his son who had already turned professional by the time his father claimed the last of those near misses in 2010.
Evans clinched his first WRC stage win in Germany in 2014 and a first podium in Argentina a year later, before having to drop down to the WRC2 class in 2016.
Evans admitted that blow only fueled his determination to make it in the WRC and a first rally victory followed - in his home event in Wales - in 2017.
He has been remarkably consistent, finishing second for the title in 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024 and, perhaps most agonisingly, to Sebastien Ogier by just four points in the final race of 2025.
He appeared condemned to be one of sport's great runners-up until the late drama of Sardinia threw up one of the championship's most thrilling finishes.
There may have been a stroke of fortune about the title win, but few can deny Evans earned it.

On Friday, Amazon committed to donating more than $1 billion over the next five years to communities neighboring data centers.
In a press release, Amazon Web Services’ CEO Matt Garman said that communities would decide how to prioritize funds across “education, job training, energy affordability, water, and energy preservation, and local priorities.”
Laying out other community commitments, Amazon also promised to ensure data centers wouldn’t increase power bills or wipe out local water supplies. Regarding the latter, Amazon promised to be “water positive” by 2030, while claiming that 75 percent of projects have already met this goal.
Rolling out these commitments, Amazon seemed bent on convincing Americans that the swelling data center backlash is based on lies. Echoing Donald Trump’s claims that foreign disinformation campaigns are fueling widespread protests, Garman urged that calls for data moratoriums must end or else American frontier AI might fall behind China’s.
According to Garman, US rivals are trying to “trick us into slowing down,” and Amazon’s commitments are meant to reassure Americans that everything’s okay and that we should instead plow ahead, as Trump endlessly advocates.
However, advocates at Stand.Earth—a global nonprofit that’s been fighting for environmental protections in communities hosting data centers—told Ars that Amazon is the one being “misleading” by spreading “corporate propaganda.” Seemingly in crisis mode as billions of dollars in data center projects have been blocked nationwide, Amazon’s promised donations represent “a flailing attempt at damage control for the harm its data center build-out has already caused,” Stand.Earth said.
Most problematic, Stand.Earth suggested, is Amazon’s plan to back a power plant that experts expect will become the largest source of US climate pollution. Glaringly, Amazon’s data center commitments don’t mention the power plant and scarcely address pollution, apart from promising to exclusively rely on back-up generators that use the lowest possible emissions.

How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
- Published
Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China.
Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%.
Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked.
Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market.
The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world.
Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year.
"India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC.
More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period.
"China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI).
If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava.
On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address, external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues".
But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC.
That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods.
To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones.
"Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava.
It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment.
Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank.
"Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production.
Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends.
China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output.
Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year.
A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava.
On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies.
"Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li.
"If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same."
The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava.
But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals – affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations – areas where India still falls short.
India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds.
"Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India."
More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sectors to reduce its trade asymmetry, says Li. Sectors like pharmaceuticals could be a natural fit with China's population aging and healthcare costs rising.
"But narrowing a $112bn deficit won't come from finding niche export sectors alone," he adds.
"The key question is whether Beijing is ready and willing to make concessions on market access as part of the broader normalisation. Alternatively, India will need to find its own leverage to force that conversation."

The Sentinelese, living on North Sentinel Island in the Bay of Bengal, are one of the most isolated peoples on earth.
Part of an archipelago governed by India, it is prohibited by law to venture within 5km of their island. And when a missionary did manage to land on the beach in 2018, he was killed by bow and arrow.
Yet none of that was to deter influencer Mykhailo Polyakov, who last year filmed himself arriving on North Sentinel Island, and leaving a can of coke on the beach.
Features writer Elle Hunt documents the rise of a new breed of influencer, travelling around the world, and streaming to millions their attempts to contact the uncontacted – despite the warnings of indigenous rights groups that the consequences could be fatal, both for the social media stars and the communities they risk exposing to disease.
Helen Pidd also speaks to Ecuadorian indigenous rights activist María José Andrade Cerda about the rights and wrongs of this new world.

A video purportedly showing a resourceful monkey rescuing a dog from floodwaters circulated online in late September and early October 2026. 
The 10-second clip allegedly shows a rainy village scene featuring a monkey wading in water and pulling a dog to the top of a log.
For example, an X post (archived) featured the video with a Thai-language text caption translating to English as, "If we're gonna make it, we've gotta make it together, right?" That clip, shared Sept. 27, made the rounds at the same time Thai authorities were reporting about fatalities from flooding following an unusually heavy rainfall. (The same user posted longer, authentic-appearing videos allegedly showing snakes, dogs, puppies and a cow during flooding.)
That X post received millions of views, as did an Instagram post (archived) displaying the clip with the onscreen caption, "Viral: Monkey Grabs A Dog And Climbs Onto A Floating Log Amid Raging Floodwaters." Other users widely shared the video on Facebook (archived), TikTok (archived) and X (archived). Some specifically claimed a person recorded the video in Thailand.
Some commenters praised the monkey for its alleged act of kindness, while others said they believed someone created the clip using artificial intelligence.
In sum, the video was fake and bore signs indicating it was AI-generated, among those its precise 10-second duration, an inauthentic-sounding audio track and unnatural-looking video artifacts. 
Moreover, reverse image search results matching single frames from the video indicated the oldest post (archived) hosting it resided on the Thai-language Facebook page เรื่องร้อนสตอรี่, a title that means Hot Story in English. That post and others on the page were labeled "AI content."
We emailed the Facebook page's owner to ask whether they created the video with AI or shared it from someone else's post and will update this article if we receive further details.
Examining the video
The video exhibits natural-seeming camera movements and zooms, and realistic visuals of rain falling onto the water in a flooded village. At the beginning, the outline of the clip's frame faintly indicates the camera's point of view may be from behind a window frame, a car window or similar setup, providing the impression of realism.
The signs of fakery far outweigh any indicators of realism, however. For example, we downloaded the video and used Adobe Premiere video-editing software to determine the clip's exact duration. The clip runs at 24 frames per second and lasts exactly 10 seconds and zero addtional frames in length — a common AI-generated video duration. We didn't find a longer version of the clip that would support the alternative explanation that it might have been an authentic video trimmed down to a precise 10 seconds.
The audio track features the sound of falling rain, followed by unrealistic sounds of the dog plopping down on the log and making whining noises that don't appear to match the visuals. Also, at the moment of the plop, the dog's front right paw lands on a pile of debris that doesn't appear to move. (Bear in mind that anyone can add inauthentic audio to a video with authentic visuals, so fake audio alone does not automatically mean the whole video is fake.)
Perhaps one of the key indicators of AI generation or other visual fakery is visible in the animals' movements just before the monkey releases the dog. From the 5-second mark to the 6-second mark, the monkey appears to pick up the dog for the last time to fully situate it on the log. An unnatural video artifact appears at that moment — at about the 00:05:13 mark — when the dog's front right leg raises up and off of the log. For a single frame, the leg appears as a thinner, sharper representation of itself as the vertical black shape in the middle of the yellow circle in the montage below. The vertical black shape doesn't appear in the preceding or subsequent frames:
(Ches Vichet via Facebook, Snopes illustration)
On the subject of odd visuals, several blue objects appear to show up only after the camera zooms in to show the closer view of the two animals. For example, one small light-blue item resembling a hair tie appears to either surface or otherwise inexplicably appear on the left side of the debris pile just after the 7-second mark.
(Ches Vichet via Facebook, Snopes illustration)
AI detection tools and fake animal rescue videos
Scanning the video with AI detection tools produced inconsistent results. The tools we used included Hive's AI-generated & deepfake content detection, Nvidia's synthetic video detector, Pangram's AI image detector (screenshots only), Tencent's Zhuque AI image and video detector and ZeroGPT's AI video detector.
Snopes doesn't rely solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability. Instead, we consider the tools' results as individual data points among many when judging the authenticity of images, text and videos.
During our research process, we made note of numerous other videos allegedly showing animals rescuing other animals (or people) from water. Those clips generally exhibited more-obvious visual indicators of AI, such as inconsistent blurring and smoothness, that the monkey-saving-dog video didn't.
Also, we considered the possibility that the "rescue" may have been staged like other examples of fake animal rescue videos hosted online. Kerry Burton-Galley, a spokesperson for the Lady Freethinker organization, which states as its purpose to "end cruelty for all beings," told us by email that most staged animal rescue content involves humans seeming to rescue animals, adding "but it's certainly not unheard of for videos to feature two or more animals, including one animal apparently coming to another's aid." She continued:
AI-generated animal content is becoming increasingly troubling and will likely pose an even greater challenge as the technology advances. While no real animal is directly harmed in creating a fully AI-generated video, realistic fake rescue content can make it increasingly difficult for people to distinguish genuine rescues from fabricated ones. That can erode public trust and potentially affect donations and support for legitimate rescue organizations doing lifesaving work.
For further reading, we previously reported the facts about a video showing an elephant throwing grass on its head.

One imam in Houston has been videoed with some of his supporters calling for Muslim business owners to stop selling haram products, like pork, alcohol and lottery tickets, that are prohibited under Islamic religious law.
As far as Snopes could tell, the request was coming from one individual imam and is not a coordinated or widespread movement. The imam's messaging is directed toward Muslim business owners, not all business owners, and is framed as a request rather than an order. No such wider order has been issued.
Under the First Amendment, all American have the right to freedom of speech and freedom of religion.
In September 2026, a claim spread online that Muslims in Texas are ordering local businesses to stop selling products Islam considers "haram" (forbidden), such as pork, alcohol and lottery tickets, within 30 days.
Multiple Facebook users posted similar captions saying Muslims have "taken to the streets in Houston" and other Texas cities, going "store to store" issuing "threats" of protests or more "if there's a continued noncompliance" (archived, archived).
Snopes readers searched our site and contacted us looking for more information regarding the rumor.
In short, the claim is exaggerated.
Footage does show one Houston imam, Qasim ibn Ali Khan, protesting with signs and asking Muslim convenience store owners to stop selling products deemed haram. One video posted on Khan's TikTok account in May 2025 (screenshotted), that features no signs of being generated using artificial intelligence, shows him telling employees at two Houston convenience stores that he planned to demonstrate if the staff did not remove haram products within 30 days. He did not specify where he planned to hold such demonstrations, only saying they would take place "around the city." Therefore, there is an element of truth to the claim.
Khan posted a follow-up video in July 2025 (screenshotted) showing him and his supporters protesting outside one of the convenience stores that features in the May 2025 clip.
It was not possible to determine whether the stores removed their haram products.
Similarly, it was not possible to find evidence of an "order" being issued — Khan specifically says in first the recording that he has no power to enforce his request — nor evidence of a coordinated, widespread movement to get businesses to stop selling haram products. Furthermore, Khan's rhetoric in the video shows he was making a request of specifically Muslim-owned businesses.
As such, we rate the claim mostly false.
Snopes attempted to contact Khan for comment, but got no response. We will update this article if we hear back.
Forbidden products across religions
Each of the world's religions, and the denominations within them, have different interpretations of religious law.
Using dietary restrictions as an example, Christian denominations rarely impose restrictions on what people can eat, though some practice abstinence from drinking alcohol. Hinduism promotes, but does not mandate, vegetarianism; Jainism requires vegetarianism, among other restrictions; observant Jews must follow kosher; and Islamic dietary law requires Muslims to not drink alcohol or consume pork.
As stated above, the grouping of forbidden practices in Islam is called "haram." In contrast, approved practices are called "halal," which is why some food products have a halal mark.
Texas Republicans, Islam and the First Amendment
Ahead of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, Republicans in Texas have made the idea that Muslims wish to implement Shariah law (Islamic religious law) in the United States a talking point in their campaigns.
(It should be noted: the phrase Shariah law can be interpreted in various ways to mean different things. In this case, Republicans appear to mean fundamentalist Shariah law, the strictest form, which applies Shariah principles to all matters of justice).
On Sept. 6, 2026, Amy Mekelburg — who is known for posting anti-Muslim videos online and who founded an organization the Southern Poverty Law Center considers an anti-Muslim hate group — posted one of Khan's TikTok videos to X. The footage shows Khan speaking outside a purportedly Muslim-owned convenience store. It's likely this is the origin of the claim that Muslims were ordering a ban on haram products.
In the clip, Khan says he asked the store to stop selling products deemed haram and that Muslim merchants should have "a higher standard," but he also states that he and his followers have no authority to force anyone to stop selling haram products:
We can't stop them, of course, this is the United States of America, and people have the freedom to sell what they want, as long as they're supported by the United States government.
Khan is correct — the First Amendment guarantees both freedom of speech and freedom of religion. As Texas Gov. Greg Abbott reportedly said during a September bill signing, according to the Texas Council for American-Islamic Relations, "Texas law and Texas courts govern those businesses and those neighborhoods. No ranting imam can change that."
In the video, Khan also says his request is being made specifically to Muslim business owners, not all businesses, as suggested in the social media posts spreading the claim in question:
Of course, you have the right to sell what you want, but as a Muslim, you should have higher principles, higher code of ethics that are supported by the Quran and the Sunnah [teachings] of Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
Despite thorough searches, it was not possible to find evidence of a widespread campaign making similar requests to businesses, Muslim-owned or otherwise.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
The winner of the Nobel Prize for medicine was announced early this morning. Did you win your office pool? Do you think another research team was robbed? Send me all your hot takes at [email protected].
Now without further ado:
2026 prize awarded to U.S. and German scientists for optogenetics research
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel are the joint recipients of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics,” the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, Sweden announced on Monday.
Deisseroth, a professor at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, Hegemann, a professor at Humboldt University in Berlin and Nagel, a professor at the University of Würzburg, Germany, developed a method that uses light, combined with genetic modifications of neurons, to switch on or off individual cells in a living brain. This makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behavior in the brain, and is being studied as a treatment for disease. Read more here.
(Oh and are you wondering whether human Nobel prize winners are about to become an endangered species, now that AI is around? This former medical school dean is asking the same question in a new First Opinion.)
The advocates trying to make stem cells happen
As STAT’s Margaret Manto was tooling around a peptide conference last month, she heard a lot about another regenerative medicine: stem cells. Proponents for peptides argue that stem cells are also a revolutionary treatment, though the data doesn’t bear that out.
Normally, that would be a problem for winning FDA approval. But Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s health department seems much more open to these kinds of treatments. As Margaret writes: “The stem cell industry sees the FDA’s tentative embrace of peptides as its chance to get a foot in the door — and bring stem cells from the grey market to millions of Americans.” What could that mean for eager patients? Read more here.
Could we one day vaccinate against every cancer?
In August, two drug companies announced that their mRNA vaccine, combined with an immunotherapy drug, had substantially cut the risk of the return of melanoma. That news raised an exciting possibility — that personalized vaccines could one day protect us from many types of cancer. But days later, a German drugmaker said it was ending its trial of a colorectal vaccine after early data showed the treatment wasn’t working.
That tale of two vaccines has experts scratching their heads. Read about how they’re making sense of the results, and what that might teach us about which cancers can be beaten by vaccines — and which will require more creative approaches. (And if that’s not enough incentive, there’s also a really helpful explanation of how cancer vaccines rally the body’s immune system.)
‘It’s been a little shocking to hear the level of despair’
Faithful readers know that STAT’s Bob Herman has been turning out hit after hit on the crisis in employer-based health insurance, chronicling the extreme financial pressure facing many American business owners. In honor of today’s new installment, I asked what’s surprised him most over the course of his reporting. Here’s what he told me:
“I have covered health insurance for well over a decade, and there’s never been a time when employers and workers have been happy or excited about their options. It’s always been ‘expensive.’ But it’s been a little shocking to hear the level of despair and concern among businesses and policy experts. GLP-1s, in particular, are pushing so many employers to the brink.
I’ve also been surprised to learn about some behind-the-scenes behaviors of the health care industry toward employers, most of which don’t look great! One is in my new story today — how a hospital tried to strong-arm an employer to pay more than $230,000 for an outpatient procedure, then backed off after realizing it made a billing mistake (but still got a hefty price). Health insurers embed some wild terms in contracts with employers, and “savings” sometimes don’t mean savings at all for businesses. It’s very easy to get taken advantage of, even for vigilant employers.”
Energy drinks are dangerous for teens. Why don’t we do more to protect them?
I can’t lie — I definitely drank a Red Bull or two to fuel my college all-nighters. But those drinks never left me feeling especially great. Which makes sense: Research shows that energy drinks aren’t safe for teenagers. At high levels, too much caffeine pushes the teen heart and brain into overdrive and can cause acute illness.
Colleges should help their students avoid these dangerous consequences. But things are moving in the opposite direction, writes Kent Sepkowitz in a new First Opinion. Schools are teaming up with brands like Celsius and Monster Energy for sports sponsorships. What will it take to stop the “energy drink cabal?” Read Sepkowitz’s diagnosis.
Good news, bad news on opioids
More young people are being treated for opioid use disorder with medications. But fewer are staying on that treatment for at least six months. That’s according to a new paper in JAMA. Experts aren’t quite sure why, but some point to the challenge of accessing drugs like buprenorphine and methadone when you’re under 18.
As Theresa Gaffney explains, “Until late 2024, federal law required minors to have two documented “failed” attempts at recovery without medication before they could start methadone. But even without that requirement, many of the specialized clinics that provide it won’t accept minors. Buprenorphine has historically been easier for doctors to prescribe, but recent research shows that few residential treatment facilities for adolescents actually offer it.”

It’s a wild time for retro gaming. Thanks to decompilations and recompilations of classic titles, those games are becoming unshackled from their proprietary code and original hardware to be ported to new devices or updated in ways to completely change the original game. Ever imagined skateboarding in Call of Duty? Or playing the original Halo right in your web browser, complete with multiplayer?
Reverse-engineered games: All the news on video game decomps, recomps, VR and web and 3D ports
These are unofficial versions of games, so they may sit in a legal gray area. It seems unlikely that Nintendo, for example, is particularly happy about people finding ways to play The Legend of Zelda on non-Nintendo hardware. Many of these projects are also made with the assistance of AI, which, for some people, is a non-starter given ethical or environmental concerns surrounding the technology.
Below, you’ll find our coverage of gaming decomps, recomps, and all the other ways gamers are reverse-engineering games to go previously unimaginable places.
- Here’s a video of Half-Life: Alyx running natively on a Vision Pro. Take a look. It was “made possible” thanks in part to Valve’s ARM port of the game it made for the Steam Frame and with some help from Claude.
- Just think: You could be playing Halo in a web browser right now. The video game decompilation movement has done it again. Not only do we have 128 player Halo across Windows, Linux, and Android , you can also just fire it up in a web browser thanks to OpenHaloCE and immediately start campaign or a huge multiplayer match. It’s not just one dev: lots of people made this happen.
- This unofficial Lego Racers remake runs in your browser with split-screen and online multiplayer. The classic game decompilation movement has produced yet another amazing feat: 1999’s Lego Racers isn’t just back, the excellent Mario-Kart-meets-Lego game is anywhere you want it to be. NavigatorSharp’s fan recreation Step On It works in a web browser on desktop or phone, and you can find builds for Android, Mac, Windows PC and Linux (including the Steam Deck) right here too.
- How an online community took back the Legend of Zelda I don’t have a first memory of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time because It’s been in my life for as long as I can remember. Before I had the coordination to play the game myself, I would watch my older brothers play it for hours on end. When I could finally play through it myself, it felt like flying. I chase that dopamine hit once every year or two by playing through Ocarina of Time, which normally requires dusting off my old GameCube and hoping the disk isn’t too scratched to read. But for the last several months, I haven’t been playing Ocarina of Time on a Nintendo console at all. 20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.
Link: WHO appreciates the signing of these milestone agreements

This story appeared in The Logoff, a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here.
Trump’s plan to buy votes, briefly explained
Can Trump bribe his way out of a midterm disaster?
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is trying to bribe his way out of a midterm disaster.
What’s happening? Over the weekend, Trump announced a plan to send $90 payments to more than 20 million Americans 65 years and older, drawing from a pool of money called the Medicare Improvement Fund.
Trump, in a post, described the payments as part of a strategy to “substantially LOWER costs for our Seniors” — but the money, a single nonrecurring payment set to go out this month, was reportedly already earmarked for other programs before Trump decided to redirect it.
Why now? Trump, facing a potentially catastrophic midterms for his party, has been looking for any way to turn out (Republican) voters — up to and including offering them cash, either implicitly or explicitly, in return for their support.
In the implicit category: these $90 payments and a smaller number of $500 Affordable Care Act refunds (fewer than 1 million) that began going out last week.
Much more explicitly, however, he’s also promising Americans $5,000 if they reelect Republicans in the midterms.
Trump has directly linked Medicare payments with the promised checks: “Because I delivered on this very important issue for the American People,” he wrote in a post, “they can also rest assured the highly popular $5,000 Trump Dividend will be distributed to every U.S. Citizen if, and when, the Republicans win the Midterm Elections!”
Will it work? It’s hard to say for sure, but it feels unlikely: The Medicare payments are relatively small, while the ACA payments are going out to relatively few voters. Polling suggests that voters are not fans of the promised $5,000 checks, and even fewer believe that they’re going to happen (they’re almost certainly correct).
What else should I know? Direct payments to Americans — real or promised — are not the only way Trump is trying to sway the midterms in his favor. He’s also continuing to spend taxpayer dollars on a propagandistic ad campaign, which he personally directed.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

This year, members of Seattle Mountain Rescue have been setting off into the wilds of the US Pacific Northwest wearing an unusual piece of kit.
They’ve been hiking into the wilderness with powered assistive devices attached to their hips and legs. Designed to increase lower-body strength when climbing or carrying heavy loads, these pieces of equipment are being tested to see if they can boost rescuers’ speed and endurance when it matters most—during searches for stranded people.
Devices like these are called human exoskeletons. They attach to parts of the body to create an external—or “exo”—mechanical structure. This powered frame enhances the wearer’s physical capabilities.
In physically demanding fields, workers are increasingly using these devices during strenuous tasks. IKEA has used SuitX exoskeletons for several years now. These assist warehouse workers with handling heavy materials. Ford, Boeing, and Mazda Toyota have also all adopted the tech on some of their assembly lines.
In Finland, a recent project called ExoPELA assessed whether exoskeletons could reduce muscle load and strain in rescue and firefighting work. It found noticeable benefits for users in certain real-world tasks.
And in early 2026, the Ukrainian military revealed its soldiers had been using Hypershell exoskeletons on the front lines to help with carrying artillery shells. According to test results, soldiers wearing the devices “become less fatigued, work faster, and maintain combat effectiveness for longer,” Colonel Vitalii Serdiuk told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper in March.
Multiple consumer and clinical devices, designed for everyday assistance, rehabilitation and exercise, are also now available. Some estimates have valued the total sector at around $500 million (£370 million) currently, and predict it could double or triple in size by the mid-2030s.
Exoskeleton technology has progressed significantly over the past decade. This has largely been thanks to robotic motors, sensors, and control systems becoming more affordable and accessible. However, the concept of augmenting human performance with exoskeleton-like devices dates back much earlier.

Injured Assefa narrowly misses world record in Berlin
- Published
An injured Tigst Assefa hobbled over the line at the Berlin Marathon on Sunday after looking set to smash the women's world record.
The Ethiopian still won with the third-fastest time in history in two hours 11 minutes four seconds.
But the 29-year-old, a silver medallist at the Paris Olympics two years ago, had been cruising to a new record before fading in the final stages.
Kenyan athlete Ruth Chepngetich's time of 2:09:56, set at the 2024 Chicago Marathon, remains the world record time, though that result is overshadowed by the three-year doping ban she received in 2025.
Assefa, the 2026 London Marathon winner, started rapidly and led the field by a minute at the 15km mark. She was ahead of the record pace at 35km and is a renowned fast finisher - but began to suffer clear discomfort and her pace slowed.
However she still broke the Berlin course record of 2:11:53 that she set in 2023 - which was also her previous personal best.
In addition, she improved on her time of 2:15:41 at the London Marathon earlier this year.
"We have to bow our heads to this performance. She was on a world record course for most of the race but then something happened to her tendon," said race director Mark Milde.
"To finish like this, I've never seen something like this. The pain is hard to imagine.
"With a heavy heart, we saw her set a course record, but it could have been a lot more."
The top five finishers were all from Ethiopia, with Bedatu Hirpa second and Dera Dida third.
Guye Adola - another Ethiopian - won the men's race with a time of 2:02:50.

Amazon has made a series of new public commitments to communities where it’s building data centers, including making an official announcement that it no longer uses nondisclosure agreements in its arrangements with county officials.
In a blog post published Friday, CEO Matt Garman detailed the steps the company says it’s already taking around data centers. In addition to stopping the use of NDAs, Garman says $1 billion will be invested over the next five years in communities that house the company’s data centers. The money will go toward free community college programs, workforce training, and energy efficiency upgrades for schools, homes, and community buildings.
In the post, Garman acknowledged how the fierce backlash against data centers across the country is hampering the AI buildout.
“Right now there are over 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the country,” he wrote. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to [the AI] race, and the consequences would last generations. As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”
Nondisclosure agreements have become a key point of contention amid the massive data center buildout. Typically, local officials who sign NDAs with data centers looking to develop projects in their area are unable to share information with the public, including the energy and water use of certain projects. Many NDAs bar officials from revealing even basic information—like the tech companies involved in building out the data center. In July, the New York Times reported on how secret agreements at all levels of government were crucial in building out plans for Hyperion, its massive data center in Louisiana.
There has been a rush of recent local legislation attempting to address the secretive paperwork. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, and Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer have all cracked down on data center NDAs in recent executive orders. Multiple states, including New York, New Jersey, Indiana, and Ohio, have considered recent legislation banning the practice.
At the federal level, a bipartisan group of lawmakers recently introduced the No Secrets for Data Centers Act in the House. Earlier this week, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD), one of the bill’s sponsors sent letters to Amazon, Google, Meta, and Oracle demanding information on their use of data center NDAs; Amazon told the Wall Street Journal that it was no longer using NDAs. (Google, Meta, and Oracle did not return the Journal’s request for comment.)
Amazon has been at the center of some high-profile controversies around NDAs. In Tucson, Arizona, Amazon was revealed last year to be the tenant of a controversial data center thanks to a public records request from a local outlet; an NDA had been in place barring county officials from sharing the identity of the end tenant. (Amazon has since exited that project.) In South Bend, Indiana, where the company has invested more than $13 billion into a massive data center campus, some elected officials have claimed that local government employees have been unable to answer questions about the project due to signing NDAs with the company.
Thanks to the opaque nature of data center financing and construction, end tenants like Amazon are often not the companies directly interfacing with government officials. As the Houston Chronicle reported last month, a top official in Wharton County, Texas, signed an NDA not with Amazon, but with contractor VisionFirst Advisors, which prevented him from sharing details about the Amazon project.
Amazon did not respond to WIRED’s queries about whether the promises around NDAs also extend to its contractors.
Much of the new blog from Garman is also dedicated to dispelling what he calls “misinformation and outright lies” around data centers and their water use, energy use, the use of diesel generators, and impacts on communities. “This build out is so important geopolitically that there are widespread reports of various countries intentionally seeding misinformation in the U.S. about data centers to trick us into slowing down,” he wrote.
As WIRED has reported, the idea that China is intentionally seeding widespread dissent and misinformation around data centers is a consistent message coming from the White House and tech leaders. Experts, however, say that this narrative is widely overblown, and that there is little evidence of Chinese misinformation driving the data center backlash.

Tripura: TIPRA Motha wins over 2000 seats in TTAADC village council polls
Though 4,597 seats were supposed to go for polls under 587 village committees, voting took place in 2,950 seats
The TIPRA Motha party, an alliance partner of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in Tripura won 2,670 seats leaving 470 to BJP in the Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council (TTAADC) village council polls, results of which were declared on Monday.
BJP’s another ally IPFT won 16 seats while 83 seats were won by independent candidates. Oppositions CPIM and Congress won 38 and 10 seats as they contested independent.
The counting of the votes began at 8am. Tensions escalated at some counting centres with protests and road blockades in Sepahijala and Dhalai districts.
Tension also prevailed at Tulasikhar block in Khowai district where security forces allegedly resorted to lathi charge following a confrontation outside a counting centre.
TIPRA Motha party chief Pradyot Bikram Kishore Manikya Debbarma wrote on his Facebook page, “Today’s result will restore the power of the grassroots back to the people. The long struggle in the Supreme Court which I personally fought to ensure that our constitutional rights is restored. Which ever party wins today the most important thing is that the people have won. This is the power of Tiprasa”.
Though 4,597 seats were supposed to go for polls under 587 village committees, voting took place in 2,950 seats as 1,644 seats were elected unopposed including 1,561 from TIPRA Motha party, 81 from BJP, one each from CPIM and an independent.
The Supreme Court, earlier, directed the state Election Commission to hold the village council polls by September first week following a petition filed by TIPRA Motha party supremo Pradyot Kishore Debbarma.
The five-year term of the elected village committees ended in 2021 but the election could not be conducted due to Covid-19 pandemic.
The 28-seated TTAADC poll held this April where the TIPRA Motha party emerged victorious securing 24 seats, reducing its estranged ally Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) by half of its previous tally - winning only 4 seats this time as against 8 in the last tribal council elections.

Twelve arrested for allegedly running cat trafficking ring in Vietnam
- Published
Twelve men have been arrested in Vietnam after allegedly confessing to stealing and selling around 2,700 cats, Ho Chi Minh City police have said.
Cat traps, fur removal machines and measuring scales were among the items seized during the investigation. The men are suspected of taking the pets to be slaughtered for food.
Police allege the suspects roamed through residential areas in small groups on motorbikes at night to steal the cats.
The men reportedly used pieces of fish as bait, placing traps outside houses where they knew cats were kept, state media reported. Thirteen of the rescued felines have since been returned to their owners.
According to the animal protection organisation Humane World for Animals, an estimated five million dogs and one million cats are captured, stolen, trafficked and slaughtered for meat in Vietnam every year.
The consumption of dog and cat meat is legal in the country, where many restaurants openly advertise it on their menu. But vendors require permits that show the origin of the animals.
Each group allegedly stole an average of four to 10 cats per night, according to a police statement in Ho Chi Minh City police department's official newspaper.
On 8 July, police said they seized 50 cats, two weighing scales, 55 cat traps, 14 bags, 13 mobile phones, seven motorbikes, two fur-removing machines and 6.7 million Vietnamese dong ($257; £195).
The 12 suspects were then brought in for questioning, and police say they confessed to stealing around 2,700 cats.
Of the 50 cats that were seized, 13 have been returned to their owners, while the remaining are being kept at the animal welfare centre HavePaws.
While the consumption of dog and cat meat remains more common in Vietnam than other Asian countries, campaigners say attitudes are changing.
A 2023 survey commissioned by Humane World for Animals found growing public opposition, particularly among younger people and pet owners, with 71% backing a ban on the consumption and trade of cat meat.
In June, more than 400 cats destined for slaughter were rescued after authorities dismantled another alleged feline theft ring, the animal welfare group said.

I print all the time, and not just because I test printers, but because I like paper. It doesn't matter if they're documents, photos, posters, or banners; I like artifacts—everything is better in physical form. And it's not just dinosaurs like me; while eschewing digital media, Gen Z is embracing printed matter, too (see, the kids are alright).
I've lost track of how many photo books I've printed over the years—mostly one-offs of little projects, fun things for friends, and maybe five copies at most. I'm not a photographer anymore, but old habits die hard, especially when you see the way people react to paper books. The response to a book, versus showing someone your latest Instagram post, is not even comparable.
With the holiday season kicking off, it seems apropos to point out that photo books make great gifts, as do mugs, prints, and my personal favorite for kids: photo puzzles. I've tested dozens of printing services over the years, and one of my favorites for holiday gifts is Staples.
You can order Staples prints online through the company's website, which features a variety of tools to help you design your photo gift, be it a mug, print, or puzzle. The print quality is great, and the online tools are well done and easy to use. But while ordering online is convenient, it's not why I like Staples for printing. It's because I can go to my local store and talk to actual human beings about my printing needs.
Printing can be tricky, and preparing your digital files exactly how the printer wants them isn't always easy. Best practice is to provide a high-res, flattened PDF file in CMYK color, but if you don't know what that means or how to get your file into the right format, fear not. The best way to print, even if you do know how to format it accurately, is to bring the file to your local Staples and talk to the print and marketing specialists there. They can catch potential issues before you print, and in most cases they can print a proof (sometimes at a reduced size, but still a proof) so you can see what you're getting beforehand. This is one advantage over online-only services.
Another big advantage is that you can get your gifts the same day if you pick up in-store. If you're in a rush this holiday season, remember that tip. You can even order online and pick up in-store to save yourself a trip.
Want to really step up your game? Here's my pro tip. Head to your local Staples to place your order, but have them print it at a Staples production center. Tell the store to have the production center send proofs for you to approve in person. This eliminates the same-day advantage, as it will likely take several days—sometimes as much as two weeks—but the printing quality will be better.
What's the quality like? I printed a couple of 11-ounce mugs—other options include a 15-ounce mug and a 17-ounce travel mug—and the results were on par with other services I've tested. I happen to like the shape of the Staples mugs a little more than what I got from others, but that's more personal preference than anything. For the design, you can choose a premade template and upload a photo of your choice, or you can start from scratch and design your own mug. As with all Staples printing services, you can choose same-day pickup if you want five or fewer. For larger orders, you'll need to get them delivered.
The photo options, like mounted prints, are nice. The print quality here lags behind dedicated photo services like our top picks, Mpix and Printique, but for the price it's quite good (both Mpix and Printique are more expensive). They offer canvas prints, metal prints, foam-backed prints, and posters up to 36 by 48 inches.
Staples is also a great place for business printing. I'm in the process of transitioning back to running a business, and the first thing I did wasn't setting up an Instagram account or doing anything with social media. The first thing I did was print business cards. Staples online business card maker is fantastic. And if I had a physical presence for my business, I'd have printed banners and posters and signs and everything else. Because we live in the real world, and if you want your business to succeed offline, you're going to need to print.

PQ in power, CAQ wiped off the map: Key takeaways from Quebec's election
Parti Québécois will form a minority government
Quebec's electoral map has been completely redrawn, with the Parti Québécois securing enough seats to form a minority government.
Paul St-Pierre Plamondon succeeded in growing his party from only three seats in 2022 to 59 on Monday.
But the PQ leader didn't get the majority he coveted, which will make it more difficult to follow through on his plans — including holding a referendum on Quebec independence.
Here is a closer look at where things stand and what to expect from the next government.
PQ dreams big
In his victory speech, St-Pierre Plamondon promised to work with other parties and be "direct and transparent" with Prime Minister Mark Carney, setting the stage for a tense relationship with Ottawa.
He also spoke in English, addressing his "English-speaking friends in Quebec."
"I just want to let you know very clearly that I'll be the premier of everyone in Quebec," he said, adding, "we share the same future."
Near the end of his speech, St-Pierre Plamondon told supporters he still dreams of making Quebec a country, speaking of the "courageous struggle of francophones" to preserve their culture.
"We deserve it just as much as any other people who possess their own country and democracy," he said.
In practical terms, however, a referendum doesn't seem likely — at least in the near term.
The PQ would now need the backing of Québec Solidaire, the only other sovereigntist party in the National Assembly, to push forward with a referendum.
St-Pierre Plamondon said he would delay a referendum until 2029 or 2030, after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office, but minority governments in Quebec typically last less than two years.
CAQ wiped out
Just four years after winning a massive majority, the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) appears to be entirely wiped off the map.
The party failed to win a single seat.
Christine Fréchette, who took over as premier from François Legault, failed to win over voters frustrated after eight years of CAQ rule.
"I have Quebec tattooed on my heart," she said in her concession speech, noting she was the second woman to lead the province. "I gave everything I could."
There will be questions about the future viability of the party, which had little grassroots support and no longer has a single MNA.
It was co-founded by Legault as an alternative to the old debates between the Liberals and Parti Québécois over sovereignty — a dynamic that appears likely to play out once again at the National Assembly.
Liberals in opposition
The Liberals are in a stronger-than-expected position after Monday, jumping from 19 seats to a projected 40.
Speaking to supporters, Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said Quebec voters elected a National Assembly without a majority, so the PQ will have an obligation to consider proposals coming from other parties.
He said the Liberals will be reviewing proposals put forward by the PQ and considering if they are in the province’s best interest.
“Preparing your referendum will find you facing a clear opponent in the Liberal Party,” Milliard said.
Switching to English, he said his party will collaborate on many issues, but “there is no way we will collaborate on a potential referendum.”
Conservative breakthrough
The Conservatives also had a good night, jumping from zero seats in 2022 to 19. The party could prove to be a partner to the PQ on some of its shared priorities.
Leader Éric Duhaime, who campaigned on tax and spending cuts, will now have a seat at the National Assembly.
“Tonight, hope has returned to Quebec,” Duhaime said. “We have just written a page in history.”
Time for electoral reform?
During the campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon — alongside the Conservatives and Québec Solidaire — promised to finally overhaul the province's voting system. Monday’s results will only add urgency to that pledge.
For the first time in Quebec history, the PQ is projected to form the government with less than 30 per cent of the popular vote.
It is a historic anomaly that will immediately renew scrutiny of the province's first-past-the-post electoral system.

‘Deleted voter filing Form 6 not false declaration’: Election Commission tells Bombay High Court amid SIR row
The Bombay High Court was hearing a petition filed by a Santa Cruz family of seven members who were removed from the draft electoral roll for switching address.
The Election Commission of India on Monday told the Bombay High Court that a deleted voter filing Form 6 for re-inclusion into the voter list during a Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise would not amount to filing a false declaration.
The Bombay High Court was hearing a petition filed by Santa Cruz resident Paresh Salgaonkar, who, along with six family members, was removed from the draft electoral roll for changing their address within the same constituency prior to the enumeration phase. The Salgaonkars submitted Form 8, which is used for address changes or correcting entries in the existing voter roll, on December 2, 2025, two days before the initial deadline of the enumeration phase. Their names were also missing in the final roll that came out on February 21.
Also Read I ‘Who modified Form 6?’: SC seeks record from EC over voter form changes
‘If citizens excluded, what will we do with SIR?’
Deep Dive
The court questioned whether the procedure adopted by the Election Commission for this was in consonance with the Representation of the People’s Act and its provisions for revision exercises.
“If citizens are excluded what will we do with your SIR? If citizens are being removed from the list then what is the purpose of this entire SIR process then?” the bench comprising of justices Valmiki Menezes and Amit Jamsandekar, said.
Adv Gaurish Agni, representing the ECI, told the Court that once the final roll is notified it is “as though the roll is starting completely afresh.”
“The old roll goes out of the window once the new roll is notified. The old roll of 2002 is gone. That can’t form the basis of any transfer forms. The whole perspective changes when we treat this as if this is the first roll,” Adv Agni told the High Court.
He stated that the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, are to treat a special intensive revision “as though we are preparing the roll for the first time.” “The previous roll only serves as a database for getting data for preparing the enumeration roll,” he said.
Salgaonkar's opposition to filing Form 6
Referring to the case of Paresh Salgaonkar, the Election Commission argued that it was not possible for them to have accepted his Form 8 since “his name was already deleted from the draft roll.” “If you have not submitted the enumeration form, the name gets deleted from the draft roll. If his name is not there in the draft roll. Form 8 cannot be submitted independently when your name is not on the draft roll,” he said.
The HC, countered, saying that effectively in the SIR “you are not removing people from the draft roll but effectively from the existing roll... Your argument now is that since SIR is underway, we shouldn’t look at the existing roll and only focus on the draft roll... We just cannot ignore the existing list,” the bench said.
The HC also said that since Salgaonkar was changing his address but staying as a voter in his own constituency, filing Form 6 would amount to submitting a false declaration. Form 6 is used registering a new voter.
“No [existing] voter should sign this. We’re saying they should not sign this,” the bench countered.
ECI, however, told the court that Salgaonkar would be “applying for inclusion” and submitting a declaration that his name is not in any other constituency was not an untrue statement. “He’s in the same constituency. He has changed the part. He is a new voter in a new part,” Adv Agni added.
Salgaonkar approached the HC after he was told his only option was to file Form 6 to enter the voter roll. His appeals before the District Election Officer and Chief Electoral Officer were both rejected after the final roll was declared. Salgaonkar has refused to fill Form 6, saying that doing so would amount to filing a false declaration stating that he’s neither a first-time voter nor had shifted from another constituency. Neither of the two mandatory options was applicable in his case, he alleged.
